title: Obituary: David Mark Dickson
text:
GRAY – It is with heavy hearts that we announce the passing of David Mark Dickson CPO, USCG retired, a cherished father, dedicated friend, and all-around good guy, who left us on Sept. 26, 2026, at the age of 72.
Born on April 29, 1954 in Hanover Mass., later during his formative years moving to East Sandwich, Cape Cod. Dave was a man of many passions and an even bigger heart.
Dave had a lifelong love for working on and restoring old cars, pouring his time and talent into reviving these classic beauties. Whether it was polishing chrome or tinkering under the hood, he found joy in every turn of the wrench. His other great loves included hitting the beach, where he spent countless hours soaking up the sun and casting lines, fishing for stripers and sharing stories with friends.
Dave entered the USCG in 1975 and served proudly for 23 years. The month after retirement he started as building and grounds supervisor for the Town of Windham where he worked hard for 19 years. He was widely respected as a supervisor and mentor to those who worked under him.
A hard worker through and through, David always put his family first, providing for them and showing up as a steady and loving presence in their lives. He had an adventurous spirit, and his travels took him 48 states driving his 40-foot Class A motorhome, creating a treasure trove of memories along the way. He also often traveled to Mexico and many Caribbean Islands.
David’s warmth and character touched everyone who knew him. He will be deeply missed by his family, friends, and all who had the pleasure of sharing a moment or two with him.
David is survived by his wife Linda; daughter, Kristia Dickson, son, Corey Dickson; sisters Gail Staples and Linda Carpenter (James); grandchildren Savannah Dickson, Nadia Dickson, Lauryn Dickson, Jaxson Dickson and his “little bud” Nicholas Dickson; his beloved, constantly attached to his hip, Black Lab, Thelma; loyal and caring friends Chipper Quatrano and The “Gumshoes”.
He was predeceased by his parents Herbert and Susie (Adams) Dickson; brother, Peter Dickson; son, Joshua David Dickson.
Memorial services will be held at 12 p.m. on Saturday Oct. 3, at Dolby Blais and Segee, 434 River Rd., Windham. Family and friends are invited to join us before the service at 11 a.m. for visitation as we share our favorite stories, memories, and a few laughs, just as David would have wanted. Burial and celebration of life will be at a later date

title: Woman accused of ‘extreme’ neglect that led to 12-year-old daughter’s death
text:
GADSDEN, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) — Police in Alabama have arrested a woman in connection with the death of a 12-year-old girl.
Leslie Denise Wilson, 35, is charged with felony murder in the death of her daughter, who had cerebral palsy, according to prosecutors.
Neglect allegations detailed in complaint
According to the complaint, between May 1 and June 17, Wilson subjected the child to “ongoing and extreme medical and/or physical neglect causing serious physical injury.”
The complaint said the child died as a result.
Gadsden police said officers initially responded to what was reported as a natural death. Because of the child’s age and the circumstances surrounding the death, the Gadsden Police Department’s Juvenile Unit and the Alabama Department of Human Resources began an investigation.
Aniah’s Law hearing held
An Aniah’s Law hearing was held Tuesday for Wilson.
Detective Alec Burgess with the Gadsden Police Department’s Major Crimes Division testified at the hearing and described what he saw when he was called to the home on reports of a natural death.
Burgess recalled finding a 12-year-old girl in a bedroom with marks on her body and live maggots inside her diaper. He described the girl as malnourished and dehydrated, and said she had pneumonia.
According to Burgess, the 12-year-old weighed 32 pounds and depended on a feeding tube. He said her younger siblings had been caring for her and that there was limited food inside the home.
Autopsy ruled homicide
An autopsy ruled the child’s death a homicide, and investigators developed evidence of abuse and neglect, according to police. At the hearing, Burgess said the autopsy showed the girl died from sepsis.
“Seeing a child, because I have children of my own, it’s heartbreaking. Prayers are with the family and the parents, and the family that is going through this hard time. Not only with that family, we want to pray for our police department. It’s tough to see our law enforcement going through the same thing because it hurts them also,” said Etowah County Assistant Coroner Dantez Robinson.
Police did not share the child’s name due to the nature of the case and her age.
Etowah County Judge Joe Nabors denied bond for Wilson.
Gadsden police said the case remains an active investigation.

title: US military withdraws from Iraq, ending years-long mission
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. military has formally ended its mission against ISIS in Iraq, completing the withdrawal of American and coalition forces from the country after a 12-year campaign.
U.S. Central Command announced Wednesday that U.S. forces and equipment had completed their departure from Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq, the main operational hub for Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve.
The base had hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and coalition personnel supporting counter-ISIS operations there.
The withdrawal marks the conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq and follows a transition plan announced by the United States and Iraq in September 2024.
“The orderly departure of Coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq,” Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Wednesday.
Parnell said the milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat and shifts responsibility for the country’s security to Iraqi forces.
The departure also closes another chapter in more than two decades of U.S. military involvement in Iraq.
The United States invaded Iraq in 2003 under Operation Iraqi Freedom, leading to the overthrow of Saddam Hussein. American forces withdrew in 2011 but returned three years later as ISIS seized large portions of Iraq and neighboring Syria.
CENTCOM established Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve in 2014 to advise, assist and support partner forces fighting ISIS. Iraq declared territorial victory over the terrorist group in 2017, but the U.S.-led mission continued as Iraqi and Kurdish forces worked to prevent its resurgence.
American and coalition forces began their latest withdrawal from federal Iraq in October 2025. That process concluded Wednesday with the removal of remaining personnel and equipment from Erbil Air Base.
CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said ISIS “no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security” and said Iraqi security forces, including Kurdish Peshmerga forces, now have the capacity and operational independence to manage threats inside the country.
That does not mean the U.S. relationship with Iraq — or the broader fight against ISIS — is over.
The Pentagon says the wartime coalition mission is transitioning to a more traditional bilateral defense relationship between Washington and Baghdad.
The Pentagon also says responsibility for other security challenges, including Iran-aligned militias operating inside Iraq, now primarily rests with the Iraqi government. U.S. officials say Washington remains committed to preventing ISIS from rebuilding its capabilities in the country.
Operation Inherent Resolve itself is also continuing outside Iraq. Its joint task force is now headquartered in Jordan, and CENTCOM says U.S. forces will continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria alongside coalition partners and the Syrian government.
President Donald Trump called the withdrawal a “decisive victory” Wednesday, saying it was time for American forces to leave Iraq.
“I had a choice to stay or to leave, and felt, without question, that it was time for America to go home!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

title: Woman found dead outside of car after vehicle hits pole in Parkman
text:
Woman found dead outside of car after vehicle hits pole in Parkman, Maine
A woman from Parkman is dead after police say she went off the road, crashed into a utility pole and was thrown from her vehicle.
A Piscataquis County Sheriff's Office deputy, Guilford Fire Department and Mayo Ambulance were called to Crow Hill Road in Parkman at about 11:20 p.m. on Tuesday.
When emergency responders arrived, they found the vehicle, and the deputy started looking for the driver. Her body was found nearby after she was thrown from the vehicle.
The driver, Tracy Bonney-Corson, 61, was pronounced dead at the scene.
The cause of the crash was under investigation on Wednesday.

title: Roman Anthony out for playoffs with another right hand injury
text:
NEW YORK — Roman Anthony is expected to miss the rest of the postseason for the Boston Red Sox because of new damage to his right hand sustained in an AL Wild Card Series opener against the New York Yankees.
It is not yet clear whether he will need surgery. Anthony was sidelined from early May to late August because of an injury to the same hand.
“We did everything we could to be back this year and play, which we did,” Anthony said Wednesday in the tunnel outside the Red Sox clubhouse at Yankee Stadium before Game 2. “Going forward, we haven’t really even talked about it today.”
Batting leadoff as Boston’s designated hitter in his playoff debut Tuesday night, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against Cam Schlittler, then was removed for a pinch hitter with the Red Sox trailing by two runs in the sixth inning of a 9-0 loss.
Manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings.
“After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%,” Anthony said. “For me, it was to a point where it was tolerable and I was taking certain swings that were sketchy, and I was still able to come back and recover enough to just be in there every single day. But ultimately I just took a few swings here recently where that wasn’t the case.”
The team sent Anthony to Boston in a car after the game. He arrived about 3 a.m. and had new MRIs on Wednesday morning.
“Additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren’t there before,” Tracy said.
The 22-year-old Anthony returned to Massachusetts because the medical staff there was familiar with his injury from earlier this season.
“My thoughts are kind of all over the place,” he said. “Feelings and emotions of, you work all this year to put yourself in a position to just be good enough to go in the playoffs and for this to happen, it just doesn’t feel real.”
Anthony wasn’t sure whether the injury is something he’ll have to manage going forward.
“Given the point where we were at this year and all the different things that I tried and the different shots that I took and the routes that I went, I think — never really rested a ton, right? — so I don’t necessarily know the answer to that,” he said.
“Once we saw it today, it was more so about like, all right, this is what it is. You can’t go. It’s not in the team’s best interest for you to play tonight. So get back there. Root your guys on and be a good teammate. And then once, like I said, once we get past the series, it will be one of those things where we reassess regardless of what happens and kind of go from there.”
Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29.
“There’s been periods of time since he’s come back where he’ll get a zinger and feel something. And then it dissipates and we’re good to go,” Tracy said. “That’s not been an uncommon occurrence since he’s come back. But yesterday, as you went through those two at-bats, it got worse.”
The club announced that Anthony was diagnosed with a right hand strain, and Major League Baseball approved a Red Sox roster substitution. Anthony was replaced on the Wild Card Series roster by infielder Curtis Mead, obtained from Washington in late July for pitcher Connelly Early.
According to MLB rules, Anthony is ineligible to return until the American League Championship Series — if the Red Sox advance that far.
“I’ve been experiencing some things with the swings and the check-swings over the past six weeks. Last night just felt a little bit more intense, a little bit more worse than past swings that have been lingering a little bit longer than the ones I was used to,” Anthony said.
“It was just super alarming and it got to a point where it was tough to grip a bat. I knew then and there that this was a little bit more similar to the one earlier in the year. That’s why we decided to go get imaging.”
Mead got hit by a pitch in his first game with the Red Sox at the Athletics on July 27 and was placed on the injured list because of a broken left wrist. He hasn’t played in the big leagues since.
Mead was on the bench for Game 2 against the Yankees. Jahmai Jones was set to hit leadoff as the DH with the Red Sox one loss from elimination, followed in the batting order by catcher Adley Rutschman, first baseman Willson Contreras, right fielder Wilyer Abreu, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, third baseman Caleb Durbin, second baseman Nick Sogard, shortstop Trevor Story and left fielder Nate Eaton.
Sonny Gray was set to start on the mound for Boston against one of his former teams. Left-hander Max Fried was scheduled to pitch for New York.
One of baseball’s premier prospects when he debuted in the majors last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBI and a .735 OPS in 55 games this season.
“Hopefully he’s going to be healthy for next year,” Abreu said. “It’s a big loss for us, but we still have to play the game and try to win the game today.”

title: LETTERS: Let's start talking to people, not about them
text:
As a Winslow resident, a member of the Winslow Town Council, and a board member of the Waterville Opportunities Recovery and Resource Center (WORRC), I have had the opportunity to see firsthand why a place like WORRC is needed in our community.
I understand that when something new comes into a neighborhood, it can raise questions and even create some anxiety. I believe the best way to address that is through openness and understanding about what WORRC actually is – and what it is not. The home at 21 Elm Street, in Waterville, is currently being renovated to become a Recovery & Resource Center. WORRC is not a homeless shelter or residential treatment facility. It will provide a safe welcoming place where people can find recovery and peer support, help navigating housing and employment, educational opportunities, basic necessities, family support and connections to healthcare, treatment, and other community resources.
I think it’s time we change the conversation. Instead of talking about the homeless, the person struggling with addiction, or the family that is having a difficult time, perhaps we should start talking to them. Ask what they need. Listen. And then help connect them with the resources that can help them move forward.
WORRC believes in a helping hand up, not simply a handout. Sometimes that hand is the first step toward hope, stability, and independence. WORRC is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, and making these services available requires community support. Donations are greatly needed and appreciated. Contributions may be mailed to WORRC, 21 Elm Street, Waterville, ME 04901. For more information, call (207) 649-3271.
I believe our communities are stronger when we help people find a way forward – and sometimes all someone needs is for someone to reach out a hand.
Doris Labranche
Winslow

title: Maine ethics commission won’t investigate whether lawmaker broke confidentiality
text:
The Maine ethics commission voted Wednesday not to investigate whether a Republican State House leader violated confidentiality laws when she shared a letter with the media that House Speaker Ryan Fecteau said questioned his integrity.
Assistant House Republican Leader Katrina Smith, R-Palermo, filed a letter in July with the Maine Commission on Governmental Ethics and Election Practices seeking “an independent review of the legal and ethical boundaries” of Fecteau, D-Biddeford, holding simultaneous roles in the Legislature and as the head of the Biddeford Housing Authority.
Jonathan Wayne, executive director of the commission, initially interpreted Smith’s request as a formal complaint, which would have triggered a confidentiality clause.
Smith, however, actually requested an “advisory opinion,” which does not have the same requirement.
The contents of Smith’s letter, which outlined concerns about a possible conflict of interest between Fecteau’s two positions, appeared in full online in the Biddeford Buzz and in part on the Maine Wire the day after she submitted it.
Fecteau subsequently asked the commission to investigate whether Smith’s letter appearing online violated the confidentiality requirement.
Choosing not to, he said, would set “a terrible precedent.”
“Lawmakers could be subject to bait and switch requests that are immediately shared with the media to then create an appearance of wrongdoing,” he said.
Biddeford Housing wasn’t scared off by the news articles, Fecteau said, but for some employers, that could be enough to withdraw an offer.
“This is not a political game,” he said. “This has very serious consequences for the livelihoods of those who seek and serve in public office.”
To open an investigation, though, the commission first had to determine whether Smith’s letter constituted a formal complaint.
The commission ultimately decided Wednesday that it didn’t, effectively closing the discussion.
But while members made the decision unanimously, they also made it grudgingly.
If a person wishes to file a complaint with the commission they have to agree, in writing, not to share the details of the complaint until the commission decides whether to hear the issue. If they don’t agree, the commission won’t consider the matter.
“It’s clear to me that Assistant Leader Smith never completed the process of filing a complaint and never agreed to keep it confidential,” said William Schneider, commission chair.
Commissioner Sarah LeClaire suggested the law be clarified “so it’s not used in a weaponized way to get a letter out to the press that the public will assume is an investigation,” she said.
“I don’t like what I see in this case,” LeClaire added. “I don’t like the idea of the possibility that this commission was used for some sort of press grab.”

title: Rangeley downtown sidewalk work to restart
text:
Sidewalk construction will restart in downtown Rangeley on Oct. 5, according to a Facebook post from the town office.
The focus will be from Lake Street to the Alpine Shop. In addition to the construction, a new crosswalk with flashing lights will be installed in front of Rangeley Lakes Builders Supply. An ADA compliant parking space will be created in front of Sarge’s Sports Pub & Grub.
This is the second phase of construction in a sidewalk improvement project that began this spring, with lanes closed to traffic between Allen Street and Mike Cerminara Landscaping on Main Street.
Work should be confined to the shoulders of Main Street, with the possibility of occasional lane closures, except for the crosswalk, which will require single-lane closures to get both halves of the street painted, town manager Joe Roach said.
The downtown work is projected to take three weeks, depending on weather, the post said.

title: MDI road damaged by 2024 storms to be closed during October for permanent fixes
text:
Seawall Road on Mount Desert Island will be temporarily closed through October while the state fixes a section of road damaged by severe back-to-back winter storms in January 2024.
The construction follows a more-than-two-year dispute over which government entity — the Maine Department of Transportation, town of Southwest Harbor, or Acadia National Park — should bear financial responsibility for the repairs and future maintenance.
The project has been delayed several times, including this past summer.
The road connects Manset and Seawall, villages within Southwest Harbor, to the southern edge of Acadia and Tremont. The shorefront road is essential to locals and popular among tourists visiting the park’s quieter areas, including less-congested trails like Wonderland and Ship Harbor.
The project, focused on less than a mile of roadway roughly between Beaver Lodge Lane and Acadia’s Seawall Campground, is intended to make it “more resilient to future storm events,” according to MDOT. The battered roadway abuts Seawall Pond.
The detour will divert traffic to Route 102 from Southwest Harbor to Tremont. The closures will force locals, visitors and emergency vehicles to take longer detours, cutting off Seawall Campground from easy access to nearby businesses.
The closure, announced Wednesday, will begin Oct. 5 and will last up to 28 days, according to state officials, who believe the job will be complete by Oct. 30.
Ellsworth contractor R F Jordan & Sons Construction Inc. will complete the work for $915,820, funded by the National Park Service and the U.S. Department of the Interior, according to MDOT.
Last year, Acadia received congressional funding for storm-related damages, which will be used to improve Seawall Road. The funding was used through the Good Neighbor Authority, which allows the park service to partner with state and local governments to restore and maintain public land.
The project will install new gabion baskets, which are wired containers filled with rocks or concrete used for erosion control, along the oceanfront and a reinforced concrete culvert that allows for fish passage, particularly eels, state officials said.
In 2024, the road was rendered impassable for several months following back-to-back winter storms that churned up heavy surf that battered the roadway. It was temporarily fixed by local contractors the following summer, but, as climate change causes sea levels to rise, bringing more intense storms, the road’s quick fixes weren’t expected to withstand future damage.
An MDOT spokesperson previously estimated the repairs would cost up to $1.45 million. The spokesperson did not respond to an inquiry Wednesday from the Bangor Daily News.

title: Firefighter killed in BASE jumping accident, fire department confirms
text:
SALT LAKE CITY (Gray News) - A firefighter in Utah died during a BASE jumping accident, the fire department confirmed.
Gabe Reilly died in a BASE jumping accident in Cache County on Sept. 27, according to the Salt Lake City Fire Department. He was 27.
Reilly served as a firefighter for the department for four years. The fire department said that he was “following in the footsteps of his father.” The fire department said his father was also a firefighter who retired from the Salt Lake City Fire Department in 2024.
“Gabe was known for his infectious smile, kind-heartedness, and his free-spirited nature,” the department said in a Facebook post. “Gabe’s commitment to the department, his fellow firefighters, and the community will not be forgotten.”
The fire department did not provide further information regarding Reilly’s death. The agency asked the public to respect his family’s privacy as they grieve his loss.
“On behalf of the Salt Lake City Fire Department, we extend our deepest condolences to the entire Reilly family. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, and fellow firefighters during this difficult time,” the department said.
BASE jumping is an extreme sport similar to skydiving. Instead of jumping out of a plane, BASE jumpers launch themselves from high locations such as mountain cliffs and bridges. The name itself is an acronym for possible jump spots: building, antenna, span or earth.

title: Insomnia is linked to higher risk of dementia and stroke, study finds
text:
(Gray News) - New research suggests insomnia may be linked to some serious long-term health risks.
A recent study published in “Sleep Medicine Reviews” found people with insomnia had a 26% higher risk of stroke.
The study also found that insomnia is linked to a higher risk of dementia, depression, suicide and hospitalizations.
Researchers analyzed 20 comprehensive review studies from multiple countries.
Another study, published on Sept. 9 in the journal “Neurology,” found that insomnia is a “modifiable risk factor” for cognitive decline.
In the study, 2,750 people underwent annual neurological assessments and brain imaging, along with evaluations of their sleep habits.
According to the study’s data, insomnia was linked to a 40% increased risk of cognitive impairment. It also found that people with insomnia who increased their sleep time or used medication to help them sleep did not experience as much harm to their cognitive health.
According to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 12% of Americans said they’ve been diagnosed with chronic insomnia.
Experts said staying on a regular sleep schedule is important.
According to Dr. Diego Carvalho, assistant professor of neurology and sleep specialist at the Mayo Clinic Center for Sleep Medicine, research shows that sleep helps clear unneeded synapses and waste from the brain that accumulates during the day. It is also necessary for memory consolidation, emotional regulation and overall brain health.
To get a good night’s sleep, experts suggest putting your phone and other distractions away about 30 to 60 minutes before bed. Practicing relaxing habits before bed and keeping your bedroom dark, quiet and cool can also help.
If insomnia persists after making these changes, experts say you should consult a doctor or sleep specialist.

title: Normand J. Bosse
text:
Normand J. Bosse, 72, of East Boothbay, Maine, passed away peacefully on Sept. 20, 2026, after a brief illness.
Born on Nov. 27, 1953, in North Adams, Massachusetts to Armand and Cecile Bosse, Normand grew up with a deep love for mathematics and computer science. He was a 1971 graduate of Nashua Senior High School in Nashua, New Hampshire and received a bachelor of science degree in applied mathematics from the University of Massachusetts at Lowell.
He had a long and varied career as a software engineer for several companies including Wang Labs and Thomson Financial.
In 1993, he married the love of his life, Ann (Pierce), and together they shared 33 wonderful years of marriage.
Norm was known for his sense of humor and love of the ocean, plus a deep commitment to all things computer-related, and always enjoyed working on his computer - learning everything he could about an assortment of topics (there was always something new to learn!) - and taking computer-related classes online, plus ham radio, Zooming with his best friend Roy, his friends and family, swimming at the Y, kayaking, drives and adventures along the coast of Maine and gazing out at the ocean while deep in thought.
In addition to his wife, Ann, he is survived by his sisters Susanne Wall (Nathaniel) of Culpeper, Virginia, and Christine Pelleti er (David) of Merrimack, New Hampshire and their children, Danielle, Nikki and Chip; his best friend Roy Bays and his wife Gloria; his cousins, including Ron Colonna and Barbara Jean Vivenzio; as well as many other loving family members and friends and his beloved cats, Wookie and Romeo.
The family asks that memorial donations be made to Boothbay Region YMCA, Boothbay Harbor, Maine.

title: King bill would expand veterans' access to costly medications
text:
Maine Veterans’ Homes and similar facilities nationwide could receive reimbursement for certain high-cost medications under a bipartisan bill co-sponsored by U.S. Sen. Angus King, I-Maine.
The “Providing Veterans Essential Medications Act” would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to reimburse state veterans’ homes for medications that exceed 8.5% of their per diem rate. Alternatively, the department could provide the medications directly, improving veterans’ access to expensive treatments.
Maine has six state veterans’ homes. They are located in Scarborough, South Paris, Augusta, Bangor, Machias and Caribou.
The bill would extend an arrangement already available to many private nursing homes that contract with the VA. Currently, the department does not reimburse state veterans’ homes for high-cost medications for severely disabled veterans, although it covers those medications for veterans living outside the facilities.
“Our men and women in uniform didn’t hesitate when it came time to answer the call and serve the nation — we shouldn’t hesitate to make their retirement from service as comfortable as possible,” King said.
“If the VA covers veterans’ medications when they are living at a private nursing home, those cost reimbursements should be the same when veterans choose to enter a facility that specializes in taking care of veterans.”
King is the bill’s lead co-sponsor with U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind.
The bill, King said, “is a crucial piece of legislation that will ensure our veterans continue to receive the care they have earned, regardless of where they choose to live.”
Arguing that veteran’s homes should never have to turn away elderly and disabled veterans because lifesaving drugs are too expensive, Banks said the bill “will help states cover those costs and expedite care for our nation’s heroes.”
‘Clear and consequential gap’
Brad Klawitter, CEO of Maine Veterans’ Homes, said the bill addresses a “clear and consequential gap” in federal policy.
“Reimbursement for high-cost medications is essential to our ability to continue serving veterans in our communities, including those with complex medical needs,” he added.

title: Matt Dunlap wants to represent the Maine district he's spent his life in
text:
State Auditor Matt Dunlap wants to represent the Maine congressional district he's spent his life in
Dunlap won the four-way Democratic primary for CD2 in a ranked-choice voting tabulation in June
State Auditor Matt Dunlap wants to represent the Maine congressional district he's spent his life in
Dunlap won the four-way Democratic primary for CD2 in a ranked-choice voting tabulation in June
For Democratic congressional candidate Matt Dunlap, who beat out three others to take on former Gov. Paul LePage in the race to represent Maine's 2nd District, it has always been about connecting with people.
"That's something that, you know, it sounds so simple, but so few people really do it," he said.
Dunlap grew up in the Bar Harbor area and has been in Old Town for the majority of his adult life. Now, he's running to represent the congressional district he's spent his life in.
He is a former legislator and the former Maine secretary of state, and he is now the state auditor.
"I have never stopped walking with people and sharing their journey. I was born in the district. I've spent my whole life here. I've worked in the district my whole life," Dunlap said.
Dunlap got in the race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District first, challenging incumbent Democratic Congressman Jared Golden to a primary. Golden eventually announced he would not seek reelection. After that announcement, State Sen. Joe Baldacci, social worker Paige Loud and former Capitol Hill staffer Jordan Wood entered the race.
Dunlap said getting in early helped him, and after winning a four-way ranked-choice voting tabulation in the Democratic primary, he said his primary opponents are behind him.
"I mean, the day after the tabulation, Jordan Wood sent me a picture of his house with my sign in his lawn. He said, 'I've already maxed out to you. I have a house party for you.' Joe endorsed and co-sponsored that house party with Paige," Dunlap said.
Now, Dunlap is focused on the issues.
"I think that the one thing that I hear about every single day, because we make a lot of phone calls, is health care issues, people's access to health care and how they pay for it," he said.
Dunlap added that universal healthcare is one of his top priorities and that he blames President Donald Trump for the affordability challenges many people are facing.
"With the war in Iran, the cost of heating oil has just about doubled. The price of gasoline is way up, which means the cost of groceries goes up. Everything goes up, except wages," Dunlap said.
Dunlap now has the tough task of trying to keep a conservative district blue.
"There's no stone in the forest with a sword in it that you can pull out and become declared the rightful king of the realm," Dunlap said. "Sometimes when people ask me like, 'What's that campaign look like?' What they're saying is, 'What is the magic campaign ad? What's the piece that convinces people?' And the reality is, there is nothing. You have to get out and you have to meet people where they are. You have to listen to them."
Dunlap's other priorities include labor issues and a woman's right to choose.

title: ‘How ridiculous’: 11-year-old goes to court after receiving citation for riding a motorbike
text:
SEMINOLE COUNTY, Fla. (WKMG) - An 11-year-old boy appeared in court this week alongside his parents and attorney.
Cade Kirchner was charged with one count of misdemeanor failure to register his motorbike, a vehicle police said he was not old enough to ride.
“We’ll enter a plea of not guilty,” Kirchner’s attorney said in court.
Body camera video obtained showed Cade being fingerprinted, ticketed and issued a court summons.
In the video, Cade can be heard saying he knew his e-bike was actually a motorcycle.
An officer in the video told Cade he was issuing one ticket instead of six possible criminal violations.
“So you’re getting one ticket today. OK? You could have gotten six criminal violations, but I’m giving you one,” the officer said.
The officer also told Cade that signing the ticket did not mean he was admitting guilt.
“OK, all right. You know, this is a motorcycle, you know, you can’t be riding it, all right? So just because you signed this ticket doesn’t mean you’re admitting to any guilt. OK, buddy?” the officer said.
Police said the motorbike was capable of traveling 50 MPH and was powered by a 4,500-watt motor.
After court
After the hearing, Cade’s father, Chris Kirchner, commented on the court appearance.
“How ridiculous that he had to miss school for that,” Chris Kirchner said.
Samuel Filler, the attorney representing Cade, said he expects the case to be resolved.
“We will get it all resolved, no doubt in my mind,” Filler said.

text:
CAPE COD, Mass. (CNN) — A rare two-headed diamondback terrapin hatchling was brought to marine wildlife officials in New England for assessment, according to the Cape Wildlife Center.
The turtle was discovered at a nesting site on Cape Cod.
The hatchling weighs roughly as much as a nickel, the center said.
The center said the turtle has a rare developmental anomaly called bicephaly, in which two independent and functional heads grow from a single body.
The center said it is closely monitoring the appetite, growth and behavior of the hatchling.
The center said it has seen only two other bicephalic cases in the last five years.

title: Weather Discussion 9/30/26
Third school budget try passes first step with Wiscasset voters
text:
As with the first two tries at a 2026-27 Wiscasset school budget, the latest offer withstood all attempts Sept. 29 to pare the school committee's proposal. The $10.6 million offer, with a local ask down 2.54% from 2025-26, goes to a vote at the polls Nov. 3.
The special town meeting in Wiscasset Middle High School's Stover Auditorium saw the most comments from Richard Lutes. On multiple warrant articles, he proposed smaller sums.
"I am still of the school that we are spending too much money in this town on what we have and what we have available to us, and considering today's climate and the amount of students, and the projected amount of students in the state of Maine," Lutes told fellow residents.
He recommended replacing the proposed $3,623,149 for regular instruction with $3,476,745. That amendment and all others failed in a show of raised yellow slips of paper.
On special education instruction, Chet Grover asked how and why the proposal went from the last budget offer's $2,716,468 to this one's $2,648,194. Chair Tracey Whitney answered, "We dropped a special ed teacher, we went half-time on a social worker, we dropped some substitutes and tech supplies, we dropped dues and fees, we dropped training and conferences, we dropped some tuition reimbursement and legal fees, we dropped some contracted services, a deaf interpreter and a PT (physical therapist)."
"Why couldn't we have arrived at that in the original budget (proposal)," Grover asked.
"We had students we felt were going to need those services," and who have not left, Whitney said. "It won't be the same amount of services ... We're hoping that we can restructure enough to be able to cover this."
One woman said services are being cut at the federal level, too, and she hoped the children would not suffer for the cuts. More attention is better than less attention, she said.
In a required secret ballot vote, the following question passed 52-14: "To see what sum the Town will be authorized to raise and appropriate in additional local funds for school purposes under the Maine Revised Statutes, Title 20-A, section 15690. The Wiscasset School Committee recommends $2,806,703 which exceeds the State's Essential Programs and Services allocation model by $2,756,703 as required to fund the budget recommended by the school Committee. The school committee gives the following reasons for exceeding the State's Essential Programs and Services funding model by $2,756,703: The additional local funds represent local costs to support the Wiscasset School Department school programs that are not included in the State's funding model, including costs for co-curricular and extra-curricular activities, transportation, school and system administration, and special education services."
The budget offer faces a validation referendum Nov. 3. Polls are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at Wiscasset Community Center.
The referendum vote is where the first two offers fell: 535 yes votes to 547 no's June 9; and 228-250 on Sept. 1.

title: Parents of college hockey player who collapsed during workout want coaches put on leave
text:
TEMPE, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - The parents of an Arizona State University hockey player who collapsed during a team workout last month and is unlikely to fully recover are calling for the coaches to be removed amid the investigation.
Matthew Mayich, a sophomore defenseman from Ontario, Canada, collapsed on Aug. 20 during an outdoor workout in Tempe, Arizona. The 21-year-old is still in the hospital and unlikely to fully recover, according to his family’s attorney.
In a statement provided on Tuesday through their attorney, Mayich’s parents, John and Christina, said they want the coaches involved in the workout removed during the investigation over concerns of possible retaliation.
“The coaches who ran that workout on August 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn’t have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day,” the statement read in part.
Mayich’s parents said they want the truth and accountability for what happened to their son.
The full statement is below:
“We’ve heard some things about what our family wants that aren’t right, so we want to be clear. We want this team to have a great season, and we’ll be cheering for you. But the coaches who ran that workout on August 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn’t have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day. And there are plenty of former college and pro players in the Valley who could step in and help.
“Nobody should keep quiet about what they think should happen because they believe that’s what we want. It isn’t. If anyone wants to know what we want, ask us. We want the truth, and we want it done in a way that lets the boys focus on hockey instead of wondering whether their coaches think they talked.
“Mostly, we want accountability for what happened to our son, and we want his teammates to be safe.”
Players challenge ASU’s report on workout
The statement comes a day after seven anonymous players sent a letter to ASU President Michael Crow challenging the university’s report on what happened the day Mayich collapsed.
The players’ letter claims former Green Beret Timothy Ziesel, who led the workout, was brought in with no background check or safety certifications. It was originally described as a team-building exercise, but in reality, it was a “military-style conditioning session,” players said.
The anonymous players reported that the only water break given lasted seconds, and only eight players got water. Mayich reportedly was not among them.
They said the workout continued even when some began falling to their knees and vomiting.
Like Mayich’s parents, the players are calling for the coaching staff to be placed on leave. They also asked that the investigation be turned over to an outside agency.
Trainer’s attorney pushes back on players’ account
Ziesel’s attorney, Buddy Rake, is pushing back on players’ accounts of the workout, saying no players vomited or were denied water.
He also said that Ziesel couldn’t have denied water to players since “he didn’t determine water breaks.” He added that water breaks were determined by coaching staff and based on the university’s hydration policy.
“The workout was not punishing unless you consider flutter kicks, pushups, planks, and sprints punishing,” said Rake in an emailed statement to Arizona’s Family. “Have you ever seen a D1 preseason workout?”
Rake explained that ASU’s hydration policy requires trainers to supervise pre-hydration requirements. Before exercise, he said ASU athletes under supervision are required to hydrate at least four hours prior and drink 8 to 12 fluid ounces about 10 to 15 minutes before starting the exercise.
The lawyer added that he has emails from a coach stating that Mayich didn’t show signs of struggle until after Ziesel left. During the workout, there were six coaches and trainers present, according to Rake.
“As Tim’s [Ziesel’s] attorney, I continue to be of the opinion that the family and parents of Matthew receive complete transparency. Instead of focusing on a non-existent hard workout, the focus should be on how could this happen during a workout that was not as hard as an average D1 conditioning program,” Rake said.
“There is not a definition of a military workout,” he added.
Rake claimed that Mayich’s case went off track by “trying to find blame before facts were known.” In his emailed statement, he listed questions about the case, including:
- What qualifies as a “military-style” workout?
- What conditioning was actually provided?
- Was water available and would it have made a difference?
- What was the temperature in Canada where Matthew was training beforehand?
- What kind of physical condition was Mayich in when he arrived in Arizona?
- What activities did Mayich participate in leading up to the incident?
ASU police are investigating the circumstances of the workout. They will submit their report to the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office for review.

title: Should you buy a house now or wait?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Should you buy a house now or wait?
Key takeaways
- The housing market has become more friendly for homebuyers recently, but even so, many prospective buyers are sidelined by record-high prices.
- If your credit score is strong, your employment is stable and you have enough savings to cover a down payment and closing costs, buying now can still be a smart move.
- But if your personal finances are not ideal at the moment, or if home values in your area are on the decline, it might be better to wait.
Buy now, or wait? That’s the question prospective homeowners have been struggling to answer as home prices keep skyrocketing and rates keep rising.
So, is it a good time to buy a home? Or is it better to wait on the sidelines, in the hopes that either prices or rates see a significant drop soon? The combination of high home prices and mortgage rates has led many would-be buyers to pick the “wait” side of the equation, but these considerations can help you determine the way forward.
Is now a good time to buy a house?
No matter which way the real estate market is leaning, buying now means you can start building equity immediately. It also means avoiding the potential for mortgage rate fluctuations later: Rising rates can wreak havoc on your monthly budget, and they also result in paying more in interest over the life of the loan.
While they have backed off from the high of 8% hit in late 2023, they’re still elevated. Currently, mortgage rates are at their highest level in more than 18 months, with the 30-year fixed rate averaging 7.08% as of late September, according to Bankrate’s weekly survey of large lenders.
Home prices are also sky-high, with NAR’s data reflecting 38 consecutive months of year-over-year increases. The median sale price of an existing home in the U.S. was $429,100 in August 2026 — the highest August price ever recorded by the National Association of Realtors (NAR). Together, these factors might dissuade you from buying right now, and that’s understandable.
On the bright side, housing inventory is finally expanding a bit. There were 1.62 million homes for sale at the end of October 2025, marking the first time since November 2019 that inventory exceeded 1.6 million units, NAR says. That represented a 4.9-month supply of unsold inventory, up from 4.6 months in July 2026 and 4.6 months in August 2025.
If you’re ready to buy and you find a place you want to call home, pull the trigger. Timing the market is nearly impossible, and over the course of the 5 to 10 years you own the home, you’re likely to recoup your investment.
Whenever you buy, don't overpay for the loan
Bankrate research finds 87% of Americans overpay for their home loans. For the typical borrower, that adds up to $3,343 in extra costs each year. Don’t settle for the first offer — be sure to shop around.
How to know if you should buy a house or wait
Ultimately, the decision of when to buy a home is up to you, and it hinges on highly personal factors — the birth of a child, job changes, divorce, a death in the family. Life goes on, whether the timing is perfect or not. These questions can help guide your decision if you’re anxious to become a homeowner and start house-hunting.
- How is your credit? Before you start house-hunting, check your credit score. If you have demonstrated that you are a low-risk borrower with a history of on-time payments, you’ll be in line for the lowest mortgage rates a lender offers.
- Have you saved enough for a down payment? In addition to paying your bills on time, you should be sitting on a sizable chunk of change for a down payment. The more you can pay upfront, the less you’ll have to borrow (and so the less interest you’ll have to pay). You should also consider closing costs and other mortgage-related expenses
- Are you able to afford homeownership? More goes into the cost of owning a home than just the mortgage payment. You’ll need to be sure you can afford insurance costs, property taxes and any maintenance or emergencies that inevitably pop up along the way.
- How long are you planning to stay in the home? Beyond the purchase price, buying a home comes with closing costs that can run thousands more. So, to justify those one-time transaction costs, it’s wise to be reasonably certain that you won’t move again anytime soon — or that you’ll be financially stable enough to hold on to the property and rent it out. Selling a home very soon after buying can have serious tax implications.
- Are home values in your area dropping? The country’s overall median home price may be soaring to new heights, but some individual areas have still seen price declines. Such declines may not be done yet, so it could pay to be patient for a bit longer.
- Is the inventory in your area increasing substantially? When there are more properties on the market to choose from, buyers enjoy more bargaining power. Many areas have seen a jump in inventory recently, which certainly helps.

Know your local market
Deciding whether to buy a house now or wait depends a lot on where you want to call home. Regardless of national headlines, real estate is a local game and can vary greatly from one market to another, even within the same state or metro area.
Consider this Redfin data from North Carolina’s Research Triangle cities of Raleigh and Chapel Hill, only about 30 miles from each other: In mid-2025, both cities had relatively similar median home prices of $450,000 and $495,000, respectively. But they’ve gone in opposite directions recently.
In Raleigh, the median price dipped to about $422,000, down 6% in a year. Meanwhile, the median price in Chapel Hill soared to nearly $660,000 in August 2026, up nearly 20% over the past year. They’re close in proximity, with similar pricing, but one market is in decline while the other is on the upswing. That can make a big difference for your buying strategy.
This is just one example of local markets going in different directions – and it’s another reason why it’s so hard to say whether it’s a “good” or “bad” time to buy. In today’s homebuying market, it’s more important than ever to find a real estate agent who really knows your local area — down to your specific neighborhood — and can help you successfully navigate its unique quirks
Next steps
Trying to buy a house right now might feel overwhelming, but waiting too long can present challenges as well. Review your finances in detail, and think about how much you’re able to pay upfront as a down payment. Your credit score is the single most important factor in determining your mortgage rate, so make sure you’ve cleaned up any outstanding issues.
Be sure to take the pulse of the town in which you’re hoping to live. Then, talk with an experienced local real estate agent to figure out whether you should buy now or wait until you’ve saved up enough to do a deal now.
Frequently asked questions
-  Should you wait for mortgage rates to drop? No. It’s almost impossible to know where mortgage rates are headed. The best advice: If you’re financially and emotionally ready to buy a house, then you should do so regardless of where mortgage rates are.
-  Is now a bad time to buy a house? Buying a house is a deeply personal decision, based on where you are in life. If you live in a one-bedroom apartment and are expecting twins, for instance, it’s a great time to buy a house, no matter what’s happening in the economy. Base your decision on your own individual circumstances rather than what’s happening in the housing market.
-  Is the housing market going to crash? Housing experts do not think so. While there is certainly some economic uncertainty swirling right now, most experts believe that the housing market will not crash. Home prices may decline in some areas, but it won’t be catastrophic — think of it as more of a soft landing.
-  What if there’s a recession? Talk of a possible recession has been increasing lately, and as you might imagine, recessions are a risky time to buy a home. If you lose your job, for example, a lender will be much less likely to approve your loan application. Even if a recession doesn’t affect you directly, if your geographic area is hard-hit, that could have a serious effect on the local real estate market. Fewer people with the means to buy means a lower chance of homes selling, which could keep homeowners from listing and decrease your options as a buyer. There are some potential upsides to buying a home during a recession, though, if you’re financially able to do so. Notably, there will be less competition, which could help you find a great property that you otherwise couldn’t.

title: Election officials aim to reassure voters ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Election officials from some of the largest jurisdictions in the country met in Washington to address voter concerns ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
Los Angeles County, Calif. Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan said officials want voters to trust the process.
“We want voters to be assured that we’re ready and we want voters to be focused on their readiness,” Logan said.
Dallas County, Texas Elections Administrator Paul Adams said officials are focused on communicating with voters about election procedures.
“It is very important that we give a strong message of clarity to the voters, that they understand what is going on, they understand the procedures we are following,” Adams said.
In recent weeks, federal updates and decisions have affected the elections system, including Supreme Court opinions on mail-in ballots and redistricting maps, and a White House push to address what it calls long-term voter corruption.
On Wednesday, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the indictment of 10 foreign nationals for making false claims of citizenship in order to vote.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said voter fraud affects public confidence in elections.
“Voter fraud erodes the public’s trust in our electoral system and it’s vital to our democratic process that we do everything that we can to restore that trust,” Blanche said.
Aaron Blacksberg, of the Institute for Responsive Government, said many proposed federal changes have not taken effect.
“The executive branch, the federal government, the President, the various agencies announced attempted changes and almost all of them of any substance for voters have not come into effect,” Blacksberg said.
Blacksberg said voters should learn election procedures before heading to the polls.
“Know the rules, go vote,” Blacksberg said.

title: Author George Jreije wants to broaden horizons at Portland’s Mechanics’ Hall
text:
Lebanese American author George Jreije was a sophomore at Clark University majoring in political science and business when a good book flipped a switch in his head, prompting him to ask a question: Could he write something that would provoke the same sense of wonder he’d just experienced?
Nearly 10 years later, Jreije has turned that curiosity into a career that includes writing, freelance book editing and public speaking.
A writer of young adult fantasy fiction, Jreije has written four novels, and short stories that have appeared in magazines such as Scholastic’s Scope and Bangarang, in addition to two upcoming graphic novels. His works incorporate elements of Arab culture alongside a prominent theme of searching for belonging while being split between two cultures.
One of Jreije’s ultimate goals as a writer is to foster literacy and an appreciation for storytelling among younger generations — something he hopes to continue in his role as Mechanics’ Hall’s next writer-in-residence.
The yearlong position, which he started last Tuesday, gives Jreije a dedicated workspace in the hall, a $2,500 honorarium, and opportunities to connect and share his work with the library community.
“I think that the more synergy we can create, the more we can bring cultural elements to the institutions that are these mainstays and these beacons of culture, I think that good things can happen,” said Jreije.
Over the next year, Jreije plans to break beyond the “classics” of literature and encourage more conversation and exposure to genre fiction such as sci-fi, fantasy, horror and children’s literature.
“My spin is going to be inclusivity; let’s make this something that is a more inclusive experience that challenges folks to think outside of what they’re comfortable with,” said Jreije.
Jreije said he has many ideas for what he wants to do with the position, including hosting conversations with local authors or starting a book club.
“I’m an ideas person, and maybe not all of them are feasible, but I’m hoping and dreaming for some of them,” he said.
Jreije was previously a writer-in-residence for the Concord Free Library in Concord, Massachusetts, which left him with a few lessons he plans to keep in mind at Mechanics’ Hall.
“I can’t impose my preferences on patrons, on staff. I have to meet people where they are, and I think in doing so, and getting to know them and them getting to know me, that’s actually how I can get them closer to embodying my excitement for books,” he said.
DRAWING FROM EXPERIENCE
Although Jreije has never attended a school for alchemy or found a ring that houses an all-powerful jinn — unlike the protagonists of his Shad Halid and Bashir Boutros book series — he has drawn on the experience of growing up in a first-generation immigrant household to craft stories that resonate with him and his readers.
He described growing up in the shadow of the Iraq War, how the conflict put a target on the back of all Arabs regardless of what country they came from, and how it resulted in rude comments from people about his background.
“It made me pause and think about how, as humans, we like to put ourselves in buckets and put other people into buckets, and I wanted to explore that in my writing,” Jreije said.
Jreije pulled inspiration from Lebanese culinary tradition, folklore and geography; many of his stories take their protagonists outside the U.S. and to Lebanon. Jreije also incorporated what he described as some of the “sillier parts” of Lebanese culture, such as controlling parents or the experience of being held to a high standard.
“My books are not just about being Lebanese, but being Lebanese American,” said Jreije. “That third culture experience, and not quite feeling Arab enough, while not quite feeling American enough.”
But above all else, Jreije feels that reading and writing remain important because of their ability to foster empathy and compassion for different points of view.
“What we see happening so often in society is that people struggle to put themselves in the shoes of others,” said Jreije. “And I think that books allow one to become better and better at empathizing with the other, but also critically thinking and asking the questions that will lead them to understand.”

title: Swedish goaltending tandem set to stop pucks for Maine men’s hockey
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Two Swedish netminders will be stopping pucks for the Black Bears this season.
“It’s been great. It’s nice to be able to talk some Swedish. We’re talking out on the ice too and everywhere. Yeah, it’s been awesome. Yeah, he’s a great guy, so it’s been fun,” said Albin Boija, senior goaltender.
“It’s been a long time since I’ve been able to talk Swedish in the locker room, so I’m enjoying it big time. We have a Norwegian and a Finnish guy too that talks pretty good Swedish. It’s just fun,” said Petter Wickström Stumer, junior goaltender.
Boija was an All-American two years ago and will be looking to bounce back after turning in an .899 save percentage last season.
“Definitely a down year, and I think something I hadn’t really gone through before. So, you learn from it and definitely get stronger out of it. I’m excited and motivated, for sure. (I’m) definitely bringing my A-game, bringing it every night, doing everything I can for the team to make us better and ultimately win games and save pucks,” said Boija.
Wickström Stumer comes to Orono as a transfer from Canisius.
“It’s been nothing but good. It’s been a fun summer. It’s been a good two-and-a-half months. The time has flown by, and I’m really excited to be here. I feel like we have a great group, and that’s why I came here. I came here to win. I came here to play fun hockey, and I think we’re going to do that this season,” said Wickström Stumer.
The Black Bears start the season with a trip to Holy Cross on Friday at 7 p.m.
Maine’s home opener is against Quinnipiac on Friday of next week at 7 p.m.
It’s Alfond Arena’s 50th season.

title: MaineHousing awards a record $2.7 million to help agencies run winter warming shelters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MaineHousing has awarded a record $2.72 million in funding to 12 warming shelters from York County to Presque Isle this winter.
The funding will support safe, heated spaces in Bangor, Lewiston and Portland, as well as Augusta, Biddeford, Brunswick, Ellsworth, Orland, Presque Isle and Waterville. The facilities will offer a combined 474 beds for people during cold and dangerous winter weather, and most plan to stay open through April.
“Dangerous winter weather can put lives at risk, especially for people experiencing homelessness or housing instability,” MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan said in a news release Tuesday afternoon.
This year’s funding is the most money doled out in the five years that MaineHousing has offered this program. Last year, the Legislature gave the agency $2.3 million to distribute.
The organizations running the shelters can use the funding from the quasi-governmental agency for staffing, supplies, transportation, extended hours and other operating costs. Recipients of the warming shelter grants will work with their municipalities, emergency management officials and community partners to connect people in need to a warming shelter.
“We are grateful to the governor and the Maine Legislature for making these funds available,” Brennan said. “This investment helps local organizations prepare before winter and respond when dangerous weather threatens Maine people.”
Biddeford-based Seeds of Hope is the top recipient of this year’s funding. The nonprofit will get more than $660,000 — about $304,000 to support its 55-bed facility in Biddeford, and nearly $361,000 to operate a nightly warming shelter in Portland.
Seeds of Hope stepped forward in early September to operate the Portland shelter after the city sought an agency to run a winter shelter following the closure of its shelter for asylum seekers.
Portland Mayor Mark Dion said at the time that he had some concerns with Seeds of Hope taking the shelter on, noting that the city’s past partners couldn’t handle the capacity needs in Maine’s most populous area.
But Seeds of Hope Director Vassie Fowler said her staff is experienced in managing high-needs populations, complex situations and the operational demands that come with running a full-capacity warming center.
Still, the $360,720 for this winter’s shelter is less than the roughly $400,000 that the city received last year to operate a shelter that only opened based on certain thresholds. This year, the plan is for the facility to be open every night, regardless of temperature or snowfall.
Fowler declined to comment on the funding Wednesday.
Alter L/A, a 24-hour warming shelter in the Lewiston and Auburn area, received just under $390,000 for a 112-bed facility. That funding will primarily go toward staffing, said Kevin Boilard, the executive director.
The shelter employs around 25 people and plans to bring on an additional 12 to 15 staff members for the colder months. Last year, the shelter served more than 700 people, with an average of 112 per 24-hour period. It’s thought to be the only 24/7 warming shelter in the Twin Cities, Boilard said.
“The intention is not just to house (people), but to bring them in, make them warm and connect them to stability and the structure that most are looking for,” he said.
The other nine agencies receiving funding are:
- Augusta Overnight, $375,750 for 50 beds in Augusta
- Bangor Area Homeless Shelter, $10,000 for 5 beds in Bangor
- Brick Church, $427,650 for 65 beds in Bangor
- Tedford Housing, $225,450 for 30 beds in Brunswick
- Healthy Acadia, $263,025 for 35 beds in Ellsworth
- HOME Inc., $28,611 for 18 beds in Orland
- State Street Church, $52,000 for 18 beds in Portland
- Homeless Services of Aroostook, $112,725 for 15 beds in Presque Isle
- Mid-Maine Homeless Shelter, $172,845 for 23 beds in Waterville
The shelter funding is a piece of broader winter preparedness efforts across the state. MaineHousing also runs the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) and the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which both help eligible households with heating costs and emergencies.
Heating costs have soared in Maine, with the price of heating oil hitting a record $6.02 per gallon last week.
Steve Hoad, of Windsor, is just one of a large number of Maine homeowners who use heating oil to keep their homes warm during the winter. Hoad told the Portland Press Herald in early September that his farmhouse will cost him thousands more to keep warm this winter. He’s exactly the kind of person HEAP aims to help.
“We know many families are concerned about heating costs,” Brennan said. “Programs such as HEAP can help thousands of Maine households each year, and we urge people to seek help before they face a crisis.”
Staff Writer Emily Duggan contributed to this story.

title: Kingfield to hold election for vacant Select Board seat
text:
Kingfield residents will elect a new member to the Select Board in December.
Following the resignation of Hunter Lander in August, the board voted Sept. 21 to hold a special election Dec. 8 to fill the vacant seat. The board has been operating with four members since.
This was the second meeting in a row where the vacancy was debated. At a Sept. 8 meeting, after discussing the challenges that a four-person board could have in getting business done, opinions were split over whether to hold a special election or wait until the annual town meeting in June, causing the discussion to be tabled until Sept. 21.
Board member Kim Jordan said the town could not wait until June to fill the seat. That option would risk splitting votes on a number of important decisions.
“I think in our last meeting that we had, we had two tie votes, and we didn’t get anywhere with those discussions,” Jordan said. She said the town “voted for us to have a five-member board for that very reason.
“We’ve got some pretty serious stuff that’s coming up in front of us with the Bowdoin College thing, the school withdrawal,” she added. “I mean, we can’t keep having tied votes.”
Morgan Dunham, chairman of the board, noted the learning curve for a new member and expressed hesitance about filling the seat immediately.
“To have a new person come on the board,” Dunham said. “It takes us back a couple of steps. Just explaining everything and someone learning something new. It’s a little bit frustrating.”
Jordan explained that the new member will need to get trained regardless of when they are elected. She said that at least two community members have expressed interest in running for the position.
A motion to set the election date almost didn’t pass. Jordan and Christopher Rushton voted in favor of the motion. Dunham initially voted against but changed her vote to pass the motion. David Davol did not vote.

title: Maine Marathon competitor ran 100 miles to raise money for warming center
text:
Maine Marathon competitor ran 100 miles through Bangor to raise money for warming center
Brad Eslin, of Bangor, is among the thousands of runners who will be competing in the Maine Marathon on Sunday, Oct. 4.
Eslin is an avid competitive runner and earned the nickname "Brad Crazy."
"Early-morning runs, sub-zero temperatures, frozen beard, and this runner friend of mine, her name is Kelly, she was like, 'Man, you are Brad Crazy,' and it just kind of stuck," Eslin said.
In August, Eslin ran 100 miles through the city of Bangor to raise awareness of homelessness in the community. The "Brad Crazy Hundo for the Homeless" event turned attention into action and helped raise more than $18,000 for the Well Warming Center, which is run by Jericho Road Ministries.
"Part of my route is just littered with homeless people, off and on, different days, and this one particular morning just struck me. I was just crying as I was running thinking, 'What can I do to help this?'" Eslin said.
It took Eslin 21 hours, 31 minutes and 35 seconds to finish that 100-mile run.
Eslin has competed in the Boston Marathon five times, and he is ready to do it again in 2027.
A master plumber by trade, he's even named his business after his passion: Marathon Plumbing and Drain Service.
Eslin said the Maine Marathon is important and special to him.
"It was actually one of my first marathons, not the first marathon, but one of," he said. "They seem to give back a lot to the community. They are very community-based. I just love how much they do that. I love running and they seem to fit that profile pretty good."
The Maine Marathon starts at 7:45 a.m. Sunday in Portland's Back Cove, which is also where the race will finish.

title: Man dragged to death by subway train after his bag gets caught in doors
text:
NEW YORK (AP) - A man was dragged to death by a New York City subway train when a bag he was carrying got stuck in the door during the Monday evening rush hour commute, police said.
Yaw Boahene, 57, was exiting the train at a Brooklyn subway station around 6 p.m. when his bag, which police described as a shopping bag, snagged in the closing train doors. The Brooklyn resident was pulled onto the tracks and run over by the train as it left the station, police said in a statement.
Officers arrived to find Boahene “unconscious and unresponsive” on the train tracks, police said. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
The medical examiner’s office will determine the cause of death. The police investigation is ongoing.
The Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which runs the subway system, said both the train operator and conductor have been removed from service, as is routine while the investigation continues. The agency said the train was one of the fleet’s newest models. It was inspected after the man’s death and also previously in July, and no mechanical issues were found.
Dragging deaths happen from time to time on the nation’s largest subway system. In 2022, a 20-year-old commuter was killed after his backpack or a piece of his clothing got stuck in the door as he was trying to get onto a train at the Columbus Circle station in upper Manhattan.

title: Trump’s new AI-powered government website contradicts his claims on the 2020 election and a third term
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration has lauded its revamped website America.gov as a way to simplify Americans’ access to information and services scattered across a plethora of agency sites, but President Donald Trump probably won’t like some of the answers his new site says are sourced from government information.
Asking the site — which says it’s sourced via artificial intelligence from “official government sources” — questions about who won the 2020 election or about the name of the federal department that operates out of the Pentagon yields answers contrary to those Trump himself frequently proclaims.
As Trump was still speaking at Tuesday’s launch event, however, the site began modifying its answers. Asked again about the 2020 election, it replied that it couldn’t answer “political questions,” a response it also gave to inquiries about whether Trump had been impeached or convicted of felony charges.
The Associated Press asked about:
The 2020 presidential election
“Official federal sources do not show that widespread fraud changed the 2020 presidential election outcome. Isolated election crimes did occur and have been prosecuted.”
Since Trump, a Republican, lost the 2020 election to Democrat Joe Biden, he has repeatedly falsely claimed that victory was “stolen” from him and asserted that widespread fraud occurred. Repeated audits and recounts found no significant fraud in the presidential election, and Trump’s own administration said the election was clean.
Trump running for president in 2028
“The 22nd Amendment says that no person shall be elected President more than twice. Donald J. Trump has already been elected twice (2016 and 2024). I am not giving legal advice.”
Trump has frequently suggested he wants to seek a third term, posting about mounting another campaign, donning 2028 caps and discussing ways to make it happen — even as he’s acknowledged the Constitution prohibits it. He had only been back in the White House for a couple of months when he told NBC News, “There are methods which you could” use to seek a third term.
The Pentagon
“The Pentagon is the headquarters of the Department of Defense.”
Last year, Trump signed an executive order aimed at rebranding the Department of Defense as the Department of War, complaining that the Department of Defense’s name was “woke.”
Human action as cause of climate change
“Federal climate-science pages say recent warming is largely from human greenhouse-gas emissions, mainly burning fossil fuels. Earth’s climate has also changed for natural reasons over long periods.”
Trump, who has called climate change a “hoax,” previously issued an executive order that directed the Environmental Protection Agency to submit a report on “the legality and continuing applicability” of the endangerment finding. Conservatives and some congressional Republicans have long sought to undo what they consider overly restrictive and economically damaging rules to limit greenhouse gases that cause global warming.
Presidential salaries
The chatbot said that “some presidents have declined to keep that pay,” mentioning Trump but listing George Washington, Herbert Hoover and John F. Kennedy as refusing their salaries before Trump.
During his remarks Tuesday, Trump, a real estate mogul who took in about $1.2 billion from various crypto holdings last year, said he was the first U.S. president to forgo a salary, something that he has said before.
___
Kinnard reported from Columbia, S.C.

title: DOJ files complaint against judges over immigration enforcement surge comments
text:
Department of Justice files complaint against judges over immigration enforcement surge comments
The Department of Justice filed a complaint Wednesday against federal judges in Minnesota over their remarks to the media about the pressure on their courthouse during Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge.
The complaint alleges the seven judges — nominated by Democrats and Republican presidents — violated judicial ethics by speaking to The New York Times about their experience dealing with a flood of cases during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge crackdown that led to thousands of arrests in the Twin Cities.
The complaint escalates the department's battle with the federal judiciary, which has halted administration priorities, dismissed high-profile prosecutions and accused government lawyers in some cases of failing to comply with court orders.
The department is demanding that the judges recuse themselves from all criminal or civil cases involving the Department of Homeland Security, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters, because of what he described as “obvious bias they have shown" in their remarks to the newspaper.
“When we have a situation like we have now, where you have a judge, a couple of judges, just not only violating the canons in our view, but also showing bias in what they’re saying, we have no choice but to act to defend not only our prosecutors, but also DHS,” Blanche said.
The judge at the center of the story, Patrick Schiltz, accused the government in January of failing to comply with nearly 100 court orders. He said in a ruling that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a part of DHS, "is not a law unto itself.”
Schiltz, who was nominated by Republican President George W. Bush and served as a law clerk for Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, told the newspaper that what happened in Minnesota's federal court last winter “created a grave threat to the rule of law.”
In a statement Wednesday, a spokesperson for the Minnesota court said legal experts have confirmed that the judges were acting “well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges” in speaking to the newspaper. Schiltz also said in a statement that his comments did not violate any ethical rules.
“Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges" may speak or write "on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence,'" Schiltz said in a statement. “That is exactly what I did."
The complaint was filed with the chief judge of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which oversees federal judges in Minnesota.
The Republican administration has railed against what it describes as “activist judges” who officials say are intent on thwarting Trump’s agenda. Yet some of the most critical and unfavorable court rulings have come from judges nominated by Trump and other Republican presidents.
