title: UMaine men’s hockey team looks to regain its culture
text:
ORONO — On Tuesday, Ben Barr thanked the University of Maine men’s hockey team on behalf of himself and the entire coaching staff. They’re all getting their 40 winks every night, sound sleep from head hitting pillow to morning alarm, and that’s due in large part to the effort the Black Bears put in every day.
“I expect them to bring effort and attitude, and they’ve been bringing that every practice since we started,” Barr said after Tuesday’s practice. “That doesn’t mean we go out and win just because we work hard. There’s another level for that, but at least we know we’ll be in the fight with the work ethic I think we’ve established so far.”
The season opens this weekend with a pair of games at Holy Cross. The Black Bears, as Barr put it, are trying to find the program’s soul again.
Go ahead and call this a resetting season for the Black Bears, who followed the 2025 Hockey East championship with an 18-14-3 record last season. A few years ago, when Barr was starting a program rebuild, that would have been a cause for minor jubilation as a positive step.
A Hockey East crown and two straight appearances in the NCAA tournament changed expectations. A season with 18 wins isn’t progress anymore, it’s disappointment.
The 2025-26 season was one of upheaval across college hockey. For the first time, players from the three Canadian major junior leagues and Canadian colleges (U Sports) were NCAA eligible. It turned the recruiting landscape into the wild west. Yeah, this guy can play but is he a fit for our program? Often the question was met with a shrug and the hope that things would work out.
At Maine, the influx of CHL players was a mixed bag. Of the nine players Barr brought in from the CHL or U Sports last season, five have already left via the transfer portal. Good hockey players? Yes. The right fit for Maine’s blue-collar culture? No.
“For three or four years, we were building something. We were trying to do it a certain way. Then the whole world tips upside down as far as the NCAA stuff’s concerned. You have a little bit of a turbulent year as far some of the decisions we make,” said Barr, now in his sixth season as Maine’s head coach.
Barr can take blame for last season’s team culture issues, which reached its nadir in a December home loss to rival New Hampshire, but players know it starts with them. Team captain Owen Fowler knows what kind of team he wants to see on the ice. Fowler wants the Black Bears to use their size to forecheck hard and play gritty hockey, looking to erode the stamina of opponents.
“We’re going to wear teams down a lot. Kind of similar to my first year (that Hockey East title season), where there were definitely a lot of games we won in the third period,” Fowler said.
Maine has 15 newcomers on a 28-player roster. That’s a lot of turnover, Barr admits. Nine of the newcomers are transfers with college hockey experience. They bring a higher maturity level, and that’s a good thing.
If that maturity manifests as players willing to go after rebounds and tipped pucks to score goals, and guys who set screens to get a teammate an open shot, it will be a very good thing. Last season’s top four scorers are gone. Brandon Holt graduated. Josh Nadeau signed a pro contract with Montreal. Justin Poirier and Miguel Marques transferred.
“We have enough good hockey players on this team to go out against anybody. The execution piece is just finding that little bit of extra will. That will be the challenge,” Barr said.
Assistant captain Sully Scholle said he’s done talking about last season. The focus has to be on the now. Assistant captain Max Scott said this season’s team already feels like a tighter-knit group that last year’s ever was. Barr sees that, too, and noted that they care about each other, and that’s been evident for a couple months.
It didn’t take Barr long to lift Maine into college hockey’s upper tier again after more than a decade outside of it. Ups and downs are a given, and Barr noted that camaraderie and a willingness to work hard doesn’t translate into 10 goals a game.
It’s a sturdy foundation, though, and one the Black Bears need. It’s what will help determine if last season was a hiccup, or the start of a trend.

title: Remember: Abortion kills human life

title: Maine E-ZPass introduces new tags featuring local sports team logos
text:
Maine E-ZPass can help you root, root, root for the home team
You can now show support for some of your favorite local sports teams using your E-ZPass tag from the Maine Turnpike Authority.
On Wednesday, the MTA introduced four new branded sticker tags. The tags are $20, and you can get them with the logos of the Portland Hearts of Pine, Portland Sea Dogs, or two different logos for the Boston Red Sox.
All of the proceeds from Portland Hearts of Pine sticker tags will benefit the Hearts of Pine Foundation, a nonprofit that uses soccer to build connections through after-school programs, local partnerships and investments.
The MTA says a Maine Mariners tag will be available soon and that it plans to build more partnerships with professional teams across New England and collegiate teams with ties to Maine.
In March, the MTA announced it would start offering sticker tags, in addition to the traditional hard-covered transponders.
The hard-covered transponders are $15 and the non-sports branded sticker tags are $5.
“We are constantly looking for smart technology that can improve cost efficiency, reduce our environmental impact, and make travel easier. When we can pair those benefits with something creative and personal, it is a win for Maine drivers,” said Andre Briere, Executive Director, Maine Turnpike Authority.
Sticker tags are available in person at the E-ZPass customer service office on Congress Street in Portland, by searching Maine E-ZPass on the new MTA app, or online. The new sticker tags are optional. Users do not need to replace existing transponders.
The MTA says the sticker tags use passive RFID technology, eliminating the need for an internal battery, and require significantly less plastic than traditional transponders. The tags also provide added protection against theft or unauthorized use. Because each tag adheres directly to the vehicle’s windshield, it is automatically deactivated if removed and cannot be moved from vehicle to vehicle like traditional transponders.

title: ‘Super oversize’ load’s journey to South Portland taking longer than expected
text:
The transport of a “super oversize” load — approximately 220 feet long and roughly 20 feet wide — to South Portland has been delayed.
The heat recovery steam generator began its two-night journey from Jay on Tuesday night, and was originally due to arrive in South Portland by 6 a.m. Thursday.
But because its progress has been slower than anticipated, it’s now due to arrive in South Portland next Tuesday morning, with incremental progress each night, according to the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office.
Wednesday night, it was to travel from Turner to Oxford, including over Jumper Bridge. Over Thursday night, the generator will travel from Oxford to Gray, resulting in traffic delays on Route 26 in Mechanic Falls and Poland. It will be staged in Gray over the weekend and moved to Buxton on Sunday night.
Monday night will be the final push before it arrives in South Portland the next morning. Law enforcement officers, utility crews and other personnel are assisting the transport of the generator, which weighs more than 683,000 pounds.
These generators are typically used at industrial facilities or power plants, and while it’s on the road, it spans two travel lanes. Residents and businesses have been asked to avoid parking along the route while the load is being transported to avoid obstruction, and drivers have been encouraged to plan ahead and allow extra travel time.
It’s the first of nine oversize loads planned along this route. The schedule for the remaining eight loads will be released once the current one is complete, according to the Maine Department of Transportation.
A spokesman for the MDOT did not say whether the delay will impact the timelines for the other loads.
A spokesman for Barnhart Crane & Rigging, the company overseeing the transport, did not immediately respond to questions about the timeline.

title: Hegseth announces a new drone command, cuts to 20% of generals in US military
text:
QUANTICO, Va. (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced some major changes to the U.S. military on Wednesday in what he called his “State of the Force” address, including establishing a new drone command and cutting 20% of the nation’s generals and admirals.
The Pentagon also will launch an effort to study the future of warfare that will be led in part by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Hegseth said. The Defense Department will create an Office of Religious Affairs and plans to build a new base for the first time in 40 years, he added.
Hegseth made the announcements to junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia — the second year in a row that he has given such an address. But this time, the U.S. military is seven months into a war with Iran with no clear end in sight, has captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and killed more than 200 people in strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats in Latin America, among other actions worldwide.
The speech is not a usual fixture among Pentagon leaders. While Hegseth’s predecessors have regularly addressed troops and top officers, they have traditionally done so in small or private settings.
The Pentagon chief, however, again led with how he has drastically retooled the U.S. military by targeting what he calls “woke” culture — through a rollback of diversity programs, a review of ground combat units with female troops and a new screening program for “testosterone deficiency” among male personnel — as well as attacks on the media for the coverage of the military.
Hegseth announces a new drone-focused warfare command
The Pentagon chief announced the intention to create a new four-star command to oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities in what he called “the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history.”
He acknowledged that “the pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it.” Iran commonly uses cheap drones, including those that have killed U.S. troops during the seven-month war. Hegseth pointed to Ukraine’s pioneering use of drones to combat Russian forces — something American forces have learned from firsthand.
“Ukraine’s lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt,” Hegseth said.
However, a U.S. Army unit based in Europe that specialized in drone warfare was ordered recently to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion.
A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers subsequently asked the Army to explain the order, given that the world’s battlefields are rapidly evolving and military tactics increasingly rely on uncrewed systems to fight.
The plans for a drone command come as the U.S. is in a stalemate with Iran over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy shipping corridor. The war has forced American forces in the region to expend hundreds of expensive missile interceptors to defend against Iran’s missile and drone attacks, which have still managed to kill and wound U.S. troops.
Hegseth repeated claims that the U.S. military has destroyed Iran’s navy, air force and defense systems as well as many of its leaders and its industrial base. But Tehran has continued intermittently to launch drone and missile attacks against at U.S. or allied bases, while maintaining its ability to strike commercial and military ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
During his speech, Hegseth touted the Trump administration’s major investments in the defense industry and push for contractors to speed up their work to expand the nation’s weapons arsenals. But experts say U.S. military contractors will need at least three years to replenish stockpiles of key weapons systems used heavily in the Iran war.
Hegseth faces questions from lawmakers over cuts to general ranks
Hegseth said he directed the military services to double the 10% reduction he ordered last spring for roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027.
“I call it accountability and long overdue,” he said.
Some members of Congress have criticized the war and the drawdown of munitions stockpiles, while calling the latest cuts to the general ranks a “purge” that will take years to rebuild.
“He’s got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth. “He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it.”
Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth’s reasoning.
“If it’s simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first,” Rounds said.
Musk and Gingrich to lead a study of future warfare
In innovating the next wave of weapons systems, Hegseth announced an effort to study the future of warfare led by Musk, Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries.
Hegseth said the work “will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes.” He pointed to the need to dominate “any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon.”
This month, the U.S. confirmed for the first time that it had deployed weapons in space, a remarkable revelation after previous warnings about countries such as Russia possibly weaponizing a global frontier long agreed in treaties to be used for only peaceful purposes.
Among the other announcements was the unveiling of a plan to build a new military base, with Hegseth inviting all 50 states to compete for the chance to play host to 15,000 to 25,000 service members. He also announced a plan to make every military base self-powered.
___
Finley reported from Washington, and Kinnard from Columbia, South Carolina. Associated Press writer Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Learning new tricks — The surprising way new hobbies boost your brain as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Forget the old adage: You can’t teach an old dog new tricks.
Picking up a new hobby later in life isn’t just fun — it’s also one of the best things you can do for your brain. From line dancing to sourdough starters to pickleball, small leaps outside your comfort zone can spark change in how your brain works.
“The brain still learns” — it just needs patience
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, says the idea that older adults can’t pick up new skills doesn’t hold up once you actually watch them try.
“I hear this all the time, that you can’t teach an old dog new tricks. And then I walk into a senior community, and they’re like teenagers sitting there texting, and they’re on their phone and they’re taking videos and QR codes,” Cradduck said. “They learned that at an older age because I had to learn it at an older age.”
Cradduck said the brain just needs a little more time and patience to learn as we age.
“And you need to make it relevant to the time,” Cradduck said. “So grab a grandkid and learn a whole bunch.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, says that discomfort is actually doing something good beneath the surface.
“When you challenge it like that, you create new connections. The brain is always changing. New connections, what we call neuroplasticity,” Rogers said. “And also you’re waking up the brain, and that’s a good thing. So it makes you just stay alert and all that. And you can look at reaction time to things actually improve.”
From line dancing nerves to a new rhythm
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, shared her own recent experience stepping outside her comfort zone.
“I always get nervous when I’m learning something new, and I get nervous with the technology. But I have this experience I’ve had in the back of my mind I wanted to learn line dancing,” O’Rourke said. “And my yoga studio is teaching a three-hour line dancing class. Then I’m at this event the other day and they’re line dancing and I could tell I was sitting there like, should I go? Should I not go? So I just jumped in there.”
“My heart was pounding, and there was a woman behind me helping me, go to the right, to the left, and she really helped me,” O’Rourke said. “As nervous as I was, I got into this rhythm with them, and it really helped me realize one — I had to face the fear and do it anyway and then keep doing it. And I just got so excited.”
Cradduck says even something as simple as walking is a workout for the brain.
“The more you can make those connections in the brain, and then the feet, the movement of the feet — you don’t think about what it takes with your brain to actually just walk,” Cradduck said. “And so walking is actually really brain exercise. It really is, especially for our aged community. And so learning how to dance, learning something with rhythm — the arts, those things are amazing.”
New activities, new purpose
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose says the same principle is already built into many independent living communities.
“That’s why in independent living, there’s so many activities where they might be teaching new language, they’re teaching history. They’re giving all kinds of new things to introduce people to, because that helps people live longer and live better,” Ambrose said.
Rogers shared an example from her own life, learning pickleball in Wichita — and Ambrose took a sourdough baking class through her real estate office.
“And I’m not really that much of a cook or a baker,” Ambrose said. “But I took a sourdough class in my real estate office. One of the realtors was teaching it, and I picked up my mom. I said, ‘Hey, I’m coming to pick you up,’ She didn’t know what we’re doing, so that was really fun for her and I to do it together.”
Ambrose said it was like a science experiment.
“Every morning you’re like, ‘Oh, I gotta go check my dough,’” she said.
What if you can’t be physically active?
Cradduck says the lesson isn’t limited to people who can move freely.
“There are some people that are impaired, and they can’t do the physical. So go to your grandkid’s ball game. Maybe you don’t know the rules of soccer, maybe you don’t know all the rules of baseball or football — and learn the game and learn and connect,” Cradduck said. “It’s all going to give you so much more purpose and so much more connection. The more you do and the more you connect.”
Rogers said the biggest thing is that you’re exercising your brain.
Key takeaways
- Learning new skills sharpens your brain health.
- Pairing curiosity with experience keeps you engaged and builds connection across generations.
- Embracing new tricks builds generational bridges.

title: Federal prosecutors charge Venezuelan man shot by ICE agent in Texas with assaulting an officer
text:
Federal prosecutors charge Venezuelan man shot by ICE agent in Texas with assaulting an officer
Federal prosecutors on Tuesday announced an assault charge against a Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in his car by a federal immigration agent in Texas, accusing the man of striking an officer with his side mirror while trying to drive away.
Video: ICE shooting in Texas sparks outrage (Sept. 20)
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint. Garces Perez, whose attorney has said he still has a bullet lodged in his back from the Sept. 20 shooting, made an initial court appearance in an Austin federal court on Tuesday, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Western District of Texas.
A nine-page affidavit from a Department of Homeland Security agent amounts to the government's fullest public account to date of the shooting in the Texas capital, which has set off protests and outrage from Democrats over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The document includes photos taken from body-worn cameras but no video was released, and the complaint did not say whether the agent allegedly struck by the side mirror sustained any injuries.
The accusations against Garces Perez are reminiscent of previous claims made by immigration agents after high-profile shootings, in which officers have similarly accused drivers of weaponizing their vehicles. In a handful of cases, those allegations have been undermined or walked back after the release of body-worn camera footage, and have renewed scrutiny about the DHS's reliance on vehicular stops to execute arrests.
Garces Perez was in the custody of U.S. Marshals after being removed from a federal detention center in South Texas, according to court documents filed by federal prosecutors. Separately, Garces Perez's attorneys have filed a lawsuit seeking to stop his removal from the U.S.
During the federal court hearing Tuesday, Garces Perez was in “extremely bad medical condition,” his lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said, describing him as light-headed, nauseated and confused about what was happening. For the nine days since he has been incarcerated, Lincoln-Goldfinch said, Garces Perez has not stopped pleading for surgery to remove the bullet, which is preventing him from moving his arm without pain. DHS did not immediately respond to questions on Tuesday afternoon about Garces Perez's medical treatment.
If convicted, Garces Perez faces up to 20 years in prison.
Affidavit says agent was struck in torso by side mirror
According to an affidavit signed by a DHS agent, officers first saw Garces Perez's car parked outside of a restaurant with its emergency flashers on. They decided to pull him over after conducting a database check that showed the car was registered to Garces Perez who had a final order of removal from the U.S.
The agents said that they turned on their lights to execute the stop, but in the same filing, Garces Perez told investigators that an unmarked SUV followed him and then abruptly cut him off on the side of the road.
Garces Perez, who was making a DoorDash delivery, provided his driver's license through a crack in the window, but ignored agents' requests to step out of the car, the complaint said. Garces Perez told investigators that he declined to exit because he had asked for officers to wait to apprehend him until his wife could come retrieve his car. Court documents describe the interaction as initially conversational, with a tone that was “pleasant and not aggressive.”
About a minute later, according to court records, Garces Perez “abruptly” closed the window and drove off. One of the officers, who is referred to only by his initials, was struck in his torso with the driver’s side view mirror when Garces Perez tried to drive away, the documents say.
Officer who fired wasn't wearing body camera
The unnamed officer who shot Garces Perez wasn’t wearing a body camera. The other officer involved in the chase was wearing a camera, but only caught up to the chase after Garces Perez had been shot, according to the affidavit.
ICE has previously said its field officers nationwide will have body-worn cameras by the end of September.
The affidavit included screenshots from previously unreleased body-worn camera footage of the officer’s initial interactions with ICE agents. The first of three photos appears to show the officer standing in front of Garces Perez’s driver’s door mirror; the second shows the officer resting his hands on the hood and side of Garces Perez’s car, with the mirror close to or touching the officer’s abdomen; and the third appears to show the car pulling away.
Lincoln-Goldfinch called on DHS to release the full body-worn camera footage, rather than screenshots that she said could be misleading.
“This is an example of the government playing games with my client’s life and safety,” she said.
The Austin Police Department last week released video from its officers. But that footage did not show the shooting or the moment that Garces Perez allegedly tried driving away.
Conflicting accounts of lead-up to shooting
The affidavit includes Garces Perez providing his account to federal investigators, which paints a contrasting picture of the lead-up to the shooting than what federal prosecutors described.
According to the affidavit, Garces Perez said that a law enforcement SUV struck his car after a brief chase and caused it to spin before an agent opened fire, shooting him in the back. By contrast, U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons said in a statement that Garces Perez tried to strike an officer with his car, “causing the officer to fire his pistol."
Garces Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to make appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum. President Trump ended the program on his first day in office.
Garces Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to his lawyer. She said a judge issued a deportation order after Garces Perez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.
Others have faced charges following ICE shootings
The shooting occurred amid a surge in ICE enforcement across the U.S. during President Donald Trump’s second term. ICE reported more than 50,000 monthly arrests in July and August — a first for the agency.
Immigration officers have come under intense scrutiny for shootings that have occurred since Trump took office in January 2025 — at least 10 of which have been fatal. On a few occasions, federal law enforcement has charged the person shot by immigration officers with assault.
A woman shot several times by Border Patrol officers in Chicago and a man shot in the leg by an ICE agent in Minneapolis were both accused of assaulting officers, but in both cases the charges were dropped. The ICE officer in Minneapolis has since been charged with lying about getting assaulted before shooting the man in the leg.
___
Riddle reported from Los Angeles.

title: REVIEW POTPOURRI: Writers, television and Beethoven
text:
Malcolm Cowley
Author Malcolm Cowley (1898-1981) spent a number of years in Paris during the 1920s and made the acquaintance of other writers beginning their careers – in particular Ernest Hemingway and Scott Fitzgerald. In 1934, he wrote a fascinating memoir of that period, Exile’s Return, which I have read twice since buying it at the Gorham State College bookstore back in 1969 when I was a freshman and suffering from a burning hunger to read every book of great literature before I was 30 – an early delusion of grandeur.
I remember most vividly Cowley’s account of the 1929 joint suicide of the incredibly wealthy Bostonian/poet Harry Crosby and his mistress, Josephine Rotch, in a New York City studio apartment. Crosby was quite rigidly committed to the life of a free spirit in Paris, away from his stuffy wealthy family, which included an aunt married to J.P. Morgan.
Both Crosby and his wife Caresse were also philanderers in their very open marriage predilections; hence, Miss Rotch whom Crosby met in Venice. By the late 1920s, Crosby and Rotch dabbled in Satanism and the cult of suicide with the above-mentioned tragedy.
Another chapter in the book mentioned the life of simplicity living in a farmhouse with his first wife, a woodstove, kerosene lamp, a windup phonograph with piles of dusty dance records and lots of books and more books endlessly crowding their space.
When Exile’s Return was published in 1934, it was trashed by the reviewers over the age of 35 and praised by those under 35.
Some quotes from the older reviewers shared by Cowley in his 1980 book of memories about the 1930s, The Dream of the Golden Mountains:
“Mr. Hemingway is growing dim. So are his colleagues… Cowley’s exiles a little group of serious thinking drunkards….They felt there was something superb in starving for three days while waiting for Papa’s next check…vocational narcissism.”
Interestingly, the sales for that first year – 983 copies. A later revised edition in the 1950s sold more copies and received more favorable reviews.
Both Cowley and Harry Crosby were friends with the poet Hart Crane (Unfortunately I find Crane’s poetry all but unreadable.); in 1929, Cowley’s first wife Peggy ran off with Crane, three years later Crane also committed suicide.
In 1943, while working for Viking Publishers, Cowley developed the Viking Portable Library, a series of inexpensive paperback anthologies devoted either to one writer or to a genre – essays, poems, etc. He first edited a volume devoted to Hemingway and combined stories and bleeding chunks of novels with critical commentary and historic context.
An even more momentous Portable Library anthology came out in 1944 on William Faulkner whose fame had been declining and his novels – Light in August; As I Lay Dying; and The Sound and the Fury, etc. – going out of print.
Cowley’s advocacy and appreciation of Faulkner’s literary genius jump-started that Southerner’s career, leading to the 1950 Nobel Prize for literature.
In 1969, Malcolm Cowley lectured at Colby College on Maine’s own great original, Gardner poet Edwin Arlington Robinson. Unfortunately, according to an acquaintance of those years, Richard Cary – who was curator of Colby’s rare books collection and a professor of American literature – Cowley mainly focused on Robinson’s drinking.
The Closer
In watching the two very captivating TV series, The Closer with Kyra Sedgwick and its successor Major Crimes, starring Mary McDonnell, I have found G.W. Bailey’s Lieutenant Provenza increasingly stealing the show – one particularly snippy comment is Provenza referring to an ignorant smug investigator as “Detective Cheech!”, along with various very subtle facial expressions.
Beethoven’s 9th Symphony
Highly recommended is the YouTube of Leonard Bernstein’s 1964 New York Philharmonic recording of Beethoven’s 9th Symphony. I own shelves of 9ths and could recommend easily 25 other recordings and broadcasts for their own individual approach.
Listening today (September 26, 2026) to Bernstein conducting it, I was bowled over by the sweeping intensity, his sense of buildup from the first to last bar and the supreme reverence in both the singing and playing.
The Ode to Joy designation of the last movement with its choir and soloists would truly describe the first three movements.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Maine must review offshore wind alternatives now
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Sept. 22 WMTW report on Maine’s lawsuit challenging the U.S. Department of the Interior’s buyout termination of Gulf of Maine offshore wind leases read: “The lawsuit argues that the cancellations could negatively impact Maine’s plans for future offshore wind development and other renewable energy goals.”
So, just what are Maine’s plans for future offshore wind development? Now is exactly the right time to explore that question.
Previous to the Trump administration holding offshore wind hostage, Maine announced plans to develop an offshore wind manufacturing, assembling and launching facility on Sears Island. Those plans failed to adequately consider a number of other, viable options and failed to generate sufficient funding.
During today’s offshore wind pause — even as Clearway Energy pursues an 800-megawatt onshore wind project in Aroostook County — Maine needs to consider the least environmentally damaging and most economically beneficial offshore wind development strategy.
Developing two currently industrialized ports for offshore wind that would coordinate manufacturing, assembly and launching, a strategy used elsewhere and for the Aqua Ventus quarter-scale turbine now operating near Castine, almost certainly would reduce environmental harm, save costs and spread development’s fiscal benefits across a greater segment of the Maine coast than the previously failed offshore plan.
Climate change poses a clear and present threat to Maine’s future. Clean, renewable energy production helps reduce climate change impacts. Prudence points to further research now into whether offshore wind can be part of Maine’s adaptation.
Steve Miller
Islesboro

title: 3 high school football games to watch in Week 5
text:
This season, Varsity Maine reporters will offer up suggestions each week for three games that are worth a drive to watch in person, with a brief explanation of why we think these games are worth a fan’s time.
Portland (4-0) at Thornton Academy (4-0), 1 p.m. Saturday
The midway point of the season features a rematch of last year’s Class A championship game, which Thornton won, 28-0. In fact, these two teams have played in the past three Class A title games, with Thornton holding a 2-1 advantage. The Trojans, to no one’s surprise, are chugging along again in Class A South, scoring 45.5 points per game while allowing only seven per game. Quarterback Noah Fullerton has done well spreading the ball to multiple playmakers, like Quinn Cook and Logan LeBlanc. The defense, meanwhile, has two shutouts in the first four games.
Portland has answered any questions about potential growing pains under new head coach Dylan Rottkov. Even after the graduation of the program’s all-time scoring leader, Cordell Jones, the Bulldogs are averaging 34.8 points, featuring a rushing attack led by senior Alex Martin and sophomore David Gomes. The pair combined for over 300 yards in a 39-13 win over Windham on Sept. 18. Saturday’s game could be another a Class A final preview.
Cony (4-0) at Lawrence (4-0), 7 p.m. Friday
It’s air vs. ground in this rivalry matchup at Keyes Field in Fairfield, and the winner will earn a firm grasp on the No. 1 spot in the Class B North Crabtree standings.
Coach B.L. Lippert’s air attack offense is once again on display for Cony, which has averaged 30.5 points in the first four games. Junior quarterback Drew Lindquist (599 passing yards, 7 touchdown passes, 1 interception) has done well leading the offense in his first season as the starter, equally spreading the ball to seniors Landen Perry (14 receptions, 243 yards, 3 TDs) and Da’Marion Raymond (12 receptions, 139 yards, 2 TDs).
The Bulldogs are off to a hot start behind new head coach Pete Curtis. Nothing has changed in the offensive approach, as Lawrence has ridden its ground-and-pound attack to a 4-0 record. Keegan Littlefield (52 carries, 494 yards, 4 TDs), a senior, leads that attack, along with junior Jaiden Hebert (52 carries, 298 yards, 5 TDs) and senior Hunter Curtis (18 carries, 119 yards, 2 TDs).
This is always one of the best back-and-forth rivalries in central Maine. The Bulldogs knocked Cony out of the playoffs in 2023 (B North final) and 2024 (B North semifinal), and Cony beat Lawrence 46-14 during the regular season last year.
Morse (3-1) at Freeport (3-1), 6 p.m. Friday
Halfway into the season, there’s a three-way battle at the top of the Class D South Crabtree standings, and it includes these two Midcoast schools. After reaching the regional final last season, Morse has steamed on in its first four games, with wins over Mountain Valley, Dirigo and Lisbon. Quarterback Dylan Root has been Morse’s biggest weapon, making plays with his arm and his feet.
Freeport jumped out to a 3-0 start, including a 29-28 win over defending state champion Winthrop on Sept. 11, before falling 14-6 to defending North champion Winslow last week. Quarterback Andrew Thomas has been Freeport’s most consistent offensive threat. He rushed for 151 yards and a touchdown against Winthrop.

title: Nearly 684,000-pound load is taking longer than expected to reach Maine coast
text:
The “super oversize” load crawling across Maine will take longer than expected to reach the Maine coast.
The nearly 684,000-pound load, which departed Tuesday evening from Jay, was originally expected to reach Turner Island in South Portland on Wednesday night, according to the Maine State Police.
Now it’s not expected to reach its destination until next Tuesday.
That’s because the load didn’t reach Jumper Bridge in Turner in time, the state police said Wednesday.
The load is a heat recovery steam generator from the former Androscoggin Mill on Riley Road, according to the Sun Journal.
The load is 20 feet wide, more than 19 feet tall and 219 feet long, requiring it to take up most of the road as it slowly makes its way south.
It will resume the journey Wednesday night, traveling from Turner to Oxford. Then on Thursday night, it will travel to Gray, where it will remain until Sunday night before slouching toward Buxton. The convoy will complete its journey into South Portland Monday night into Tuesday morning.
Its ultimate destination, Turner Island in South Portland, is the location of a shipping company and gas terminal.

title: 2 killed, 1 injured after man allegedly shoots 3 coworkers at United Rentals, police say
text:
AUGUSTA COUNTY, Va. (WHSV/Gray News) - A man in Virginia is accused of killing two of his coworkers at United Rentals.
Marvin Grant, 37, was wanted for a shooting in Manassas City that was reported at 7:11 a.m. Wednesday.
Manassas City Police Department said Grant shot his coworkers at United Rentals around 7 a.m., then left the scene.
Police said Ricky Lamont, 48, and Christopher Serrano, 33, were both taken to the hospital but later died. The third victim remains in the hospital.
A Virginia State Police trooper saw Grant’s vehicle on southbound Interstate 81 in Augusta County before Grant pulled into the rest area at mile marker 232.
Troopers attempted a traffic stop. Grant then exited the vehicle, got back inside, and continued driving, prompting a pursuit.
Grant pulled over at mile marker 227 and exited the car with a firearm pointed at his head.
Police said Grant shot himself and was taken to a hospital, where he died.
Virginia State Police say troopers did not use force during the incident, which remains under investigation.

title: Rick Bennett can help unify a house divided
text:
“A house divided against itself cannot stand.”
In these times of division and danger, Abraham Lincoln’s prophetic words still ring true today. Our democracy cannot stand without an informed, aroused, consensus-seeking voting public.
The current level of public conversation is a petty, mindless, toxic gabble: polls, personal scandals, campaign strategies, money raised for campaign war chests. But in Maine’s current political race, I know of one candidate who persistently strives to raise the level of public conversation to: issues, policies, political platforms, voting records.
I know of one candidate who has consistently sought mutual understanding, consensus and bipartisan collaboration. I know of one candidate whose statecraft, long service in our state Senate and persistent voice of sense and sanity entitle him to stand in Lincoln’s long shadow.
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, please join me in voting for Richard Bennett, independent candidate for the governorship of Maine.
Steve Turner
Mechanic Falls

title: Man accused of exposing himself to children on a school bus twice in one week
text:
TOWN OF WATERTOWN, N.Y. (WWNY/Gray News) - A man is accused of exposing himself to children on a school bus twice in one week
Daniel Iles, 32, is charged with two counts of public lewdness and two counts of child endangerment, according to the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office.
Iles allegedly exposed his genitals while driving next to a school bus on Interstate 81 in Town of Watertown, New York. A 16-year-old student reported seeing the man fondling himself, according to officials.
A week later on Sept. 22, Iles allegedly exposed himself again while driving next to a school bus, also on Interstate 81 in the Town of Watertown, New York. A 16-year-old student reported the incident and officials said they were unsure whether the same student witnessed both incidents.
School resource officers reviewed video from the buses’ surveillance cameras that confirmed the reported incidents.
The cameras captured the license plate number, which led to Iles’ arrest.
Iles was arraigned on the charges and released.

title: Camden Hills girls soccer is team to beat in Class A North
text:
Not too long ago, the Camden Hills High School girls soccer team from Rockport set a state record by stringing together a 71-game unbeaten streak. From 2017 to 2021, the Windjammers went 70-0-1 before finally losing, 1-0, to rival Bangor.
They won four consecutive state Class A championships between 2016-19.
They have continued to be contenders, but Bangor has been a thorn in their sides, beating them in the Class A North championship game the past three seasons.
Camden Hills also reached the title game in 2022 only to lose to Brunswick 5-1.
Head coach Meredith Messer’s Windjammers have firmly established themselves as the team to beat in Class A North this fall with a 7-0 record that includes an 8-0 victory over Bangor and a 10-1 win over Brunswick.
Camden Hills has outscored its opponents 56-2.
And the future is bright as there are only two seniors on the roster and just one of them starts.
“The core group played together last year and played together for their club team in the offseason,” Messer said. “They have gotten to know each other better. They are a year older and a year stronger.”
Messer said her team is “firing on all cylinders” and has a strong culture.
“They like playing with each other and are super supportive of each other. They could care less who scores the goals. They want to execute and have fun,” Messer said.
The Windjammers feature one of the state’s best and most dynamic players in striker/attacking midfielder Molly Williams.
Williams was an All-Northern Maine State Team selection a year ago, as well as an All-Northern Maine Class A Regional choice.
Williams, a junior, is closing in on 100 career goals and is around the 20 mark this season, according to Messer.
But what makes Camden Hills so potent is its scoring depth.
Messer said if opponents key on Williams with double and triple-teams, “we have so many other people who can score.”
Strikers freshman Remi Caton and junior Eve Domareki are both around the 10-goal mark and sophomore Elsa Schwalm has three goals and a healthy bunch of assists, Messer said.
Domareki’s sister, sophomore midfielder Liv Domareki, supplies the Windjammers with a long-distance threat and senior striker Thea Laukka has picked up several assists with her crosses into the penalty area.
Liv Domareki, a Northern Maine Class A Regional All-Star team selection a year ago, and sophomore Cate Middleton are solid mainstays in the midfield and nicely complement Williams when she is in the number 10 role (attacking midfielder).
The back line is stellar with junior Maia Andrews and sophomore Nathalie Nelson in the middle and freshman Colette Nowak and junior Maggie McCarthy on the outside.
Sophomores Eliza Gallant and Charley Hall share the goalkeeping chores.
“They’re both getting the experience that they need,” said Messer, who felt her 2025 team “overachieved” by getting to the Class A North final where it was beaten by Bangor, 4-1.
Bangor would go on to win its second straight state title.
Messer’s Windjammers will travel to Bangor to play the Rams on Oct. 17, and she said “I expect them to give us a good match. I’m looking forward to that.”
The Rams have lost All-Americans and prolific scorers Clara Oldenburg and Georgie Stephenson to graduation and a Connecticut prep school, respectively, and influential midfielder Gabby Gordon has been lost for the season due to injury.
She pointed out that both Bangor and Brunswick have first-year coaches in Nick Christensen and Jimmy Pelletier, respectively, and it takes teams a while to adapt to their new coaches’ “philosophy, formations and style of play.”
Camden Hills will play again at 7 p.m. Thursday when the team travels to Lewiston.

title: Relief as nor'easter misses Mount Desert Island
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — Last week, residents around MDI prepared for a potential nor’easter to slam into the island. Luckily, a high-pressure system kept the winds and waves farther south, and the storm barely grazed the island.
But, as the storm approached land, members of the United States Coast Guard were gearing up to make sure mariners around the island had someone to call in case of an emergency.
On Sept. 24, as harbors around the island were slowly emptying, dinghies were coming out, and people were preparing for a storm that was slowly creeping up the east coast and was expected to form a nor’easter to much of New England.
Jake Shelters, USCG Station Southwest’s Officer in Charge, noted that the storm dissipated before reaching MDI.
“New Jersey, New York, and maybe New Hampshire and southern Maine experienced something much, much bigger, and the storm was supposed to move up the coast, and we were supposed to receive it Saturday-Sunday time frame,” Shelters said.
That wasn’t the case, though, as the storm lost all its steam before reaching MDI. It did, however, deliver almost 24 hours of rain and wind.
“I’m no meteorologist, but I know there was a good high-pressure system that stuck right on our coast and fended us off for most of it,” said Shelters. “So that storm was supposed to sweep right up here, but instead lingered south of us until it petered out, and we kind of just got the tail end of it.”
Despite all the prep from mariners, island residents, and emergency services, the storm produced only 20-30 mph winds and 7-8 foot waves. At the USCG Station Southwest Harbor, this is a double-edged sword. During these big storms, there’s an opportunity to train and get out in big water, but the downside is that these storms can also wreak havoc on mariners and create situations the USCG needs to help with.
Shelters said “Mariners around here are pretty smart, most people on the water are pretty prudent and avoid being out there in a storm.
“We were out there every day trying to find some good seas,” he continued, explaining that, during these storms, the Coast Guard takes time to practice towing and other rescues that might come about in bad weather. “Nothing too big out there. Well, we were hoping for a little bigger to knock the dust off and get some good training.”
This storm did not call for any rescues or the assistance of the Coast Guard, according to Shelters, though he added that Station Southwest is always ready and training. “Whenever a storm comes through, we’ll go out and do a myriad of drills with two boats going back and forth, and that’s really it, you know, just taking advantage of that, those seas, to prepare the crews and get everybody operating,” he said.
“We’ll still push out there, and the crew’s really focused on training to pick up a disabled boat, put it in tow, and get it back to the harbor. Or even picking up persons in the water if that’s the case. So they’re training for every scenario they might face. Passing the pump, we call it, or taking that dewatering pump and passing it from one boat to another.”
Shelters offered advice for future storms that could help save Coast Guard resources and allow them to return lost dinghies and gear to mariners. He explained that if a report of a dinghy or paddleboard comes in, they have to treat it as if someone was on that vessel until they can confirm otherwise.
“We’ll be out searching for quite a while, and it’s taking us away from potentially other emergencies,” said Shelters. “If it’s a big storm and it’s probably pretty apparent that something was blown from shore or dock, we still have to treat it as if someone is in the water until we can prove that that’s not the case, and that timeline to do that can be drastically reduced if we pick it up and there’s a phone number we can call,” he explained.
Shelters urged people to make sure their dinghies or small boats, including paddleboards, are secured before a storm, and to label them in some manner. The Coast Guard offers stickers to put on smaller vessels that aren’t registered, or even gear that blows away. Shelters said, at a minimum, to put on contact info somewhere with a Sharpie so they can call and confirm everyone is ok and not in the water.

title: Letter to the Editor: A Different Time
Inside the 2026 Pemaquid Oyster Festival
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mine Oyster Raw Bar & Gathering Place hosted the 23rd Pemaquid Oyster Festival in Boothbay Harbor, Sept. 26-27, featuring freshly shucked oysters of the Damariscotta River region. Event-goers sampled oysters from The Pemaquid Oyster Company, Mook Sea Farm, Norumbega Oyster Inc., Dodge Cove Marine Farm, Glidden Point Oyster Farms, Blackstone Point Oysters, Pleasant Cove Oyster Farm, Heron Island Oyster Company, Great Salt Bay Oyster Co. and Carlisle Oyster Farm. The festival is an annual fundraiser for the Edward A. Myers Marine Conservation Fund, which has awarded over $250,000 through grants and scholarships to Lincoln County non-profit groups that work in marine conservation and education. A tribute table to Myers, featuring his work boots, served as an homage to the South Bristol resident, shellfish farmer and mentor to many of the river's early oyster growers.
A kick-off dinner, the Oyster & Wine Extravaganza, offered a six-course, oyster-forward dinner paired with wines from this year's featured sommelier, Sierra Fahrman of Browne Trading Market in Portland. Mine Oyster Chef Ralph Smith designed the menu.
The weather seemed to deter few from attending the festival, though the oyster shucking contest was smaller than in past years. This year, shuckers Andy Rogers (defending champion) of Jolie Rogers Raw Bar in Wiscasset and up-and-comer Firat Kozan of Yeti Boys Food Truck faced off for a $500 prize from sponsor First National Bank, presented by Alyssa Allen. Virginia Shaffer judged the competition. Rogers won, defending his title for the third time, and securing an opportunity to advance to the 60th annual U.S. National Oyster Shucking Championship in Maryland. Rogers has attended the national competition several times, placing fifth in 2025. As well, Rogers placed second in an international competition earlier this year on Prince Edward Island.
Live music, across two stages, included the Hadacol Bouncers, the Liz Lannon Blues Band, the Old Blues Kats, Primo Cubano, and the Oystermen.
The exhibit tent moved inside this year due to weather. Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences, Boothbay Sea and Science Center (BSSC), Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust, Maine Aquaculture Innovation Center and many local artists displayed educational materials and paintings, prints, decor, ceramics and more. A silent auction, both online and in-person, concluded at the festival's end.
Proceeds from the festival targeted seven regional initiatives to support in 2025. Boothbay Region Land Trust and Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust were awarded funds for water quality sampling and monitoring. Lincoln Academy, South Bristol School, Great Salt Bay School and BSSC were awarded grants for marine education. Carpenter's Boat Shop in Bristol also received funds. Municipalities were also granted funds for pump stations, and some search and rescue teams were gifted GPS navigational equipment. The Fish Ladder Project, several fire stations, Maine Aquaculture Association, and many more were listed as prior grant recipients.

title: Cloudy but warm this afternoon
text:
Cloudy but warm this afternoon
Cloudy but warm this afternoon
Wednesday will be mostly cloudy, but a few rays of sunshine are possible in the evening. Temperatures today will be close to 70 degrees, which is slightly warmer than what we would normally expect. Tonight will be mild with temperatures in the low 50s, and patchy fog is possible.
Thursday will feature more sunshine with partly cloudy conditions. Temperatures will start to ramp up, leading to a warm few days in the mid to upper 70s on Thursday and Friday. A few locations might get as high as 80, making for a warm way to start October.
A cold front will move through on Friday, which could bring rain chances and a few rumbles of thunder along with it. Showers will first arrive in mountain areas in the morning and push towards the coast by the evening. The cold front will also drop our high temperatures back into the mid 60s for the weekend.

title: Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness highlights painful historic trauma with 'Orange Shirt Day'
TSA officers no longer allowed to sit during ID checks, union says
text:
(CNN) — A union representing Transportation Security Administration officers said workers who check boarding passes and IDs will no longer be able to sit down while doing their job.
The TSA is removing all chairs at the check-in site, according to a branch of the American Federation of Government Employees union. Workers will now have to stand during their shifts.
The union said the chairs provide support for officers, and forcing them to stand all day goes against safety and common decency.
The policy change comes nearly two months after David Cummins took over as TSA administrator.

title: ‘Taking Care of Granny’: Hear this caregiver’s story of dementia, dignity and finding help
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of The Aging Untold Podcast, Dugan Meredith, who documents caring for his mother-in-law online through the “Taking Care of Granny” social media feeds, joins us to talk about what it’s really like to become a caregiver and how his family found their way through it.
Caring for an aging loved one can reshape a family, and it’s a responsibility more men are shouldering than ever before.
Watch the full podcast episode:
Today, an estimated 21 million men are in caregiving roles, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. They are navigating the daily challenges of aging and illness alongside their own jobs and children.
Meredith’s mother-in-law, known online as Granny, was originally living with her oldest daughter in the Charleston, South Carolina, area. Meredith described the signs that led the family to seek a diagnosis.
“She was experiencing symptoms, showing signs, forgetting how to go pick up the grandchildren from school, getting lost,” Meredith said. “Talking to random strangers and inviting them back to the house.”
The turning point came when Granny tried to cook soup by putting it in a baking pan in the oven instead of putting it in a pot and placing it on the stove. Granny was later diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia, also known as FTD.
Dividing caregiving duties wasn’t planned — it just happened
When Granny moved in with Meredith and his wife, there wasn’t a formal plan for who would do what.
“I think it was decided for us,” Meredith said. The family originally intended to split time with another sister-in-law, but when she had to return to full-time work, “the responsibility fell squarely on our shoulders,” Meredith said.
For a time, Meredith’s wife took Granny to work with her during the day and Dugan took over caregiving duties in the evenings. Eventually, his wife’s employer could no longer accommodate the arrangement, prompting the family to hire outside help.
Learning to ‘meet her where she’s at’
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, asked Meredith to reflect on his experience as a man stepping into a caregiving role that required hiring help rather than “fixing” the problem himself.
“Granny coming to live with us was a struggle for me mentally,” Meredith said. “I was exhausted because I could not figure out why I could not get a 72-, 73-year-old woman to understand, you can’t do this — it will hurt you.”
Meredith described one moment when Granny wanted to cut her hair and used a lighter to try to burn off a piece of it after he took away her scissors and said they would take her to get her hair cut.
“I could not understand in my mind, why does this woman do this? Why can I not get her to understand she’s going to hurt herself?” he said.
Meredith said he came to the realization that he needed to meet Granny where she is.
“Sam taught me that very early on,” Meredith said, referring to Aging Untold expert and gerontologist Sam Cradduck. “You have to meet them where they are.”
Meredith emphasized that lesson for other men in a similar situation.
“For men out there, you’re not going to fix it. The only thing you can do to help the situation is to swallow your pride, swallow your ego and learn to meet them where they’re at,” Meredith said.
Decoding Granny’s signature word: ‘heavy’
Viewers of Meredith’s videos on TikTok and Facebook are familiar with Granny’s repeated word, “heavy.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, asked how the family figures out what she means.
“What is she trying to tell me? Is her stomach hurt? Is her food cold? Is her food too hot?” Meredith said. “When she says ‘my heavy is heavy,’ I keep reiterating, and eventually she’ll move a certain way, she’ll do something with her hands, she’ll nod with her head, and we’ll figure it out.”
Meredith said much of the communication comes down to body language and behaviors learned from living with Granny every day.
Why Meredith started sharing the journey online
Meredith said the decision to document his caregiving journey online came from feeling isolated.
“I felt like I was alone. I felt like nobody in the world understood what was going on within my mind and in my heart,” Meredith said.
He recalled sitting at his kitchen table with a cup of coffee, recording himself talking about his frustrations before posting the video to TikTok. That post led him to a community of other caregivers he didn’t know existed.
Meredith said he’s still learning to manage the volume of response, including tens of thousands of messages and comments.
“You go through a whirlwind of emotions just reading the comments or the messages that come in,” he said.
Meredith said the online community has helped his family tremendously.
“For every one negative person, there’s 500 positives,” he said, and people in that community provide tips, which Meredith uses.
“Not only are they helping us, but they are helping the others that are reading the comments,” Meredith said.
The ‘sandwich generation’ and the cost of care
O’Rourke noted that Meredith and his wife are also raising children while caring for Granny — a dynamic often called the “sandwich generation.”
“We are 100% the sandwich generation,” Meredith said.
In the beginning, he said, the couple struggled to give their children enough attention because of the protocols required to care for Granny. Hiring additional caregivers allowed them “to still be parents for our children and give them the attention that they need and that they deserve as well.”
Meredith also spoke about the cost of care. The family looked into memory care facilities before deciding on the private route, which he described as the more affordable option.
“You go look at nice memory care facilities — we’re talking $10,000 to $15,000 a month,” Meredith said.
He said monetizing the family’s social media content has helped cover the cost of keeping Granny comfortable at home.
“Everyone always asks, are you going to keep her here until her last breath. We will,” Meredith said.
Meredith is also the founder of a nonprofit, also called Taking Care of Granny, which he said is focused solely on helping caregivers.
He said the idea for a nonprofit came from a conversation with another caregiver who documents caring for his wife, who has Parkinson’s disease.
“He was the one that started the idea with me. He was like, ‘What about a nonprofit? You do a nonprofit to provide care to the caregivers,’” Meredith said. “I was like, I like that idea. I don’t know how I’m going to do it, but let me start digging into it.”
Where things stand today
Asked how Granny is doing now, Meredith said the disease has progressed. The family now purees her food because of trouble swallowing, and he’s noticed her shuffling her feet while walking, so the family has removed rugs and other trip hazards from the house.
Hospice has also brought in a medical bed to help prevent falls.
“The disease has progressed, and we’re at that point now,” Meredith said. “But given what we’ve been through, I would say she’s doing well.”
See the full interview with Dugan Meredith
How to follow Taking Care of Granny
Key takeaways
- Male caregiving. An estimated 21 million men are currently in caregiving roles for aging or ill loved ones, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving.
- Meet them where they are. Dugan Meredith emphasized that trying to reason with a loved one with dementia rarely works. Caregivers need to adapt to the person’s reality instead.
- The “sandwich generation” faces unique pressure. Balancing young children and an aging parent or relative at the same time requires intentional systems so neither gets neglected.
- Online communities can ease caregiver isolation. Sharing the caregiving journey publicly connected Meredith with a wider community of caregivers facing similar experiences.

title: Norway tax revaluation sparks petition to recall elected officials
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
At least 50 Norway residents attending a special Select Board meeting Sept. 29 learned that the board could not legally alter or delay implementation of the town’s recently completed tax revaluation.
By the end of the meeting, most of them threw their support behind a resident’s petition for an elected official recall ordinance.
The petition is being led by Matt Glatz, the owner of a multiunit home who said its value increased by 200% as a result of the revaluation.
Glatz has become a vocal critic of the revaluation process, which he and other residents said was rushed and mistake-ridden, and is a conflict of interest for Norway’s sworn tax assessor.
Glatz had filed a request at the Town Office in September to have the Select Board draft and pass an ordinance allowing residents to petition to recall elected officials.
As he explained to property owners after Monday’s meeting adjourned, the Select Board has up to six months before taking any action on his request.
But if a petition signed by at least 300 voters is presented to the town, the board is required to publicly acknowledge the matter and schedule a vote at either a special or annual town meeting.
Most of the people lingering after the meeting indicated they would sign such a petition. Glatz said he will have it available Nov. 3 at the fire department and polling place during federal and state elections.
At the start of Monday’s meeting, the Select Board voted to enter executive session for consultation with its attorney, as allowed by state law.
The meeting agenda stated after the executive session the board would discuss and vote on the 2026 tax commitment.
However, when the executive session ended Chair Sarah Carter announced there would be no discussion or vote. She read the following statement, made on behalf of the five-member board:
“The Select Board understands the concerns raised by members of the public regarding the recent revaluation,” Carter said. “After conferring with the town attorney, however, the board understands that it does not have the legal authority to interfere with the assessor’s valuation determination.
“Therefore, there will be no discussion and vote this evening. In an effort to address the concerns of the public, the town is drafting an FAQ (frequently asked questions sheet) which will be made public as soon as possible.”
Carter encouraged any residents who feel their revaluations were done incorrectly to follow the proper abatement appeal process according to state law, and to contact town assessor John O’Donnell with additional questions.
About 1,000 property owners in town will see a tax decreases as a result of the revaluation. But values and tax payments are increasing for more than 3,400, many significantly.
Town Manager Jill Lathan said O’Donnell is expected to commit property taxes by Oct. 1. She anticipates tax bills will be mailed by mid-October.
O’Donnell has become a touchpoint for residents upset with their revaluations. He became Norway’s tax assessor in a stipend position three years ago and is a sworn town official.
The town contracted with his appraisal business, John E. O’Donnell & Associates, to conduct its revaluation.
Town officials and residents are in agreement that a revaluation is long overdue, having been last conducted 19 years ago.
Glatz, and others, allege that his company’s staff cut corners during the reevaluation, misrepresenting building uses, failing to measure structures and incorrectly assigning condition grades and comparative properties to determine values, among other issues.
Property owners have the burden of individually researching discrepancies and state appraisal standards to challenge a private business owner who also has the power as a sworn town official to acknowledge or deny their disputes.
“John O’Donnell is the jury, judge and executioner,” Glatz and others have said during several Select Board meetings and interviews with the Advertiser Democrat.
While a crowd waited in the Town Office conference room and traded anecdotes, one resident said the 200-year-old home he purchased for $240,000 is valued at $900,000.
Another owner of an older home told him that factors impacting his valuation could include age, condition and foundation condition. He said his house has no foundation. Others urged him to review his property card and request an abatement.

title: Death Notice: Jayson J. E. Carver
Kingfield to hold election for vacant Select Board seat
text:
Kingfield residents will elect a new member to the Select Board in December.
Following the resignation of Hunter Lander in August, the board voted Sept. 21 to hold a special election Dec. 8 to fill the vacant seat. The board has been operating with four members since.
This was the second meeting in a row where the vacancy was debated. At a Sept. 8 meeting, after discussing the challenges that a four-person board could have in getting business done, opinions were split over whether to hold a special election or wait until the annual town meeting in June, causing the discussion to be tabled until Sept. 21.
Board member Kim Jordan said the town could not wait until June to fill the seat. That option would risk splitting votes on a number of important decisions.
“I think in our last meeting that we had, we had two tie votes, and we didn’t get anywhere with those discussions,” Jordan said. She said the town “voted for us to have a five-member board for that very reason.
“We’ve got some pretty serious stuff that’s coming up in front of us with the Bowdoin College thing, the school withdrawal,” she added. “I mean, we can’t keep having tied votes.”
Morgan Dunham, chairman of the board, noted the learning curve for a new member and expressed hesitance about filling the seat immediately.
“To have a new person come on the board,” Dunham said. “It takes us back a couple of steps. Just explaining everything and someone learning something new. It’s a little bit frustrating.”
Jordan explained that the new member will need to get trained regardless of when they are elected. She said that at least two community members have expressed interest in running for the position.
A motion to set the election date almost didn’t pass. Jordan and Christopher Rushton voted in favor of the motion. Dunham initially voted against but changed her vote to pass the motion. David Davol did not vote.

title: A $450M art collection is poised to break Van Gogh and Cézanne’s auction records
text:
A $450M art collection is poised to break Van Gogh and Cézanne’s auction records
In New York this fall, Sotheby’s will put up for auction a rare Vincent van Gogh painting, not seen for half a century, which it expects will sell for a staggering $180 million and set a new auction record.
Related video: A painting bought for $30 at an estate sale may soon sell at auction for up to $250,000
That would normally be enough buzz for a marquee November evening sale — but there’s more. The auction house will also follow it up with a rare Paul Cézanne painting (also not seen for the last five decades), that it has estimated “in the region” of $120 million and hope will set a second record for the night.
The two masterworks have both been held by the same family since the 1970s — and will sell alongside ten of their other collected artworks including a Monet and a Renoir, that together, Sotheby’s is promoting as the “El Dorado” of private art collections. If all goes as planned, the auction house will clean up $450 million (or more) in less than an hour.
“It’s one of the greatest remaining collections of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art in private hands,” said Helena Newman, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, who also referred to the group of artworks as “a mini Musée d’Orsay.”
“It had this legendary, mythical status as one of the greats,” she said. “But now there is the reveal, and people will get the chance to see what it comprises.”
Philip Hook, a former senior director at Sotheby’s said the mystery of the collection was a “constant” throughout his career.
“What was in it? How good was it? The thing was, no one really knew,” Hook told journalists at a press view in London on Wednesday morning. One reason was because the Blaquier-Arrieta family never lent the pictures to museums, he said. The other was because they were based in Argentina. “This seemed a very, very long way away” in the ‘90s and noughties, he continued.
The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, owned by the late Argentinian businessman Carlos Pedro Blaquier and the art patron Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, is the latest mega-collector sell-off that the art market has relied on for the past few seasons to buoy its sales. It follows the collections of media magnate SI Newhouse, Microsoft founder Paul G Allen, socialite and art patron Pauline Karpidas, and Estée Lauder heir Leonard A. Lauder — the last of which included the $236 million Klimt that became the second-most expensive work of art to ever sell at auction.
The lots are being sold by the children of the Blaquier-Arrieta family after Nelly’s death in 2020 and Carlos’ in 2023. Blaquier was president of a sugar mill, and Nelly served on international committees for major museums, and guided their collection. They were one of the most powerful families in Argentina. But for the last decade of Blaquier’s life, he was investigated for crimes against humanity, for allegedly detaining activists during the Argentina’s brutal military dictatorship from 1976-83, which the BBC reported that he denied. He never stood trial before his death, according to his obituary in La Nacion. A spokesperson for Sothebys said that he was never convicted and always maintained his innocence.
While the upcoming sale will take place in New York, the works were unveiled together for the first time in London on Wednesday morning. That’s where the Blaquiers procured much of their collection, traveling during the summer months to purchase directly from Lefevre Gallery, a major player in Impressionist and Modern art until its closure at the turn of the 21st century.
If both top lots set new records, it will be the second time both artist’s records have been broken in the same night, as part of the same collection. Christie’s historic 2022 sale of Paul Allen’s works led to the $117 million sale of Van Gogh’s landscape “Verger avec cyprès” and $137.7 million sale of Cézanne’s mountain scene “La Montagne Sainte-Victoire,” both painted in 1888.
This Van Gogh painting, titled “Chataignier en fleurs roses et blanches,” which was not on show in London but instead on its way to Hong Kong where it will be displayed ahead of the auction later this year, was made in the last two months of the artist’s life in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise.
Van Gogh had only just been released from the psychiatric facility in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he’d voluntarily admitted himself for a year, and Sotheby’s notes the “vigor” and “optimism” of the period.
“It’s an amazing, exuberant palette,” Newman said, noting that there’s only a “handful” of works still out there from the end of the artist’s life. Several hang in the Musée d’Orsay, including one of his portraits of the physician who treated him, Doctor Paul Gachet.
The neighboring Cézanne work, “Arlequin,” a vibrant color-clashing work that took centerstage in Sotheby’s London gallery on Wednesday morning, is from a set of four Harlequin paintings, and is the only one not held by a museum, the press release noted. It passed through the hands of important French art dealers Ambroise Vollard, Paul Durand-Ruel and Paul Rosenberg, and exhibited in seminal Cézanne exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Tate in London and the Art Institute of Chicago before it was eventually sold to the Blaquier family in 1975.
Now, their collection is being marketed as one of the last great tranches of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art — a period of art that has become a safety net during economic turbulence. How the health of the art market at its highest end will fare as these collections dwindle remains to be seen. Newman acknowledged that it is a generational shift as collections that formed from the 1960s-80s come to market now as their owners age and pass.
For the — very few — collectors in the world who can afford their own museum-worthy collection, Newman says this is a rare opportunity. “It’s a moment for those collectors, both established and new, to be competing, and that will be very interesting for us all to see.”

text:
'Light of our lives': Actor Chad Lowe mourns death of 13-year-old daughter
Actor Chad Lowe and producer Kim Painter's 13-year-old daughter, Fiona Hepler Lowe, has died, according to media reports.
The couple announced their daughter's death on Tuesday in a statement to People magazine, saying, "We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona." The family said Fiona was smart, creative and loved to dance.
"She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents," the family said. "In fact, she was the light of our lives."
In the statement, the family also shared the national suicide and crisis helpline. "Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time. If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988."
Fiona was born on Nov. 16, 2012. Lowe and Painter share two other daughters together, 17-year-old Mabel Painter Lowe and 10-year-old Nixie Barbara Lowe.
Lowe, the younger brother of actor Rob Lowe, won an Emmy Award for his supporting role in "Life Goes On" as a young man living with HIV.
This story contains discussion of suicide. Help is available if you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters. Call or text 988 for help.

title: Gavin P. Martin Foundation donates $2,500 to Edgecomb Fire Dept.
text:
Gavin Martin lived a short, but remarkable life. Martin worked as a volunteer fireman in two communities. He began his public service in his hometown of Verona, New Jersey and later served in Edgecomb.
Shortly after his death in December 2025 at age 21, his family set up the Gavin P. Martin Foundation which benefits local fire departments. A board of directors was set up and, with a sponsorship from the Verona Local Policemen’s Benevolent Association No. 72, the foundation was established.
The fundraiser collected donations and sponsorships resulting into the contribution into the foundation.
According to its website, the Gavin P. Martin Foundation transforms compassion into action by supporting community-based initiatives that embody service, entrepreneurship and dedication. “We honor Gavin's legacy by investing in young and old alike, empowering service organizations, fostering entrepreneurial spirit, advancing vocational training, and strengthening civic engagement,” the website reads.

title: Kids pick up money habits earlier than parents realize, expert says
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Children begin picking up on money habits much earlier than most parents realize, according to Teresa Murray, a consumer watchdog with US PIRG.
“We may think sometimes that our children aren’t paying attention to us when they’re three or four years old — oh no, kids are smart, and they learn from us,” Murray said. “And some of that happens really early.”
Murray said a parent’s financial behavior often becomes a child’s first money lesson, whether intentional or not.
“If they see their parents making careless or irresponsible choices, then they will probably learn that behavior very quickly,” Murray said.
Murray recommends using real situations, like birthday money, to teach kids how to think ahead about spending.
“Say a kid got $100 total in birthday money from grandparents and aunts and uncles and stuff — go and sit down with the kid and say, ‘Hey, what are you going to do with that money?’” Murray said. “I mean, their eyes are going to glaze over the math, but you need to teach kids how to think ahead with their money.”
Murray said parents can also share their own financial priorities with children in simple, age-appropriate terms.
“It doesn’t even hurt to share that with the kids a little bit — like, don’t lay it on heavy, don’t depress them,” Murray said. “But it’s like, yeah, we were planning on getting new furniture for the deck, but gosh, our refrigerator broke, so now we have to wait. Model that kind of behavior, model that kind of language. Kids are smart. They’ll understand.”
Murray said building these habits early can give children a head start once they begin managing money on their own.
Beyond money habits, experts also recommend talking with children early about what personal information they share on tablets and smartphones — a conversation focused less on finances and more on safety.
