title: Current credit card interest rates
text:
Current credit card interest rates
The average credit card interest rate is 19.63%, down from a record-high 20.79% set on Aug. 14, 2024.
Current credit card interest rates
Bankrate Data Center
Since 1976, Bankrate has been the go-to source for personal finance data, publishing average rates on the most popular financial products and tracking the experience of consumers nationwide.
See more
Historical interest rates
How are credit card rates set?
The typical credit card rate formula is the Prime Rate plus a profit margin set by the card issuer. On average, this margin often runs between 12% and 13%. The Prime Rate is currently 6.75%. It’s typically 3 percentage points higher than the federal funds rate, which is set by the Federal Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee.
Essentially, the federal funds rate is the interest rate that banks charge each other for short-term (generally overnight) loans. The Prime Rate is a benchmark for what banks charge their most creditworthy customers. It serves as a basis for many financial products.
Credit cards have a higher markup than other loans, such as mortgages and auto loans, because credit cards represent unsecured debt. That means they aren’t backed by an underlying asset such as a home or car that a lender can seize if the borrower doesn’t pay them back.
How the CARD Act changed credit card rate calculations
The CARD Act, which took effect in 2010, altered the way credit card rates were set. Previously, credit card issuers had much more flexibility in terms of when they could change customers’ rates. Now, the easiest way for them to adjust rates (especially on existing balances) is to tie the rate to an index such as the Prime Rate.
If the Prime Rate changes, almost all credit card agreements are written in a way that the adjustment affects cardholders’ new and existing balances without any special notice required. The exact timing of the change varies. Sometimes the issuer uses the Prime Rate on your statement date. It might also be the first day of the month or the last day of the month or another date of their choosing.
Card issuers can change the rate on existing customers’ new purchases with 45 days’ notice. And they have a lot of flexibility regarding new offers just coming onto the market.
Money tip: The most important thing to know with respect to credit card rate adjustments is that Federal Reserve rate changes (up or down) generally pass through to customers within a month or two. And these Fed rate changes affect new and existing credit card balances.

How do credit card rates affect you?
Most credit cards bill on a monthly cycle. If you pay your credit card purchases in full, you aren’t charged interest and you typically receive an interest-free grace period of at least 21 days. For example, if your billing statement is generated on the 1st of the month, you usually have until at least the 22nd of that month to pay without interest accruing. Depending on when you made the purchase, you might actually have close to two months without owing interest (if you bought something early in the billing cycle).
However, if you carry a balance from one billing cycle to the next, it’s a completely different story. Credit card rates are usually expressed as APRs — annual percentage rates. But taking this a level deeper, what actually happens when you carry a balance is that the card issuer assesses a daily interest rate (typically the APR divided by the 365 days in a year) on your average daily balance during a given billing cycle. The most important thing for consumers to understand is that, when they carry balances, interest is accruing every single day (and usually at a hefty interest rate). That’s why it’s essential to pay down credit card debt as quickly as possible.
Let’s say you have $5,000 of credit card debt and your interest rate is 20% APR. If you only make minimum payments, you will be in debt for about 23 years and you’ll end up paying about $7,723 in interest, according to Bankrate’s calculator.
Keep in mind: An interest-free grace period applies only to purchases. If you’ve made a balance transfer or taken a cash advance, different APRs could apply and there may not be any grace period for those transactions.
-  Our methodology When we refer to the average credit card rate, we mean the average midpoint of the APR ranges assessed by 111 popular credit cards offered by the 50 largest U.S.-based credit card issuers. Most credit cards charge different interest rates to different customers based upon their creditworthiness. A consumer with an excellent credit score, for example, might be charged 14.99%. That same card might charge as high as, say, 24.99% to someone with a lower credit score. In that example, we would use 19.99% (the midpoint between 14.99% and 24.99%) in our average credit card rate calculations.

title: A closer look at the candidates for the Portland City Council at-large race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The decision by Portland City Councilor April Fournier to not seek reelection has created a three-way race for one of the council’s three at-large seats that features a former mayor and two candidates who have run unsuccessfully before.
The Portland Press Herald spoke to each candidate ahead of the Nov. 3 election to ask why they are running and what their priorities are.
This is the first of three previews for City Council races that will run in the coming days. Early voting in the state of Maine begins Oct. 5. For polling locations, or to request an absentee ballot, go to portlandmaine.gov/elections-voting.
ATIIM BOYKIN
Atiim Boykin has seen the effects of gentrification in places like San Francisco — where he went to college and began a career in social work — but doesn’t believe it’s too late for Portland. He wants to keep artists and other working class creatives in the city.
“It’s an economic engine that’s overlooked,” he said. “Artists get washed out as soon as (a city) gets attractive.”
Boykin, 50, first ran for the District 2 seat in 2024 but was unsuccessful. He said he got involved because he realized he’d already been doing public service-related work for a long time.
Boykin is a mental health clinician, and believes his experience could help the city tackle its issues with homelessness, substance use and behavioral health. In 2015, he helped found San Francisco’s first-of-its-kind Young Adult Court, a program for individuals aged 18 to 25 facing felony and misdemeanor charges.
He said the city needs some kind of resource hub where segmented services could be brought under one roof to “fill in gaps” and help address safety issues downtown. Right now, he said, Portland is essentially playing “whack-a-mole,” and could use his experience to employ “diversion before crisis” models that are successful in other cities rather than “going straight to enforcement.”
Boykin also sees housing as a key issue, and specifically housing that’s affordable to the teachers, nurses, artists and service workers “who keep this city running.”
He said local hospitals and schools have available land and should partner with the city or developers to build housing for traveling nurses and teachers. He wants to see mixed-use live/work spaces built, and points specifically to “empty Bayside lots” as a potential home.
However, Boykin also alluded to the city’s inclusionary zoning policy — which requires large housing projects to have at least 25% affordable units — as something that needs to be revisited in order to get more shovels in the ground.
He and his wife moved to Portland in 2018, and he said he wants to be part of shaping Portland’s future for his daughter.
“Other cities have suffered growing pains that hollowed out their neighborhoods and priced out the people who built them. I refuse that fate for Portland,” he said. “Twenty years as a clinician taught me how to hold a community through hard change. That is the work I want to bring to City Hall.”
While Boykin is a registered Democrat, he said local political candidates shouldn’t “lead with the party.”
“You lead with (being a) nonpartisan listener,” he said.
He’s also not afraid to identify himself to voters as a musician and poet while seeking support for the at-large seat.
“I thought it could translate well. It’s just a different stage,” he said.
JOEY BRUNELLE
If voters don’t recognize the name, there’s a good chance they’ve seen Joey Brunelle walking downtown Portland, or at a public meeting, forum or event. Or, if the name is familiar, they may have seen one of Brunelle’s Reddit posts sparking a virtual debate over city issues.
“I do try to be everywhere,” he said when asked about his active presence. “I’ve learned over the years that issues are all interconnected.”
He said he’s tried not to pigeonhole himself into being an advocate for just one issue, and sees himself as a candidate that could unite people to collaborate on solutions.
Brunelle believes local government in Portland is stuck in an “old-school mentality” where the city acts as a corporation with the public as its customers.
“In reality, city government is just us,” he said. “I really want to expand how people can participate meaningfully. Let’s bring in people who have the passion and expertise to work on a variety of issues, and empower them to actually help fix problems.”
While never popularly elected, Brunelle, 41, has been involved in city politics for a decade. He ran for office in 2017 and 2018, and was recently named chair of the newly formed Civilian Police Review Board.
Like other candidates, he’s hearing themes when knocking on doors: concerns about affordability, pedestrian safety, climate change and immigration enforcement. He’s shared a series of policy proposals on social media, including plans for tackling pedestrian safety, housing production, property taxes and more.
He’s advocating for environmental policies like a “scrubber wash” ban to prevent cruise ships from discharging dirty water into Casco Bay.
He said increases in local property taxes are not sustainable, and that the council needs to do a better job of lobbying for state and federal changes. A local or state hotel/lodging tax would help, he said.
Brunelle works as a web developer and graphic designer. As a West End resident, he’s constantly traversing Congress Street, and often sees the problems with homelessness and substance use that impact the business community.
He said the public concerns are real, but Portland isn’t the first city to confront these issues, and there’s a wide policy gap between “hand-waving” the issue away as a systemic problem that can’t be fixed and reverting to the “lock ’em all up” policies of the 1980s.
“Look outside Maine for what has worked elsewhere,” he said, referring to things like increasing police foot patrols.
Brunelle said he shares values with the Maine Democratic Socialists of America, but doesn’t agree with some of their tactics and didn’t receive their endorsement. He was recently endorsed by councilors Pious Ali and April Fournier.
He also points out to potential voters that he is the only Clean Elections candidate in the race, which means the maximum individual campaign contribution is $5, with the ability to qualify for additional money through the Clean Elections fund.
When asked how he’s different from his opponents, he said he’s seen enough in local politics to know that elected officials can’t fix anything by themselves.
“I feel like I have a good sense of where the problems are with our process, and how we can unlock more action,” he said. “People are hungry for action.”
KATE SNYDER
Kate Snyder didn’t point to just one issue as the inspiration for her return to city politics. It’s simply a love for public service, she said.
Snyder, now 56, served as the city’s mayor from 2019-2023. Before that, she was on the school board from 2007-2013. In both instances, she said, a break in service spurred her to get back in.
“I care a lot about this city, ” she said. “I’m raising my hand for City Council because I think I can help. To me this is just a natural continuation of everything I’ve done here.”
Snyder’s previous experience at City Hall was tumultuous, but she said it gave her the experience to be able to deal with unforeseen challenges. Three months after she was elected mayor, Portland declared a state of emergency due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Her term also saw Black Lives Matter protests and the rise of homeless encampments.
“We never know what’s around the corner,” she said. “I ask voters to think about how candidates will navigate unforeseeable challenges that will come our way. I think I can help us address the known problems and the unknowable ones.”
During recent door-knocking, campaign events and house parties, Snyder said voters are concerned about housing affordability, transportation safety and homelessness.
She hears concerns about property taxes and tells people she wants to make sure spending reflects reality, and that the tax dollars spent are in line with Portlanders’ priorities.
Snyder wants the city to take advantage of its new zoning policies passed during ReCode to get more housing built, and said the current inclusionary zoning policy “doesn’t seem to be fostering the increase in housing we’d hope to see.”
She wants more emphasis on attracting and retaining businesses downtown, and sees the homelessness and substance use issues as a major impediment. Losing Reny’s was a big hit, she said, and she’d love to see a local grocer option downtown.
To do that, the substance use crisis needs to be prioritized by increasing access to detox beds, she said, adding that even when she was mayor, they would often run into the issue of beds not being available. Snyder also knows Portland can’t do it alone.
“We’ve done a lot of work on homelessness and shelters, we need to do the same for substance use and mental health,” she said.
A recent campaign finance report from Snyder shows contributions from Mayor Mark Dion, Angus King III and former city manager Jon Jennings.
When asked how she believes she fits into the progressive versus moderate political spectrum on the council, Snyder said she recently faced a similar question while at a forum at DiMillo’s restaurant.
“I have a record, I have experience, I think it’s not too hard to know who I am,” she said. “If people decide my approach to local governance is right for this time I will be so happy and honored to serve, and that’s really the decision of voters.”
Maria Maffucci, who had also qualified to run for the at-large seat, dropped out of the race in early September.

title: Hegseth announces a new drone command, cuts to 20% of generals in US military
text:
QUANTICO, Va. (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced some major changes to the U.S. military on Wednesday in what he called his “State of the Force” address, including establishing a new drone command and cutting 20% of the nation’s generals and admirals.
The Pentagon also will launch an effort to study the future of warfare that will be led in part by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Hegseth said. The Defense Department will create an Office of Religious Affairs and plans to build a new base for the first time in 40 years, he added.
Hegseth made the announcements to junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia — the second year in a row that he has given such an address. But this time, the U.S. military is seven months into a war with Iran with no clear end in sight, has captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and killed more than 200 people in strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats in Latin America, among other actions worldwide.
The speech is not a usual fixture among Pentagon leaders. While Hegseth’s predecessors have regularly addressed troops and top officers, they have traditionally done so in small or private settings.
The Pentagon chief, however, again led with how he has drastically retooled the U.S. military by targeting what he calls “woke” culture — through a rollback of diversity programs, a review of ground combat units with female troops and a new screening program for “testosterone deficiency” among male personnel — as well as attacks on the media for the coverage of the military.
Hegseth announces a new drone-focused warfare command
The Pentagon chief announced the intention to create a new four-star command to oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities in what he called “the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history.”
He acknowledged that “the pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it.” Iran commonly uses cheap drones, including those that have killed U.S. troops during the seven-month war. Hegseth pointed to Ukraine’s pioneering use of drones to combat Russian forces — something American forces have learned from firsthand.
“Ukraine’s lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt,” Hegseth said.
However, a U.S. Army unit based in Europe that specialized in drone warfare was ordered recently to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion.
A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers subsequently asked the Army to explain the order, given that the world’s battlefields are rapidly evolving and military tactics increasingly rely on uncrewed systems to fight.
The plans for a drone command come as the U.S. is in a stalemate with Iran over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy shipping corridor. The war has forced American forces in the region to expend hundreds of expensive missile interceptors to defend against Iran’s missile and drone attacks, which have still managed to kill and wound U.S. troops.
Hegseth repeated claims that the U.S. military has destroyed Iran’s navy, air force and defense systems as well as many of its leaders and its industrial base. But Tehran has continued intermittently to launch drone and missile attacks against at U.S. or allied bases, while maintaining its ability to strike commercial and military ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
During his speech, Hegseth touted the Trump administration’s major investments in the defense industry and push for contractors to speed up their work to expand the nation’s weapons arsenals. But experts say U.S. military contractors will need at least three years to replenish stockpiles of key weapons systems used heavily in the Iran war.
Hegseth faces questions from lawmakers over cuts to general ranks
Hegseth said he directed the military services to double the 10% reduction he ordered last spring for roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027.
“I call it accountability and long overdue,” he said.
Some members of Congress have criticized the war and the drawdown of munitions stockpiles, while calling the latest cuts to the general ranks a “purge” that will take years to rebuild.
“He’s got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth. “He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it.”
Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth’s reasoning.
“If it’s simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first,” Rounds said.
Musk and Gingrich to lead a study of future warfare
In innovating the next wave of weapons systems, Hegseth announced an effort to study the future of warfare led by Musk, Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries.
Hegseth said the work “will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes.” He pointed to the need to dominate “any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon.”
This month, the U.S. confirmed for the first time that it had deployed weapons in space, a remarkable revelation after previous warnings about countries such as Russia possibly weaponizing a global frontier long agreed in treaties to be used for only peaceful purposes.
Among the other announcements was the unveiling of a plan to build a new military base, with Hegseth inviting all 50 states to compete for the chance to play host to 15,000 to 25,000 service members. He also announced a plan to make every military base self-powered.
___
Finley reported from Washington, and Kinnard from Columbia, South Carolina. Associated Press writer Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

title: US military withdraws from Iraq, ending years-long mission
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. military has formally ended its mission against ISIS in Iraq, completing the withdrawal of American and coalition forces from the country after a 12-year campaign.
U.S. Central Command announced Wednesday that U.S. forces and equipment had completed their departure from Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq, the main operational hub for Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve.
The base had hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and coalition personnel supporting counter-ISIS operations there.
The withdrawal marks the conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq and follows a transition plan announced by the United States and Iraq in September 2024.
“The orderly departure of Coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq,” Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Wednesday.
Parnell said the milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat and shifts responsibility for the country’s security to Iraqi forces.
The departure also closes another chapter in more than two decades of U.S. military involvement in Iraq.
The United States invaded Iraq in 2003 under Operation Iraqi Freedom, leading to the overthrow of Saddam Hussein. American forces withdrew in 2011 but returned three years later as ISIS seized large portions of Iraq and neighboring Syria.
CENTCOM established Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve in 2014 to advise, assist and support partner forces fighting ISIS. Iraq declared territorial victory over the terrorist group in 2017, but the U.S.-led mission continued as Iraqi and Kurdish forces worked to prevent its resurgence.
American and coalition forces began their latest withdrawal from federal Iraq in October 2025. That process concluded Wednesday with the removal of remaining personnel and equipment from Erbil Air Base.
CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said ISIS “no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security” and said Iraqi security forces, including Kurdish Peshmerga forces, now have the capacity and operational independence to manage threats inside the country.
That does not mean the U.S. relationship with Iraq — or the broader fight against ISIS — is over.
The Pentagon says the wartime coalition mission is transitioning to a more traditional bilateral defense relationship between Washington and Baghdad.
The Pentagon also says responsibility for other security challenges, including Iran-aligned militias operating inside Iraq, now primarily rests with the Iraqi government. U.S. officials say Washington remains committed to preventing ISIS from rebuilding its capabilities in the country.
Operation Inherent Resolve itself is also continuing outside Iraq. Its joint task force is now headquartered in Jordan, and CENTCOM says U.S. forces will continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria alongside coalition partners and the Syrian government.
President Donald Trump called the withdrawal a “decisive victory” Wednesday, saying it was time for American forces to leave Iraq.
“I had a choice to stay or to leave, and felt, without question, that it was time for America to go home!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

title: Red Sox swept out of playoffs by Yankees
text:
NEW YORK — Max Fried dominated Boston in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the New York Yankees romped over the Red Sox 9-2 Wednesday night for a two-game AL Wild Card Series sweep.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston’s 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke the game open with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBI that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, was eliminated by the Yankees in the first round for the second straight year. The Red Sox hit .117 in the two-game series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and were outscored 18-2.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García’s fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead, and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just entered in relief. Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay Bellinger, who won a World Series with New York in 2000.
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, a throwing error, a stolen base, a bunt single and an intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger’s homer.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series opener, hadn’t pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation but entered to start the sixth. On a two-strike pitch to Jones, Crochet bounced a sweeper off catcher Adley Rutschman’s chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled out. The Yankees appealed, and the call was reversed by the video umpire.
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled, and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Austin Wells’ sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout, and Rice, who had four hits and six RBI in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats to make it 8-1.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
Nick Sogard hit a solo homer off Will Warren in the seventh.
UP NEXT
New York right-hander Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.

title: Election officials aim to reassure voters ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Election officials from some of the largest jurisdictions in the country met in Washington to address voter concerns ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
Los Angeles County, Calif. Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan said officials want voters to trust the process.
“We want voters to be assured that we’re ready and we want voters to be focused on their readiness,” Logan said.
Dallas County, Texas Elections Administrator Paul Adams said officials are focused on communicating with voters about election procedures.
“It is very important that we give a strong message of clarity to the voters, that they understand what is going on, they understand the procedures we are following,” Adams said.
In recent weeks, federal updates and decisions have affected the elections system, including Supreme Court opinions on mail-in ballots and redistricting maps, and a White House push to address what it calls long-term voter corruption.
On Wednesday, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the indictment of 10 foreign nationals for making false claims of citizenship in order to vote.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said voter fraud affects public confidence in elections.
“Voter fraud erodes the public’s trust in our electoral system and it’s vital to our democratic process that we do everything that we can to restore that trust,” Blanche said.
Aaron Blacksberg, of the Institute for Responsive Government, said many proposed federal changes have not taken effect.
“The executive branch, the federal government, the President, the various agencies announced attempted changes and almost all of them of any substance for voters have not come into effect,” Blacksberg said.
Blacksberg said voters should learn election procedures before heading to the polls.
“Know the rules, go vote,” Blacksberg said.

title: Elmet Technologies of Lewiston awarded $36M defense contract
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Defense Logistics Agency, which manages the nation’s global supply chain, has awarded a $36 million contract to Elmet Technologies of Lewiston to provide molybdenum and tungsten alloys, and precision wire for the National Defense Stockpile.
The materials, known as refractory metals, are key components for the defense and aerospace industries and are used in jet engine components and high performance defense systems.
Tungsten is the strongest metal in the world with the highest tensile strength. It’s very dense and has the highest melting point of any metal. Molybdenum has similar properties, but to a lesser degree.
They are also among the raw materials produced primarily in China and restricted from export since 2025 for national security reasons.
Under the contract, Elmet Technologies will supply the government with titanium-zirconium-molybdenum, or TZM alloy billets, bar stock, and ingots, as well as specialized molybdenum and tungsten wire.
TZM is a molybdenum alloy strengthened with small additions of titanium and zirconium, allowing it to retain its strength at higher temperatures than pure molybdenum, making it well suited to aerospace and defense applications where materials must perform under extreme heat and stress.
Elmet Technologies’ plant is at 1560 Lisbon St.

title: Woman accused of firing at home of Rihanna indicted on attempted murder and other felony counts
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A Florida woman accused of driving across the country to fire a rifle at Rihanna and A$AP Rocky’s home, hitting a trailer the celebrity couple was inside and a nursery where their kids were, has been indicted by a grand jury on 14 felony counts including attempted murder.
The indictment against 36-year-old Ivanna Lisette Ortiz of Orlando was unsealed Wednesday by a Los Angeles County judge.
Ortiz, appearing in court wearing yellow jail clothes, spoke only to her attorney, who entered a not guilty plea for her. The judge then ordered her held on $2.6 million bail.
The move came a day after another judge ruled that Ortiz is mentally competent to stand trial. The secret grand jury proceedings were held as Ortiz was undergoing months of psychiatric evaluation. The jurors returned their indictment June 18, but it was kept under wraps for three months until the judge ruled on her competency. Now, a case that appeared stalled — possibly permanently — is on a fast track to trial.
No one was injured in the March 8 shooting. Authorities allege Ortiz drove a Tesla up to the gates of the Beverly Hills-area property of the singing superstar and her rap star partner, A$AP Rocky, pointed an AR-15 style rifle out the window and fired at least 20 rounds toward the property and the neighboring house.
“This is a person who wanted to kill Rihanna,” Deputy District Attorney Alexander Bott said outside court. “Everyone else was collateral damage.”
Bullets tore through the Airstream trailer, according to a police report. Shots also struck the wall of their home’s nursery, where their three small children were with their nanny. Rihanna’s mother and several staffers also were in the home, and authorities say she also fired shots toward a neighbor’s house.
Both Rihanna and her mother, Monica Fenty, testified to the grand jury, as did Hollywood agent Tracey Jacobs, the owner of the neighboring house who was home at the time and is listed among the victims in the indictment.
Their testimony remains under seal but will become public in about two weeks unless the defense seeks to keep them secret and the judge agrees.
Rihanna told investigators just after the shooting that she “suddenly heard approximately ten loud sounds like something banging on metal,” and pulled Rocky out of a bed and onto the ground. She said she opened curtains and saw bullet marks in the windshield right in front of where she had been standing.
Deputy Public Defender Derek Dillman, Ortiz’s attorney, did not speak to reporters outside the courtroom, and a message seeking comment from the public defender’s office on the indictment was not immediately answered. Other than her not guilty pleas, her lawyers have not publicly addressed the charges, saying only that they would work to defend her rights.
Investigators said that on the day of her arrest, Ortiz told them: “I wasn’t attempting murder.”
Ortiz was charged with very similar counts in March. The new indictment supersedes those charges. The secret grand jury proceedings allow prosecutors to skip California’s preliminary hearing process, where evidence must be presented publicly to see if a trial is merited.
The indictment also charges Ortiz with 10 counts of assault with an assault weapon — one for each of the people on the two properties — and three counts of shooting at an inhabited dwelling or camper. It names the couple’s three children Rza, Riot and Rocki, all under age 5, as victims. The assault weapon counts carry a stiffer sentence than the original charges of assault with a semiautomatic firearm. Ortiz was the registered owner of the rifle, which she obtained in Florida, authorities said.
She could get life in prison if convicted of all counts.
Reports have been sealed on the psychiatric evaluations that paused the case shortly after it began, and there was no public discussion of the details of her mental state.
Prosecutors have not said anything about a motive or cited any connection between Rihanna and Ortiz, a longtime licensed speech pathologist. But in videos posted on Facebook and YouTube in the months before the shooting, Ortiz made increasingly angry comments on Rihanna that sometimes took the form of threats, at one point calling her a “devil.”
A nine-time Grammy Award winner, Rihanna has had 14 No. 1 hits on the Billboard Hot 100, including “We Found Love,” “Work,” “Umbrella” and “Disturbia.”

title: Woman sues hospital over wrong-leg amputation: ‘Every day is a struggle’
text:
MARIETTA, Ohio (WTAP/Gray News) - An Ohio couple is suing a hospital and surgical team after a procedure they say resulted in the amputation of the wrong leg.
Sharon Jacks went to Selby General Hospital for an elective right-leg amputation below the knee. Surgeons instead amputated her left leg.
Lawsuit details allegations
According to the lawsuit, Sharon Jacks made the decision to have her right leg amputated below the knee because of cancer in that leg. The lawsuit’s general allegations section states that before surgery, the correct leg was checked off and marked.
“When Mrs. Jacks went in to have an elective right leg amputation below the knee because of cancer that she had in that leg, she made the tough decision. It wasn’t easy in and of itself to do that, and prior to the surgery, from what I can determine, everything was checked off as to the correct leg. It was marked the correct leg. Everything seemed to be in order,” said Brad Layne, the Jacks family attorney.
In September 2025, Sharon Jacks went in for a below-the-knee amputation for a chronic ulcer. The lawsuit states that documented safety timeouts were conducted twice during the procedure.
Life as a double amputee
Sharon Jacks and her husband, Dannie, are now dealing with the effects of her being a double amputee.
“You can imagine somebody that’s a double amputee now, there’s prosthetics, there’s transportation modifications, there’s housing modifications,” Layne said.
Dannie Jacks quit his job to take care of his wife.
“She certainly couldn’t be left home as a double amputee trying to manage property or manage their home that was not set up for that,” Layne said.
Layne said Sharon Jacks is an Army veteran, a determined and tough person.
“Every day is a struggle. She has to transport herself from a board to a wheelchair just to get to the bathroom or to get into the bed or to change clothes or to go anywhere,” Layne said.
Hospital response
Selby General Hospital issued a statement, calling the incident “an adverse surgical event.”
“Our proactive review of what took place confirmed this was an avoidable event, and that our expected operating room procedures were not followed. Those involved were held accountable for their actions and are no longer in their positions,” the hospital system said.
Exhibit 2, page 24 of the lawsuit states a wrongful-site amputation is a catastrophic, foreseeable and preventable patient safety event classified by the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations as a never event.

title: As heating costs surge, fire officials urge caution with woodstoves and space heaters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) — As home heating oil hits record highs in Maine, local fire officials worry families could turn to risky heating alternatives to stay warm.
Last week, Maine heating oil reached a record-high $6.02 a gallon. As temperatures drop, Waterville Fire Chief Jason Frost remembers 2008 in Skowhegan, when soaring fuel prices triggered a dangerous surge in chimney and structure fires.
“People were putting in wood stove installations that just were not kosher and we did see a lot of chimney fires that year, and probably double the amount of structure fires that we usually see from improper wood stove installations,” Frost said.
Frost says makeshift setups and unseasoned, green wood were the biggest culprits. He recommends timber sit stacked outside for a full year to dry, otherwise moisture leaves behind a dangerous hazard.
“It’s wet and it creates all the sugars in there, in the woods, and that’s what creates creosote,” Frost said. “Creosote will build up in your chimney over time if you’re not burning it off. That creosote plugs the chimney up, and then you end up having a chimney fire.”
Beyond woodstoves, Frost warns that older portable space heaters without automatic tip-over shutoffs are a major hazard. He advises homeowners to use only modern, UL-listed units.
He understands families are facing tight budgets, but emphasizes that his department will help ensure safety where they can, offering free chimney inspections and advice.
“I’d rather be proactive,” Frost said. “If you are unsure, if you don’t know about your installations, if you just want us to just take a look, we are more than willing to come out and do what we can to help you out so that we don’t end up in a situation where you have to call 911.”
Frost says whether you need an inspection or simply a working smoke detector, reach out before striking that first match.
Homeowners can find the state’s official woodstove installation standards prepared by the Office of State Fire Marshal and the Maine Office of Energy Resources here, or pick up a printed copy at the Waterville Fire Department.

title: Roman Anthony out for playoffs with another right hand injury
text:
NEW YORK — Roman Anthony is expected to miss the rest of the postseason for the Boston Red Sox because of new damage to his right hand sustained in an AL Wild Card Series opener against the New York Yankees.
It is not yet clear whether he will need surgery. Anthony was sidelined from early May to late August because of an injury to the same hand.
“We did everything we could to be back this year and play, which we did,” Anthony said Wednesday in the tunnel outside the Red Sox clubhouse at Yankee Stadium before Game 2. “Going forward, we haven’t really even talked about it today.”
Batting leadoff as Boston’s designated hitter in his playoff debut Tuesday night, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against Cam Schlittler, then was removed for a pinch hitter with the Red Sox trailing by two runs in the sixth inning of a 9-0 loss.
Manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings.
“After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%,” Anthony said. “For me, it was to a point where it was tolerable and I was taking certain swings that were sketchy, and I was still able to come back and recover enough to just be in there every single day. But ultimately I just took a few swings here recently where that wasn’t the case.”
The team sent Anthony to Boston in a car after the game. He arrived about 3 a.m. and had new MRIs on Wednesday morning.
“Additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren’t there before,” Tracy said.
The 22-year-old Anthony returned to Massachusetts because the medical staff there was familiar with his injury from earlier this season.
“My thoughts are kind of all over the place,” he said. “Feelings and emotions of, you work all this year to put yourself in a position to just be good enough to go in the playoffs and for this to happen, it just doesn’t feel real.”
Anthony wasn’t sure whether the injury is something he’ll have to manage going forward.
“Given the point where we were at this year and all the different things that I tried and the different shots that I took and the routes that I went, I think — never really rested a ton, right? — so I don’t necessarily know the answer to that,” he said.
“Once we saw it today, it was more so about like, all right, this is what it is. You can’t go. It’s not in the team’s best interest for you to play tonight. So get back there. Root your guys on and be a good teammate. And then once, like I said, once we get past the series, it will be one of those things where we reassess regardless of what happens and kind of go from there.”
Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29.
“There’s been periods of time since he’s come back where he’ll get a zinger and feel something. And then it dissipates and we’re good to go,” Tracy said. “That’s not been an uncommon occurrence since he’s come back. But yesterday, as you went through those two at-bats, it got worse.”
The club announced that Anthony was diagnosed with a right hand strain, and Major League Baseball approved a Red Sox roster substitution. Anthony was replaced on the Wild Card Series roster by infielder Curtis Mead, obtained from Washington in late July for pitcher Connelly Early.
According to MLB rules, Anthony is ineligible to return until the American League Championship Series — if the Red Sox advance that far.
“I’ve been experiencing some things with the swings and the check-swings over the past six weeks. Last night just felt a little bit more intense, a little bit more worse than past swings that have been lingering a little bit longer than the ones I was used to,” Anthony said.
“It was just super alarming and it got to a point where it was tough to grip a bat. I knew then and there that this was a little bit more similar to the one earlier in the year. That’s why we decided to go get imaging.”
Mead got hit by a pitch in his first game with the Red Sox at the Athletics on July 27 and was placed on the injured list because of a broken left wrist. He hasn’t played in the big leagues since.
Mead was on the bench for Game 2 against the Yankees. Jahmai Jones was set to hit leadoff as the DH with the Red Sox one loss from elimination, followed in the batting order by catcher Adley Rutschman, first baseman Willson Contreras, right fielder Wilyer Abreu, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, third baseman Caleb Durbin, second baseman Nick Sogard, shortstop Trevor Story and left fielder Nate Eaton.
Sonny Gray was set to start on the mound for Boston against one of his former teams. Left-hander Max Fried was scheduled to pitch for New York.
One of baseball’s premier prospects when he debuted in the majors last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBI and a .735 OPS in 55 games this season.
“Hopefully he’s going to be healthy for next year,” Abreu said. “It’s a big loss for us, but we still have to play the game and try to win the game today.”

title: From shorts to sweaters: Bar Harbor shifts gears for fall tourism
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR, Maine (WABI) - A new season brings new opportunities for Maine tourism.
Even as shorts turn into sweaters, Bar Harbor remains a top pick for visitors.
It was another busy summer season in the town on Mount Desert Island, but as the leaves change, so does the approach to tourism.
“I think we start to see the character of the traveler change, where a lot of the summer is overall families, and then as you get into kids going back to school, it tends to be younger families, newlyweds or some of our older population that wants to come out and visit that doesn’t have the kids in school anymore,” explained Everal Eaton, executive director of the Bar Harbor Chamber of Commerce.
Arriving to town via RV, Blake Daughtery and Kelley D’Souza, from Oklahoma and Kansas respectively, came to visit Acadia National Park with a group of friends.
“We actually planned specifically around the fall time for the fall colors,” D’Souza said. “We were told it was actually one of the most beautiful national parks, so we had to make a stop.”
Tourism turnout this year did not come without challenges, namely rising gas prices and Bar Harbor’s ordinance imposing cruise ship passenger limits.
Located on Rodick Street, Side Street Cafe said it experienced an increase in both food and labor costs.
“A lot of it is just the increased expenses for everybody. When the fuel price goes up, that means farmers have to pay more for fuel and that means they have to charge more for their product,” described the cafe’s Director of Operations Bo Jennings.
While the summer season may be cooling down, many businesses are opting for year-round offerings to keep Bar Harbor a destination for locals and visitors alike.
New this year, Oli’s Trolley will be open throughout the year for private events and as a shuttle.
“Just because we saw a need and people are constantly asking and so we wanted to help provide a service,” Oli’s Trolley CEO Elizabeth Sturm said.
While food operations shut down in the winter at Side Street Cafe, the building will remain open to host live music, comedy shows, and other events.
“What we learned last offseason is that people are yearning for experiences here in Bar Harbor,” Jennings explained. “People want to get out of their homes. They want to get out and see their community members and hang out with their friends and laugh and sing along and we’re here to provide that for them.”
For the Chamber of Commerce, a packed schedule across all seasons is key to supporting the local economy.
“We are very fortunate that a lot of our businesses are locally owned mom-and-pop stores,” Eaton said. “So, when you come to Bar Harbor and visit, you’re directly helping the people that live here year round.“
Beyond peak leaf-peeping in a couple of weeks, Bar Harbor has many events in store for the fall, including the MDI Marathon in October and the Bar Harbor Bed Races in November.

title: Maine Coastal Program announces $299,057 in habitat restoration planning grants
text:
The Maine Office of Community Affairs’ Maine Coastal Program (MCP) awarded $299,057 to four municipalities and service providers for projects to develop habitat restoration plans in support of community resilience.
Communities depend on healthy coastal habitats to buffer storm surge, maintain clean water, and absorb rising seas. The funded projects demonstrate how coastal communities across Maine are prioritizing habitat restoration for ecological and community resilience.
The funding for these grants comes from a one-time Habitat Restoration Planning opportunity through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Office of Coastal Management. The grants will support projects focused on tidal marsh restoration design, road crossing assessments and prioritization, and natural resource inventories. Projects will begin in Fall 2026.
The four selected projects are:
- Town of Boothbay: “Town-wide Crossing Assessment and Prioritization.” The town will hire a consultant to conduct road crossing assessments and evaluate every crossing in Boothbay for coastal habitat restoration potential and climate hazard vulnerability. With this evaluation, the Town of Boothbay will have the tools available to prioritize projects to create a resilient coastal community.
- Town of Gouldsboro: “Preliminary Natural Resource Inventory and Infrastructure Vulnerability Assessment of the Sand Cove area in Gouldsboro, ME.” The town will hire a consultant to map sea level rise, storm surge threats, basic infrastructure, and natural resources of Grand Marsh. These data and calculations will enable the town to assess how proposed coastal transportation improvements interact with the protection of the existing dune, freshwater, and intertidal wetlands in the study area.
- Downeast Salmon Federation (DSF): “Point Street Resilient Crossing Design Supplement.” DSF will work with a consultant to improve habitat resiliency through infrastructure upgrades. This work includes culvert replacement design, geotechnical assessments, and improvements to water infrastructure at the Point Street crossing of the West Branch Pleasant River (WBPR) in Addison, Maine.
- Kennebec Estuary Land Trust (KELT): “Planning for the restoration and enhancement of resilience of Popham area tidal marshes.” KELT will hire a consultant to evaluate the Popham marshes’ vegetation and existing conditions to understand its resiliency to changing water levels. Developing a plan for marsh rehabilitation and evaluating its potential absorption capability can help prepare the Phippsburg area and its associated infrastructure for future flood events.
For inquiries about the Habitat Restoration Planning Grant Program, contact Erin Campbell at erin.grace.campbell@maine.gov.

title: How much does it cost to go to college now? What the data shows
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How much does it cost to go to college now? What the data shows
The cost of tuition at a public, four-year institution has doubled from 30 years ago, even after adjusting for inflation. Is the same true for what students are actually paying?
Prices advertised by colleges have increased significantly over the past several decades, but the actual amount students are spending has remained relatively flat due to more grant aid coming from colleges and universities.
The average cost of in-state tuition at a public, four-year institution was $11,950 during the 2025-26 school year, according to College Board.
The average cost of tuition at a private institution is also much higher at $45,000. That's about a 75% increase from 30 years before. The cost of tuition and fees does not include housing, food, books or other necessary living expenses.
The average annual published cost of tuition peaked around 2020 for both private and public four-year institutions, after adjusting for inflation. In the years following, average tuition went down slightly.
Adjusting for inflation converts data from prior years into what the tuition would equal in 2025, the most recent year with data. It allows for a direct comparison from the most recent published cost of tuition to the cost 30 years ago.
What is college tuition, and what does it include?
There's a big difference between the advertised tuition, the total estimated cost of attendance and the actual amount paid after aid.
For example, the advertised total cost of attendance includes tuition and fees along with estimated housing, food, books and other costs.
Most students in undergraduate programs don’t pay the full "sticker price" to attend, according to College Board. The total estimated cost of attendance, including expenses like housing and food at public, in-state institutions, was $30,990, but after estimated grant aid, it's closer to $21,340.
What is the most expensive college tuition by state?
Vermont had the most expensive in-state tuition for public institutions during the 2025-26 school year at $18,090. New Hampshire and New Jersey weren't too far behind. Florida was the most affordable for students in-state to attend college with an average of $6,360.
For out-of-state students, Michigan was the most expensive at more than $45,000, and South Dakota was the most affordable at about $13,000.
Use the interactive map below to see the average tuition at a public institution during the 2025-26 school year. Data shows the average cost of tuition and fees for each state and may not represent what someone actually paid to attend a university.

title: Maine approves deer hunt for MDI town after nearly century-long ban
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Maine wildlife officials have approved a special deer hunt in Tremont, allowing the Mount Desert Island town to reopen to deer hunting for the first time since 1931.
Tremont voters approved the hunt by a 314-227 vote in May after years of concerns about deer-related property damage, vehicle collisions and other conflicts.
The Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife adopted the rule Sept. 16, and it took effect Wednesday, Sept. 30.
The special hunt will take place each November from 2026 through 2028 unless the Tremont Select Board or IFW suspends it after a season. Only antlerless deer may be harvested, and hunters may use shotguns or archery equipment from fixed blinds.
Hunters must obtain permission from the Tremont Town Office and register harvested deer at a tagging station designated by the town. The town will administer permit selection for residents and nonresidents. Deer harvested during the special hunt will be in addition to the statewide bag limit.
The final rule followed a public comment period that drew 21 written comments: 12 opposed, four in support and five that were mixed or unclear. Several opponents called for more study of the deer population before the hunt began.
Tremont is among the most deer-impacted towns in Maine, and IFW estimated the average deer density in Wildlife Management District 26, which includes MDI, at about 30 to 35 deer per square mile over the past three years. IFW noted that studies generally suggest deer densities should be maintained below 15 to 25 deer per square mile when forest health is a priority.

title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow transgender medical care restrictions in prison
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to let it enforce restrictions on gender-affirming care in federal prisons.
The emergency appeal comes after lower courts blocked officials from immediately carrying out the policy adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump.
U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered the government to continue providing gender-affirming care like hormone therapy.
The Trump administration argues that the policy was properly adopted and the judge overstepped. It halts surgeries, hormones and social accommodations like wigs while allowing mental health therapy to continue.
It was adopted after an executive order required the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”
The government asked the high court to freeze Lamberth’s order while the lawsuit continues to play out, saying the Bureau of Prisons had “determined that sex-trait-modification surgeries, hormone interventions in general, and social accommodations could no longer be justified as treatment for gender dysphoria.”
The agency said in 2025 that it was providing hormone therapy to more than 600 inmates.
The bureau doesn’t dispute that gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects, including depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts, Lamberth wrote. The Washington-based judge was nominated to the bench by President Ronald Reagan.
A divided appeals court panel left the order in place.
ACLU attorneys for the inmates said the policy is “a direct threat to the well-being of transgender people in federal custody and an open violation of their fundamental rights,” and withholding necessary gender-affirming healthcare constitutes cruel and unusual punishment.
The conservative-majority Supreme Court has previously upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender youth, and restricting sports participation by transgender athletes in women’s sports.
It has also handed down shorter-term decisions allowing the Trump administration to move ahead for now with other policies rolling back protections for transgender people serving in the military and holding a passport consistent with their gender identity.

title: ‘Absolutely devastated’: Patriots rookie tight end announces death of newborn son
text:
‘Absolutely devastated’: Patriots rookie tight end announces death of newborn son
New England Patriots rookie tight end Eli Raridon and his wife announced the loss of their first child.
Related video: Ed Sheeran address Macklemore/Robert Kraft controversy on stage
The couple shared a post on Instagram Tuesday, saying their son, Peter James Raridon, died as a result of anencephaly, a fatal birth defect in "which he would not survive outside the womb."
"While we are absolutely devastated that we were unable to bring our baby boy home, I am grateful to have loved him deeply, kept him safe, and had been his home for the past 9 months before he was called back to Heaven," Eli and his wife, Anna, said in a joint post.
The couple said Peter was diagnosed during a 20-week anatomy scan.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, anencephaly is a serious birth defect where, during pregnancy, the neural tube that helps form the baby’s brain, skull, spine and backbone does not close all the way. At birth, babies with anencephaly often do not have a front part of their brain, a cerebrum or bone or skin covering the brain.
The CDC said about 1 in every 4,762 babies is born with anencephaly in the United States. There is no cure or treatment.
"I believe our little boy was lovingly knitted together in the womb by God, knowing how deeply he would be loved by our families, our friends, Eli, and me," the post read. "Though his time with us was brief, his life still precious, his purpose still meaningful, and he will forever be a part of our story."
The post continued, saying, "I have loved you every second of your life & will miss you every second of mine. What a sweet sweet reunion ours will be."

title: New Bangor crisis receiving center holds ribbon cutting ceremony
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - With the aim to open on October 5th, the new Bangor crisis receiving center held ribbon cutting ceremony on Wednesday.
“The opening of the crisis receiving center here in Bangor represents a new front door for individuals experiencing a mental health, substance use or suicidal crisis. Breaking down stigma, providing immediate low barrier support in a welcoming space,” said Sarah Squirrell, Director of the Office of Behavioral Health.
The new Bangor Crisis Receiving Center is one of three in the state of Maine.
The first opened in Portland in February of 2022.
According to Gov. Mills, that location has served more than 3,500 people.
“More than half of them have visited just once or twice. And more than 90% of them left the center with a clear plan for what to do next,” said Mills.
In the wake of the 2023 mass shooting in Lewiston, the Maine legislature approved funding for two new centers in Lewiston and Bangor.
Once open, the Bangor center will be accessible 24/7 to anyone ages 14 and older.
“A key component of a safe place to go is really connection. And that power of connection is magnified when individuals with lived experience and expertise, peers, are there to help. Which is why our crisis receiving model includes talented peer specialists. Peer specialists play an important role in building trust quickly, reducing fear for individuals, and opening that door to healing and recovery. Peer support also provides hope, And with this center in Bangor, we strengthen compassionate response and we build hope,” said Squirrell.
The center is located inside of Community Health and Counseling Services at 68 First St.

title: As heating costs surge, fire officials urge caution with woodstoves and space heaters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) — As home heating oil hits record highs in Maine, local fire officials worry families could turn to risky heating alternatives to stay warm.
Last week, Maine heating oil reached a record-high $6.02 a gallon. As temperatures drop, Waterville Fire Chief Jason Frost remembers 2008 in Skowhegan, when soaring fuel prices triggered a dangerous surge in chimney and structure fires.
“People were putting in wood stove installations that just were not kosher and we did see a lot of chimney fires that year, and probably double the amount of structure fires that we usually see from improper wood stove installations,” Frost said.
Frost says makeshift setups and unseasoned, green wood were the biggest culprits. He recommends timber sit stacked outside for a full year to dry, otherwise moisture leaves behind a dangerous hazard.
“It’s wet and it creates all the sugars in there, in the woods, and that’s what creates creosote,” Frost said. “Creosote will build up in your chimney over time if you’re not burning it off. That creosote plugs the chimney up, and then you end up having a chimney fire.”
Beyond woodstoves, Frost warns that older portable space heaters without automatic tip-over shutoffs are a major hazard. He advises homeowners to use only modern, UL-listed units.
He understands families are facing tight budgets, but emphasizes that his department will help ensure safety where they can, offering free chimney inspections and advice.
“I’d rather be proactive,” Frost said. “If you are unsure, if you don’t know about your installations, if you just want us to just take a look, we are more than willing to come out and do what we can to help you out so that we don’t end up in a situation where you have to call 911.”
Frost says whether you need an inspection or simply a working smoke detector, reach out before striking that first match.
Homeowners can find the state’s official woodstove installation standards prepared by the Office of State Fire Marshal and the Maine Office of Energy Resources here, or pick up a printed copy at the Waterville Fire Department.

What Cornell's Jane Doe told investigators in 2024 prompts fresh questions in reopened investigation
text:
Transcript shows woman told Cornell police 2 years ago she was 100% confident she was raped
A woman who filed a lawsuit saying she was sexually assaulted by seven men at a Cornell University fraternity house told police weeks after the incident that she could “say with 100% confidence I was raped,” according to a report by CBS New York, which said it obtained a transcript of her interview with investigators.
Video above: Attorney of former student who alleges she was raped speaks
The transcript, which has not been publicly released, raises new questions surrounding the local district attorney's decision not to prosecute anyone at the time.
In recent days, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has maintained the woman's first account to police didn't include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex. Yet, he also said he had reopened the investigation based on new information in the woman's lawsuit, which was filed this month.
The woman initially went to Cornell's campus police about three weeks after the alleged attack that began on Oct. 19, 2024, then went back on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, to be interviewed.
“Yes. It was coercion, yes,” she told a campus police officer, according to the transcript obtained by CBS. According to CBS News, she said she was “completely and totally incapacitated” before some of the sexual abuse.
The woman acknowledged she had been drinking alcohol and used drugs the night she visited the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, and that she had gaps in her memory.
She also told police she was comfortable with an initial sexual encounter with two of the men, but not with what happened later in the night, when other men began to enter the room.
“And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard," she told police, according to the transcript. “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," it said she told investigators.
Video above: District Attorney Van Houten speaks
The woman, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in the lawsuit, filed a complaint Sept. 16 saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. She became completely incapacitated while fraternity members were sexually assaulting her, she said.
The district attorney, Van Houten, didn't immediately respond to emails and phone messages from The Associated Press on Wednesday, but he told CBS News he never saw the transcript of the woman's interview when his office declined to bring charges, and relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer but signed by the accuser.
Van Houten has released a summary of that statement, with some of her direct quotes included. He has defended his office’s decision not to do additional investigation after the woman first came forward in 2024.
“There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided,” Van Houten told CNN earlier this week.
Cornell University first publicly disclosed that it was investigating the woman's allegations on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day she first went to police. The school sent students an email alert warning them that a person had reported they had been sexually assaulted at a fraternity house and coerced into consuming drugs. Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity the same day.
In another public statement to students in late November 2024, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said campus police were investigating “deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence” at the fraternity house.
Later, Cornell appointed a task force designed to address sexual assault on campus. But with the district attorney's decision not to pursue charges and the university's internal disciplinary investigation being shielded from the public, attention on the matter waned.
Cornell said in a statement this week that it supported the decision to reopen the criminal investigation, adding that its own investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled. The Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus, but the university has declined to release more information on discipline for individual students, citing privacy rules.
Help is available: For help in the U.S., call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 or chat 24/7 on online.rainn.org.

title: Stephen King opens up about his new novel and a new ‘Carrie’ series
text:
It’s hard to imagine Stephen King needing another writer to make him look good.
But the Maine author says that’s what happened when he worked with Peter Straub. The two first collaborated on a dark fantasy called “The Talisman” in 1984 and then on the 2001 sequel, “Black House.”
Before Straub died in 2022 at 79, he wrote to King with ideas for a third book in the series. King thought the ideas were so powerful, so on point, that he used them as a basis for the new novel “Other Worlds Than These.” It goes on sale Oct. 6, with both authors’ names on the cover.
King wishes he had been able to work with Straub one more time, but is glad to have had the partnership at all.
“Oh man, he was so good. He was a better stylist than I ever was, and I thought this is going to make me look so good if I collaborate with him, and it really did,” said King in mid-September. “We kept saying we’re going to do it (a third book) next year, but I had things to finish and he had things to finish. Then time just ran out.”
The day after “Other Worlds Than These” comes out, Prime will debut a new limited series based on “Carrie,” King’s first book. The 1974 novel was made into a Hollywood film in 1976, starring Sissy Spacek. The new series stars Summer H. Howell and was created and written by Mike Flanagan, who has done several TV or film projects based on King’s work, including “The Life of Chuck” and “Dr. Sleep.”
King said he really likes the way the story has been updated to the present, with Carrie’s fellow students using cellphones and social media to bully and humiliate her.
“It’s really smart and it expands on the book, which was fairly slim. The miniseries is all about social media and it’s fantastic,” said King. “It’s a timeless story, which is too bad. You would hope at some point we as human beings would stop bullying each other for no good reason.”
NO SLOWING DOWN
At 79, King continues to be a pop culture powerhouse. He’s written more than 65 novels or novellas and his books have sold some 400 million copies. More than 80 films or TV series have been based on his work. Colleges around the country have held courses dedicated to his work.
Born in Portland and raised largely in Durham, King went to high school in Lisbon Falls and graduated with a degree in English from the University of Maine in 1970. He and his wife, Tabitha, have lived in Maine ever since. Their longtime Bangor home, a tourist attraction for its resemblance to a haunted house, now houses the couple’s charitable foundation and King’s archives. These days, King spends a little more than half the year in Maine and the rest in Florida.
King had only been a published author for a few years when he met Straub, in London, in the late 1970s. Straub had had success writing about the supernatural with his 1975 novel, “Julia.”
“The Talisman” focused on Jack Sawyer, who at the age of 12 starts an epic quest, walking from New Hampshire to the California coast to find a way to save his dying mother’s life. His trek takes him to the Territories, a parallel medieval universe, where people have lookalike counterparts known as twinners. Jack’s mother’s twinner is queen of the Territories, and is also dying.
“Black House” continues with Sawyer in his 30s, leaving his job as a police officer to live in small-town Wisconsin. A series of murders involving young children draws him out of retirement and into different worlds.
In “Other Worlds Than These,” Sawyer is called to journey to strange worlds again. He has to stop a rampaging group of infected teenagers in America-side and battle the forces of the mysterious Gullet at the edge of Mid-World. The book also wraps up the various worlds of King’s Dark Tower series.
Before Straub died, he sent King a letter with ideas for a third book. He also sent him the book “Redheaded Peckerwood” by artist and photographer Christian Patterson. The book uses photographs to retrace the route of teenagers Charles Starkweather and Caril Ann Fugate on a killing spree through Nebraska in the 1950s.
“Peter said to me, ‘Maybe somebody gets possesed by the spirit of Charles Starkweather and they go into the Territories, and all this stuff happens,” said King. “I thought, ‘Oh man, this is just tailor-made for a suspense novel.’ It really made me want to write this book.”
DO YOUR THING
As for the new “Carrie” series, King said he was sent scripts, had casting approval and was credited as an executive producer. But he really wasn’t very involved. He said he doesn’t like to use his approval power unless he feels he really has to, which is almost never.
“Making a film is different (than writing a book). My thought is, you do your thing and we’ll see what happens,” King said.
Besides Howell as Carrie, the cast includes Samantha Sloyan as her mother and Matthew Lillard as the high school principal. Though the book is set in a fictional Maine town, filming for the series took place in western Canada. Because Canada and states like Massachussetts and New York offer lucrative financial incentives and tax credits to production companies, Maine has rarely been the location of a big-budget King film or TV show in recent years. Film advocates have tried to increase Maine’s film incentives several times in recent years, without much success.
King liked the new series and was particularly impressed with the gym shower scene, where classmates taunt Carrie because she doesn’t realize she’s having her period. Her mother never explained it to her.
In the original movie, the scene is steamy and dreamlike, showing girls in the shower through what King called “a male gaze.” But in the new version, Carrie is crumpled on the floor of the shower while her classmates, fully clothed, crowd around her, recording her humiliation on their cellphones.
“Teenagers still bully each other, but with social media it’s supercharged,” said King. “He (Flanagan) really caught that idea with his shot of all these kids taking cellphone photos of this girl who’s in terror. It’s a wonderful moment.”
King is also happy that while Flanagan updated some things, he didn’t change the story basics, which include a girl who is mercilessly bullied but who has hidden powers.
“It doesn’t reinvent the wheel. The prom scene, the pig’s blood, it’s all there,” King said.

title: Dental clinic uses minimally invasive care, hospital partnerships to treat children’s teeth
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - St. Apollonia Dental Clinic is using a minimally invasive approach to treat tooth decay in children and has partnered with local hospitals to provide dental care for children who need general anesthesia.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found in 2024 that about 11% of children between 2 and 5 years old had primary teeth with untreated decay. Julie Tucci, executive director of St. Apollonia Dental Clinic, said treating tooth decay and cavities in young children has been a challenge, which led the clinic to adopt an approach that does not always require filling a tooth.
“So this practice embraces the minimally invasive dental care that is spreading across the country, which they don’t always have to fill a tooth. Sometimes they can put some treatment on it that arrests the decay so they don’t have to drill tooth structure away,” Tucci said.
Pediatric dental care differs from adult care
Tucci said a child’s dental care is different from an adult’s.
“When they have their first teeth, their primary teeth, a dentist, a pediatric dentist does two more years of residency in order to be able to work on those. And it’s not just the structure of the teeth, it’s behavior management, it’s all the things that need to be considered for a child,” Tucci said.
Hospital partnerships support extensive care
Tucci said partnerships with local hospitals have helped children who need more extensive dental work. The clinic has collaborated with Northern Light AR Gould and Houlton Regional Hospitals to provide dental treatment for children who need general anesthesia.
“We also are very fortunate to have two local hospitals that let our pediatric dentists go in and take children to the hospital who need to have general anesthesia to have their dental work done,” Tucci said.
Tucci said having that option close to home isn’t available in every community.
“I know from being in organizations across the state that that’s not happening everywhere. We are very, very, very fortunate that our local hospitals are 100% behind the work that’s being done here for the kids,” Tucci said.

title: Aging Untold: Meet the man behind ‘Taking Care of Granny;’ and how learning new things boosts your brain
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we shatter the notion that you are ever too old to try something new and share how to break through doubt and embrace fresh adventures.
Plus, we highlight the rising number of male caregivers with creator Dugan Meredith — the force behind “Taking Care of Granny” — who shares essential lessons and resources for families navigating care.
Learning something new, such as picking up a new hobby later in life, can be fun, and it also sharpens your brain health, keeps you engaged and builds connections across generations, according to the Aging Untold experts.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, says the discomfort is actually doing something good beneath the surface.
“The brain is always changing. New connections, what we call neuroplasticity,” Rogers said. “And also you’re waking up the brain, and that’s a good thing. So it makes you just stay alert and all that. And you can look at reaction time to things actually improve.”
See the full story to find out how learning boosts your brain and which new skills the Aging Untold experts have challenged themselves to learn.
When Dugan Meredith started to open up and share what life is like as a caregiver for his mother-in-law, Granny, he never imagined how much support he would find through an online community.
Granny showed signs that something was wrong when she was forgetting how to go pick up the grandchildren from school, getting lost and inviting strangers back to the house. Then, Granny was diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia.
One day, Meredith was sitting at his kitchen table with a cup of coffee, recording himself as he talked about his frustrations before posting the video to TikTok.
That led him to a community of other caregivers he didn’t know existed.
