title: Maine getting federal money to help reduce suicide by veterans
text:
Maine getting federal money to help reduce suicide by veterans
Maine is getting $1.35 million from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs to help prevent suicides by veterans in Maine.
The money will be shared by Easterseals Maine and the Maine Department of Defense, Veterans and Emergency Management.
The money for Maine is part of $112 million in grants awarded to 191 organizations nationwide to support suicide prevention efforts.
The money comes from the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program (SSG Fox SPGP) and will become available at the start of fiscal year 2027.
According to the VA, there are approximately 105,000 veterans living in Maine. That is roughly 8% of the total adult population, giving Maine one of the highest veteran populations per capita in the country.
According to data from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, 43 Maine veterans died by suicide in 2022. That year, the suicide rate among veterans in Maine was nearly double the rate among non-military members.
While Maine’s veteran suicide rate was similar to the national average, it was higher than every New England state except Vermont and more than double the rate in Massachusetts.
The VA says reaching veterans in need of help can be a challenge. The VA says 61% of veterans who died by suicide in 2023 — the most recent year for which data is available – were not receiving VA healthcare in the last year of their lives.
“Community organizations play a vital role in strengthening the support network available to Maine Veterans,” said Medical Center Director Tracye B. Davis. “These grants provide Veterans with lifesaving support and ensure they have access to the care and resources they deserve right here in our community.”
In fiscal year 2026 through September 20, the VA answered more than 1.3 million calls, chats and texts from veterans in need through the Veterans Crisis Line, a 7.1% increase over the prior year.
In 2018, the federal government launched RISK ID, a comprehensive suicide risk evaluation screening that helps the VA flag and care for at-risk veterans.
In May 2026, the VA announced it was screening veterans for suicide risk and providing comprehensive evaluations. Through August 2026, the VA completed more than 5.5 million suicide risk screenings, approximately 100,000 more veterans screened in 2025.

title: Study ranks the most and least affordable states for retirees
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold)— Where retirees choose to live can make a significant difference in how far their savings go — and a study from Retirement Living identifies the states that offer the most financial breathing room.
Retirement Living ranked states based on housing costs, cost of living and tax-friendliness. Ella Gomes, a media relations specialist at Retirement Living, said the findings reflect a growing affordability challenge for retirees nationwide.
“Retirement affordability matters more than ever because many Americans are facing higher housing costs, health care expenses and everyday living costs than they did just a few years ago,” Gomes said. “And at Retirement Living, we wanted to understand which states provide retirees with the best opportunity to make their savings last longer.”
West Virginia ranked first as the most affordable state for retirees, with the lowest housing costs in the nation, according to the study. Median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the state is $643 a month. Mississippi, Alabama, Oklahoma and Arkansas round out the top five.
“What’s especially interesting is that these states aren’t just inexpensive in one area,” Gomes said. “They consistently perform well across housing, cost of living and taxes, making them well-rounded options for retirees who are looking to max their retirement savings.”
California tops the list of least affordable states for retirees, followed by Hawaii, Washington state, Oregon and Colorado.
“Here we see almost the opposite regional trend where the least affordable states are heavily concentrated in the West and the Northeast,” Gomes said. “Half of the bottom 10 are Western states, while New Jersey, Massachusetts, New York — those represent the Northeast. And these regions tend to have much higher housing costs, but they’re also more expensive when it comes to everyday expenses like groceries and transportation and taxes.”
For retirees considering relocation, Gomes said looking beyond a single expense category is essential. Day-to-day costs, health care access and proximity to specialists should all factor into the decision.
“It’s not only important to account for healthcare costs, but also picking a location where you can ensure you’ll have access to quality care and specialists for however your needs change over time,” Gomes said.
Retirement Living ranked all 50 states in the study. The full rankings and methodology are available on the organization’s website.

title: Maine’s Blue Economy will form its future
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rhiannon Hampson serves on the Maine Blue Economy Week Planning Committee and is vice president for economic development at the Gulf of Maine Research Institute.
Long before we ever knew it as Maine, people lived and worked along the more than 3,500 miles of coastline we call home. For thousands of years, the Gulf of Maine has sustained our communities — we have harvested these waters, building our lives around its tides and seasons.
Our relationship with the sea has never been static. The movement of people and industry, changes in fish populations and the shifting demands of trade have continually pushed Maine’s coastal communities to reinvent themselves, to innovate and adapt.
That instinct to adapt is one of Maine’s oldest strengths. We see it in the fishing boats steaming out at dawn — evolving from small wooden dories to the fast boats that thrill kids and adults at summertime races, and now moving toward electrification. It shows up in the aquaculture farms growing food for their neighbors, and it drives the innovation of researchers and entrepreneurs who are creating solutions to the challenges those fishermen and farmers face.
The numbers set the stage but do not tell the whole story. The almost $6.8 billion in economic activity and 90,000 jobs supported by Maine’s ocean-related businesses are not legacy numbers. They are dynamic and reflect an economy that is still changing. The legislatively established Blue Economy Task Force 2.0 identified five sectors of opportunity for growth here in Maine: aquaculture and marine vegetation, marine biotechnology, ocean data and research, resilient coastal infrastructure and sustainable boatbuilding and marine propulsion.
This growth is not guaranteed, but the challenges we face can define our opportunity to support it. Climate change is not only rapidly warming the Gulf of Maine and reshaping the species available to our fishermen, but it is also pressuring our roads and working waterfronts — critical infrastructure for a thriving economy.
Few places in the country are as well positioned as Maine to turn those challenges into new solutions given the expertise we have developed here through investment in our colleges, scientific institutions and coastal industries. That expertise and experience in responding to these pressures and shifts are why our researchers, engineers, educators and community development organizations are in demand nationally as other states seek to solve these challenges.
This is why we are convening Maine’s first Blue Economy Week (Sept. 29-Oct. 2), because the time is now. It is a way to have scientists, investors, students, fishermen and educators come together to chart our course. It is an opportunity to collectively ask: How do we keep and build upon what Maine already does well while continuing to innovate to meet this moment?
We have never been a state that waits for the future to arrive, an identity demonstrated by our motto, Dirigo: “I lead.”
The blue economy is not a departure from our story; it is just the next chapter. We hope you will join us in writing it.

title: Man accused of exposing himself to children on a school bus twice in one week
text:
TOWN OF WATERTOWN, N.Y. (WWNY/Gray News) - A man is accused of exposing himself to children on a school bus twice in one week
Daniel Iles, 32, is charged with two counts of public lewdness and two counts of child endangerment, according to the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office.
Iles allegedly exposed his genitals while driving next to a school bus on Interstate 81 in Town of Watertown, New York. A 16-year-old student reported seeing the man fondling himself, according to officials.
A week later on Sept. 22, Iles allegedly exposed himself again while driving next to a school bus, also on Interstate 81 in the Town of Watertown, New York. A 16-year-old student reported the incident and officials said they were unsure whether the same student witnessed both incidents.
School resource officers reviewed video from the buses’ surveillance cameras that confirmed the reported incidents.
The cameras captured the license plate number, which led to Iles’ arrest.
Iles was arraigned on the charges and released.

VETERANS CORNER: I wish all was good at VA
text:
Good day my friends, I wish all was good but such is not the case. Oh, I’m not the barer of doom and gloom but I try my best to deal with the truth and to the betterment of our veterans and families.
The cafeteria talk of the day targets the VA once more and how unhappy the employees are and how fearful they are of their jobs. There has been so much turn over it makes anyone wonder about what will happen next and to whom. It seems through my observation that those receiving less are more fearful and are seen less. They are working faster and harder and really don’t have time to be sociable anymore. I personally, after more than 45 years of arduous service to all who may have needed me find the lack of interplay and silence defining.
I always enjoyed the chit chat we shared throughout the day. Now it’s just, “hi” as they pass by. They don’t want to be seen socializing. This makes for a very caustic environment. Where does this all begin? From what I have been told it starts in the administration office. You have to be very careful of what you do or say. A fearful environment is not a very good environment. The only people that I can really speak with are those who can say, “I don’t give a damn, I have been here for 30 years so they can do what they want”.
That is my major source of information lately. Some of the negatives that must be topics to be avoided are the ones I like to write about; not because they are fun or good but because they are full of meaning and truth and let me know why people I really care about have become so withdrawn. I don’t know why but the names Tracye Davis and Ryan Lilly comes up very often, or perhaps I do know, or believe I do. I have never been convinced otherwise and I have written those names many times. Unfortunately, there has never been one time I have written those names in a good way. I believe some of the reasons are because there has never been anything good that came out of those names. Of course, that is my opinion, but realize those opinions come from somewhere. I just don’t make them up and this isn’t a best selling novel.
This week we have several issues presented not only by employees but by veterans and their families. One issue mentioned in the elevator while heading for the seventh floor was that of all the duck defecation on all the sidewalks, and some veterans struggling to avoid such while trying to navigate a wheelchair. It is a smelly thing to get on your shoes and on the wheels of your chair. Julie and I have to navigate it almost every day. Don’t take me wrong, we love our ducks and how friendly they are. They waddle across the street at their own pace and when they have young it is quite cute. However, they do some times have an arrogant side and will stop in the middle of the road until you shoe them out. Anyway, you have to realize they came here because it is safe and have their babies. So, what once was a dozen is now a hundred. Ducks like many of God’s little creatures like safety and well being. When they have their young they train them, then they prepare them for a long journey to Mexico for the winter. The problem is they are territorial. So, when they leave and return in the spring their once upon a time babies call this home also, and they are now ready to breed also. The same happens with deer. They multiply until they become a problem. Hunting only takes so many. We’ve even had a season on them in years past. How do you do that with ducks on your porch? Oh well, I’m sure administration will come up with a solution.
Our next problem facing we veterans on the VA campus is the allocation and dispersement of our annual budget of approximately $385 million. Which serves 53,000 veterans. That would allow each vet a little more than $700 for care. However, that hasn’t included the physical plant or payroll and miscellaneous. So, the government may stretch to $571 million. That is more realistic, yet we still have to squeeze the physical plant and payroll. So, let’s pay the administration and cut the medical. In my opinion the VA farming out the medical seems to be more costly, with hotels, restaurants, tolls and mileage. That doesn’t seem correct for me, how about you? My math may not be totally accurate, but it’s close.
The way I see it we are going the wrong way. We lose doctors and staff at an ever increasing rate yet administration is strong. What does that tell us? People being promoted to positions they aren’t qualified for just causes more attrition as was the case of Dr. Jeff Walawander. He couldn’t run the hospital with his young years and lack of experience so he left for another group. He was a fine, loved dentist but a poor administrator, “Murphy’s Law” coming from the desk of the administrator, and they know that’s true as most of them should not be there either. “The old days are gone”.
In the old days you came up through the ranks and knew as you grew. Today, the rules are different; it’s the color of your skin or your sex and quoters of each. We are in a sad state of affairs. It’s time for our secretary Collins to do what he is paid the big bucks for, “leadership”.
My last two negatives are in the back and front of our beloved Togus building. No, I am not referring to the sinking of the “Fisher House”, although that is an unanswered issue. It’s rumored that maybe insurance may pay for it, but would they if they had proof that they were warned? No, our immediate problems as veterans, and remember this facility belongs to us, can be changed, I’m working on it. Problem one is our little entrance bridge has been condemned as unsafe. I have been told we may be looking north of one million dollars. So, when you come to work either come in the back gate or use the bare right avenue to the facility. Who is responsible for facility and grounds maintenance?
Last but not least I have been informed that all the handicapped entrances in the rear of the building are closed, not admissible. Is that even legal? I am not sure perhaps one of you will fill me in, as I do my weekly pass through the corridors. It is a hospital and not all who work or volunteer there are OK with stairs. The only real handicap entrance I know of is the gym/pool entrance. Why lock it? It doesn’t make any sense but that should be expected from this administration. Paranoia is a very powerful thing as is power itself. Keep your eyes open. I don’t mention names. Remember, veterans are the reason VA exists and freedom is spelled VETERAN. Love and respect those who make it all possible.
Remember that old and sometimes haggard, unkempt fellow wandering in our facility once stood tall, handsome and was admired. Time and pain changes much over time but kindness and respect puts a smile on ones face and tends to draw the shoulders up and improve the gate, if possible. Have a great and safe weekend and God be with you all.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: ‘His loss is deeply personal’: Police officer found dead hours after disappearing while wakeboarding, chief says
text:
PUEBLO COUNTY, Colo. (Gray News) - A police officer in Colorado was found dead hours after disappearing while wakeboarding.
On Sunday, Colorado Parks and Wildlife said in a post that officers were searching for a missing person in “the area of Peck Creek/west-central area of” the park following a single boat incident.
The report came in around 5:30 p.m.
The following day, it was announced that the missing person was found at about 2 a.m. The body of the victim, who was in 48 feet of water, was recovered 45 minutes later with the assistance of a remotely operated vehicle.
Pueblo Police identified the victim as Cpl. Stephen Biggs. The department said that he was in a wakeboarding accident.
Pueblo Police said that Biggs had been a member of the department since 2010, serving as a patrol training officer and with the SWAT team. They noted that Biggs was the recipient of 10 letters of commendation, three Medal of Valor awards and the Distinguished Service award.
“Working with Stephen was an honor, and his loss is deeply personal,” Pueblo Police Department Chief Chris Noeller said in the news release. “His courage, dedication, and commitment to his fellow officers meant so much to our department. I was proud to serve with him, and I will miss him. My heart is with his family, his friends, and everyone in our department who is grieving his loss.”
Pueblo Police said that the late officer’s patrol car will be parked at the department’s headquarters as a sign of respect.

title: Transport of massive equipment through Maine will take longer than expected
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Transport of massive equipment through Maine underway, but taking longer
The transport of a massive piece of equipment from Jay to South Portland is underway, but is now expected to take longer than initially expected.
Transport company Barnhart Crane & Rigging is moving a heat recovery steam generator from the former Pixelle/International Paper mill in Jay to Turner Island on Elm Street in South Portland.
The load is just over 219 feet long, 20 feet wide, 19.5 feet high and has a gross weight of 683,530 pounds. Due to the size, the load and support team will take up most, if not all, of the road in several areas.
"We've got a tractor pulling and a tractor pushing because the magnitude of the load would be too great for one tractor to pull and take care of on its own," said Lucien Richard, site manager for JGT2 Redevelopment, the company that owns the former mill site in Jay.
The transport made it as far as Turner on Wednesday morning and the plans are for it to move over Streaked Mountain on Wednesday night.
Turner Fire Rescue said the convoy would be moving from the area of the Turner Plaza down Route 4 to Route 117 on Wednesday evening. Significant traffic delays and temporary closures were expected at about 7 p.m. at the intersection of Route 4 and Route 117.
Route 117 will be closed from Weston Road to East Hebron Road from approximately 6:00 PM until midnight.
The convoy is expected to make it to Oxford by Thursday morning. Thursday night into Friday morning, the convoy is expected to go from Oxford to Gray and then stay staged in Gray until Sunday night. Sunday night into Monday morning, the goal is to move the equipment from Gray to Buxton and then make the final move from Buxton to South Portland overnight Monday into Tuesday.
The remaining route includes Route 4, Route 117, Route 26, Route 202, Route 22, Route 1 and then Broadway to Elm Street along the waterfront in South Portland.
That will take the roughly 90-mile route through towns like Turner, Buckfield, Paris, Norway, Oxford, Poland, Gray, Windham, and Scarborough. The route takes the convoy over Streaked Mountain.
This transport is just the first of several. Officials say eight more oversize loads will need to move along the same route, but the schedule for the remaining moves won't be set until the first delivery is complete.
All nine generators will end up at the end of Elm Street in South Portland, near the oil tanks. The massive metal boxes will be hoisted onto barges and delivered to paper mills in three different states: Alabama, Virginia and Louisiana.

title: InvestigateTV+: The crime targeting young people online
text:
(InvestigateTV) — In a matter of hours, a text conversation ends in a teen’s death, spotlighting a crime authorities say increasingly targets young people online.
Plus, a woman keeps a mysterious and embarrassing symptom to herself until an E.R. visit reveals a diagnosis on the rise among people under 50.
Then, a mother comes face-to-face with the nurse who saved her daughter decades ago.
‘Psychological warfare’
Bryce Tate’s death was the result of a crime the FBI reports is quickly growing across the country.
His father, Adam Tate, is sharing his story to educate other parents. He and his wife, Amanda, said they were initially unfamiliar with the scam police say killed their son.
“We had never heard of the term sextortion before,” Adam Tate said.
Endometrial cancer rates are rising
The biggest overall risk of developing cancer comes later in life, as the typical age for a diagnosis is 67 years old.
But recent data shows a growing number of young people are receiving the life-changing news. Researchers at the National Institutes of Health found between 2010 and 2019 the incidence of fourteen cancer types increased among people under 50.
One of those is uterine cancer, which also saw an increase in death rates at younger ages. Most uterine cancers happen in the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus.
Veterans hike and talk mental health
A small group of military veterans in the Las Vegas Valley has started a monthly ritual of joining together on hikes throughout the valley.
The group, organized by Navy veteran Nathan French, meets on the first Saturday of each month and invites military veterans across the valley to participate.
Forty years flying with newborns
A nurse who transports critically ill newborns to a Level Four NICU in the nation’s capital has marked 40 years on the job.
Janice Berry works on the transport team at Children’s National Hospital, flying with newborns to bring them to the hospital’s NICU.

title: Baby defying odds, meeting milestones as 1 of only 15 with rare genetic mutation
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A Louisiana couple says their baby girl has been defying the odds since birth.
Wren Michelle Roberts was born with a rare genetic mutation that has caused three heart defects, placed her stomach in her chest, and left her with spina bifida and no spleen.
Wren’s father, Nick Roberts, says doctors told the family their daughter is one of only about 15 such documented cases.
“The body is not being told by the brain how to properly form everything,” Nick Roberts said.
The parents added that doctors told them that Wren would likely not survive birth. But now, three weeks later, they say they are watching her meet developmental milestones.
Dr. Gabriella Bluett-Mills, Wren’s complex care pediatrician at Ochsner Children’s Hospital, said Wren is meeting milestones after spinal surgery at 1 week old.
“I’d say Wren is one in a million,” Bluett-Mills said. “I’ve never seen all of these things together before.”
Wren drinks from a bottle, takes a pacifier, yawns, coos, raises her arms and sneezes. She even cried for the first time.
“To hear her cry was just heaven, heaven sent,” Wren’s mother, Savannah Roberts, said.
Wren’s parents said they first learned something may be wrong about 20 weeks into Savannah Roberts’ pregnancy during routine tests.
Doctors later told them Wren would likely die before she was born, and then that she would not survive much longer after birth.
“We planned on having a funeral (the weekend after she was born),” Nick Roberts said.
Savannah Roberts said that, as a nurse, she sees the ugly side of things and struggled with considering all that was to come after first learning her pregnancy had complications.
But she said now, her daughter has made her believe in miracles.
“There’s a reason that it happened, and now looking at her, I’m so glad that it happened because I don’t want any other baby,” she said. “I want her.”
Bluett-Mills said Wren’s case serves as an important reminder to health care professionals.
“We don’t know every single answer,” Bluett-Mills said. “We will have to just follow along and let her lead us and kind of show us what she’s capable of doing.”
Wren’s father started the Facebook group Wren’s Warriors to provide family and friends with updates on her progress. The page now has thousands of followers.
Fundraisers to help the family with ongoing medical costs can also be found on the page.

title: Cruise ship that frequents Maine caught in Border Patrol effort targeting child porn
text:
Child porn on cruise ships: Dozens of crewmembers removed, including from ship that visited Maine
A cruise ship that makes frequent stops in Portland has been caught up in a U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) effort targeting the possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation material among cruise ship crewmembers.
CBP says, as of Friday, it has removed 87 people at the Port of Boston from cruise ships as part of Operation Tidal Wave. That includes six citizens of the Philippines removed from a Norwegian Cruise Line ship called Breakaway in Boston on Sept. 20. CBP says all six admitted to previously having child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation material.
The Breakaway stopped in Portland twice in August and four times in September, including this week.
Maine's Total Coverage is working to learn if any of the implicated crewmembers were in Maine or were detained here.
The Breakaway has a crew capacity of more than 1,600 and a guest capacity of about 3,900.
The Area Port of Boston plans to continue the operation through the end of the fiscal year.
"The success of Operation Tidal Wave reflects the unwavering dedication of our officers and partners to protect the most vulnerable," said Acting Director of Field Operations Julio Caravia. "Let the removal of these 87 be a message to others: we will not accept this exploitation and CBP will not stop identifying and arresting the individuals who participate in it."
Operation Tidal Wave also resulted in action against 27 crewmembers through the San Diego office and 15 people through the San Juan office this year.

title: 7 Mainers recommend books that should be on the big screen
text:
It’s no secret that books inspire some of Hollywood’s greatest hits. “Project Hail Mary,” “Wuthering Heights” and “The Odyssey” inspired some of the year’s biggest releases. With readers and moviegoers enjoying their favorite stories from page to screen and back again, it’s easy to read a novel cinematically. And sometimes it’s shocking when a book has not been adapted for film.
The Press Herald asked seven Maine writers, booksellers and editors about the books they think deserve dramatic adaptation.
‘The Art Thief’ by Michael Finkel
“The Art Thief” is the heist film Hollywood needs. Michael Finkel’s nonfiction chronicle follows Stephane Breitwieser, who stole more than 300 masterpieces not for profit but out of obsessive devotion to beauty. His brazen museum raids, compulsive hoarding and the bizarre international manhunt that followed read like a psychological thriller built for the screen. The story offers rich visual tableaux, moral complexity and a protagonist who is as contemptible as he is mesmerizing. Why settle for invented capers when this stranger-than-fiction chronicle already possesses every ingredient of a gripping cinematic experience?
— Sambara Seidel, manager of Nonesuch Books
‘Canon’ by Paige Lewis
There are so many books, across genres, that I’d love to see as films or miniseries or even straight-up TV shows. But the novel I most need to see adapted for screen? “Canon” by Paige Lewis. A self-described “nonbinary epic,” the book follows two unlikely and deeply imperfect heroes as they embark on holy quests. There are talking whales and oysters, mysterious islands, a grab bag of saints and villains, magic powers and spells, meditations on mental health and queerness and a whole lot of regular human neurosis and anxiety. It is profound, weird, surprising, funny, beautiful and cinematically entertaining.
– Hannah Matthews, marketing coordinator, Back Cove Books
‘My Friends’ by Fredrick Backman
“My Friends” makes me nostalgic for a time I’ve never exactly lived. While the story itself is beautiful, it is Fredrik Backman’s writing that is the most compelling. This heartbreaking, hopeful, hilarious book follows teenage Louisa, an orphan, and her unlikely partnership with middle-aged Ted as they return a piece of art to its home. On their journey, Ted explains the story of growing up with his three best friends. Both Ted and Louisa must confront what it means to love and to be loved. Backman’s circuitous story reveals something fundamental about all humans: how we handle loneliness.
– Charlotte DiAdamo, Press Herald intern
‘The Sweetness of Water’ by Nathan Harris
The Civil War just ended. Two brothers, former slaves, live in the woods behind a white couple’s Georgia farm. Their unfolding relationship and collaboration inflames the community. Every time I picked up Nathan Harris’s “The Sweetness of Water,” I felt transported into this world. It’s so vividly written. Add to that 19th-century phrasing, painful depictions of white supremacy and language so exquisite I wrote the author a fan letter. (He wrote me back! Swoon.) Short listed for the Booker Prize and selected by Oprah for her book club, this book feels like essential American reading.
– Melissa Pritchard, Maine Trust creative services director
‘The Secret History’ by Donna Tartt
It’s incomprehensible that Donna Tartt’s debut novel, “The Secret History,” with its cinematic, twisty plot, hasn’t yet been made into a film. Fans have made a parlor game out of dream-casting this inverted unraveling of a detective story on a college campus (tell me Gwyneth Paltrow and Jude Law circa “Talented Mr. Ripley” wouldn’t have made the perfect Charles and Camilla Macaulay) but at least three attempts to adapt it for film have failed. It’s not the easiest story to boil down in two hours: A cult leader-like classics professor and the clique of preppy, sociopathic students who worship him and misbehave in particularly lurid fashion, but it’s time for another try.
– Katherine K. Lee, news and culture editor
‘The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay’ by Michael Chabon
While Michael Chabon’s Pulitzer Prize winning novel, “The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay,” got the opera treatment last year, the expansive, earnest and bright story of two cousins who write a smash-hit superhero comic series during World War II is overdue for Hollywood. Joe Kavalier, a magician and escape artist, flees Nazi-occupied Prague and shows up on the doorstep of his American cousin, Sam Clay, in Brooklyn. As the nearly 700-page novel charts the duo’s ascension during the Golden Age of comic books, it also tells a gripping tale on immigration and family across time.
– Michael Colbert, books editor-at-large
‘The Southern Book Club’s Guide to Slaying Vampires’ by Grady Hendrix
Set in Charleston during the 1990s, “The Southern Book Club’s Guide to Slaying Vampires” tells the story of Patricia Campbell and the true-crime obsessed women in her tight-knit book club. Patricia’s life is far from exciting. Her husband is too busy to pay attention, her children don’t listen and her ailing mother-in-law needs constant care. All of that changes when James Harris shows up. James is handsome, well-read, mysterious and quickly has Patricia’s friends wrapped around his finger. But there’s something strange and otherworldly about James that Patricia can’t quite place, and when local children begin to go missing she can’t help but feel that he might be involved.
– Rachael Conrad, MWPA membership and program coordinator

title: Tracy Bonney-Corson, Parkman Nursing Leader And Rail Yard Brewing Co-owner, Dies In Crow Hill Road Crash
text:
Former Piscataquis County VP Of Nursing-Turned-Brewery-Owner Found Deceased After Crash In Parkman Tuesday Night
Authorities in Piscataquic County are trying to piece together the details of a deadly crash that claimed the life of one person late Tuesday evening.
According to the Piscataquis County Sheriff's Office, their communications center received a notification just before 11:30 PM, that a crash had occurred somewhere in the area of the Crow Hill Road in Parkman, so they sent authorities out to investigate.
"A deputy along with Guilford Fire and Mayo Ambulance were dispatched to the area. Upon checking the area, the deputy discovered a vehicle gone off the road and crashed into a telephone pole. The deputy started searching for the operator and found the female operator had been ejected from the vehicle."
Read More: Maine Authorities Locate Missing Blue Hill Boater
The sheriff's office says the woman, 61-year-old Tracy Bonney-Corson of Parkman, was pronounced dead by the EMTs on the scene.
Corson was well known in the Piscataquis County community as a former VP of Nursing at a local hospital for over 30 years and more recently co-owner of Rail Yard Brewing, which she opened with her long-time friend, John Riitano, last year.
Read More: New Restaurant And Brewery Opening In Milo, Maine Soon
Riitano addressed Corson's passing on the Brewery's social media page.
"It is with an extremely heavy heart that I have to report the passing of my dear friend and business partner, Tracy Bonney-Corson... During this extremely sad time, please keep Tracy's family in your thoughts and prayers. Knowing Tracy, she would not want us to skip a beat, and she would insist we keep pushing forward! Tracy loved Trivia Night and loved the community support and love you all gave us at Rail Yard. Tracy wanted Rail Yard and Rusty Rail to be a gathering place for the community, and that is just what it has become. So, in Tracy's honor, we will press on and continue to be a community hub where we can gather to celebrate the good times and be there for each other in the sad times."
The Crow Hill Road, like many rural routes across the state, can often experience muddy conditions when the weather is wet. Providing access to places like Bennett Pond, and connecting with many secondary roads like the Armstrong and Trafton Roads, it's sometimes used as a cut-through of sorts.
Earlier this summer, the town replaced a culvert along a section of the Crow Hill Road, and shut it down for an afternoon, but the closure was temporary, and there were no other known issues to the roadway.
Read More: Maine State Police Search For Suspect After Skowhegan Drug Stop
Authorities will continue to investigate Tuesday night's crash. We will update the story when more details become available.
In the meantime, we send our deepest condolences out to Corson's family, friends and community in Piscataquis County.

title: Portland’s Lincoln Middle School needs $20M in immediate repairs, per facilities report
text:
Lincoln Middle School in Portland has nearly $20 million in obsolete infrastructure that should already have been replaced, according to a new assessment of the district’s three middle schools.
The details come amid the city’s effort to reorganize its middle school programming due to low building utilization, declining enrollment and facilities issues.
The school board passed a resolution in March calling on the superintendent to study the middle schools: Lincoln, King and Lyman Moore. It scaled back from explicitly calling for a reduction to two schools, although the latest facility assessment explores the enrollment implications of shuttering Lincoln.
Since the resolution, the district has hosted community engagement sessions on the topic and solicited feedback. Administrators presented an update on the work in August, and the district is currently recruiting community members to review a proposed design framework and provide comments through a form open until Oct. 4.
Part of the process involved a facilities assessment focused on the middle school buildings.
In a Monday meeting, the board’s committee for finance, personnel and operations heard an update from the architecture firm Harriman, which was hired by the district to conduct a larger facilities master plan. Harriman is reviewing buildings across the district for that study, but began with the middle schools as the school board prepares to make decisions about the future of those spaces.
All three schools are below capacity, Lisa Sawin from Harriman told the committee, but Lincoln is the lowest, with space for about 220 additional students. Across the district, there is space for 444 additional middle school students, based on a target of 85% building utilization.
An assessment of building conditions also showed Lincoln is in the poorest condition of the three schools, while Lyman Moore is in the best. Lincoln is the oldest of the three schools, originally constructed in 1897, while King was completed in 1950 and Lyman Moore in 1954.
Lincoln’s building has reached the end of life for almost all of its features, from code compliance to plumbing to fire protection. The cost to repair Lincoln’s obsolete infrastructure — elements of the facility that should have already been replaced — is $19.5 million, and looking a decade into the future, the school will require a total of $28 million in fixes.
That’s compared to under $3 million in immediate repair costs at each of the other schools.
Those estimates don’t include the cost of any renovations for programmatic changes or improvements, just critical repairs. Lincoln’s include a heating system replacement that will cost nearly $13 million alone, and other pressing fixes to the front entrance and roof.
Based on the capacity information and cost estimates, Sawin showed board members what would happen if the district closed Lincoln, due to its excess capacity, low population and outsized facility issues.
In that situation, Moore and King would actually be slightly overenrolled, by about 115 students, and could require renovations to accommodate the new students.
The firm also modeled closing both Lincoln and King, which would require nearly doubling the capacity of Moore. They’re also planning to simulate what might happen if the district moved fifth grade to middle school to make space for pre-K in the elementary schools.
Sarah Warren, chief of strategy for Portland Public Schools, said the numbers are meant to help guide the district’s conversation, but are not a conclusion.
“No one should read this as a particular outcome that is predetermined,” she said.
Warren said the details would be presented to the working group looking at the middle school operations, whose recommendations will eventually come before the full board.
“They are kind of scary numbers, admittedly, and clearly we’re going to have to raise money down the road — not too far down the road — one way or another,” she said. “But I just want people to know that we’re using this to have good conversations and study the problem, not to get quickly to a predetermined outcome.”
Sawin, from Harriman, said the district’s elementary schools are broadly in good shape, but the high schools also need work. Portland is currently applying for a grant from the state to consolidate all of its high schools into one campus that would also include technical programming and higher education.
The last major infrastructure project in the district wrapped up in 2024, after voters approved a $64 million bond in 2017 to renovate four elementary schools: Longfellow, Lyseth, Presumpscot and Reiche. Harriman was the architect on those projects as well.
Harriman’s full facilities study is due to be completed by December.

title: Woman accused of firing at home of Rihanna indicted on attempted murder and other felony counts
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A Florida woman accused of driving across the country to fire a rifle at Rihanna and A$AP Rocky’s home, hitting a trailer the celebrity couple was inside and a nursery where their kids were, has been indicted by a grand jury on 14 felony counts including attempted murder.
The indictment against 36-year-old Ivanna Lisette Ortiz of Orlando was unsealed Wednesday by a Los Angeles County judge.
Ortiz, appearing in court wearing yellow jail clothes, spoke only to her attorney, who entered a not guilty plea for her. The judge then ordered her held on $2.6 million bail.
The move came a day after another judge ruled that Ortiz is mentally competent to stand trial. The secret grand jury proceedings were held as Ortiz was undergoing months of psychiatric evaluation. The jurors returned their indictment June 18, but it was kept under wraps for three months until the judge ruled on her competency. Now, a case that appeared stalled — possibly permanently — is on a fast track to trial.
No one was injured in the March 8 shooting. Authorities allege Ortiz drove a Tesla up to the gates of the Beverly Hills-area property of the singing superstar and her rap star partner, A$AP Rocky, pointed an AR-15 style rifle out the window and fired at least 20 rounds toward the property and the neighboring house.
“This is a person who wanted to kill Rihanna,” Deputy District Attorney Alexander Bott said outside court. “Everyone else was collateral damage.”
Bullets tore through the Airstream trailer, according to a police report. Shots also struck the wall of their home’s nursery, where their three small children were with their nanny. Rihanna’s mother and several staffers also were in the home, and authorities say she also fired shots toward a neighbor’s house.
Both Rihanna and her mother, Monica Fenty, testified to the grand jury, as did Hollywood agent Tracey Jacobs, the owner of the neighboring house who was home at the time and is listed among the victims in the indictment.
Their testimony remains under seal but will become public in about two weeks unless the defense seeks to keep them secret and the judge agrees.
Rihanna told investigators just after the shooting that she “suddenly heard approximately ten loud sounds like something banging on metal,” and pulled Rocky out of a bed and onto the ground. She said she opened curtains and saw bullet marks in the windshield right in front of where she had been standing.
Deputy Public Defender Derek Dillman, Ortiz’s attorney, did not speak to reporters outside the courtroom, and a message seeking comment from the public defender’s office on the indictment was not immediately answered. Other than her not guilty pleas, her lawyers have not publicly addressed the charges, saying only that they would work to defend her rights.
Investigators said that on the day of her arrest, Ortiz told them: “I wasn’t attempting murder.”
Ortiz was charged with very similar counts in March. The new indictment supersedes those charges. The secret grand jury proceedings allow prosecutors to skip California’s preliminary hearing process, where evidence must be presented publicly to see if a trial is merited.
The indictment also charges Ortiz with 10 counts of assault with an assault weapon — one for each of the people on the two properties — and three counts of shooting at an inhabited dwelling or camper. It names the couple’s three children Rza, Riot and Rocki, all under age 5, as victims. The assault weapon counts carry a stiffer sentence than the original charges of assault with a semiautomatic firearm. Ortiz was the registered owner of the rifle, which she obtained in Florida, authorities said.
She could get life in prison if convicted of all counts.
Reports have been sealed on the psychiatric evaluations that paused the case shortly after it began, and there was no public discussion of the details of her mental state.
Prosecutors have not said anything about a motive or cited any connection between Rihanna and Ortiz, a longtime licensed speech pathologist. But in videos posted on Facebook and YouTube in the months before the shooting, Ortiz made increasingly angry comments on Rihanna that sometimes took the form of threats, at one point calling her a “devil.”
A nine-time Grammy Award winner, Rihanna has had 14 No. 1 hits on the Billboard Hot 100, including “We Found Love,” “Work,” “Umbrella” and “Disturbia.”

title: Lincoln native, UMaine grad named Norway Savings Bank president
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NORWAY — Following an extensive search process, Norway Savings Bank is proud to announce that Darci Hamm, chief operating officer and executive vice president of NSB, has been appointed as the bank’s 18th president, effective immediately. Hamm succeeds Dan Walsh, who has served as NSB president since 2020. Walsh will remain as chief executive officer of the bank until his retirement on Dec. 31, 2027, and will continue to serve as a member of the NSB Board of Directors following his retirement.
Hamm is a native of Lincoln, where she was valedictorian of her class at Mattanawcook Academy before earning a bachelor’s degree in business administration from the University of Maine. She has served at Norway Savings Bank since 1999 as an in-store banking administrator, regional vice president of retail banking, senior vice president of retail banking and executive vice president and senior retail banking officer. In 2023, Hamm was named chief operating officer, leading the bank’s enterprise strategy, planning and execution across asset management, commercial lending, retail banking, cash management, customer care, marketing and deposit and loan operations.
“When I walked into the Norway Branch in 1999 as a new member of the NSB Team, I never imagined that one day I would have the honor of being named president of our bank,” Hamm said. “As I assume my new role, I do so with deep gratitude and appreciation for the people who make this organization so meaningful. Together, we will continue to serve solely in the best interests of our team members, our customers, and our communities, and we look forward to welcoming new individuals, families and businesses in Maine and New Hampshire to this exceptional organization and experience.”
In addition to her duties at NSB, Hamm serves on the Board of Directors for hoMEworks, which has helped thousands of Maine residents make sounder decisions in the homeownership process, and has acted as an advisor and volunteer at a multitude of nonprofits, including the Olympia Snowe Women’s Leadership Institute and Junior Achievement of Maine.
“Darci has been instrumental in carrying out the mission and purpose of Norway Savings Bank for over 25 years,” Walsh said. “She is a tireless promoter of offering a positive and fulfilling environment for team members and a top-notch experience for customers. She has also contributed countless hours outside of the bank to improving our communities, from sharing her knowledge and expertise in increasing financial literacy to volunteering for many nonprofits while encouraging fellow team members to similarly offer their time and talents. As we celebrate our 160th anniversary as a bank, Darci is exceptionally prepared to guide NSB forward.”
“For decades, Darci has served as a leader, a respected team member, and a steward of growth and advancement at NSB. Her knowledge, experience, and genuine affinity for the bank were clear during our months-long search process,” Patricia Weigel, chair of the NSB Board of Directors and the bank’s 16th president, said. “Darci personifies the bank’s high achievement and support culture. She is a true team player, leading with integrity, humility, and purpose. The positive impact Darci has on those she encounters is beyond measure.”
Hamm lives in Yarmouth with her husband Mike and has two adult children, Gavin and Evan. In addition to the University of Maine, she is also a graduate of the New England School for Financial Studies and the Graduate School of Banking at Colorado.
Founded in 1866, Norway Savings Bank is a leading mutual banking and financial services company headquartered in Norway, Maine. As of June 30, 2026, Norway Savings Bank had $2.155 billion in total assets; 25 branch locations in Maine and New Hampshire; and divisions in trust and investment services, personal banking, and business banking. It has received an “Outstanding” rating for three consecutive Community Reinvestment Act Exams from the FDIC. Norway Savings has also received the Best Place for Working Parents designation for the last five years and was recognized with the “Best Wellness Employer – Gold Certification” for the eighth year in a row by Wellness Workdays. BauerFinancial has designated the Bank the “Best of Bauer” for earning and maintaining its highest 5-star rating for 36 continuous years. For more information, visit www.norwaysavings.bank.

title: MaineHousing awards a record $2.7 million to help agencies run winter warming shelters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MaineHousing has awarded a record $2.72 million in funding to 12 warming shelters from York County to Presque Isle this winter.
The funding will support safe, heated spaces in Bangor, Lewiston and Portland, as well as Augusta, Biddeford, Brunswick, Ellsworth, Orland, Presque Isle and Waterville. The facilities will offer a combined 474 beds for people during cold and dangerous winter weather, and most plan to stay open through April.
“Dangerous winter weather can put lives at risk, especially for people experiencing homelessness or housing instability,” MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan said in a news release Tuesday afternoon.
This year’s funding is the most money doled out in the five years that MaineHousing has offered this program. Last year, the Legislature gave the agency $2.3 million to distribute.
The organizations running the shelters can use the funding from the quasi-governmental agency for staffing, supplies, transportation, extended hours and other operating costs. Recipients of the warming shelter grants will work with their municipalities, emergency management officials and community partners to connect people in need to a warming shelter.
“We are grateful to the governor and the Maine Legislature for making these funds available,” Brennan said. “This investment helps local organizations prepare before winter and respond when dangerous weather threatens Maine people.”
Biddeford-based Seeds of Hope is the top recipient of this year’s funding. The nonprofit will get more than $660,000 — about $304,000 to support its 55-bed facility in Biddeford, and nearly $361,000 to operate a nightly warming shelter in Portland.
Seeds of Hope stepped forward in early September to operate the Portland shelter after the city sought an agency to run a winter shelter following the closure of its shelter for asylum seekers.
Portland Mayor Mark Dion said at the time that he had some concerns with Seeds of Hope taking the shelter on, noting that the city’s past partners couldn’t handle the capacity needs in Maine’s most populous area.
But Seeds of Hope Director Vassie Fowler said her staff is experienced in managing high-needs populations, complex situations and the operational demands that come with running a full-capacity warming center.
Still, the $360,720 for this winter’s shelter is less than the roughly $400,000 that the city received last year to operate a shelter that only opened based on certain thresholds. This year, the plan is for the facility to be open every night, regardless of temperature or snowfall.
Fowler declined to comment on the funding Wednesday.
Alter L/A, a 24-hour warming shelter in the Lewiston and Auburn area, received just under $390,000 for a 112-bed facility. That funding will primarily go toward staffing, said Kevin Boilard, the executive director.
The shelter employs around 25 people and plans to bring on an additional 12 to 15 staff members for the colder months. Last year, the shelter served more than 700 people, with an average of 112 per 24-hour period. It’s thought to be the only 24/7 warming shelter in the Twin Cities, Boilard said.
“The intention is not just to house (people), but to bring them in, make them warm and connect them to stability and the structure that most are looking for,” he said.
The other nine agencies receiving funding are:
- Augusta Overnight, $375,750 for 50 beds in Augusta
- Bangor Area Homeless Shelter, $10,000 for 5 beds in Bangor
- Brick Church, $427,650 for 65 beds in Bangor
- Tedford Housing, $225,450 for 30 beds in Brunswick
- Healthy Acadia, $263,025 for 35 beds in Ellsworth
- HOME Inc., $28,611 for 18 beds in Orland
- State Street Church, $52,000 for 18 beds in Portland
- Homeless Services of Aroostook, $112,725 for 15 beds in Presque Isle
- Mid-Maine Homeless Shelter, $172,845 for 23 beds in Waterville
The shelter funding is a piece of broader winter preparedness efforts across the state. MaineHousing also runs the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) and the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which both help eligible households with heating costs and emergencies.
Heating costs have soared in Maine, with the price of heating oil hitting a record $6.02 per gallon last week.
Steve Hoad, of Windsor, is just one of a large number of Maine homeowners who use heating oil to keep their homes warm during the winter. Hoad told the Portland Press Herald in early September that his farmhouse will cost him thousands more to keep warm this winter. He’s exactly the kind of person HEAP aims to help.
“We know many families are concerned about heating costs,” Brennan said. “Programs such as HEAP can help thousands of Maine households each year, and we urge people to seek help before they face a crisis.”
Staff Writer Emily Duggan contributed to this story.

title: Federal court halts Tennessee's first execution a woman in 200 years at last minute
text:
Tennessee governor orders outside investigation and halts executions after inmate survives lethal injection attempt
Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death Wednesday for a 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug. A death penalty expert said it was an unprecedented failure, and Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee halted the one remaining execution for the rest of the year.
Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn’t been told about her condition.
She had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay.
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday.
Gov. Bill Lee said in a statement that he has ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and that the remaining scheduled execution will not take place this year.
“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” he said.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that they “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”
The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is “singular and unparalleled.”
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Media witnesses detail the execution process
Media witnesses observing from a separate room said officials raised curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney.
“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love,” she said in her “last” words. She described herself as at peace.
But Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head and asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. It was not clear what she was referencing.
By 8:26 p.m., execution witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered.
Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday to the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit court and a district court.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution: In May state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. The case garnered widespread attention in part because of a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer’s body, and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s.
Stay of execution was swiftly appealed
Pike was initially scheduled to be put to death in the morning, and witnesses had gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay. That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.
The attorney general’s office appealed to the Supreme Court, saying that halting the execution at the last moment traumatized Slemmer’s family and rewarded “abusive delay tactics” by Pike’s attorneys.
Later in the day, the high court cleared the way for the execution to proceed. The conservative majority did not explain their order, while the three liberal members signed a dissent that said Pike’s claims deserved a closer look.
Pike did not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argued that the state should consider her age at the time, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse.
Case renewed debate on the death penalty for teens
As the execution date drew near, debate renewed over the death penalty for young offenders.
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike’s death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds in Tennessee have had such sentences vacated.
After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn’t “put the brakes on.”
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in a statement.
Victim's mother says she is waiting for death sentence
Slemmer’s mother had traveled to Nashville in the hopes of witnessing the execution of her daughter’s killer. She told The Associated Press on Saturday that she had waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.
“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” May Martinez told The Associated Press in a telephone interview on Saturday.
Martinez could not be immediately reached by telephone for comment after the execution was halted.
The killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satan, into her body.
Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.
Executions of women are rare in the US
Since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976, 18 women have been put to death, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday.
Tennessee announced in 2024 that it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged that it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were tested properly.
___
This story has been updated to correct that Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. local time, not 11 a.m. and that the lawyers filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee Supreme Court, not U.S.
___
Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, Ed White in Detroit, Hallie Golden in Seattle and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

title: Letter: It’s time for Congress to rein in political spending
text:
As we approach the November election, political spending in Maine and around the country has started to skyrocket. Political ad spending for the midterm election is expected to exceed $11 billion for the first time, shattering the previous midterm record of $8.9 billion set in 2022.
Mainers are tired of this pay-to-play system. In recent years, we’ve passed several new laws to help rein in the dominance of money in our political system. In 2023, Maine passed a historic referendum to ban foreign government spending in state elections. The initiative passed with 86% support, the largest margin of victory of any referendum in Maine’s history.
As part of this new law, the Maine Ethics Commission is required to issue an annual report about money in politics. The commission recently issued their third annual report. The report outlines different amendments in Congress that are aiming to address unlimited and unchecked political spending. The commission collected public comments from Maine voters to be included in the report and the testimonials are overwhelmingly positive, with the vast majority calling for Maine’s congressional delegation to do something about the problem.
I urge your readers to visit the Maine Ethics Commission website and look for their 2026 Report on Proposed Amendments to the U.S. Constitution. Learn about the different amendments in Congress and then ask your representatives to help address the issue of money in politics.
Chris Cayer
Stratton

title: UMaine men’s hockey team looks to regain its culture
text:
ORONO — On Tuesday, Ben Barr thanked the University of Maine men’s hockey team on behalf of himself and the entire coaching staff. They’re all getting their 40 winks every night, sound sleep from head hitting pillow to morning alarm, and that’s due in large part to the effort the Black Bears put in every day.
“I expect them to bring effort and attitude, and they’ve been bringing that every practice since we started,” Barr said after Tuesday’s practice. “That doesn’t mean we go out and win just because we work hard. There’s another level for that, but at least we know we’ll be in the fight with the work ethic I think we’ve established so far.”
The season opens this weekend with a pair of games at Holy Cross. The Black Bears, as Barr put it, are trying to find the program’s soul again.
Go ahead and call this a resetting season for the Black Bears, who followed the 2025 Hockey East championship with an 18-14-3 record last season. A few years ago, when Barr was starting a program rebuild, that would have been a cause for minor jubilation as a positive step.
A Hockey East crown and two straight appearances in the NCAA tournament changed expectations. A season with 18 wins isn’t progress anymore, it’s disappointment.
The 2025-26 season was one of upheaval across college hockey. For the first time, players from the three Canadian major junior leagues and Canadian colleges (U Sports) were NCAA eligible. It turned the recruiting landscape into the wild west. Yeah, this guy can play but is he a fit for our program? Often the question was met with a shrug and the hope that things would work out.
At Maine, the influx of CHL players was a mixed bag. Of the nine players Barr brought in from the CHL or U Sports last season, five have already left via the transfer portal. Good hockey players? Yes. The right fit for Maine’s blue-collar culture? No.
“For three or four years, we were building something. We were trying to do it a certain way. Then the whole world tips upside down as far as the NCAA stuff’s concerned. You have a little bit of a turbulent year as far some of the decisions we make,” said Barr, now in his sixth season as Maine’s head coach.
Barr can take blame for last season’s team culture issues, which reached its nadir in a December home loss to rival New Hampshire, but players know it starts with them. Team captain Owen Fowler knows what kind of team he wants to see on the ice. Fowler wants the Black Bears to use their size to forecheck hard and play gritty hockey, looking to erode the stamina of opponents.
“We’re going to wear teams down a lot. Kind of similar to my first year (that Hockey East title season), where there were definitely a lot of games we won in the third period,” Fowler said.
Maine has 15 newcomers on a 28-player roster. That’s a lot of turnover, Barr admits. Nine of the newcomers are transfers with college hockey experience. They bring a higher maturity level, and that’s a good thing.
If that maturity manifests as players willing to go after rebounds and tipped pucks to score goals, and guys who set screens to get a teammate an open shot, it will be a very good thing. Last season’s top four scorers are gone. Brandon Holt graduated. Josh Nadeau signed a pro contract with Montreal. Justin Poirier and Miguel Marques transferred.
“We have enough good hockey players on this team to go out against anybody. The execution piece is just finding that little bit of extra will. That will be the challenge,” Barr said.
Assistant captain Sully Scholle said he’s done talking about last season. The focus has to be on the now. Assistant captain Max Scott said this season’s team already feels like a tighter-knit group that last year’s ever was. Barr sees that, too, and noted that they care about each other, and that’s been evident for a couple months.
It didn’t take Barr long to lift Maine into college hockey’s upper tier again after more than a decade outside of it. Ups and downs are a given, and Barr noted that camaraderie and a willingness to work hard doesn’t translate into 10 goals a game.
It’s a sturdy foundation, though, and one the Black Bears need. It’s what will help determine if last season was a hiccup, or the start of a trend.

title: Rick Bennett can help unify a house divided
text:
“A house divided against itself cannot stand.”
In these times of division and danger, Abraham Lincoln’s prophetic words still ring true today. Our democracy cannot stand without an informed, aroused, consensus-seeking voting public.
The current level of public conversation is a petty, mindless, toxic gabble: polls, personal scandals, campaign strategies, money raised for campaign war chests. But in Maine’s current political race, I know of one candidate who persistently strives to raise the level of public conversation to: issues, policies, political platforms, voting records.
I know of one candidate who has consistently sought mutual understanding, consensus and bipartisan collaboration. I know of one candidate whose statecraft, long service in our state Senate and persistent voice of sense and sanity entitle him to stand in Lincoln’s long shadow.
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, please join me in voting for Richard Bennett, independent candidate for the governorship of Maine.
Steve Turner
Mechanic Falls

title: TSA officers no longer allowed to sit during ID checks, union says
text:
(CNN) — A union representing Transportation Security Administration officers said workers who check boarding passes and IDs will no longer be able to sit down while doing their job.
The TSA is removing all chairs at the check-in site, according to a branch of the American Federation of Government Employees union. Workers will now have to stand during their shifts.
The union said the chairs provide support for officers, and forcing them to stand all day goes against safety and common decency.
The policy change comes nearly two months after David Cummins took over as TSA administrator.

title: Peaks Island author and illustrator finds inspiration in an astronaut’s journey
text:
Earlier this year, NASA invited author and illustrator Jamie Hogan to watch the SpaceX Crew-12 launch into space. Hogan was working on a children’s book at the time detailing the life of the astronaut Jessica Meir. During this mission, Meir would be leading the crew on their journey to the cosmos. The invitation was an easy RSVP.
Jessica Meir’s fascination with space took root in her childhood growing up in Maine. Caribou is home to some of the darkest night skies in the eastern United States. Jamie Hogan’s new book, “The Cosmic Journey of Jessica Meir,” tells the story of Meir’s life, following her dream of becoming an astronaut. Meir’s ever-expanding life is what Hogan says brought her the title.
Jamie Hogan spoke with the Press Herald about the inspiration and creative process behind her book — out later this fall — about the Maine astronaut who reached for the stars.
I’d love to hear a bit about the inspiration for this story: Jessica Meir. How did you find her story?
Jessica Meir was up on the International Space Station — she was in the paper, and that’s where I read about her. At the time, I was developing my previous book, called “Sky Watcher.” In that book, Jessica Meir appears on the cover of this boy’s comic, so I was starting to learn about her. I thought her pursuits, her education and her passions all just seemed really visual to me. When it comes to picture books, the words are super important, but really, the pictures tell a lot of the story. The fact that she was a scientist, but she was doing things like diving in Antarctica with penguins to study their lung capacity, I just thought, “That’s the kind of thing that is exciting for kids to read about — that somebody is out having these risky adventures in pursuit of science.”
It’s a lifelong learning process to be an illustrator, to be doing books for kids, because you’re really trying to take important things about the world and distill them for children to be curious about. So in “Sky Watcher,” the theme is about light pollution, but it’s really about a boy going from the city, where he can’t see the stars, to someplace that looks a lot like Maine to see them. He has this epiphany there that the stars are there, and they’re real. Once I put Jessica into that book, I was determined she was going to be my next subject.
This book is based on a NASA astronaut. But you also show a history of interest in the natural world and the night sky in your illustrations. What’s your relationship to the sky? Why is that a scene you return to?
I have a memory of where I grew up in New Hampshire. My parents ran a motel, and I lived right near Franconia Notch in the White Mountains. They woke my sister and me up one night and said, “There’s Northern Lights. You need to come outside.” And it was just a really cool thing that I think we have to witness. We have to bear witness to nature and the wilderness. But it’s in us too. We’re also animals. I think it’s important to convey that. I live that and I want to share that.
I know you talk about the research that goes into illustrating, but this book requires research for your subject matter as well. How do you balance researching for your art and then also researching, in this case, for the narrative?
They both feed each other. I have an 11-by-14 ring-bound sketchbook that I consider my vessel of everything. I glue in things I cut out of the newspaper — articles about Jessica. When I went to Caribou, I said to the librarian, “You must have an archive on her.” And she’s like, “Yes, we do. Here it is.”
I was going through these folders, and I got to see her yearbook. She said that her dream was to go for a spacewalk. So there’s that piece of it too, that she’s been dedicated to the idea of being an astronaut since she was 5. That narrative is pretty much everywhere about her — that she knew as a child that’s what she wanted to do. She didn’t let go of that.
The drawing comes after I’ve done a lot of research, and then I start to think about how I am going to visualize this. Then my process usually begins with a storyboard.
I know you have illustrated many children’s books. What made you want to start writing them as well?
When I first started illustrating, I was doing things for newspapers and magazines, illustrating current events or things about food or culture. It was all for adults. It really wasn’t until I moved to Maine, had a child in 1996 and started buying kids’ books and reading to kids. Reading to my daughter changed my life. I felt like I wanted to do this. I wanted to illustrate a book. I wanted to write a book. It was becoming a parent and really being in the market for kids’ books and appreciating what amazing nuggets they are when they work well. Kids just want to hear them over and over again. They remember them even when they’re older.
Annabelle Allen is a writer living in Brooklyn, N.Y.

title: AN ENVIRONMENTALIST VOICE: The splitting of America
text:
It seems that most of what our politicians do is fight and call each other insulting names. Who benefits from this demonizing? Not the American people on the right or the left. The world is changing fast, and our government is not working well enough to deal with it.
But two groups of people do benefit from the gridlock in Congress: demonizing politicians and billionaires. Some politicians are naturally gifted at insulting, demonizing, and riling up their followers to fear, hate, and blame the politicians’ opponents. It’s easy to spot these politicians. Just listen for a few minutes, and if you start hating other Americans, you’ve got a demonizing politician. If he can make us mad enough, we may vote for him.
But how does this demonizing affect our country? Abraham Lincoln said, “A house divided against itself cannot stand.” Splitting America by making us hate each other certainly weakens us. It makes us less healthy, because chronic anger is bad for the heart. And it spoils our days: makes us less happy. And let’s face it. We all want America to be great for ourselves and our children. We are just listening to different media; different silos, so we are hearing completely different ways to make our country great. Nobody wants to harm their own country.
The other group of people who benefit from gridlock in Congress is the super-wealthy. They have loopholes that allow them to avoid paying anything in taxes, and the government leaves them alone: lets them do what they want. If our government began working together well, it might close some loopholes and regulate the super-wealthy in ways they wouldn’t like, but that would benefit 99 percent of us. But the billionaires donate enough campaign money to control our elections, and if they want, they can continue to support politicians who will keep insulting and fighting, rather than trying to solve problems.
Fortunately, the solution is simple. Identify the demonizers and stop listening to them, regardless of their political party. Vote for politicians who have respect for everyone. Then our leaders can start working together to make America great, again. If the demonizing politicians are consistently defeated, they will leave us alone.
The views of the author of this column are not necessarily those of The Town Line newspaper, its staff and board of directors.
Richard Thomas, Ph.D. is a recently retired psychologist in Waterville who specialized in treating trauma, addiction, depression, and anxiety.
