title: Hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin gives record $3B to Carnegie Mellon to build Miami campus
text:
Carnegie Mellon University announced Wednesday that hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin is donating $3 billion, with the bulk of the money for a new campus in Miami focused on societal challenges.
The Pittsburgh-based private research university said the gift is the largest ever single gift to a U.S. university. Other donations topping the billion-dollar mark include $1.8 billion from former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg to Johns Hopkins University in 2018. And Nike co-founder Phil Knight and his wife, Penny, also have been prolific donors, including a $2 billion gift to Oregon Health & Science University in 2025.
Griffin’s gift includes $2 billion to build a new 35-acre campus in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood, just north of downtown. The campus is expected to enroll around 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and doctoral students. Construction is scheduled to begin next year.
Rather than academic majors, it will focus on what the university and Griffin described in a news release as “grand challenge areas,” such as human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation.
The rest of the money will be divided evenly between the Pittsburgh campus’ computer science program, which will be renamed after Griffin, and other unspecified projects on the main campus.
“Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems,” Carnegie Mellon’s President Farnam Jahanian said in a news release praising Griffin. “ Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others.”
Colleges are facing growing pressure to prepare students for a workforce that is rapidly being transformed by AI. Job postings including AI and machine learning in the skills requirements or job title are exploding.
At the same time, financial pressures on higher education are mounting. International enrollment is dropping, just as many states are seeing their classes of high school seniors begin to shrink because of U.S. demographic changes. Meanwhile, expenses like fuel, healthcare and technology are rising.
Griffin, a GOP megadonor who founded the Citadel investment firm, owns a waterfront home in Miami, which is part of a growing metropolitan area whose population tops 6.4 million.
The area already is home to the University of Miami, a private research university; Florida International University, a public research university; and Miami Dade College, which started out as a community college but also offers some four-year degrees. Combined, enrollment at the three schools totals around 135,000. Several smaller private colleges are also based in the area.
But Griffin, who has donated over the years to causes such as medical research, charter schools and other universities, saw room for something new.
“The opportunity to bring Carnegie Mellon to Miami places our city at the heart of humanistic and scientific advancement and amplifies the University’s international reach and impact,” said Griffin, who is joining Carnegie Mellon’s Board of Trustees, in a news release.
Even before the announcement, Carnegie Mellon had growing ties to Florida, a state where conservatives have increased their influence on higher education.
Its computer science department runs a program designed to teach middle school students in Florida and several other states about AI. The university also is involved in a partnership with the Gates Foundation to deploy AI-powered course materials for introductory math classes at Miami Dade College.

title: How can we trust Susan Collins on the environment?
text:
I heat my home with a heat pump. It keeps the house warm through a Maine winter and costs less than the oil it replaced. It was one reason I was so disappointed that Sen. Susan Collins voted to advance the 2025 budget bill that rolled back the tax credits that help other Maine families make the same switch.
Sen. Collins often positions herself as an environmentalist, but her voting record doesn’t always reflect that. She earned a 0% rating from the League of Conservation Voters in 2024 and 31% in 2025, alongside her vote against the Inflation Reduction Act. Most recently, Collins voted to confirm Eighth Circuit judge Justin Smith, whose record as Missouri’s deputy attorney general included backing industry challenges to state clean water protections.
On May 18, Collins voted to confirm Stevan Pearce as director of the Bureau of Land Management, which oversees more than 245 million acres of public lands. Pearce has a track record of supporting the sell-off of public lands, conflicts of interest with the oil and gas industry and a history of trying to shrink and block the designation of national monuments.
Maine’s clean air, rivers and reduced dependence on heating oil didn’t happen by accident. Given her recent votes, how can Mainers trust Sen. Collins to protect our environment from big oil and gas?
Stephen Simpson
Portland

title: Surfer, fishermen team up to rescue 2 people and a dog from capsized boat
text:
Surfer, fishermen team up to rescue 2 people and a dog from capsized boat
A surfer and two fishermen rescued two people and a dog after their boat capsized in rough waters off Florida's shores.
Surfer, fishermen team up to rescue 2 people and a dog from capsized boat
A surfer and two fishermen rescued two people and a dog after their boat capsized in rough waters off Florida's shores.
A surfer and two local fishermen worked together Saturday to rescue two people and a dog after their boat capsized in rough waters off Palm Beach Shores in Florida.
AJ Castronovo, a surfer, witnessed the incident while riding waves.
"The second wave came; it was bigger, already breaking, and unfortunately, I noticed there was a boat," Castronovo said. "It was right in front of the wave. That wave came and just absolutely rolled the boat over on its side. Both people were ejected from the boat."
Castronovo quickly swam toward the capsized boat to help but found himself in danger as another wave approached.
"This boat is now coming at me. I figured this is about it for me; the boat is coming at me sideways, another wave behind it, nowhere for me to go," he said.
Miraculously, Castronovo managed to swim underneath the overturned boat, where he found the two people in distress.
"They seemed like they were breathing in water, weren’t doing too well," he said.
Castronovo pulled the pair onto his surfboard and began swimming them to safety. Soon, a local fisherman, Chad Smith, and his son arrived on a boat to assist.
"Chad Smith came up like he’s done it 100 times," Castronovo said.
Together, they hoisted the man and woman onto the fishermen’s boat.
As the rescue concluded, Castronovo recalled a surprising moment.
"He starts pulling away, and we hear another surfer saying, 'Hey, hey, what’s going on?' He lifts his hand up in the air and says, 'I got the dog,'" Castronovo said.
Authorities said the two people were taken to the hospital and are okay.
"If the people are out there, I hope you’re safe and get a new boat," Castronovo said.
Local fire rescue and the sheriff's office responded to the incident, too.

title: It’s not about the quantity of Collins’ votes, it’s about the quality
text:
It is an undeniable fact that, in our nation’s history, the current administration has the least qualified and most incompetent cabinet members heading our important agencies.
While Sen. Susan Collins frequently cites her record of never missing a vote in the Senate, it is the merit of those votes that matters. If readers followed the Maine Sunday Telegram’s column on how our legislators voted in the prior week, they may recall that she votes for Trump’s right-wing judge nominees. If they check further, they will find that Collins’ vote was one of those that put the notorious Florida District Court Judge Aileen Cannon on the bench during Trump’s first term.
Mainers deserve more than a rubber stamp when the U.S. Senate acts on important nominations and policy issues.
Ervin Snyder
Brunswick

title: Resident Evil: Funny Scary
text:
Resident Evil, directed by Zach Cregger, hit theatres on Sept. 18. Cregger based the film off of the Resident Evil videogame franchise from 1996. He is not the first to be inspired by this videogame, which has a six film series and a reboot from 2021 preceding this film. However, as the 2021 reboot had performed poorly, and the fandom remained eager for more, this was the perfect opportunity for another shot.
While I hadn’t seen the earlier films or played the videogame, I knew that I had to see this movie when I heard that Cregger was directing it. Being a fan of his earlier works, Weapons and Barbarian, I went to the theatres with high expectations. I was not disappointed.
The film stars Austin Abrams, who plays Bryan, a medical courier. Despite being a pretty average guy, Bryan soon finds himself playing a big role in stopping a virus that has leaked from a lab. The virus transforms people into mutated monsters.
What drew me into the film was Austin Abrams’s acting. The way Abrams plays Bryan reminds me of how any Gen-Z person would go about stopping monsters. He lacks survival skills. He can hardly shoot a gun. He constantly cracks sarcastic and self-deprecating jokes. Who could be a better person to save the world?
In addition to Austin Abrams’s fantastic acting, the suspense and jump-scares in this film are well executed. Each time Bryan seems to have made it away from the monsters, something jumps out and he tries to run away, facing many obstacles along the way. To add to this, the whole movie takes place at night, creating tension with Bryan’s use of his flashlight to see otherwise invisible evils.
This film has a lot of body horror, as well as a decent amount of gore. I’m not a huge fan of body horror, and feel like some parts went a little too far, but the suspense wouldn’t have been as intense without most of it. Much of the thrill was about not knowing what was around the corner and the body horror gave Bryan, and us, something to genuinely be afraid of.
Notably, some recent horror movies have commented on real world issues. In Obsession, a horror film that came out just this past May, it’s hard to miss the deeper meaning connecting Bear and Nikki’s relationship to issues of consent and obsession in relationships today.
However, I didn’t see much of a connection between Resident Evil and the real world. The one element that I did notice was Bryan’s phone call to his partner. Early on in the movie, he called her to discuss his doubts about being a father and being ready to have a baby with her. This relates to the modern struggles of parenthood, and it had the potential to prompt an important discussion for viewers, but Creggler didn’t spend enough time analyzing this to make it that impactful.
Other reviewers seem to agree on the fact that this movie isn’t trying to start a serious conversation about the real world. For example, film critic Owen Gleiberman said in a recent Variety review, “‘Resident Evil’ is a light and funky viral beastie thriller. Is it a good movie? Let’s call it a sweetly executed piece of escapist trivia.”
But that’s not a bad thing. Many people go to the movies to escape the stress of their real life and watching Resident Evil is a great way to escape our world and enter a dystopian world that is somehow both funny and scary.
Overall, Resident Evil is a great reboot. Unlike the other movies in the franchise, it takes the unique path of making the protagonist an average guy with minimal survival skills. This makes the film relatable and entertaining. If you’re a fan of suspense, comedy, body horror and dystopia, I would definitely recommend watching this film.

Trump touts $54 billion South Korea investment in Alaska gas pipeline
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump announced plans Wednesday for South Korea to invest $54 billion in a liquefied natural gas project in Alaska.
The project is expected to be completed in three years and would construct an 800-mile pipeline carrying natural gas from Alaska’s North Slope to the southern part of the state for export to Asian markets.
White House Correspondent Jon Decker asked Trump whether there was consideration of constructing another oil refinery in Alaska to lower gasoline prices, noting that energy costs in the state are high.
“I was in Alaska just a few weeks ago. Energy costs are exceedingly high. Is there any consideration of constructing another oil refinery - for gasoline to bring these prices down,” Decker asked.
“Gasoline prices in Alaska are going to tumble well as soon as the war ends which is going to be soon. Prices are going to come way down regardless. But gasoline prices, because of this project and a couple of others in Alaska are going to tumble,” Trump said.
Trump also commented on the Senate race between Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola (D). Peltola lost her bid for reelection to the House in 2024.
Decker asked Trump why he thought the race was as close as polls indicate.
“If the people of Alaska knew what I know, and I know the real facts, there wouldn’t even be a race,” Trump said.
Trump said he plans to travel to Alaska in the weeks before the midterms to energize Republicans and help Sullivan win a third term in the U.S. Senate.

title: Kids pick up money habits earlier than parents realize, expert says
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Children begin picking up on money habits much earlier than most parents realize, according to Teresa Murray, a consumer watchdog with US PIRG.
“We may think sometimes that our children aren’t paying attention to us when they’re three or four years old — oh no, kids are smart, and they learn from us,” Murray said. “And some of that happens really early.”
Murray said a parent’s financial behavior often becomes a child’s first money lesson, whether intentional or not.
“If they see their parents making careless or irresponsible choices, then they will probably learn that behavior very quickly,” Murray said.
Murray recommends using real situations, like birthday money, to teach kids how to think ahead about spending.
“Say a kid got $100 total in birthday money from grandparents and aunts and uncles and stuff — go and sit down with the kid and say, ‘Hey, what are you going to do with that money?’” Murray said. “I mean, their eyes are going to glaze over the math, but you need to teach kids how to think ahead with their money.”
Murray said parents can also share their own financial priorities with children in simple, age-appropriate terms.
“It doesn’t even hurt to share that with the kids a little bit — like, don’t lay it on heavy, don’t depress them,” Murray said. “But it’s like, yeah, we were planning on getting new furniture for the deck, but gosh, our refrigerator broke, so now we have to wait. Model that kind of behavior, model that kind of language. Kids are smart. They’ll understand.”
Murray said building these habits early can give children a head start once they begin managing money on their own.
Beyond money habits, experts also recommend talking with children early about what personal information they share on tablets and smartphones — a conversation focused less on finances and more on safety.

title: Great Falls Construction wraps up Biddeford Primary School addition

text:
Education and community leaders and students officially opened the doors last week to the $9 million expansion, which had been under construction since Sept. 2024.
Education and community leaders and students officially opened the doors last week to the $9 million Biddeford Primary School expansion, which had been under construction since September 2024.
The expansion was designed by local Mobile Studio Design and Haley Ward Inc., which is headquartered in Bangor. Gorham-based Great Falls Construction was the builder.
The two-story addition creates a unified early-learning campus for students from pre-kindergarten through second grade. It includes 16 modern classrooms and learning spaces designed specifically for young children, provides room for Head Start, and allows for the potential to expand pre-K opportunities in the future.
An outdoor classroom space has also been added to the campus.
The $9 million expansion was funded by a voter-approved bond as an alternative to a costly renovation of the aging John F. Kennedy Memorial School. The addition to Biddeford Primary versus renovating the older building was estimated to save taxpayers as much as $16 million.
JFK closed in June 2025 and the town is evaluating potential reuses for the building.
The new wing at Biddeford Primary School fulfills the district’s long-term vision for bringing all Pre-K through second grade students together, reducing school transitions during children’s earliest educational years.
“This project is about much more than additional classrooms; it is about creating stability, belonging and opportunity for our youngest learners,” said Jeremy Ray, Biddeford’s superintendent.

title: ‘Super oversize’ load’s journey to South Portland taking longer than expected
text:
The transport of a “super oversize” load — approximately 220 feet long and roughly 20 feet wide — to South Portland has been delayed.
The heat recovery steam generator began its two-night journey from Jay on Tuesday night, and was originally due to arrive in South Portland by 6 a.m. Thursday.
But because its progress has been slower than anticipated, it’s now due to arrive in South Portland next Tuesday morning, with incremental progress each night, according to the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office.
Wednesday night, it was to travel from Turner to Oxford, including over Jumper Bridge. Over Thursday night, the generator will travel from Oxford to Gray, resulting in traffic delays on Route 26 in Mechanic Falls and Poland. It will be staged in Gray over the weekend and moved to Buxton on Sunday night.
Monday night will be the final push before it arrives in South Portland the next morning. Law enforcement officers, utility crews and other personnel are assisting the transport of the generator, which weighs more than 683,000 pounds.
These generators are typically used at industrial facilities or power plants, and while it’s on the road, it spans two travel lanes. Residents and businesses have been asked to avoid parking along the route while the load is being transported to avoid obstruction, and drivers have been encouraged to plan ahead and allow extra travel time.
It’s the first of nine oversize loads planned along this route. The schedule for the remaining eight loads will be released once the current one is complete, according to the Maine Department of Transportation.
A spokesman for the MDOT did not say whether the delay will impact the timelines for the other loads.
A spokesman for Barnhart Crane & Rigging, the company overseeing the transport, did not immediately respond to questions about the timeline.

New Bangor crisis receiving center holds ribbon cutting ceremony

BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - With the aim to open on October 5th, the new Bangor crisis receiving center held ribbon cutting ceremony on Wednesday.
“The opening of the crisis receiving center here in Bangor represents a new front door for individuals experiencing a mental health, substance use or suicidal crisis. Breaking down stigma, providing immediate low barrier support in a welcoming space,” said Sarah Squirrell, Director of the Office of Behavioral Health.
The new Bangor Crisis Receiving Center is one of three in the state of Maine.
The first opened in Portland in February of 2022.
According to Gov. Mills, that location has served more than 3,500 people.
“More than half of them have visited just once or twice. And more than 90% of them left the center with a clear plan for what to do next,” said Mills.
In the wake of the 2023 mass shooting in Lewiston, the Maine legislature approved funding for two new centers in Lewiston and Bangor.
Once open, the Bangor center will be accessible 24/7 to anyone ages 14 and older.
“A key component of a safe place to go is really connection. And that power of connection is magnified when individuals with lived experience and expertise, peers, are there to help. Which is why our crisis receiving model includes talented peer specialists. Peer specialists play an important role in building trust quickly, reducing fear for individuals, and opening that door to healing and recovery. Peer support also provides hope, And with this center in Bangor, we strengthen compassionate response and we build hope,” said Squirrell.
The center is located inside of Community Health and Counseling Services at 68 First St.

Controversial Bangor councilor running for reelection wants the city to have a mayor
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Bangor Daily News is profiling all 12 Bangor City Council candidates ahead of the election this fall. Read more coverage of Bangor’s local election here.
Of the nine sitting Bangor city councilors, perhaps no one has drawn more attention than Joe Leonard.
The councilor has been censured three times and acquired a reputation as a polarizing personality. Some Bangor residents hate Leonard for his outbursts and feel he behaves inappropriately; others love him for his passion and willingness to stand by his beliefs.
Leonard is the only councilor running for reelection of the three whose terms are up this year. He gained his seat in a competitive special election in 2022 after two unsuccessful runs and won reelection in 2023.
“People want to see bold individuals that mean what they say and that actually want to do things, not just say things,” Leonard said. “And that’s me, at the end of the day.”
Leonard, 36, has lived in Bangor for nearly 10 years and works as an enrollment specialist for the clean energy company Ampion. He also works as a substitute teacher and tutor, and previously served as an Army National Guard officer, an artificial intelligence consultant and a manager for his family’s restaurant, Evenrood’s.
He also serves on the boards of Penquis CAP, a local anti-poverty nonprofit, and the Maine Rail Group.
Leonard is a Democrat but added that he considers himself a “Maine nationalist” and wants to prioritize Bangor residents regardless of political affiliation.
He knows he’s controversial, but Leonard said he’s running for council again because some constituents asked him too. He sees a lot of discontent among both Democrats and Republicans and said people want to see “that their local government actually works.”
His top priority if he wins reelection would be to change Bangor’s government structure by implementing voting wards and an elected mayor, goals he ran on when he was first elected.
Adding wards would improve representation, and having a full-time mayor with real executive authority would help the city more quickly address pressing issues, Leonard argued.
“We take too long to deliberate on issues,” he said of the council. “I think the people deserve to have a legislative arm of the city and an executive arm of the city. I think that’s a more effective government at the end of the day.”
Despite growing frustration around what many residents see as inaction on the council, Leonard said he thinks this past year has been more action-oriented than any other year he’s been on it.
“This was the most robust and progressive budget that the city of Bangor has seen in a long time,” he said of the budget council passed in June, noting the numerous new staff positions that were added. Leonard said he was particularly proud that the council added eight new firefighters.
“If I have it my way, I want to continue adding more positions to the city, because we need more services,” he said.
Leonard also wants to “figure out a way to expand where the money for our budget comes from,” such as enterprise funds. He said he’s interested in looking into municipally controlled energy.
He also wants the city to invest in housing and improve regional and state collaboration around homelessness.
Although the project drew backlash from a vocal group of residents, Leonard said he sees the Yellen Pines housing development for homeless residents, for which the council recently approved a tax reimbursement deal, as an example of cost savings for the city’s taxpayers. He often points to the high law enforcement and emergency services costs associated with homelessness.
Leonard also wants to build on the city’s Street Plus program by turning it into an in-house downtown ambassador program within a city department like public health or police, rather than one that is contracted out.
Unlike many other council candidates this year who are pushing for restrictive policies around syringe service providers, Leonard said he sees adding more syringe disposal boxes around the city as the appropriate solution for concerns around needle litter.
He also wants to ban automatic license plate readers and said he and other councilors are currently working on an ordinance that will do so.
Leonard’s been embroiled in a long list of controversies in his time on the council.
Most recently, he drew ire from some residents and in conservative media during a debate over Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity. During a council meeting, Leonard blasted ICE and President Donald Trump, calling him a “rapist, pedophile, fascist president” and prompting a walkout by one of his colleagues on the council.
Leonard was censured in November for another outburst during which he raised his middle finger at a local neo-Nazi and threw a pen in response to racist, antisemitic comments made at a public meeting.
“I know I can be viewed as a bombastic person. I know that there are some people who don’t like that I go about politics the way that I do,” he said at the time. “But I refuse to accept any criticism over denouncing and defying Nazism.”
He was also censured for what the council determined to be “inappropriate” accusations he made against a city employee in a public meeting last year, and for comments he made about two colleagues on the council.
The accusations against former finance director David Little cost the city nearly $100,000 in severance pay and legal fees, and an independent investigation found that the finance department was allocating resources fairly, contrary to Leonard’s claims.
Does Leonard have any regrets about his behavior on the council?
“No, not a single one,” he said.
Leonard knows he’s a contentious figure. He’s “received a death threat or two,” he said with a laugh. But, “I’m an action-oriented guy and I’m not going to pretend that I’m going to be okay with council doing nothing,” he said.
He added, “And on the throwing the pen at the Nazi thing, if people really have an issue with me doing that, okay. I mean, I’m not going to apologize.”

title: Roman Anthony out for playoffs with another right hand injury
text:
NEW YORK — Roman Anthony is expected to miss the rest of the postseason for the Boston Red Sox because of new damage to his right hand sustained in an AL Wild Card Series opener against the New York Yankees.
It is not yet clear whether he will need surgery. Anthony was sidelined from early May to late August because of an injury to the same hand.
“We did everything we could to be back this year and play, which we did,” Anthony said Wednesday in the tunnel outside the Red Sox clubhouse at Yankee Stadium before Game 2. “Going forward, we haven’t really even talked about it today.”
Batting leadoff as Boston’s designated hitter in his playoff debut Tuesday night, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against Cam Schlittler, then was removed for a pinch hitter with the Red Sox trailing by two runs in the sixth inning of a 9-0 loss.
Manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings.
“After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%,” Anthony said. “For me, it was to a point where it was tolerable and I was taking certain swings that were sketchy, and I was still able to come back and recover enough to just be in there every single day. But ultimately I just took a few swings here recently where that wasn’t the case.”
The team sent Anthony to Boston in a car after the game. He arrived about 3 a.m. and had new MRIs on Wednesday morning.
“Additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren’t there before,” Tracy said.
The 22-year-old Anthony returned to Massachusetts because the medical staff there was familiar with his injury from earlier this season.
“My thoughts are kind of all over the place,” he said. “Feelings and emotions of, you work all this year to put yourself in a position to just be good enough to go in the playoffs and for this to happen, it just doesn’t feel real.”
Anthony wasn’t sure whether the injury is something he’ll have to manage going forward.
“Given the point where we were at this year and all the different things that I tried and the different shots that I took and the routes that I went, I think — never really rested a ton, right? — so I don’t necessarily know the answer to that,” he said.
“Once we saw it today, it was more so about like, all right, this is what it is. You can’t go. It’s not in the team’s best interest for you to play tonight. So get back there. Root your guys on and be a good teammate. And then once, like I said, once we get past the series, it will be one of those things where we reassess regardless of what happens and kind of go from there.”
Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29.
“There’s been periods of time since he’s come back where he’ll get a zinger and feel something. And then it dissipates and we’re good to go,” Tracy said. “That’s not been an uncommon occurrence since he’s come back. But yesterday, as you went through those two at-bats, it got worse.”
The club announced that Anthony was diagnosed with a right hand strain, and Major League Baseball approved a Red Sox roster substitution. Anthony was replaced on the Wild Card Series roster by infielder Curtis Mead, obtained from Washington in late July for pitcher Connelly Early.
According to MLB rules, Anthony is ineligible to return until the American League Championship Series — if the Red Sox advance that far.
“I’ve been experiencing some things with the swings and the check-swings over the past six weeks. Last night just felt a little bit more intense, a little bit more worse than past swings that have been lingering a little bit longer than the ones I was used to,” Anthony said.
“It was just super alarming and it got to a point where it was tough to grip a bat. I knew then and there that this was a little bit more similar to the one earlier in the year. That’s why we decided to go get imaging.”
Mead got hit by a pitch in his first game with the Red Sox at the Athletics on July 27 and was placed on the injured list because of a broken left wrist. He hasn’t played in the big leagues since.
Mead was on the bench for Game 2 against the Yankees. Jahmai Jones was set to hit leadoff as the DH with the Red Sox one loss from elimination, followed in the batting order by catcher Adley Rutschman, first baseman Willson Contreras, right fielder Wilyer Abreu, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, third baseman Caleb Durbin, second baseman Nick Sogard, shortstop Trevor Story and left fielder Nate Eaton.
Sonny Gray was set to start on the mound for Boston against one of his former teams. Left-hander Max Fried was scheduled to pitch for New York.
One of baseball’s premier prospects when he debuted in the majors last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBI and a .735 OPS in 55 games this season.
“Hopefully he’s going to be healthy for next year,” Abreu said. “It’s a big loss for us, but we still have to play the game and try to win the game today.”

title: Bond denied for man accused of killing Kentucky trooper
text:
BOWLING GREEN, Ky. (WSMV/WKYT/Gray News) - A judge denied bond for the 51-year-old Tennessee man charged with murder in the shooting of Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips.
Emonnie Branch of Portland, Tennessee, appeared in a Warren County court in Kentucky Tuesday morning.
Prosecutors argued that Branch is a flight risk and a danger to the community.
Prosecutors cite criminal history
Branch allegedly gave police a false name and has an extensive criminal history, including fraud, robbery and assault involving a minor. Prosecutors also said the incident involving the state trooper was captured on video.
After hearing those arguments, the judge denied bond for Branch.
Branch is charged with the murder of a first responder/peace officer after Kentucky State Police said Phillips, 28, was fatally shot during a traffic stop on Interstate 65 in Warren County.
Arrest in Jefferson County
Louisville police used a grappler to secure the car and Branch in Jefferson County about four hours after the shooting.
Branch also has an outstanding warrant from Tennessee for a probation violation. His attorney said extradition had not yet been discussed.
Branch’s next hearing in the Kentucky case is scheduled for Friday morning.

title: Arnold Schwarzenegger Is Back ... As Santa Claus in ‘The Man With the Bag’ Trailer
text:
Arnold Schwarzenegger Becomes Santa Claus in ‘The Man With the Bag’ Trailer
Arnold Schwarzenegger. Champion bodybuilder. Movie star. Governor. Fitness advocate. And now ... Santa Claus.
Truly, one of the all-time great resumes. Don’t you wish your LinkedIn page looked like that?
Although best known as an action star and a sentient killer robot from a time when rogue artificial intelligence setting off an apocalypse felt like wholesome escapist fun, Schwarzenegger made several Christmas movies during his ’90s peak, including the holiday favorite Jingle All the Way and his one directorial effort, the TV movie Christmas in Connecticut starring Dyan Cannon and Kris Kristofferson.
Now he’s back (sorry) playing Santa himself in the streaming comedy The Man With the Bag. In the film, he’s teamed with one of his spiritual successors in the action realm, Reacher star Alan Ritchson, who Santa recruits to help him get back his stolen bag from a disgruntled elf (Awkwafina).
You can check out Schwarzenegger as Santa — looking a little buffer than Saint Nick usually does, but still sporting that big white beard — in The Man With the Bag trailer below:
READ MORE: Every Arnold Schwarzenegger Movie Ever, Ranked From Worst to Best
Here is the film’s official synopsis:
When Santa’s (Schwarzenegger) iconic red bag is stolen by a rogue elf with a grudge (Awkwafina), Christmas is suddenly at risk. With his biggest night of the year fast-approaching, Santa recruits a thief (Ritchson) from his ‘Naughty List’ who quickly assembles a crew of criminally skilled misfits — with a little help from elves and reindeer — to pull off the most unexpected heist of their lives. Packed with holiday magic, big laughs, and plenty of heart, THE MAN WITH THE BAG is a holiday heist adventure about second chances, unlikely friendships, and discovering that sometimes even Santa needs a little help delivering Christmas.
The Man With the Bag premieres on Prime Video on December 2. I can’t wait.

title: Tick Reauthorization Act signed into law
text:
Tick Reauthorization Act signed into law
The new law is aimed at combating Lyme and other tick-borne diseases.
Tick Reauthorization Act signed into law
The new law is aimed at combating Lyme and other tick-borne diseases.
The Tick Reauthorization Act, introduced by Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., is now law after being signed by President Donald Trump. The law is aimed at combating Lyme and other tick-borne diseases. Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, was also an original co-sponsor of the bill.
The bipartisan measure extends funding through 2030 for regional research centers, as well as Centers for Disease Control and Prevention grants to state health departments to improve research, treatment and awareness. Officials say it will also require the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to continue implementing and updating its strategy to fight the diseases.
It also provides funding for Lyme disease vaccine trials at the MaineHealth Institute of Research.
This comes as the number of cases of Lyme disease continues to reach record-high levels in Maine, with more than 4,200 cases reported statewide last year.
The senators named the bill after the late Sen. Kay Hagan, D-N.C., who died in October 2019 due to complications from the Powassan virus, a tick-borne disease.

title: ‘His loss is deeply personal’: Police officer found dead hours after disappearing while wakeboarding, chief says
text:
PUEBLO COUNTY, Colo. (Gray News) - A police officer in Colorado was found dead hours after disappearing while wakeboarding.
On Sunday, Colorado Parks and Wildlife said in a post that officers were searching for a missing person in “the area of Peck Creek/west-central area of” the park following a single boat incident.
The report came in around 5:30 p.m.
The following day, it was announced that the missing person was found at about 2 a.m. The body of the victim, who was in 48 feet of water, was recovered 45 minutes later with the assistance of a remotely operated vehicle.
Pueblo Police identified the victim as Cpl. Stephen Biggs. The department said that he was in a wakeboarding accident.
Pueblo Police said that Biggs had been a member of the department since 2010, serving as a patrol training officer and with the SWAT team. They noted that Biggs was the recipient of 10 letters of commendation, three Medal of Valor awards and the Distinguished Service award.
“Working with Stephen was an honor, and his loss is deeply personal,” Pueblo Police Department Chief Chris Noeller said in the news release. “His courage, dedication, and commitment to his fellow officers meant so much to our department. I was proud to serve with him, and I will miss him. My heart is with his family, his friends, and everyone in our department who is grieving his loss.”
Pueblo Police said that the late officer’s patrol car will be parked at the department’s headquarters as a sign of respect.

title: Central Maine Power removes job postings after Public Utilities Commission staff recommendation to deny temporary rate hike
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Central Maine Power (CMP) is removing all job postings from its website after Maine Public Utilities Commission (PUC) staff members called for the agency to deny the company’s request for a temporary rate increase, a CMP spokesperson confirmed to Maine’s Total Coverage.
As of Monday, CMP had 70 job postings listed.
CMP is requesting a $189 million increase to help upgrade equipment that failed or got close to failing this summer. But a number of groups have objected to the proposal, including the Maine Office of the Public Advocate, the Maine Department of Energy Resources, Efficiency Maine Trust, AARP Maine, CMP Ratepayers Unite and the Natural Resources Council of Maine.
In a recommended ruling, PUC staff members said the commission’s policy only allows it to approve rate changes if there are no objections to an amount, which is not the case in this instance.
CMP president and CEO Linda Ball released a statement reacting to the recommended ruling, which said that the recommendation “carries consequences that extend well beyond the rate case itself.”
“Prolonged revenue uncertainty puts pressure on the infrastructure investments, workforce, financing capacity, and grant-funded modernization efforts that customers and communities depend upon. Unfortunately, the consequences of prolonged uncertainty are no longer theoretical,” Ball said in her statement. “CMP has already been forced to defer planned capital work, including projects intended to strengthen reliability, improve resilience, and modernize the system, and will continue to do so. CMP will now also be forced to evaluate workforce levels and hiring plans that support current operations and future needs.”
Ball also sent a letter to CMP employees on Monday. In the letter, Ball said that the company will need to evaluate current workforce levels, hiring plans and apprenticeship programs as a result of the recommendation from PUC staff members.
“No decisions have been made beyond those already communicated, but it would be irresponsible not to assess all available options given the current circumstances,” Ball said in her letter, which was shared with Maine’s Total Coverage by a CMP employee.
PUC staff members noted in their recommended ruling, however, that the decision does not necessarily foreclose CMP from seeking a temporary rate increase later in the process should a clear agreement be reached between the parties.
“I think everybody recognizes we want costs as low as possible, but low also needs to be thoughtful,” said Patrick C. Woodcock, president of the Maine State Chamber of Commerce. “Just as in how you manage your house, you don’t want to put off investments that may increase costs later down the road.”
The PUC is expected to consider the recommendation at its meeting next Tuesday, Oct. 6. Parties must file comments or exceptions to the staff members’ recommended decision by 12 p.m. on Monday, Oct. 5, in order for the PUC to consider them in its deliberation on the matter.

title: ‘Psychological warfare’: Family shares heartbreaking loss to sextortion to save others
text:
(Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or a loved one need help, call or text the Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988.)
NITRO, W. Va. (InvestigateTV) — Bryce Tate’s death was the result of a crime the FBI reports is quickly growing across the country.
His father, Adam Tate, is sharing his story to educate other parents. He and his wife, Amanda, said they were initially unfamiliar with the scam police say killed their son.
“We had never heard of the term sextortion before,” Adam Tate said.
Sextortion involves someone coercing a minor to create sexually explicit images or videos, then threatening to release the material unless payment is received, often in the form of gift cards or cryptocurrency.
A 2025 survey found one in five teens have experienced sextortion.
Bryce Tate was a sophomore at Nitro High School. His father described him as “always smiling, full of energy, goofy, dancing.”
“It was the greatest thing in the world, to be able to get home and see his smiling face, and be able to pick him up, and hug him, kiss him, and wrestle him, and it was just so much fun,” Adam Tate said.
“You know, there’s nothing but good memories. And that we’re thankful for.”
The Kanawha County Sheriff’s Department investigated Bryce Tate’s death as a case of sextortion.
“It was just a normal day. My son tells my wife, ‘I’m gonna go take a shower.’ Just normal conversations. There was no red flag. There was nothing that would make you question that there was something going on,” Adam Tate said.
The texts began after school
On the evening of Nov. 6, Bryce Tate received a text message after school while he was working out at the gym. The message came from someone claiming to be a teenage girl interested in him.
Bryce Tate had never met or spoken with the girl, but she had information about him that was accurate. The first text arrived just after 4:30 p.m.
The conversation continued at the gym and as Amanda Tate picked her son up and drove him home.
“And around 7:25, 7:27, somewhere in that area, my wife heard a loud noise,” Adam Tate said. “I said, well, Amanda... He might have fell. Something might have broke. And she walks into the man cave, and that’s where she finds him. You know, and I hear her screaming on the phone.”
Adam Tate would get home as fast as he could.
“In my mind, as his father, I felt like if I would have got there sooner, I could have done something,” he said.
The sound Amanda Tate heard was a gunshot. Bryce Tate had died.
Answers come nearly two weeks later
Over the next 12 days, through Bryce Tate’s funeral and the investigation into his death, Adam and Amanda Tate could think of no reason why their son would have done something like this.
“This crime happened in such a short period of time, we’re talking a three-hour period. My son didn’t struggle with mental health. He wasn’t bullied. There was no heartbreak. There was, he would have otherwise never done something like this,” Adam Tate said.
Nearly two weeks after their son’s death, detectives asked the Tates to come to the sheriff’s department.
“They performed a forensics audit on his phone. And they told us that he was a victim of sextortion,” Adam Tate said. “So, it was nice to get that answer, but then more questions came up, like, what is sextortion?”
Deputies and the FBI believe the person Bryce Tate had been texting was a professional extortionist posing as a teenage girl.
After Bryce Tate received pictures from the other number and was enticed to send compromising pictures of himself, the extortionist revealed himself. He threatened to release the images publicly, ruining Bryce Tate’s life and his family’s life, unless he paid a ransom.
“They wanted $500. My son offered him $30. He only had $30 and, uh, he offered that to him and that wasn’t enough money. So, the next thing that they do is, they coerce them into taking their own lives,” Adam Tate said. “So, this isn’t something that he just thought of on his own. You know, they coach him into that.”
Tate said the extortionist sent Bryce 120 texts in a span of 20 minutes.
“A text message every 10 seconds to keep them engaged by design to keep them in that panic. And they put this imaginary timer, like if you don’t do this within this amount of time, all these images will be released,” he saiid. “And they just keep them in a state of panic. And it’s psychological warfare. And they just, they pile it on. I mean, they just, they max pressure.”
Tate said that pressure becomes all-consuming for kids, who feel unable to put the phone down and see a way out. He said that’s why it’s important for parents to talk with their children.
“Stop believing that this can’t happen to your family because it can. If it can happen to my family, it can happen to yours. So please take a moment and just simply have a conversation with your kid,” Adam Tate said.
Tate and his wife say that Bryce was the “biggest blessing in my lifetime.”
“For my wife and I, and anybody who had the privilege of knowing my son, he was a blessing. And what I refuse to do, what I will not allow to happen, is these cowards write the ending to my son’s story. That will not happen,” Adam Tate said.
No arrests have been made in Bryce Tate’s case.
The Kanawha County Sheriff’s Office says it’s working with the FBI on the investigation.
Advocacy since Bryce’s death
In April 2026, Nitro High School hosted a basketball tournament in Bryce Tate’s honor. The two-day event also served as an opportunity to educate families on sextortion.
The advocacy work of Bryce Tate’s parents reached the West Virginia State Capitol. In 2026, Bryce’s Law went into effect, criminalizing sextortion and outlining penalties.
Parents sharing their stories of loss and pushing for change is why Wisconsin has several laws to stop and prevent sextortion. As of April 2026, victims of sexual extortion can file a civil suit for monetary damages against their perpetrator rather than relying on a criminal case. It also allows a victim’s family to file a wrongful death lawsuit against a perpetrator if their loved one’s suicide was largely a result of that crime.
The state also passed laws allocating more resources to investigating internet crimes against children and awareness campaigns in public schools.
If you or someone you know is struggling with distress or a mental health crisis, help is available. Call or text the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Services are free and confidential.

title: Let’s have an honest discussion about Social Security
text:
Lenny Shine’s Aug. 22 op-ed (“Don’t fall for Republican distractions”) argues that the Social Security contribution cap unfairly favors higher earners because, once they earn more than $184,500, they “cease to pay a nickel into the program.” He calls eliminating that cap a matter of making them pay their “fair share.”
He leaves out an important fact: America’s working families who earn in excess of $184,500 will receive no additional Social Security retirement benefit based on those “excess” earnings. That is an important omission. Pay nothing in, get nothing out. How is that not “paying a fair share”?
Should American working families who earn more than $184,500 in a year be required to pay more into Social Security without receiving any additional benefit for those additional contributions?
If we are going to have an honest and helpful discussion about the challenges faced by Social Security, we should do so based on an honest and accurate statement of the facts.
Daniel Kagan
Lewiston

title: As heating oil prices hit record highs, Mainers eye winter with growing trepidation
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The band was playing and the carnival rides were spinning on a warm, sunny afternoon at the Farmington Fair, the kind of bright September day that makes winter feel safely far off.
But the nights have been getting colder, and Krista Hinkley was worried.
“Oil prices are absolutely outrageous, and we’re concerned that we’re not going to even make it through the winter,” she said.
Hinkley lives in Jay with her three kids, her husband and her mother. They’re trying to cut back where they can, chasing discounts and even eating less food.
And she’s not just worried about her own family. Hinkley works as a mobile hearing aid provider and said many of her clients don’t know how they’re going to afford oil either.
“They’re not going to make it through the winter,” Hinkley said. “There’s some who are on extremely low incomes. There’s no way they could afford even 100 gallons, and that’s really the biggest concern.”
Heating oil prices in Maine hit a record high last week, at $6.02 a gallon on average. That means it’ll now cost an extra $740 to fill a standard 250-gallon tank, according to the state Department of Energy Resources.
On top of the global market turmoil triggered by the U.S.-Iran war, heating oil, which is similar to diesel, is also affected by limited refining capacity, which has taken a hit from fighting in the Middle East and in Ukraine.
“So, as a result, we’re seeing very tight supplies for diesel and heating oil,” Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association.
Wolfe said the Northeast consumes 82% of the country’s heating oil, meaning that the fallout from higher prices is also concentrated here, at a time when households are already stretched by more expensive gasoline.
“They now have an additional upwards of $200 a month for home heating oil. So, this is putting significant pressure on lower income families,” Wolfe said.
“We’re seeing about the highest demand that we have seen for assistance and for services, especially this early in the season,” said Jason Parent, CEO of Avec Community Action, which administers the federally funded Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, in Aroostook, Washington and Hancock Counties.
This year, he said, they’re also seeing more demand from middle-income households who don’t qualify for federal aid.
And even for those who do qualify, the early season demand for assistance is hard to meet, because federal funding typically isn’t available until November.
“We’ve had some households that have been without fuel now for over a month and are just at the critical point where they’re like, ‘It’s starting to become unbearable for us now,'” Parent said.
MaineHousing said the state does have about $4 million in federal funding left over from last year, which could help bridge some of the gap. They are urging anyone who thinks they may need help this winter to apply as soon as possible, either online through its website, or by phone, or in person at their local community action agency.
All of this is playing out weeks ahead of the midterm elections, and Democrats in Maine and across the country are laying the affordability issue at the feet of Republicans. But at the Farmington Fair, Joe Nelson, who lives in Temple, said he’s seen prices go up and down under both parties.
“I mean, I’m not too happy about the gas prices being the way they are, or the oil prices. Neither one of them,” Nelson said. “I was also around in ’78 when Jimmy Carter was here, and everything went through the roof as well.”
Nelson also pointed to the last big energy price spike under former President Joe Biden, triggered by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when Republicans were the ones trying to harness voter anger over rising costs.
But as the national parties jockey for position in the political horserace, Stewart Wyman has just been burned by the results of an actual horserace.
“I don’t think I won,” Wyman said, with a laugh, after a pack of harness racers barrel across the finish line. “I had the 5 horse, which did terrible.”
Wyman, who lives in Farmington and made a career in the public school system, said he’s not feeling much better about his heating oil prospects.
“It’s kind of scary going into the winter, knowing right now what the prices are going to be,” he said. “And I’m not sure they’re going to drop a whole heck of a lot in the short term.”
Wyman said he’s been waiting as long as possible to fill his tank. But said with nighttime temperatures starting to dip into the 30s, he’s not sure how much longer he can hold out.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: FTC opens probe into OpenAI and Anthropic
text:
FTC is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over possible risks to consumers
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has opened an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other artificial intelligence companies over dangers their technology may pose to consumers, the agency said Wednesday.
OpenAI and Anthropic, both AI giants, and other tech companies in recent months have disclosed examples of their AI agents going beyond human instructions, finding their way onto the internet and hacking external websites.
Related video above: “Tremendous self-policing”: Trump unveils voluntary AI safety accord with tech leaders
An FTC spokesperson confirmed the investigation but declined further comment. The investigation was first reported by the New York Post, which said it has been underway for months.
Representatives for Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to messages for comment on Wednesday.
Concerns around the dangers powerful AI models may pose to humanity have led some of the top AI developers to call for a slowdown. The CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, said this month that the industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet.
OpenAI, meanwhile, recently delayed the launch of its newest model this week over safety concerns.

title: Data center bill falls short in Senate as lawmakers take final votes before midterms
text:
Data center bill falls short in Senate as lawmakers take final votes before midterms
A bill that attempts to address voter worries about data centers and their impact on energy costs failed to advance in the Senate on Wednesday, falling victim to an election-year clash on how best to address a growing concern.
Before leaving Washington to campaign, Senate Republicans reserved one of the chamber's final votes for a bill they hoped would underscore efforts to address the impact data centers have on voters' monthly energy bills. The bill needed 60 votes to advance, but fell short, 57—43.
The bill is a modest one. It requires utility regulators to consider adopting a federal standard that charges large power customers a rate that covers the cost of the system upgrades needed to serve them. Democrats say it amounts to a suggestion and that more is needed. Republicans say the bill sends a message to regulators to act.
The bill’s sponsor, Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, is in a tough reelection battle and has been labeled in campaign ads as the “face of data centers” by his Democratic challenger, former Sen. Sherrod Brown.
“You all know this is the only game in town,” Husted told reporters in advocating for his bill. “This bill passing is the only way to get a chance to prove to the American people before the midterm elections whose side you're on.”
Senate Democrats say the bill isn't tough enough
The measure passed the House by a vote of 417-3. It needed support from at least seven Democratic senators to proceed to a final vote, but that didn't happen given the criticism from within their ranks that it doesn't go far enough and knowing that passage could give Husted's reelection prospects a lift.
“The bill is a fraud, plain and simple,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said.
Democrats have offered competing proposals. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. sponsored legislation that would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to issue rules for large electricity customers that requires them to pay for necessary grid upgrades.
“They want it optional, which means zero. We want it mandatory,” Schumer said.
Republicans are looking to position Democrats as obstructionists who are blocking progress on key voter concerns. Husted's bill is one example. Another would be the bill from Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., that would bar members of Congress from purchasing individual stocks. The issue is a popular one with candidates running for office this election cycle, but also includes voter identification requirements that Democrats have called a poison pill.
Thune teed up both bills for procedural votes and both failed to meet the 60-vote threshold for advancing.
“Both pieces of legislation strike at the very heart of issues that the American people care deeply about, passionately about, and we'll see if the Democrats are willing to take yes for an answer," Thune said.
Data centers have become a top campaign issue
The House and Senate are both expected to be out of session for all of October. The House left in mid-September, canceling nearly two weeks of votes as Republicans were anxious to get on the campaign trail in a bid to keep their majority in the next Congress.
President Donald Trump has embraced the building of more data centers, but there is growing wariness from voters. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans.
And a majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.
In Ohio, a data center hot spot with closely contested races for governor and U.S. Senate, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a recent memo that Husted is vulnerable to losing his seat because of the centers. Husted helped promote Ohio as a destination for data centers while serving as lieutenant governor.
The Ohio race is seen as vital to determining control of the Senate, helping explain why the data center bill has generated so much scrutiny and is so hotly contested despite the overwhelming vote it received in the House.
Speaking on the Senate floor before the vote, Husted said that the bill requires states to at least confront the issue of data centers paying their own way for their power and the grid improvements needed to serve them. He said the bill could hardly get broader support than it did in the House, but by blocking the bill in the Senate, Democrats would be showing they don’t care about the issue of affordability.
“Let’s hold data centers accountable and let’s stop blocking a path to affordability,” Husted said.

title: Obituary: Thelma E. Eye Goggin Brooks
text:
WATERVILLE – Thelma E. Eye Goggin Brooks, 101, passed away on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026, at the Oak Grove Center in Waterville, Maine, where she recently celebrated her 101st birthday. She was born on Sept. 10, 1925, in Calais, Maine, the eldest of three children of Chester William Eye and Mary Elizabeth “Bessie” Edmonds Eye.
At the time of her death, Thelma held the title of the longest living member of her family tree, going back generations and hundreds of years.
She was educated in the Calais school system and graduated from Calais Academy in the class of 1942. Shortly after graduation, her family moved to Gardiner and she moved to Rome, N.Y. where she worked for the Army Air Depot for the next three years, after which time she moved back to Maine.
She married William “Bill” Goggin in Gardiner, Maine in May 1946 and they began their family together, raising four children. Thelma was active in the community and with the schools, she often subbing a class, coaching a team, or teaching swimming to local children during the summers.
In 1971, due to the death of her son in Vietnam, she suddenly became a Gold Star Mother. One of the downsides of living a long life, she experienced the loss of many of her family members as well as the loss of all four of her children.
During her working years and into the early years of her retirement, Thelma was very involved with genealogy and her family tree. She also was a published author of some of her genealogy researches and families that she also did research for.
A few years before her retirement, she moved to Waterville where she met her second husband, Earl Brooks and they married in 1979. After she retired, she worked at the library in Waterville and was active in the local stamp club and often played cards on Saturday nights with her friends, well into her 90’s.
Thelma was predeceased by her father Chester in 1947 and her mother Bessie in 2003; her brother Donald Eye in 1985 and her sister Shirley Williams in 2015; her son Richard in 1971, her son Kenneth in 1994 and most recently her son Chester and her daughter Donna both in 2024. Also predeceased by her nephew Daniel Williams in 2024; as well as both of her former husbands.
She is survived by two grandsons, Joel Goggin of California and Tom Stevens of Randolph, Maine; four great grandsons, Chris and Zachary Goggin of Waterville; Ben and Luke Stevens of Randolph; one nephew and Guardian, Jeffery Williams of Portland; two nieces, Liz (Eye) Helton and Julie (Eye) Gilmore of Nevada; one great niece in Maine, Shannon (Williams) May, three great nieces Jamie Richards, Carrie Arcoraci and Rachel Gilmore and one great nephew, Adam Gilmore, all from Nevada, and several great nephews and nieces in Nevada.
Thelma requested no visiting hours and no funeral. She wished to be cremated, and her ashes buried in the family lot in Calais, where she will be laid to rest next to her parents and her son Kenneth.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of Aable Cremation Service in Waterville. An online guestbook may be signed, condolences and memories shared at http://www.aablecremationservice.com.

title: New England’s winter forests need the Roadless Rule
text:
Anneka Williams is a writer and climate scientist who is originally from Vermont’s Mad River Valley. She currently serves as the policy director for Winter Wildlands Alliance.
Growing up in New England instilled in me a deep appreciation for trees. In the summers my family would hike sections of trail all over the state, relishing the shade provided by a dense, leafy canopy of sugar maple, beech and birch trees. In the winter, the trees would shed their leaves and my friends and I would go find hidden powder stashes, carving quick turns between tight glades.
While trees feel like an abundant resource in Vermont today, forests haven’t always been
plentiful in this part of the country. In the 17th century, early European settlers established the foundation for a booming logging industry across the Northeast. 
As the number of settlers grew through the 18th and 19th centuries, forests were cleared and converted to agricultural land and much of the region lost its major old growth forests, shifting lumber operations west because there simply weren’t enough trees left. Over the last century, New England forests have recovered through practices aimed at balancing timber harvesting with conservation and other uses, but much of New England is a patchwork of roads and very few large roadless areas are left.
The roadless areas that remain are vital resources for outdoor recreation and watershed
protection. But they are currently under threat. Last June, the Trump administration’s U.S. Department of Agriculture moved to rescind the Roadless Rule under the guise of more local forest control and wildfire management. 
The Roadless Rule is a piece of federal policy enacted in 2001. It protects more than 58 million acres of “inventoried roadless areas” — pieces of undeveloped land within the national forest system that remain in their natural, undeveloped state. These places offer abundant opportunities for outdoor recreation in all seasons, including undeveloped terrain that makes human-powered winter recreation some of the best in the country, while also protecting clean watersheds and natural ecosystem qualities.
While the rescission of the Roadless Rule doesn’t automatically greenlight logging and road development, it does remove an important layer of protection that has implications for the character of New England’s wild, unroaded lands and for backcountry winter recreationists.
New England is home to two national forests: the Green Mountain National Forest (GMNF) in Vermont and the White Mountain National Forest (WMNF) in New Hampshire and western Maine. GMNF, which is approximately 400,000 acres total, holds approximately 80,000 acres of inventoried roadless areas. WMNF is approximately 800,000 acres and encompasses an estimated 368,000 acres of inventoried roadless areas.
Collectively that’s roughly 448,000 acres of roadless areas across New England. These areas encompass lots of terrain for winter recreation, including world-class backcountry skiing in Jefferson Ravine, the Wildcat Valley Trail, maintained backcountry glades around Baldface Knob and sections of snowmobile trails.
When I think about roadless areas in New England, I picture quiet glades nestled in heavily forested areas, lovingly maintained and enjoyed by local communities. I picture second-growth forests that have worked hard to reach their current density. I picture the places I visit on my skis or snowshoes in search of untracked powder, wild experiences and the stillness of a forest stand in the middle of winter.
These are the places that create a community of people around shared outdoor experiences and that provide the backdrop for photographs that define entire regions. They are the places I think about when I think of home.
At a moment filled with attempts to sell off our public lands and dramatic cuts in funding and staff to the agency we rely on to manage our national forests, having a policy like the Roadless Rule to protect these places is more important than ever.
Intact forests are on the chopping block and it’s up to all of us to use our voices to speak for these places during the Roadless Rule Draft Environmental Impact Statement comment period. I hope that if you’re reading this you will reflect on what untrammeled forests mean for you, how outdoor recreation has played a role in your life and join me in standing up for those places and experiences now and for future generations.
The Forest Service is holding a public comment period on the Roadless Rule right now. Submit your comment before Oct. 6.

title: Harry and Meghan blame paparazzi for security scare at children’s school
text:
Harry and Meghan blame 'extraordinarily reckless' paparazzi for security scare at children’s school
Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex have condemned what they described as “extraordinarily reckless” behavior by international photographers who they say sparked a security scare at their children’s school.
Private security and school staff are understood to have spotted two young men carrying backpacks, later identified as international photographers, walking around the school and stopping to look into the grounds.
A spokesperson for the Sussexes called the incident on Monday “an extraordinary lack of judgment” and an “unacceptable intrusion” after the photographers were seen “walking the perimeter of the school.”
“It is concerning enough that certain European paparazzi appear unwilling to respect the privacy of children at school,” the spokesperson said. “But to behave in this manner in these particular circumstances, and so soon after the incident at RAF Fairford, demonstrates an extraordinary lack of judgment.”
The spokesperson continued, “Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school.”
British media outlets have taken care not to identify the location of the school or the Sussexes’ residence following a request from the Independent Press Standards Organisation, though their rules do not apply to representatives working for international media outlets.
Prince Harry has long expressed concerns over his family’s security, even before they returned to the U.K. in late August. Earlier this month, they moved Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, from a previous school just days into the start of the academic term due to security practicalities.
When Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties in 2020, the British government decided to downgrade their level of taxpayer-funded security – a decision which the duke fought unsuccessfully in the courts for years. In one of those rulings, the U.K.’s Home Office argued it was not appropriate for wealthy individuals to buy protective security from specialist police officers.
Harry has continued pressing for protection, often drawing comparisons of what his wife has faced with that of his mother, Diana, who died in 1997 in a high-speed car crash while paparazzi were following her.
This latest incident comes as the couple are reportedly waiting on an official risk assessment now they have returned to the U.K. from Montecito, California.
The couple has been asked to provide authorities with as much detail as possible about their new daily routines, including trips such as the school run, addresses routinely visited, routes taken and more, according to The Telegraph newspaper earlier this month. That information, along with any other evidence considered relevant, will be used by a branch of the U.K.’s Home Office to evaluate any changes to the level of threat they face.

title: OPINIONS: Get Big Money Out of Politics
text:
COMMUNITY COMMENTARY
by Bonnie Sammons
Mid-Maine Citizens Climate
Lobby Chapter, Belgrade
For many years I have observed with dismay, and anger, the increasing influence of big money on our elections. I submitted the testimony below to the Maine Ethics Commission in support of an amendment to our constitution that will return to the states the power to place reasonable limits on campaign spending. Such an amendment is urgently needed.
Over the last several years, I have worked with American Promise to do what I can as a volunteer to solve the problem of big money in politics. I have talked with many friends, family members, and colleagues about this issue. Nearly everyone recognizes that this is an enormous problem that impedes our democracy. However, reactions often reflect a cynical view of what is possible, especially in the current polarized political climate. “That is never going to happen” is a typical comment. When I point out the vast majority of citizens, regardless of political party, recognize the negative impact of big money in politics and support ending it; this is a unifying issue that can be a win for all of us; that 25 states have already signified readiness to ratify an amendment; that a bill for the amendment has been introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives; and, finally, that there is a very good chance this amendment can be added to our constitution in the near future. Many people see a glimmer of hope on the horizon for ending the flow of dark money, foreign money, and billionaire money that buy our politicians and dilutes the influence of everyday citizens.
As you are well aware, in 2023 Maine passed, with an amazing 86 percent support, a referendum, Question 2, banning foreign government spending in state elections and calling on Congress to pass the For Our Freedom Amendment. Lawsuits subsequently filed claim the referendum violates the First Amendment rights of big corporations and foreign government entities, enabled by the SCOTUS Citizens United decision in 2010 that wrongly called political spending free speech. Because of this and other disastrous SCOTUS decisions, a constitutional amendment is critically needed to correct the current protocols that prevent even basic transparency and reasonable regulation of campaign finance.
The $100 million spent between 2020 and 2023 (83 percent of the total!) to influence Maine ballot initiatives does not come from Maine citizens but from outside influencers who are attempting to, and succeeding in, promoting their own interests, not the interests of the people of this state or of the country. This is not democracy.
Yes, I do believe we can correct this dysfunctional system. This is not a partisan issue. As noted above, a large majority of Republicans, Democrats and independents agree: getting the money out of our political system is critical for the functioning of a government of, by and for the people. I urge every citizen therefore to learn more about this proposed constitutional amendment and support it by contacting your representatives. https://americanpromise.net/for-our-freedom-amendment/.

title: Baby defying odds, meeting milestones as 1 of only 15 with rare genetic mutation
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A Louisiana couple says their baby girl has been defying the odds since birth.
Wren Michelle Roberts was born with a rare genetic mutation that has caused three heart defects, placed her stomach in her chest, and left her with spina bifida and no spleen.
Wren’s father, Nick Roberts, says doctors told the family their daughter is one of only about 15 such documented cases.
“The body is not being told by the brain how to properly form everything,” Nick Roberts said.
The parents added that doctors told them that Wren would likely not survive birth. But now, three weeks later, they say they are watching her meet developmental milestones.
Dr. Gabriella Bluett-Mills, Wren’s complex care pediatrician at Ochsner Children’s Hospital, said Wren is meeting milestones after spinal surgery at 1 week old.
“I’d say Wren is one in a million,” Bluett-Mills said. “I’ve never seen all of these things together before.”
Wren drinks from a bottle, takes a pacifier, yawns, coos, raises her arms and sneezes. She even cried for the first time.
“To hear her cry was just heaven, heaven sent,” Wren’s mother, Savannah Roberts, said.
Wren’s parents said they first learned something may be wrong about 20 weeks into Savannah Roberts’ pregnancy during routine tests.
Doctors later told them Wren would likely die before she was born, and then that she would not survive much longer after birth.
“We planned on having a funeral (the weekend after she was born),” Nick Roberts said.
Savannah Roberts said that, as a nurse, she sees the ugly side of things and struggled with considering all that was to come after first learning her pregnancy had complications.
But she said now, her daughter has made her believe in miracles.
“There’s a reason that it happened, and now looking at her, I’m so glad that it happened because I don’t want any other baby,” she said. “I want her.”
Bluett-Mills said Wren’s case serves as an important reminder to health care professionals.
“We don’t know every single answer,” Bluett-Mills said. “We will have to just follow along and let her lead us and kind of show us what she’s capable of doing.”
Wren’s father started the Facebook group Wren’s Warriors to provide family and friends with updates on her progress. The page now has thousands of followers.
Fundraisers to help the family with ongoing medical costs can also be found on the page.
