title: New York man sentenced in St. Albans marijuana grow house mortgage fraud
text:
BANGOR — A New York man who admitted to fraudulently applying for a mortgage to buy a house he used for an illegal cannabis growing operation was spared prison time Wednesday.
Ken Yiu, 49, of Brooklyn, was sentenced to time served in prison — one day — and three years of supervised release, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Maine said in a statement.
U.S. District Judge Stacey D. Neumann handed down the sentence during a hearing at the federal court in Bangor.
Yiu pleaded guilty in December 2025 to one count of mortgage fraud and one count of maintaining a marijuana-involved premises. In exchange, prosecutors dismissed one count of bank fraud, court records show.
An emailed message to Yiu’s attorney, Ronald W. Bourget of the Augusta law firm Bourget & Banda, was not returned Wednesday morning.
A grand jury indicted Yiu in February 2025, court records show. Authorities arrested him in Queens, New York, the next month and he was released from custody on a $20,000 bond and ordered to stay in New York except for court proceedings in Maine.
According to federal prosecutors, Yiu applied in July 2020 for an $80,000, 25-year fixed-rate mortgage to purchase a property in St. Albans. He indicated the property was going to be his primary residence.
Instead, federal prosecutors wrote in court filings, Yiu used the property to house a large-scale cannabis cultivation operation. Yiu never intended to live at the St. Albans property, prosecutors said.
Real estate records at the Somerset County Registry of Deeds show the home, purchased in August 2020, is at 294 Hartland Road.
Court records only identify the victim bank as “Maine bank 1.” But filings at the Registry of Deeds indicate Kennebec Savings Bank issued Yiu the mortgage.
Yiu sold the property earlier this month, on Sept. 2, to De Xing Li, of Brooklyn, New York, records show. The mortgage was discharged Sept. 4.
Prosecutors were not seeking restitution in the case because Yiu had sold the property and satisfied the debt before sentencing, Assistant U.S. Attorney Alisa Ross wrote in a court filing earlier this month.
From September 2020 to January 2024, Yiu used the property to manufacture and distribute marijuana, prosecutors said.
On Dec. 13, 2024, federal agents interviewed Yiu in Brooklyn, according to prosecutors. Yiu admitted to “growing weed” at the St. Albans property until January 2024. He told the agents he sold the marijuana to buyers in Massachusetts.
Federal agents executed a search warrant at the property Jan. 8, 2025, and confirmed it was being used to grow and distribute marijuana, prosecutors said.
Neither Yiu nor the property was licensed through the Maine Office of Cannabis Policy.
Yiu’s case was one of a handful that made its way to federal court amid a crackdown on illegal cannabis grow houses in rural Maine, in 2024 and 2025. Many of the raids were in Somerset County.
Many busts at the rural properties resulted in arrests of people of Asian descent. Federal prosecutors in Maine have pointed to a possible link between Chinese criminal organizations and the grow houses, which they estimated totaled at least 100.
The Maine Office of Cannabis Policy confirmed in late 2024 that more than 120 previously illicit grows had entered the state’s licensed medical caregiver program.

title: Couple sued by lobster co-op over fraud scheme sells marina to pay off penalty
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A couple accused of defrauding a Maine lobsterman’s cooperative have paid their court-ordered penalty in full after selling a Winter Harbor marine facility and ferry terminal for $3.2 million.
Anthony and Josette Pettegrow were ordered to pay just over $3.8 million after they were sued in federal court in 2019 by Lobster 207 over a fraud scheme connected to the couple’s Trenton lobster pound.
Joseph Townsend, a local philanthropist and conservationist, purchased Winter Harbor Marine Center, which serves as the terminal for a ferry to Bar Harbor, according to a town official.
The sale closes a yearslong legal saga between the owners of the Trenton Bridge Lobster Pound and Maine Lobstering Union Local 207, a group of fishermen that pooled money to operate a wholesale lobster business.
The conflict arose after the cooperative purchased Anthony and Josette Pettegrow’s wholesale lobster business for $4 million in 2017 and then later alleged that the family swindled the group by violating the sale terms.
The couple and their son Warren Pettegrow, who was hired as CEO of the business, were accused of embezzling funds, submitting fraudulent invoices, surcharging lobster products and violating the sale contract by operating a competing wholesale outfit.
Following the Winter Harbor sale, the Pettegrows paid the cooperative just over $3.8 million — their share of the $5 million settlement awarded to the group, according to David Johnson, an attorney for Lobster 207.
The couple’s co-defendants, including their son Warren Pettegrow, had already paid their shares of the settlement, according to court documents.
The Pettegrows own several local businesses including the Trenton Bridge Lobster Pound, which was at the center of the alleged fraud scheme and is a staple for many visitors on their way to Mount Desert Island.
The Winter Harbor Marine Center was sold to Mosquito Harbor Holdings, according to real estate transfer records. The Ellsworth-based company was established in May 2026, according to filings with Maine’s Department of the Secretary of State.
Joseph Townsend, a member of the Schoodic Institute’s Board of Directors and head of a Pennsylvania park preservation nonprofit, was behind the purchase, according to a Winter Harbor town official. Last year, Townsend and his wife JoAnn purchased a historic former church in Winter Harbor to house local nonprofit Winter Harbor Music.
Townsend did not respond Tuesday to an inquiry from the Bangor Daily News.
The Schoodic Institute previously leased the site for a 20-year term to provide researchers with direct ocean access and to ensure the marina and ferry service would continue operating. That agreement was dissolved during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to a local realty group.
The marine facility, which offers 13 registered moorings, was first listed for sale a year ago by LandVest-Christie’s for $4.95 million.
The Pettegrows filed for bankruptcy last year, following the $5 million settlement between the parties. The union argued they did so to avoid paying the judgment, according to court records. The Trenton lobster pound also filed for bankruptcy but has remained open for business.

title: How can we trust Susan Collins on the environment?
text:
I heat my home with a heat pump. It keeps the house warm through a Maine winter and costs less than the oil it replaced. It was one reason I was so disappointed that Sen. Susan Collins voted to advance the 2025 budget bill that rolled back the tax credits that help other Maine families make the same switch.
Sen. Collins often positions herself as an environmentalist, but her voting record doesn’t always reflect that. She earned a 0% rating from the League of Conservation Voters in 2024 and 31% in 2025, alongside her vote against the Inflation Reduction Act. Most recently, Collins voted to confirm Eighth Circuit judge Justin Smith, whose record as Missouri’s deputy attorney general included backing industry challenges to state clean water protections.
On May 18, Collins voted to confirm Stevan Pearce as director of the Bureau of Land Management, which oversees more than 245 million acres of public lands. Pearce has a track record of supporting the sell-off of public lands, conflicts of interest with the oil and gas industry and a history of trying to shrink and block the designation of national monuments.
Maine’s clean air, rivers and reduced dependence on heating oil didn’t happen by accident. Given her recent votes, how can Mainers trust Sen. Collins to protect our environment from big oil and gas?
Stephen Simpson
Portland

title: How to take advantage of the campaign spending bonanza
text:
Dan Kolbert is a builder in Portland.
As summer turns to fall, the electoral campaigns in Maine are sure to heat up. Unprecedented sums of money are expected to flow into the state, in an effort to sway people one way or the other.
As a concerned citizen, I am anxious about the impact of all this spending. My first thought, like many of you no doubt, is “How do I get mine?”
Recently in Dallas, President Trump made his most important electoral reform yet, when he promised to buy our votes. Along with centralizing voter rolls under his control, sending the military to patrol voting sites and withholding funds from Democratic states, he is transforming our country in ways no one could have imagined. It is an exciting time to be a voter in America!
Unfortunately, he set a price for our votes, and apparently believes that all votes should cost the same. This seems shockingly short-sighted. If, as many analysts think, we hold the key to control of the Senate, shouldn’t we command top dollar for our votes? Does he really think our precious Maine votes are worth the same as those of people from Massachusetts? Fortunately, there is still time before the November elections, so let’s hope that he reconsiders this poorly thought out position.
We must, however, remain realists. For obscure historical reasons, vote-buying has negative connotations, and it seems likely that we won’t get our promised $5,000 before November. With that in mind, I have assembled a short list of alternatives that, while requiring more effort, promise greater gain for those with a little gumption.
Start a radio station.
There are a limited number of media outlets in Maine, and it seems likely that the ad budgets will quickly swamp the available slots. Campaigns will be desperate for alternatives. Put a speaker in your window and call it a low-power FM station. Play Chumbawumba’s “I Get Knocked Down” on the hour, every hour, and reserve the remaining 56 1/2 minutes for advertising.
Form a PAC.
There are plenty of identified groups — anti-abortion, pro-choice, gun rights and so on. But there are thousands of people just waiting for someone to stand up for their interests. Tax deductions for travel hockey teams. Banning lawn mowers on Sundays before 9 a.m. Making weed less smelly. Priority parking for big pickups. Campaigns will be so desperate to pick up a half dozen votes by Halloween that they’ll pull up to your house with truckloads of cash.
Become a pundit.
The short-lived Graham Platner campaign proved that there’s an insatiable appetite nationally for people who can explain our out-of-the-way state to a nationwide audience. Most people think of us as folks who talk funny and wear Grundens and plaid. Well, lean into it!
Listen to a few hours of Tim Sample and you’ll be able to pull off a 30- second interview on national news without breaking a sweat. Learn how to talk at length without getting to the point. Learn how to pronounce “Wytopitlock.” Pretend you like Moxie. You’ll have mobile TV trucks lined up around the block.
Those are just a few of the ideas out there. What are yours? Have fun.
As the old saying goes, the personal is political. And there’s nothing more personal than getting paid. Thank you for your attention to this matter!

title: Letter: Vote for Matt Dunlap for our environment
text:
In the 1970s, I never saw a tick while gardening. Today, what with the ticks and the trips to the doctor for antibiotics, the outdoor work and play that sustain Maine people no longer feel safe.
As the Natural Resources Council has reported, Maine experienced a huge explosion in its tick population and a 20-fold increase in Lyme disease between 2000 and 2016. Paul LePage, as governor from 2011 to 2019, blocked or vetoed climate change initiatives. He hindered state-level research on the link between a warming climate and restricted tracking of its link to the spread of tick-borne disease, leaving Maine unprepared.
Matt Dunlap, a candidate for the U.S. House in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, is committed to climate action and research to prepare Maine for the future due to warming water, land and air. He is endorsed by the League of Conservation Voters (LCV) Action Fund, which works to elect candidates who will fight to lower energy costs, build a clean energy economy with good paying jobs, and protect our communities’ air and water.
Vote for Matt Dunlap for Congress.
Carole Beal
Blue Hill

Maine’s highest court will hear appeals at 3 high schools next week
text:
Starting in Staceyville on Tuesday, Maine Supreme Judicial Court justices will hear appeals cases at three Maine high schools next week.
Oral arguments begin at 9 a.m. Oct. 6, at Katahdin Middle/High School in Stacyville. The three cases include appeals of a murder conviction and 50-year sentence, a revocation of bail based on allegedly unreliable testimony and a request for unredacted public documents.
The practice of appellate law is rarely seen on television or in the movies. The court created the program 21 years ago to give students an opportunity to see how the appeals court functions.
The court will hear a total of nine appellate cases. Justices will also hear arguments at Bath’s Morse High School on Wednesday and at Kennebunk High School on Thursday.
The court has visited about 40 schools to hold actual appellate hearings. Last year, they went to Northern Kennebec Valley High School in Bingham, Oak Hill High School in Wales and Falmouth High School.
These are real oral arguments in real appeals before the court. All justices will be there, although a justice may be recused in a particular case and therefore would not participate in the argument on that case, said Matthew Pollack, the court’s executive clerk.
Each school’s gym, cafeteria or auditorium is transformed into a courtroom so students can observe the appellate process. Students receive copies of the briefs in advance and, after each argument, the lawyers will answer questions from students.
“We hope that providing real-time exposure to the third branch of government supplements the students’ civics education and exposes Maine learners to the concept of justice, ” Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill said in a Tuesday release.
Creating a courtroom environment in a high school takes great effort on the part of the school administration and staff and we appreciate their extensive efforts, she said.
The three opening day cases in Stacyville are slated for 9 a.m., 10 a.m. and 11 a.m.
In the first case, State of Maine v. Chad T. McDougal, the appellant wants justices to vacate the lower court’s decision to revoke his probation based on what he alleges is unreliable hearsay testimony and written statements to police.
McDougal denies allegations that he punched the woman in the eye and he is appealing the decision because in each retelling of the alleged assault to police, 911 dispatchers and medical staff, the alleged victim changed her story.
In the second case, John D. Clopper v. Maine Public Employees Retirement System, Clopper alleges that when he filed Freedom of Access Act requests for public records from the Maine Public Employees Retirement System, he was given nearly 4,000 pages of blacked-out documents with most of the text redacted.
He asks that the documents be released without redactions or with redactions that only obscure what’s protected from disclosure by statute.
In the final opening day case, Lorenze Labonte wants a new trial based on what he said are multiple trial court errors.
Last year Labonte was found guilty of murder by a jury in York Superior Court and sentenced to 50 years in the Maine state prison. Labonte alleges that the trial court erred in its authentication of evidence: admission of calls from jail; leading questions in direct examination; authentication of cell phone records; and sufficiency of evidence.
When the cases are decided, the schools will receive a link to the decisions to share with the students.
The schedule for all the high school hearings and the appellant’s briefs are available on the Supreme Judicial Court’s schedule page. The hearings will also be live streamed.

title: 3 things to know about the redevelopment of the Kennebec Arsenal
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Almost 20 years after it was purchased for redevelopment, the Kennebec Arsenal is sitting in disrepair.
Four years after Augusta city officials deemed the buildings to be dangerous, the city of Augusta and Main Street I LLC, the property’s owner, have reached a proposed settlement on its future development.
Here are three things to know about the Kennebec Arsenal and the next steps on the road to redevelopment.
VACANT FOR ALMOST 20 YEARS
Tom Niemann, a North Carolina developer and the primary owner of the limited liability company that owns the Arsenal, bought the property from the state of Maine in 2007 for $280,000 with the agreement he would preserve, maintain and repair the property to keep its value as a historic place.
The original plans were to develop the buildings into a mixed-use site with retail, office space, a boutique hotel and residences. But since the sale almost 20 years ago, little progress has been made.
The Kennebec Arsenal, a group of eight granite buildings overlooking the Kennebec River, was built by the federal government between 1828 and 1838 and is a National Historic Landmark. The building is considered to be one of the best examples of an early 19th-century military depot, according to Maine Preservation.
However, due to the lack of activity over the past two decades, the property has deteriorated significantly.
The lack of action in developing or maintaining the property has been the subject of repeated legal action from the state and Augusta city officials and complaints from community members.
PAST LEGAL ACTION
City and state officials have expressed frustration with the lack of progress a number of times.
State officials sued Niemann in 2013 for neglecting the property, requesting it be returned to the state or alternatively seeking a $1 million bond and assurances from Niemann that he would protect, preserve and develop the property. Niemann denied the allegations, and the lawsuit was later dropped after an agreement was reached in which Niemann said he would better maintain the site going forward.
In 2017, Niemann’s company paid $60,000 owed to the Greater Augusta Utility District for liens and stormwater fees to avoid foreclosure.
Augusta residents formed the Concerned Citizens for Augusta Historical Preservation of the Kennebec Arsenal group and urged city councilors to take action in 2021 after growing frustration with the lack of development.
In August 2022, the Augusta City Council declared the property dangerous and gave Niemann 90 days to address the building concerns before pursuing further legal action. Niemann’s company filed a complaint shortly thereafter requesting the dangerous building determination be reviewed in the Kennebec County Superior Court.
PARTIES PROPOSE TO SETTLE
Now, both parties have reached a proposed settlement that could resolve the litigation pending City Council approval.
The settlement proposal states that Main Street I LLC is in the process of finalizing a funding plan for redeveloping the property. If the plan is not finalized 90 days after the settlement agreement is approved, litigation will continue.
City Manager Jared Mills said Main Street I is pursuing funding from private investors and financial institutions involving low-income housing tax credits. Mills also said Main Street I has obtained permits for the construction of residential buildings with some office space.
Main Street I would also be obligated to obtain certificates of occupancy, a document stating a building adheres to codes and is safe to occupy, from the city for the six buildings slated to be redeveloped within one year of the funding plan finalization. If it fails to receive the certificates, Main Street I would be required to pay the city $60,000 and the city would obtain a court order requiring the company to address any remaining violations within three months.
Main Street I would be required to pay the city $75,000 as a settlement payment when the funding plan is finalized.
Main Street I would be required to replace its sole managing member, Niemann Capital LLC, with a panel of three co-managers: Mike Scholtz, an investor; Richard Parkhurst, a local developer focused on renovating old buildings in Augusta; and Niemann Capital.
A third-party construction manager would be appointed to oversee the redevelopment, and Parkhurst or another person or entity approved by city officials will serve as clerk of the works for the redevelopment. Main Street I would be required to provide a weekly progress report and will be responsible for paying the cost of the clerk of the works.
Mills said the riverfront property has seven main buildings and one accessory structure. Six buildings are currently involved in the permitting process, with the seventh likely to be developed later.
Main Street I would be free to redevelop the seventh building, known as the Old Max, on the same or a different timeline. Mills said Main Street I will likely be using the Old Max building as a staging area for construction, meaning its development would have to come later.
The Old Max building was built between 1907 and 1909 as a maximum security building for the Maine Insane Asylum, according to the Maine Historic Preservation Commission.
Both parties will dismiss the pending litigation if the terms of the settlement are followed. Legal action may continue if they are not.
Niemann declined to comment on the settlement proposal as it is still an outstanding legal matter.
The City Council will consider the proposed agreement during its meeting Thursday in City Council chambers at City Hall, 16 Cony St.

title: ‘How ridiculous’: 11-year-old goes to court after receiving citation for riding a motorbike
text:
SEMINOLE COUNTY, Fla. (WKMG) - An 11-year-old boy appeared in court this week alongside his parents and attorney.
Cade Kirchner was charged with one count of misdemeanor failure to register his motorbike, a vehicle police said he was not old enough to ride.
“We’ll enter a plea of not guilty,” Kirchner’s attorney said in court.
Body camera video obtained showed Cade being fingerprinted, ticketed and issued a court summons.
In the video, Cade can be heard saying he knew his e-bike was actually a motorcycle.
An officer in the video told Cade he was issuing one ticket instead of six possible criminal violations.
“So you’re getting one ticket today. OK? You could have gotten six criminal violations, but I’m giving you one,” the officer said.
The officer also told Cade that signing the ticket did not mean he was admitting guilt.
“OK, all right. You know, this is a motorcycle, you know, you can’t be riding it, all right? So just because you signed this ticket doesn’t mean you’re admitting to any guilt. OK, buddy?” the officer said.
Police said the motorbike was capable of traveling 50 MPH and was powered by a 4,500-watt motor.
After court
After the hearing, Cade’s father, Chris Kirchner, commented on the court appearance.
“How ridiculous that he had to miss school for that,” Chris Kirchner said.
Samuel Filler, the attorney representing Cade, said he expects the case to be resolved.
“We will get it all resolved, no doubt in my mind,” Filler said.

title: High gas prices are spurring states to waive taxes and regulations amid midterm election
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — State officials nationwide are focusing on rising gas and diesel prices tied to the war in Iran, offering gas tax holidays and other measures to ease costs as affordability remains a top voter concern in the critical midterm elections.
The high gas prices took center stage in Ohio on Wednesday, as lawmakers passed a 90-day state gas tax holiday with broad bipartisan support. Ohio is among at least one-fifth of states that have implemented some form of fuel tax relief, with many taking action within the past week, according to an Associated Press review.
Some states have suspended their fuel taxes. Others have temporarily reduced taxes. And still more have targeted relief only to farmers, loggers and others who use a special type of diesel fuel.
The average price of regular gasoline stood at $4.43 a gallon on Wednesday, up roughly 50% since the war with Iran began, according to the AAA motor club. The average price of diesel was $6.41 a gallon — just a few cents shy of a record high set last week.
Here’s what to know about states’ actions on fuel taxes:
Ohio governor’s race at center of fuel tax action
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s office said he plans to sign legislation that will suspend the 38.5-cent-per-gallon gasoline tax and 47-cent-per-gallon diesel tax through the remainder of this year. The plan taps $725 million from the state’s general fund to pay for roads and bridges typically funded by fuel taxes.
Republican legislative leaders scrambled to recall lawmakers to the Statehouse after Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton called for a gas tax holiday last week and rival Republican Vivek Ramaswamy announced a plan to do the same a few hours later. The two are locked in a closely fought contest to succeed DeWine, a term-limited Republican. Democrats criticized Ramaswamy for taking credit for Acton’s idea, while Ramaswamy’s allies said his plan had substance and Acton’s consisted of “tweets.”
Ramaswamy’s running mate, Rob McColley, is the Ohio Senate president. On Wednesday, McColley used a technical maneuver to quickly close debate on the measure, suggesting Democrats were preparing for nothing more than “theatrics.” Senate Democratic Leader Nickie Antonio said one proposal would have called for an end to the Iran war.
Republican state Sen. Michele Reynolds, a co-sponsor of the legislation, said it “will provide much-needed relief to Ohioans at a time when they are feeling the pressure of gas prices continuing to rise.”
In the House, Democratic state Rep. Allison Russo, a candidate for secretary of state, accused Republicans of an election-year “stunt” that will save Ohioans an average of $55 over the next three months.
Several states have already halted or reduced gas taxes
In March, Georgia became the first state to suspend its fuel taxes after the war in the Middle East sent prices spiraling. Republican Gov. Brian Kemp extended the tax break into June. More recently, he announced a 30-day resumption of the motor fuel tax holiday, which began Tuesday.
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun, a Republican, has extended a fuel tax exemption multiple times since spring, with the current version running through Oct. 5.
A six-month, 6-cent reduction in Utah’s fuel tax is in effect through the end of this year. Illinois and Kentucky have more modest fuel tax breaks in effect, delaying increases that were due to take effect in July.
Some states have relaxed diesel fuel regulations
In the past week, Republican governors in Alabama, Louisiana, Nebraska and Texas all have taken steps to provide fuel tax relief for the agricultural industry amid the harvest season.
The executive orders target dyed diesel fuel, which is exempt from state taxes but normally can be used only for off-road machinery like tractors, logging equipment and irrigation pumps. The orders temporarily waive enforcement of those rules, allowing the tax-exempt diesel fuel to be used in vehicles driven on highways.
Governors noted that reduced costs for transporting crops could affect grocery prices.
California ends restrictions on cheaper fuel blends
The Environmental Protection Agency allowed an annual switch to cheaper, winter-blended fuels beginning Sept. 1, a couple of weeks earlier than normal. The change could save up to 15 cents a gallon, according to data from the National Association of Convenience Stores.
But California sets its own stricter environmental fuel standards. In many parts of the state, summer-blended fuel is required through Oct. 31. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom ended the summer fuel requirement Monday, citing a recent state law that requires a reevaluation of regulations when retail gas prices rise substantially.
Fuel tax changes may have a delayed effect for consumers
State actions intended to provide relief from high fuel prices don’t always have the effect some consumers expect. That’s partly because fuel price volatility could cause costs to rise even as tax rates fall. But that’s also because taxes typically are charged at the wholesale level, not at the retail pump.
“Customers expect the day that a gas tax holiday takes effect that the price at every pump will be reduced by that amount. But it’s way more complicated than that,” said Jeff Lenard, a spokesperson for the National Association of Convenience Stores.
“The costs and the changes happen further upstream,” he said. “The retailer may also have product that has already been paid for with taxes that needs to be sold before you can acquire the new fuel that is not taxed and you can lower the price.”
___
Lieb reported from Jefferson City, Missouri.

title: Cornell gang rape allegation leads to renewed scrutiny of laws on intoxication and consent
text:
(AP) - A woman’s account of being sexually assaulted at a Cornell University fraternity house has advocates and lawmakers renewing their criticism of a New York law that makes it more difficult to prosecute people who have taken advantage of others too intoxicated to consent to sex.
Under state law, rape charges generally need to involve force or a clear refusal of sex, unless the victim is physically helpless due to being unconscious, or mentally incapacitated due to being drugged without their consent.
Those limitations have led to something nicknamed the “voluntary intoxication loophole.” Prosecutors can’t easily bring charges against someone who engaged in sex with someone who voluntarily became intoxicated to the point where their ability to say “yes” or “no” to sex was compromised.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited that law as he defended his office’s initial decision not to file criminal charges against any of the men sued by a woman who says she was the victim of a gang rape at Cornell in 2024.
Van Houten said that in her sworn statement to campus police in 2024, the woman didn’t allege that she became intoxicated against her will, or was physically forced into sex or was unconscious when it happened.
“That’s victim blaming, straight up,” in state law, said Stefan Turkheimer, vice president of public policy for RAINN, the largest anti-sexual violence organization in the U.S. “It prevents a lot of cases from coming forward, where prosecutors are reluctant to try to push forward on a case where the person is incapacitated due to voluntary intoxication.”
New York lawmakers renew push to change the law
New York state lawmakers have considered bills to change the law over the years, though the proposals have stalled, despite support from prominent district attorneys and advocates.
Jeffrey Dinowitz, a state Assembly member who has sponsored such measures starting back in 2019, said the Cornell case is “exactly the type of situation this legislation would address” and hoped that there would be additional urgency in the coming legislative session to change the law.
“It’s just outrageous and it makes me angry that we haven’t passed this yet,” he said, adding that “it would at least ensure that the survivor would get justice.”
The woman, identified only by a pseudonym in the civil lawsuit, filed the complaint Sept. 16, saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house on the Ivy League campus in October 2024 after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. She became completely incapacitated while frat members were sexually assaulting her, the lawsuit alleges.
Van Houten has since reopened the investigation, saying he would consider presenting the case to a grand jury for their consideration. But in a written statement issued Monday, he said his initial decision not to charge relied heavily on a statement the woman gave to police that was given to his office, in which he said she had described some of the male students exhibiting incapacitation but not herself.
Police have not released that document, and the prosecutor’s statement only included sparse redacted pieces of that document in his explanation.
Other states with intoxication laws are moving to change them
New York is one of 19 states with rape or sexual assault laws that consider intoxicated victims to be mentally incapacitated only if they became drunk or were drugged without their knowledge or consent, according to research by The Associated Press and a report published in The Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law.
Many of those laws have been in place for a long time. But states have been gradually moving to change them.
After the Minnesota Supreme Court overturned a sexual misconduct conviction in 2021 because the incapacitated victim had voluntarily become intoxicated, the state legislature revised its laws later that year to allow charges to be brought no matter whether an incapacitated victim had voluntarily or involuntarily become intoxicated. Michigan made a similar revision to its sexual assault laws in 2023, and Texas followed in 2025.
“That business of whether the victim was voluntarily intoxicated or involuntarily intoxicated should really not matter in the vast majority of cases, if not all of them,” said Chinmoy Gulrajani, a psychiatry professor at the University of Minnesota who has researched state sexual assault laws. That’s because “the assailant should have known that this is not a person who is in their right state of mind.”
Turkheimer said these laws can have a disproportionate effect on campuses, where people may be experiencing alcohol or drugs in social settings for the first time. He said mental incapacitation laws aren’t about someone having just a few drinks, but about situations in which a person has lost the capacity to consent.
“The movement is, to look at a person who is incapacitated, regardless of how they got there, and actually give that person protection,” he said. “This is a situation where a person has reached a state where they lack the capacity to consent. And in that situation, the law should be protecting those people because they simply can’t protect themselves.”

title: Death Notice: Michael Machacek
Route 69 And Route 9 Intersection In Newburgh Switching To Four-way Stop October 6th
text:
In just one week, motorists who travel along Routes 69 and Route 9/Route 202 in the Newburgh area will encounter a new traffic pattern along their commute.
Read More: Route 1A Paving Project Starts Monday In Brewer And Holden
As of October 6th, the intersection of those roads will become a full 4-way stop, and surrounding towns are trying to get the word out, so drivers aren't caught off guard.
Towns of Winterport and Hampden posted a notice on their social media pages.
"The Town of Winterport has been notified that the intersection of Route 69 and Route 9 will be converted to a full 4-way stop next week...Please use caution when traveling through the intersection and be aware of the new traffic pattern."
The town of Newburgh will also be affected by this, and took to their facebook page to address the changes, and ask folks to plan accordingly, as the there will be a time of transition as people get used to the new rules.
"The DOT will be placing all signage needed and flashing stop signs next week... They will be putting message boards out in these areas as well to notify drivers of the traffic pattern change. We know this will bring some frustrations for a bit while everyone gets used to the new pattern of everyone stopping. We ask that you give yourself a few extra minutes especially in those morning and evening commutes when the traffic flow there is heavier."
Earlier this summer, Maine DOT crews were in the same area working on tree and brush removal, along with taking other actions to make that specific area safer for folks traveling on the roads.
Read More: Old Town Bridge Closure Coming For Winter Prep Work
According to the Maine DOT website, crews also flatten slopes at the intersection, as well as removed guardrails so folks could see farther down the road. Maine DOT crews also paved about 500 feet at this intersection, and positioned a flashing beacon there "to alert drivers approaching the area."
Brittany Roberts from the Maine DOT says the decision was made after some other measures that were put into play did not result and safer travels for motorists.
"This intersection has historically been a high crash location. MaineDOT previously added signage intended to improve intersection visibility, but crash patterns did not improve significantly. Following a review by MaineDOT’s Safety Office, the office recommended converting the intersection to an all-way stop. MaineDOT met with town officials two months ago to review the project, and the town is aware of the changeover next week."
The change is supposed to take place next Tuesday, October 6th, if the weather allows. If there are issues with the weather, they will move the official change date to October 8th.

title: Military academies will no longer give tenure to civilian faculty, Hegseth says
text:
Military academies will no longer give tenure to civilian faculty, Hegseth says, to focus on 'warfighting'
The Defense Department will no longer appoint civilians as tenured college faculty at the United States' military service academies, according to a memo signed Tuesday by Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Video above: Hegseth says "diversity is not our strength" in speech
The memo describes the decision to stop granting tenure to civilian faculty as part of an effort to refocus the military academies on warfighting.
"To ensure our educational institutions remain firmly focused on this warfighting mission, we must address the structural mechanisms that have allowed civilian academic norms to dilute our focus on lethality," the memo said.
The tenure designation generally comes with a career-long academic appointment at a college. Advocates say the job security is a crucial component of academic freedom, as it broadly protects faculty from being fired over their research or teaching. Hegseth's directive apparently would not remove the designation from faculty members who are currently tenured.
The U.S. Military Academy at West Point, the U.S. Naval Academy, and the U.S. Air Force Academy all did not immediately respond to questions, and officials at the Pentagon did not offer further details on the plan when reached for comment.
The percentage of faculty who are civilians varies by military academy. It is highest at the United States Naval Academy, where roughly half of the 600 faculty members are civilians. The academies hire civilian faculty to offer expertise in topics and disciplines that military officers don't study as part of their careers, such as English and the humanities.
Hegseth's decision follows broader conservative attacks on tenured faculty appointments in higher education. Those efforts to rein in tenure are often presented as bids to rein in academics with liberal views.
In Hegseth's memo Tuesday, tenure was described as a factor that contributed to "academic stagnation, faculty complacency, and institutional inability to adapt to emerging needs. Additionally, it contributes to curriculum that drifts from the mission of educating our warfighters to the research priorities of the tenured academics."
Traditionally, tenured professors can be terminated only under extreme circumstances, such as professional misconduct or a financial emergency. Advocates say it's especially important to maintain tenure as controversy grows over scholarly discussions about history, race, gender and sexuality.
The decision Tuesday is part of a broader push from Hegseth to remake the military's education apparatus. Earlier this year, the Pentagon severed longstanding ties with prestigious universities that had been a pipeline for military leadership, forging new relationships with Christian schools and public universities.
The Pentagon has also attempted to reorient the K-12 schools it operates for military families. It introduced a course centered on Western civilization and Christianity, part of an effort to redirect the education system toward what the administration considers patriotic values and classical learning.

title: Let’s have an honest discussion about Social Security
text:
Lenny Shine’s Aug. 22 op-ed (“Don’t fall for Republican distractions”) argues that the Social Security contribution cap unfairly favors higher earners because, once they earn more than $184,500, they “cease to pay a nickel into the program.” He calls eliminating that cap a matter of making them pay their “fair share.”
He leaves out an important fact: America’s working families who earn in excess of $184,500 will receive no additional Social Security retirement benefit based on those “excess” earnings. That is an important omission. Pay nothing in, get nothing out. How is that not “paying a fair share”?
Should American working families who earn more than $184,500 in a year be required to pay more into Social Security without receiving any additional benefit for those additional contributions?
If we are going to have an honest and helpful discussion about the challenges faced by Social Security, we should do so based on an honest and accurate statement of the facts.
Daniel Kagan
Lewiston

title: Maine must review offshore wind alternatives now
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Sept. 22 WMTW report on Maine’s lawsuit challenging the U.S. Department of the Interior’s buyout termination of Gulf of Maine offshore wind leases read: “The lawsuit argues that the cancellations could negatively impact Maine’s plans for future offshore wind development and other renewable energy goals.”
So, just what are Maine’s plans for future offshore wind development? Now is exactly the right time to explore that question.
Previous to the Trump administration holding offshore wind hostage, Maine announced plans to develop an offshore wind manufacturing, assembling and launching facility on Sears Island. Those plans failed to adequately consider a number of other, viable options and failed to generate sufficient funding.
During today’s offshore wind pause — even as Clearway Energy pursues an 800-megawatt onshore wind project in Aroostook County — Maine needs to consider the least environmentally damaging and most economically beneficial offshore wind development strategy.
Developing two currently industrialized ports for offshore wind that would coordinate manufacturing, assembly and launching, a strategy used elsewhere and for the Aqua Ventus quarter-scale turbine now operating near Castine, almost certainly would reduce environmental harm, save costs and spread development’s fiscal benefits across a greater segment of the Maine coast than the previously failed offshore plan.
Climate change poses a clear and present threat to Maine’s future. Clean, renewable energy production helps reduce climate change impacts. Prudence points to further research now into whether offshore wind can be part of Maine’s adaptation.
Steve Miller
Islesboro

title: Current credit card interest rates
text:
Current credit card interest rates
The average credit card interest rate is 19.63%, down from a record-high 20.79% set on Aug. 14, 2024.
Current credit card interest rates
Bankrate Data Center
Since 1976, Bankrate has been the go-to source for personal finance data, publishing average rates on the most popular financial products and tracking the experience of consumers nationwide.
See more
Historical interest rates
How are credit card rates set?
The typical credit card rate formula is the Prime Rate plus a profit margin set by the card issuer. On average, this margin often runs between 12% and 13%. The Prime Rate is currently 6.75%. It’s typically 3 percentage points higher than the federal funds rate, which is set by the Federal Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee.
Essentially, the federal funds rate is the interest rate that banks charge each other for short-term (generally overnight) loans. The Prime Rate is a benchmark for what banks charge their most creditworthy customers. It serves as a basis for many financial products.
Credit cards have a higher markup than other loans, such as mortgages and auto loans, because credit cards represent unsecured debt. That means they aren’t backed by an underlying asset such as a home or car that a lender can seize if the borrower doesn’t pay them back.
How the CARD Act changed credit card rate calculations
The CARD Act, which took effect in 2010, altered the way credit card rates were set. Previously, credit card issuers had much more flexibility in terms of when they could change customers’ rates. Now, the easiest way for them to adjust rates (especially on existing balances) is to tie the rate to an index such as the Prime Rate.
If the Prime Rate changes, almost all credit card agreements are written in a way that the adjustment affects cardholders’ new and existing balances without any special notice required. The exact timing of the change varies. Sometimes the issuer uses the Prime Rate on your statement date. It might also be the first day of the month or the last day of the month or another date of their choosing.
Card issuers can change the rate on existing customers’ new purchases with 45 days’ notice. And they have a lot of flexibility regarding new offers just coming onto the market.
Money tip: The most important thing to know with respect to credit card rate adjustments is that Federal Reserve rate changes (up or down) generally pass through to customers within a month or two. And these Fed rate changes affect new and existing credit card balances.

How do credit card rates affect you?
Most credit cards bill on a monthly cycle. If you pay your credit card purchases in full, you aren’t charged interest and you typically receive an interest-free grace period of at least 21 days. For example, if your billing statement is generated on the 1st of the month, you usually have until at least the 22nd of that month to pay without interest accruing. Depending on when you made the purchase, you might actually have close to two months without owing interest (if you bought something early in the billing cycle).
However, if you carry a balance from one billing cycle to the next, it’s a completely different story. Credit card rates are usually expressed as APRs — annual percentage rates. But taking this a level deeper, what actually happens when you carry a balance is that the card issuer assesses a daily interest rate (typically the APR divided by the 365 days in a year) on your average daily balance during a given billing cycle. The most important thing for consumers to understand is that, when they carry balances, interest is accruing every single day (and usually at a hefty interest rate). That’s why it’s essential to pay down credit card debt as quickly as possible.
Let’s say you have $5,000 of credit card debt and your interest rate is 20% APR. If you only make minimum payments, you will be in debt for about 23 years and you’ll end up paying about $7,723 in interest, according to Bankrate’s calculator.
Keep in mind: An interest-free grace period applies only to purchases. If you’ve made a balance transfer or taken a cash advance, different APRs could apply and there may not be any grace period for those transactions.

Most credit cards charge different interest rates to different customers based upon their creditworthiness. A consumer with an excellent credit score, for example, might be charged 14.99%. That same card might charge as high as, say, 24.99% to someone with a lower credit score. In that example, we would use 19.99% (the midpoint between 14.99% and 24.99%) in our average credit card rate calculations.

title: Las Vegas veteran group uses monthly hikes to address mental health
text:
LAS VEGAS (InvestigateTV) — A small group of military veterans in the Las Vegas Valley has started a monthly ritual of joining together on hikes throughout the valley.
The group, organized by Navy veteran Nathan French, meets on the first Saturday of each month and invites military veterans across the valley to participate.
It’s a mission aimed at supporting mental health and a lifeline for others. The suicide rate among veterans are more than twice the overall national average, according to the Department of Veteran Affairs.
How the group started
French began walking several years ago after suffering a heart attack, initially to improve his physical health. He said he found his mental health improved more than his physical condition as a result.
Three years ago, French walked 22 miles on Veterans Suicide Awareness Day. A local group later asked him to organize weekly walks, and he agreed to a monthly schedule instead.
The group has only been active for a few months and currently has roughly 90 followers on its Facebook page. On this particular hike, around eight or nine veterans attended and together they covered three and a half to four miles.
What happens on the trail
Leake, who filmed the story on his phone and hiked alongside the group, said the veterans connected quickly despite many not knowing each other beforehand.
“A couple of Army vets, who had never met each other ever in their lives, start talking about, ‘Oh, where were you deployed?’ They start speaking that same lingo, and all of a sudden you feel like you have a comrade that you didn’t know 30 minutes ago,” Leake said.
Leake said the conversation grew more fluid as the hike progressed.
At the summit, with a view overlooking Henderson, participants took a moment of remembrance for those they had lost or to reflect on their own experiences.
“You kind of saw exhales. You saw the shoulders loosen. I think that shows something like this works,” Leake said.
Mental health and the veteran community
Leake said younger veterans in particular are still working through barriers to discussing mental health openly.
“I feel like it is the younger veterans, a lot of the time, who are still struggling to talk about it. I think that’s what it comes down to, a feeling like it’s okay to open up about these things,” Leake said.
He said the hikes are intended as a preventative measure for veterans who may be experiencing mental health struggles.
“This is meant to be a preventative effort. This is meant to help those people who may be having struggles with those issues,” Leake said.
The Veterans Social Club is also involved in organizing the hikes. The Las Vegas Valley has a large veteran population, and organizers said they hope the group continues to grow.

title: MDI town restricts garage access after bear sightings
text:
The fate of the three dumpsters at the Mount Desert Town Garage has taken a backseat to what Town Manager Alex Kimball describes as a more pressing matter: a mother bear and her two cubs.
“For at least the past two nights, a mother bear and her two cubs have been spotted at the dumpsters at the town garage,” Kimball wrote in a September 29 email. “They are definitely feeding at the dumpsters, and will almost certainly keep coming back as long as the food source is available to them.”
Earlier in September, a mother bear and two cubs had been spotted in multiple areas in Mount Desert, prompting the town to send out a news flash, writing, “as fall approaches, black bears are more active in areas of the Town of Mount Desert. Bears are searching for food to prepare for winter, and household garbage is a major attractant. We have received reports that bears have been spotted on Beech Hill Cross Road, Ripples Road, and Pretty Marsh.”
Now, a family of bears has been hanging out at the town garage on Sargent Drive, a place which has been in the news lately as the town tries to determine the best course of action for the three dumpsters located there that have been determined to be an insurance liability.
Household trash is often an attractant to the bears.
“They appear to be somewhat bold already, and are ignoring wildlife deterrents already in place. We need to stop this behavior immediately in order to keep them from becoming any more acclimated to the area. While it is possible that this is the same trio seen in the Somesville-Beech Hill area recently, there is no way to know for sure,” Kimball explained.
The town will be placing temporary barricades in front of the garage’s entryways as well as signs explaining why those barricades are there.
The signs, Kimball said, will also be “pleading with people to stop dropping off their trash at the location. This will need to be in place at least until we stop having bear sightings at a minimum. If we do not take these steps immediately, the area will be an enormous hazard to both the bears and the residents. The Town of Mount Desert can’t possibly more strongly request of residents to NOT dump any trash at the location after hours. If they do so, they are reinforcing to the bears that the town garage is in fact still a viable food source.”
There will be no public access to the town garage other than between 7 a.m. and 3 p.m.
“The dumpsters will be removed from the facility at night to reduce the attraction to the bears,” Kimball explained.

title: US can deport the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque on foreign policy grounds, judge rules
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — The U.S. can deport the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque — an outspoken advocate of Palestinian rights — on the grounds that he is a threat to national security, an immigration judge ruled Wednesday.
Salah Sarsour was detained in Milwaukee in March by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers. A federal judge ordered Sarsour’s release in June, saying he raised a “substantial” claim that the Trump administration was targeting him for speaking out against Israel and advocating for Palestinian rights.
Sarsour said in a statement that the ruling was “deeply disappointing,” but that he intends to appeal.
“I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” Sarsour said.
The government says Sarsour’s decades-old terrorism convictions in Israel make him a threat to national security in the U.S. and accuse him of lying about it on his green card application.
Immigration Judge Jayme Salinardi agreed but tossed out the claim that Sarsour lied on his green card application.
Sarsour says he fears for his life if he is deported to the West Bank
Sarsour, who was born in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was imprisoned in Israel in 1988 after confessing to throwing a Molotov cocktail and stones at Israeli military personnel. In 1995, he was convicted of attempting to hold weapons and ammunition. Sarsour denies committing those crimes. His attorneys say he was tortured and coerced into confessing in both instances.
Sarsour does not have a criminal record in the U.S., where he has lived since 1993. His attorneys say the U.S. government has known about Sarsour’s convictions in Israel since he arrived. He is president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee.
Deportation to the West Bank, “means the end of my life,” Sarsour told The Associated Press in a Tuesday interview.
One of his attorneys, Patrick Taurel, told the AP that Sarsour’s earlier treatment by Israeli authorities is “probably a good indicator of what awaits him” if he is deported.
At a status hearing Wednesday, Taurel pressed the judge to specify that Sarsour can only be deported to Israel and the Palestinian territories. Jordan, a country with which Sarsour has no connection, is listed as a possible destination on the deportation order.
Sarsour was instructed by immigration officers to list Jordan as his home country on an immigration form because his preferred entry — “Palestine” — is not a fully independent, unified state. But he “has no right to reside in Jordan,” attorney Patrick Taurel said.
Salinardi refused.
“That issue is preserved on appeal,” he said.
Attorney says Sarsour will fight deportation
Taurel said on Wednesday that Sarsour is being unfairly targeted.
“If Salah can be deported for his speech in support of Palestinian rights, anyone can face the same fate,” Taurel said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a rare memo in June 2025 saying Sarsour could be deported on the same grounds as Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi, both advocates for Palestinian rights whom the Trump administration has tried to expel, according to court documents.
Before the judge’s ruling, Taurel said Sarsour would fight his removal and would likely need to demonstrate that he would face torture by Israel if he were deported.
“It’s a very high bar, although I think we can meet it in this case, given what Salah has already experienced, and given the government of Israel’s treatment of people similarly situated” to him,” Taurel said.
Appeals in Sarsour’s case are due in 30 days. Salinardi did not schedule a future court date on Wednesday, and announced he is retiring and that Judge Craig Defoe will oversee the case going forward.
Sarsour says he was tortured and coerced into confessions
Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour when he was convicted in Israel, testified in August that Sarsour was coerced into confessing and that he wasn’t convicted of any charge tying him to a terrorist organization.
Boulos also testified that Sarsour was tortured while in the custody of the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency. The Department of Homeland Security questioned Boulos about the torture allegations, questioning how he could know it was true.
Sarsour’s current defense team has asked why U.S. authorities waited until this year to detain him. Taurel said the government has known about Sarsour’s time behind bars in Israel for decades and that Sarsour never concealed that information from U.S. immigration authorities.
Experts on forced confessions and the treatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli prisons also testified in Sarsour’s defense. Israeli military courts have faced repeated scrutiny over allegations of limited due process and the high conviction rate of Palestinians. Israel rejects the claims.
In June, U.S. District Judge James Patrick Hanlon ordered Sarsour released from custody pending his immigration case. Hanlon found Sarsour could have a case arguing the U.S. government was retaliating in violation of his free speech rights and that attorneys for ICE and DHS had not explained why Sarsour was suddenly considered a threat after decades of legal residency.
The Trump administration has appealed Hanlon’s decision to release Sarsour from ICE detention.
Sarsour, who has Type 2 diabetes, lost more than 30 pounds (14 kilograms) while detained by ICE, and his blood sugar levels were checked only once a month, putting him at risk of organ failure or death, his attorneys said.
An investigation by KFF Health News and The Associated Press found that hundreds of detainees in at least 33 states have filed federal lawsuits with similar allegations of medical neglect.
Sarsour is among several people who have been arrested in the U.S. and threatened with deportation after speaking out in favor of Palestinians since the start of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2023.
___
Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Portland-Thornton football grudge match, and other storylines for Week 5
text:
It’s clear by this point of the season which Maine high school football teams have potent offenses.
Now it’s time to find out if they also have the goods on defense.
CLASS A BATTLE
Saturday in Saco, two of the top three teams in the Varsity Maine poll meet when No. 3 Portland (4-0) takes on No. 1 Thornton Academy (4-0). These teams have met in three consecutive Class A title games. Thornton won in an upset in 2023 and rolled to a 28-0 win in 2025; Portland dominated in its 2024 victory.
Since 2018, Thornton has played in seven straight Class A championship games and is 72-8 against Maine teams (73-12 overall). Portland and Oxford Hills are the only in-state teams to beat Thornton more than once (both three times).
In its three-plus seasons back in Class A, Portland is 32-5 against Maine opponents (33-6 overall). Three of its five in-state losses were against Thornton (the other two vs. Bonny Eagle).
Both teams are more balanced offensively this season after the graduation of Thornton’s Fitzpatrick Trophy winner, Connor Ayoob, and Portland’s Cordell Jones, the Varsity Maine Male Athlete of the Year in 2025-26.
Thornton’s second-year starting quarterback, Noah Fullerton (26 of 32, 381 yards), has more touchdown passes (8) than incompletions (6) and hasn’t thrown an interception. He was 9 of 10 for 156 yards and 2 TDs last Friday in a 42-0 win against Westbrook.
Brennan Tabor (40 carries, 353 yards) and Josiah Blain (31 carries, 207 yards) are sharing the running reps with Caleb Parenteau (20 carries, 148 yards), who has been effective in a backup role. Thornton is averaging 328 yards and 45.4 points per game.
Portland sophomore David Gomes (38 carries, 414 yards) has emerged as a strong complement to top back Alex Martin (62 carries, 629 yards). With solid play from quarterback Reece Wildes (32 of 52, 499 yards), the Bulldogs are averaging 409 yards and 34.8 points.
This will be a competitive step up for both teams, though Thornton has beaten New Hampshire nemesis Bedford and South Portland (2-2). Portland’s four opponents are a combined 3-12.
Expect both Portland’s 10.1 yards per carry average and Fullerton’s 81.3% completion rate to dip Saturday. The winner will likely be the team that comes closest to its average production.
VARIETY IN TWO FORMS
Fun fact: This is the first time since 2018 that Cony vs. Lawrence will take place at Keyes Field in Fairfield. The B North rivals both enter Friday’s game 4-0. Cony’s spread offense, featuring a diverse passing game, contrasts sharply with the wing-T stylings that have defined Lawrence for decades.
“Lawrence can attack the A, B, C and D gap. They make you defend the full width of the field with their run game. That’s a challenge,” said Cony coach BL Lippert. “Against us, teams are always going to try to take away one thing and then we adapt.”
Lawrence and Cony have each beaten Fryeburg Academy, Skowhegan and Mt. Blue. In those three games, Lawrence had a cumulative 72-point margin. Cony (plus-25) had to rally to pull out wins against Fryeburg and Skowhegan.
Look for Lawrence’s top backs, Keegan Littlefield and Jaiden Hebert, to continue to chew up big yardage. The Bulldogs’ defense will try to dial up some pressure in an attempt to get Cony junior quarterback Drew Lindquist (55 of 87, 692 yards, 8 TDs, 1 INT) a bit flustered.
ANYTHING LEFT IN THE TANK?
How much energy will Marshwood and Noble have after Marshwood’s 52-51 win last week? That game had no punts, no turnovers and 10 lead changes — eight in the second half.
Marshwood (4-0) has momentum but now enters the heart of its B South schedule with a trip to Falmouth (2-2), which has won two straight.
After being pummeled by Marshwood’s wing-T (47 carries, 384 yards), the banged-up Knights (2-2) now have to figure out another option-style ground-and-pound offense in Massabesic’s Veer offense.
Massabesic (3-1) doesn’t have gaudy offensive numbers, but its 213-81 edge in rushing yards per game is telling. Plus, opposing QBs are completing less than 44% of their passes.
First-year Massabesic coach Cory Woodsome credits his offensive line — tackles Gavin Pomerleau and Isaac Best, guards Cam Goodson and Turner Knox, center Eli Tibbetts and tight end Nolan Pomerleau — for the team’s success. Best, Goodson and Knox are sophomores.
“It’s the guys up front. We really instill in these guys the importance of playing with a low pad level,” Woodsome said. “This style is how everybody used to teach blocking. The low man wins.”

title: Hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin gives biggest gift in US college history to rethink education for the AI era
text:
(AP) - Carnegie Mellon University announced Wednesday that hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin is donating $3 billion, with the bulk of the money for a new campus in Miami focused on societal challenges.
The Pittsburgh-based private research university said the gift is the largest ever single gift to a U.S. university. Other donations topping the billion-dollar mark include $1.8 billion from former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg to Johns Hopkins University in 2018. And Nike co-founder Phil Knight and his wife, Penny, also have been prolific donors, including a $2 billion gift to Oregon Health & Science University in 2025.
Griffin’s gift includes $2 billion to build a new 35-acre campus in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood, just north of downtown. The campus is expected to enroll around 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and doctoral students. Construction is scheduled to begin next year.
Rather than academic majors, it will focus on what the university and Griffin described in a news release as “grand challenge areas,” such as human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation.
The rest of the money will be divided evenly between the Pittsburgh campus’ computer science program, which will be renamed after Griffin, and other unspecified projects on the main campus.
“Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems,” Carnegie Mellon’s President Farnam Jahanian said in a news release praising Griffin. “ Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others.”
Colleges are facing growing pressure to prepare students for a workforce that is rapidly being transformed by AI. Job postings including AI and machine learning in the skills requirements or job title are exploding.
At the same time, financial pressures on higher education are mounting. International enrollment is dropping, just as many states are seeing their classes of high school seniors begin to shrink because of U.S. demographic changes. Meanwhile, expenses like fuel, healthcare and technology are rising.
Griffin, a GOP megadonor who founded the Citadel investment firm, owns a waterfront home in Miami, which is part of a growing metropolitan area whose population tops 6.4 million.
The area already is home to the University of Miami, a private research university; Florida International University, a public research university; and Miami Dade College, which started out as a community college but also offers some four-year degrees. Combined, enrollment at the three schools totals around 135,000. Several smaller private colleges are also based in the area.
But Griffin, who has donated over the years to causes such as medical research, charter schools and other universities, saw room for something new.
“The opportunity to bring Carnegie Mellon to Miami places our city at the heart of humanistic and scientific advancement and amplifies the University’s international reach and impact,” said Griffin, who is joining Carnegie Mellon’s Board of Trustees, in a news release.
Even before the announcement, Carnegie Mellon had growing ties to Florida, a state where conservatives have increased their influence on higher education.
Its computer science department runs a program designed to teach middle school students in Florida and several other states about AI. The university also is involved in a partnership with the Gates Foundation to deploy AI-powered course materials for introductory math classes at Miami Dade College.

title: The US military says its withdrawal of troops from Iraq is complete
text:
The US military says its withdrawal of troops from Iraq is complete
The U.S. military announced on Wednesday that it has completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group. The last U.S. troops left an air base in northern Iraq under a deal between Baghdad and Washington.
Related video: Trump criticizes UK for releasing suspects in alleged terror plot targeting base used by US
The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups' strongholds.
Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country's increasing strength and sovereignty.
The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region. Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought — with little success so far — to disarm.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an “orderly departure” from the air base in Irbil, in northern Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” he said. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a “new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against IS and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons.
U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight the Islamic State group, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory.
With the extremist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down.
U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen’s Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.
The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.
While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet.
Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.
The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in Iraq's Kurdish region have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems.
The Kurdish regional government's Peshmerga Ministry said the Kurdish region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the statement said.
Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal.
“The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty,” Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.
He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that “any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means.”

title: Literacy Volunteers of Bangor seeks tutors amid rise in reading, writing help requests
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor-area learning organization is looking for volunteer tutors after seeing an uptick in students seeking help with reading and writing comprehension.
For nearly 60 years, Literacy Volunteers of Bangor has operated as a nonprofit helping adults improve their handle on reading and writing in English.
“About 70% of our adult students right now are immigrants. So, they’ve come from all around the globe, and they’re needing to understand English. Being able to speak it, read it, write in English. They’re often on a track to be U.S. citizens,” Mary Marin Taylor, Executive Director of Literacy Volunteers of Bangor said.
But it goes beyond just reading and writing. A lot of times, volunteers are giving students lessons on skills that are rarely taught, even in school.
“How do you read a paystub? What is a paystub? Why is a paystub important? How does it relate to your life? It was those types of things that we worked on. In this particular case the person I was matched with needed life skills. How do you budget? That money coming in, how do you use it going out,” volunteer Bob Jonah said.
For about a year and a half, Jonah has been volunteering with LVB. For him, the fulfilling part is seeing a person become a new version of themselves over time.
“To watch the confidence level is amazing. To go from not understanding a lot of things to understanding many things. And that’s been, for me, the excitement of doing what I’m doing,” Jonah said.
“I’ve been blessed with seeing just generations of families really change because one adult in that family came forward and asked for help, and it was transformative in terms of what they were able to do differently moving forward, and what they were able to teach their children and how it affected their family unit,” Marin Taylor said.
Similar to a matchmaking website, LVB pairs students and potential tutors based on how well they would work together.
“We prioritize learning each party, like every tutor, every student. And we’re going to make sure that geographically you’re in the same region, timewise you have the same availability, but we’re also going to look at the characteristics and maybe the background of either and just ensure as much as possible that two people can work together and learn from each other,” Marin Taylor said.
While educators are considered a natural fit for these kinds of roles, anybody with a will to help others is welcomed.
“There are people knocking on the door on a regular basis at Literacy Volunteers and think of them as your neighbors. If your neighbor is knocking on your door, and they ask, ‘can you help me with this?’ what would you do? I’d help them. That’s what we’re looking for, is people that can step up with whatever experiences they’ve had in their life, no matter their age, and answer that door,” Jonah said.
For those interested in getting involved as a volunteer, LVB is offering certification training. Classes begin October 19th and continue for the following four weeks.
For more information or to sign up, head to LVBangor.org .
