title: Appalachian Mountain Club celebrates 150 years of finding a balance
Human rights groups ask UN panel to help end ICE's effort to hide locations of detainees
text:
Human rights advocates asked a United Nations panel to intervene Wednesday to help end a new U.S. government practice of withholding from families and lawyers the whereabouts of thousands of detainees facing deportation.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement removed the names of detainees with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System on Sept. 15 in an apparent effort to speed up their deportations. The change, which ICE did not announce and has not explained, applies to more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who are in ICE custody.
The move has interfered with detainees’ ability to challenge looming deportations by impeding access to their lawyers while devastating families who lost track of their loved ones, immigration lawyers say.
A coalition of more than 30 groups who advocate for noncitizens in the U.S. petitioned the U.N.’s Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances to declare the policy a violation of international law and to push for its end.
“A system with no transparency is a system with no accountability, and that should terrify all of us,” said Sarah Decker, an attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, one of the petition’s signatories. “Disappearing people into a network of remote detention sites, hiding their whereabouts, and cutting off their access to outside help is the definition of an enforced disappearance.”
Separately, on Wednesday, more than 45 House Democrats led by Reps. Luz Rivas and Veronica Escobar urged ICE to restore the names to the locator, calling the practice of concealing them “contrary to foundational principles of the American legal system.”
ICE’s parent agency denied Wednesday that its practices amount to disappearing people, saying all detainees “have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”
“The appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. “That said, DHS has a stringent law enforcement assessment in place that abides by due process under the U.S. Constitution.”
Detainees can typically call relatives if they have money in their commissary accounts, while calls to their legal representatives are supposed to be free.
Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal. That typically means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed. They still have several legal options to challenge their detention and deportation. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.
The petition to the U.N. said the policy has already “obstructed legal counsel from accessing their clients in detention, preventing interventions to seek immigration relief, challenge unconstitutional detention, and block unlawful deportations.”
It cited examples of several detainees, including a mother and 7-year-old daughter who were challenging their detention at a Texas facility but lost access to their lawyers as they faced deportation to Venezuela. Only after a judge ordered ICE to disclose their whereabouts did the agency do so, about 18 hours later, and release them from custody, the petition said.
One man reported intense stress and that the “darkest thoughts imaginable went through” his mind after the whereabouts of his elderly disabled mother were abruptly removed from the system, according to the petition.
The petition said ICE’s online locator, launched in 2010, has become “an even more crucial tool” as President Donald Trump’s administration has carried out a sweeping campaign to arrest and deport people who are in the country illegally. It noted that the U.N. working group had lobbied for the locator’s creation and its 2024 expansion to include people detained by the Border Patrol.
The petition asked the U.N. group to urge ICE to publicly list all detainees’ locations within an hour of their arrest and give detainees’ lawyers 24 hours’ notice before a transfer. The U.N. group, which was formed in 1980, helps families locate loved ones who have reportedly been subjected to enforced disappearance by government agents. It has five members and is currently chaired by Grazyna Baranowska of Poland.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Warm Thursday Ahead, Rain Returns Friday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Wednesday. We’re closing out the month of September with another quiet evening across northern Maine, and dry weather will continue through the day Thursday. Before we get there, some patchy fog could develop overnight and linger into the Thursday morning commute. Once that fog burns off, plenty of sunshine and a warm southwest flow will help temperatures climb well above average during the afternoon. Our next round of showers arrives late Thursday night into Friday, followed by a noticeably cooler but drier start to the weekend.
Skies become mostly clear to partly cloudy overnight, while winds remain light enough for areas of fog to develop toward Thursday morning. The latest guidance shows the potential for patchy fog across portions of Aroostook County, with some locations potentially seeing reduced visibility around sunrise. Any fog that develops should gradually lift through the morning as temperatures begin to warm and southwest winds increase.
September certainly brought its share of temperature swings across northern Maine. Caribou spent much of the first three weeks of the month near or below average, before a much warmer stretch arrived late last week. High temperatures reached the mid 70s from September 24th through the 26th, running around 10 to 12 degrees above average on some of those days. Temperatures cooled back down to end the month, with today’s high near 62 degrees sitting much closer to normal for the final day of September.
The warm weather makes another appearance as we begin October.
Thursday looks like a great day across the region once any morning fog clears out. Plenty of sunshine is expected through much of the day, while southwest winds help temperatures climb quickly into the 70s. Changes then arrive Thursday night as clouds increase and showers begin approaching northern Maine from the northwest.
Friday looks considerably more unsettled, with showers becoming widespread as a weak cold front moves across the state. Rainfall totals generally look to fall between a half inch and an inch, although some localized areas could see a little more. While this will certainly provide some welcome rainfall, it still does not look like enough to provide significant relief from the ongoing drought conditions.
High temperatures Thursday look to climb into the lower to mid 70s across nearly all of Aroostook County. Presque Isle and Houlton both look to reach around 75 degrees, while Caribou and Fort Kent climb into the lower 70s. With Caribou’s average high now around 61 degrees, Thursday afternoon will run more than 10 degrees above normal for the beginning of October. Southwest winds around 5 to 15 mph could also gust to around 20 to 25 mph at times during the afternoon.
Behind Friday’s cold front, much cooler air arrives for the weekend. Saturday looks sunny and dry, but high temperatures only reach the mid to upper 50s across northern Aroostook County, with readings closer to 60 farther south. Saturday night will turn even colder, with temperatures potentially falling into the upper 20s and lower 30s across much of the region, bringing another potential frost or freeze concern.
For more details on Thursday’s warm-up, Friday’s rainfall and the much cooler weather arriving for the weekend, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Judge approves Paramount's settlement with states over Warner buyout, allowing merger to soon close
text:
Judge approves Paramount's settlement with states over Warner buyout, allowing merger to soon close
A federal judge has now granted approval to Paramount's settlement agreement with 12 states that sued over the company's takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, allowing the companies to soon close their $81 billion mega merger.
In a Wednesday order, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín ruled that the proposed consent decree was a "fair, reasonable, and good faith approach to address the competitive harms" alleged by the states' lawsuit. Paramount previously called the antitrust challenge the last hurdle ahead of closing its Warner merger, and signaled that it aims to close its Warner acquisition as soon as early October.
Shortly after Martínez-Olguín's ruling on Wednesday afternoon, the company announced that Ynon Kreiz — current chief executive at toy giant Mattel — will join Paramount on Oct. 5 and serve as co-CEO alongside David Ellison of the combined company.
A Paramount-Warner marriage will bring together two of Hollywood's last five legacy studios. HBO Max, a library full of titles including "Harry Potter" and cable networks such as CNN will also find themselves under the same roof with CBS, the likes of the "Top Gun" franchise and the Paramount+ streaming service.
Top prosecutors from 12 states — led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta — sued in July with an initial goal of blocking the merger altogether. They alleged a Paramount-Warner combo would "extinguish competition" and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly movie theatergoers and cable customers.
Last week, the states agreed to settle these claims through new commitments from Paramount, including pledges to increase film production in the U.S. over the next five years, commit millions of dollars to a fund aimed at supporting workers displaced by the merger and establish new editorial monitoring of CNN and CBS.
When announcing the deal on Sept. 21, Bonta said the settlement was about "protecting people's careers, the lives they've built here in California, the livelihoods their families rely on," while maintaining it was not a vote of support for the merger.
Many critics of the tie-up, however, quickly decried the deal as capitulating to corporate pressure and said the proposed terms were too weak. Martínez-Olguín didn't greenlight the terms right away — maintaining at a hearing on Thursday that the court isn't merely a "rubber stamp" on a settlement of this kind and that she, like many others, still had questions.
The judge granted outside critics of the settlement — including members of the Block The Merger coalition and the League of United Latin American Citizens — a brief window to share their opposition with the court through amicus briefs. She also instructed Paramount and the settling states to respond to a letter from Democratic Sen. Cory Booker, who called for a more thorough review of the deal.
By Wednesday's order, however, she concluded that the hopes for settlement terms to go further "do not rise to the level of legal violations upon which the Court can reject the parties' negotiated resolution."
The Block the Merger coalition on Wednesday maintained the settlement was a "toothless" deal.
"Allowing the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery merger to move forward with no meaningful structural remedies will cost jobs, mute creativity, weaken independent journalism, and damage our First Amendment rights," Block the Merger said in a statement. But, the coalition added, "if there is one discernible benefit to the approval of this corporate takeover, it's that people are now wide awake and paying attention –- and their anger is not going to fade away."
The Writers Guild of America, which had filed its own suit shortly after the states in July, also reached a settlement agreement with Paramount last week — concluding that it couldn't continue its legal fight alone.

title: Belgrade names Fayette accountant as new town manager
text:
After an almost five-month search, Belgrade appointed a new town manager effective Oct. 19.
Michael Carlson has spent 30 years as a certified public accountant and has five years of experience as a selectboard member in Fayette. Selectboard chair Carol Johnson announced Carlson’s hiring Tuesday.
Johnson highlighted Carlson’s familiarity with accounting, audits and regulatory compliance and his experience in municipal government in the announcement.
Carlson’s salary will be $99,500 per year, and his contract is for a three-year term.
In Fayette, Carlson has been involved in budgeting, capital planning, policy work and day-to-day municipal decision-making. Johnson said this gave him a practical understanding of what it takes to support a community effectively.
“We have every confidence that Mike’s fiscal responsibility, proven grant-writing skills and resilient leadership style will make him an excellent fit,” Johnson wrote.
Carlson and Johnson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Town Clerk Mary Vogel, who is also the tax collector, was appointed interim town manager following the May 1 resignation of Lorna Dee Nichols.

title: He worked to create a ‘normal’ life in Maine’s prisons. Now he’s stepping down.
text:
MAINE STATE PRISON — Two men in shorts and T-shirts stood on a walkway chatting on a clear Wednesday morning in September. Rows of flowers and carrots planted nearby soaked up the sun. Both men were out for a walk before work.
In separate cases in 1999 and 2009, these men were each convicted of murder. The bountiful gardens, personal laptops, permission for remote work and largely unsupervised time are all part of their lives at Maine State Prison. Barbed wire at the top of a fence was visible in the distance, but up close it appeared this conversation could’ve happened at any local park.
A lot has changed in Maine’s correctional system under the leadership of Randall Liberty, commissioner of Maine’s Department of Corrections, who walked up to the men wearing a tan suit.
“What’s going on, guys?” Liberty asked.
His dad served time in prison when Liberty was a child. That, combined with Liberty’s years in the military and law enforcement, formed his belief that people in prison should be treated with respect, life inside should be as normal as possible, and the main goal should be to rehabilitate.
Liberty traveled to Istanbul last year to promote these reforms, which he calls the Maine Model of Corrections. He recently hosted representatives from Israel, Ireland and Norway, and delegations from at least 14 states have come to see it in action.
The Brennan Center for Justice, a national, nonpartisan policy institute that is studying Maine’s prison system, said other states are right to look here as an example, and that Liberty’s attempt to spread the changes statewide is unique. The group issued a new report that calls Maine a “pioneer,” and says the results so far are promising, particularly in reducing violence among inmates and staff uses of force.
The model is widely respected within Maine, too, although people on both sides of the political aisle have questions about the results. Even Liberty acknowledged that for all the attention the Maine model is getting, the transformation from a system focused on punishment to one focused on rehabilitation is unfinished.
But he won’t be leading the charge to finish it.
Liberty, 62, will step down as commissioner on Oct. 1, shortly before Gov. Janet Mills, who appointed him, leaves office.
While Maine started some of the prison reforms before he took the helm, Liberty’s personal mark on the system is visible everywhere, like in a CBS national news segment this month in which Liberty donned a beekeeping suit in the state prison’s garden where inmates can learn the trade.
Brennan Center Justice Program director Ram Subramanian said he thinks Liberty has gotten people below him at the Department of Corrections on board with the vision, and he’s begun the difficult work of changing the culture among inmates themselves, whose buy-in is as important as the staff’s.
“I do hope it continues,” Subramanian said. “I hope they build on their successes.”
MUTUAL RESPECT
The Maine Model is built on the idea that being locked up for years is punishment enough. Once people are inside, the system should help address chronic problems in their lives and prepare them to be productive when they leave, since about 95% will walk out of the prison doors.
A culture of mutual respect among staff and inmates is essential, Liberty said, and acts as a kind of security system. He calls the people incarcerated in the eight state-run facilities he oversees “residents,” and said everyone should care about each other’s wellbeing.
As he led Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram journalists through the state prison this month, just a few staff watched over hundreds of inmates in the building where they played basketball and pickleball, lifted weights, spent time in the chapel and bought food at the commissary window.
Liberty uses every opportunity to enforce the culture he wants to see. Walking briskly by the weight room, an inmate made a flippant remark to a reporter about the quality of the food at the prison. Liberty, in mid-stride, pivoted to ask a staff member for the inmate’s name.
“That’s not how we act in this community,” Liberty said later. “If you’ve got a problem with the food, reach out to me. We’ll figure something out.”
Several inmates stopped the commissioner to ask about an issue and Liberty offered a way to follow up. One called the commissioner “brother” as they parted ways.
This culture may explain why there’s much less violence reported in the prisons. Between 2017-2024, rates fell by 36%, and those for staff use of force fell by 69%, the Brennan Center found.
Inmates told the researchers that violence was far less of a concern for them than it had been in prior years or in other facilities.
Brennan’s report said this is a key metric of success of a corrections system. Yet in most places, “immediate safety concerns and harsh punishment often take precedence,” the center wrote.
It may be one reason why Maine now has an easier time retaining corrections officers and filling positions in prisons than other states, but culture change takes time, Liberty acknowledged. In the Brennan Center survey, 41% of incarcerated men said staff did not treat inmates with respect. That’s 16 points better than a similar survey of prisoners in five other states the Urban Institute did last year, but still shows room for growth.
“It takes persistence to really move the needle,” Subramanian said.
DAD WAS INCARCERATED
When Liberty was just a kid, he visited his own father at the Maine State Prison. In his memoir published this year, “Liberty’s Prison: The Inmate’s Son Who Radically Reformed An American Prison,” co-written with freelance writer Christine Graf, they said the facility at the time was designed to “overwhelm inmates with feelings of ‘horror and remorse.’”
As recently as 2013, the Press Herald reported that staff, inmates and advocates called the prison’s culture “toxic,” and inmates were treated in a way that was “more punitive than rehabilitative.” A prison worker union representative said at the time, “No one wants to work in corrections.”
In part because of his dad, Liberty believes there are six root causes of incarceration: substance abuse, mental illness, poverty, neglect, educational deficiencies and trauma.
As described in the book, his dad checked at least four of those boxes and was arrested more times than anyone in the family can remember. Those stints in prison did not help his dad address the core of his problems.
When Liberty later worked for the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office, he went to crime scenes and saw hundreds of homes where, “I looked at those kids and, you know, that was me,” he said.
Society had let his family down in some respects, he said, especially during one winter when the family of four kids went without running water for three months because the pipes froze. Now thinking about the men and women in the state’s prisons, Liberty said, “All of the systems leading up to incarceration have failed them in one way or the other.”
“We’re the stop of last resort to help these people.”
He’s boosted substance use and mental health treatments in the prisons, and he’s not afraid to try new things. He pointed to what he considers the “gold standard” for the Maine model: a prison unit that looks almost like a college dorm with blue painted walls. Instead of staying for four years, though, inmates could be here for decades.
Dan Roberts, who’s served 21 years of a 55-year sentence for murder (which he said he is still appealing), leaned against the door to his room that has a single bed, a hand-painted mural and two small mounted televisions.
He said he keeps one always tuned to financial news channels so he can call his daughter and advise her on stock trades.
This area, which houses 25-30 people, used to be for solitary confinement. Inmates would exercise by walking in circles in a dog pen. Now it’s the opposite. They have an open kitchen, a long fish tank in the common area, and their own gym and showers. They can walk around the outdoor gardens where they can grow and pick their own food.
Inmates say those amenities are an incentive to behave well and give them a sense of purpose.
Liberty said he understands it can be surprising and hard to see someone convicted of murder living a somewhat “normal” life. He said after he talks to victims or their families they generally — but not always — support the Maine model’s reforms.
Some of the money inmates earn goes toward paying restitution. They also pay child support and cover some of the costs of their incarceration, which Liberty said improves public safety and accountability. Maine has done more around inmate remote work than any other state, according to the Alliance for Higher Education in Prison.
Another man who lives in the unit and was convicted of murder expects to leave prison in six years. The Press Herald is not naming him at the request of a member of the family of the person he killed, who said seeing him in this story could retraumatize the victim’s other family members.
The inmate said that with the money he’s earned working remotely, he recently bought a house.
“I’m just trying to set myself up for when I do get out,” he said. “Education, employment, stable housing — these are all things that help the recidivism rate drop.”
DISCONNECT ON THE GROUND
When Liberty took over as warden of the Maine State Prison in 2015 and then as commissioner in 2019, there was already some momentum for reform, said Subramanian from the Brennan Center. Corrections officials in various states have embraced the idea that prison shouldn’t necessarily be a horrible place, he said.
Maine stands out for its push to expand reforms to all of its prisons and as many inmates as possible, he said. Currently, 170 inmates in Maine are full-time college students, 12 are graduate students, and four are PhD candidates, Liberty said. Others learn woodworking, upholstery, welding or culinary skills, and get trained as commercial drivers or to work in hospitality.
Liberty said opportunities to work, study, and have computers need to grow in order for more of Maine’s approximately 2,100 inmates to get access.
Foster Bates is president of the state prison’s NAACP branch and has been incarcerated for 25 years serving a life sentence for a murder he maintains he did not commit. He said in an interview this spring that he appreciates the programs at the state prison, but that it can be hard to take advantage of them because some are restricted to a few dozen people, and because of lock-ins in the prison.
“Residents here don’t have a problem with the policy. We have an issue with the disconnect of how it’s being implemented,” Bates said.
“It’s challenging for some who are incarcerated to have a perspective of where we are nationally, where Maine was 10 years ago, and where Maine is today,” Liberty said. “Prison isn’t an easy experience regardless of how many opportunities they have.”
The Department of Corrections did not provide lock-in data, but said there has been a reduction.
Bates said he wished Liberty wouldn’t retire. “He’s leaving behind a legacy that can be built upon, but I think it could be destroyed,” he said.
Gubernatorial candidates Democrat Hannah Pingree and Republican Bobby Charles did not answer questions about how they would approach corrections. Independent Rick Bennett said he supports the Maine Model and that rehabilitation and humane treatment belong in the corrections system.
Areas for improvement documented by the Brennan Center include access to healthcare, which got particularly low marks from incarcerated women; the process for inmates to file grievances; and the system’s capacity to prepare people for release.
Just 10% of incarcerated men and 2% of women told the Brennan Center that the facility they’re in does a good job at preparing people to leave. Liberty said he wants to see Maine put more money toward transitional housing.
Still, recidivism is down under his leadership. The Brennan Center noted an 8% drop between people released in 2014 and 2022, the most recent year data is available, though the researchers said it will take more time to know for sure if it’s because of the reforms.
“These initial results show what prison officials and systems can accomplish with limited budgets amid shifting political winds,” the report said. In a sign of Liberty’s cooperation with the study, he’s scheduled to do a presentation with Brennan’s staff in Belfast, Ireland, in October.
State Senator Scott Cyrway, the top Republican on the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee, said he has “a lot of respect” for Liberty, whom he served with at the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office. The senator commended the culture Liberty has been able to foster in the prisons.
But Cyrway is skeptical of the results the Maine Model has produced. He thinks reductions in recidivism could be because Maine has recently made some conduct that used to be criminal into civil offenses. He worries the focus is being taken off of accountability, and he wants to see more support for drug addiction before people are released from prison.
Though his tenure is up on Oct. 1, Liberty is not going far. He plans to work three days a week for Amend, a prison reform program under the University of California San Francisco. In that capacity, he’ll still be leading tours of Maine’s prisons for people from other states and countries.
He’ll also focus on improving access to education, remote work and internet for inmates in Maine, without having to do the administrative duties that come with being commissioner.
“This will allow me to focus on those things I think really make a difference,” he said.
But it also means he’ll no longer be the guy calling the shots.
“In the last eight years, I’ve been hiring people that are like minded, believe in redemption and are forward thinking,” Liberty said. “It’s time for people behind me to step up.”

title: Maine Men's Hockey relying on Swedish goaltending
2 Steves and a propeller
text:
Wiscasset's Steve Erskine said his grandfather Roy B. Rowe and Rowe's brothers Clarke and Frank started Eastern Steamship Company and owned the Winter Harbor and another steamboat. Winter Harbor did the Boothbay-Wiscasset mail run with over 100 passengers aboard, Erskine, of Wiscasset, said. He told Wiscasset Newspaper Sept. 24, Route 27’s paving “gradually put them out of business.” He has a logbook he said shows a Boothbay-Wiscasset trip with seven passengers.
Its income lost to the changing times, Erskine said the Winter Harbor was tied up “just abaft on the port side” of the Luther Little, which, along with its fellow four-masted schooner Hesper, became Wiscasset’s oft-captured image of two vessels in their final resting place.
The Rowe brothers could not afford Winter Harbor’s repairs and they “just left it abandoned,” Erskine said. “And then she went to the bottom in a hurricane, and that was history," Erskine said.
Not quite history for the Winter Harbor’s propeller, however.
Wiscasset author and Wiscasset Newspaper news contributor and columnist Phil Di Vece wrote in his book "Wiscasset And Its Times," divers cut off and brought up the propeller in 1978.
In last week's interview, Erskine recalled when, several years ago, friend Sidney Gammon was Wiscasset’s harbor master. “He said ‘Your granddad’s propeller is stored down at the storage locker and I’ve been told to clean out the locker, so would you like to have it?’ And then I said, ‘Yeah, I’d love to have it.’” Erskine considered it a “piece of Wiscasset history,” and wanted to preserve it.
Erskine worked at Bath Iron Works then and the company, he said, was going to soda-blast the propeller and put a preservative on it. “I had a group of 10 people and we were going to build an informational kiosk down at the waterfront, (telling) a little about the Winter Harbor and … Hesper and the Luther Little,” and return the propeller for display there.
He said publicity about the propeller’s being out of town hands led to the end of that prospect and the propeller went back to the town before it could be worked on.
Sept. 15, Steve Christiansen — known to Wiscasset Newspaper readers as a great resource in Phil Di Vece’s Salt ‘n Spar columns — told Wiscasset selectmen the old steel propeller, now sitting unpreserved at the waterfront, is "slowly eating itself to death." Christiansen said the Winter Harbor owner’s grandson (Erskine) told him he’d still like to improve the propeller’s condition for the town.
As this was the public comment portion, selectmen made no comment. Erskine told Wiscasset Newspaper he plans to talk with Town Manager Dennis Simmons about the idea.
Christiansen told Wiscasset Newspaper Sept. 22, when he was a kid, he could, in extreme low tides, see the Winter Harbor's ribwork. He said he has always known Erskine. Their fathers worked together at Mason Station.
"Hopefully, (this) will come to fruition," Christiansen said of the possible work on the propeller. "It's kind of sitting there rusting into oblivion ... I just think it's nice of Steve to want to do that."
Why does Christiansen like sharing Wiscasset's history, whether with Phil Di Vece for a column, or at a selectmen's meeting? Christiansen explained, his family goes back 290 years in Wiscasset. As a kid, he'd often look at Fanny Chase's book, "Wiscasset in Pownalborough." He has his great grandmother's copy she received as a Christmas gift in 1941.
"So I was always interested in stuff in Wiscasset, from my great grandmother's perspective. And my mother has a pretty good memory of stuff, and so I've just had an interest ... only because I've been here for so darn long. And I just think history is important, and I like talk in about it, and I've got a lot of stuff," he added.
Erskine is one of the captains on Maine's First Ship's the Virginia. He said he's a 40-year member of Wiscasset Yacht Club and that his roots run deep in the Boothbay area. "It's in my blood, and it means a lot to me."
Erskine said his mother Priscilla Rowe became, in 1949, the fifth female ever on the East Coast to get a hundred-ton captain’s license. At 12, she was captain of a 28-foot swampscott dorey taking people to Squirrel and Cabbage islands, Erskine said.
Erskine also recalled the late Ruth Applin, a Wiscasset Boston Post Cane honoree, telling him her senior class trip was on the Winter Harbor. He said she told him two seniors got a couple of empty pint bottles out of the trash and put ice tea in them; the two were up on the forecastle sipping when Erskine's grandfather, a "teetotaler ... grabbed them away from them and threw (the bottles) overboard and said 'I won't have any drinking on my boat.'"

title: MaineDOT to make high-crash Newburgh intersection an all-way stop
Super cars bring smiles to kids facing life-changing illnesses
text:
Super cars bring smiles to kids facing life-changing illnesses
Fifteen supercars roared out of Wyler Family Automotive headquarters in Cincinnati, Ohio, each carrying a special passenger — children fighting life-changing illnesses.
"You get to ride in these cars, I mean look at them, they're goated, I mean they are good, they go fast," said Alex Piening, one of the young participants.
The event, called "Super Cars for Super Kids," paired children with drivers of luxury vehicles, creating moments of joy and excitement.
Warren Watson, who drove a Lamborghini Revuelto, shared his thoughts on the experience.
"I get to drive this car every day, but when they come out, they see the colors of the car, they see the doors, the speed, they really love it," Watson said. "So that's what we get out of this event. To see them smile and laugh and take their mind off of things they are going through, and be a kid."
For six years, The Wyler Fast Lane has hosted patients and families from the Ronald McDonald House, offering them a high-speed escape from their daily challenges.
"If the community is going to support us, we have to do our part and support the community," said Graham Wyler. "An event like this lets us show our passion—automotive, cool cars—supporting the community is the perfect combination."
The excitement was evident among the children, including Waylon Ott, who received a kidney transplant a few years ago.
Reflecting on the experience, Ott expressed gratitude for the event.
"It means a lot to me and the other kids who are riding, and we are thankful that they rent these cars out that we ride. It's pretty special to us, and we love that and are thankful for that to happen," he said.
With engines revving and hearts racing, the event brought smiles and unforgettable memories to children and families, proving that a little speed can make a big difference.

title: Auburn’s Flock cameras will come down, city officials say
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Auburn City Council voted in August to terminate its agreement with Flock Safety and request cameras and equipment be removed.
- Flock Safety initially responded to the city’s termination of the agreement, but did not address removal of cameras and equipment until Monday and are scheduling it.
- Should cameras and equipment remain in place, city officials said the city will remove them.
AUBURN — Residents and city councilors have noted in recent weeks that license plate recognition cameras remain up around town about a month after the city’s agreement with Flock Safety was terminated and months after funding was removed for them from the city budget.
That is about to change.
City officials said Tuesday that Flock Safety officials reported that camera removal is being scheduled.
“However they do not have a timeline for us right now,” said city spokesperson Liz Allen. “They understand the removal is overdue, and they are working to get this accomplished.”
After removing funding for the cameras in May from the the city’s proposed 2026-27 budget the City Council terminated its contract with Flock Safety and requested cameras be removed in August.
Because the terms of Auburn and Flock Safety’s agreement states equipment would be removed within a “commercially reasonable” period of time, the city has interpreted that time period to mean six to eight weeks, Allen said.
Should the cameras and equipment remain up at the end of that period, the city will remove them, Allen said.
Flock data access and data sharing with surrounding law enforcement agencies ended when the agreement was terminated, Allen said.
Auburn police began using Flock Safety cameras, acquired through a federal grant, in 2025. A $24,000 request by the police department in the 2027 budget to carry on the program was denied by the City Council when residents began airing concerns about the use of the technology. The cameras were installed by the department without public input or a council vote.
Republican state lawmakers Laurel Libby and Quentin Chapman, both of Auburn, and David Boyer, of Poland, spearheaded a citizens initiative proposing a new ordinance banning the automatic license-plate-reading technology from Auburn streets. The petition drew 1,800 of the required 1,568 signatures, receiving over 1,200 signatures on Election Day in June alone.
City councilors opted Sept. 21 not to adopt the ordinance, which automatically sent the matter to a special election to be held in four to six months.
City Councilor Rachel Randall of Ward 1 said she was pleased to learn the city has a clear next step to remove Flock Safety equipment, and that she will only be satisfied when the cameras are physically removed, not just turned off.
“I’ve seen reports from other communities raising concerns about cameras being reconnected or reactivated without the municipality’s authorization, so for me, physical removal is important,” Randall said.
Kelly Butler, Auburn City Ward 4 councilor, said Tuesday that it is important that, as a community, Auburn residents balance operational considerations with protecting the privacy of residents. People should expect the city is in a contractual process that takes time to reach completion, she said.
“As we move through the process, information sharing with the community in a manner that offers clear confirmation of status of the equipment while the physical removal is underway is essential,” Butler said. “Overall, I think the shared goal here is to complete the contractual process (in a timely way), share accurate information with our community and assure our residents that their privacy is a priority to the city and council.”

title: Maine’s deluge of political ads is crowding out small businesses
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Jason and January Furchak, owners of Holy Cannoli in Waterville, enforce a hard line of neutrality in the bakery, often turning down requests for rallies, meetings and issue-based signs from politicians and organizers of all stripes.
They’re not neutral about their baked goods, aggressively advertising on WABI to reach hundreds of thousands of potential customers on top of highlighting their offerings to tens of thousands of followers on social media.
Their TV advertising push forces Holy Cannoli to compete, just like car dealerships, shops, colleges and professional services firms across the state, with an onslaught of political advertising in a heated midterm election season.
Led by a U.S. Senate race between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson expected to generate almost $400 million in ad spending, this year’s deluge of ads means fewer slots available and higher prices for local businesses. Rates have skyrocketed for the outside groups that are dominating the Senate race.
“They limit our number of air spots for the next 40 days leading up to Election Day,” Jason Furchak said of the stations. “So I get a little less bang for my buck.”
That dynamic is playing out across the state, with businesses finding alternative ways to reach customers at a time when political campaigns and outside groups are pouring millions of dollars into the state’s TV stations and other media, and to their out-of-state corporate owners to rack up prime advertising real estate for their candidates.
In Bangor, outside groups have paid as much as $7,500 for a single 30-second ad during WABI’s 6 p.m. newscast this fall, according to filings with the Federal Communications Commission. That compares with $3,000 for a spot in the same newscast at a similar time in 2024.
Candidates have paid about the same as in 2024, since federal law requires stations to sell them airtime at their lowest rate in the 60 days before an election, a discount that doesn’t apply to super PACs and other outside groups.
Businesses need to compete with both groups. Elizabeth Sutherland, CEO of the Bangor-based marketing firm Sutherland Weston, said the month before a primary and October “tend to be real trigger points.” In both 2024 and this year, “the season where advertising inventory is tight and pricing is really expensive is lengthening,” she said.
“We could see the writing on the wall, and we got a little more aggressive about making decisions earlier in the year, so we didn’t have to fight for things now,” she said of her team and their clients, a mix of professional service and direct-to-consumer sales businesses.
New business owners, she said, should consider holding off on traditional TV advertising until after Election Day, and instead “get creative” with more ads online, print, signs or through local chambers of commerce. An additional factor for advertisers is that they may not want to run ads squeezed between two negative spots from competing sides, Sutherland said.
“You can’t escape it,” Brent Littlefield, a Republican strategist who works for former Gov. Paul LePage, said, noting Maine has grown increasingly competitive politically, and on the airwaves, over the last 15 years. “Especially in the current day with people moving to various forms of entertainment, local broadcast TV stations and the station owners see election time as a major cash infusion.”
Experts noted it’s challenging to compare the 2026 cycle to 2024 or 2020, because of the variety of media options and shifting rules and disclosure requirements on social media. Campaigns execute different strategies across broadcast, cable and streaming platforms as well as on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
Ads on TV still often dominate discussion, with a spike in demand and fewer slots available. Sutherland said sales managers at local TV stations work with advertisers to ensure the stations don’t lose business with regular clients after the wild election season.
The Furchaks, who have owned the Holy Cannoli since 2019, aren’t seeing higher prices this election cycle because they’re on an annual plan for a certain number of 30- or 15-second spots. WABI let them know months ago that they’ll be on the air less during the busy Senate race as well as the competitive 2nd Congressional District and governor’s races.
The station then makes up for it on the other side of the election, airing more than the usual number of spots for the bakery around Thanksgiving and Christmas. The grab-and-go style of the business benefits from customers who may be 15 minutes away or as far as Bar Harbor.
“They have a viewership of 300,000 that’s just north and east of us, hitting about a third of the state,” he said.
Emily Cain, a Democratic strategist who said she saw back-to-back ads for the Senate, gubernatorial and 2nd Congressional District race during a recent football game, said the constant stream is “the nature of things” every election. That’s because campaigns know they work.
“In today’s short attention span world, if you’re not showing up everywhere, you’re missing an opportunity to communicate with people,” she said.
BDN writer Michael Shepherd contributed to this report.

title: Join me in voting for Charlotte Nutt
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Dear Editor:
I’ve lived in Edgecomb for 20 years, and over the past year that I’ve gotten to know Charlotte Nutt, she has made a huge impression on me. In the time I’ve known her, it’s clear she is a great person who truly cares about this place and is always there to support our town whenever we need her.
While I've known her for a year, Charlotte’s roots here go way back. Her dad, David Nutt, spent years as a local boat builder, and her late mom, Dr. Judy Sandick, took care of so many of us at St. Andrews and Miles Memorial Hospital. Growing up on the peninsula, Charlotte went to local public schools, played field hockey, swam at the Y, and spent summers working as a deckhand on Schooner Eastwind. She knows what life on the coast is like because she lived it.
Through her work in municipal planning, Charlotte understands how important it is to support our town governments. She knows solutions shouldn't be forced down from Augusta, but developed by listening to local towns and giving us the tools to handle our own planning.
She’s also focused on the issues hitting us hardest right now, especially housing. So many young families, tradesmen, teachers, and seniors are getting priced out of the towns where they grew up or work. Charlotte wants to fix that by building more housing, protecting existing homes, and keeping working families here. That same care goes into protecting our working waterfronts, small businesses, and local industries that keep our coast alive.
In the year I’ve known Charlotte, she’s proven to be someone who genuinely cares and is always ready to pitch in. Please join me in voting for Charlotte Nutt for House District 48 this November.
Cara R. Gaffney
Edgecomb

title: Trump’s new AI-powered government website contradicts his claims on the 2020 election and a third term
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration has lauded its revamped website America.gov as a way to simplify Americans’ access to information and services scattered across a plethora of agency sites, but President Donald Trump probably won’t like some of the answers his new site says are sourced from government information.
Asking the site — which says it’s sourced via artificial intelligence from “official government sources” — questions about who won the 2020 election or about the name of the federal department that operates out of the Pentagon yields answers contrary to those Trump himself frequently proclaims.
As Trump was still speaking at Tuesday’s launch event, however, the site began modifying its answers. Asked again about the 2020 election, it replied that it couldn’t answer “political questions,” a response it also gave to inquiries about whether Trump had been impeached or convicted of felony charges.
The Associated Press asked about:
The 2020 presidential election
“Official federal sources do not show that widespread fraud changed the 2020 presidential election outcome. Isolated election crimes did occur and have been prosecuted.”
Since Trump, a Republican, lost the 2020 election to Democrat Joe Biden, he has repeatedly falsely claimed that victory was “stolen” from him and asserted that widespread fraud occurred. Repeated audits and recounts found no significant fraud in the presidential election, and Trump’s own administration said the election was clean.
Trump running for president in 2028
“The 22nd Amendment says that no person shall be elected President more than twice. Donald J. Trump has already been elected twice (2016 and 2024). I am not giving legal advice.”
Trump has frequently suggested he wants to seek a third term, posting about mounting another campaign, donning 2028 caps and discussing ways to make it happen — even as he’s acknowledged the Constitution prohibits it. He had only been back in the White House for a couple of months when he told NBC News, “There are methods which you could” use to seek a third term.
The Pentagon
“The Pentagon is the headquarters of the Department of Defense.”
Last year, Trump signed an executive order aimed at rebranding the Department of Defense as the Department of War, complaining that the Department of Defense’s name was “woke.”
Human action as cause of climate change
“Federal climate-science pages say recent warming is largely from human greenhouse-gas emissions, mainly burning fossil fuels. Earth’s climate has also changed for natural reasons over long periods.”
Trump, who has called climate change a “hoax,” previously issued an executive order that directed the Environmental Protection Agency to submit a report on “the legality and continuing applicability” of the endangerment finding. Conservatives and some congressional Republicans have long sought to undo what they consider overly restrictive and economically damaging rules to limit greenhouse gases that cause global warming.
Presidential salaries
The chatbot said that “some presidents have declined to keep that pay,” mentioning Trump but listing George Washington, Herbert Hoover and John F. Kennedy as refusing their salaries before Trump.
During his remarks Tuesday, Trump, a real estate mogul who took in about $1.2 billion from various crypto holdings last year, said he was the first U.S. president to forgo a salary, something that he has said before.
___
Kinnard reported from Columbia, S.C.

title: Netanyahu says a pilot on a FlyDubai flight stabbed another and apparently tried to crash the plane
text:
Pilot stabs fellow pilot on flight to Israel before passengers intervene to stop attack
Warning: Video above may be graphic; viewer discretion advised
A pilot stabbed a fellow pilot Wednesday on a flight to Israel before passengers burst into the cockpit and wrestled with the attacker as the plane descended sharply and passengers screamed, witnesses said. The jetliner was stabilized and made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
It was not clear what motivated the attack, which led Israel to scramble warplanes amid concerns about a possible hijacking. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saudi Arabia arrested the pilot, who was not identified.
The shaken passengers from the FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv landed Wednesday evening in Israel on another flight, as onlookers cheered.
“We’re going to die,” passenger Naama Bershadski recalled thinking as she closed her eyes and prayed for a good ending.
Aviation experts were surprised that the plane did not crash after an descent so extreme that most of the rudder was ripped off the tail.
A video shared by Netanyahu's office showed passenger Yaniv Hayoun, who grappled with the attacker, wearing a bloodied shirt and hugging the prime minister, who told him: “I look at you and I see a lion. I see a great hero."
Video above, translated: Brother of FlyDubai passenger speaks about flight where captain was stabbed
Responders said they knew they had seconds to act
After a passenger saw one pilot stab the other and called out for help, Yaniv said, he and others pushed their way into the cockpit, where he saw the unharmed pilot apparently trying to destroy the controls, Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported.
“The door apparently wasn’t locked, and we managed to open it somehow,” Hayoun told journalists. “What made it difficult for us was the (other) pilot himself. He had been stabbed and was on the other side of the door.”
As people wrestled with the attacker, Yaniv said he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television. Then other crew members took over. FlyDubai said the aircraft was secured by on-duty crew “who diverted and landed the aircraft safely.”
Another passenger in the scrum, Tzvika Manes, told Channel 12 it took many minutes to subdue the attacking pilot.
A third responder, dentist Shota Musayev, told journalists the passengers realized they had just seconds to take control of the plane before a “critical event.” They also feared another attacker might be on the plane, so “we spread a few more people inside the plane so that if something happened, we would be able to simply take control.”
Musayev then attended to the wounded pilot: “He was just praying the whole time and was in contact with me, and I was afraid we would really lose him.”
Netanyahu identified the Indian pilot as Capt. Smit Machchhar and noted his “extraordinary bravery.” The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was in stable condition.
“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” Netanyahu said on X. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.”
When the struggle was over, video footage on social media reviewed by The Associated Press showed two men on the plane's floor, bloodied and wounded. The captain and first officer were injured, according to a statement by Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, where the plane landed at 9:45 a.m., an hour after making a distress call.
Among the passengers who intervened were members of the Israeli security forces and air marshals, according to a person familiar with a probe by Saudi Arabia and regional partners. The person was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
FlyDubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while an investigation takes place. Saudi authorities also said an investigation was underway.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, heightened security threats. The country is a week away from the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which has triggered a series of wars, and is weeks away from an election.
A panicked mayday call as the flight sought place to land
A person who heard the flight’s communications with air traffic control described the plane being turned away by Saudi Arabia and Jordan before eventually landing in Tabuk, while passengers screamed in the background.
The person said the pilot’s voice was trembling as he called “mayday” and said a hijacking was taking place and ambulances would be needed. But Saudi Arabia initially denied clearance to land and directed him to Jordan. The plane was told to wait for clearance from the Jordanian military and then turned away.
The pilot then returned to Saudi Arabia and said he had to land in Tabuk. The air control operators gave no reason for the refusals. The person who heard the communications spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said he spoke with his counterpart in the UAE and they agreed to work together “against extremist elements seeking to harm security and undermine stability in the region.” The general Civil Aviation Authority of the UAE said it was investigating a security incident.
An official confirmed that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a hijacking. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because the incident was under investigation.
Aviation experts marvel that the plane didn't crash
In the chaos about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk about an hour later, according to Flightradar24, which identified the aircraft as a Boeing 737 Max 8.
“Suddenly the aircraft started to fall down, like, a massive turbulence, like a massive G force, for 20 or 30 seconds,” passenger Almog Italie said.
Former United Airlines pilot and aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said he was surprised that the plane was able to land safely after most of the rudder was ripped off the tail during the extreme descent.
“That was a serious descent and strong aerodynamic forces on that rudder for that to happen. I’m just amazed the aircraft didn’t come apart,” Arroyo said.
Another aviation safety expert, Jeff Guzzetti, said that given the rate of descent, it may not have been possible for the plane to level out if it had fallen below 10,000 feet.
“It is remarkable they were able to pull out of that dive. What saved them is there was enough altitude left for them to recover,” said Guzzetti, who used to investigate crashes for the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration in the U.S.
Israelis have made emergency landings in Saudi Arabia before
Israelis were targeted in a string of hijackings and airplane attacks by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s. Israel has not experienced a hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world, including on Israel-bound flights.
The emergency landing in Saudi Arabia was not the first for a plane carrying Israelis home. The kingdom does not have formal diplomatic ties with Israel, but ended its longstanding ban on Israeli flights overflying its territory in 2022.
Since then, Saudi Arabia has coordinated emergency landings for Israeli passengers, including in 2023 when a plane experienced an electrical malfunction.
The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalized ties in 2020. FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates airlines.
Magdy reported from Cairo and Metz from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Adam Schreck in Bangkok and Ami Ben Tov in Tel Aviv, Israel, contributed to this report.

title: Firefighter killed in BASE jumping accident, fire department confirms
text:
SALT LAKE CITY (Gray News) - A firefighter in Utah died during a BASE jumping accident, the fire department confirmed.
Gabe Reilly died in a BASE jumping accident in Cache County on Sept. 27, according to the Salt Lake City Fire Department. He was 27.
Reilly served as a firefighter for the department for four years. The fire department said that he was “following in the footsteps of his father.” The fire department said his father was also a firefighter who retired from the Salt Lake City Fire Department in 2024.
“Gabe was known for his infectious smile, kind-heartedness, and his free-spirited nature,” the department said in a Facebook post. “Gabe’s commitment to the department, his fellow firefighters, and the community will not be forgotten.”
The fire department did not provide further information regarding Reilly’s death. The agency asked the public to respect his family’s privacy as they grieve his loss.
“On behalf of the Salt Lake City Fire Department, we extend our deepest condolences to the entire Reilly family. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, and fellow firefighters during this difficult time,” the department said.
BASE jumping is an extreme sport similar to skydiving. Instead of jumping out of a plane, BASE jumpers launch themselves from high locations such as mountain cliffs and bridges. The name itself is an acronym for possible jump spots: building, antenna, span or earth.

title: Tick Reauthorization Act officially signed into law
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A new federal law aims to combat the growing threat of tick-borne illnesses in Maine and across the country.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-ME, and Sen. Tina Smith, D-MN, announced the Kay Hagan Tick Reauthorization Act has officially been signed into law.
The bipartisan measure extends funding through 2030 for regional research centers and provides CDC grants to state health departments to improve testing, tracking, and treatment.
It comes as Maine continues to see record-high levels of Lyme disease, with more than 4,200 cases reported statewide last year.
The funding also supports local efforts, including Lyme disease vaccine trials at MaineHealth Institute for Research.

title: Maine must review offshore wind alternatives now
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Sept. 22 WMTW report on Maine’s lawsuit challenging the U.S. Department of the Interior’s buyout termination of Gulf of Maine offshore wind leases read: “The lawsuit argues that the cancellations could negatively impact Maine’s plans for future offshore wind development and other renewable energy goals.”
So, just what are Maine’s plans for future offshore wind development? Now is exactly the right time to explore that question.
Previous to the Trump administration holding offshore wind hostage, Maine announced plans to develop an offshore wind manufacturing, assembling and launching facility on Sears Island. Those plans failed to adequately consider a number of other, viable options and failed to generate sufficient funding.
During today’s offshore wind pause — even as Clearway Energy pursues an 800-megawatt onshore wind project in Aroostook County — Maine needs to consider the least environmentally damaging and most economically beneficial offshore wind development strategy.
Developing two currently industrialized ports for offshore wind that would coordinate manufacturing, assembly and launching, a strategy used elsewhere and for the Aqua Ventus quarter-scale turbine now operating near Castine, almost certainly would reduce environmental harm, save costs and spread development’s fiscal benefits across a greater segment of the Maine coast than the previously failed offshore plan.
Climate change poses a clear and present threat to Maine’s future. Clean, renewable energy production helps reduce climate change impacts. Prudence points to further research now into whether offshore wind can be part of Maine’s adaptation.
Steve Miller
Islesboro

title: Teen charged with attempted murder in Lewiston shooting
text:
LEWISTON — A second person, a 15-year-old local teen, has been charged with attempted murder in connection with a shooting downtown on Sunday afternoon, police Lt. Derrick St. Laurent said Wednesday.
Police charged the boy with attempted murder and reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon in the 3 p.m. shooting at Walnut and Shawmut streets.
The teen, who was not identified because he is a juvenile, has been taken to Long Creek Youth Development Center in South Portland.
Earlier in the week, police arrested 20-year-old Mohammud Osman after the city’s Flock cameras zeroed in on a vehicle that had been driven away from the area of the shooting.
Police said Osman was near the vehicle when investigators tracked it down.
Osman was charged with reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, discharging a weapon near a dwelling and driving with a suspended license.
Police did not say what led them to charge the 15-year-old with attempted murder, a felony punishable by up to 30 years in prison.
No victim was found when police investigated the Sunday shooting.
Police are investigating a number of shootings that have vexed the city over the past few weeks, and since the start of the previous summer in particular.
Investigators said the Flock cameras helped lead them to both suspects in the Sunday afternoon shooting.

title: Landowner Banned from North Maine Woods Speaks Out
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - A North Maine Woods landowner has been issued a lifetime ban and says he can no longer access his property. Mark Thomas was banned from the North Maine Woods in October of 2025. Now, he’s speaking out about what led to his ban and the issues it’s caused him and his family.
Mark Thomas owns nearly 400 acres within the North Maine Woods. For nearly a year he has not been able to reach that property due to being issued a lifetime ban. He calls the accusations unverified and incorrect and says he’d never harm the area. “I love those woods up there. I literally stop in the spring and pick up trash because guys snowmobile down all the roads and I pick everything from gum wrappers to empty beer cans. It’s the most beautiful place in the world to me where I come from. It’s gorgeous. I cherish the place. I love it. I respect it and I want to bring my kid up there to have the memories that I had with my dad and the last thing I would do is do something harmful to the place.”
Thomas denies every accusation against him. He says he never bypassed a gate and bought a season pass every year. He says the trespassing charge was dropped and denies vandalizing a bridge. He says a worker he hired stole the outhouse he’s been accused of taking and later confessed. The situation has not only affected him, but his family as well. “I’ve never stolen a thing in my life and never would and I have the money to buy something if I want it and it was just bizarre. I have 2 kids. I have my son and then me and my wife are in the process of becoming legal guardians of a 15-year-old boy that lost both his parents at a very young age. He moved in with us back in November and he loves the outdoors and this whole summer came and went. It makes me wanna cry and they’re like, “Let’s go up to camp.”, and I haven’t even told them because I keep thinking this is like a nightmare I’m gonna wake up from.”
Thomas says there is no appeal process. He just wants the ban lifted to reach and maintain his property, and enjoy it with family and friends. We reached out to North Maine Woods Inc. for this story. Their response is in our report from yesterday on the ban found here, Landowner Banned from North Maine Woods

title: Man arrested on suspicion of planning an attack on the Texas Capitol, authorities say
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A 40-year-old man was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas Capitol, authorities said.
The Texas Department of Public Safety said in a statement that it received “credible information about an individual planning a violent attack” for Thursday in Austin.
The tip came in Tuesday evening, and SWAT officers made the arrest about 3 a.m. Wednesday at a residence in Converse, near San Antonio.
Benny Caldera Jr. was jailed and could face charges including felony terroristic threat against a public servant, the DPS statement said.
Messages were left seeking comment from John Bunk, an attorney listed for Caldera.
Officials did not provide details about the alleged plot, citing the ongoing investigation.
DPS notified state lawmakers about the threat and arrest early Wednesday. The Capitol remained open during regular operating hours.
Texas Senate Secretary Patsy Spaw said in a notice that there will be increased security at the Capitol during the investigation.
Gov. Greg Abbott said the state DPS was assisted by the FBI in making the arrest.
“Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol,” the governor said in a statement on social media.

title: ‘Psychological warfare’: Family shares heartbreaking loss to sextortion to save others
text:
(Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or a loved one need help, call or text the Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988.)
NITRO, W. Va. (InvestigateTV) — Bryce Tate’s death was the result of a crime the FBI reports is quickly growing across the country.
His father, Adam Tate, is sharing his story to educate other parents. He and his wife, Amanda, said they were initially unfamiliar with the scam police say killed their son.
“We had never heard of the term sextortion before,” Adam Tate said.
Sextortion involves someone coercing a minor to create sexually explicit images or videos, then threatening to release the material unless payment is received, often in the form of gift cards or cryptocurrency.
A 2025 survey found one in five teens have experienced sextortion.
Bryce Tate was a sophomore at Nitro High School. His father described him as “always smiling, full of energy, goofy, dancing.”
“It was the greatest thing in the world, to be able to get home and see his smiling face, and be able to pick him up, and hug him, kiss him, and wrestle him, and it was just so much fun,” Adam Tate said.
“You know, there’s nothing but good memories. And that we’re thankful for.”
The Kanawha County Sheriff’s Department investigated Bryce Tate’s death as a case of sextortion.
“It was just a normal day. My son tells my wife, ‘I’m gonna go take a shower.’ Just normal conversations. There was no red flag. There was nothing that would make you question that there was something going on,” Adam Tate said.
The texts began after school
On the evening of Nov. 6, Bryce Tate received a text message after school while he was working out at the gym. The message came from someone claiming to be a teenage girl interested in him.
Bryce Tate had never met or spoken with the girl, but she had information about him that was accurate. The first text arrived just after 4:30 p.m.
The conversation continued at the gym and as Amanda Tate picked her son up and drove him home.
“And around 7:25, 7:27, somewhere in that area, my wife heard a loud noise,” Adam Tate said. “I said, well, Amanda... He might have fell. Something might have broke. And she walks into the man cave, and that’s where she finds him. You know, and I hear her screaming on the phone.”
Adam Tate would get home as fast as he could.
“In my mind, as his father, I felt like if I would have got there sooner, I could have done something,” he said.
The sound Amanda Tate heard was a gunshot. Bryce Tate had died.
Answers come nearly two weeks later
Over the next 12 days, through Bryce Tate’s funeral and the investigation into his death, Adam and Amanda Tate could think of no reason why their son would have done something like this.
“This crime happened in such a short period of time, we’re talking a three-hour period. My son didn’t struggle with mental health. He wasn’t bullied. There was no heartbreak. There was, he would have otherwise never done something like this,” Adam Tate said.
Nearly two weeks after their son’s death, detectives asked the Tates to come to the sheriff’s department.
“They performed a forensics audit on his phone. And they told us that he was a victim of sextortion,” Adam Tate said. “So, it was nice to get that answer, but then more questions came up, like, what is sextortion?”
Deputies and the FBI believe the person Bryce Tate had been texting was a professional extortionist posing as a teenage girl.
After Bryce Tate received pictures from the other number and was enticed to send compromising pictures of himself, the extortionist revealed himself. He threatened to release the images publicly, ruining Bryce Tate’s life and his family’s life, unless he paid a ransom.
“They wanted $500. My son offered him $30. He only had $30 and, uh, he offered that to him and that wasn’t enough money. So, the next thing that they do is, they coerce them into taking their own lives,” Adam Tate said. “So, this isn’t something that he just thought of on his own. You know, they coach him into that.”
Tate said the extortionist sent Bryce 120 texts in a span of 20 minutes.
“A text message every 10 seconds to keep them engaged by design to keep them in that panic. And they put this imaginary timer, like if you don’t do this within this amount of time, all these images will be released,” he saiid. “And they just keep them in a state of panic. And it’s psychological warfare. And they just, they pile it on. I mean, they just, they max pressure.”
Tate said that pressure becomes all-consuming for kids, who feel unable to put the phone down and see a way out. He said that’s why it’s important for parents to talk with their children.
“Stop believing that this can’t happen to your family because it can. If it can happen to my family, it can happen to yours. So please take a moment and just simply have a conversation with your kid,” Adam Tate said.
Tate and his wife say that Bryce was the “biggest blessing in my lifetime.”
“For my wife and I, and anybody who had the privilege of knowing my son, he was a blessing. And what I refuse to do, what I will not allow to happen, is these cowards write the ending to my son’s story. That will not happen,” Adam Tate said.
No arrests have been made in Bryce Tate’s case.
The Kanawha County Sheriff’s Office says it’s working with the FBI on the investigation.
Advocacy since Bryce’s death
In April 2026, Nitro High School hosted a basketball tournament in Bryce Tate’s honor. The two-day event also served as an opportunity to educate families on sextortion.
The advocacy work of Bryce Tate’s parents reached the West Virginia State Capitol. In 2026, Bryce’s Law went into effect, criminalizing sextortion and outlining penalties.
Parents sharing their stories of loss and pushing for change is why Wisconsin has several laws to stop and prevent sextortion. As of April 2026, victims of sexual extortion can file a civil suit for monetary damages against their perpetrator rather than relying on a criminal case. It also allows a victim’s family to file a wrongful death lawsuit against a perpetrator if their loved one’s suicide was largely a result of that crime.
The state also passed laws allocating more resources to investigating internet crimes against children and awareness campaigns in public schools.
If you or someone you know is struggling with distress or a mental health crisis, help is available. Call or text the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Services are free and confidential.

title: Las Vegas veteran group uses monthly hikes to address mental health
text:
LAS VEGAS (InvestigateTV) — A small group of military veterans in the Las Vegas Valley has started a monthly ritual of joining together on hikes throughout the valley.
The group, organized by Navy veteran Nathan French, meets on the first Saturday of each month and invites military veterans across the valley to participate.
It’s a mission aimed at supporting mental health and a lifeline for others. The suicide rate among veterans are more than twice the overall national average, according to the Department of Veteran Affairs.
How the group started
French began walking several years ago after suffering a heart attack, initially to improve his physical health. He said he found his mental health improved more than his physical condition as a result.
Three years ago, French walked 22 miles on Veterans Suicide Awareness Day. A local group later asked him to organize weekly walks, and he agreed to a monthly schedule instead.
The group has only been active for a few months and currently has roughly 90 followers on its Facebook page. On this particular hike, around eight or nine veterans attended and together they covered three and a half to four miles.
What happens on the trail
Leake, who filmed the story on his phone and hiked alongside the group, said the veterans connected quickly despite many not knowing each other beforehand.
“A couple of Army vets, who had never met each other ever in their lives, start talking about, ‘Oh, where were you deployed?’ They start speaking that same lingo, and all of a sudden you feel like you have a comrade that you didn’t know 30 minutes ago,” Leake said.
Leake said the conversation grew more fluid as the hike progressed.
At the summit, with a view overlooking Henderson, participants took a moment of remembrance for those they had lost or to reflect on their own experiences.
“You kind of saw exhales. You saw the shoulders loosen. I think that shows something like this works,” Leake said.
Mental health and the veteran community
Leake said younger veterans in particular are still working through barriers to discussing mental health openly.
“I feel like it is the younger veterans, a lot of the time, who are still struggling to talk about it. I think that’s what it comes down to, a feeling like it’s okay to open up about these things,” Leake said.
He said the hikes are intended as a preventative measure for veterans who may be experiencing mental health struggles.
“This is meant to be a preventative effort. This is meant to help those people who may be having struggles with those issues,” Leake said.
The Veterans Social Club is also involved in organizing the hikes. The Las Vegas Valley has a large veteran population, and organizers said they hope the group continues to grow.
