title: Judge keeps Venezuelan delivery driver shot by ICE in custody for alleged assault
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in his car by a federal immigration agent in Texas will remain in custody on charges that he assaulted an officer while trying to escape arrest, a federal judge ruled on Wednesday.
Judge Dustin Howell said that the case against Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, should proceed after prosecutors showed body-worn camera footage of the interaction where Garces Perez allegedly struck a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with his driver’s side mirror during the encounter in Austin.
Garces Perez is charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted. His case has sparked widespread outrage across the Texas capital city and brought renewed criticism from Democrats about President Donald Trump’s aggressive crackdown on immigration.
With a bullet still lodged in his back, Garces Perez appeared in court in a wheelchair and his attorneys said he still urgently needs medical care 10 days after being shot. He also wore a sling on his arm and needed help putting on a headset to receive a translation of the proceedings.
The defense argued that the camera footage of the encounter wasn’t conclusive since it didn’t fully capture the moment when Garces Perez tried to flee.
The defense also noted that the federal official who investigated the stop couldn’t confirm whether the ICE agent was actually hit by the car mirror, since he did not interview the ICE agent directly. The officer allegedly struck by the car mirror was not wearing a body-worn camera.
Footage presented Wednesday in court shows officers pulling Garces Perez over Sept. 20 in Austin, where he was making deliveries for DoorDash. The video showed Garces Perez giving officers his drivers license through a crack in his window and then asking in Spanish if he can park his car so that a relative could come retrieve it. The officer demanded Garces Perez get out of the car multiple times, to which he asked if he could park his own car so a family member could come retrieve it. After a back and forth, Garces Perez abruptly and rapidly drives off.
Prosecutors showed a video from cameras a nearby business of the high-speed chase that ensued through residential streets. But the shooting itself was not captured on the footage shared in court.
The federal officer who shot Garces Perez wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The immigration officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned the camera off during the pursuit.
Garces Perez said he was struck by a law enforcement SUV and spun around before he was shot. Federal officers told investigators, however, that Garces Perez attempted to strike an officer with his car at the end of the chase before the unidentified officer fired his weapon.
The accusations against Garces Perez recall previous claims made by immigration agents after other high-profile shootings similarly accusing drivers of weaponizing their vehicles. In a handful of cases, the allegations have been undermined or walked back after the release of body-worn camera footage, drawing renewed scrutiny about the DHS’s reliance on vehicular stops to execute arrests.
Garces Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to make appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day of returning to office.
Garces Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to his lawyer. She said a judge issued a deportation order after Garces Perez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.
His attorneys have filed a lawsuit seeking to stop his removal from the U.S.
___
Riddle reported from Los Angeles.

title: Aging Maine schools are impacting students' education
text:
Aging Maine schools are impacting students' education
Maine Department of Education records reviewed by 8 Investigates show 95 schools sought grants for capital construction projects during the 2024-25 school year, but only two received funding
Aging Maine schools are impacting students' education
Maine Department of Education records reviewed by 8 Investigates show 95 schools sought grants for capital construction projects during the 2024-25 school year, but only two received funding
Aging school buildings are disrupting learning for millions of students across the United States.
According to a new report from the Government Accountability Office, during the 2024-25 school year, 19% of schools across the country closed for at least one day because of structural issues. The disruptions affected an estimated 2 million students, who collectively lost more than 3 million days of learning.
“Before a school closes, yes, you're seeing things like discomfort, distraction, disruption to learning way before you see building closures,” said Jackie Nowicki, the GAO’s director of pre-K-12 issues.
Students in Maine are experiencing those problems firsthand.
“One teacher whose classroom was in the basement said that children needed to wear rain boots on rainy days because, you know, her classroom would flood," Nowicki said. “We had another teacher explain to us that there was a little waterfall in her classroom, you know, as the ceiling leaked.”
In recent years, schools in Portland and Cape Elizabeth have temporarily closed because of mold. Earlier this year, Poland Community School closed for a week because of water damage.
As part of its research, the GAO visited school districts in three states, including Maine. Nowicki said Maine was selected in part because researchers wanted to examine a variety of settings, including a state in the Northeast, where school buildings tend to be older.
In Maine, schools have struggled to secure state funding for building upgrades. District leaders told researchers that because grants are awarded based on need, the system can create an incentive for schools to let their buildings fall into disrepair to qualify for funding.
Maine Department of Education records reviewed by 8 Investigates show 95 schools sought grants for capital construction projects during the 2024-25 school year, but only two received funding.
According to the report, schools have $11 billion in deferred maintenance.
“States and districts are really starting to realize that this issue is too big for anyone to handle alone, and they are going to need to think outside the box, and they're really going to need to engage their communities,” Nowicki said.
A Maine commission tasked with addressing the problem recommended targeted funding for routine maintenance so schools can address facility problems before they reach a breaking point. That may require support from donors and public-private partnerships.

title: The unlocked mind: How exercise sparks our best breakthroughs
text:
We’ve all been there: sitting at a desk, staring at a screen or a blank page, trying to force a solution to a tough problem. When we focus intentionally on a single issue, our minds can get trapped in a loop. We analyze, overthink, and often end up hitting a mental brick wall.
As a board member at both our MDI YMCA and MDI Health, I spend a lot of time thinking about community issues, strategic planning, and complex challenges. But I’ve learned over the years that my best ideas rarely happen in the boardroom or while staring at a to-do list. They happen when I’m running, biking, weightlifting or just moving my body.

title: Mother accused of leaving 4 children, including 2-month-old, home alone during cruise
text:
NORTH MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (WSVN) — A 29-year-old mother was arrested Monday after police said she left her four children home alone while she went on a cruise.
Nathalie Belizaire was arrested on four counts of child neglect, according to authorities.
“You were arrested for four counts of child neglect,” a judge said.
Cruise ticket posted on social media
Officials said that on Sept. 24, Belizaire posted what appeared to be a cruise ticket for a Carnival cruise line on social media.
That same day, she allegedly told a man, possibly the father of her 2-month-old daughter, that she would be “dropping the children off with their great-grandmother.”
“One baby, the baby was born in July of this year. Who just leaves a baby alone like that?” the judge said.
A few days later, the man said he went to the home and found the children by themselves.
Police forced their way into the home and found the children “hiding in the bathroom.”
“There you are,” an officer said, according to body camera video of the encounter.
The children appeared to be shaken, the video showed.
“Just two of you? Three? Four?” an officer asked.
Investigators said Belizaire left all four children, including a 2-month-old and a 2-year-old, without adult supervision.
Mother arrested at port
Police said Belizaire traveled out of town aboard the cruise ship. She disembarked Monday and was arrested at the Port of Miami, where officials were waiting for her.
She was taken into custody by the North Miami Beach Police Department.
The judge ordered no contact between Belizaire and the children.
“No contact with the alleged victims either directly, indirectly, in person, in writing, by telephone, or through third parties. You must stay at least 500 feet away from the victims. They’re home and school at all times,” the judge said.
The judge set bond at $10,000.

title: Survivor, doctor warn of rising endometrial cancer rates among younger women
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (InvestigateTV) - The biggest overall risk of developing cancer comes later in life, as the typical age for a diagnosis is 67 years old.
But recent data shows a growing number of young people are receiving the life-changing news. Researchers at the National Institutes of Health found between 2010 and 2019 the incidence of fourteen cancer types increased among people under 50.
One of those is uterine cancer, which also saw an increase in death rates at younger ages. Most uterine cancers happen in the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus.
A life-changing diagnosis
Amy Nissen said her first symptom appeared in March 2024 — abnormal vaginal bleeding.
“It was the heaviest vaginal bleeding I’d ever had in my entire life,” Nissen said. “I could never get ahead of it. I could never get it under control. I had been having my period for 30-some years and never had to take a change of clothes to work, and now I was having to take a change of clothes.”
Nissen said she searched the internet for answers but found most references to endometrial cancer focused on post-menopausal women over 60, which led her to dismiss the possibility.
“It was one of those things that I was so embarrassed about it,” she said. “I didn’t really bring it up to anybody.”
The bleeding eventually brought her to the emergency room, and soon after, a diagnosis.
She would find out a day before her 43rd birthday that she had endometrial cancer.
“I wasn’t really grasping it yet,” Nissen said. “It was still such a shock.”
Rates rising among younger women
Endometrial cancer rates are increasing nationally. According to pharmaceutical company GSK, more than 160 women are diagnosed every day. GSK estimates 62,000 cases were diagnosed and 12,500 deaths resulted from the disease in 2025, making it the most common form of gynecologic cancer in America.
Dr. Lindsey McAlarnen, a gynecologic oncologist at Nebraska Medicine, said more women in their 20s, 30s and 40s are receiving this diagnosis. She said growing rates of obesity are a contributing factor.
“We see that obesity in general is a risk factor for uterine cancer, but it’s also a risk factor for uterine cancer coming back or recurrence,” McAlarnen said. “Really living a healthy lifestyle and being at a healthy weight is beneficial for all of our patients.”
McAlarnen said abnormal bleeding is the key warning sign women should not ignore.
“Either heavy bleeding or in somebody who has gone through menopause and stopped having periods, any type of bleeding that shows up after they’ve had no bleeding for a year, that’s a reason to see your doctor or provider, because it could be a cancer growing in the lining of the uterus,” she said.
Additional symptoms of endometrial cancer include new or unusual discharge and persistent pelvic pain.
McAlarnen said survival rates exceed 95% when the cancer is caught at stage one, but drop sharply if it spreads.
“I’ve seen too many older women who thought that getting a period again was normal or who thought that having a little bit of spotting with wiping wasn’t something to worry about,” she said. “And then if you leave it untreated for even a year, cancer can spread and that can really impact your chances of survival.”
Treatment and recovery
Nissen was diagnosed early and no chemotherapy was required.
“I opted for a total hysterectomy,” Nissen said. “I know that’s not the choice for all women. It was what was right for me and where I was in life.”
The procedure is a minimally invasive robotic surgery performed by a doctor, completed in a couple of hours, with patients typically able to go home the same day.
Nissen said she is doing well since the surgery and goes in for regular monitoring.
Nissen and McAlarnen are partnering on GSK’s “Don’t Be Embarrassed” campaign to encourage women to speak openly with their doctors about symptoms.
“The more conversations we can have, the more it chips away at that stigma,” Nissen said. “Somebody maybe if they’re hearing my story will go, hey, I haven’t been talking about it but I have something really similar to this going on. I should go get that checked out. Because it can change your life and it could even save your life if you go to your doctor.”
“Don’t be afraid to come in and start that conversation,” McAlarnen said.
McAlarnen also cautioned women against taking hormones — including pills or topical products — without first consulting a doctor, warning that excess hormones can lead to endometrial cancer.

title: How businesses can do well by doing good
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Business leaders have many priorities. Near the top of the list is the bottom line: creating jobs, growing the business and getting ahead financially.
But there is more to doing business than making money. Another priority should be doing good.
Not only is it the right thing to do, but thinking beyond the bottom line can have a positive financial impact over the long haul. From volunteering for a local nonprofit and making charitable donations to treating employees, customers and colleagues with kindness, there are countless ways to give back.
Here’s why doing good can lead to doing well.
Doing good builds goodwill. I think of goodwill as the accumulation of people knowing, liking and trusting you. Every positive interaction, fulfilled promise, helpful introduction, thoughtful gesture and successful project makes a small deposit in your goodwill bank account. On the flip side, showing up late, canceling at the last minute or failing to follow through can result in a withdrawal. Goodwill may be difficult to measure, but its impact is very real.
Goodwill can’t be bought. It has to be earned. When people in your community or professional network see you going above and beyond to help others, that says something about you. It shows that you’re not just about the paycheck. Of course, that only works if you aren’t doing good simply so you can post about it and promote your generosity. Do good because you mean it. When you operate with humility and sincerity, people notice.
Remember the formula: know, like and trust. You cannot put your hands on goodwill the way you can equipment or inventory, but it can have enormous value. It lives in your reputation and your relationships. It gives people the confidence to do business with you. Over time, that can translate into prospect calls, client referrals, repeat business and signed contracts.
Goodwill makes business easier. When people already know, like and trust you, they are more likely to return your call, take a meeting, make an introduction, consider your proposal or give you an opportunity. Think about the difference between a cold email and a warm introduction. Relationships remove friction from business. And ultimately, business is about people.
Your network is your net worth. The stronger your network, the more opportunities you have to connect people, solve problems and create opportunities. Goodwill makes that network even more valuable. And it compounds over time. Twenty or 30 years of doing good, keeping your word and treating people well creates something a competitor cannot simply replicate with an advertising campaign.
Generosity builds goodwill. Generosity doesn’t have to mean making a large charitable donation or spending a weekend volunteering. Goodwill is built day after day, interaction after interaction. Congratulate people on their successes. Write a handwritten note. Make an introduction. Help someone when there is nothing immediately in it for you. Reliability builds goodwill, too. Meet deadlines. Keep promises. Treat everyone with respect.
Build goodwill before you need it. Relationships should not begin when you need a favor, a referral or a new client. Build them long before that. Make deposits in your goodwill account consistently so that someday, when you do need help, people want to help you. If you’re constantly asking and rarely giving, that account eventually runs low. And remember that goodwill can be destroyed much faster than it is built. A reputation that took decades to establish can be damaged by arrogance, dishonesty or broken promises.
Public relations is fundamentally about building goodwill. Whether through community involvement, earned media, thought leadership or simply being a helpful resource, good PR builds positive relationships. But you have to bring value to the table. You can’t just sell. You have to solve people’s problems, whether that means providing useful information, helping a journalist tell a better story or connecting two people who should know each other.
Even beyond PR, business has always been, and will always be, a goodwill game.
The takeaway
Ask yourself this question: How much goodwill have you built among the people who know, like and trust you?
You may never be able to put an exact number on it, but you can keep making deposits.
Do the right thing. Build goodwill. And do well by doing good.

title: Who qualifies for $500 ACA refund check? Payments start going out
text:
Who qualifies for $500 ACA refund check? Payments start going out
The Trump administration started sending $500 refunds to some Affordable Care Act enrollees on Wednesday who the White House said were overcharged for healthcare by the Biden administration.
The Treasury Department issued the rebate checks to just shy of 1 million enrollees across 30 states, with the White House alleging they were overcharged for exchange fees.
“The relief begins with refunding everyone who was overcharged, and the rebates are going out in just a few weeks,” President Donald Trump said.
Related video above | As Affordable Care Act enrollment declines and premiums increase, will Congress take action?
Enrollees who can expect refunds are those who do not receive premium assistance.
The 30 states included are Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
Trump in his address accused former President Joe Biden’s administration of “gross mismanagement” of ACA funds, without providing evidence, and said that the Biden administration collected user fees from insurance companies that consumers paid through higher premiums.
In a fact sheet, the White House claimed that Biden’s administration “accumulated a significant surplus of funds that were not used to benefit the Americans who paid these higher premiums.”
It said the rebates would be sent out beginning in October. Officials confirmed that those rebate checks have begun to go out.
Critics called the move a “gimmick” that doesn’t represent a plan for addressing soaring healthcare costs.
Challenging Trump’s claim that the Biden administration mismanaged funds, Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said it’s entirely possible that the funds Trump has promised came from fees collected during Trump’s first term. His first administration collected more user fees from insurers than it spent, resulting in an estimated $1 billion in unspent funds, according to KFF analysis.
It is unclear whether the $500 rebate represents what each enrollee may have overpaid, where the money for the rebates would come from and whether it requires congressional approval for disbursement.
Roughly 19 million people receive insurance through the Affordable Care Act exchange.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles called Wednesday for the release of records involving his Democratic opponent’s spouse during a morning appearance in Rockland.
Charles is requesting the release of records involving Jason Mann, the husband of Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree, and his video production work with the Island Institute and North Haven Sustainable Housing.
In 2022, While Pingree was director of the Governor’s Office of Policy, Innovation and the Future, the Island Institute was awarded with a $37,000 grant, followed by a Community Resilience Partnership grant.
That same year, the Island Institute released a film titled ‘Climate of Change’, directed by Mann.
Mann, now the executive director of North Haven Sustainable Housing, also produced a video for that nonprofit while Pingree served as its president in 2023.
Speaking outside the Maine State Ferry Service terminal Wednesday, Charles said voters deserve complete transparency over state spending.
“Accountability matters, and that is because when state dollars are taken from taxpayers, they are not expected to be stolen or misapplied or misused or given to family. They are expected to be used for the good purposes for which the government decides to use them, and when they are not used that way, you have a betrayal of trust,” Charles said. “If public money was never paid to Jason Mann or if appropriate recusal procedures were followed, the documents will establish that.“
Pingree rejected the allegations.
“This attack is completely made up. My husband has never benefited from any grant or program my office had any role in. Not one,” Pingree said. “This is exactly what Mainers have come to expect from DC lobbyist Bobby Charles. He won his primary on hateful, AI-generated memes, and now he’s running the same playbook in the general election. It isn’t working. His campaign is trailing in the polls and in fundraising because Mainers are tired of fake attacks and want leaders who will work on the issues that matter to them.”
The Island Institute also denied the allegations.
“No federal or state dollars were used by Island Institute for this film series, and we acknowledge the private funders at the end of the film,” The nonprofit stated. “The Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future (GOPIF) grants cited by the Charles campaign were restricted for work with Chebeague, Long Island and Monhegan, to enroll those communities in the Community Resilience Partnership.”
If elected governor, Charles said he would place inspectors general in every state agency, clarify conflict-of-interest policies, and abolish the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future.

title: College student falls 70 feet off overpass while trying to avoid truck in multi-car crash
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) - A Kansas college student survived falling 70 feet from an overpass while trying to avoid being hit by an oncoming truck during a multi-car crash.
Kyra Kinnison and Sara Celeen are close friends after they met at Kansas State University over two years ago.
“[Kyra is] just a really amazing person, very sweet and helpful. She’s always there if you need something,” Celeen said.
It’s a friendship that was almost lost. Kinnison, 21, and her boyfriend were traveling separately to Salina last Friday night when they encountered a hazard on highway K-18.
“[Her boyfriend] swerved around it and stopped. And [Kyra] pulled over to the side of the road, and then, a vehicle crashed into his vehicle,” Celeen said.
But it didn’t stop there, as more oncoming cars piled up behind, causing a multi-vehicle crash. Kinnison, who was walking along the shoulder on the overpass, was in the path of danger with a truck coming at full speed in her direction.
“She jumped back to get out of the way, and the railing is not very good; you can easily lean over it and fall,” Celeen said.
Kinnison fell 70 feet and suffered serious injuries.
“She had fractures on her back, some of her vertebrae, her pelvis and her tailbone,” Celeen said.
But despite all odds, Kinnison can still walk. Her family from North Carolina paid her a visit in the hospital, alongside Celeen.
“I’m just glad she’s not paralyzed for life,” Celeen said. “There really was a guardian angel out there, looking out for her.”
But what still lies ahead in Kinnison’s journey is healing and the financial cost of it. That’s why Celeen is raising money on GoFundMe, and the community is already rallying behind her.
“It’s just amazing the community we have here. Everyone that’s been supporting her is just amazing,” Celeen said.

title: MaineHousing awards record $2.7 million for winter warming shelters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - As winter approaches, critical relief is on the way for unsheltered Mainers.
MaineHousing has awarded a record $2.7 million to fund nearly 475 beds at short-term warming shelters this season.
Twelve organizations across eight of Maine’s nine homeless-service hubs will receive grants, marking the largest investment and highest number of beds in the program’s five-year history.
The heated shelters will offer overnight protection from life-threatening cold through April 30th, with funds going toward staffing, supplies and extended operating hours.
The Bangor Area Homeless Shelter is receiving five beds in the amount of $10,000 while the Brick Church in Bangor is receiving 65 beds amounting to $427,650.
Healthy Acadia in Ellsworth is receiving $263,025 and 35 beds, while the Augusta Overnight Shelter in Augusta is getting 50 beds at $375,750.
The Mid-Maine Homeless Shelter in Waterville received $172,845 for 23 beds.
After L/A in Lewiston received $389,972 for 112 beds, Home INC. in Orlan got $28,611 for 18 beds, Homeless of Aroostook in Presque Isle received $112,725 for 15 beds, Seeds of Hope in Biddeford got $303,790 for 55 beds, Portland’s Seeds of Hope received $360,720 for 48 beds, State Street Church in Portland got $52,000 for 18 beds, and Tedford Housing in Brunswick got $225,450 for 30 beds.

title: Fat Bear Week crowns its 2026 champion
text:
KATMAI, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - A bear who wasn’t supposed to make it to the final round of Fat Bear Week just carried the whole thing.
It was the 12th year of the popular Fat Bear Week tournament. During the tournament, the internet votes on which of the brown bears in Katmai National Park and Preserve did the best job getting enormous before winter.
A winner was crowned after polls closed Tuesday at fatbearweek.org.
Bear 89, better known as “Backpack,” was voted the 2026 Fat Bear Week champion. It came down to a margin of 5,091 votes, with Backpack beating Bear 910 by 103,344 votes to 98,253 to win the title.
It’s a fitting finish for a bear who spent much of Monday neck-and-neck with his competition.
In the semifinal, Backpack trailed Bear 164, nicknamed “Bucky,” for most of the day before surging ahead by roughly 3,000 votes.
Officials called it the tightest race they had seen in Fat Bear Week.
“This is the first time, this is unprecedented. We have never had a race this close,” Sarah Bruce, a park ranger with Katmai National Park and Preserve, said. “For most of the day, Bear 164 — nicknamed Bucky — he was ahead of 89. And so, I think some fans out there were campaigning hard for Bear 89 and were able to just get some votes in for him.
“This is the first time we’ve ever seen a bear come up from behind and win the semifinals.”
Backpack earned his nickname as a cub by riding on his mother’s back instead of swimming alongside her. His mother, Bear 435 “Holly,” won Fat Bear Week in 2019 but hasn’t been seen at the river in years.
Bear 89’s final opponent also came from a famous bloodline. Bear 910, the lone female in the final, is the daughter of former Fat Bear Week champion Bear 409, named “Beadnose.”
“She’s looking really good to be able to support another litter,” Bruce said. “That is really cool to see mama bears get really fat supporting their cubs.”
This year, it was the fans who came to the tournament hungry.
A crush of traffic overwhelmed the voting site on opening day, forcing Katmai to extend first-round voting.
“THE BEARS HAVE BROKEN THE INTERNET,” the park wrote on Facebook. “Literally.”
Explore.org, which hosts the tournament, said, “We had our biggest Day 1 turnout of all time and experienced some system overload.”
The organization later switched to a different platform ahead of the final.
“There are more polls this year. There’s more rounds of voting. There’s four more bears than we usually have,” Bruce said. “And even just comparing it poll to poll, the numbers have increased in an insane way that I don’t think anybody was expecting.”
The bracket was brutal from the start.
Last year’s champion, Bear 32, “Chunk,” lost to Bear 164 in the first round. It was a heavyweight clash that normally wouldn’t happen until much later in the tournament. Chunk entered this year still living with a completely broken mandible, a broken canine and broken front teeth. Rangers say he kept packing on weight anyway.
While the contest is light-hearted entertainment, the stakes for the bears are real. Katmai’s brown bears lose roughly a third of their body weight during hibernation. Bruce said that during their late-summer feeding frenzy, they can eat as much as 200,000 calories a day and gain up to two pounds daily.
“A fat bear is a successful bear,” Bruce said.
Fat Bear Week began in 2014 as a one-day Facebook event called “Fat Bear Tuesday,” drawing fewer than 1,700 votes.
Last year, more than 1.7 million votes came in from upward of 100 countries.
This year, the bears kept tipping the scales. Fans cast about 2.5 million votes across the tournament, according to results posted by explore.org, well above last year’s total.
“I don’t think anybody would have thought that this would happen,” Bruce said.

title: Rare two-headed turtle hatchling found on Cape Cod
text:
CAPE COD, Mass. (CNN) — A rare two-headed diamondback terrapin hatchling was brought to marine wildlife officials in New England for assessment, according to the Cape Wildlife Center.
The turtle was discovered at a nesting site on Cape Cod.
The hatchling weighs roughly as much as a nickel, the center said.
The center said the turtle has a rare developmental anomaly called bicephaly, in which two independent and functional heads grow from a single body.
The center said it is closely monitoring the appetite, growth and behavior of the hatchling.
The center said it has seen only two other bicephalic cases in the last five years.

title: A pilot on a flight carrying Israelis stabbed another and apparently tried to crash, Netanyahu says
text:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — A copilot stabbed a captain in an apparent attempt to crash a jetliner as it was flying 174 people to Israel on Wednesday. But passengers burst into the cockpit and wrestled with the attacker even as the plane descended sharply, witnesses and Israel’s government said.
The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The shaken passengers from the FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv landed Wednesday evening in Israel on another flight, as onlookers cheered. Israel’s emergency services said they treated three passengers with minor injuries.
It was not clear what motivated the attack, which led Israel to scramble warplanes amid concerns about a possible hijacking. In a CNN interview aired on Wednesday evening, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attacker was an Omani national and was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia, where he was arrested.
Aviation experts were surprised the plane did not crash after a descent so extreme that most of the rudder was ripped off the tail.
“We’re going to die,” passenger Naama Bershadski recalled thinking as she closed her eyes and prayed.
A video shared by Netanyahu’s office showed passenger Yaniv Hayoun, who grappled with the attacker, wearing a bloodied shirt and hugging the prime minister, who told Hayoun: “I look at you and I see a lion. I see a great hero.”
President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu discussed the incident “at length” by telephone and that it seemed as though the copilot “was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job. And, he stabbed the pilot.”
Responders said they knew they had seconds to act
Hayoun, who Netanyahu identified as a plumber, said he and others pushed their way into the cockpit, where he saw the alleged attacker seemingly trying to destroy the controls.
“The door apparently wasn’t locked, and we managed to open it,” Hayoun told journalists at the airport. “What made it difficult for us was the (other) pilot himself. He had been stabbed and was on the other side of the door.”
Hayoun told Netanyahu that as people wrestled with the attacker, he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television shows. Then other crew members took over. FlyDubai said the aircraft was secured by on-duty crew “who diverted and landed the aircraft safely.”
Another responder, dentist Shota Musayev, told journalists they realized they had just seconds to take control of the plane before a “critical event.” They also feared another attacker might be on the plane, so “we spread a few more people inside the plane so that if something happened, we would be able to simply take control.”
Musayev then attended to the wounded pilot: “He was just praying the whole time and was in contact with me, and I was afraid we would really lose him.”
Video footage on social media reviewed by The Associated Press showed two men on the plane’s floor, bloodied and wounded.
Netanyahu identified the captain as Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen, and noted his “extraordinary bravery.” The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was hospitalized in stable condition.
“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” Netanyahu said on X. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.”
Israel’s foreign ministry said the people on board were from Israel, India and the United Arab Emirates. The U.S. State Department said four passengers had American citizenship.
FlyDubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while an investigation takes place. Netanyahu said that he spoke with the UAE’s president, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.
The incident came at a busy travel time as the Jewish High Holy Days with school and work breaks wrap up. In addition, national elections will be held on Oct. 27 and many Israelis plan to fly back to vote, since Israel doesn’t permit absentee voting from abroad.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, heightened security threats. The country is a week away from the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which has triggered a series of wars.
Aviation experts marvel that the plane didn’t crash
In the chaos about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk about an hour later, according to Flightradar24, which identified the aircraft as a Boeing 737 Max 8.
According to a statement by Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, the plane landed there at 9:45 a.m., an hour after making a distress call.
“Suddenly the aircraft started to fall down, like, a massive turbulence, like a massive G force, for 20 or 30 seconds,” passenger Almog Italie said.
Former United Airlines pilot and aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said he was surprised that the plane was able to land safely after most of the rudder was ripped off the tail during the extreme descent.
“That was a serious descent and strong aerodynamic forces on that rudder for that to happen. I’m just amazed the aircraft didn’t come apart,” Arroyo said.
Another aviation safety expert, Jeff Guzzetti, said that given the rate of descent, it may not have been possible for the plane to level out if it had fallen below 10,000 feet.
“It is remarkable they were able to pull out of that dive. What saved them is there was enough altitude left for them to recover,” said Guzzetti, who used to investigate crashes for the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration in the U.S.
A panicked mayday call as the flight sought place to land
A person who heard the flight’s communications with air traffic control described the plane being turned away by Saudi Arabia and Jordan before eventually landing in Tabuk, while passengers screamed in the background.
The person said the pilot’s voice was trembling as he called “mayday” and said a hijacking was taking place and ambulances would be needed. But Saudi Arabia initially denied clearance to land and directed him to Jordan. The plane was told to wait for clearance from the Jordanian military and then turned away.
The pilot then returned to Saudi Arabia and said he had to land in Tabuk. The air control operators gave no reason for the refusals. The person who heard the communications spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said he spoke with his counterpart in the UAE and they agreed to work together “against extremist elements seeking to harm security and undermine stability in the region.” The general Civil Aviation Authority of the UAE said it was investigating a security incident.
An official confirmed that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a hijacking. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because the incident was under investigation.
Israelis have made emergency landings in Saudi Arabia before
Israelis were targeted in a string of hijackings and airplane attacks by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s. Israel has not experienced a hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world, including on Israel-bound flights.
The emergency landing in Saudi Arabia was not the first for a plane carrying Israelis home. The kingdom does not have formal diplomatic ties with Israel, but ended its longstanding ban on Israeli flights overflying its territory in 2022.
Since then, Saudi Arabia has coordinated emergency landings for Israeli passengers, including in 2023 when a plane experienced an electrical malfunction.
The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalized ties in 2020. FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates airlines.
___
Magdy reported from Cairo, Scharf from Jerusalem and Funk from Omaha, Nebraska. Associated Press writers Sam Metz, Aamer Madhani and Josef Federman in Jerusalem, Ami Ben Tov in Tel Aviv, Israel, Adam Schreck in Bangkok, Darlene Superville in Washington and Giovanna Dell’Orto in Minneapolis contributed to this report.

title: Country over party means time’s up for Susan Collins
text:
This lifelong Republican says it’s time for Sen. Collins to go. The reason is simple: her support for Trump.
I have written the senator for more than eight years, always asking for a response. I’ve never gotten one. Odd, considering when I’ve written to Sen. King, I’ve gotten three pages of soggy prose that didn’t address the point.
But the issue is Collins’ support for Trump; her votes for his minions who are harming the American order and her limp opposition when it’s apparent her vote isn’t needed shows me she’s chosen party over country.
I am no particular fan of Mr. Jackson, but I am sure he will stand in robust opposition to the menace in the White House. Country over party.
Earle Wingate
Peru

title: Newcastle Realty welcomes John Pedlowe
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Newcastle Realty is pleased to announce that John Pedlowe of Wiscasset has joined the company as a real estate agent.
Pedlowe brings an extensive professional background in government, strategy consulting, international development, and project management. Throughout his career, he has worked with complex organizations and projects where careful analysis, clear communication and attention to detail were essential— skills he now brings to helping buyers and sellers navigate real estate decisions.
His interest in real estate is also personal. Pedlowe has firsthand experience buying, selling and restoring several residential properties, including historic homes. Through those projects, he developed a particular appreciation for the craftsmanship and character of older homes as well as a practical understanding of renovations, property condition and preparing a home for its next owner.
“John brings an impressive combination of professional experience, sound judgment and a genuine appreciation for midcoast Maine,” said Hannah Hilton, president of Newcastle Realty. “He is thoughtful, detail-oriented and committed to understanding what matters to his clients. We’re delighted to welcome him to Newcastle Realty.”
As he begins his real estate career in Maine, Pedlowe will be mentored by veteran Newcastle Realty agent Clint Miller, drawing on Miller’s extensive experience and knowledge of the Maine market.
A California native whose life and career have taken him around the country and the world, Pedlowe and his family now proudly call Wiscasset home. title: Maine ethics commission won’t investigate whether lawmaker broke confidentiality
text:
The Maine ethics commission voted Wednesday not to investigate whether a Republican State House leader violated confidentiality laws when she shared a letter with the media that House Speaker Ryan Fecteau said questioned his integrity.
Assistant House Republican Leader Katrina Smith, R-Palermo, filed a letter in July with the Maine Commission on Governmental Ethics and Election Practices seeking “an independent review of the legal and ethical boundaries” of Fecteau, D-Biddeford, holding simultaneous roles in the Legislature and as the head of the Biddeford Housing Authority.
Jonathan Wayne, executive director of the commission, initially interpreted Smith’s request as a formal complaint, which would have triggered a confidentiality clause.
Smith, however, actually requested an “advisory opinion,” which does not have the same requirement.
The contents of Smith’s letter, which outlined concerns about a possible conflict of interest between Fecteau’s two positions, appeared in full online in the Biddeford Buzz and in part on the Maine Wire the day after she submitted it.
Fecteau subsequently asked the commission to investigate whether Smith’s letter appearing online violated the confidentiality requirement.
Choosing not to, he said, would set “a terrible precedent.”
“Lawmakers could be subject to bait and switch requests that are immediately shared with the media to then create an appearance of wrongdoing,” he said.
Biddeford Housing wasn’t scared off by the news articles, Fecteau said, but for some employers, that could be enough to withdraw an offer.
“This is not a political game,” he said. “This has very serious consequences for the livelihoods of those who seek and serve in public office.”
To open an investigation, though, the commission first had to determine whether Smith’s letter constituted a formal complaint.
The commission ultimately decided Wednesday that it didn’t, effectively closing the discussion.
But while members made the decision unanimously, they also made it grudgingly.
If a person wishes to file a complaint with the commission they have to agree, in writing, not to share the details of the complaint until the commission decides whether to hear the issue. If they don’t agree, the commission won’t consider the matter.
“It’s clear to me that Assistant Leader Smith never completed the process of filing a complaint and never agreed to keep it confidential,” said William Schneider, commission chair.
Commissioner Sarah LeClaire suggested the law be clarified “so it’s not used in a weaponized way to get a letter out to the press that the public will assume is an investigation,” she said.
“I don’t like what I see in this case,” LeClaire added. “I don’t like the idea of the possibility that this commission was used for some sort of press grab.”

title: Woman charged after 2 children found dead inside home by deputies, authorities say
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — A homeowner in South Carolina is facing charges after authorities say two children were found dead at the home on Tuesday.
Justine May, 31, was booked into the Charleston County jail on two counts of homicide by child neglect, court records showed.
May will remain in custody after waiving her right to a bond hearing on Wednesday. She is scheduled for an initial court appearance Nov. 20.
Charleston County authorities said they were called to the home on Pinewood Drive for a welfare check Tuesday afternoon when they found the two children dead inside.
The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division Department of Child Fatalities and the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office are both investigating.
May’s ex-boyfriend, Zachary Deacon, also found himself in custody recently after being arrested on Sept. 11. The Charleston County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded that day to the same home regarding a reported mental health crisis.
Deacon’s charges include harassment in the second degree after May alleged that Deacon continued to contact her after prior domestic violence.
Family members of May said they had called law enforcement within the last month regarding the well-being of May and the children who were in her care.
Documents stated that Deacon had previously called May delusional, spiraling and in need of getting a grip on reality while referencing involvement with social services.
On Sept. 13, May herself posted on social media screenshots of concerned text messages and emails allegedly from family, with an email specifically expressing concerns about her parenting.
Deacon has since been released on bond, but a judge has ordered him not to have contact with May or the children as a condition of his release.
The Charleston County Coroner’s Office did not immediately release the cause of death for the two children, as investigators said the case remains under investigation.

title: 3 high school football games to watch in Week 5
text:
This season, Varsity Maine reporters will offer up suggestions each week for three games that are worth a drive to watch in person, with a brief explanation of why we think these games are worth a fan’s time.
Portland (4-0) at Thornton Academy (4-0), 1 p.m. Saturday
The midway point of the season features a rematch of last year’s Class A championship game, which Thornton won, 28-0. In fact, these two teams have played in the past three Class A title games, with Thornton holding a 2-1 advantage. The Trojans, to no one’s surprise, are chugging along again in Class A South, scoring 45.5 points per game while allowing only seven per game. Quarterback Noah Fullerton has done well spreading the ball to multiple playmakers, like Quinn Cook and Logan LeBlanc. The defense, meanwhile, has two shutouts in the first four games.
Portland has answered any questions about potential growing pains under new head coach Dylan Rottkov. Even after the graduation of the program’s all-time scoring leader, Cordell Jones, the Bulldogs are averaging 34.8 points, featuring a rushing attack led by senior Alex Martin and sophomore David Gomes. The pair combined for over 300 yards in a 39-13 win over Windham on Sept. 18. Saturday’s game could be another a Class A final preview.
Cony (4-0) at Lawrence (4-0), 7 p.m. Friday
It’s air vs. ground in this rivalry matchup at Keyes Field in Fairfield, and the winner will earn a firm grasp on the No. 1 spot in the Class B North Crabtree standings.
Coach B.L. Lippert’s air attack offense is once again on display for Cony, which has averaged 30.5 points in the first four games. Junior quarterback Drew Lindquist (599 passing yards, 7 touchdown passes, 1 interception) has done well leading the offense in his first season as the starter, equally spreading the ball to seniors Landen Perry (14 receptions, 243 yards, 3 TDs) and Da’Marion Raymond (12 receptions, 139 yards, 2 TDs).
The Bulldogs are off to a hot start behind new head coach Pete Curtis. Nothing has changed in the offensive approach, as Lawrence has ridden its ground-and-pound attack to a 4-0 record. Keegan Littlefield (52 carries, 494 yards, 4 TDs), a senior, leads that attack, along with junior Jaiden Hebert (52 carries, 298 yards, 5 TDs) and senior Hunter Curtis (18 carries, 119 yards, 2 TDs).
This is always one of the best back-and-forth rivalries in central Maine. The Bulldogs knocked Cony out of the playoffs in 2023 (B North final) and 2024 (B North semifinal), and Cony beat Lawrence 46-14 during the regular season last year.
Morse (3-1) at Freeport (3-1), 6 p.m. Friday
Halfway into the season, there’s a three-way battle at the top of the Class D South Crabtree standings, and it includes these two Midcoast schools. After reaching the regional final last season, Morse has steamed on in its first four games, with wins over Mountain Valley, Dirigo and Lisbon. Quarterback Dylan Root has been Morse’s biggest weapon, making plays with his arm and his feet.
Freeport jumped out to a 3-0 start, including a 29-28 win over defending state champion Winthrop on Sept. 11, before falling 14-6 to defending North champion Winslow last week. Quarterback Andrew Thomas has been Freeport’s most consistent offensive threat. He rushed for 151 yards and a touchdown against Winthrop.

text:

title: FOR YOUR HEALTH: Recovering from an ankle sprain
text:
Ankle sprains are a common injury caused by a stretch or tear of one or more of the ligaments (tough bands connecting bones) that support your ankle. Most ankle injuries are caused by rolling or twisting the ankle. Symptoms include pain, swelling, change in color, and not being able to put weight on the ankle. X-rays may be needed to rule out broken bones or other injuries.
When your ankle is unstable for at least si months after initial injury, it is called chronic ankle instability. This can occur when you do not do enough exercise therapy, also known as rehab, after the initial ankle sprain. Not doing rehab can lead to another injury. Patients often say their ankle “gives out.” Pain and swelling can last if you are active too soon or if there is an unrecognized injury.
HOW LONG DOES IT TAKE TO RECOVER FROM AN ANKLE SPRAIN?
Time to recovery depends on how severe the injury is. A mild sprain involves stretching or tiny tears in the ligament; recovery takes one to two weeks. Moderate sprains involve a partial ligament tear; recovery takes two to four weeks. You should tape the ankle or wear a brace to protect the joint. In severe sprains, the ligament tears completely; recovery takes six to eight weeks. Supporting the injured ligaments and preventing movement with a semirigid or walking boot may be needed to protect the joint, but your doctor will most likely tell you to start moving again by 10 days to help with faster return to activities. High ankle sprains are more severe injuries. Average recovery time is eight to 12 weeks.
HOW CAN I BECOME ACTIVE AGAIN?
Wearing outer ankle support, such as a brace or tape, for 12 months while playing high-risk sports can lower your risk of re-injury. Your doctor will give you an exercise program similar to the one presented here to help you heal and return to your normal daily activities. Some patients may need referral to formal physical therapy.
COMMON REHAB PROGRAM EXERCISES
Early Ankle Sprain Exercises
Use pain, swelling, range of motion, and how stable your ankle feels as a guide during the early phase of injury. Some good exercises to try:
Towel stretch: Seated in a chair or on the ground with your leg straight in front of you, loop a towel around the ball of your foot. Pull the towel toward you to stretch your calf. Hold the stretch for 30 seconds, then relax. Repeat three to five times.
Ankle pumps: Seated in a chair or on the ground with your leg straight, flex (Picture 2A) and extend (Picture 2B) the ankle. Move your foot up and down. Do two sets of 15.
Ankle circles: Seated in a chair or on the ground with your leg straight, move your ankle in a circular motion both clockwise and counterclockwise. Do two sets of 15.
Alphabet writing: Write the alphabet in the air with your big toe while moving only your foot and ankle. This exercise promotes movement in all planes. Start with small movements and then increase as tolerated. Do 2 sets of ABCs.
Standing calf stretch: Stand facing a wall; put your injured foot behind the uninjured foot while keeping your injured foot pointing straight toward the wall. Slowly lean forward while keeping the back knee straight and the heel on the ground. Hold stretch for 30 seconds and then relax. Repeat 3 to 5 times.
Bent-knee calf stretch: Stand facing a wall; place your injured foot behind the uninjured foot, keeping your injured foot pointing straight toward the wall. Slowly lean forward while keeping the back knee slightly bent and the heel on the ground. Hold the stretch for 30 seconds and then relax. Repeat 3 to 5 times.

title: With rate hike in flux, Central Maine Power delays Baldwin-area infrastructure project
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Power, citing financial uncertainty, is delaying work on the Baldwin Resiliency Project, a large-scale plan to upgrade the power grid in Baldwin, Sebago and Steep Falls.
The decision to delay the project comes as Maine Public Utilities Commission staff recently recommended that regulators deny CMP’s request for $70 million in raised rates, which would increase the average household power bill by $7. The increase was requested in April to soften the “significant financial distress” hitting the utility, which saw its financial outlook downgraded this summer to “negative” under a $100 million cash flow deficit.
In an Aug. 27 letter to the Maine Department of Energy, CMP said that, given the uncertainty around the outcome of the rate proceeding, the utility was “temporarily deferring parts of the implementation schedule of (the) project,” effective Aug. 28. Once there is certainty around the funding, the letter said, work will resume “as expeditiously as practicable.”
A final decision on the rate hike is due at the utility board’s Oct. 6 meeting.
In 2024, CMP received a $1.6 million grant from the Department of Energy for the Baldwin Resiliency Project. The work includes upgrading 348 poles, adding 16 poles, and replacing 10.3 miles of overhead line. The grant funding comes in addition to $5 million in CMP funding.
The distribution line being revamped, Baldwin Circuit 691D1, is the company’s third-worst performing line based on the three-year average System Average Interruption Frequency Index, while the Baldwin and Shaw Mills substations serve a combined 5,100 customers, CMP said.
Prior to deferment, construction on the project was due to begin in January. CMP said all pre-construction engineering and design work has been completed.
Standish Town Manager Tashia Pinkham said that while she recognized the importance of maintaining and upgrading Maine’s electric infrastructure, Standish did not support CMP’s proposed temporary rate increase, and would like to see a thorough review of the proposal by the Maine Public Utilities Commission before any rate hike is approved.
Rebecca Schultz, of the Natural Resources Council of Maine, condemned CMP’s decision to delay utility work unless the rate hike goes through, and noted that the company overspent its budget by $239 million in recent years.

title: How to take advantage of the campaign spending bonanza
text:
Dan Kolbert is a builder in Portland.
As summer turns to fall, the electoral campaigns in Maine are sure to heat up. Unprecedented sums of money are expected to flow into the state, in an effort to sway people one way or the other.
As a concerned citizen, I am anxious about the impact of all this spending. My first thought, like many of you no doubt, is “How do I get mine?”
Recently in Dallas, President Trump made his most important electoral reform yet, when he promised to buy our votes. Along with centralizing voter rolls under his control, sending the military to patrol voting sites and withholding funds from Democratic states, he is transforming our country in ways no one could have imagined. It is an exciting time to be a voter in America!
Unfortunately, he set a price for our votes, and apparently believes that all votes should cost the same. This seems shockingly short-sighted. If, as many analysts think, we hold the key to control of the Senate, shouldn’t we command top dollar for our votes? Does he really think our precious Maine votes are worth the same as those of people from Massachusetts? Fortunately, there is still time before the November elections, so let’s hope that he reconsiders this poorly thought out position.
We must, however, remain realists. For obscure historical reasons, vote-buying has negative connotations, and it seems likely that we won’t get our promised $5,000 before November. With that in mind, I have assembled a short list of alternatives that, while requiring more effort, promise greater gain for those with a little gumption.
Start a radio station.
There are a limited number of media outlets in Maine, and it seems likely that the ad budgets will quickly swamp the available slots. Campaigns will be desperate for alternatives. Put a speaker in your window and call it a low-power FM station. Play Chumbawumba’s “I Get Knocked Down” on the hour, every hour, and reserve the remaining 56 1/2 minutes for advertising.
Form a PAC.
There are plenty of identified groups — anti-abortion, pro-choice, gun rights and so on. But there are thousands of people just waiting for someone to stand up for their interests. Tax deductions for travel hockey teams. Banning lawn mowers on Sundays before 9 a.m. Making weed less smelly. Priority parking for big pickups. Campaigns will be so desperate to pick up a half dozen votes by Halloween that they’ll pull up to your house with truckloads of cash.
Become a pundit.
The short-lived Graham Platner campaign proved that there’s an insatiable appetite nationally for people who can explain our out-of-the-way state to a nationwide audience. Most people think of us as folks who talk funny and wear Grundens and plaid. Well, lean into it!
Listen to a few hours of Tim Sample and you’ll be able to pull off a 30- second interview on national news without breaking a sweat. Learn how to talk at length without getting to the point. Learn how to pronounce “Wytopitlock.” Pretend you like Moxie. You’ll have mobile TV trucks lined up around the block.
Those are just a few of the ideas out there. What are yours? Have fun.
As the old saying goes, the personal is political. And there’s nothing more personal than getting paid. Thank you for your attention to this matter!

title: Story, song at Alna Meetinghouse Oct. 3
text:
Historic Alna, in partnership with the Sheepscot Arts Preserve, will host The Outhouse Association at the Alna Meetinghouse, 1789 Alna Road, Alna, on Saturday, Oct. 3, from 4 to 6 p.m.
Hailing from Eagle Island in East Penobscot Bay, The Outhouse Association is the acoustic duo of Ian Ludders and Tony Scott, who play a salty, piney, infectious brand of hyper-local music — songs about farming, fishing, fixing engines, and digging for clams that you probably haven’t heard before and certainly won’t forget. Between songs, the duo pays tribute to the grit and humor of life in the great state of Maine, sharing stories and observations from the coast. They will also discuss Ludders’ new book, “The Log of the Herring Pumper BERYL,” a genre-bending work of local history that immerses readers in the scale-spattered herring season of 1955, mixing primary documents and oral history in a folkloric blend that harmonizes readily with the Outhouse Association’s wide-ranging repertoire.
Admission is free, though donations to support the maintenance, preservation, restoration, and use of Alna’s historic buildings will be gratefully accepted. For more information, email historicalna@gmail.com. Information about Historic Alna and other upcoming events may be found at historicalna.org/events
After the performance, a dinner with the artists will be offered at the Sheepscot Arts Preserve, co-sponsored with Gallery Paraply. Seating is limited to 25. Reservations may be made at galleryparaply.com

The world's largest oat milk producer has joined an unusual climate journalism campaign
text:
The world's largest oat milk producer has joined an unusual climate journalism campaign
Oatly, the world's largest producer of oat milk, is sending a new message to its consumers: most people want their governments to take action on climate change.
Splashed on the side of the Swedish company's cartons is messaging from the “89 Percent Project,” a campaign launched by Covering Climate Now, a global journalism nonprofit.
Newsrooms traditionally try not to associate with organized advocacy efforts, but the unorthodox campaign has been gaining traction. Participating news organizations have amplified research that 80% to 89% of people worldwide want their governments to confront climate change.
Oatly's new cartons were first released in Sweden and have since been rolled out to other European nations, including Belgium and Germany. The cartons are expected to be on U.S. shelves by January, said Caroline Reid, senior sustainability director at Oatly.
“Companies should be taking much more responsibility, not only in reducing their own environmental footprint, but really working out how they can use their platform to drive a positive future,” Reid said at an event last week during New York Climate Week.
Behind the '89 Percent Project'
In addition to producing stories on climate change, Covering Climate Now promotes reporting on the issue through journalism trainings, newsroom collaborations and press awards. It launched the “89 Percent Project” last year and describes it as a global collaborative journalism initiative.
The project takes its name from a 2024 study in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Nature Climate Change. Based on a survey of nearly 130,000 people across 125 countries, the study found that 89% of people want intensified political action on climate change.
Most people who want climate action don’t realize they are in the “silent majority,” said Mark Hertsgaard, executive director of Covering Climate Now. But that is beginning to change, as “elements of civil society all around the world pick up this 89% message and spread it themselves.”
The project launched with several media partners, including The Guardian, Agence France-Presse and El País. In April, Japanese TV stations said over the next two years they would air announcements about how the majority of Japanese people want stronger climate action. In June, in a separate initiative, 136 Japanese news outlets also began spreading this messaging via social media platforms, news releases, and other forms of public communication.
Numerous polls, surveys and scientific studies in the U.S. have long found that a majority want the government to take more action on climate change, even if the issue is rarely brought up in political campaigns.
In a 2022 poll, The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that nearly two-thirds of Americans thought the federal government was not doing enough to fight climate change, which is primarily caused by the release of greenhouse gases when coal, oil and gas are burned.
That same year, a study based on responses from more than 6,000 Americans and published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Nature Communications found that most Americans underestimate the prevalence of support for major climate change mitigation policies and climate concern. While 66% to 80% of Americans support these policies, Americans think only 37% to 43% do.
“We felt that we, and our fellow journalists, were really missing the story here,” said Hertsgaard, adding he believed the industry was inadvertently “misrepresenting a big part of the climate story, which is that most people around the world want this tackled.”
Oat milk company boosts climate message
Oatly’s milk carton campaign is subtle, especially when compared to the more well-known 1980s U.S. milk carton campaign that put photos of missing children on cartons to spread awareness about their cases.
The new cartons feature two stacked text boxes on one side of the carton.
The much smaller top box reads: “Politicians! These eleven words represent people not interested in climate action.” The lower box, which takes up most of the carton's side, has an 89-word message that makes the case that most people want their governments to take climate action and that doing so could lead to political wins.
Reid, with Oatly, first read about the climate project in The Guardian. As a company selling alternatives to cow milk, which has negative consequences for emissions and in the ecosystem due to feed and waste, she said the project “aligns with what we’re trying to do. We’re trying to engage people and make them want to do something different.”
Every organization, political party and brand can play a bigger role in contributing to societal net zero, meaning as much carbon is being absorbed as is released into the atmosphere, and driving the transition to renewable energy, Reid said.
Project treads fine line between journalism and advocacy
President Donald Trump has periodically railed about climate change and policies meant to address it, including transitioning to carbon-free energy like wind and solar. During the 2025 U.N. General Assembly, Trump called climate change a “con job” and renewable energy the “Green Scam.”
This narrative, which goes against years of science that has established that human-caused emissions are driving the climate to change, has pushed some organizations to take a stronger stand in rebutting the administration and go a step further to advocate for solutions.
Covering Climate Now's project straddles a tightrope between advocacy and journalism, which experts say has pros and cons.
“The economic failures of so many news outlets have led to a rise in independent journalism that operates outside the norms established by legacy media outlets,” said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation. “There is plenty of room for advocacy in journalism.”
Clay Calvert, who specializes in First Amendment and freedom of expression issues at the University of Florida, said two dangers arise when journalism organizations partner with companies.
The first is that the journalism group will pull its punches and self-censor negative information about the corporate partner. The second is that the journalism organization will favorably portray its corporate partner in news coverage.
“There really needs to be a wall of separation in any newsroom between the interests of the journalism entity, including its readers and viewers, and those of its corporate partners,” Calvert said. “Sometimes creating and maintaining that separation is easier said than done.”
No money has changed hands between Covering Climate Now and Oatly, according to Hertsgaard, who called the company an “ally.”
“As a journalist, I feel like we have to have the courage to not just report the facts, but to draw the connections,” Hertsgaard said. “Now, if that amounts to advocacy, then that’s an advocacy I’m comfortable with.”
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed to this report.

title: Mother accused of killing her 4-year-old daughter after custody hearing, police say
text:
HOUSTON (KHOU) — Police allege a mother killed her 4-year-old daughter, then shot herself Tuesday.
Police said the shooting followed a court hearing in which the girl’s father gained custody of the child.
Authorities said the child’s stepfather and a babysitter were downstairs at the home when they heard shots upstairs.
“What we believe happened today is that the 4-year-old’s mother, who’s the 30-year-old who was transported, had a custody hearing earlier today. After that custody hearing, they came home. The stepfather and a babysitter were downstairs. They heard gunshots upstairs, went upstairs and found the victims up there,” Lt. Larry Crowson, with the Houston Police Department, said.
The 30-year-old mother is expected to survive.
