title: Governor pushes for investigation into Cornell’s handling of fraternity gang rape allegation
text:
(AP) - New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Tuesday called for an investigation into Cornell University’s response to a 2024 gang rape allegation in which a woman says she was sexually assaulted by seven students after being plied with alcohol and drugs.
The woman filed a lawsuit this month saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Cornell’s campus in October 2024. Her suit says the assault occurred after she was pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol, to the point where she was incapable of consenting to sex.
The woman reported the incident to Cornell’s campus police department, but the local district attorney’s office opted not to prosecute anyone at the time. It reopened the criminal investigation Monday as public outrage built over the woman’s allegations.
Hochul calls for an outside law firm to investigate Cornell’s response
Hochul, a Democrat, said she supported Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s decision to reopen his investigation, but said bigger questions remain about Cornell’s reporting, response, and prevention systems, as well as its campus culture. The governor called for an outside law firm to be hired to independently investigate the university’s response.
“The allegations in this case are nothing short of horrifying,” Hochul said in a statement. “For any student to come forward after an experience like this takes extraordinary courage. No student should ever be left wondering whether the institutions meant to protect them will listen and act.”
An email seeking comment was sent to Cornell on Tuesday.
Prosecutor defends decision not to bring charges
In several media interviews on Tuesday, Van Houten argued that while the male students involved did things that were “morally wrong,” the woman’s initial account of the incident to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex.
“She went to the police because she knew it wasn’t right,” Van Houten told CNN.
Van Houten has not released the victim’s sworn statement to police, but instead released a summary with some of her direct quotes included. He also defended his office’s decision not to do additional investigation after the woman, who was identified in court filings by the pseudonym Jane Doe, initially spoke to police.
“There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided,” Van Houten said.
Van Houten’s office did not talk directly to the victim, but the district attorney had told the police that he would sit down with her to explain the law.
Cornell supports reopening investigation
Shortly after the woman first made her allegations in 2024, Cornell publicly disclosed that it was investigating “serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house.” It also announced that the fraternity and several students had been suspended, and that parallel police and school investigations were underway.
On Monday, the university said in a statement that it supported the decision to reopen the criminal investigation, adding that its own investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled. The Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus. Cornell has declined to release more information on discipline for individual students, citing privacy rules.
The woman’s complaint accuses the university of not preventing the alleged assaults and of failing to properly address sexual violence on campus. It includes a photo that it says shows a group chat between frat members discussing the night’s events.
Van Houten called the photo a “red herring,” saying that it had no bearing on the legal analysis of the case.
“We received it, but it was not relevant to the assessment of whether Jane Doe consented or whether there was any evidence of lack of consent on her part as defined by the penal law,” he said.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

title: CTL begins Song and Story Community Series
text:
The Center for Teaching and Learning held its first “Song and Story” session Thursday, Sept. 24. Musician and educator Annie Nixon and CTL’s Head of School Katy Inman welcomed a group of children ages four and under to the school’s Reading Room, where they gathered to sing songs accompanied by Nixon’s guitar music, and enjoy thematically connected books, read by Inman.
Favorite music and story connections from the first session were songs and books that featured apples. Future Song and Story sessions will continue to focus on seasonal themes and recurring favorite songs that help build connection in the group. The meetings will be held on Thursdays from 10:30 to 11:15 a.m. each week that school is in session. They are free to attend on a drop-in basis: no registration or regular attendance is required.
Song and Story represents a way for CTL to give back to the community by sharing two traditions that its students and teachers value deeply: connection through books and music. Each day CTL students begin by gathering together as a student body to read a poem and sing a song during their daily morning meeting. As Inman explains, “Song and Story extends this combined music and literacy time to the broader Midcoast community and offers a space for caregivers of young children to connect with one another during the week.”
To attend future Song and Story sessions, visit CTL at 119 Cross Point Road in Edgecomb on Thursdays from 10:30 to 11:15 a.m. To learn more about CTL, visit c-t-l.org or call 207-882-9706.

title: Iran indicates it's received an official US response to its latest offer on ending the war
text:
Iran indicates it's received an official US response to its latest offer on ending the war
Iranian officials indicated Wednesday they have received an official U.S. response to Tehran's latest proposal to end the seven-month war, which U.S. President Donald Trump had publicly rejected just days earlier.
Previous video: President Trump rejects Iran's latest proposal as war enters its eighth month
The officials did not say what the response contained, and whether it was a rejection or not.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented the U.S. response to President Masoud Pezeshkian at a Cabinet meeting, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani told the state-run IRNA news agency.
“We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition and will firmly stand up for the rights of the Iranian people,” Pezeshkian said. “The agreement must now be based on a win-win strategy.”
The Cabinet meeting follows Araghchi's return to Iran after travelling to New York for the U.N. General Assembly last week. While there, officials held indirect talks with U.S. officials and also met with Qatari and Pakistani mediators on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders.
Araghchi briefed the Cabinet on his trip to New York and the meetings he held there, including Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which Mohajerani said had been conveyed through mediators.
Araghchi last week said he floated the proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Trump swiftly rejected the proposal, saying Iran wanted to make a deal because it was “losing so badly” but that its offer "would not be acceptable.”
Despite Trump's public rebuffing, mediators continued working with Iran and the United States on trying to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the strait, according to officials who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration says it is is pushing forward with economic warfare against Tehran as the prospects of the two sides coming to an agreement appears uncertain.
The U.S. Treasury Department unveiled new sanctions on Tuesday targeting people and companies around the globe that it accuses of being financial facilitators or enablers of Iran’s military supply chain.
The latest action by the U.S. administration is part of the administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast” campaign, aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines” for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government.
Ten individuals and entities based in Iran, Hong Kong and Pakistan now face sanctions over accusations of procuring weapons and weapon components for Iran’s defense ministry as it fights its now seven-month war against the U.S.
Iran's economy is spiraling further
Iran's economy, which was under heavy strain before the war started, has been in a freefall since the conflict began in late February.
The country's currency fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging more than 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar in a stark reflection of how the war in the Middle East has steadily eroded the Iranian economy.
The latest decline came just 27 days after the rial hit its previous record low of 2.2 million to the dollar on Sept. 2. The currency has repeatedly reached new lows since the war began in February.
Trump on Tuesday said that Iran is “failing very badly, very badly” and predicted anew that the war will be “over with very, very soon.”
At the onset of the conflict, he had predicted that the war would last just weeks. More recently, Trump said he expects it won't end until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the U.S.
Iran executes 2 men on charges of violence during January protests
Also on Wednesday, two men were executed in Iran over their role in violence during nationwide anti-government protests in January, the state-run IRNA news agency reported.
Citing the country's judiciary, IRNA said the men took part in unrest in the northeastern city of Mashhad that left four members of the security forces dead earlier this year. Their death sentences were upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court before being carried out Wednesday morning.
The unrest began Dec. 28 amid anger over Iran’s collapsing currency and worsening economy and quickly spread across the country, with demonstrators increasingly calling for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic. Iranian authorities responded with a deadly crackdown.
Rights groups say thousands were killed and tens of thousands arrested, while Iranian authorities have reported a substantially lower death toll.

title: Country over party means time’s up for Susan Collins

title: Absentee voting: how to go about it
text:
This is the first in a series detailing the processes of the upcoming mid-term election.
With the November 3 mid-term election quickly approaching, many voters want to know how to vote by absentee ballot.
In Maine, any registered voter may request and vote by absentee ballot for any election (with no reason required) through the Thursday prior to the election date. After that date, a special circumstances application must be completed.
Voters can request an absentee ballot up to 90 days prior to election day (60 days before a primary election). Absentee ballots become available for 30 days prior to each election. If available earlier, ballots can be mailed to those who have requested them. In-person absentee voting cannot begin before 30 days preceding election day.
Absentee ballots may be obtained in person, by telephone or by mail. An immediate family member may also obtain a ballot for the voter. Homeless people may register and vote.
Immediate family member means a person’s spouse, parent, grandparent, child, grandchild, sister, half-sister, brother, half-brother, step-parent, step-grandparent, step-child, step-grandchild, step-sister, step-brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, son-in-law, daughter-in-law, guardian, former guardian, domestic partner, the half-brother or half-sister of a person’s spouse, or the spouse of a person’s half-brother or half-sister.
A mailed or telephone request must be done through the voter’s municipal office (town or city clerks’ office).
Once the ballot is completed by the voter, it can be returned to the town office by the immediate family member who obtained the ballot. If the ballot is being returned by a different immediate family member, a signature is required from the immediate family member who returns the ballot.
Ballots may also be returned by depositing the ballot in a secure drop box provided by most municipalities.
Absentee ballots must be returned before 8 p.m., on election day.
If you have any questions regarding obtaining an absentee ballot, contact your municipality’s clerk’s office.
Absenttee ballots became available October 3.
Roland Hallee has 40 years experience in conducting elections, the last 25 years as warden in Waterville.

title: The 10 largest credit unions in the US
text:
The 10 largest credit unions in the US
Key takeaways
- With over $200 billion in assets, Navy Federal is by far the largest credit union in the U.S.
- Most of the 10 largest credit unions restrict membership, but PenFed and Alliant are notable exceptions — anyone can join.
- Federal data shows that credit unions are growing steadily.
While the top ten largest credit unions still hold significantly less in assets than even the top five largest banks, they have been growing considerably in recent years.
In six years, total assets in federally insured credit unions have risen by over 48%, increasing from $1.64 trillion in March 2020 to just under $2.5 trillion in the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
Credit Unions may be drawing customers with their community focus, not-for-profit setup and tendency to offer competitive annual percentage yields (APYs).
The 10 largest credit unions collectively hold approximately $392.6 billion worth of deposits and $456.4 billion in total assets, according to the most recent NCUA data.
Here’s a breakdown of the biggest credit unions in the U.S. by total assets as of September 2026.
Some of these credit unions restrict membership based on factors such as residence or profession. Others — such as Pentagon Federal Credit Union (PenFed) and Alliant — make it easy for anyone to join.
Assets vs. deposits
You’ll see references to two different (large) numbers on this page — a credit union’s total assets and its total deposits.
- Deposits refers to the amount of money that members have put into deposit accounts, such as checking and savings accounts.
- Assets include deposits but also other financial instruments, like loans and investments.
1. Navy Federal Credit Union
Navy Federal is the largest credit union in the country. It has more than 15 and a half million members and holds over $170 billion in deposits. The credit union offers a full suite of financial products and services, including deposit products like checking and savings accounts along with credit products like credit cards and auto loans.
In order to be a member, you or a family/household member must have a tie to the armed forces, the U.S. Department of Defense or the National Guard.
- Assets: $204.46 billion
- Headquarters: Vienna, Virginia
- Footprint: More than 300 branches in 31 states and Washington, D.C.
- Members: 15.52 million
2. State Employees’ Credit Union
Chartered in 1937, State Employees’ is the second-largest credit union in the U.S. With just over $50 billion in deposits, State Employees’ has nearly 3 million members. Membership is open primarily to North Carolina state employees and their families.
- Assets: $59.97 billion
- Headquarters: Raleigh, North Carolina
- Footprint: Nearly 270 branches in North Carolina, plus CO-OP shared branches
- Members: 3 million
3. SchoolsFirst Federal Credit Union
SchoolsFirst is a California-based institution servicing nearly 1.6 million members. The credit union holds more than $30 billion in total deposits. The credit union serves educational communities in California.
As such, membership is open to current or retired school employees living in California or those with a family member who belongs to the credit union. Membership is also open to employees living in California whose company primarily offers direct services to a school or district in California, or college students enrolled in eligible education programs with a student teaching requirement.
- Assets: $37.23 billion
- Headquarters: Santa Ana, California
- Footprint: More than 70 branches in California
- Members: 1.58 million
4. Boeing Employees Credit Union
Boeing Employees’ Credit Union (BECU) is the fifth-largest credit union in the U.S. and the largest credit union in Washington state. BECU has nearly 1.6 million members, and holds more than $25 billion in deposits. Membership is currently open to those who live, work or go to school in Washington state, but residents of select counties in Oregon, Idaho and South Carolina, and those who are affiliated with partner companies and organizations are also eligible.
- Assets: $29.62 billion
- Headquarters: Tukwila, Washington
- Footprint: About 70 branches in Washington and South Carolina plus CO-OP shared branches
- Members: 1.6 million
5. Pentagon Federal Credit Union
Pentagon Federal Credit Union has more than 2.7 million members and deposits totaling over $25 billion. The credit union has branches scattered across the U.S., but provides a full spectrum of financial products, including certificates of deposit, money market, checking accounts and savings accounts. Unlike many other credit unions, PenFed membership is open to anyone.
- Assets: $29.2 billion
- Headquarters: McLean, Virginia
- Footprint: 38 branches in 10 states, Washington, D.C. and three territories
- Members: 2.75 million
6. First Technology Credit Union
First Tech is a California-based credit union that has branches in a variety of Western states (and Georgia). It offers a variety of account options and does over $24 billion in deposits. While there are membership requirements, you may be able to qualify depending on where you work, live or worship.
- Assets: $27.88 billion
- Headquarters: San Jose, California
- Footprint: 30+ branches in California, Colorado, Georgia, Idaho, Massachusetts, Oregon, Texas and Washington
- Members: 1.87 million
7. America First Credit Union
Founded in 1939, America First Credit Union is a Utah-based institution, which is where most of its branches can be found.
America First has 1.6 million members with nearly $23 billion worth of deposits. Membership is open primarily to those who live, work or attend school or church in Salt Lake, Utah and Juab Counties, but it’s also open to those who reside in portions of Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Idaho and Oregon.
- Assets: $25.99 billion
- Headquarters: Riverdale, Utah
- Footprint: More than 110 branches in Utah, Idaho, Oregon, New Mexico, Arizona and Nevada
- Members: 1.58 million
8. Mountain America Credit Union
Mountain America serves more than 1.4 million members in Western states and holds more than $20 billion in deposits.
Membership eligibility is mostly limited to those living in select parts of Utah, but it can also be extended to family and household members. Additionally, employees and volunteers of select organizations are eligible to join.
- Assets: $22.85 billion
- Headquarters: Sandy, Utah
- Footprint: More than 100 branches in Utah, Arizona, Idaho, Nevada and Montana
- Members: 1.46 million
9. Golden 1 Credit Union

title: Marine harvesters alarmed over planned midcoast dredging project
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A proposal by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to dredge a portion of the St. George River is raising alarm bells over its potential impact on the marine environment.
The issue was raised at the Monday night meeting of the St. George Select Board.
The plan by the Army Corps is to conduct what it calls maintenance dredging and remove about 80,000 cubic yards of material, primarily fine grain silty material, and low levels of sand along the 16-foot-wide federal channel and anchorage that starts off Lyman Morse’s shipyard and proceeds south in the river.
St. George Board Chair Jane Conrad said the concern is that stirring up this silt will smother flats and kill off things such as clams and other marine life.
Tammy Willey, who represents St. George on the Georges River Regional Shellfish Management Committee, said the dredging could have a major environmental and economic impact.
“There are more questions than answers,” Conrad said. “We all have a vested interest in the fishing and aquaculture industry.”
Danny Staples of Cushing, who chairs the five-town committee, agreed. He said an economic and environmental impact study needs to be done and presented to the towns before the decision to dredge is made.
He said there are 75 families whose livelihoods depend on harvesting shellfish from that section of the river. There is also concern that it could impact migrating smelts, alewives and even small lobsters that are in the river. Staples said Friendship lobstermen are concerned about the impact of dumping the dredged soils in waters where there is lobstering.
The shellfish committee consists of representatives from Thomaston, St. George, South Thomaston, Warren and Cushing.
The dredging is expected to occur in 2027.
Staples said in other rivers where dredging has occurred there have been significant loss of shellfish and that it took 7 to 10 years to recover.
In 2011, the Phippsburg Shellfish Committee notified the Army Corps about similar concerns and how there were significant adverse economic impacts from earlier dredging in the Kennebec River.
David Madore, deputy commissioner of the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, said the DEP must issue a water quality certification for proposed dredging activity, and the Maine Coastal Program must issue a consistency determination under the Coastal Zone Management Act before dredging would occur. Madore said the Army Corps has not yet filed anything for those permits.
Questions were mailed Tuesday afternoon to the Army Corps.
Congress approved $175,000 for a study of the dredging in the fiscal year 2024 budget.
One of the benefits of the dredging is to allow larger boats to navigate the river and reach the Lyman Morse facility in Thomaston at more times than high tide.
In March 2026, Thomaston discussed potential municipal dredging and coordination with the Army Corps and said there would be a follow-up discussion with Lyman Morse.
Joshua Moore of Lyman Morse said the dredging is not exclusively for Lyman Morse but will benefit the entire Thomaston Harbor. He pointed out that at low tide, boats can bump the bottom at the 90-degree turn to enter the harbor.
He said he believes, but was not certain, the last dredging there was in the late 1970s.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Penobscot dam owner replaces faulty poles on line where July failure killed fish
text:
The owner of the Penobscot River dam that shut down in July after a transmission crossarm broke and likely killed thousands of fish said it is replacing faulty poles along the 30-mile power line.
Brookfield Renewable N.A. said the new poles are part of an annual maintenance program it has run for 10 years. In that time, failures on the line have twice caused automatic shutdowns of the Ripogenus Dam that left thousands of fish dead from a lack of water, according to the Maine Council of Trout Unlimited.
The work comes as federal regulators near a decision on renewing the dam’s license. The July fish kill brought a new round of complaints from conservation groups and nearby landowners who say Brookfield has let maintenance slide. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has asked the company to account for every repair on the line since 2016.
The July crossarm failure sparked a small fire that shut down the dam, which is roughly 30 miles west of Millinocket. The earlier shutdown came in 2023, after lightning struck poles and other equipment at McKay Station, the hydroelectric plant tied to the dam.
Great Lakes Hydro America, the Brookfield subsidiary that operates the dam, is the license applicant. Trout Unlimited is among the many groups and landowners that have filed comments with the commission, much of it about maintenance and irregular water flows. Trout Unlimited and dam neighbors told regulators the crossarm failures show Brookfield is not keeping up.
Brookfield has told federal regulators it spent $3 million on maintenance to improve reliability. Trout Unlimited questioned that figure in its filing, pointing to the two recent failures.
In an Aug. 27 letter, the commission asked Brookfield for an itemized accounting, by location and date, of all inspections, maintenance and rehabilitation work on the transmission line since 2016. The company has 60 days to respond.
Brookfield spokesperson David Heidrich told the Bangor Daily News that the annual maintenance is meant to reduce risk and improve reliability, but it cannot rule out an unexpected failure. He compared it to a car owner who keeps up with inspections and service and still has a mechanical problem.
The crossarm failures “should not be viewed as evidence that the program was inadequate, but rather as recognition that even well-maintained infrastructure can experience unexpected failures,” Heidrich said.
In a July 31 filing with federal regulators, Brookfield said the crossarm broke because of “age-related internal deterioration” that could not be seen from the outside.
McKay Station is shut down in the evenings through Oct. 10 for seasonal maintenance, including work on the transmission lines, and will be shut again in December, Heidrich said. During those outages, water will be released through deep gates at the dam and routed through the upper gorge.
Lori Valigra reports on the environment for the BDN’s Maine Focus investigative team. Email her at lvaligra@bangordailynews.com. Support for this reporting is provided by the Unity Foundation, a fund at the Maine Community Foundation and donations by BDN readers.

title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow transgender medical care restrictions in prison
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to let it enforce restrictions on gender-affirming care in federal prisons.
The emergency appeal comes after lower courts blocked officials from immediately carrying out the policy adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump.
U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered the government to continue providing gender-affirming care like hormone therapy.
The Trump administration argues that the policy was properly adopted and the judge overstepped. It halts surgeries, hormones and social accommodations like wigs while allowing mental health therapy to continue.
It was adopted after an executive order required the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”
The government asked the high court to freeze Lamberth’s order while the lawsuit continues to play out, saying the Bureau of Prisons had “determined that sex-trait-modification surgeries, hormone interventions in general, and social accommodations could no longer be justified as treatment for gender dysphoria.”
The agency said in 2025 that it was providing hormone therapy to more than 600 inmates.
The bureau doesn’t dispute that gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects, including depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts, Lamberth wrote. The Washington-based judge was nominated to the bench by President Ronald Reagan.
A divided appeals court panel left the order in place.
ACLU attorneys for the inmates said the policy is “a direct threat to the well-being of transgender people in federal custody and an open violation of their fundamental rights,” and withholding necessary gender-affirming healthcare constitutes cruel and unusual punishment.
The conservative-majority Supreme Court has previously upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender youth, and restricting sports participation by transgender athletes in women’s sports.
It has also handed down shorter-term decisions allowing the Trump administration to move ahead for now with other policies rolling back protections for transgender people serving in the military and holding a passport consistent with their gender identity.

title: Hawks? Hawkeyes? GOP senator mistakes basketball mascots in probing Jack Smith
text:
GOP senator Schmitt mistakes basketball mascots in attempt to link Jack Smith to Fani Willis
In Sen. Eric Schmitt's effort to trip up former Trump prosecutor Jack Smith on Tuesday, the Missouri Republican seemed to mistake basketball teams playing about 650 miles apart.
Watch the heated exchange in the video player above.
Schmitt accused Smith of perjuring himself during a Senate hearing after repeatedly prodding him about whether he'd attended an NBA game in Atlanta on the evening of Feb. 3, 2024. The hometown Hawks were playing the Golden State Warriors.
Schmitt appeared to be trying to set Smith in Atlanta at the time Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis was facing scrutiny for her romantic relationship with Nathan Wade, the special state prosecutor she hired for the county's election-interference case against Trump.
Video below: Sen. Eric Schmitt laughs off backfired Jack Smith questioning: "Who knew Jack Smith was a Caitlin Clark fan?"
“So your testimony today is that you did not go to a Hawks game on Feb. 3, 2024. Is that correct?” Schmitt asks sharply. “What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warriors-Hawks game on Feb. 2, 2024?”
Smith said he didn't think he had visited Atlanta as special prosecutor, and was even more certain he hadn't attended an Atlanta Hawks game.
He did, however, recall attending a University of Iowa women's game at the University of Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024, recalling the game as one where then-Iowa star Caitlin Clark was playing.
“Could it then be that the University of Iowa was the Hawkeyes?” Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota interjected. “Perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully.”

title: Mother accused of leaving 4 children, including 2-month-old, home alone during cruise
text:
NORTH MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (WSVN) — A 29-year-old mother was arrested Monday after police said she left her four children home alone while she went on a cruise.
Nathalie Belizaire was arrested on four counts of child neglect, according to authorities.
“You were arrested for four counts of child neglect,” a judge said.
Cruise ticket posted on social media
Officials said that on Sept. 24, Belizaire posted what appeared to be a cruise ticket for a Carnival cruise line on social media.
That same day, she allegedly told a man, possibly the father of her 2-month-old daughter, that she would be “dropping the children off with their great-grandmother.”
“One baby, the baby was born in July of this year. Who just leaves a baby alone like that?” the judge said.
A few days later, the man said he went to the home and found the children by themselves.
Police forced their way into the home and found the children “hiding in the bathroom.”
“There you are,” an officer said, according to body camera video of the encounter.
The children appeared to be shaken, the video showed.
“Just two of you? Three? Four?” an officer asked.
Investigators said Belizaire left all four children, including a 2-month-old and a 2-year-old, without adult supervision.
Mother arrested at port
Police said Belizaire traveled out of town aboard the cruise ship. She disembarked Monday and was arrested at the Port of Miami, where officials were waiting for her.
She was taken into custody by the North Miami Beach Police Department.
The judge ordered no contact between Belizaire and the children.
“No contact with the alleged victims either directly, indirectly, in person, in writing, by telephone, or through third parties. You must stay at least 500 feet away from the victims. They’re home and school at all times,” the judge said.
The judge set bond at $10,000.

title: Obituary: Jayson J. E. Carver
text:
RANDOLPH – Jayson J. E. Carver, 54, of Randolph, Maine, formerly of Wayne, Maine, and known for his unwavering dedication and love for the outdoors, peacefully passed away at his home on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.
He was born on July 5, 1972, in Augusta, Maine. Jayson graduated from Maranacook Community High School and spent four years furthering his education at the University of Maine in Orono. He was a lifelong resident of Maine, deeply connected to its natural beauty. His spirit was as vast and as free as the landscapes he cherished.
Jayson was a “hell of a worker,” a description that perfectly encapsulates his strong work ethic and commitment to his craft. He dedicated his career as a laborer in the construction industry, where his skill and diligence were always evident. Beyond his professional life, Jayson found immense joy in simple pleasures. He was an avid fisherman, finding peace and contentment by the water. His love for skiing and the great outdoors was profound, and he held a special affection for Carrabassett Valley and the cherished family camp, places where he made countless memories.
Jayson is survived by his mother Karen Paige and his stepfather William, and his cherished nephew Jared Carver. He was predeceased by his father James Carver.
At Jayson’s request there will not be a service; his ashes will be spread by family in Carrabassett Valley while listening to his favorite song, “Simple Man”.
He will be remembered for his strong hands, his generous spirit, and his deep appreciation for the natural world. His legacy lives on in the memories he created and the lives he touched. Jayson lived and died according to his own rules.
Arrangements and guidance are in the care of Staples Funeral Home and Cremation Care, 53 Brunswick Avenue, Gardiner, Maine.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared with the family on the obituary page of the Staples Funeral Home website http://www.staplesfuneralhome.com.

title: How to write a check: A step-by-step guide
text:
How to write a check: A step-by-step guide
Key takeaways
- Writing a check requires six steps: date, payee name, amount in numbers, amount in words, memo (optional) and your signature.
- Always use blue or black ink — never pencil — to prevent alterations and fraud.
- The numerical amount and the written amount must match exactly, or the bank may reject or delay your check.
- Check fraud has surged in recent years, so take precautions like filling all blank spaces, storing checks securely and mailing them safely.
These days, most payments happen with a tap, swipe or a few clicks — but checks aren’t gone yet. Americans still wrote roughly nine billion checks in 2025, and checks remain common for rent payments, large purchases, gifts and business transactions.
Whether you’re writing your first check or your first one in a long time, getting it right matters. A mistake can lead to delays, late fees or a bounced check. Use this step-by-step guide to fill out a check correctly the first time.
What you need to write a check
- A checking account with enough money to cover the check amount
- A pen with blue or black ink
- The payee’s full, correct name
- The exact dollar amount you’re paying
How to fill out a check in 6 steps
Before writing a check, you’ll need to have a checking account with sufficient funds to cover the amount of the check. Then, follow these steps to fill one out.
1. Write the date
Write the current date on the line in the top right-hand corner. This tells the bank and the recipient when you wrote the check. You can use numbers or write out the entire date — either “3/4/2026” or “March 4, 2026” works.
Some people write a future date hoping the recipient will wait to cash the check. However, most banks will process checks immediately regardless of the date written. If you need to delay a payment, use your bank’s scheduled payment feature instead.
2. Write who the check is payable to
On the line that says “Pay to the order of,” write the full name of the individual or company you’re paying. This person or entity is called the payee. Use their complete, legal name rather than a nickname to avoid confusion. If you’re paying a business, confirm its official name. Some businesses operate under multiple names or may use a different business name when accepting checks.
You can write “Cash” if you don’t know the payee’s name, but this is risky — anyone can cash or deposit a check made out to cash. It’s much safer to write a specific name.
3. Write the check amount in numbers
In the small box to the right of the payee line, write the numerical dollar amount clearly. For example, if you’re writing a check for one hundred dollars and thirty cents, write “$100.30.”
Write clearly and start as close to the dollar sign as possible so no one can add digits in front of your number.
4. Write the amount in words
On the line below “Pay to the order of,” spell out the dollar amount in words. This amount must match the numerical amount exactly. Write the cents as a fraction over 100.
Examples:
- $100.30 becomes “One hundred and 30/100”
- $50.00 becomes “Fifty and 00/100”
- $1,250.75 becomes “One thousand two hundred fifty and 75/100”
Even if you’re writing a check for a round dollar amount, include “00/100” for the cents portion. This prevents someone from adding cents to your check. Draw a line through any remaining blank space to further prevent fraud.
5. Write a memo (optional but recommended)
The memo line at the bottom left is optional, but using it is smart. Write a brief note about the check’s purpose — for example, “Rent — March 2026” or “Invoice #4521.” This helps with your own recordkeeping and ensures the recipient can apply the payment correctly.
Some companies specifically request that you write your account number or invoice number in the memo field.
6. Sign the check
Sign your name clearly on the line at the bottom right corner of the check. Your signature authorizes the bank to pay the stated amount to the payee. Without it, the check is invalid. Use the same signature that’s on file with your bank — mismatched signatures can cause processing delays.
How to write a check safely: Fraud prevention tips
Following these best practices helps prevent fraud, processing errors or payment delays.
- Always use pen, never pencil. Write with blue or black ink only. Pencil can be erased and altered. Avoid other ink colors like red or green, which can cause problems with check-scanning equipment.
- Write clearly. If your handwriting is hard to read, print in block letters. Unclear writing is one of the most common reasons banks reject checks.
- Fill all blank spaces. Draw a line through any unused space after the written amount and start numbers as close to the dollar sign as possible. This prevents someone from adding words or digits.
- Double-check everything before signing. Make sure the numerical amount matches the written amount, the payee’s name is spelled correctly and all required fields are filled in.
- Keep records. Write down each check number, amount, payee and date in your check register or a budgeting app. Take a photo of the check before mailing it.
- Store checks and mail them securely. Keep unused checks in a secure place at home — never in your car or bag. When mailing checks, drop them inside the post office or use your bank’s online bill pay to avoid mailing them at all. If checks are stolen, contact your bank immediately.
Why you still need checks in 2026
Even as check usage has dropped, there are situations where checks are still commonly used or even required:
- Rent payments. Many landlords, especially individual property owners, still prefer or require checks.
- Large purchases. Some transactions like security deposits, contractor payments and vehicle purchases may call for a cashier’s check or certified check rather than a personal check.
- Gifts. Checks remain a common way to give money for weddings, graduations and holidays, especially across generations.
- Government and legal payments. Some courts, local government offices and tax authorities still accept or require checks for certain filings and fees.
- Business payments. Small businesses and sole proprietors frequently use checks for invoicing and accounts payable.
If you find yourself writing checks often, it’s worth making sure your checking account provides checks at a low cost (or free). Some accounts include free checks as a benefit.
Types of checks and when to use each one
Not every payment calls for a personal check. Here’s how the main types compare:
- Personal checks
- Personal checks are the standard checks from your checking account, used for everyday payments. They’re drawn directly from your account balance. Best for routine bills, rent and personal payments.
- Cashier’s checks
- Cashier’s checks are issued and guaranteed by the bank itself. You pay the bank upfront, and they draw the check from the bank’s own funds. They typically cost $10–$15 and are often required for large transactions like home closings or vehicle purchases.
- Certified checks
- Certified checks are personal checks that the bank has verified and guaranteed. The bank confirms you have sufficient funds and sets that money aside. They offer more security than a standard personal check. To understand the difference between cashier’s checks and certified checks, see our detailed comparison.
- Money orders
- Money orders function similarly to cashier’s checks but are available at more locations — post offices, grocery stores, convenience stores — and are typically cheaper, between $1 and $5. They’re good for smaller amounts.
Where to get checks
- From your bank: Most banks provide checks, but they’re often more expensive than other options. Some checking accounts include free checks — check your account details first.
- Third-party check printers: Companies that specialize in printing checks typically charge less than banks. You’ll need your account number and routing number to order.
- Online ordering: Many services let you order checks online and have them delivered to your home. This is often the most convenient and least expensive option.
Next steps

title: Survivor, doctor warn of rising endometrial cancer rates among younger women
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (InvestigateTV) - The biggest overall risk of developing cancer comes later in life, as the typical age for a diagnosis is 67 years old.
But recent data shows a growing number of young people are receiving the life-changing news. Researchers at the National Institutes of Health found between 2010 and 2019 the incidence of fourteen cancer types increased among people under 50.
One of those is uterine cancer, which also saw an increase in death rates at younger ages. Most uterine cancers happen in the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus.
A life-changing diagnosis
Amy Nissen said her first symptom appeared in March 2024 — abnormal vaginal bleeding.
“It was the heaviest vaginal bleeding I’d ever had in my entire life,” Nissen said. “I could never get ahead of it. I could never get it under control. I had been having my period for 30-some years and never had to take a change of clothes to work, and now I was having to take a change of clothes.”
Nissen said she searched the internet for answers but found most references to endometrial cancer focused on post-menopausal women over 60, which led her to dismiss the possibility.
“It was one of those things that I was so embarrassed about it,” she said. “I didn’t really bring it up to anybody.”
The bleeding eventually brought her to the emergency room, and soon after, a diagnosis.
She would find out a day before her 43rd birthday that she had endometrial cancer.
“I wasn’t really grasping it yet,” Nissen said. “It was still such a shock.”
Rates rising among younger women
Endometrial cancer rates are increasing nationally. According to pharmaceutical company GSK, more than 160 women are diagnosed every day. GSK estimates 62,000 cases were diagnosed and 12,500 deaths resulted from the disease in 2025, making it the most common form of gynecologic cancer in America.
Dr. Lindsey McAlarnen, a gynecologic oncologist at Nebraska Medicine, said more women in their 20s, 30s and 40s are receiving this diagnosis. She said growing rates of obesity are a contributing factor.
“We see that obesity in general is a risk factor for uterine cancer, but it’s also a risk factor for uterine cancer coming back or recurrence,” McAlarnen said. “Really living a healthy lifestyle and being at a healthy weight is beneficial for all of our patients.”
McAlarnen said abnormal bleeding is the key warning sign women should not ignore.
“Either heavy bleeding or in somebody who has gone through menopause and stopped having periods, any type of bleeding that shows up after they’ve had no bleeding for a year, that’s a reason to see your doctor or provider, because it could be a cancer growing in the lining of the uterus,” she said.
Additional symptoms of endometrial cancer include new or unusual discharge and persistent pelvic pain.
McAlarnen said survival rates exceed 95% when the cancer is caught at stage one, but drop sharply if it spreads.
“I’ve seen too many older women who thought that getting a period again was normal or who thought that having a little bit of spotting with wiping wasn’t something to worry about,” she said. “And then if you leave it untreated for even a year, cancer can spread and that can really impact your chances of survival.”
Treatment and recovery
Nissen was diagnosed early and no chemotherapy was required.
“I opted for a total hysterectomy,” Nissen said. “I know that’s not the choice for all women. It was what was right for me and where I was in life.”
The procedure is a minimally invasive robotic surgery performed by a doctor, completed in a couple of hours, with patients typically able to go home the same day.
Nissen said she is doing well since the surgery and goes in for regular monitoring.
Nissen and McAlarnen are partnering on GSK’s “Don’t Be Embarrassed” campaign to encourage women to speak openly with their doctors about symptoms.
“The more conversations we can have, the more it chips away at that stigma,” Nissen said. “Somebody maybe if they’re hearing my story will go, hey, I haven’t been talking about it but I have something really similar to this going on. I should go get that checked out. Because it can change your life and it could even save your life if you go to your doctor.”
“Don’t be afraid to come in and start that conversation,” McAlarnen said.
McAlarnen also cautioned women against taking hormones — including pills or topical products — without first consulting a doctor, warning that excess hormones can lead to endometrial cancer.

title: The US military says its withdrawal of troops from Iraq is complete
text:
BAGHDAD (AP) — The U.S. military announced Wednesday that it completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group and prompting President Donald Trump to hail the conclusion of “a very expensive excursion into Hell.”
The last U.S. troops left an air base in northern Iraq under a deal between Baghdad and Washington.
Trump, in a social media post, described the withdrawal by a Sept. 30 deadline as “orderly.” Appearing soon after at a White House event celebrating Hispanics, he spoke at length about the withdrawal and said, “It’s been a long time with very bad decision making that got us involved in this quagmire in the first place. It was a quagmire. For many, many years it lasted. But soon that part of history will be over.”
He said the shift was a victory for the U.S., Iraq and a sign of victory over the Islamic State group.
The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups’ strongholds.
Trump’s comments came as his own decision earlier this year to launch the war with Iran has been compared to the Iraq war for its undefined mission as it nears its seventh month.
Appearing at the White House, Trump made that comparison, arguing both that his one-day military action in Venezuela earlier this year to capture now former President Nicolás Maduro and the Iran war compared favorably, taking far less time and with fewer deaths of U.S. troops.
In recent years, Washington has sought to shift its focus from the Middle East toward Asia, but that shift has been inconsistent, with the Pentagon alternating between reducing its Mideast presence and then finding itself engaging in new conflicts — including the ongoing war in Iran.
Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country’s increasing strength and sovereignty.
The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region, where many fear a resurgence of the Islamic State group as well as more attacks by Iran-linked groups, possibly emboldened by the departure of U.S. forces.
Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought to disarm, with little success so far.
A new phase in Iraq after decades of US involvement
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an “orderly departure” from the air base in Irbil, in northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” he said. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
He added that the U.S. military “will continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a “new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against IS and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons.
Trump in his remarks on Wednesday lavished praise on al-Zaidi, calling him “outstanding,” a “fantastic guy, friend of mine,” and someone who “will hopefully be able to handle things very well.” He also appeared to try to take credit for al-Zaidi’s leadership, saying that the Iraqi leader was “running for election” and “wasn’t given even a chance and I endorsed him and politicked for him a little bit, and he ended up winning in a virtual landslide.”
Al-Zaidi was not on the ballot but was selected as prime minister when Iraq’s dominant parliamentary bloc nominated him after weeks of internal debate among its member parties and Trump publicly announcing his opposition to the coalition’s previous choice.
U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight the Islamic State group, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory.
With the extremist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down.
U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen’s Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.
The future of militias remains unclear
The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.
While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet.
Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.
The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in Iraq’s Kurdish region have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems.
The Kurdish regional government’s Peshmerga Ministry said the Kurdish region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the statement said.
Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal.
“The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty,” Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.
He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that “any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means.”
Kataib Hezbollah leader Ahmad al-Hamidawi took a somewhat more conciliatory tone, calling on the group’s fighters to halt their military activities “with the exception of targeting hostile aircraft violating the country’s airspace.”
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, said in a statement that negotiations with the government over the regulation of weapons have not resulted in an agreement and that it was “not bound by any timeline or agreement” announced by the government or political entity. The group said it is open to “any dialogue that guarantees Iraq’s sovereignty and dignity.”
___
Price reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Abby Sewell in Istanbul contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: Lois J. (Haley) Henry
text:
WILTON/FARMINGTON – Lois J. (Haley) Henry, 92, passed away peacefully at her home on Sept. 9, 2026. She was born Oct. 24, 1933, in Phillips, the youngest child of Wilfred and Helen (White) Haley. A resident of the Wilton/Farmington area for most of her life, Lois spent her final four years living with her daughter and son-in-law in Fenton, Missouri.
Lois came from humble beginnings but decided as a young child that she would make the most of the opportunities she was given. She was a self-driven student, graduating with honors at Wilton Academy in 1952. She continued her education with two years of nurses’ training at Eastern Maine General Hospital, but left to begin a family, marrying Clifford E. Henry Jr. They soon moved to Naples, Italy, where he was stationed in the US Navy.
She returned to Maine with her three young children in 1961 following his sudden passing, and enrolled at Farmington State Teachers College, earning her bachelor’s degree in 1966 and beginning her career as a teacher in Wilton. In 1971, she earned a master’s degree in education.
Lois also earned a reputation as a devoted and no-nonsense English teacher during her 25-year career, working tirelessly to instill in her students an appreciation for proper grammar.
This devotion continued into retirement, working with those who asked her for assistance and even with those who weren’t aware they needed help – she rarely hesitated to correct someone who strayed from the rules.
Lois accepted Jesus as her Savior while in the fifth grade, that faith helping to guide her throughout her life. As an adult, she served as a Sunday School teacher and in several other church roles. She joined Farmington Baptist Church in 1994, becoming an active part of its growth and outreach, including several years of volunteer work at the local food pantry. After moving to Missouri, she became a joyful member of Calvary Fellowship Church in Fenton, where she made many new friends.
Lois enjoyed a wide variety of activities and interests. She was gifted with an artistic flair, and her interests included painting in oils and watercolors, poetry, knitting and crocheting, creating stuffed dolls, and writing and illustrating personalized books for her grandchildren. She also enjoyed outdoor activities and was an avid reader.
Lois is survived by her children, Alan Henry, Gary Henry and his wife Tarrye (Stoddard), and Jo Ann (Henry) Guarino and her husband John. She also leaves seven grandchildren: Sarah Guarino, Jennifer Guarino, Brendan Henry, Trevor Henry, Amy Guarino, Nicholas Guarino, and Skyler Henry; and four great-grandchildren.
In addition to her husband and parents, she was predeceased by her siblings, Ronald Haley, Mae (Haley) Fairbanks, Grace (McFarland) Marsinko, Raymond McFarland, John Haley, W. Clayton Haley, Pauline Haley, and Robert Haley.
A celebration of her life will be held Saturday, October 10, at 11 a.m., at Farmington Baptist Church, 194 Whittier Road, followed by interment at Lakeview Cemetery in Wilton.
Family and friends are encouraged to visit Lois’ Book of Memories at
http://www.wilesrc.com to leave words of comfort, share a story or photos. Honored to be caring for the family of Lois J. Henry is Wiles Remembrance Center – Farmington.
In lieu of flowers, donations in Lois’s memory to a local food pantry would be appreciated.

title: New England’s winter forests need the Roadless Rule
text:
Anneka Williams is a writer and climate scientist who is originally from Vermont’s Mad River Valley. She currently serves as the policy director for Winter Wildlands Alliance.
Growing up in New England instilled in me a deep appreciation for trees. In the summers my family would hike sections of trail all over the state, relishing the shade provided by a dense, leafy canopy of sugar maple, beech and birch trees. In the winter, the trees would shed their leaves and my friends and I would go find hidden powder stashes, carving quick turns between tight glades.
While trees feel like an abundant resource in Vermont today, forests haven’t always been
plentiful in this part of the country. In the 17th century, early European settlers established the foundation for a booming logging industry across the Northeast. 
As the number of settlers grew through the 18th and 19th centuries, forests were cleared and converted to agricultural land and much of the region lost its major old growth forests, shifting lumber operations west because there simply weren’t enough trees left. Over the last century, New England forests have recovered through practices aimed at balancing timber harvesting with conservation and other uses, but much of New England is a patchwork of roads and very few large roadless areas are left.
The roadless areas that remain are vital resources for outdoor recreation and watershed
protection. But they are currently under threat. Last June, the Trump administration’s U.S. Department of Agriculture moved to rescind the Roadless Rule under the guise of more local forest control and wildfire management. 
The Roadless Rule is a piece of federal policy enacted in 2001. It protects more than 58 million acres of “inventoried roadless areas” — pieces of undeveloped land within the national forest system that remain in their natural, undeveloped state. These places offer abundant opportunities for outdoor recreation in all seasons, including undeveloped terrain that makes human-powered winter recreation some of the best in the country, while also protecting clean watersheds and natural ecosystem qualities.
While the rescission of the Roadless Rule doesn’t automatically greenlight logging and road development, it does remove an important layer of protection that has implications for the character of New England’s wild, unroaded lands and for backcountry winter recreationists.
New England is home to two national forests: the Green Mountain National Forest (GMNF) in Vermont and the White Mountain National Forest (WMNF) in New Hampshire and western Maine. GMNF, which is approximately 400,000 acres total, holds approximately 80,000 acres of inventoried roadless areas. WMNF is approximately 800,000 acres and encompasses an estimated 368,000 acres of inventoried roadless areas.
Collectively that’s roughly 448,000 acres of roadless areas across New England. These areas encompass lots of terrain for winter recreation, including world-class backcountry skiing in Jefferson Ravine, the Wildcat Valley Trail, maintained backcountry glades around Baldface Knob and sections of snowmobile trails.
When I think about roadless areas in New England, I picture quiet glades nestled in heavily forested areas, lovingly maintained and enjoyed by local communities. I picture second-growth forests that have worked hard to reach their current density. I picture the places I visit on my skis or snowshoes in search of untracked powder, wild experiences and the stillness of a forest stand in the middle of winter.
These are the places that create a community of people around shared outdoor experiences and that provide the backdrop for photographs that define entire regions. They are the places I think about when I think of home.
At a moment filled with attempts to sell off our public lands and dramatic cuts in funding and staff to the agency we rely on to manage our national forests, having a policy like the Roadless Rule to protect these places is more important than ever.
Intact forests are on the chopping block and it’s up to all of us to use our voices to speak for these places during the Roadless Rule Draft Environmental Impact Statement comment period. I hope that if you’re reading this you will reflect on what untrammeled forests mean for you, how outdoor recreation has played a role in your life and join me in standing up for those places and experiences now and for future generations.
The Forest Service is holding a public comment period on the Roadless Rule right now. Submit your comment before Oct. 6.

title: Up and Down the Kennebec Valley: Medical history in central Kennebec Valley
text:
Dr. Stephen Barton
Stephen Barton was another very early doctor in the central Kennebec Valley. As usual, sources differ as to exactly how early and in what town(s), and about many other aspects of his life.
Find a Grave, calling him Dr. Stephen Barton Sr., says he was born June 10, 1740, in Sutton, Massachusetts. Linwood Lowden, in his history of Windsor, Maine, added the (unsourced) assertion that Barton “became interested in medicine early in life.”
He married Dorothy Moore (1747 -1838) on May 28, 1765. Sources disagree spectacularly widely on their children, some of whom might have lived rather unusual lives for the time (see box).
A history of Oxford, Massachusetts, found on line (Oxford and Sutton are neighboring towns, south of Worcester) says Barton studied medicine with “Dr. Green, of Leicester.” Lowden’s version is Dr. Greene, of Oxford.
(The first reference might be to Dr. John Green, 1736 – 1799, of Worcester, the town east of Leicester, who taught other would-be doctors, according to on-line medical biographies; and/or his son, John Green, who was trained by his father and practiced with him until the father died. The first Dr. John Green trained more than 100 doctors.)
(Another on-line reference names Dr. Samuel Green, who in the early 1700s lived in a village on the line between Leicester and Oxford and taught so many future doctors that his house is sometimes called Massachusetts’ first medical school. AI [for what it’s worth] says Stephen Barton was one of his students.)-
Barton was in business in Oxford as a trader (1764 -1766) and “landlord at the old tavern” (1766 -1769). He and his wife were both well educated, the Oxford history says; it calls him “a good citizen” and “one of the leading organizers of the ‘Social Library’.”
Barton was also “a good physician; charitably inclined, and, it is said, lost much by never presenting bills to his patrons.”
Henry Kingsbury’s summary of Barton’s life in the medical chapter in his 1892 Kennebec County history says it was 1774 when Barton came from Oxford to Vassalboro. He practiced in Vassalboro until 1788, when he returned to Oxford.
Laurel Thatcher Ulrich, in her 1990 “A Midwife’s Tale,” said Barton was in Vassalboro by 1775, joining a brother and other family members. He practiced medicine in Vassalboro from 1775 to 1787, she wrote, “spent the next decade in Oxford [Massachusetts] and died shortly after returning to Maine.”
Lowden wrote that “Dr. Barton made his first trip to Maine in 1767,” without further information. In 1776, he said, Barton and three of his brothers settled in Vassalboro.
The Oxford history says Barton “with his sons” moved to either Vassalboro or Winslow about 1776.
Alma Pierce Robbins said in her Vassalboro history that in March, 1776, Barton “was elected Town Clerk and carried on much of Town business for several years.”
Another reference in Kingsbury’s history names Barton as Vassalboro town meeting moderator in 1777. (Readers might remember from last week’s story that Vassalboro voters in 1788 recognized Dr. Obadiah Williams in the same way, as, Kingsbury wrote, “the one deemed the leading man in town.”)
In his chapter on Vassalboro, Kingsbury wrote that Barton was elected Vassalboro’s treasurer in 1777, and in 1778 a select board member, serving for two years. He was also elected town clerk in 1777 and served through 1780, when Jedediah Barton succeeded him; elected again in 1784, he was succeeded by Flint Barton in 1787. FamilySearch identifies them as the two older of Stephen’s younger brothers, Jedediah born in 1747 and Flint in 1749.
(Kingsbury said Flint Barton, a blacksmith, moved to Sidney, then part of Vassalboro, in 1773 from Sutton, Massachusetts, and built a sawmill. He and his wife, Lydia (Crosby) had 12 sons. Flint was elected a selectman in 1792 [the year Sidney separated from Vassalboro], serving for four years; and in 1801 was chosen town treasurer. Sidney’s Barton Cemetery, which has the graves of 22 Bartons, including Flint and Lydia, says Flint was born Dec. 3, 1749, and died May 12, 1833. Lydia, born Nov. 23, 1758, died Nov. 24, 1821.)
Between his official duties, Stephen Barton practiced medicine in Vassalboro. Lowden offered information compiled from the doctor’s “ledger book.” He summarized:
“Most of Dr. Barton’s practice while he lived in Vassalboro seemed to consist of pulling teeth, applying dressings, bleeding patients, inducing vomiting, dispensing pills and elixirs, applying plasters and opening abscesses.”
He listed some of the doctor’s “most frequent prescriptions,” which included salve for burns; different kinds of plasters (either bandages or casts, in modern terms); “pill chochia” (Lowden translated as “red pill”); “Aqua Briopia” (“invigorating water”); and “Mugs of Toddy and cider” (after which Lowden wrote “Purpose ?)”
Barton’s wife, Dorothy Moore, was a sister of Martha Ballard, the Kennebec Valley midwife made famous through her diary. Robbins quoted an entry from the diary showing Barton was in Vassalboro in the summer of 1785. On Aug. 26, Martha Ballard wrote, “Dr. Barton came to Cobose (Cobbosseecontee) dined here and went home to Vassalboro in the afternoon. I went to see them up the rips….”
On Oct. 22, 1785, Martha Ballard dined at the Bartons’.
In 1786, Robbins wrote, Barton “had to be relieved from being Town Clerk as he was moving to Windsor to live with his son. He died there in 1803.”
However, the Oxford history says Barton went back to Oxford about 1790, and in 1794, received town permission to build a “mechanical shop.”
Sometime later – 1800, Lowden said – the family came back to Maine. Lowden said after two years in Augusta and a year in Vassalboro, “Dr. Barton moved his family in 1803 to Windsor where the family lived many years in a log cabin.”
Ulrich, Lowden and the Oxford history agree that Barton died Oct. 21, 1804, and, in the history’s words, “at his request was buried at the side of a large boulder on the spot on which he spent the first night on going into the wilderness. This rock has been faced and now [the history was published in 1892] bears his monumental inscription.”
Kingsbury said Barton died of consumption in 1805, two years after settling in Windsor in 1803. He, too, mentioned a monument marking the place “where he and his sons [Elijah and Gideon] bivouacked the night they entered the woods.”
Lowden agreed the doctor’s grave was near the boulder where he and Elijah and Gideon “had camped their first night in Windsor.” Writing in 1993, he did not mention an inscription.
Warning: untangling the contradictions in this genealogy could be a life-time job.
FamilySearch says Stephen and Dorothy (Moore) Barton had 13 children between 1765 and 1791. Laurel Thacher Ulrich confirmed the 1765: Dorothy was “almost five months pregnant at marriage,” she wrote. She said the first daughter was named Pamela, and the next Clarissa.
A history of Oxford, Maine, found on line lists a dozen Barton children. Find a Grave lists on one page five, born between 1773 and 1784, and on another page adds another son. The Find a Grave list:
— Parthenia Barton Pitts, born in Vassalboro in 1773; married Shubael Pitts on Nov. 18, 1792, in Hallowell; and died there Sept. 1, 1794, aged 21;
— Capt. Stephen Barton, Jr., born Aug.18, 1774, in Oxford, Massachusetts; in 1804 married Sarah “Sally” Stone (1783 – 1851), with whom he had two sons and three daughters; died in 1862. The older son, Capt. Stephen Barton, III, was born in 1806 and died May 6, 1865, in the District of Columbia, at age 59. The youngest daughter, Clara Barton, was born Dec. 25, 1821, and became famous for her medical work during and after the Civil War and for founding the American Red Cross; she died April 12, 1912.
— Hannah Barton Davis, born in Vassalboro July 20, 1776. She married Massachusetts militia General Jonathan Davis (1761 – 1838) on Oct. 4, 1822, after having born him two illegitimate sons in 1798 and 1799, Find a Grave says, and after his first wife, Sarah Hammond, died Feb. 4, 1822. Ulrich explained that Davis was Hannah’s employer, and his wife was an invalid.
Ulrich added that the younger son “killed himself out of humiliation while a student at Brown.” Hannah died Feb. 12, 1859, in Massachusetts.
— Dorothy “Dolly” Barton Learned, born Aug. 27, 1778, in Vassalboro. On Sept. 21, 1793 (age 15), in Oxford, she became the third of four wives of Capt. Jeremiah Learned (born in Oxford Jan. 12, 1732; his second wife had died Sept. 2, 1793). Capt. Learned had two sons and two daughters by his first wife, all older than their stepmother; he and Dorothy had a daughter and three sons between April 28, 1793 (when Dorothy was 14, before they married), and June 28, 1799. Dorothy died July 14, 1799.
— Elijah Moore Barton, born Aug. 10, 1784, in Vassalboro. He married Sarah “Salley” Fairfield, born March 31, 1783, in Vassalboro; Find a Grave says their two sons were born in 1808 and 1820 in Windsor, where Elijah was buried after he died Feb. 22, 1839. Sarah’s death date is unknown.
— Deacon Gideon Barton, born June 18, 1786, in Vassalboro, where, the donor of this information wrote, Dr. Stephen Barton had settled in 1774. Gideon moved “with his father” to Windsor in 1803. After Stephen died in 1805 (per this source), Gideon married Sarah Pierce; they had eight sons and six daughters, and named their second son Stephen (his older brother was Samuel). Gideon died May 30, 1878.
Here is the Oxford history’s list of Stephen and Dorothy’s 12 children, starting with five apparently born in Oxford (though Pamela and Clarissa married and lived in Maine): Elijah M., 1765 -1769; Gideon, 1767-1770; Pamela, Nov. 28, 1768 – Nov. 16, 1836; Clarissa H., Sept. 10, 1770 – 1843; Stephen, born Aug. 18, 1774, death date unlisted.
Born in Maine were: Hannah, July 20, 1776; Parthena, 1780; twins Dolly and Polly, 1782; Elijah M., 1784; and Gideon, 1786. After Stephen and Dorothy returned to Oxford, they had one more son, Luke, born Sept. 3, 1791.
Henry Kingsbury confirmed Gideon Barton’s existence: he was a deacon, died in 1878, and one of his sons, also Deacon Gideon Barton, lived in Vassalboro in 1892. This grandson of Stephen Barton was born in Windsor, one of 13 children; Kingsbury wrote that he claimed the family “wore out two log houses.”
And for one more comparison, FamilySearch’s Barton list: Elijah Moore, 1765 – 1769; Gideon, 1767 – 1770; Pamela “Permelia” 1768 – 1836; Clarissa Harlow, 1770 -1843; Parthenia, 1772 -1794; Capt. Stephen, 1774 – 1862; Hannah, 1776 -1859; Dorothy “Dolly” 1778 – 1799; Mary, 1782 -1835; Elijah Moore, 1784 -1839; Gideon, Sr., 1786 -1878; Anna, 1787 – ??; and Luke, 1791 -1837.
Names with dates consistent on all three lists are Stephen, 1774 – 1865; Hannah, 1776 -1859; Elijah Moore, 1784 -1839; and Deacon Gideon, 1786 – 1878. Dorothy and Parthenia also appear on all three, with different birth dates – Dorothy was either the fifth or the eighth child, and Pathenia or Parthena varies from first to fifth to seventh.
In his history of Windsor, Lowden wrote that Barton’s Brook (in 1799 called Wonnamdogus Stream) flows through a corner of the Barton lot. Sometime after the spring of 1816, he said, a mill “appears to have been built” on the stream by Elijah and Gideon Barton and others.
Gideon Barton was captain of a company raised to resist the British during the War of 1812; he and his men were among those sent to Belfast briefly in September 1814. He opened one of the first stores in West Windsor, in 1814.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!
