title: Cruise ships visiting Maine this summer caught up in federal child sex abuse sweep
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A crew member who served on a cruise ship that visited Maine this week is one of dozens of cruise ship employees who have been arrested in a sweeping federal operation targeting people in possession of child sex abuse materials.
A handful of the cruise ships identified by federal officials in the operation have visited Maine ports this summer.
Bobby Prieto, 35, who worked on the Norwegian Jewel, was arrested on Monday, a day before the ship visited Bar Harbor. Prieto, a citizen of the Philippines, was arrested after customs officials found multiple media files on his two cellphones depicting Prieto sexually assaulting a young girl, according to the District of Massachusetts U.S. Attorney’s Office.
Before arriving in Bar Harbor, the Norwegian Jewel was in Portland Monday, according to an online cruise ship tracker. It is scheduled to arrive Wednesday in Saint John, New Brunswick.
Authorities have arrested 87 cruise ship crewmembers in Boston since mid-August for child sex abuse related charges, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection officials.
The arrests, which will lead to deportation or prosecution, are part of Operation Tidal Wave, a sprawling, multi-agency federal raid targeting child sex abuse crimes among cruise ship crew members, customs officials said.
The arrests come at a time when large ship visits to Bar Harbor are on the decline, as local residents have voted to cut back on the number and type of ships that can visit. Supporters of the limits, which restrict cruise ships to disembarking no more than 1,000 passengers per day during the months of July and August, say that the volume of ships and passengers in recent years has hurt the town.
The cap, which can only be enforced during the town’s peak tourist months, does not apply to large ships that were reserved prior to March 2022. The ships Norwegian Jewel and Norwegian Breakaway, both of which made their reservations prior to the limits being adopted, and which have both visited Bar Harbor this summer, are among the ships identified by federal officials as part of the investigation.
The Breakaway, carrying nearly 4,000 guests, was targeted by the federal operation on Sept. 20, when officials removed six crew members from the vessel in Boston. Those six employees allegedly admitted to previously possessing child sex abuse or exploitation materials, according to customs authorities.
The Norwegian cruise ship’s seven-day New England-Canada voyage includes a stop in Portland, according to the company’s website. Its next arrival in Portland will be on Oct. 6.
The Breakaway vessel visited Eastport for the first time last week, according to a Facebook post from the Eastport Port Authority. Its visit, which was widely celebrated by area locals, came just days after the arrests.
But once news of the arrests reached Eastport Tuesday, locals expressed concern about cruise ships stopping at the Washington County coastal city.
“The point that I think is most important is that there is no community discussion about any of the downsides of this level of cruise tourism,” wrote one Facebook user who posted about the arrests. “And that water and air pollution brought to us by these big ships are not the only downside. Local kids were on one of these ships in June. Our community leaders need to help protect us from the negative impacts.”
Another user who commented on the post said her eighth-grade class traveled on the Breakaway.
“Ickkkkk,” another commentator wrote. “Well if anything this is a good PSA to keep a closer eye on our children’s whereabouts when cruise ships are in town.”
In mid-August, authorities arrested an additional 11 crew members of the Breakaway and Holland America Line’s Volendam, which also visited Eastport throughout the summer, according to Cruise Hive, a cruise ship blog.
All of the accused have been identified as foreign nationals, according to the agencies.
“The safety, security, and well-being of our guests are of paramount importance, and we remain committed to maintaining a safe and secure environment across our fleet,” Norwegian Cruise Lines told USA TODAY in mid-August, adding the cruise is fully cooperating with authorities.
Prior to the Boston arrest and expedited deportations, federal authorities removed 27 crewmembers from six ships in San Diego in April, and 15 employees — one of whom faces federal prosecution — from ships in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in June and July, according to customs officials.

title: He worked to create a ‘normal’ life in Maine’s prisons. Now he’s stepping down.
text:
MAINE STATE PRISON — Two men in shorts and T-shirts stood on a walkway chatting on a clear Wednesday morning in September. Rows of flowers and carrots planted nearby soaked up the sun. Both men were out for a walk before work.
In separate cases in 1999 and 2009, these men were each convicted of murder. The bountiful gardens, personal laptops, permission for remote work and largely unsupervised time are all part of their lives at Maine State Prison. Barbed wire at the top of a fence was visible in the distance, but up close it appeared this conversation could’ve happened at any local park.
A lot has changed in Maine’s correctional system under the leadership of Randall Liberty, commissioner of Maine’s Department of Corrections, who walked up to the men wearing a tan suit.
“What’s going on, guys?” Liberty asked.
His dad served time in prison when Liberty was a child. That, combined with Liberty’s years in the military and law enforcement, formed his belief that people in prison should be treated with respect, life inside should be as normal as possible, and the main goal should be to rehabilitate.
Liberty traveled to Istanbul last year to promote these reforms, which he calls the Maine Model of Corrections. He recently hosted representatives from Israel, Ireland and Norway, and delegations from at least 14 states have come to see it in action.
The Brennan Center for Justice, a national, nonpartisan policy institute that is studying Maine’s prison system, said other states are right to look here as an example, and that Liberty’s attempt to spread the changes statewide is unique. The group issued a new report that calls Maine a “pioneer,” and says the results so far are promising, particularly in reducing violence among inmates and staff uses of force.
The model is widely respected within Maine, too, although people on both sides of the political aisle have questions about the results. Even Liberty acknowledged that for all the attention the Maine model is getting, the transformation from a system focused on punishment to one focused on rehabilitation is unfinished.
But he won’t be leading the charge to finish it.
Liberty, 62, will step down as commissioner on Oct. 1, shortly before Gov. Janet Mills, who appointed him, leaves office.
While Maine started some of the prison reforms before he took the helm, Liberty’s personal mark on the system is visible everywhere, like in a CBS national news segment this month in which Liberty donned a beekeeping suit in the state prison’s garden where inmates can learn the trade.
Brennan Center Justice Program director Ram Subramanian said he thinks Liberty has gotten people below him at the Department of Corrections on board with the vision, and he’s begun the difficult work of changing the culture among inmates themselves, whose buy-in is as important as the staff’s.
“I do hope it continues,” Subramanian said. “I hope they build on their successes.”
MUTUAL RESPECT
The Maine Model is built on the idea that being locked up for years is punishment enough. Once people are inside, the system should help address chronic problems in their lives and prepare them to be productive when they leave, since about 95% will walk out of the prison doors.
A culture of mutual respect among staff and inmates is essential, Liberty said, and acts as a kind of security system. He calls the people incarcerated in the eight state-run facilities he oversees “residents,” and said everyone should care about each other’s wellbeing.
As he led Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram journalists through the state prison this month, just a few staff watched over hundreds of inmates in the building where they played basketball and pickleball, lifted weights, spent time in the chapel and bought food at the commissary window.
Liberty uses every opportunity to enforce the culture he wants to see. Walking briskly by the weight room, an inmate made a flippant remark to a reporter about the quality of the food at the prison. Liberty, in mid-stride, pivoted to ask a staff member for the inmate’s name.
“That’s not how we act in this community,” Liberty said later. “If you’ve got a problem with the food, reach out to me. We’ll figure something out.”
Several inmates stopped the commissioner to ask about an issue and Liberty offered a way to follow up. One called the commissioner “brother” as they parted ways.
This culture may explain why there’s much less violence reported in the prisons. Between 2017-2024, rates fell by 36%, and those for staff use of force fell by 69%, the Brennan Center found.
Inmates told the researchers that violence was far less of a concern for them than it had been in prior years or in other facilities.
Brennan’s report said this is a key metric of success of a corrections system. Yet in most places, “immediate safety concerns and harsh punishment often take precedence,” the center wrote.
It may be one reason why Maine now has an easier time retaining corrections officers and filling positions in prisons than other states, but culture change takes time, Liberty acknowledged. In the Brennan Center survey, 41% of incarcerated men said staff did not treat inmates with respect. That’s 16 points better than a similar survey of prisoners in five other states the Urban Institute did last year, but still shows room for growth.
“It takes persistence to really move the needle,” Subramanian said.
DAD WAS INCARCERATED
When Liberty was just a kid, he visited his own father at the Maine State Prison. In his memoir published this year, “Liberty’s Prison: The Inmate’s Son Who Radically Reformed An American Prison,” co-written with freelance writer Christine Graf, they said the facility at the time was designed to “overwhelm inmates with feelings of ‘horror and remorse.’”
As recently as 2013, the Press Herald reported that staff, inmates and advocates called the prison’s culture “toxic,” and inmates were treated in a way that was “more punitive than rehabilitative.” A prison worker union representative said at the time, “No one wants to work in corrections.”
In part because of his dad, Liberty believes there are six root causes of incarceration: substance abuse, mental illness, poverty, neglect, educational deficiencies and trauma.
As described in the book, his dad checked at least four of those boxes and was arrested more times than anyone in the family can remember. Those stints in prison did not help his dad address the core of his problems.
When Liberty later worked for the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office, he went to crime scenes and saw hundreds of homes where, “I looked at those kids and, you know, that was me,” he said.
Society had let his family down in some respects, he said, especially during one winter when the family of four kids went without running water for three months because the pipes froze. Now thinking about the men and women in the state’s prisons, Liberty said, “All of the systems leading up to incarceration have failed them in one way or the other.”
“We’re the stop of last resort to help these people.”
He’s boosted substance use and mental health treatments in the prisons, and he’s not afraid to try new things. He pointed to what he considers the “gold standard” for the Maine model: a prison unit that looks almost like a college dorm with blue painted walls. Instead of staying for four years, though, inmates could be here for decades.
Dan Roberts, who’s served 21 years of a 55-year sentence for murder (which he said he is still appealing), leaned against the door to his room that has a single bed, a hand-painted mural and two small mounted televisions.
He said he keeps one always tuned to financial news channels so he can call his daughter and advise her on stock trades.
This area, which houses 25-30 people, used to be for solitary confinement. Inmates would exercise by walking in circles in a dog pen. Now it’s the opposite. They have an open kitchen, a long fish tank in the common area, and their own gym and showers. They can walk around the outdoor gardens where they can grow and pick their own food.
Inmates say those amenities are an incentive to behave well and give them a sense of purpose.
Liberty said he understands it can be surprising and hard to see someone convicted of murder living a somewhat “normal” life. He said after he talks to victims or their families they generally — but not always — support the Maine model’s reforms.
Some of the money inmates earn goes toward paying restitution. They also pay child support and cover some of the costs of their incarceration, which Liberty said improves public safety and accountability. Maine has done more around inmate remote work than any other state, according to the Alliance for Higher Education in Prison.
Another man who lives in the unit and was convicted of murder expects to leave prison in six years. The Press Herald is not naming him at the request of a member of the family of the person he killed, who said seeing him in this story could retraumatize the victim’s other family members.
The inmate said that with the money he’s earned working remotely, he recently bought a house.
“I’m just trying to set myself up for when I do get out,” he said. “Education, employment, stable housing — these are all things that help the recidivism rate drop.”
DISCONNECT ON THE GROUND
When Liberty took over as warden of the Maine State Prison in 2015 and then as commissioner in 2019, there was already some momentum for reform, said Subramanian from the Brennan Center. Corrections officials in various states have embraced the idea that prison shouldn’t necessarily be a horrible place, he said.
Maine stands out for its push to expand reforms to all of its prisons and as many inmates as possible, he said. Currently, 170 inmates in Maine are full-time college students, 12 are graduate students, and four are PhD candidates, Liberty said. Others learn woodworking, upholstery, welding or culinary skills, and get trained as commercial drivers or to work in hospitality.
Liberty said opportunities to work, study, and have computers need to grow in order for more of Maine’s approximately 2,100 inmates to get access.
Foster Bates is president of the state prison’s NAACP branch and has been incarcerated for 25 years serving a life sentence for a murder he maintains he did not commit. He said in an interview this spring that he appreciates the programs at the state prison, but that it can be hard to take advantage of them because some are restricted to a few dozen people, and because of lock-ins in the prison.
“Residents here don’t have a problem with the policy. We have an issue with the disconnect of how it’s being implemented,” Bates said.
“It’s challenging for some who are incarcerated to have a perspective of where we are nationally, where Maine was 10 years ago, and where Maine is today,” Liberty said. “Prison isn’t an easy experience regardless of how many opportunities they have.”
The Department of Corrections did not provide lock-in data, but said there has been a reduction.
Bates said he wished Liberty wouldn’t retire. “He’s leaving behind a legacy that can be built upon, but I think it could be destroyed,” he said.
Gubernatorial candidates Democrat Hannah Pingree and Republican Bobby Charles did not answer questions about how they would approach corrections. Independent Rick Bennett said he supports the Maine Model and that rehabilitation and humane treatment belong in the corrections system.
Areas for improvement documented by the Brennan Center include access to healthcare, which got particularly low marks from incarcerated women; the process for inmates to file grievances; and the system’s capacity to prepare people for release.
Just 10% of incarcerated men and 2% of women told the Brennan Center that the facility they’re in does a good job at preparing people to leave. Liberty said he wants to see Maine put more money toward transitional housing.
Still, recidivism is down under his leadership. The Brennan Center noted an 8% drop between people released in 2014 and 2022, the most recent year data is available, though the researchers said it will take more time to know for sure if it’s because of the reforms.
“These initial results show what prison officials and systems can accomplish with limited budgets amid shifting political winds,” the report said. In a sign of Liberty’s cooperation with the study, he’s scheduled to do a presentation with Brennan’s staff in Belfast, Ireland, in October.
State Senator Scott Cyrway, the top Republican on the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee, said he has “a lot of respect” for Liberty, whom he served with at the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office. The senator commended the culture Liberty has been able to foster in the prisons.
But Cyrway is skeptical of the results the Maine Model has produced. He thinks reductions in recidivism could be because Maine has recently made some conduct that used to be criminal into civil offenses. He worries the focus is being taken off of accountability, and he wants to see more support for drug addiction before people are released from prison.
Though his tenure is up on Oct. 1, Liberty is not going far. He plans to work three days a week for Amend, a prison reform program under the University of California San Francisco. In that capacity, he’ll still be leading tours of Maine’s prisons for people from other states and countries.
He’ll also focus on improving access to education, remote work and internet for inmates in Maine, without having to do the administrative duties that come with being commissioner.
“This will allow me to focus on those things I think really make a difference,” he said.
But it also means he’ll no longer be the guy calling the shots.
“In the last eight years, I’ve been hiring people that are like minded, believe in redemption and are forward thinking,” Liberty said. “It’s time for people behind me to step up.”

title: Mount Desert Warrant Committee rejects AOS reorg plan
text:
MOUNT DESERT — The Mount Desert Warrant Committee weighed in on the proposed school district reorganization on Tuesday night, with a unanimous vote to recommend voters reject the plan when it goes to the ballot in November.
Mount Desert Island Regional School System Superintendent Mike Zboray attended the meeting to speak to the committee about why the district is proposing a reorganization. He talked about the reorganization in broad strokes.
Other towns on MDI have already taken a stance on the reorganization. Both the Bar Harbor Warrant Committee and Town Council have voted to recommend rejection of the proposed reorganization. The Tremont Select Board also voted to recommend the rejection of the proposed plan.
A handful of Mount Desert residents attended the Sept. 29 meeting to share their thoughts on the plan and ask Zboray questions.
One aspect of the proposed reorganization plan that residents kept coming back to was the consolidation of school district leadership into one board. In the proposal, the RSU would be governed by one board consisting of 15 members. Each town in the RSU would have a fixed number of representatives on the board, with Mount Desert and Bar Harbor each receiving three voting seats.
Residents raised concerns about potentially losing governing power in the new model, especially as it pertains to the town’s elementary school. Zboray assured residents that the current board that makes decisions about the regional high school considers each town equally when weighing decisions.
Gail Marshall, a member of the Mount Desert Elementary School Board, shared her stance on the proposed reorganization at the meeting. Despite being pro-consolidation, she explained that she does not support this proposal and sees it as too focused on administration rather than education.
“I don’t favor this kind of reorganization that simply shifts the tax burden without using that as a leverage to provide a vision for what our educational system and structure should look like for the next 20-30 years,” said Marshall. “It’s not about where people are going to send their kids to school this fall or next fall, it’s future planning and that’s what this should be about.”
She acknowledged that the current administrative structure, which requires Zboray to attend monthly meetings of each individual town’s elementary school board in addition to the high school, is problematic. Although, she reiterated that she did not see this reorganization as the solution.
“I think there’s more we can do to make this more humane for the superintendent who really does have a job description that’s not ok just in terms of meeting times,” said Marshall. “I think we can work on stuff like that too.”
Meeting attendees also brought up concerns about losing ownership of the Mount Desert Elementary School building which would be turned over to the RSU if the reorganization plan passed. One resident brought up other RSUs in the state where towns have voted to close one of the elementary schools in the district or exit the district altogether.
The RSU 63 Board of Directors voted to approve closure of Eddington Elementary School in April, citing annual savings and logistical efficiencies according to reporting by WABI. This November, the towns in RSU 63 will vote on whether or not to approve the closure.
If all three towns vote “yes” to approve the closure, it will pass and the district will move forward. If the vote is split among the district towns, according to Maine law, the dissenting towns become responsible for covering the net savings the district would forfeit by not closing the school.
Zboray responded by saying he reached out to legal counsel for clarity on the law as to whether that financial liability would be a one-time payment for the dissenting town. He assured the group that the decision to close a school within an RSU would not be made lightly or without extensive work to gain feedback from district towns before going to a vote.
Warrant Committee member Kathy Miller added that she appreciates the work that went into developing the reorganization plan and the problems with the current administrative structure but suggested the district look into smaller solutions.
“I would like to see some of those discrete problems with their discrete solutions and not necessarily this big thing,” said Miller. “So, I think if there are ways to get better education and provide what students need all over the island, let’s find some other solutions to that. I don’t think that this is necessarily it.”
After an hour, Warrant Committee Chair Phil Lichtenstein read the referendum out loud and brought the motion to a vote. It received a unanimous rejection by the 12 members in attendance.
The reorganization proposal will appear on the ballot in Mount Desert on Nov. 3.

title: Rick Bennett can help unify a house divided
text:
“A house divided against itself cannot stand.”
In these times of division and danger, Abraham Lincoln’s prophetic words still ring true today. Our democracy cannot stand without an informed, aroused, consensus-seeking voting public.
The current level of public conversation is a petty, mindless, toxic gabble: polls, personal scandals, campaign strategies, money raised for campaign war chests. But in Maine’s current political race, I know of one candidate who persistently strives to raise the level of public conversation to: issues, policies, political platforms, voting records.
I know of one candidate who has consistently sought mutual understanding, consensus and bipartisan collaboration. I know of one candidate whose statecraft, long service in our state Senate and persistent voice of sense and sanity entitle him to stand in Lincoln’s long shadow.
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, please join me in voting for Richard Bennett, independent candidate for the governorship of Maine.
Steve Turner
Mechanic Falls

title: The rise and fall of America's deadly love affair with the cigarette
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cancer stick. Coffin nail. Cowboy killer. Those are nicknames, through the decades, for the cigarette — the once-glamorous desideratum of American society that has been tied to tens of millions of U.S. deaths.
The cigarette is not an invention of the United States. And while Marlboro is a top-selling international brand, more than 100 countries make cigarettes. The largest manufacturer is in China.
But U.S. ingenuity drastically altered the global tobacco industry. And American culture embraced it in the 20th century, making it — for a time — a symbol of stylish adulthood in U.S. movies and media, and omnipresent in bars, restaurants, airplanes and even hospitals.
Smoking became “a right of passage for many young people,” and by the 1950s nearly half of U.S. adults smoked, says K. Michael Cummings, a tobacco history scholar at the Medical University of South Carolina.
“I remember making ashtrays for my parents for Mother’s Day and Father’s Day gifts,” says Cummings, 73. “I remember giving cartons of cigarettes as Christmas gifts. I mean, smoking was so common. It was just part of Americana.”
Early versions of cigarettes can be traced back thousands of years to the Mayans. But hand-rolling each cigarette was time-consuming and labor intensive.
That changed in the 1880s, when a Virginia inventor named John Bansack invented an automated cigarette-rolling machine that could make smokes 50 times faster. Early tobacco magnate James Buchanan Duke invested in the technology, and used it — along with the development of more palatable tobacco blends — to build the cigarette business into a major American industry.
Cigarettes were clearly addictive, and the idea that smoking could kill was long suspected. Automaker Henry Ford warned against cigarettes in the 1910s, putting out a brochure in 1914 that called them “little white slavers” and argued they were habit-forming bad for health, and were associated with bad morals.
A watershed moment came in 1964 with an authoritative U.S. surgeon general report that said smoking causes illness and death, helping to lead the way to warning labels on cigarette packs, bans on cigarette commercials, and restrictions on where people could light up.
The dangers of smoking began to sink in to the public consciousness, though it took decades for smoking rates to plummet to the historically low levels they’re at now. The chain-smoking writer Kurt Vonnegut Jr., who favored Pall Malls, in 1968 penned that “the public health authorities never mention the main reason many Americans have for smoking heavily, which is that smoking is a fairly sure, fairly honorable form of suicide.”
___
Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more American objects, click here. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

title: Literacy Volunteers of Bangor seeks tutors amid rise in reading, writing help requests
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor-area learning organization is looking for volunteer tutors after seeing an uptick in students seeking help with reading and writing comprehension.
For nearly 60 years, Literacy Volunteers of Bangor has operated as a nonprofit helping adults improve their handle on reading and writing in English.
“About 70% of our adult students right now are immigrants. So, they’ve come from all around the globe, and they’re needing to understand English. Being able to speak it, read it, write in English. They’re often on a track to be U.S. citizens,” Mary Marin Taylor, Executive Director of Literacy Volunteers of Bangor said.
But it goes beyond just reading and writing. A lot of times, volunteers are giving students lessons on skills that are rarely taught, even in school.
“How do you read a paystub? What is a paystub? Why is a paystub important? How does it relate to your life? It was those types of things that we worked on. In this particular case the person I was matched with needed life skills. How do you budget? That money coming in, how do you use it going out,” volunteer Bob Jonah said.
For about a year and a half, Jonah has been volunteering with LVB. For him, the fulfilling part is seeing a person become a new version of themselves over time.
“To watch the confidence level is amazing. To go from not understanding a lot of things to understanding many things. And that’s been, for me, the excitement of doing what I’m doing,” Jonah said.
“I’ve been blessed with seeing just generations of families really change because one adult in that family came forward and asked for help, and it was transformative in terms of what they were able to do differently moving forward, and what they were able to teach their children and how it affected their family unit,” Marin Taylor said.
Similar to a matchmaking website, LVB pairs students and potential tutors based on how well they would work together.
“We prioritize learning each party, like every tutor, every student. And we’re going to make sure that geographically you’re in the same region, timewise you have the same availability, but we’re also going to look at the characteristics and maybe the background of either and just ensure as much as possible that two people can work together and learn from each other,” Marin Taylor said.
While educators are considered a natural fit for these kinds of roles, anybody with a will to help others is welcomed.
“There are people knocking on the door on a regular basis at Literacy Volunteers and think of them as your neighbors. If your neighbor is knocking on your door, and they ask, ‘can you help me with this?’ what would you do? I’d help them. That’s what we’re looking for, is people that can step up with whatever experiences they’ve had in their life, no matter their age, and answer that door,” Jonah said.
For those interested in getting involved as a volunteer, LVB is offering certification training. Classes begin October 19th and continue for the following four weeks.
For more information or to sign up, head to LVBangor.org .

title: Senate blocks bill aimed at keeping data center costs off electric bills
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Senate blocks bill aimed at keeping data center costs off electric bills
A Senate bill aimed at addressing higher electric costs tied to expanding data centers failed to advance, with Democrats arguing it did not go far enough.
Senate blocks bill aimed at keeping data center costs off electric bills
A Senate bill aimed at addressing higher electric costs tied to expanding data centers failed to advance, with Democrats arguing it did not go far enough.
The Senate failed to advance a bill on Wednesday aimed at addressing higher electric bills as data centers expand across the country, falling three votes short despite bipartisan agreement on its goal.
The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 votes needed to move forward. The measure had previously passed the House 417-3.
Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, said, "This bill is the only path that we can take today that will lower electricity prices."
Senate Democrats blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act, arguing it did not adequately address the issue.
Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., said, "Let me be clear, this is nothing more than a messaging bill on the eve of an election."
The bill would have required state utility regulators to consider making large power users, such as data centers, pay for the grid upgrades needed to serve them. However, it would not have mandated states to adopt that standard.
Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said, "Senate Democrats want to make it mandatory for data centers to cover their own costs by law."
Democrats have backed competing proposals that would go further. Heinrich's GRID Savings Act would direct federal regulators to require large electricity customers such as data centers to pay for infrastructure needed to connect them to the grid.
Rep. Mike Johnson, R-La., said the Ratepayer Protection Act was "a codification of President Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge."
The debate over data centers is growing beyond Washington, as communities across the country weigh the promise of new investment against concerns over electric bills and environmental impact.
A recent AP-NORC/University of Chicago poll found about 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers, while 63% are concerned about their impact on electricity prices.
Taylor Enterline, a Pennsylvania resident, said during a recent community meeting, "We really need strict regulations in place to protect ourselves from data centers."
Trump has previously said communities that reject data centers risk "being backwards and poor."
When asked about local concerns, Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, said, "Nobody has to allow a data center in their hometown if they don't want. I mean, the people of the town will decide. But you know, I think that the places that have allowed data centers in voluntarily have seen the data centers produce more power than they consume, electricity prices have gone down."
New economic data released Wednesday shows investment in AI infrastructure, such as data centers, is helping power economic growth.
With the bill's failure, Congress has not imposed any new federal protections on data-center-related grid costs. Much of the responsibility remains with states, utility regulators and the agreements that communities strike with companies.
The White House has its Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which participating tech companies have voluntarily agreed to cover new power and grid costs their data centers create rather than passing those costs on to existing customers. Husted's legislation was designed to codify key elements of that pledge.
Tech companies have been making significant deals with local communities to build data centers.
Meta says teachers in Louisiana's Richland Parish received annual bonuses of up to $50,000 because of increased tax revenue associated with its data center project.
And on Tuesday, Amazon Web Services agreed to contribute $10 million toward a new career and technical education school in King George County, Virginia, as part of a planned $6 billion data center investment.
Trump said Tuesday that people living near data centers could eventually see what he called a "dividend."
The question remains whether those benefits outweigh concerns over power costs, water use and the impact on local communities.

title: California couple accused of killing son-in-law in public park have been charged with murder
text:
DUBLIN, Calif. (AP) — A California couple has been charged with murder after authorities say they shot their son-in-law to death Saturday in a public park, days before he and the couple’s daughter were set for a hearing in a bitter divorce case.
Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, were due in court Wednesday for an arraignment on the charges. The Associated Press was not able to reach an attorney for the couple prior to the court appearance. Their daughter, Candice Jang, could not be reached, though she appeared virtually at Wednesday’s hearing.
Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for The New York Times, was shot to death in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin, east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple, who were still near the scene, Dublin Police Services said in a news release.
Court records show McKinsey’s killing came during a contentious divorce with Jang and a custody battle over the couple’s three young children. In petitions for restraining orders filed last year, the couple accused each other of physical, emotional and psychological abuse going back more than a decade. McKinsey, who is transgender, alleged that both Jang and her parents were verbally and physically abusive regarding a gender transition he underwent years ago.
In his petition for a protection order, McKinsey alleged that Chen had directed anti-LGBTQ slurs at him and his oldest child.
He also accused Jang of being physically and emotionally abusive during medical procedures related to his transition. He alleged Zhang punched him in the chest while he was recovering from double mastectomy surgery.
Victim had been charged with misdemeanor child abuse
McKinsey was arrested last October and charged with misdemeanor child abuse for allegedly hitting their oldest son. Police said he acknowledged having slapped the child. Prosecutors also charged him with endangering their youngest child after deputies responded to the family’s home to talk with him and found their 2-year-old had been left home alone, according to court documents.
McKinsey pleaded not guilty to the charges and alleged in court records that he had been set up by his wife, who had left the house without telling him the child was sleeping in a crib upstairs. He was released from jail on the condition that he complete 12 parenting classes. At the time of his killing, McKinsey was out on bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program.
It was also in October that Jang obtained a domestic violence protection order against McKinsey.
Jang said in her filing that in 2010 McKinsey had grabbed her by the forearms during one argument and caused her to hit the corner of a coffee table, fracturing a vertebra in her upper back. She also said that in 2023 she called the police to their home after McKinsey pushed their oldest son hard on the head. Jang also accused McKinsey of emotionally abusing her mother.
Victim filed a competing protective order request
McKinsey in December filed his own request for domestic violence protection against Jang, alleging years of abuse that included her hitting him in the head with a frying pan. He later filed for divorce and sought more time with the three children, noting that he had been limited to two hours of supervised visits per week since last fall, Alameda County court documents show.
In late August, McKinsey was granted unsupervised visits in public twice a week.
The killing occurred a week before a hearing was scheduled in McKinsey and Jang’s divorce case. The couple had been married since July 2011.
McKinsey joined The New York Times in January 2023. He was director of engineering for New York Times Games and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the paper said. A spokesperson declined to comment further.

title: Ex-NFL star Antonio Brown set to appear in Miami court for expected plea agreement
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Former NFL star wide receiver Antonio Brown is scheduled to be in a Miami courtroom Wednesday to accept a plea deal that will let him avoid prison time on a reduced charge in an attempted murder case, according to his attorney.
Defense attorney Mark Eiglarsh has said Brown will plead no contest to aggravated assault and be sentenced to probation. He also said adjudication will be withheld, meaning Brown will not be considered a convicted felon.
Brown could have faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the original charge. Eiglarsh has said the agreement with prosecutors was too good to turn down. The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office said previously that details would be clarified at the hearing.
Brown is accused of grabbing a handgun from a security staffer after a celebrity boxing match in Miami on May 16, 2025, and firing two shots at a man he had been in a fistfight with earlier, according to an arrest warrant. Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu told investigators that one of the bullets grazed his neck.
Brown has said on social media that he was defending himself from an attack and others were trying to steal jewelry from him.
Florida’s Stand Your Ground law allows people who believe they face death or serious injury to use deadly force to defend themselves without a duty to retreat.
Richard Cooper, an attorney for Nantambu, has called the plea deal a fair one. He has said Nantambu forgives Brown and would not cooperate with law enforcement.
Brown, 38, spent 12 years in the NFL and was an All-Pro wide receiver who last played in 2021 for Tampa Bay, including winning a Super Bowl with quarterback Tom Brady.
Over the course of his career, much of it spent with Pittsburgh, he had 928 receptions for more than 12,000 yards and accounted for 88 total touchdowns, including punt returns and one pass.
During a 2021 game with Tampa Bay against the New York Jets, Brown took off his jersey, shoulder pads and gloves and ran off the field, leading to his release by the Buccaneers and effectively ending his career.
Brown has dealt with several legal problems over the years. He previously was accused of battery of a moving truck driver, several domestic violence charges, failure to pay child support and other incidents.
Brown was extradited in November 2025 from Dubai, where he has business interests, after an arrest warrant on the attempted murder charge was issued in June of the same year.

title: Additional repairs to Seawall Road to begin in October
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SEAWALL — In July 2024, the community came together to repair a washed-out section of road that runs through Seawall in Southwest Harbor and Acadia National Park land. The road is vital infrastructure connecting Southwest Harbor with Tremont and Bass Harbor.
On Oct. 5, the state plans to close the road again for additional repairs spanning no more than 28 days.
At the Sept. 22 Select Board meeting, Town Manager Karen Reddersen announced that the state would move forward with repairs to the road running through Seawall.
Back-to-back storms in January 2024 caused severe damage to Route 102A at Seawall, followed by another storm with a massive tide in March. The road was shut down until July, before the community rallied and repaired the damaged section.
That repair has served residents and visitors on Mount Desert Island to date with no issues.
Concerns about the road being completely closed off were brought up at the meeting, with Reddersen noting, “We talked about the one-way traffic, about it needing to be one way or another because there was some discussion about maybe it could be open some days.”
Reddersen also said that emergency responders would need to be informed so they could adjust their response.
“We did put forth the idea of moving the start date to Oct. 13 because then the campground would be closed and the bus service would be closed,” said Reddersen.
Reddersen confirmed the road would be fully closed with a detour, which would add 16 minutes and approximately 8 miles.
Local business owners also raised concerns, including Charlotte Gill, owner of Charlotte’s Legendary Lobster Pound and The Seawall Motel. “Seawall Road is not just a roadway, it’s a way of life,” said Gill. “A lot of people are depending on the crews who are coming in to do this work, and they have some pretty big shoes to fill.”
Gill was one of the locals in 2024 who helped with the repairs and delivered food and drinks to the workers while they voluntarily fixed the roadway over a five-day span. “When Seawall Road was left in pieces for five months, our local companies were heroes. They came together and put it back together in five days, and they did a remarkable job,” said Gill.
Gill’s business sits directly in the Seawall area and will potentially be affected when construction starts. “I do wish the state could wait until after the Columbus Day/Indigenous Peoples’ Day weekend to begin, but whenever they start, I wish the crews good weather, good luck, and Godspeed. This road matters enormously to the people who live and work along it, as well as to all those who come from near and far to enjoy its beauty. We’ll all be rooting for them to get it right.”
Maine Department of Transportation has placed a sign with closure information at the turnoff to Seawall in Southwest Harbor.
Spencer Roberts with MDOT confirmed the Oct. 5 date as the beginning of closure. “The project location is on Route 102A and begins 0.07 of a mile south of Beaver Lodge Lane and extends south 0.42 of a mile,” said Roberts.
Local contractor RF Jordan will do the construction work, with federal funding covering the cost of repairs.
“It’s the first time that type of funding has been provided anywhere in the nation, so we’re happy and grateful that they’re doing the project,” said Reddersen at the Sept. 22 meeting.
Additionally, once the 28 days have passed, Special Provision Section 107 states that “The contractor will be assessed Supplemental Liquidated Damages at the rate of $2500 per calendar day that 102A is closed to traffic beyond 28 calendar days.”

title: From scout fundraiser to fall staple: Inside Davis Family Farm’s 10-acre corn maze
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
KENDUSKEAG, Maine (WABI) - What started out as a simple fundraiser for local Cub Scouts has quickly grown into one of the region’s most anticipated autumn destinations.
Now in its third year of operation, Davis Family Farm in Kenduskeag has become a go-to seasonal hub for families across central Maine, blending traditional agriculture with community entertainment.
The Region’s Largest Corn Maze
The centerpiece of this year’s festivities is a sprawling 10-acre corn maze, which farm operators say is now the largest in Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts. The labyrinth expanded significantly from last year’s six-acre footprint.
Navigating the full adult maze can take anywhere from two to three hours.
“It’s the real deal,” said Davis, a fifth-generation farmer. “I’m not saying you have to pack a lunch, but you probably oughta bring a water.”
For younger visitors, the farm offers a smaller children’s maze complete with prizes at the finish.
Accessible Fun for All Generations
Beyond the maze, the farm was designed to be welcoming to every member of the family. Attractions include a pumpkin patch, pedal tractors, a corn play box, pumpkin and apple slingshots, and a giant slide accessed through a hay bale pyramid.
Accessibility was a top priority when designing the farm’s signature wagon ride.
“The ticket includes an accessible wagon ride. We’re really proud of that wagon,” Davis said. “I have set it up so there’s a ramp on the back so it’s accessible. I don’t know anybody that has something like that.”
Local food trucks, hot dogs, and popcorn are also on hand, alongside friendly farm animals ready for a visit once guests emerge from the stalks.
Giving Back to the Community
Community support remains at the heart of Davis Family Farm’s mission.
The farm has scheduled three “night mazes,” with 10% of ticket sales directly benefiting local high school Project Graduation programs. Additionally, on Oct. 10, the farm will partner with Tiller & Rye and Uno’s Pizzeria & Grill to host a special benefit for the Old Town Animal Orphanage.
For tickets, operating hours, and event schedules, visit the farm’s official page by following the link.

title: Why I voted against removing George Mitchell’s name from building, scholarship
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Donna Loring is a Penobscot Nation citizen, Vietnam War veteran, former tribal representative to the Maine Legislature and former chief of the Penobscot Nation Police Department. She is a member of the University of Maine System Board of Trustees.
I was one of five members of the University of Maine System Board of Trustees who voted against removing former Sen. George Mitchell’s name from the George J. Mitchell Center for Sustainability Solutions and the George J. Mitchell Peace Scholarship.
I want to explain why.
My vote was not a declaration that every allegation concerning Mitchell is false. I do not know that. But neither has there been a finding that he committed wrongdoing. The university’s own task force acknowledged that fact.
There is a difference between an allegation, an association and a finding of wrongdoing. I believe a university, perhaps more than almost any other institution, has an obligation to recognize those distinctions.
But there was something else weighing heavily on me when I voted: legacy.
A legacy is not simply a name attached to a building, center or scholarship. It is the record of what a person has done with a lifetime.
George Mitchell represented Maine in the U.S. Senate for 15 years, eventually becoming Senate majority leader. After leaving the Senate, he undertook the extraordinarily difficult task of chairing the peace negotiations in Northern Ireland. He spent more than 22 months in those negotiations and made more than 100 trips across the Atlantic.
Those negotiations produced the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, helping bring an end to three decades of violence in Northern Ireland in which thousands of people had died. President Bill Clinton awarded Mitchell the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, for his leadership in the Northern Ireland peace process.
That is part of Mitchell’s legacy.
So are thousands of young people from Maine who have received Mitchell Scholarships. What began with 20 scholars in 1995 has grown into a community of more than 4,000 scholars and alumni. Mitchell used money remaining from his Senate campaign fund, after offering refunds to contributors, to help establish the scholarship program.
Only days before our vote, Mitchell Scholars and supporters gathered again to celebrate that continuing work.
That is also part of his legacy.
I recognize that institutions in Ireland have also reconsidered or removed Mitchell’s name from scholarships associated with him. I understand why universities and other institutions are struggling with these questions. The allegations surrounding Jeffrey Epstein are deeply disturbing, and association with him understandably raises serious questions.
But difficult questions should cause a university to examine history more carefully, not less.
My concern is what standard we establish when we remove an honor because of allegations and reputational damage when there has been no finding of wrongdoing.
The university system’s own commemorative naming policy says removal should occur only in “extraordinary circumstances.” It says removal “must not be undertaken lightly.” The policy also asks those making such decisions to respect “the considered judgments of the past” while recognizing “the fallibility of their own judgments.”
Students who wanted Mitchell’s name removed deserved to be heard. So did faculty, alumni and members of the public. Listening to them is part of our responsibility as trustees.
We also have an obligation to exercise our own judgment, examine the evidence and consider the precedent our decisions establish.
I worry about a standard in which reputational harm can outweigh the absence of a finding of wrongdoing. Reputations can change quickly. Public opinion can change quickly. The principles by which a university makes consequential decisions should be more durable.
And I worry about what happens to legacy.
We should not ignore the questions raised about Mitchell’s association with Epstein. We should not minimize them, and we should certainly not prevent students from examining them. But neither should those questions cause us to diminish everything else.
More than 4,000 Mitchell Scholars are part of the historical record.
Fifteen years representing Maine in the Senate are part of that record.
And the Good Friday Agreement is part of that record.
History is rarely neat enough to divide human beings into columns marked good and bad. Universities should be among the places where we confront that complexity rather than remove it.
Tell the whole story.
Tell students what Mitchell accomplished. Tell them about his association with Epstein. Tell them what has been alleged. Tell them what Mitchell has denied. Most importantly, distinguish between what has been established and what has not.
Then allow people to wrestle with the complete record.
I respect that other trustees reached a different conclusion. It was a difficult decision, and I do not question the sincerity of those who voted to remove the name.
But I could not vote to diminish a lifetime of documented public service based on allegations for which there has been no finding of wrongdoing.
For me, this was about more than George Mitchell.
It was about evidence. It was about fairness. It was about the responsibility of a university to preserve and examine history rather than simplify it. It was about a university’s responsibility to educate its students.
And it was about legacy.
That is why I voted no.

title: Landowner banned from North Maine Woods
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - A landowner in the North Maine Woods has been issued a lifetime ban and says he is no longer able to access his 400-acre property.
Mark Thomas was banned from the North Maine Woods on Oct.24, 2025. In a letter from North Maine Woods Incorporated to Thomas, officials claim since 2020 he committed several violations of Maine Inland Fish and Wildlife laws. The letter informed Thomas that he had been banned from the North Maine Woods and that if he’s found within an area he doesn’t have deeded access to he may face trespassing charges.
Organization responds
North Maine Woods Inc. Executive Director Bill Greaves wrote in a statement:
“North Maine Woods is a non-profit organization that manages public access on approximately 3.5 million acres of private timberlands. Public recreational access on these private lands is by permission. While the majority of public users are respectful of this permissive open access, on occasion there are users who are not and abuse this privilege. On such occasions, NMW takes steps to address this behavior, which can include prohibiting a person from using private lands for recreational use - i.e., those individuals no longer have permission.
“Each time a visitor enters the North Maine Woods, they agree to a Land Use and Camping Permit. Also, NMW prohibitions for recreational users are specific to permissive use and access. These steps help ensure permissive open access can remain for the majority of recreational users, especially during this time of year as we enter hunting season. Each individual situation is case-specific. NMW does not typically share details of such behaviors specific to any individuals out of privacy respect but may do so with cooperating law enforcement agencies. When a FOIA request is submitted to a government agency, this information then becomes available to the public. Whether someone has permission to use private lands is a wholly separate issue from whether an individual has, or does not have, certain property rights.”
Landowner disputes claims
Thomas calls the accusations unverified and incorrect and says he’d never harm the area.
“I love those woods up there. I literally stop in the spring and pick up trash because guys snowmobile down all the roads and I pick everything from gum wrappers to empty beer cans. It’s the most beautiful place in the world to me where I come from. It’s gorgeous. I cherish the place. I love it. I respect it and I want to bring my kid up there to have the memories that I had with my dad and the last thing I would do is do something harmful to the place,” he said.
Thomas denies every accusation against him. He says he never bypassed a gate and bought a season pass every year. He says the trespassing charge was dropped and denies vandalizing a bridge. He says a worker he hired stole the outhouse he’s been accused of taking and later confessed.
Family affected
Thomas said the situation has not only affected him, but his family as well.
“I’ve never stolen a thing in my life and never would and I have the money to buy something if I want it and it was just bizarre. I have 2 kids. I have my son and then me and my wife are in the process of becoming legal guardians of a 15-year-old boy that lost both his parents at a very young age. He moved in with us back in November and he loves the outdoors and this whole summer came and went. It makes me wanna cry and they’re like, ‘Let’s go up to camp,’ and I haven’t even told them because I keep thinking this is like a nightmare I’m gonna wake up from.”
Thomas says there is no appeal process. He just wants the ban lifted to reach and maintain his property, and enjoy it with family and friends.

title: Aging Untold: Meet the man behind ‘Taking Care of Granny;’ and how learning new things boosts your brain
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we shatter the notion that you are ever too old to try something new and share how to break through doubt and embrace fresh adventures.
Plus, we highlight the rising number of male caregivers with creator Dugan Meredith — the force behind “Taking Care of Granny” — who shares essential lessons and resources for families navigating care.
Learning something new, such as picking up a new hobby later in life, can be fun, and it also sharpens your brain health, keeps you engaged and builds connections across generations, according to the Aging Untold experts.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, says the discomfort is actually doing something good beneath the surface.
“The brain is always changing. New connections, what we call neuroplasticity,” Rogers said. “And also you’re waking up the brain, and that’s a good thing. So it makes you just stay alert and all that. And you can look at reaction time to things actually improve.”
See the full story to find out how learning boosts your brain and which new skills the Aging Untold experts have challenged themselves to learn.
When Dugan Meredith started to open up and share what life is like as a caregiver for his mother-in-law, Granny, he never imagined how much support he would find through an online community.
Granny showed signs that something was wrong when she was forgetting how to go pick up the grandchildren from school, getting lost and inviting strangers back to the house. Then, Granny was diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia.
One day, Meredith was sitting at his kitchen table with a cup of coffee, recording himself as he talked about his frustrations before posting the video to TikTok.
That led him to a community of other caregivers he didn’t know existed.

title: MaineHousing awards a record $2.7 million to help agencies run winter warming shelters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MaineHousing has awarded a record $2.72 million in funding to 12 warming shelters from York County to Presque Isle this winter.
The funding will support safe, heated spaces in Bangor, Lewiston and Portland, as well as Augusta, Biddeford, Brunswick, Ellsworth, Orland, Presque Isle and Waterville. The facilities will offer a combined 474 beds for people during cold and dangerous winter weather, and most plan to stay open through April.
“Dangerous winter weather can put lives at risk, especially for people experiencing homelessness or housing instability,” MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan said in a news release Tuesday afternoon.
This year’s funding is the most money doled out in the five years that MaineHousing has offered this program. Last year, the Legislature gave the agency $2.3 million to distribute.
The organizations running the shelters can use the funding from the quasi-governmental agency for staffing, supplies, transportation, extended hours and other operating costs. Recipients of the warming shelter grants will work with their municipalities, emergency management officials and community partners to connect people in need to a warming shelter.
“We are grateful to the governor and the Maine Legislature for making these funds available,” Brennan said. “This investment helps local organizations prepare before winter and respond when dangerous weather threatens Maine people.”
Biddeford-based Seeds of Hope is the top recipient of this year’s funding. The nonprofit will get more than $660,000 — about $304,000 to support its 55-bed facility in Biddeford, and nearly $361,000 to operate a nightly warming shelter in Portland.
Seeds of Hope stepped forward in early September to operate the Portland shelter after the city sought an agency to run a winter shelter following the closure of its shelter for asylum seekers.
Portland Mayor Mark Dion said at the time that he had some concerns with Seeds of Hope taking the shelter on, noting that the city’s past partners couldn’t handle the capacity needs in Maine’s most populous area.
But Seeds of Hope Director Vassie Fowler said her staff is experienced in managing high-needs populations, complex situations and the operational demands that come with running a full-capacity warming center.
Still, the $360,720 for this winter’s shelter is less than the roughly $400,000 that the city received last year to operate a shelter that only opened based on certain thresholds. This year, the plan is for the facility to be open every night, regardless of temperature or snowfall.
Fowler declined to comment on the funding Wednesday.
Alter L/A, a 24-hour warming shelter in the Lewiston and Auburn area, received just under $390,000 for a 112-bed facility. That funding will primarily go toward staffing, said Kevin Boilard, the executive director.
The shelter employs around 25 people and plans to bring on an additional 12 to 15 staff members for the colder months. Last year, the shelter served more than 700 people, with an average of 112 per 24-hour period. It’s thought to be the only 24/7 warming shelter in the Twin Cities, Boilard said.
“The intention is not just to house (people), but to bring them in, make them warm and connect them to stability and the structure that most are looking for,” he said.
The other nine agencies receiving funding are:
- Augusta Overnight, $375,750 for 50 beds in Augusta
- Bangor Area Homeless Shelter, $10,000 for 5 beds in Bangor
- Brick Church, $427,650 for 65 beds in Bangor
- Tedford Housing, $225,450 for 30 beds in Brunswick
- Healthy Acadia, $263,025 for 35 beds in Ellsworth
- HOME Inc., $28,611 for 18 beds in Orland
- State Street Church, $52,000 for 18 beds in Portland
- Homeless Services of Aroostook, $112,725 for 15 beds in Presque Isle
- Mid-Maine Homeless Shelter, $172,845 for 23 beds in Waterville
The shelter funding is a piece of broader winter preparedness efforts across the state. MaineHousing also runs the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) and the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which both help eligible households with heating costs and emergencies.
Heating costs have soared in Maine, with the price of heating oil hitting a record $6.02 per gallon last week.
Steve Hoad, of Windsor, is just one of a large number of Maine homeowners who use heating oil to keep their homes warm during the winter. Hoad told the Portland Press Herald in early September that his farmhouse will cost him thousands more to keep warm this winter. He’s exactly the kind of person HEAP aims to help.
“We know many families are concerned about heating costs,” Brennan said. “Programs such as HEAP can help thousands of Maine households each year, and we urge people to seek help before they face a crisis.”
Staff Writer Emily Duggan contributed to this story.

title: Massachusetts man pleads guilty to drug, gun conspiracy tied to trafficking in Maine
text:
Massachusetts man pleads guilty to drug, gun conspiracy tied to trafficking in Maine
A Massachusetts man has admitted to supplying fentanyl and cocaine in Maine and New Hampshire and trading drugs for cash and firearms, federal prosecutors say.
Massachusetts man pleads guilty to drug, gun conspiracy tied to trafficking in Maine
A Massachusetts man has admitted to supplying fentanyl and cocaine in Maine and New Hampshire and trading drugs for cash and firearms, federal prosecutors say.
A Lawrence, Massachusetts man pleaded guilty Tuesday to federal charges stemming from an interstate drug and firearm trafficking network that distributed fentanyl and cocaine in Maine and New Hampshire, federal prosecutors said.
Officials say 26-year-old Nilbel Ventura Amaro, also known as "Nino," “Megamind,” “Ben” and “Migo,” pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston to conspiracy to distribute, manufacture and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances and conspiracy to possess firearms in furtherance of drug trafficking.
U.S. Senior District Court Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton scheduled sentencing for Jan. 6, 2027.
Federal prosecutors said Ventura Amaro was an associate of the Trinitarios transnational criminal organization and operated a drug trafficking network in Maine in coordination with members of the group.
According to prosecutors, Ventura Amaro supplied drugs to Trinitarios members and associates, as well as Mackenzie Bimpson, whom authorities described as a large-scale dealer in drugs and firearms. Prosecutors said Ventura Amaro sold fentanyl and cocaine to Bimpson and received cash and firearms in exchange.
The investigation also uncovered photos, videos and conversations among defendants that prosecutors said documented the drug and gun trafficking conspiracy.
Ventura Amaro was among five people charged in June in connection with the network.
Prosecutors also said Ventura Amaro was kidnapped by alleged members of the Trinitarios in May 2024 after he took over drug distribution in parts of New Hampshire and Maine. Two Trinitarios members were charged in June 2025 in connection with that alleged kidnapping and are awaiting trial, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.
The drug conspiracy charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, at least three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $1 million.
The firearm conspiracy charge also carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, up to five years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000.

title: ‘She’s gone’: Foster family mourns baby girl found dead in dumpster as mother arrested
text:
LOS ANGELES (KCAL/KCBS) - The foster family of a woman who was arrested after police say her 4-month-old daughter was found dead in a Los Angeles dumpster are speaking out amid their grief.
The Los Angeles Police Department says a woman found a 4-month-old girl in a dumpster around 10:30 p.m. Monday outside a South Los Angeles housing project. The baby was taken to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
Laura Lacy believes the baby was her 4-month-old foster granddaughter Luna; though she is still waiting on the coroner to confirm her identity.
“She’s gone, but it’s OK. The Lord has her,” Lacy said through tears.
Lacy says she and her husband, Herman Johnson, raised Luna while allowing her 19-year-old foster daughter, Takiyah Babers, who is also the baby’s mother, to visit her. The couple were worried Babers was suffering from postpartum depression, Johnson says.
Johnson and his wife dropped off Luna with Babers at the housing project Monday.
“She called me yesterday, told me to drop the baby off. I should have just kept her, like I started to do, but that’s just a back thought. It’s a sad situation. The baby can’t protect herself. She was just an innocent little baby,” Johnson said.
Lacy says the couple were at their home in Inglewood when they saw the news and rushed over, fearing the worst. Then, they couldn’t find Luna.
At the start of the police investigation, the foster family stood together – until officers put Babers in handcuffs and led her away. Police say she was booked for murder.
Lacy says she believes Babers is responsible for what happened.
“Why would you throw her away? She didn’t do anything,” Lacy said. “What did you call me to bring her home for? Why would you call me... and then do this to her? I don’t believe this. I’m still in disbelief.”
Police say Babers’ bail was set at $2 million. The case will be presented to the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office for filing consideration.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: Fat Bear Week crowns its 2026 champion
text:
KATMAI, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - A bear who wasn’t supposed to make it to the final round of Fat Bear Week just carried the whole thing.
It was the 12th year of the popular Fat Bear Week tournament. During the tournament, the internet votes on which of the brown bears in Katmai National Park and Preserve did the best job getting enormous before winter.
A winner was crowned after polls closed Tuesday at fatbearweek.org.
Bear 89, better known as “Backpack,” was voted the 2026 Fat Bear Week champion. It came down to a margin of 5,091 votes, with Backpack beating Bear 910 by 103,344 votes to 98,253 to win the title.
It’s a fitting finish for a bear who spent much of Monday neck-and-neck with his competition.
In the semifinal, Backpack trailed Bear 164, nicknamed “Bucky,” for most of the day before surging ahead by roughly 3,000 votes.
Officials called it the tightest race they had seen in Fat Bear Week.
“This is the first time, this is unprecedented. We have never had a race this close,” Sarah Bruce, a park ranger with Katmai National Park and Preserve, said. “For most of the day, Bear 164 — nicknamed Bucky — he was ahead of 89. And so, I think some fans out there were campaigning hard for Bear 89 and were able to just get some votes in for him.
“This is the first time we’ve ever seen a bear come up from behind and win the semifinals.”
Backpack earned his nickname as a cub by riding on his mother’s back instead of swimming alongside her. His mother, Bear 435 “Holly,” won Fat Bear Week in 2019 but hasn’t been seen at the river in years.
Bear 89’s final opponent also came from a famous bloodline. Bear 910, the lone female in the final, is the daughter of former Fat Bear Week champion Bear 409, named “Beadnose.”
“She’s looking really good to be able to support another litter,” Bruce said. “That is really cool to see mama bears get really fat supporting their cubs.”
This year, it was the fans who came to the tournament hungry.
A crush of traffic overwhelmed the voting site on opening day, forcing Katmai to extend first-round voting.
“THE BEARS HAVE BROKEN THE INTERNET,” the park wrote on Facebook. “Literally.”
Explore.org, which hosts the tournament, said, “We had our biggest Day 1 turnout of all time and experienced some system overload.”
The organization later switched to a different platform ahead of the final.
“There are more polls this year. There’s more rounds of voting. There’s four more bears than we usually have,” Bruce said. “And even just comparing it poll to poll, the numbers have increased in an insane way that I don’t think anybody was expecting.”
The bracket was brutal from the start.
Last year’s champion, Bear 32, “Chunk,” lost to Bear 164 in the first round. It was a heavyweight clash that normally wouldn’t happen until much later in the tournament. Chunk entered this year still living with a completely broken mandible, a broken canine and broken front teeth. Rangers say he kept packing on weight anyway.
While the contest is light-hearted entertainment, the stakes for the bears are real. Katmai’s brown bears lose roughly a third of their body weight during hibernation. Bruce said that during their late-summer feeding frenzy, they can eat as much as 200,000 calories a day and gain up to two pounds daily.
“A fat bear is a successful bear,” Bruce said.
Fat Bear Week began in 2014 as a one-day Facebook event called “Fat Bear Tuesday,” drawing fewer than 1,700 votes.
Last year, more than 1.7 million votes came in from upward of 100 countries.
This year, the bears kept tipping the scales. Fans cast about 2.5 million votes across the tournament, according to results posted by explore.org, well above last year’s total.
“I don’t think anybody would have thought that this would happen,” Bruce said.

title: A new AI-powered helmet could transform firefighting
text:
A new AI-powered helmet could transform firefighting
A new artificial intelligence and augmented reality helmet, tested in Oklahoma City, is designed to help firefighters navigate through smoke, locate victims faster and improve safety during emergencies.
Moving in zero visibility and extreme heat with only seconds to find someone inside is the reality firefighters face when responding to burning buildings. The C-Thru system, developed by Qwake Technologies, uses AI and augmented reality to help firefighters see through smoke while also transmitting their visuals to commanders outside.
“If we have found a way to move a car through a city with all of the hazards, why have we not found a way to help a firefighter navigate to the screams of the baby in the back room?” said Sam Cossman, CEO of Qwake Technologies.
The Oklahoma City Fire Department was one of 30 fire departments nationwide selected for a Homeland Security field assessment of the technology. Victor Stagnaro, CEO of the National Fallen Firefighters Foundation, explained the system’s impact.
“It changes that equation. Search-and-rescue is roughly half the time than what it used to be using this technology. A shorter search means a shorter exposure,” Stagnaro said.
Cossman said 81% of firefighters in the assessment reported better orientation in zero-visibility conditions, and less experienced firefighters completed their primary searches faster.
Oklahoma City fire Chief Richard Kelley said testing technology like this is a critical part of their mission.
“We owe it to the residents that we serve every day. We have to do our best to be able to identify what is the best way to effect the rescue. What is the best way to save a life? What is the best way to make sure that that family member is reunited back with their loved ones? And we’ll do it at all costs to make that happen,” Kelley said.
The system has moved beyond testing and is now being used in real-world scenarios.
“We are very much at the beginning of this journey,” Cossman said.

title: Woman sues hospital over wrong-leg amputation: ‘Every day is a struggle’
text:
MARIETTA, Ohio (WTAP/Gray News) - An Ohio couple is suing a hospital and surgical team after a procedure they say resulted in the amputation of the wrong leg.
Sharon Jacks went to Selby General Hospital for an elective right-leg amputation below the knee. Surgeons instead amputated her left leg.
Lawsuit details allegations
According to the lawsuit, Sharon Jacks made the decision to have her right leg amputated below the knee because of cancer in that leg. The lawsuit’s general allegations section states that before surgery, the correct leg was checked off and marked.
“When Mrs. Jacks went in to have an elective right leg amputation below the knee because of cancer that she had in that leg, she made the tough decision. It wasn’t easy in and of itself to do that, and prior to the surgery, from what I can determine, everything was checked off as to the correct leg. It was marked the correct leg. Everything seemed to be in order,” said Brad Layne, the Jacks family attorney.
In September 2025, Sharon Jacks went in for a below-the-knee amputation for a chronic ulcer. The lawsuit states that documented safety timeouts were conducted twice during the procedure.
Life as a double amputee
Sharon Jacks and her husband, Dannie, are now dealing with the effects of her being a double amputee.
“You can imagine somebody that’s a double amputee now, there’s prosthetics, there’s transportation modifications, there’s housing modifications,” Layne said.
Dannie Jacks quit his job to take care of his wife.
“She certainly couldn’t be left home as a double amputee trying to manage property or manage their home that was not set up for that,” Layne said.
Layne said Sharon Jacks is an Army veteran, a determined and tough person.
“Every day is a struggle. She has to transport herself from a board to a wheelchair just to get to the bathroom or to get into the bed or to change clothes or to go anywhere,” Layne said.
Hospital response
Selby General Hospital issued a statement, calling the incident “an adverse surgical event.”
“Our proactive review of what took place confirmed this was an avoidable event, and that our expected operating room procedures were not followed. Those involved were held accountable for their actions and are no longer in their positions,” the hospital system said.
Exhibit 2, page 24 of the lawsuit states a wrongful-site amputation is a catastrophic, foreseeable and preventable patient safety event classified by the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations as a never event.

title: 3 high school football games to watch in Week 5
text:
This season, Varsity Maine reporters will offer up suggestions each week for three games that are worth a drive to watch in person, with a brief explanation of why we think these games are worth a fan’s time.
Portland (4-0) at Thornton Academy (4-0), 1 p.m. Saturday
The midway point of the season features a rematch of last year’s Class A championship game, which Thornton won, 28-0. In fact, these two teams have played in the past three Class A title games, with Thornton holding a 2-1 advantage. The Trojans, to no one’s surprise, are chugging along again in Class A South, scoring 45.5 points per game while allowing only seven per game. Quarterback Noah Fullerton has done well spreading the ball to multiple playmakers, like Quinn Cook and Logan LeBlanc. The defense, meanwhile, has two shutouts in the first four games.
Portland has answered any questions about potential growing pains under new head coach Dylan Rottkov. Even after the graduation of the program’s all-time scoring leader, Cordell Jones, the Bulldogs are averaging 34.8 points, featuring a rushing attack led by senior Alex Martin and sophomore David Gomes. The pair combined for over 300 yards in a 39-13 win over Windham on Sept. 18. Saturday’s game could be another a Class A final preview.
Cony (4-0) at Lawrence (4-0), 7 p.m. Friday
It’s air vs. ground in this rivalry matchup at Keyes Field in Fairfield, and the winner will earn a firm grasp on the No. 1 spot in the Class B North Crabtree standings.
Coach B.L. Lippert’s air attack offense is once again on display for Cony, which has averaged 30.5 points in the first four games. Junior quarterback Drew Lindquist (599 passing yards, 7 touchdown passes, 1 interception) has done well leading the offense in his first season as the starter, equally spreading the ball to seniors Landen Perry (14 receptions, 243 yards, 3 TDs) and Da’Marion Raymond (12 receptions, 139 yards, 2 TDs).
The Bulldogs are off to a hot start behind new head coach Pete Curtis. Nothing has changed in the offensive approach, as Lawrence has ridden its ground-and-pound attack to a 4-0 record. Keegan Littlefield (52 carries, 494 yards, 4 TDs), a senior, leads that attack, along with junior Jaiden Hebert (52 carries, 298 yards, 5 TDs) and senior Hunter Curtis (18 carries, 119 yards, 2 TDs).
This is always one of the best back-and-forth rivalries in central Maine. The Bulldogs knocked Cony out of the playoffs in 2023 (B North final) and 2024 (B North semifinal), and Cony beat Lawrence 46-14 during the regular season last year.
