title: Maine Air National Guard is a finalist to house a new, advanced air refueling wing
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Air National Guard is a finalist to house a new, advanced air refueling wing
The Bangor Air National Guard base is a finalist in the Air Force selection process as a potential location to house a new KC-46A air refueling squadron.
Senators Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Angus King, I-Maine, announced on Tuesday that Bangor is one of four finalists chosen from an initial field of 14 Air National Guard bases,
“This announcement from the Air Force is an important step toward equipping the MAINEiacs with the advanced aircraft they need to carry out their critical mission,” said Collins and King in a joint statement. “Bangor’s strategic location and the proven excellence of the 101st Air Refueling Wing make a compelling case for bringing the KC-46 to Maine. We will continue to press for Bangor’s selection as the selection process continues.”
There will now be more site analysis and evaluation of the four finalists and a decision about the preferred location for the KC-46A Main Operating Base 9 is expected in the second quarter of Fiscal Year 2027.
The other finalists are: Forbes Field Air National Guard Base in Topeka, Kansas; Key Field Air National Guard Base in Meridian, Mississippi; and McGhee Tyson Air National Guard Base in Alcoa, Tennessee.
If selected, Bangor would gain significantly more advanced refueling capabilities as the KC-46A Pegasus would replace, over time, the aging KC-135 Stratotankers currently assigned to the 101st Air Refueling Wing. The first aircraft would be expected to arrive in 2030.
In 2025, the Maine Air National Guard says the 101st Air Refueling Wing completed 780 flying missions with over 2,500 flying hours logged. The MAINEiacs moved over 1,200 personnel and approximately 230 airmen deployed.
The KC-46A Pegasus is larger than the KC-135 Stratotanker and uses a fly-by-wire boom controlled by an operator stationed in the forward cockpit utilizing a 3D camera-based Remote Vision System (RVS) as opposed to the traditional flying boom operated by a crew member lying prone in a rear windowed station utilized in the KC-135.
The KC-46A also has significant payload space and has a modern defensive suite, including an integrated threat-detection and self-defense suite (such as radar warning receivers and infrared countermeasures) to allow it to operate closer to contested airspace.

title: He worked to create a ‘normal’ life in Maine’s prisons. Now he’s stepping down.
text:
MAINE STATE PRISON — Two men in shorts and T-shirts stood on a walkway chatting on a clear Wednesday morning in September. Rows of flowers and carrots planted nearby soaked up the sun. Both men were out for a walk before work.
In separate cases in 1999 and 2009, these men were each convicted of murder. The bountiful gardens, personal laptops, permission for remote work and largely unsupervised time are all part of their lives at Maine State Prison. Barbed wire at the top of a fence was visible in the distance, but up close it appeared this conversation could’ve happened at any local park.
A lot has changed in Maine’s correctional system under the leadership of Randall Liberty, commissioner of Maine’s Department of Corrections, who walked up to the men wearing a tan suit.
“What’s going on, guys?” Liberty asked.
His dad served time in prison when Liberty was a child. That, combined with Liberty’s years in the military and law enforcement, formed his belief that people in prison should be treated with respect, life inside should be as normal as possible, and the main goal should be to rehabilitate.
Liberty traveled to Istanbul last year to promote these reforms, which he calls the Maine Model of Corrections. He recently hosted representatives from Israel, Ireland and Norway, and delegations from at least 14 states have come to see it in action.
The Brennan Center for Justice, a national, nonpartisan policy institute that is studying Maine’s prison system, said other states are right to look here as an example, and that Liberty’s attempt to spread the changes statewide is unique. The group issued a new report that calls Maine a “pioneer,” and says the results so far are promising, particularly in reducing violence among inmates and staff uses of force.
The model is widely respected within Maine, too, although people on both sides of the political aisle have questions about the results. Even Liberty acknowledged that for all the attention the Maine model is getting, the transformation from a system focused on punishment to one focused on rehabilitation is unfinished.
But he won’t be leading the charge to finish it.
Liberty, 62, will step down as commissioner on Oct. 1, shortly before Gov. Janet Mills, who appointed him, leaves office.
While Maine started some of the prison reforms before he took the helm, Liberty’s personal mark on the system is visible everywhere, like in a CBS national news segment this month in which Liberty donned a beekeeping suit in the state prison’s garden where inmates can learn the trade.
Brennan Center Justice Program director Ram Subramanian said he thinks Liberty has gotten people below him at the Department of Corrections on board with the vision, and he’s begun the difficult work of changing the culture among inmates themselves, whose buy-in is as important as the staff’s.
“I do hope it continues,” Subramanian said. “I hope they build on their successes.”
MUTUAL RESPECT
The Maine Model is built on the idea that being locked up for years is punishment enough. Once people are inside, the system should help address chronic problems in their lives and prepare them to be productive when they leave, since about 95% will walk out of the prison doors.
A culture of mutual respect among staff and inmates is essential, Liberty said, and acts as a kind of security system. He calls the people incarcerated in the eight state-run facilities he oversees “residents,” and said everyone should care about each other’s wellbeing.
As he led Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram journalists through the state prison this month, just a few staff watched over hundreds of inmates in the building where they played basketball and pickleball, lifted weights, spent time in the chapel and bought food at the commissary window.
Liberty uses every opportunity to enforce the culture he wants to see. Walking briskly by the weight room, an inmate made a flippant remark to a reporter about the quality of the food at the prison. Liberty, in mid-stride, pivoted to ask a staff member for the inmate’s name.
“That’s not how we act in this community,” Liberty said later. “If you’ve got a problem with the food, reach out to me. We’ll figure something out.”
Several inmates stopped the commissioner to ask about an issue and Liberty offered a way to follow up. One called the commissioner “brother” as they parted ways.
This culture may explain why there’s much less violence reported in the prisons. Between 2017-2024, rates fell by 36%, and those for staff use of force fell by 69%, the Brennan Center found.
Inmates told the researchers that violence was far less of a concern for them than it had been in prior years or in other facilities.
Brennan’s report said this is a key metric of success of a corrections system. Yet in most places, “immediate safety concerns and harsh punishment often take precedence,” the center wrote.
It may be one reason why Maine now has an easier time retaining corrections officers and filling positions in prisons than other states, but culture change takes time, Liberty acknowledged. In the Brennan Center survey, 41% of incarcerated men said staff did not treat inmates with respect. That’s 16 points better than a similar survey of prisoners in five other states the Urban Institute did last year, but still shows room for growth.
“It takes persistence to really move the needle,” Subramanian said.
DAD WAS INCARCERATED
When Liberty was just a kid, he visited his own father at the Maine State Prison. In his memoir published this year, “Liberty’s Prison: The Inmate’s Son Who Radically Reformed An American Prison,” co-written with freelance writer Christine Graf, they said the facility at the time was designed to “overwhelm inmates with feelings of ‘horror and remorse.’”
As recently as 2013, the Press Herald reported that staff, inmates and advocates called the prison’s culture “toxic,” and inmates were treated in a way that was “more punitive than rehabilitative.” A prison worker union representative said at the time, “No one wants to work in corrections.”
In part because of his dad, Liberty believes there are six root causes of incarceration: substance abuse, mental illness, poverty, neglect, educational deficiencies and trauma.
As described in the book, his dad checked at least four of those boxes and was arrested more times than anyone in the family can remember. Those stints in prison did not help his dad address the core of his problems.
When Liberty later worked for the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office, he went to crime scenes and saw hundreds of homes where, “I looked at those kids and, you know, that was me,” he said.
Society had let his family down in some respects, he said, especially during one winter when the family of four kids went without running water for three months because the pipes froze. Now thinking about the men and women in the state’s prisons, Liberty said, “All of the systems leading up to incarceration have failed them in one way or the other.”
“We’re the stop of last resort to help these people.”
He’s boosted substance use and mental health treatments in the prisons, and he’s not afraid to try new things. He pointed to what he considers the “gold standard” for the Maine model: a prison unit that looks almost like a college dorm with blue painted walls. Instead of staying for four years, though, inmates could be here for decades.
Dan Roberts, who’s served 21 years of a 55-year sentence for murder (which he said he is still appealing), leaned against the door to his room that has a single bed, a hand-painted mural and two small mounted televisions.
He said he keeps one always tuned to financial news channels so he can call his daughter and advise her on stock trades.
This area, which houses 25-30 people, used to be for solitary confinement. Inmates would exercise by walking in circles in a dog pen. Now it’s the opposite. They have an open kitchen, a long fish tank in the common area, and their own gym and showers. They can walk around the outdoor gardens where they can grow and pick their own food.
Inmates say those amenities are an incentive to behave well and give them a sense of purpose.
Liberty said he understands it can be surprising and hard to see someone convicted of murder living a somewhat “normal” life. He said after he talks to victims or their families they generally — but not always — support the Maine model’s reforms.
Some of the money inmates earn goes toward paying restitution. They also pay child support and cover some of the costs of their incarceration, which Liberty said improves public safety and accountability. Maine has done more around inmate remote work than any other state, according to the Alliance for Higher Education in Prison.
Another man who lives in the unit and was convicted of murder expects to leave prison in six years. The Press Herald is not naming him at the request of a member of the family of the person he killed, who said seeing him in this story could retraumatize the victim’s other family members.
The inmate said that with the money he’s earned working remotely, he recently bought a house.
“I’m just trying to set myself up for when I do get out,” he said. “Education, employment, stable housing — these are all things that help the recidivism rate drop.”
DISCONNECT ON THE GROUND
When Liberty took over as warden of the Maine State Prison in 2015 and then as commissioner in 2019, there was already some momentum for reform, said Subramanian from the Brennan Center. Corrections officials in various states have embraced the idea that prison shouldn’t necessarily be a horrible place, he said.
Maine stands out for its push to expand reforms to all of its prisons and as many inmates as possible, he said. Currently, 170 inmates in Maine are full-time college students, 12 are graduate students, and four are PhD candidates, Liberty said. Others learn woodworking, upholstery, welding or culinary skills, and get trained as commercial drivers or to work in hospitality.
Liberty said opportunities to work, study, and have computers need to grow in order for more of Maine’s approximately 2,100 inmates to get access.
Foster Bates is president of the state prison’s NAACP branch and has been incarcerated for 25 years serving a life sentence for a murder he maintains he did not commit. He said in an interview this spring that he appreciates the programs at the state prison, but that it can be hard to take advantage of them because some are restricted to a few dozen people, and because of lock-ins in the prison.
“Residents here don’t have a problem with the policy. We have an issue with the disconnect of how it’s being implemented,” Bates said.
“It’s challenging for some who are incarcerated to have a perspective of where we are nationally, where Maine was 10 years ago, and where Maine is today,” Liberty said. “Prison isn’t an easy experience regardless of how many opportunities they have.”
The Department of Corrections did not provide lock-in data, but said there has been a reduction.
Bates said he wished Liberty wouldn’t retire. “He’s leaving behind a legacy that can be built upon, but I think it could be destroyed,” he said.
Gubernatorial candidates Democrat Hannah Pingree and Republican Bobby Charles did not answer questions about how they would approach corrections. Independent Rick Bennett said he supports the Maine Model and that rehabilitation and humane treatment belong in the corrections system.
Areas for improvement documented by the Brennan Center include access to healthcare, which got particularly low marks from incarcerated women; the process for inmates to file grievances; and the system’s capacity to prepare people for release.
Just 10% of incarcerated men and 2% of women told the Brennan Center that the facility they’re in does a good job at preparing people to leave. Liberty said he wants to see Maine put more money toward transitional housing.
Still, recidivism is down under his leadership. The Brennan Center noted an 8% drop between people released in 2014 and 2022, the most recent year data is available, though the researchers said it will take more time to know for sure if it’s because of the reforms.
“These initial results show what prison officials and systems can accomplish with limited budgets amid shifting political winds,” the report said. In a sign of Liberty’s cooperation with the study, he’s scheduled to do a presentation with Brennan’s staff in Belfast, Ireland, in October.
State Senator Scott Cyrway, the top Republican on the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee, said he has “a lot of respect” for Liberty, whom he served with at the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office. The senator commended the culture Liberty has been able to foster in the prisons.
But Cyrway is skeptical of the results the Maine Model has produced. He thinks reductions in recidivism could be because Maine has recently made some conduct that used to be criminal into civil offenses. He worries the focus is being taken off of accountability, and he wants to see more support for drug addiction before people are released from prison.
Though his tenure is up on Oct. 1, Liberty is not going far. He plans to work three days a week for Amend, a prison reform program under the University of California San Francisco. In that capacity, he’ll still be leading tours of Maine’s prisons for people from other states and countries.
He’ll also focus on improving access to education, remote work and internet for inmates in Maine, without having to do the administrative duties that come with being commissioner.
“This will allow me to focus on those things I think really make a difference,” he said.
But it also means he’ll no longer be the guy calling the shots.
“In the last eight years, I’ve been hiring people that are like minded, believe in redemption and are forward thinking,” Liberty said. “It’s time for people behind me to step up.”

title: Ellsworth picks 3 adult-use cannabis vendors nearly 2 years after voter approval
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nearly two years after Ellsworth voters approved allowing adult-use cannabis stores, the city is inching closer to the opening of three retail shops along the High Street corridor.
Following a June lottery draw, the city awarded three businesses conditional approval to set up adult-use cannabis shops. Construction is underway for at least two of the stores, according to a city permit document.
The lottery came after a two-year process in which city staff and councilors weighed how to permit retail marijuana stores. Much of the discussion revolved around how to establish adult-use cannabis shops while preserving Ellsworth’s family-oriented character.
JAR Cannabis Co., which has 10 stores across Maine, one of which is limited to medical patients only, and Lighthouse Cannabis Co. were awarded adult-use approval. JAR’s Ellsworth location at 59 Downeast Highway, scheduled to open in early 2027, will be its northernmost site.
Lighthouse submitted two applications under separate limited liability companies — with identical addresses — both of which were selected in the draw. Tim Pease, the city attorney, said the city’s adult-use ordinance allows family members to submit separate applications, according to the Ellsworth American weekly newspaper.
Not all councilors were in favor of the prolonged process. Councilor Steven O’Halloran, a frequent City Hall critic, thought the licenses should have been awarded within 6 months of the referendum. He opposed the city’s lottery system, arguing there should be no limitations on the number of shops allowed in Ellsworth.
“I was not in favor of any cannabis stores but, during the referendum of ‘24, the general public voted 55 percent to have recreational marijuana,” O’Halloran told the Bangor Daily News Wednesday. “Therefore, it doesn’t matter what I want. However, I am very upset with the process they have come up with. If we’re going to have them, I believe the government should stay out of business and let the free market figure it out.”
The adult-use licensing fee has been set at $10,000, according to city officials. O’Halloran strongly objects to any such fee.
JAR co-founder Joel Pepin said the fee was on the higher end for other municipalities his businesses operate in, but there are other cities that charge even more.
The city is expected to consider the final licenses at its Dec. 21 meeting, according to Amy Kenney, the city’s communications director.
“Following the November 2024 referendum, the city needed to develop the local regulatory framework necessary to implement the voters’ decision,” Kenney said in a statement describing the many administrative hurdles in place. “Developing and adopting those regulations takes time, and staff worked carefully, diligently through the required public and legal processes to establish a clear framework before licenses could be issued.”
Although Ellsworth’s first retail marijuana store will likely open more than two years after the 2024 voter referendum, the city’s drawn-out process is not unique.
“We’ve been doing this for a long time and have seen firsthand that creating local cannabis regulations can be a complicated process, particularly for communities doing it for the first time,” JAR co-founder Joel Pepin said in a statement Wednesday to the BDN. “We’ve seen other Maine towns spend years working through their local rules before allowing adult-use businesses. I understand why municipalities want to take the time to get it right.”
JAR, founded in 2011 by three Maine friends, purchased the Route 1 location — which formerly housed Mike’s Country Store — and is now remodeling the site. Following construction, the store will go through the city’s final approval process, including a review by the code enforcement department, Pepin said.
It was not immediately clear if the adult-use Lighthouse store in Brewer is connected to the Ellsworth applications. The Brewer shop did not respond to multiple inquiries Wednesday from the BDN.
Colt and Summer Sleight, who are listed under the Lighthouse applications, did not respond Wednesday to inquiries from the BDN.
One of the Lighthouse locations will be at Maine Coast Mall, while its other site could be at 403 High Street, according to license applications submitted to the city and shared with the BDN. The sites are roughly a mile from each other.
As the three stores navigate the city’s bureaucratic approval process, the owner of one of Maine’s largest medical cannabis chains, Frank Berenyi of Marijuanaville, is suing Ellsworth over his springtime bid to set up shop on Main Street.
The administrative appeal followed a monthslong saga between Ellsworth city councilors, staff and Berenyi, who was denied a business license twice between February and April. The denials came shortly after products at Berenyi’s Waterville store tested positive for pesticides.
Berenyi’s appeal is still pending in Hancock County Superior Court. A judge extended a filing deadline for the cannabis businessman to Nov. 30 after the city failed to produce documents responsive to a May Freedom of Access Act request by Berenyi that he sought for his legal arguments.

title: Maine employers say they need workers, so why is it hard to find a good job?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Trust for Local News wanted to get a sense of how people feel about living and working in Maine. So, we commissioned a survey to find out. Over the next few weeks, we’ll be exploring the results and hearing from dozens of people who participated. You can read all about it here.
Sheila Richardson has been hanging wallpaper since her youngest was in seventh grade. She learned the skill from her grandmother and her father, then grew it into a successful business with a broad customer base near her home in Turner — all by word of mouth.
“I take pride in my work,” she said. “I don’t have to advertise.”
Now 78 and a great-grandmother, she’s still working 35 years later, despite some health issues that cropped up last year.
“I’m up and down the ladder a hundred times a day,” she said. “I’m a doer. I don’t depend on anybody else.”
Richardson’s tenacity is serving her well these days, as rising costs for materials and fuel, and a shifting economic landscape make it more challenging to work or do business in Maine.
She is one of 824 Mainers who responded to a survey conducted in July by the Siena Research Institute for the Maine Trust for Local News. It found that the job market is daunting for many across the state — 51% of respondents rated their ability to get suitable employment as “only fair” or “poor,” while 41% rated their ability to make a living wage as “not very likely” or “not at all likely.”
Asked whether they could get a job with opportunities for advancement, 32% said it was “almost certain” or “very likely,” but 27% said it was “not very likely” or “not at all likely” and 39% said it was a toss-up.
The Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram interviewed a variety of people across the state who participated in the 62-question survey. While they see some bright spots, Richardson and others say workers and businesses face increasing economic headwinds.
Richardson has been working all her life, really, running a household with four kids, helping her husband with his excavation, wood harvesting and auto repair businesses, scrimping and saving to make ends meet when times got hard.
Social Security has eased her need to work, she said, but her healthcare savings are dwindling despite Medicare. She and her husband own the ranch-style home they built themselves, but it needs a new roof, and that’s going to be costly.
She sees others struggling, too, including her son, who has his own construction and excavation business, she said. Record-high diesel prices are eating up narrow profit margins.
“It’s terribly tough right now,” Richardson said. “The price of everything has gone up and you have to charge customers what it costs. You really have to pinch pennies when you don’t have money coming in.”
SHADOW OF UNCERTAINTY
In reviewing the survey results, Maine State Economist Amanda Rector said she was surprised that only 32% of respondents were positive about the potential for job advancement, especially since Maine has a worker shortage and its rapidly aging population is expected to increase retirements.
“Responses may have been overshadowed by near-term uncertainties,” Rector said, including rising costs that have led some businesses to throttle hiring and consider downsizing if artificial intelligence is used in the workplace.
She also noted significant regional differences in views of the job market — 51% of Southern/Coastal respondents (Cumberland and York counties) said they could get suitable employment, and 38% saw potential for workplace advancement. Responses in other regions were even lower.
Rector said that’s not surprising. “That’s where a lot of economic activity is in the state,” she said.
Respondents showed similar regional trends when asked whether Maine is a place where businesses can succeed — 46% rated the business climate positively, while 52% said it’s only “fair” or “poor.” Looking at that question regionally, 57% of Southern/Coastal participants had a positive response, with significantly lower rates in other areas where business owners say they’re facing tough economic conditions.
Rector also pointed out that the survey shows strong recognition — 75% statewide — of Maine’s access to affordable adult education and job training. Both have been bolstered in recent years by the state’s community colleges, building contractors, defense contractors and the U.S. Small Business Administration.
“It’s good to see that has such a strong positive response,” she said.
LACK OF RELIABLE WORKERS
Workforce training is helping Alex Thibodeau meet some of the challenges facing Maine’s manufacturing sector, including rising costs and logistical drawbacks of being at the end of the line geographically.
Thibodeau is director of operations at Kenway Composites, an Augusta company with 50 employees that makes fiber-reinforced plastic storage tanks and other equipment for heavy industry, public infrastructure and military uses.
In recent years, Thibodeau has hired seven students from the composites manufacturing program at the Foster Career and Technical Education Center in Farmington that serves several area high schools.
“They are some of our best employees,” said Thibodeau, 59. “Technical training is one of the only salvations for manufacturers who need workers. (The training programs) are so underrated and deserve more funding going forward.”
Still, a lack of reliable workers has forced Thibodeau to turn away about $2 million in contracts in recent years, he said. His hiring expectations are pretty basic — show up every day, be willing to learn and do quality work — but he’s often disappointed, despite offering benefits, bonuses and pay ranging from $23 to $35 an hour depending on the job, he said.
Recent tariffs, inflation, higher interest rates and rising fuel prices have increased the cost of procuring materials, having them delivered to Maine and transporting goods to customers, he said. Truck deliveries now come with fuel surcharges. Tariffs on one part needed for a government contract increased the price from $80,000 to $130,000.
“We as taxpayers end up paying for that,” Thibodeau said. “One of Maine’s greatest struggles is our location. Most of the truck traffic is outbound, so you have to pay for the trip in. We are disadvantaged in a lot of ways already. We don’t need additional costs.”
STARK DIFFERENCES STATEWIDE
Thibodeau’s experience and the survey’s findings align with aspects of a Maine State Chamber of Commerce goals report released this year in advance of the 2026 gubernatorial election, said Patrick Woodcock, chamber CEO.
Economic headwinds that have pummeled Maine for years have been exacerbated by recent federal policies that have increased costs and threaten to worsen the workforce shortage, he said, including immigration enforcement activities.
In reviewing the survey results, Woodcock noted that while 57% of respondents in the Southern/Coastal region said Maine is a place where businesses can be successful, 58%-60% of respondents in the rest of the state said the exact opposite.
“I found that gap to be pretty stark,” he said. “Some pessimism has taken root. There are distinct challenges between the regions, and we have to recognize and respect those differences.”
Woodcock also noted that 85% of respondents across the state said the lack of affordable housing is a problem.
“Housing has overwhelmed a lot of Maine families,” he said. “Our members have identified affordable housing as a workforce issue. We cannot attract workers, foster economic growth and have a robust business climate without addressing affordable housing.”
On the upside, Woodcock said, Maine businesses are resilient, with an uptick in recent retail sales corroborating anecdotal feedback that this summer was a fairly strong tourism season. He noted that lodging receipts increased 12.8% in July compared to 2025, and restaurants experienced 6.8% growth, according to the latest state sales tax reports.
THE GOOD AND NOT SO GOOD
Nathan Gurtman agrees — it was a successful summer for many businesses in Maine’s hospitality industry. A chef at the York Harbor Inn, he has worked in area kitchens for 30 years.
“It was a good season,” said Gurtman, 50. “We were booked up with plenty of events and functions and our daily business was good.”
But the inn has been affected by rising costs like every other business, he said. Whether ordering special ingredients from outside Maine or fresh produce from nearby farms, food prices and delivery fees are going up.
“We make everything from scratch,” Gurtman said. “We’ve definitely seen price fluctuations due to what’s going on because fuel is more expensive, insurance is more expensive, everything related to doing business is more expensive. At the same time, we’re trying to keep our quality up and our prices reasonable.”
Despite the challenges, Gurtman said he wouldn’t want to live anywhere else. A native Mainer, he has vacationed in western Maine all his life, visits Acadia National Park at least twice a year, and swims several times a week at beaches near his home in York.
He doesn’t mind the tourist traffic that takes over Memorial Day through Labor Day because it pays the bills — for him, the town and the state.
“I understand why people come here,” he said. “I live it. I don’t take it for granted.”
Zack Gauley, 28, is on the flip side of that experience. A California native, he lives in Rumford, in western Maine, with his girlfriend, who has a job in manufacturing. He has worked seasonal jobs in the skiing and commercial fishing industries for the last five years, he said.
This year, however, his $15.10-an-hour minimum wage job making snow and running chairlifts at Black Mountain Ski Resort kept him working into spring, then he was let go, he said. At that point, the fishing boats he had worked on in the past were all crewed up.
A high school graduate, Gauley has applied for jobs at local gas stations, grocery stores and fast-food restaurants without luck, he said. He plans to expand his search to manufacturing jobs that might pay more and include job training.
“I’m dismayed with a lot of things, but I just have to apply myself a little more,” he said. “I just hope I can get a job as soon as possible, and then I can get a better job and build a life for me and my girlfriend.”

title: ‘I need help’: Restaurant staff shields and protects woman from man following her on walk
text:
MONONA, Wis. (WMTV/Gray News) - A Wisconsin woman says a routine evening walk along Monona’s Lake Loop quickly escalated into a frightening situation.
Carly Major was out walking with her dog last Saturday evening when she said she noticed a man approaching her who then began to follow her.
Major was about to make her way home but immediately changed her path when this stranger suddenly appeared behind her so she wouldn’t lead him back to her front door.
“I turned around and noticed after about half a block that he started following me,” Major said. “So I diverted my course away from my home toward the courtyard around Buck & Honey’s [restaurant].”
As Major crossed the waterway, the situation escalated. She said the man took off his shirt and ran across four lanes of traffic, attempting to cut off her route.
Scared, Major ran directly into Buck & Honey’s restaurant to seek refuge.
“I need help. I am being followed,” Major said as she entered.
Inside the Monona restaurant, an all-woman crew working that shift immediately jumped into action outside of any typical job description.
Moments later, the man walked through the front doors, asking employees for Major and her dog.
Staff members immediately formed a protective barrier, blocking his view, directing him out of the building and contacting 911.
“I was immediately taken to a place of safety where I could not be seen outside, and I just received so much support from the staff,” Major said.
Buck & Honey’s manager, Katie Leiter, said her team reacted purely out of protective instinct.
“It was like everybody was going to their battle stations. Everybody was doing their part to make sure that this guy was not going to hurt anyone,” Leiter said. “I had one of my servers run down to the park to warn a woman who was down there by herself to make sure that she was safe too.”
Staff members stayed by Major’s side, even offering their shift meals, water for both her and her dog, and a ride home.
“I love my staff and seeing them behave instinctively this way was just heartwarming,” Leiter added. “They’re amazing people, and they did the right thing.”
The Monona Police Department confirmed officers were dispatched to the restaurant last Saturday night for a report of a suspicious person following Major.
Officers ended up making contact with the man in question. Police noted he showed signs of mental illness and was driven away from the area.
For Major, the relief of having complete strangers step up in a moment of vulnerability is something she says she will carry forever.
“I have strangers that don’t know me that care about me. And knowing that people really do have each other’s backs and care means everything,” Major said.

title: Christa Gail Pike says ‘I am not afraid to die’ in letter written before execution was halted by federal court
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - In a letter written before Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee denied her clemency and before a federal court issued a stay in her Wednesday execution, Christa Gail Pike said she is not afraid to die.
Pike is the only woman on Tennessee’s death row and would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in at least 200 years.
EN ESPAÑOL | ‘No tengo miedo de morir’: Christa Gail Pike ante ejecución en Tennessee
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit issued an order Wednesday morning staying Pike’s execution “until further order of this court.”
“The court has stayed this recognizing the serious concerns about Christa’s scheduled execution,” Stephen Ferrell of the Federal Defenders Services of Eastern Tennessee said.
Pike was found guilty in 1996 of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer on the University of Tennessee campus.
Pike, along with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, planned Slemmer’s torture and killing. The case later became known as the Job Corps Murder because both Pike and Slemmer were members of Job Corps at the time.
“I would like to extend my gratitude to everyone who has supported me through these hard days,” the letter reads. “I’ve felt more love in the last two weeks than I have my entire life.”
Since Pike’s trial ended, she and her legal team have tried to change her sentence. Pike has also been supported by activist groups that oppose the death penalty, which is something she references in the letter.
“When my people showed up for me- they have showed [SIC] up and showed out!” she said. “I am humbled beyond words.”
Her petition for clemency was not granted, with Lee confirming Monday that he would not step in to keep Pike alive past her execution date.
“Whether my clemency is granted or not, I am at peace,” the letter reads. “I am not afraid to die. I am only nervous about the process.”
Pike is not the only one to have concerns about Tennessee executions. The state’s death penalty has faced scrutiny after botched executions prompted a pause from Lee. The attempted Tennessee execution of Tony Carruthers was abandoned in May after medical staff failed to establish IV access, a process that took over an hour.
Mark Fowler, the doctor who was involved in Carruthers’ attempted execution, will oversee Pike’s death sentence.
In August, Anthony Darrell Hines was put to death at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville for the 1985 murder of Catherine Jean Jackson Jenkins.
In her letter, Pike also said the public had only seen a “limited persona” of her, rather than her “true character.”
She has long been the subject of media reports and faced the court of public opinion for decades.
Pike was scheduled to be executed Wednesday morning.

title: Letter: Susan Collins has to leave the Senate sometime. Why not now?
text:
Multimillion-dollar digital advertisements tout Susan Collin’s work bringing federal funds to Maine. Let’s take a look. Defense funds, especially the big one at Bath Iron Works, would mostly be coming to Maine no matter who are our senators as the Navy needs to keep two shipyards building DDGs. And BIW has not been successful in competing for other federal contracts.
Let’s look at the future if Collins continues in the Senate. It’s likely she could be voting for two Supreme Court justices in the wake of her vote for Brett Kavanaugh. Her role as the Appropriations Committee chair would likely either be ignored by the Trump administration, as it largely has been, or be rubber stamping new war monies or tariffs. There will be no Medicare for All.
I believe she would be another enabler of the damage that President Donald Trump has done to our domestic economy and foreign policy. If Trump loses the Senate, I believe she will be largely relegated to the sidelines, no matter her seniority.
In the years after 2028, if Trump and his backers are defeated, she could spend the next four years as an ineffectual voice. If they are not, she would likely be honored and ignored, like other senators over the age of 80.
Maine is going to have to lose the seniority that it has built in Congress. I think it’s time to do it now, before any more damage can be done. Let’s start getting our new representation by electing the only real working-class senator, Troy Jackson.
Ben Fuller
Cushing

title: The scaffolding at Portland’s Trelawny Building is finally coming down
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After three years of headaches for tenants — and yet another lawsuit between the city and landlord Geoffrey Rice — the scaffolding at the Trelawny Building in downtown Portland is coming down.
According to Greg Shinberg of Shinberg Consulting, which has been managing the project, the scaffolding at 655 Congress St. should be completely removed within the next week to 10 days, weather dependent. After that, crews will use a lift to conduct repair work on the first two floors and the job will be complete.
As of Tuesday, about one-third of the scaffolding had been taken down, revealing the restored façade that was required by the city and its historic preservation office in 2023 after chunks of masonry began crumbling into the street.
Built in 1907, the building is located in the Congress Street Historic District and is subject to historic preservation code requirements.
The initial order from the city gave Rice one year to complete permanent fixes to bring it up to code, which was then extended to October 2025. At the time of the extension, in December 2024, Shinberg told staff that the project would be complete in six to eight months.
That same month, the city issued a notice of violation “based on the failure of the property owner to complete the work within the time frame set.” In a December 2025 update, Shinberg said the project was expected to be completed in mid-2026.
Shinberg said Tuesday that the project has been complicated but that he’s proud of the work that’s been done. He said the safety of workers and residents has been the number one concern throughout.
He said replacing the windows will be a second phase, but that Shinberg will likely not be involved.
Ahead of the initial court hearing in June, the building’s tenants’ union and its ground-floor business tenant said the ongoing work had created conditions that caused people to move out. A salon tenant closed and moved, and the owner of the Green Hand Bookshop said the work had been detrimental to her business.
Michelle Souliere, the store’s owner, said Wednesday that the “scaffolding barricade” coming down “will bring a much-needed breath of fresh air and freedom to the neighborhood.”
“Hopefully the heavy losses incurred during this ordeal will serve as a lesson to the city that accountability extends beyond paperwork and loopholes, and reminds them that hundreds if not thousands of Portlanders have encountered detrimental living and working conditions that could have been mitigated much earlier had better city oversight and community involvement been part of the original plan,” she said.
The city’s notice of violation told Rice that the violations could carry monetary penalties in an amount not less than $100 per day, per violation, and that penalties would be assessed beginning Oct. 14, 2025, and would continue to accrue until all violations are remedied.
City spokesperson Jessica Grondin said attorneys for the city and Rice are scheduled for a status conference on Nov. 6.
Rice, who owns dozens of properties in Portland, has faced a number of previous violations of the city’s rent control ordinance. In March, a Superior Court judge affirmed a 2025 ruling of the Portland rent board that required Rice to refund tenants he overcharged and pay $170,500 in fines.

title: How much a home equity sharing agreement could cost you
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How much a home equity sharing agreement could cost you
Key takeaways
- Home equity sharing agreements (HEAs) are costly and financially risky, requiring homeowners to give up a portion of their home’s future value for a lump-sum payment.
- Also known as home equity investments (HEIs), these products are an alternative for homeowners with poor credit or those who may not qualify for traditional home equity loans or HELOCs.
- These agreements are extremely complicated, with each company having its own formula and rules to determine how much the homeowner ultimately pays — and very little consumer protections for homeowners.
- You pay the investors after the home is sold or at the end of the 10- or 30-year period, which can add up to hundreds of thousands of dollars
They give you cash today, but you may not realize what it will cost you tomorrow.
Home equity sharing agreements (HEAs) offer a lump sum in exchange for a share of your home’s future value and are pitched to homeowners who may not qualify for a traditional HELOC or home equity loan. Also known as home equity investments (HEIs), these companies boast no monthly payments, no income requirements and no need for perfect credit. With homeowners collectively holding a record $35.8 trillion in equity as of the second quarter of 2026, what may sound like an attractive alternative to access that wealth is anything but.
Not only are the contracts incredibly complex, but homeowners also lack many of the same consumer protections they find with traditional home equity products, like HELOCs. The primary reason is that these 10- to 30-year agreements are characterized as investments, not loans.
At the end of the contract, you may owe tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars if your home goes up in value. Even a decline in your home’s value doesn’t mean you will be walking away owning nothing. The only way to pay them is to come up with a huge amount of cash, refinance your mortgage or sell your home.
“That’s really what we’re worried about, that this could be another subprime crisis,” says Andrew Pizor, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center (NCLC). “People get these now, and in 10 to 30 years, depending on how long they keep it, all of a sudden they’re going to have to make these big balloon payments. People aren’t going to be thinking about it until they have reason to need to pay. If somebody decides they want to sell their home, they want to move in retirement, they get a payoff estimate, and they’re shocked.”
Types of home equity sharing agreements
There are two common types of home equity sharing agreements. In both cases, you receive a lump sum from your investor or lender. The difference is how they get compensated.
Share of appreciation model
With this model, you’re obligated to repay the home equity sharing company your initial loan amount, plus a predetermined percentage of your home’s future appreciation, if any.
Some companies require repayment of the original investment amount plus a percentage of the appreciated value. On a home worth $450,000, let’s say you receive $75,000. The contract says the company will receive 25% of your home’s future appreciation in 10 years, on top of its original investment. So if your home appreciated in value by $150,000, you’d need to repay a total of $112,500 — [$150,000 x 0.25%] + $75,000 — at the end of the decade.
Share of home value model
With this model, instead of repaying the original lump sum you receive, you just pay a percentage of the home’s value at sale. So, if your home declines in value, the percentage you’ll pay to the investor will decrease; you could even pay back less than your original loan.
Using our example from above, let’s say your home is now worth $600,000 (after appreciating in value by $150,000). If your agreement requires you to give the company 20% of your home’s total worth, you’d owe $120,000.
How does a home equity sharing agreement work?
Unlike a traditional mortgage or HELOC, home equity agreements give a homeowner a lump sum in exchange for your home’s value. Equity sharing agreements often have terms ranging from 10 to 30 years. While you won’t have to make monthly payments, you do have to pay the investor back at the end of the contract.
“It’s not a traditional 30-year amortizing loan with monthly payments, an installment loan, but it’s definitely a loan,” says Pizor. “The reason they argue it’s not a loan is a legal trick. Buried in the contract, they say they’re actually buying an option to participate in the ownership. They say at maturity, we might not exercise the option if your property value goes down. In practice, that’s not true, because the way the contracts are structured, you’d need a huge catastrophe for that not to be worth it to them to exercise the option.”
How do you qualify for a home equity sharing agreement?
You typically don’t have to jump through as many hoops to qualify for an home equity agreement as you would with a HELOC or home equity loan. But that should be viewed as a warning sign, not a benefit.
Most HEI companies won’t consider your debt-to-income ratio, and your minimum credit score can be as low as 500. But the biggest factor in your approval may be the home itself.
Often, you’ll need a greater amount of equity in your home, about 20% to 40%. The companies have their calculations to determine how much the homes may appreciate in value. However, they often lowball or “risk-adjust” your home’s appraisal value to compensate, so it’ll always seem like the home has appreciated to some degree.
“That’s their business model,” says Pizor. “They only make money if the property goes up in value a lot. As far as we can tell, they’re not going to be marketing in a community and not going to approve a loan in a community if their AVMs (automated valuation models) suggest that it’s either going to go down in the future or just basically not go up enough.”
The legality of home equity investments
At the heart of the debate is whether HEIs are loans disguised under different names that allow companies to sidestep traditional lending rules and consumer protections. HEI companies have faced lawsuits alleging they sold predatory and deceptive products. While Pennsylvania and North Carolina officials debate the future of HEIs, Maryland, Connecticut, and Illinois are among the states that have passed regulations characterizing the products as loans. Some of the passed regulations include additional payoff disclosures, payment caps or a requirement that consumers seek counseling before entering an agreement.
Risks of home equity sharing agreements
Before signing home equity sharing agreements, homeowners need to understand what they are giving up in return and what obligations could follow them for years.
Contract terms can be complicated
At the heart of the HEI agreement is that you are giving up a share of your home’s future value in exchange for a lump sum. However, there’s no standard industry practice on how HEI companies calculate that lump sum or how much your home is worth.
One company may determine your payout either by looking at the total value of the home or how much the value has changed. Another may take the appraised value of the home, then discount it and come up with a risk-adjusted “starting property value.” The formula for figuring the company’s return can be complex too.
“Your house would have to go down, depending on which company, 15% to 25% in value over several years for them to totally lose money and for you not to owe anything,” says Pizor. “That just doesn’t happen in the American housing market.”
You may face restrictions
With an HEA, the company has a financial stake in your home, and that can come with certain conditions.
Depending on the company, it may put a lien on your house. If you can’t pay the agreement back, there is a risk of foreclosure. The investment company might not be a completely silent partner, either. You typically need approval from the HEI company before renting out, selling the home or refinancing your existing mortgage. Additionally, you might also be charged a fee for that refinance.
Also, HEIs “follow the title,” not the borrower. That means if you die with the agreement still in place, anyone who inherits the home inherits the agreement too. Though not personally liable, they will have to settle the lien by paying it in full or selling the home, which could put them in a tough position.
You may lack consumer protections
HEI providers argue their products are not loans but investments and are not bound by the same rules as traditional lenders. Legislation like the Truth in Lending Act and the Dodd-Frank Act, designed to protect consumers from predatory practices, don’t apply. In short, you won’t get the protections that typically come with a traditional home loan.
“The Dodd-Frank Act said you cannot put a forced arbitration clause into a mortgage, which means consumers have the right to go to court if there’s a dispute over the terms of the mortgage,” says Pizor. “These [HEI] agreements have arbitration clauses. So if you want to go to court, dispute it, break the contract, and say ‘I was deceived,’ you get forced into arbitration most of the time.”
The differences don’t stop there.
Under TILA’s Regulation Z, mortgage lenders are required to make a good faith determination of a borrower’s ability to repay a loan by evaluating their income, assets and employment. But HEI providers sidestep those rules because their products are characterized as investments, not loans, in most states.
What companies offer home equity sharing agreements?
You won’t find home equity sharing agreements through banks or other traditional mortgage lenders. Some of the biggest companies include:
- Hometap
- Point
- Splitero
- Unison
- Unlock
As of April 2025, the top-five HEI originators were collectively originating around $600 million a month, according to Home Equity Lending News. The industry is growing as more companies expand their reach across the country and package these investments to sell to institutional investors.
How much does a home equity sharing agreement cost?
Home equity sharing agreements often come with a list of upfront fees, like transaction fees, origination fees, title fees, escrow fees and recording fees, along with the home appraisal. But these aren’t the main costs you should be most concerned about.
After the appraisal, some lenders may apply a risk adjustment to your home’s value. This figure is what the investor uses to calculate the sum they’ll give you and your home’s appreciation at payout time.
For example, Unison’s risk adjustment is 5% of the home’s starting value. If your home appraises for $500,000, the risk-adjusted value would be $475,000, a $15,000 difference. With Point, the adjustment is 27%, putting your starting value at $365,000. That’s $135,000 below your home’s value.
This risk adjustment means that, under the agreement, you may get less value out of your home’s equity than they’d thought. Whether your home rises or falls in value, you will have to pay out more to the investment company at the agreement’s end. That’s even with rate caps that limit how fast the repayment amount can grow.
“They’re a lot like subprime mortgages. They have a big balloon payment at the end,” says Pizor. “Imagine you’re going to get a mortgage and someone says, ‘There’s only one payment at the end. I can’t tell you what the payment is and what the interest rate is until [then].’ That’s kind of what these are like.”
Some companies also tack on multipliers, which give them a larger percentage of the home’s value than the homeowner initially accessed. Even if you try to repay the entire amount you owe before the contract ends, you may have no choice but to dip into savings, refinance your mortgage or seek financing from a lender.
Often, “there’s realistically little way to make the payment. No one knows the value your home is going to be,” says Pizor. “They say maybe some time in the future, maybe when you sell, you might owe something, and we don’t know what it is.”
When does a home equity sharing agreement make sense?
For most homeowners, the answer is almost never.
The type of borrower who might want an HEI is one who doesn’t qualify for traditional home equity financing, like home equity loans or HELOCs. But these agreements are an expensive way to get cash. You’re giving an investor a claim to your home’s future appreciation, which could add up to tens of thousands of dollars, if not more. Also, the agreements are extremely complicated. They lack the regulations you will find with some other lending options.
Before considering a home equity sharing agreement, look at these alternatives:
- Home equity loans allow you to borrow against your home equity, receive a lump sum, and repay the loan with fixed monthly payments over a set period
- HELOCs — home equity lines of credit — give you a borrowing limit and allow you to take money out as needed. Both home equity loans and HELOCs use your home as collateral.
- Personal loans don’t put your home on the line but can have higher interest rates — and less flexibility — than with home-secured loans.
Yes, you’ll have to pay interest for all these options, and they have higher credit standards, but the amount will be less than the appreciation you pay the shared-equity investor. Even if your home appreciates significantly, you may end up paying more in the long run than you would for a traditional home equity product.
“They’re hiding a lot of strings; that’s the problem,” says Pizor. “You’ve probably met a lot of people whose credit is worse than it is. They could shop around for a credit union and get a loan but just end up with something bad because they haven’t looked around. The other side of that is, if your financial situation is really that bad and you can’t get an affordable loan, what’s the long-term ability to keep your house? Maybe this is the time to sell, rather than taking on debt.”
If you are still convinced an HEI is the best for you, make sure you read the fine print. Each HEI company has different contracts, terms, calculations, and restrictions. This is not the type of agreement to go it alone. Before you sign, enlist the help of a housing counselor or real estate attorney who can go over the contract with a fine-toothed comb.
Frequently asked questions
-  What happens to the contract in the case of death or divorce? In case of death or divorce, the agreement “follows the home,” no matter who becomes the new homeowner. The exact terms vary depending on the company, but generally, the heir(s) have the option of continuing the home equity sharing agreement or concluding it. This can be accomplished in two ways: either by selling the property or paying back the company’s share in some other way. In the case of divorce, the options for shared equity agreements and the marital home are typically the same. The two parties have to agree if they will sell the house and split the proceeds. In community property states, the proceeds are generally divided equally. If the home is sold, the investment firm gets paid out of the proceeds. If one spouse retains it, they retain liability for the agreement.
-  How do home equity agreements compare to home equity loans? A home equity loan is a traditional form of financing offered by a bank, credit union or online lender. It typically has stringent credit and DTI requirements for borrowers. When you take out a home equity loan, you receive a lump sum of money that you pay back in monthly installments over time. These repayments also include interest on the amount borrowed. Alternatively, a home equity agreement is offered by home equity sharing companies. The money you receive is not technically a loan, but an investment. The company is essentially buying a stake in your home. When you get an HEA, you receive a lump sum and you don’t pay anything back until you sell the house or the agreement term ends (usually 10-30 years). At that point, the company gets repaid a return on its investment. It’s either the original amount plus a percentage of the home’s appreciation, or a percentage of the home’s value at the time of the sale.
-  Can you use the funds from a home equity sharing agreement for anything? Whether it’s consolidating debt, renovating your home or taking a vacation, homeowners can typically use the funds from home equity sharing agreements for anything. But some exceptions may exist, depending on the investment company.

title: Trump orders removal of ticks and mosquitoes from nation’s capital
text:
(CNN) — President Donald Trump signed a new executive order Wednesday that aims to slash the population of mosquitoes and ticks that spread disease in Washington, D.C.
The order directs federal agencies to cut the populations of Asian tiger and Egyptian mosquitoes in the nation’s capital by 90% by 2028.
It mandates a 50% cut in the tick population within the same time frame.
The Department of Health and Human Services, the EPA and the Department of the Interior would be involved in the effort.
HHS is tasked with hosting prize competitions to find the best ways to prevent and treat mosquito and tick illnesses.
Developing non-chemical ways to reduce mosquito and tick populations would also be prioritized.

title: How to write a check: A step-by-step guide
text:
How to write a check: A step-by-step guide
Key takeaways
- Writing a check requires six steps: date, payee name, amount in numbers, amount in words, memo (optional) and your signature.
- Always use blue or black ink — never pencil — to prevent alterations and fraud.
- The numerical amount and the written amount must match exactly, or the bank may reject or delay your check.
- Check fraud has surged in recent years, so take precautions like filling all blank spaces, storing checks securely and mailing them safely.
These days, most payments happen with a tap, swipe or a few clicks — but checks aren’t gone yet. Americans still wrote roughly nine billion checks in 2025, and checks remain common for rent payments, large purchases, gifts and business transactions.
Whether you’re writing your first check or your first one in a long time, getting it right matters. A mistake can lead to delays, late fees or a bounced check. Use this step-by-step guide to fill out a check correctly the first time.
What you need to write a check
- A checking account with enough money to cover the check amount
- A pen with blue or black ink
- The payee’s full, correct name
- The exact dollar amount you’re paying
How to fill out a check in 6 steps
Before writing a check, you’ll need to have a checking account with sufficient funds to cover the amount of the check. Then, follow these steps to fill one out.
1. Write the date
Write the current date on the line in the top right-hand corner. This tells the bank and the recipient when you wrote the check. You can use numbers or write out the entire date — either “3/4/2026” or “March 4, 2026” works.
Some people write a future date hoping the recipient will wait to cash the check. However, most banks will process checks immediately regardless of the date written. If you need to delay a payment, use your bank’s scheduled payment feature instead.
2. Write who the check is payable to
On the line that says “Pay to the order of,” write the full name of the individual or company you’re paying. This person or entity is called the payee. Use their complete, legal name rather than a nickname to avoid confusion. If you’re paying a business, confirm its official name. Some businesses operate under multiple names or may use a different business name when accepting checks.
You can write “Cash” if you don’t know the payee’s name, but this is risky — anyone can cash or deposit a check made out to cash. It’s much safer to write a specific name.
3. Write the check amount in numbers
In the small box to the right of the payee line, write the numerical dollar amount clearly. For example, if you’re writing a check for one hundred dollars and thirty cents, write “$100.30.”
Write clearly and start as close to the dollar sign as possible so no one can add digits in front of your number.
4. Write the amount in words
On the line below “Pay to the order of,” spell out the dollar amount in words. This amount must match the numerical amount exactly. Write the cents as a fraction over 100.
Examples:
- $100.30 becomes “One hundred and 30/100”
- $50.00 becomes “Fifty and 00/100”
- $1,250.75 becomes “One thousand two hundred fifty and 75/100”
Even if you’re writing a check for a round dollar amount, include “00/100” for the cents portion. This prevents someone from adding cents to your check. Draw a line through any remaining blank space to further prevent fraud.
5. Write a memo (optional but recommended)
The memo line at the bottom left is optional, but using it is smart. Write a brief note about the check’s purpose — for example, “Rent — March 2026” or “Invoice #4521.” This helps with your own recordkeeping and ensures the recipient can apply the payment correctly.
Some companies specifically request that you write your account number or invoice number in the memo field.
6. Sign the check
Sign your name clearly on the line at the bottom right corner of the check. Your signature authorizes the bank to pay the stated amount to the payee. Without it, the check is invalid. Use the same signature that’s on file with your bank — mismatched signatures can cause processing delays.
How to write a check safely: Fraud prevention tips
Following these best practices helps prevent fraud, processing errors or payment delays.
- Always use pen, never pencil. Write with blue or black ink only. Pencil can be erased and altered. Avoid other ink colors like red or green, which can cause problems with check-scanning equipment.
- Write clearly. If your handwriting is hard to read, print in block letters. Unclear writing is one of the most common reasons banks reject checks.
- Fill all blank spaces. Draw a line through any unused space after the written amount and start numbers as close to the dollar sign as possible. This prevents someone from adding words or digits.
- Double-check everything before signing. Make sure the numerical amount matches the written amount, the payee’s name is spelled correctly and all required fields are filled in.
- Keep records. Write down each check number, amount, payee and date in your check register or a budgeting app. Take a photo of the check before mailing it.
- Store checks and mail them securely. Keep unused checks in a secure place at home — never in your car or bag. When mailing checks, drop them inside the post office or use your bank’s online bill pay to avoid mailing them at all. If checks are stolen, contact your bank immediately.
Why you still need checks in 2026
Even as check usage has dropped, there are situations where checks are still commonly used or even required:
- Rent payments. Many landlords, especially individual property owners, still prefer or require checks.
- Large purchases. Some transactions like security deposits, contractor payments and vehicle purchases may call for a cashier’s check or certified check rather than a personal check.
- Gifts. Checks remain a common way to give money for weddings, graduations and holidays, especially across generations.
- Government and legal payments. Some courts, local government offices and tax authorities still accept or require checks for certain filings and fees.
- Business payments. Small businesses and sole proprietors frequently use checks for invoicing and accounts payable.
If you find yourself writing checks often, it’s worth making sure your checking account provides checks at a low cost (or free). Some accounts include free checks as a benefit.
Types of checks and when to use each one
Not every payment calls for a personal check. Here’s how the main types compare:
- Personal checks
- Personal checks are the standard checks from your checking account, used for everyday payments. They’re drawn directly from your account balance. Best for routine bills, rent and personal payments.
- Cashier’s checks
- Cashier’s checks are issued and guaranteed by the bank itself. You pay the bank upfront, and they draw the check from the bank’s own funds. They typically cost $10–$15 and are often required for large transactions like home closings or vehicle purchases.
- Certified checks
- Certified checks are personal checks that the bank has verified and guaranteed. The bank confirms you have sufficient funds and sets that money aside. They offer more security than a standard personal check. To understand the difference between cashier’s checks and certified checks, see our detailed comparison.
- Money orders
- Money orders function similarly to cashier’s checks but are available at more locations — post offices, grocery stores, convenience stores — and are typically cheaper, between $1 and $5. They’re good for smaller amounts.
Where to get checks
- From your bank: Most banks provide checks, but they’re often more expensive than other options. Some checking accounts include free checks — check your account details first.
- Third-party check printers: Companies that specialize in printing checks typically charge less than banks. You’ll need your account number and routing number to order.
- Online ordering: Many services let you order checks online and have them delivered to your home. This is often the most convenient and least expensive option.
Next steps

title: Breaking ground for a new farmers market in Brunswick
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Sept. 24, well after actual ground had been broken, Brunswick-Topsham Land Trust held its ceremonial groundbreaking for its new farmers market, and, in a slightly longer future, a home for community programs and the land trust itself.
It seemed especially apt that this land trust, with agriculture central to its DNA, would come to Dionne Farm, which lies at the heart of Crystal Spring Farm along the conservation and agricultural corridor from Brunswick to Freeport.
On that day, 75 attendees heard from one of the trust’s founding spirits, former Bowdoin College professor and always-farmer, Tom Settlemire. Standing in a patch of field and near two towering conserved conifers, Settlemire recalled the rush of days in the early ’90s when he and other land trust founders learned that Crystal Spring Farm was for sale.
“We knew,” he said, “that we had to save this land from housing development. Developers could have put hundreds of houses out here. It was special farm land, some of the best in Maine, and beautiful terrain.”
The land was also on sale for nearly $700,000. “But we were rich,” Settlemire joked, “we had $4,000 in the bank. Still, we knew we had to buy this land for the community.”
And so, in a hurried and white-knuckled campaign, they did. Now, as the 75 of us in attendance that day celebrated the early work on the site (just over a mile from Brunswick center, and across the road from the current farmers market with ample, on-site parking planned), the Crystal Spring Farm land family has grown to 360 acres. Those acres include the site we stood upon, the 25-acre Dionne Farm, whose generously-supported purchase was completed in 2025 as a gift of place to our whole area.
Brunswick-Topsham Land Trust Agricultural Programs Manager Julia St.Clair then outlined the design of the new market, pointing to the “community spirit of the market” as the unchanging core that would center it. The trust’s Executive Director Kristi Hatrick thanked a number of the individuals and businesses who have made this early work possible. The morning grew brighter still; the sun was higher, warm beyond the recent equinox.
It was time for the symbolic, shovels-in-the-ground moment. Eleven worthies stepped forward, grasped a shovel each, a few planted a foot atop their shovel-blades, and everyone … posed. This circle of shovelers represented many of the groups who make the farmers market a center for our community.
People took photos, an appreciative burble rose from the assembled. Just as it should be, I thought as I lined up a photo against the backdrop of work that will host up to 50 local vendors, newly-planted shade trees, plus room for chairs and gatherings beneath a pavilion.
It will be a place where, harkening back to an early market saying from teacher and then market director, Rick Wilson, “you get to meet the face of your food.” And, as bonus, the many faces of friends and people from throughout the area.
So that seems a good way to point to the community promise of Crystal Spring and Dionne farms — putting faces to the land that sustains us, and which we must serve wisely.
A few years ago I had asked Tom Settlemire where his land wisdom originated: “That one is easy, — it was my parents!!!” he wrote. “My father told me at an early age ‘soil is the most important resource we have on earth — more than oil, gold, silver, anything. If you don’t have fertile, productive soil, you have nothing else. You can’t have people.’”
That belief lies at the heart of the land trust’s vision for the market, which will open to our community next summer.
Sandy Stott is a Brunswick resident, chair of the town’s Conservation Commission and its Steering Committee for the Restoration of Mere Brook, and a member of Brunswick-Topsham Land Trust Board of Directors. He writes for the AMC’s Appalachia and a variety of publications. He may be reached at [email protected].

Mortgage rates jump to two-year high, approach 7.5%
Current mortgage rates
The 30-year fixed mortgages in this week’s survey had an average total of 0.33 discount and origination points. Discount points are a way to lower your mortgage rate, while origination points are fees lenders charge to create, review and process your loan.

Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in August 2026 was $429,100, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.38% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,372 amounts to about 27% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 1.6% over the past year, and the median of $429,100 was an all-time high for the month of August. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late September showed national home prices grew 1.9% in the year ending in July, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation held at 3.4% in August, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have spiked amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, and 10-year Treasury yields hit 5.3% this week, well up from earlier in the year.
“Inflation as reported by PCE on Wednesday offered a potential respite for bonds but unfortunately, the trend is not our friend,” says James Sahnger of C2 Financial Corp. “Since mid-April, the 10-year has risen from 4.22% to as high as 5.30% mid-day Wednesday.”
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Christa Gail Pike says ‘I am not afraid to die’ in letter written before execution was halted by federal court
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - In a letter written before Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee denied her clemency and before a federal court issued a stay in her Wednesday execution, Christa Gail Pike said she is not afraid to die.
Pike is the only woman on Tennessee’s death row and would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in at least 200 years.
EN ESPAÑOL | ‘No tengo miedo de morir’: Christa Gail Pike ante ejecución en Tennessee
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit issued an order Wednesday morning staying Pike’s execution “until further order of this court.”
“The court has stayed this recognizing the serious concerns about Christa’s scheduled execution,” Stephen Ferrell of the Federal Defenders Services of Eastern Tennessee said.
Pike was found guilty in 1996 of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer on the University of Tennessee campus.
Pike, along with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, planned Slemmer’s torture and killing. The case later became known as the Job Corps Murder because both Pike and Slemmer were members of Job Corps at the time.
“I would like to extend my gratitude to everyone who has supported me through these hard days,” the letter reads. “I’ve felt more love in the last two weeks than I have my entire life.”
Since Pike’s trial ended, she and her legal team have tried to change her sentence. Pike has also been supported by activist groups that oppose the death penalty, which is something she references in the letter.
“When my people showed up for me- they have showed [SIC] up and showed out!” she said. “I am humbled beyond words.”
Her petition for clemency was not granted, with Lee confirming Monday that he would not step in to keep Pike alive past her execution date.
“Whether my clemency is granted or not, I am at peace,” the letter reads. “I am not afraid to die. I am only nervous about the process.”
Pike is not the only one to have concerns about Tennessee executions. The state’s death penalty has faced scrutiny after botched executions prompted a pause from Lee. The attempted Tennessee execution of Tony Carruthers was abandoned in May after medical staff failed to establish IV access, a process that took over an hour.
Mark Fowler, the doctor who was involved in Carruthers’ attempted execution, will oversee Pike’s death sentence.
In August, Anthony Darrell Hines was put to death at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville for the 1985 murder of Catherine Jean Jackson Jenkins.
In her letter, Pike also said the public had only seen a “limited persona” of her, rather than her “true character.”
She has long been the subject of media reports and faced the court of public opinion for decades.
Pike was scheduled to be executed Wednesday morning.
