title: Join me in voting for Charlotte Nutt
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Dear Editor:
I’ve lived in Edgecomb for 20 years, and over the past year that I’ve gotten to know Charlotte Nutt, she has made a huge impression on me. In the time I’ve known her, it’s clear she is a great person who truly cares about this place and is always there to support our town whenever we need her.
While I've known her for a year, Charlotte’s roots here go way back. Her dad, David Nutt, spent years as a local boat builder, and her late mom, Dr. Judy Sandick, took care of so many of us at St. Andrews and Miles Memorial Hospital. Growing up on the peninsula, Charlotte went to local public schools, played field hockey, swam at the Y, and spent summers working as a deckhand on Schooner Eastwind. She knows what life on the coast is like because she lived it.
Through her work in municipal planning, Charlotte understands how important it is to support our town governments. She knows solutions shouldn't be forced down from Augusta, but developed by listening to local towns and giving us the tools to handle our own planning.
She’s also focused on the issues hitting us hardest right now, especially housing. So many young families, tradesmen, teachers, and seniors are getting priced out of the towns where they grew up or work. Charlotte wants to fix that by building more housing, protecting existing homes, and keeping working families here. That same care goes into protecting our working waterfronts, small businesses, and local industries that keep our coast alive.
In the year I’ve known Charlotte, she’s proven to be someone who genuinely cares and is always ready to pitch in. Please join me in voting for Charlotte Nutt for House District 48 this November.
Cara R. Gaffney
Edgecomb

title: SCORES OUTDOORS: Anyone seen a wooly bear?
text:
OK! Here comes the question, again.
Has anyone seen a wooly bear caterpillar? They are usually seen in abundance in September, and I have yet to see one.
As you know, they are one of the signs of weather forcasting for the upcoming winter.
The wooly bear, the pupa to the Isabella Tiger moth, is the caterpillar that has black and rust-colored bars on its body. Old folklore claims the wooly bear is capable of predicting winter temperature with great accuracy. The body of the caterpillar is black with the rust-colored bar through the middle, and the legend goes the wider the rust-colored bar, the milder the winter.
Seeing a woolly bear caterpillar usually means that autumn has arrived and the insect is actively searching for a safe, sheltered spot to hibernate for the winter. Woolly bear caterpillars turn into the Isabella tiger moth during May and June of the spring following their birth.
The caterpillar larvae emerges from the egg in the fall and over winters in its caterpillar form. It survives winter freezes by producing a cryoprotectant – designed to protect from low temperatures – in its tissues. Once the weather warms, the larva devours all the grass and weeds it can, pupates, and becomes an adult, which then lives through the summer. It is the larvae of the species which are the subject of common folklore, which has it that the forthcoming severity of a winter can be predicted by the amount of black on the caterpillar; this is the most familiar wooly bear in North America.
But in fact, the larvae produced in the same clutch of eggs can vary from mostly red to mostly black, even when reared under the same conditions.
Scientists try to disclaim that the width of the bands is actually related to weather predictions. But I find fault in their theory. You see, the rust-colored band will grow towards the ends of the body, and the black bands decreases in size, as the larvae matures. So, if the rust-colored band expands with age, then that must mean the caterpillar is less likely to go into an early hibernation stage, and, subsequently emerge earlier in the spring, thus pointing to a mild winter.
The bristles of the wooly bear do not inject venom and will not cause irritations, injury, inflammation or swelling. However, they will play dead if picked up or disturbed. Handling them is discouraged, however, as the bristles may cause dermatitis in people with sensitive skin.
Keeping with the myth of the wooly bear’s talent, many areas around the country hold Wooly Bear festivals, such as Vermilion, Ohio, Beattyville, Kentucky, Banner Elk, North Carolina, and Lewisburg, Pennsylvania. As a matter of fact, Oil City, Pennsylvania, is producing a new character, “Oil Valley Vick,” who will predict the winter weather. It is hoped they can someday draw a crowd similar to Punxsatawney Phil on Groundhog Day.
So, if the weather predicting capabilities of the wooly bear are so profound, why are people trying to dispel that little fella’s contribution to mankind?

In baseball, what is a pitcher’s immaculate inning?

title: Woman charged after 2 children found dead inside home by deputies, authorities say
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — A homeowner in South Carolina is facing charges after authorities say two children were found dead at the home on Tuesday.
Justine May, 31, was booked into the Charleston County jail on two counts of homicide by child neglect, court records showed.
May will remain in custody after waiving her right to a bond hearing on Wednesday. She is scheduled for an initial court appearance Nov. 20.
Charleston County authorities said they were called to the home on Pinewood Drive for a welfare check Tuesday afternoon when they found the two children dead inside.
The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division Department of Child Fatalities and the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office are both investigating.
May’s ex-boyfriend, Zachary Deacon, also found himself in custody recently after being arrested on Sept. 11. The Charleston County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded that day to the same home regarding a reported mental health crisis.
Deacon’s charges include harassment in the second degree after May alleged that Deacon continued to contact her after prior domestic violence.
Family members of May said they had called law enforcement within the last month regarding the well-being of May and the children who were in her care.
Documents stated that Deacon had previously called May delusional, spiraling and in need of getting a grip on reality while referencing involvement with social services.
On Sept. 13, May herself posted on social media screenshots of concerned text messages and emails allegedly from family, with an email specifically expressing concerns about her parenting.
Deacon has since been released on bond, but a judge has ordered him not to have contact with May or the children as a condition of his release.
The Charleston County Coroner’s Office did not immediately release the cause of death for the two children, as investigators said the case remains under investigation.

title: MTA rolls out Red Sox, Sea Dogs and Hearts of Pine E-ZPass stickers
text:
Mainers can now show pride in some of their local sports teams while paying their highway tolls.
The Maine Turnpike Authority announced Wednesday that new $20 E-ZPass windshield sticker tags featuring the Boston Red Sox, Portland Sea Dogs and Portland Hearts of Pine are now available.
The MTA announced in March that it was rolling out windshield stickers as a cheaper and more environmentally friendly alternative to hardcase transponders. Unbranded stickers cost $5 compared to the $15 hardcase device, and the stickers use RFID technology, eliminating the need for a battery while using less plastic.
However, unlike the traditional device, the stickers cannot be shared between vehicles.
The new $20 sports stickers provide an optional “creative and personal” touch for Maine drivers to consider, said MTA Executive Director Andre Briere.
“We are constantly looking for smart technology that can improve cost efficiency, reduce our environmental impact, and make travel easier,” Briere said in a written statement. “When we can pair those benefits with something creative and personal, it is a win for Maine drivers.”
All of the proceeds from Portland Hearts of Pine stickers will benefit the Hearts of Pine Foundation.
“Every Hearts tag represents more than team pride — it helps us expand access to soccer, invest in places to play, and create opportunities for young people to build a sense of belonging,” Kevin Schohl, president of the Portland Hearts of Pine, said in the news release.
MTA says it plans to provide more of these “community driven” collaborations with New England sports teams in the future, and also teased that Maine Mariners stickers will be coming soon.
The stickers are available to purchase at the E-ZPass office at 2360 Congress St. in Portland, as well as through maineturnpikeauthority.com.
The MTA also released a new Maine E-ZPass App this week, through which Mainers can purchase the stickers. The app is live for Android users and coming soon for Apple users.

title: Justice Department files complaint against judges over immigration enforcement surge comments
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Justice filed a complaint Wednesday against federal judges in Minnesota over their remarks to the media about the pressure on their courthouse during Trump administration’s immigration enforcement surge.
The complaint alleges the judges seven federal judges — nominated by Democrats and Republican presidents — violated judicial ethics by speaking to The New York Times about their experience dealing with a flood of cases during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge crackdown that led to thousands of arrests in the Twin Cities.
The complaint escalates the department’s battle with the federal judiciary, which has halted administration priorities, dismissed high-profile prosecutions and accused government lawyers in some cases of failing to comply with court orders.
The department is demanding that the judges recuse themselves from all criminal or civil cases involving the Department of Homeland Security, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters, because of what he described as “obvious bias they have shown” in their remarks to the newspaper.
“When we have a situation like we have now, where you have a judge, a couple of judges, just not only violating the canons in our view, but also showing bias in what they’re saying, we have no choice but to act to defend not only our prosecutors, but also DHS,” Blanche said.
The judge at the center of the story, Patrick Schiltz, accused the government in January of failing to comply with nearly 100 court orders. He said in a ruling that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a part of DHS, “is not a law unto itself.”
Schiltz, who was nominated by Republican President George W. Bush and served as a law clerk for Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, told the newspaper that what happened in Minnesota’s federal court last winter “created a grave threat to the rule of law.”
In a statement Wednesday, a spokesperson for the Minnesota court said legal experts have confirmed that the judges were acting “well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges” in speaking to the newspaper. Schiltz also said in a statement that his comments did not violate any ethical rules.
“Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges” may speak or write “on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence,'” Schiltz said in a statement. “That is exactly what I did.”
The complaint was filed with the chief judge of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which oversees federal judges in Minnesota.
The Republican administration has railed against what it describes as “activist judges” who officials say are intent on thwarting Trump’s agenda. Yet some of the most critical and unfavorable court rulings have come from judges nominated by Trump and other Republican presidents.

title: Maine ethics commission won’t investigate whether lawmaker broke confidentiality
text:
The Maine ethics commission voted Wednesday not to investigate whether a Republican State House leader violated confidentiality laws when she shared a letter with the media that House Speaker Ryan Fecteau said questioned his integrity.
Assistant House Republican Leader Katrina Smith, R-Palermo, filed a letter in July with the Maine Commission on Governmental Ethics and Election Practices seeking “an independent review of the legal and ethical boundaries” of Fecteau, D-Biddeford, holding simultaneous roles in the Legislature and as the head of the Biddeford Housing Authority.
Jonathan Wayne, executive director of the commission, initially interpreted Smith’s request as a formal complaint, which would have triggered a confidentiality clause.
Smith, however, actually requested an “advisory opinion,” which does not have the same requirement.
The contents of Smith’s letter, which outlined concerns about a possible conflict of interest between Fecteau’s two positions, appeared in full online in the Biddeford Buzz and in part on the Maine Wire the day after she submitted it.
Fecteau subsequently asked the commission to investigate whether Smith’s letter appearing online violated the confidentiality requirement.
Choosing not to, he said, would set “a terrible precedent.”
“Lawmakers could be subject to bait and switch requests that are immediately shared with the media to then create an appearance of wrongdoing,” he said.
Biddeford Housing wasn’t scared off by the news articles, Fecteau said, but for some employers, that could be enough to withdraw an offer.
“This is not a political game,” he said. “This has very serious consequences for the livelihoods of those who seek and serve in public office.”
To open an investigation, though, the commission first had to determine whether Smith’s letter constituted a formal complaint.
The commission ultimately decided Wednesday that it didn’t, effectively closing the discussion.
But while members made the decision unanimously, they also made it grudgingly.
If a person wishes to file a complaint with the commission they have to agree, in writing, not to share the details of the complaint until the commission decides whether to hear the issue. If they don’t agree, the commission won’t consider the matter.
“It’s clear to me that Assistant Leader Smith never completed the process of filing a complaint and never agreed to keep it confidential,” said William Schneider, commission chair.
Commissioner Sarah LeClaire suggested the law be clarified “so it’s not used in a weaponized way to get a letter out to the press that the public will assume is an investigation,” she said.
“I don’t like what I see in this case,” LeClaire added. “I don’t like the idea of the possibility that this commission was used for some sort of press grab.”

title: Stephen King opens up about his new novel and a new ‘Carrie’ series
text:
It’s hard to imagine Stephen King needing another writer to make him look good.
But the Maine author says that’s what happened when he worked with Peter Straub. The two first collaborated on a dark fantasy called “The Talisman” in 1984 and then on the 2001 sequel, “Black House.”
Before Straub died in 2022 at 79, he wrote to King with ideas for a third book in the series. King thought the ideas were so powerful, so on point, that he used them as a basis for the new novel “Other Worlds Than These.” It goes on sale Oct. 6, with both authors’ names on the cover.
King wishes he had been able to work with Straub one more time, but is glad to have had the partnership at all.
“Oh man, he was so good. He was a better stylist than I ever was, and I thought this is going to make me look so good if I collaborate with him, and it really did,” said King in mid-September. “We kept saying we’re going to do it (a third book) next year, but I had things to finish and he had things to finish. Then time just ran out.”
The day after “Other Worlds Than These” comes out, Prime will debut a new limited series based on “Carrie,” King’s first book. The 1974 novel was made into a Hollywood film in 1976, starring Sissy Spacek. The new series stars Summer H. Howell and was created and written by Mike Flanagan, who has done several TV or film projects based on King’s work, including “The Life of Chuck” and “Dr. Sleep.”
King said he really likes the way the story has been updated to the present, with Carrie’s fellow students using cellphones and social media to bully and humiliate her.
“It’s really smart and it expands on the book, which was fairly slim. The miniseries is all about social media and it’s fantastic,” said King. “It’s a timeless story, which is too bad. You would hope at some point we as human beings would stop bullying each other for no good reason.”
NO SLOWING DOWN
At 79, King continues to be a pop culture powerhouse. He’s written more than 65 novels or novellas and his books have sold some 400 million copies. More than 80 films or TV series have been based on his work. Colleges around the country have held courses dedicated to his work.
Born in Portland and raised largely in Durham, King went to high school in Lisbon Falls and graduated with a degree in English from the University of Maine in 1970. He and his wife, Tabitha, have lived in Maine ever since. Their longtime Bangor home, a tourist attraction for its resemblance to a haunted house, now houses the couple’s charitable foundation and King’s archives. These days, King spends a little more than half the year in Maine and the rest in Florida.
King had only been a published author for a few years when he met Straub, in London, in the late 1970s. Straub had had success writing about the supernatural with his 1975 novel, “Julia.”
“The Talisman” focused on Jack Sawyer, who at the age of 12 starts an epic quest, walking from New Hampshire to the California coast to find a way to save his dying mother’s life. His trek takes him to the Territories, a parallel medieval universe, where people have lookalike counterparts known as twinners. Jack’s mother’s twinner is queen of the Territories, and is also dying.
“Black House” continues with Sawyer in his 30s, leaving his job as a police officer to live in small-town Wisconsin. A series of murders involving young children draws him out of retirement and into different worlds.
In “Other Worlds Than These,” Sawyer is called to journey to strange worlds again. He has to stop a rampaging group of infected teenagers in America-side and battle the forces of the mysterious Gullet at the edge of Mid-World. The book also wraps up the various worlds of King’s Dark Tower series.
Before Straub died, he sent King a letter with ideas for a third book. He also sent him the book “Redheaded Peckerwood” by artist and photographer Christian Patterson. The book uses photographs to retrace the route of teenagers Charles Starkweather and Caril Ann Fugate on a killing spree through Nebraska in the 1950s.
“Peter said to me, ‘Maybe somebody gets possesed by the spirit of Charles Starkweather and they go into the Territories, and all this stuff happens,” said King. “I thought, ‘Oh man, this is just tailor-made for a suspense novel.’ It really made me want to write this book.”
DO YOUR THING
As for the new “Carrie” series, King said he was sent scripts, had casting approval and was credited as an executive producer. But he really wasn’t very involved. He said he doesn’t like to use his approval power unless he feels he really has to, which is almost never.
“Making a film is different (than writing a book). My thought is, you do your thing and we’ll see what happens,” King said.
Besides Howell as Carrie, the cast includes Samantha Sloyan as her mother and Matthew Lillard as the high school principal. Though the book is set in a fictional Maine town, filming for the series took place in western Canada. Because Canada and states like Massachussetts and New York offer lucrative financial incentives and tax credits to production companies, Maine has rarely been the location of a big-budget King film or TV show in recent years. Film advocates have tried to increase Maine’s film incentives several times in recent years, without much success.
King liked the new series and was particularly impressed with the gym shower scene, where classmates taunt Carrie because she doesn’t realize she’s having her period. Her mother never explained it to her.
In the original movie, the scene is steamy and dreamlike, showing girls in the shower through what King called “a male gaze.” But in the new version, Carrie is crumpled on the floor of the shower while her classmates, fully clothed, crowd around her, recording her humiliation on their cellphones.
“Teenagers still bully each other, but with social media it’s supercharged,” said King. “He (Flanagan) really caught that idea with his shot of all these kids taking cellphone photos of this girl who’s in terror. It’s a wonderful moment.”
King is also happy that while Flanagan updated some things, he didn’t change the story basics, which include a girl who is mercilessly bullied but who has hidden powers.
“It doesn’t reinvent the wheel. The prom scene, the pig’s blood, it’s all there,” King said.

title: October Starting Off On A Warm Note!
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Clouds will continue linger through the first half of the night. A quick warm-up kicks off October on Thursday before a cold front brings showers Friday and cooler, fall-like air for the weekend.
Wednesday Night: Clouds & Patchy Fog
Expect cloud cover to stick around for the first part of Wednesday night, with overnight low temperatures dropping into the mid-40s to mid-50s. Patchy fog may develop late.
Thursday: Warm Start to October
Thursday looks beautiful to kick off the new month. Look for a mix of sun and clouds with inland highs climbing into the 70s. A southwest breeze gusting up to 20 mph will keep coastal areas in the mid to upper 60s. Far northern communities could see a few isolated late-day showers.
Friday: Cold Front Brings Showers
A cold front moves into northern and western Maine Friday morning, spreading scattered showers across the region. The front will slowly work toward the coast through the afternoon and early evening, with shower activity turning lighter and more scattered closer to the coast. High temperatures will depend on frontal timing: expect mid to upper 60s in the Mountains and north, while the Foothills and coast reach the upper 60s to mid 70s ahead of the front.
Weekend Outlook: Brighter Days, Chilly Nights
High pressure builds in behind the front, setting up a sunny Saturday with seasonable highs in the mid 60s. Sunday starts chilly with patchy frost possible across northern areas where lows dip into the 30s. Sunday remains bright and dry with highs from the upper 50s to mid-60s, before a chance of light showers returns Sunday night into Monday.

title: Learning new tricks — The surprising way new hobbies boost your brain as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Forget the old adage: You can’t teach an old dog new tricks.
Picking up a new hobby later in life isn’t just fun — it’s also one of the best things you can do for your brain. From line dancing to sourdough starters to pickleball, small leaps outside your comfort zone can spark change in how your brain works.
“The brain still learns” — it just needs patience
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, says the idea that older adults can’t pick up new skills doesn’t hold up once you actually watch them try.
“I hear this all the time, that you can’t teach an old dog new tricks. And then I walk into a senior community, and they’re like teenagers sitting there texting, and they’re on their phone and they’re taking videos and QR codes,” Cradduck said. “They learned that at an older age because I had to learn it at an older age.”
Cradduck said the brain just needs a little more time and patience to learn as we age.
“And you need to make it relevant to the time,” Cradduck said. “So grab a grandkid and learn a whole bunch.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, says that discomfort is actually doing something good beneath the surface.
“When you challenge it like that, you create new connections. The brain is always changing. New connections, what we call neuroplasticity,” Rogers said. “And also you’re waking up the brain, and that’s a good thing. So it makes you just stay alert and all that. And you can look at reaction time to things actually improve.”
From line dancing nerves to a new rhythm
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, shared her own recent experience stepping outside her comfort zone.
“I always get nervous when I’m learning something new, and I get nervous with the technology. But I have this experience I’ve had in the back of my mind I wanted to learn line dancing,” O’Rourke said. “And my yoga studio is teaching a three-hour line dancing class. Then I’m at this event the other day and they’re line dancing and I could tell I was sitting there like, should I go? Should I not go? So I just jumped in there.”
“My heart was pounding, and there was a woman behind me helping me, go to the right, to the left, and she really helped me,” O’Rourke said. “As nervous as I was, I got into this rhythm with them, and it really helped me realize one — I had to face the fear and do it anyway and then keep doing it. And I just got so excited.”
Cradduck says even something as simple as walking is a workout for the brain.
“The more you can make those connections in the brain, and then the feet, the movement of the feet — you don’t think about what it takes with your brain to actually just walk,” Cradduck said. “And so walking is actually really brain exercise. It really is, especially for our aged community. And so learning how to dance, learning something with rhythm — the arts, those things are amazing.”
New activities, new purpose
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose says the same principle is already built into many independent living communities.
“That’s why in independent living, there’s so many activities where they might be teaching new language, they’re teaching history. They’re giving all kinds of new things to introduce people to, because that helps people live longer and live better,” Ambrose said.
Rogers shared an example from her own life, learning pickleball in Wichita — and Ambrose took a sourdough baking class through her real estate office.
“And I’m not really that much of a cook or a baker,” Ambrose said. “But I took a sourdough class in my real estate office. One of the realtors was teaching it, and I picked up my mom. I said, ‘Hey, I’m coming to pick you up,’ She didn’t know what we’re doing, so that was really fun for her and I to do it together.”
Ambrose said it was like a science experiment.
“Every morning you’re like, ‘Oh, I gotta go check my dough,’” she said.
What if you can’t be physically active?
Cradduck says the lesson isn’t limited to people who can move freely.
“There are some people that are impaired, and they can’t do the physical. So go to your grandkid’s ball game. Maybe you don’t know the rules of soccer, maybe you don’t know all the rules of baseball or football — and learn the game and learn and connect,” Cradduck said. “It’s all going to give you so much more purpose and so much more connection. The more you do and the more you connect.”
Rogers said the biggest thing is that you’re exercising your brain.
Key takeaways
- Learning new skills sharpens your brain health.
- Pairing curiosity with experience keeps you engaged and builds connection across generations.
- Embracing new tricks builds generational bridges.

title: Bond denied for man accused of killing Kentucky trooper
text:
BOWLING GREEN, Ky. (WSMV/WKYT/Gray News) - A judge denied bond for the 51-year-old Tennessee man charged with murder in the shooting of Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips.
Emonnie Branch of Portland, Tennessee, appeared in a Warren County court in Kentucky Tuesday morning.
Prosecutors argued that Branch is a flight risk and a danger to the community.
Prosecutors cite criminal history
Branch allegedly gave police a false name and has an extensive criminal history, including fraud, robbery and assault involving a minor. Prosecutors also said the incident involving the state trooper was captured on video.
After hearing those arguments, the judge denied bond for Branch.
Branch is charged with the murder of a first responder/peace officer after Kentucky State Police said Phillips, 28, was fatally shot during a traffic stop on Interstate 65 in Warren County.
Arrest in Jefferson County
Louisville police used a grappler to secure the car and Branch in Jefferson County about four hours after the shooting.
Branch also has an outstanding warrant from Tennessee for a probation violation. His attorney said extradition had not yet been discussed.
Branch’s next hearing in the Kentucky case is scheduled for Friday morning.

title: Arrest made in hit-and-run crash that killed Nickelodeon star

Man arrested in crash that killed former 'All That' star Kianna Underwood

Man arrested in death of former 'All That' star Kianna Underwood
An arrest has been made in connection with the fatal hit-and-run crash that killed a former Nickelodeon child star.
Kianna Underwood, who starred in Nickelodeon’s popular children’s sketch comedy show, “All That,” was killed Jan. 16 in a hit-and-run crash in New York.
She was 33.
On Tuesday, 72-year-old Michael Griffiths was arrested in connection to her death, according to local media reports.
According to the New York Police Department, Underwood was crossing an intersection in the Brownsville neighborhood of Brooklyn when a black Ford Explorer SUV hit her in the morning.
While lying in the street, she was then “subsequently struck by a black and gray sedan,” NYPD said in a statement. Underwood was pronounced dead at the scene.
Police say both drivers left the scene.
Citing police reports, local news outlets report that Griffiths was taken into custody in Brooklyn this week and charged with two counts of leaving the scene of the accident.
Underwood appeared in “All That” over seven episodes in 2005. Between 1999 and 2004, Underwood voiced the character Fuchsia Glover in the Nick Jr. show, “Little Bill.”
She also spent a year on the first national tour of “Hairspray” as Little Inez.
“All That” was Underwood’s last credited role. The program helped launch multiple careers over its decade-long run, ranging from Nick Cannon, Kenan Thompson and Amanda Bynes.

title: Governor pushes for investigation into Cornell’s handling of fraternity gang rape allegation
text:
(AP) - New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Tuesday called for an investigation into Cornell University’s response to a 2024 gang rape allegation in which a woman says she was sexually assaulted by seven students after being plied with alcohol and drugs.
The woman filed a lawsuit this month saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Cornell’s campus in October 2024. Her suit says the assault occurred after she was pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol, to the point where she was incapable of consenting to sex.
The woman reported the incident to Cornell’s campus police department, but the local district attorney’s office opted not to prosecute anyone at the time. It reopened the criminal investigation Monday as public outrage built over the woman’s allegations.
Hochul calls for an outside law firm to investigate Cornell’s response
Hochul, a Democrat, said she supported Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s decision to reopen his investigation, but said bigger questions remain about Cornell’s reporting, response, and prevention systems, as well as its campus culture. The governor called for an outside law firm to be hired to independently investigate the university’s response.
“The allegations in this case are nothing short of horrifying,” Hochul said in a statement. “For any student to come forward after an experience like this takes extraordinary courage. No student should ever be left wondering whether the institutions meant to protect them will listen and act.”
An email seeking comment was sent to Cornell on Tuesday.
Prosecutor defends decision not to bring charges
In several media interviews on Tuesday, Van Houten argued that while the male students involved did things that were “morally wrong,” the woman’s initial account of the incident to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex.
“She went to the police because she knew it wasn’t right,” Van Houten told CNN.
Van Houten has not released the victim’s sworn statement to police, but instead released a summary with some of her direct quotes included. He also defended his office’s decision not to do additional investigation after the woman, who was identified in court filings by the pseudonym Jane Doe, initially spoke to police.
“There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided,” Van Houten said.
Van Houten’s office did not talk directly to the victim, but the district attorney had told the police that he would sit down with her to explain the law.
Cornell supports reopening investigation
Shortly after the woman first made her allegations in 2024, Cornell publicly disclosed that it was investigating “serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house.” It also announced that the fraternity and several students had been suspended, and that parallel police and school investigations were underway.
On Monday, the university said in a statement that it supported the decision to reopen the criminal investigation, adding that its own investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled. The Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus. Cornell has declined to release more information on discipline for individual students, citing privacy rules.
The woman’s complaint accuses the university of not preventing the alleged assaults and of failing to properly address sexual violence on campus. It includes a photo that it says shows a group chat between frat members discussing the night’s events.
Van Houten called the photo a “red herring,” saying that it had no bearing on the legal analysis of the case.
“We received it, but it was not relevant to the assessment of whether Jane Doe consented or whether there was any evidence of lack of consent on her part as defined by the penal law,” he said.

title: University of Georgia student survives fall from eighth-floor apartment window
text:
'Lucky that she's alive': University of Georgia student recovering after falling from eighth-floor apartment
A University of Georgia student is recovering in the intensive care unit after she fell from the eighth floor of an apartment building in Athens.
Related video: Pond rescue operation in Minnesota
Kristin Sargent, 21, was dancing on a couch and somehow fell out of a nearby window, according to authorities.
She landed on the pool deck, where a lounge chair may have broken her fall.
Sargent is said to have several broken bones. Her father said she is lucky to be alive.
"As you can imagine, pretty badly beaten up, and we're lucky that she's alive and we're blessed," her father, Richard Sargent, said.

title: USDA, HUD sign agreement to streamline affordable housing process
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) Tuesday, officials say will make the homeownership process easier.
“Facing a lot of America today is the lack of affordable housing,” said USDA Sec. Brooke Rollins.
HUD and the USDA are teaming up to streamline standards related to housing, including environmental review, impact, regulations and physical inspections.
“We want to deregulate, make it easier for builders to build and for buyers to buy, and we want to make supply go up and costs go down, so more Americans, particularly in the rural areas of our country, can afford to buy a home,” explained HUD Sec. Scott Turner.
The partnership stems from the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which Congress passed at the end of June. Despite President Trump’s refusal to sign the bill, it eventually became law July 11.
“This MOU signifies and signals to the American people that USDA and HUD are indeed in partnership to make these processes easier, as we have been doing from day one,” Turner added.
Both agencies say the agreement also streamlines the housing approval process by cutting red tape and eliminating unnecessary paperwork to help communities build more homes, faster.
“The unprecedented level at which we’re all working together is a game changer for the American people,” Rollins said.
Average home prices are currently at an all-time high. The national median price for a single-family home is more than $434,000, according to the National Association of Realtors.

title: Red Sox swept out of playoffs by Yankees
text:
NEW YORK — Max Fried dominated Boston in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the New York Yankees romped over the Red Sox 9-2 Wednesday night for a two-game AL Wild Card Series sweep.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston’s 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke the game open with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBI that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, was eliminated by the Yankees in the first round for the second straight year. The Red Sox hit .117 in the two-game series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and were outscored 18-2.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García’s fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead, and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just entered in relief. Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay Bellinger, who won a World Series with New York in 2000.
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, a throwing error, a stolen base, a bunt single and an intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger’s homer.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series opener, hadn’t pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation but entered to start the sixth. On a two-strike pitch to Jones, Crochet bounced a sweeper off catcher Adley Rutschman’s chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled out. The Yankees appealed, and the call was reversed by the video umpire.
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled, and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Austin Wells’ sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout, and Rice, who had four hits and six RBI in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats to make it 8-1.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
Nick Sogard hit a solo homer off Will Warren in the seventh.
UP NEXT
New York right-hander Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.

title: It’s not about the quantity of Collins’ votes, it’s about the quality
text:
It is an undeniable fact that, in our nation’s history, the current administration has the least qualified and most incompetent cabinet members heading our important agencies.
While Sen. Susan Collins frequently cites her record of never missing a vote in the Senate, it is the merit of those votes that matters. If readers followed the Maine Sunday Telegram’s column on how our legislators voted in the prior week, they may recall that she votes for Trump’s right-wing judge nominees. If they check further, they will find that Collins’ vote was one of those that put the notorious Florida District Court Judge Aileen Cannon on the bench during Trump’s first term.
Mainers deserve more than a rubber stamp when the U.S. Senate acts on important nominations and policy issues.
Ervin Snyder
Brunswick

title: Country over party means time’s up for Susan Collins
text:
This lifelong Republican says it’s time for Sen. Collins to go. The reason is simple: her support for Trump.
I have written the senator for more than eight years, always asking for a response. I’ve never gotten one. Odd, considering when I’ve written to Sen. King, I’ve gotten three pages of soggy prose that didn’t address the point.
But the issue is Collins’ support for Trump; her votes for his minions who are harming the American order and her limp opposition when it’s apparent her vote isn’t needed shows me she’s chosen party over country.
I am no particular fan of Mr. Jackson, but I am sure he will stand in robust opposition to the menace in the White House. Country over party.
Earle Wingate
Peru

title: Western Maine gravel riders find adventure, community and a reason to slow down
text:
If mountain biking is about mastering the trail, gravel riding is about seeing where the road goes.
For rider and photographer Andy Gagne, that spirit is at the heart of the Crooked River Rambler, a gravel bike ride scheduled for Sunday, Oct. 11.
“The essence of the Rambler is, ‘Let’s enjoy the ride, let’s enjoy good company, let’s enjoy just going for a bike ride, the fall weather and everyone being together,’” he said.
Gagne and Sarah Kearsley, of Norway, plan to take part in the full experience for the third year, with Gagne hoping to add the optional 10-mile extension to the standard route, which is south of Bethel in the unorganized territory along the Crooked River.
Kearsley calls the Rambler a “Western Maine holiday.” The event is festive, casual and social, she said. She and Gagne like to stop at the aid stations, spaced roughly 10 miles apart, and take their time along the route.
The two regularly ride gravel and back roads around Waterford, Albany Township and Lovell, planning routes that connect dirt roads, paved roads, logging roads and ATV trails. They use GPS to link roads together and, sometimes, to discover where those roads lead.
“It’s an adventure,” Kearsley said.
GRAVEL ROADS, BACK ROADS AND DISCOVERY
Gagne loves western Maine, but said many of the region’s paved roads have become increasingly uncomfortable for cyclists as traffic has increased. Particularly where there are no bike lanes, gravel roads and back roads can offer a safer alternative.
Kearsley, who previously lived in Portland and commuted to work by bicycle with panniers, said she became less interested in riding alongside cars after moving to rural western Maine.
Gravel riding can also be more about endurance and exploration than simply getting from one place to another, she said.
Gagne and Kearsley enjoy piecing together routes from roads and trails that may not appear to be connected. In western Maine, that can require some guesswork.
“A lot of times I have gone out there and I think there’s going to be a road that connects Point A to Point B and there’s nothing,” Gagne said. “Other times I’ll go, and it feels like I’m winning the lottery. It’s this perfect road that I didn’t know existed, and it takes me exactly where I thought it would.”
That unpredictability is part of the appeal.
“In Vermont, you could do a 50-mile ride on perfectly packed-down dirt the whole time,” Gagne said. “That’s what they have there.
“It’s a little spicier here. You have to be willing to go on some bumpier roads here and there.
“I feel like it’s catching on here.”
Gagne said he credits Albany Township residents Jordan Rowell and his wife, Haley Cushing, with doing a good job of creating a ride that fits the region. Another western Maine event, Saddleback’s Northwoods Gravel Grind, was held Sept. 12.
Mahoosuc Land Trust Stewardship Director Spenser Williams notes that, regionally, there are upward of 30 miles of gravel biking opportunities on or through lands conserved by Mahoosuc Land Trust, Western Foothills Land Trust and Greater Lovell Land Trust, including about 1 mile of the Crooked River Rambler.
A RIDE WITH A SENSE OF HUMOR
Rowell, who organizes the Crooked River Rambler with Cushing, was once told that their ride had an excellent “jorts-to-spandex ratio.”
For Rowell, co-host of the event now in its third year, that was a compliment.
“While there’s a time and a place for being serious about your craft or sport, there’s also a time to just have fun with it and be a little goofy,” he said.
That spirit is woven into the Rambler, which Rowell describes simply as “not a race.”
According to a 2023 Cycling Weekly article, the gravel boom, which was reborn in Iowa in the early 2000s, shows no signs of slowing as it has spread across the country. The Union Cycliste Internationale, cycling’s international governing body, defines gravel as a discipline that combines elements of road and mountain-bike cycling and consists primarily of distance riding over unpaved roads.
Rowell discovered cycling as a child, riding trails near his Vermont home. Around 2018, a friend convinced him to get into what he called “the highest endorphins-per-dollar” outdoor activity. He bought a beat-up mountain bike for $600 and eventually found himself riding with Cushing in Moab, Utah.
When the couple moved to western Maine in 2023, they began exploring their new home on two wheels.
Rowell sees the Rambler as an extension of that exploration.
GETTING PEOPLE INTO NATURE
For Rowell, cycling is also a way to get people into nature — and potentially turn them into advocates for the places they encounter.
That idea is central to the Crooked River Rambler, the final event in the Maine Gravel Series. About 150 riders are expected to gather Oct. 11, as Maine foliage approaches its peak. The group will include tandem riders, occasional cyclists and dedicated gravel riders.
The Rambler is designed to be accessible rather than intimidating. Rowell calls it essentially a “zero-sum event.”
“In contrast to some expensive bike events these days, ours is a low entry fee ($30 or $70) and meant to just cover the basic expenses, with some left over to donate to community partners,” he said.
Unlike mountain biking, which generally takes riders onto natural-surface trails, gravel riding typically follows established roads that have already been cleared and surfaced. The Rambler, Rowell says, falls somewhere between the two disciplines.
The route offers plenty to notice along the way: roughly a half-dozen remote ponds, mountain views, farm roads and ATV trails. Local landmarks, including the Hand on the Rock and the Kezar Falls Gorge, add history and local lore.
More importantly, Rowell hopes the ride helps people connect with the Crooked River watershed and understand what makes it special — from its inland salmon spawning grounds to the clean water flowing into Sebago Lake, the region’s largest downstream water body.
Mahoosuc Land Trust and Sebago Clean Waters are working toward protecting 25% of the Sebago Lake watershed — about 35,000 acres — over the next 15 years. This year, Greater Lovell Land Trust is joining the Rambler as a community partner, adding another dimension to an event that celebrates not only riding, but the landscape itself and the people working to protect it.
BUILDING COMMUNITY
The Rambler is also deliberately local.
With lawn parking, strong community participation and an intentionally informal atmosphere, the event has some of the feel of the long-running Songo Pond triathlon, which ended in 2017 after 26 years.
There are several ways to ride the course. The standard route is 33 miles. Riders looking for more can take the Crooked-Kezar Extension, bringing the total to 43 miles, while those wanting a shorter outing can take Melby’s cutoff for a 23-mile ride.
Rowell describes the new 10-mile extension in typically irreverent fashion. It is for the “piddle-pedalers who want to keep on pushing, blasting you on up to the finest hill country general store there ever was: the Center Lovell Market. Enjoy the Baldface views and a sneaky cute antique shop, then send it back down to the Kezar River valley floor and bring ’er on home.”
Back at the finish, riders can gather for food, libations, yard games and music, including a performance by hyperlocal musician Keith Briggs, who lives just down the road. Those who want to linger can camp Saturday and Sunday nights, with a Sunday evening campfire and s’mores.
Along the course, aid stations will offer Maine-inspired fuel, including whoopie pies, as well as pretzels and fondue.
Beneath the jorts, spandex and whoopie pies is something more fundamental: a love of being outside with other people and an appreciation for the places a bicycle can take you.
But Rowell hopes it is also something more — a reason to slow down, look around and become a little more invested in the place beneath the tires.
The idea is simple: You are more likely to care about a place once you have experienced it.

title: Troy Jackson's Gaza misstep shows him struggling with a big step up to national politics
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson’s apology this week for remarks on the Israel-Gaza war showed that the longtime state lawmaker is still finding his footing on foreign policy.
Jackson has called Israel’s response to the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas a “genocide” and called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a war criminal. In a News Center Maine interview Tuesday, he suggested some Mainers are uncomfortable calling Israel’s actions in Gaza a genocide because they are Jewish. He apologized for the generalization in a Wednesday statement but stood by the genocide charge.
The stumble comes less than 40 days before Election Day. Jackson is working through one of the most divisive issues on the left while running against strongly pro-Israel Republican Sen. Susan Collins. Jackson said in the interview the only other country he has traveled to is Canada, which borders his hometown of Allagash.
The episode showed that Jackson lacks the experience and polish of many major federal candidates, Brian Kresge, president of Congregation Beth Israel in Bangor, said.
“He’s still feeling his way through foreign policy chops,” Kresge said. “If he’s apologizing for anything to the Maine Jewish community, he should apologize for calling it a genocide.”
Jackson, a former Maine Senate president who served 20 years in Augusta, said he had “never had to deal with” the Middle East as a state lawmaker. In the same interview, he said he would push for a better relationship with Canada after President Donald Trump’s tariffs. He also sharply criticized Trump and Collins over the Iran war’s effects on the economy.
Progressives have long criticized Collins for backing military and economic aid to Israel and accepting millions of dollars from pro-Israel groups. She also supported strict guardrails or cuts to aid for Palestinians in Gaza after Hamas’ attack.
In a recent Wall Street Journal interview, Collins suggested Graham Platner had required his replacement “to be very anti-Israel, to accuse Israel of committing genocide.”
“In fact it was Hamas, the terrorist group, that killed more Jewish citizens of Israel and Americans on [Oct. 7, 2023], the greatest loss of Jewish life in a single day since the Holocaust,” Collins said.
Republicans on social media called Jackson’s remarks antisemitic, trying to tie him to Platner’s widely denounced Nazi-linked tattoo. They have also cast the episode as further proof that Jackson isn’t ready to represent Maine, especially over a five-term incumbent.
“He just repeats slogans without knowing the facts,” former Maine House Minority Leader Joe Bruno of Raymond said.
But Jackson’s allies say Mainers care far more about the economy. State Sen. Joe Baldacci, D-Bangor, dismissed concerns about Jackson’s qualifications, pointing to legislation that helped children, parents and teachers during his time in Augusta.
“He’ll know how to balance U.S. interests and stand up for American values,” Baldacci said.
On Wednesday, Jackson pledged to “always listen and work to approach these conversations with the care and respect they deserve.” He said if elected he would fight antisemitism and “work for lasting peace and security for Palestinians and Israelis.”
J Street, the liberal Zionist group that supports a two-state solution, is standing by him. Tali deGroot of J Street said the group was “proud to stand with Troy Jackson, who we know will be a champion of peace for Israelis and Palestinians alike.”
“His moral clarity on this issue stands in sharp contrast to Susan Collins, who has cosigned blank-check support for Netanyahu’s extremist policies for decades,” deGroot said.
This issue is among the most charged ones for Jews and the Democratic Party this midterm season. Amy Fried, a retired University of Maine political scientist from Bangor who is a Jewish Democrat, said Jackson is newly being asked about an issue “that some see in simple terms and others view with mixed understandings and considerations.”
Kresge, who described himself as a “liberal zionist,” said he won’t vote for Collins, calling her a “blank check” for the Trump administration. But he isn’t supporting Jackson either, saying he believes using the word “genocide” with regard to Gaza is antisemitic even though he doesn’t view the candidate as an antisemite.
“I see a guy that cares,” he said of Jackson. “But the debate among the Bangor Jewish community is, ‘Do I vote for Susan Collins, or just not at all?’”

title: New midcoast superintendent not reviving school closure talks
text:
Kermit Nickerson School opened its doors again this fall. The Swanville elementary school survived a proposal to close it last spring, but the questions behind that proposal remain: How should Regional School Unit 71 serve students across five towns as enrollment declines, buildings age and the cost of education rises?
For Superintendent Elizabeth “Liz” Ridgeway, who took office July 1 after two years of interim leadership, the challenge reaches well beyond one building. RSU 71 serves Belfast, Belmont, Morrill, Searsmont and Swanville. Its youngest students attend five elementary schools: Captain Albert Stevens and East Belfast in Belfast, Gladys Weymouth in Morrill, Ames in Searsmont and Nickerson in Swanville. Students later come together at Troy Howard Middle School and Belfast Area High School. The district’s current school listings still include all five elementary buildings.
Nickerson became the focus of the debate because it had fewer than 60 students when then-interim Superintendent Bob England proposed closing it and moving its third- through fifth-graders to Captain Albert Stevens School. England estimated the move would save about $450,000 a year, with a possible additional $90,000 if the district leased the Swanville building.
Supporters saw an opportunity to reduce costs and give students access to more resources.
Families and other residents questioned the speed of the process and what the move would mean for children and their community.
The proposal failed at a March board meeting. Although six members supported beginning the closure process and two opposed it, the measure did not meet the required two-thirds threshold under the board’s weighted voting system. Nickerson remained open for the 2026–27 school year.
The vote settled Nickerson’s immediate future. It did not settle whether RSU 71 can afford its present arrangement indefinitely, or whether a different arrangement would better serve students. Ridgeway has said it is premature to put another elementary closure on the table. She expects the district to keep discussing how many schools it operates and how it delivers elementary education.
“I think it’s important we get the (RSU 71) community involved,” Ridgeway said of the RSU 71 Board of Directors and administration, adding, “and whatever we do needs to be transparent.”
Ridgeway has seen how long those conversations can last. While cleaning out her former office at Gladys Weymouth School, where she had served as principal, she found a plan from 2004 to close the school. It was never carried out. The discovery puts the Nickerson dispute in perspective: communities in the Belfast area have been confronting versions of the same question for more than two decades.
A lasting decision will require more than comparing enrollment with building capacity. Keeping several small schools open means paying to staff, heat, maintain and transport students among them. Closing a school may reduce some of those expenses, but it can also require changes to bus routes, classrooms, staffing and services at the school receiving its students. Families may value a nearby school for reasons that do not appear in an operating budget.
The district has studied pieces of that problem over the years, including a possible consolidated elementary site and, most recently, a detailed proposal for Nickerson. The materials provided for this story, together with the district’s publicly posted budget documents, do not establish that RSU 71 has completed a current, districtwide comparison of all five elementary buildings and several possible school configurations. Such a study could show how projected enrollment, repairs, transportation, student services and costs change under each option. Without one, the board and public face another risk: debating the fate of a particular school before agreeing on what they want the elementary system to provide.
The pressure is financial as well as geographic. Voters approved RSU 71’s 2026–27 budget at a May 26 district meeting and validated it in a June 9 referendum. The district’s budget page shows that administrators examined expenses across the system, including transportation, vehicle replacement and a reorganization of elementary leadership. Those discussions reflect the difficulty of controlling local costs while maintaining programs in buildings spread across five municipalities.
Special education adds another demanding part of that calculation. Maine’s fiscal 2027 funding records list more than $6 million in relevant special education expenditures for RSU 71. That figure is not a measure of a simple funding shortfall; the state’s allocation formula has multiple components. It does show the scale of services the district must plan and pay for even as it considers changes elsewhere. During the Nickerson discussion, a behavioral health provider also raised the possibility of using the building for students with significant needs if it became vacant. Because the school stayed open, that proposal did not proceed as envisioned.
RSU 71 has already changed how it manages its elementary schools. Its reorganization places one principal over the elementary system, with assistant principals in the buildings. Ridgeway has said daily access to an administrator matters as schools respond to students’ behavioral and other support needs. She also wants staff and community organizations to coordinate more closely so students receive help without gaps or duplicated efforts.
Facilities pose another set of decisions. Voters rejected a $3.5 million bond for track and athletic improvements last November, leaving the district to look for another way to address those needs. Meanwhile, the Waldo County Technical Center, which serves students from multiple districts, is seeking state support for a new regional facility. Ridgeway has said a decision on that application is expected in January. The two projects differ in scope, but both show how future educational opportunities depend in part on expensive physical space.
Ridgeway arrives with firsthand knowledge of two of RSU 71’s elementary schools and a background that includes classroom teaching, school administration and public finance. Her task now is to help the district move from recurring arguments over individual buildings toward a shared account of what students need, what each option costs and what the five communities are willing to support.
For the moment, the five elementary schools remain open. The harder decision lies ahead: whether RSU 71 can preserve the strengths of neighborhood schools while adapting to fewer students, greater service needs and facilities that will not grow less expensive with time.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Tracy Bonney-Corson, Parkman Nursing Leader And Rail Yard Brewing Co-owner, Dies In Crow Hill Road Crash
text:
Former Piscataquis County VP Of Nursing-Turned-Brewery-Owner Found Deceased After Crash In Parkman Tuesday Night
Authorities in Piscataquic County are trying to piece together the details of a deadly crash that claimed the life of one person late Tuesday evening.
According to the Piscataquis County Sheriff's Office, their communications center received a notification just before 11:30 PM, that a crash had occurred somewhere in the area of the Crow Hill Road in Parkman, so they sent authorities out to investigate.
"A deputy along with Guilford Fire and Mayo Ambulance were dispatched to the area. Upon checking the area, the deputy discovered a vehicle gone off the road and crashed into a telephone pole. The deputy started searching for the operator and found the female operator had been ejected from the vehicle."
Read More: Maine Authorities Locate Missing Blue Hill Boater
The sheriff's office says the woman, 61-year-old Tracy Bonney-Corson of Parkman, was pronounced dead by the EMTs on the scene.
Corson was well known in the Piscataquis County community as a former VP of Nursing at a local hospital for over 30 years and more recently co-owner of Rail Yard Brewing, which she opened with her long-time friend, John Riitano, last year.
Read More: New Restaurant And Brewery Opening In Milo, Maine Soon
Riitano addressed Corson's passing on the Brewery's social media page.
"It is with an extremely heavy heart that I have to report the passing of my dear friend and business partner, Tracy Bonney-Corson... During this extremely sad time, please keep Tracy's family in your thoughts and prayers. Knowing Tracy, she would not want us to skip a beat, and she would insist we keep pushing forward! Tracy loved Trivia Night and loved the community support and love you all gave us at Rail Yard. Tracy wanted Rail Yard and Rusty Rail to be a gathering place for the community, and that is just what it has become. So, in Tracy's honor, we will press on and continue to be a community hub where we can gather to celebrate the good times and be there for each other in the sad times."
The Crow Hill Road, like many rural routes across the state, can often experience muddy conditions when the weather is wet. Providing access to places like Bennett Pond, and connecting with many secondary roads like the Armstrong and Trafton Roads, it's sometimes used as a cut-through of sorts.
Earlier this summer, the town replaced a culvert along a section of the Crow Hill Road, and shut it down for an afternoon, but the closure was temporary, and there were no other known issues to the roadway.
Read More: Maine State Police Search For Suspect After Skowhegan Drug Stop
Authorities will continue to investigate Tuesday night's crash. We will update the story when more details become available.
In the meantime, we send our deepest condolences out to Corson's family, friends and community in Piscataquis County.

title: Hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin gives biggest gift in US college history to rethink education for the AI era
text:
(AP) - Carnegie Mellon University announced Wednesday that hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin is donating $3 billion, with the bulk of the money for a new campus in Miami focused on societal challenges.
The Pittsburgh-based private research university said the gift is the largest ever single gift to a U.S. university. Other donations topping the billion-dollar mark include $1.8 billion from former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg to Johns Hopkins University in 2018. And Nike co-founder Phil Knight and his wife, Penny, also have been prolific donors, including a $2 billion gift to Oregon Health & Science University in 2025.
Griffin’s gift includes $2 billion to build a new 35-acre campus in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood, just north of downtown. The campus is expected to enroll around 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and doctoral students. Construction is scheduled to begin next year.
Rather than academic majors, it will focus on what the university and Griffin described in a news release as “grand challenge areas,” such as human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation.
The rest of the money will be divided evenly between the Pittsburgh campus’ computer science program, which will be renamed after Griffin, and other unspecified projects on the main campus.
“Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems,” Carnegie Mellon’s President Farnam Jahanian said in a news release praising Griffin. “ Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others.”
Colleges are facing growing pressure to prepare students for a workforce that is rapidly being transformed by AI. Job postings including AI and machine learning in the skills requirements or job title are exploding.
At the same time, financial pressures on higher education are mounting. International enrollment is dropping, just as many states are seeing their classes of high school seniors begin to shrink because of U.S. demographic changes. Meanwhile, expenses like fuel, healthcare and technology are rising.
Griffin, a GOP megadonor who founded the Citadel investment firm, owns a waterfront home in Miami, which is part of a growing metropolitan area whose population tops 6.4 million.
The area already is home to the University of Miami, a private research university; Florida International University, a public research university; and Miami Dade College, which started out as a community college but also offers some four-year degrees. Combined, enrollment at the three schools totals around 135,000. Several smaller private colleges are also based in the area.
But Griffin, who has donated over the years to causes such as medical research, charter schools and other universities, saw room for something new.
“The opportunity to bring Carnegie Mellon to Miami places our city at the heart of humanistic and scientific advancement and amplifies the University’s international reach and impact,” said Griffin, who is joining Carnegie Mellon’s Board of Trustees, in a news release.
Even before the announcement, Carnegie Mellon had growing ties to Florida, a state where conservatives have increased their influence on higher education.
Its computer science department runs a program designed to teach middle school students in Florida and several other states about AI. The university also is involved in a partnership with the Gates Foundation to deploy AI-powered course materials for introductory math classes at Miami Dade College.

title: UMaine men’s hockey team looks to regain its culture
text:
ORONO — On Tuesday, Ben Barr thanked the University of Maine men’s hockey team on behalf of himself and the entire coaching staff. They’re all getting their 40 winks every night, sound sleep from head hitting pillow to morning alarm, and that’s due in large part to the effort the Black Bears put in every day.
“I expect them to bring effort and attitude, and they’ve been bringing that every practice since we started,” Barr said after Tuesday’s practice. “That doesn’t mean we go out and win just because we work hard. There’s another level for that, but at least we know we’ll be in the fight with the work ethic I think we’ve established so far.”
The season opens this weekend with a pair of games at Holy Cross. The Black Bears, as Barr put it, are trying to find the program’s soul again.
Go ahead and call this a resetting season for the Black Bears, who followed the 2025 Hockey East championship with an 18-14-3 record last season. A few years ago, when Barr was starting a program rebuild, that would have been a cause for minor jubilation as a positive step.
A Hockey East crown and two straight appearances in the NCAA tournament changed expectations. A season with 18 wins isn’t progress anymore, it’s disappointment.
The 2025-26 season was one of upheaval across college hockey. For the first time, players from the three Canadian major junior leagues and Canadian colleges (U Sports) were NCAA eligible. It turned the recruiting landscape into the wild west. Yeah, this guy can play but is he a fit for our program? Often the question was met with a shrug and the hope that things would work out.
At Maine, the influx of CHL players was a mixed bag. Of the nine players Barr brought in from the CHL or U Sports last season, five have already left via the transfer portal. Good hockey players? Yes. The right fit for Maine’s blue-collar culture? No.
“For three or four years, we were building something. We were trying to do it a certain way. Then the whole world tips upside down as far as the NCAA stuff’s concerned. You have a little bit of a turbulent year as far some of the decisions we make,” said Barr, now in his sixth season as Maine’s head coach.
Barr can take blame for last season’s team culture issues, which reached its nadir in a December home loss to rival New Hampshire, but players know it starts with them. Team captain Owen Fowler knows what kind of team he wants to see on the ice. Fowler wants the Black Bears to use their size to forecheck hard and play gritty hockey, looking to erode the stamina of opponents.
“We’re going to wear teams down a lot. Kind of similar to my first year (that Hockey East title season), where there were definitely a lot of games we won in the third period,” Fowler said.
Maine has 15 newcomers on a 28-player roster. That’s a lot of turnover, Barr admits. Nine of the newcomers are transfers with college hockey experience. They bring a higher maturity level, and that’s a good thing.
If that maturity manifests as players willing to go after rebounds and tipped pucks to score goals, and guys who set screens to get a teammate an open shot, it will be a very good thing. Last season’s top four scorers are gone. Brandon Holt graduated. Josh Nadeau signed a pro contract with Montreal. Justin Poirier and Miguel Marques transferred.
“We have enough good hockey players on this team to go out against anybody. The execution piece is just finding that little bit of extra will. That will be the challenge,” Barr said.
Assistant captain Sully Scholle said he’s done talking about last season. The focus has to be on the now. Assistant captain Max Scott said this season’s team already feels like a tighter-knit group that last year’s ever was. Barr sees that, too, and noted that they care about each other, and that’s been evident for a couple months.
It didn’t take Barr long to lift Maine into college hockey’s upper tier again after more than a decade outside of it. Ups and downs are a given, and Barr noted that camaraderie and a willingness to work hard doesn’t translate into 10 goals a game.
It’s a sturdy foundation, though, and one the Black Bears need. It’s what will help determine if last season was a hiccup, or the start of a trend.

title: College student falls 70 feet off overpass while trying to avoid truck in multi-car crash
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) - A Kansas college student survived falling 70 feet from an overpass while trying to avoid being hit by an oncoming truck during a multi-car crash.
Kyra Kinnison and Sara Celeen are close friends after they met at Kansas State University over two years ago.
“[Kyra is] just a really amazing person, very sweet and helpful. She’s always there if you need something,” Celeen said.
It’s a friendship that was almost lost. Kinnison, 21, and her boyfriend were traveling separately to Salina last Friday night when they encountered a hazard on highway K-18.
“[Her boyfriend] swerved around it and stopped. And [Kyra] pulled over to the side of the road, and then, a vehicle crashed into his vehicle,” Celeen said.
But it didn’t stop there, as more oncoming cars piled up behind, causing a multi-vehicle crash. Kinnison, who was walking along the shoulder on the overpass, was in the path of danger with a truck coming at full speed in her direction.
“She jumped back to get out of the way, and the railing is not very good; you can easily lean over it and fall,” Celeen said.
Kinnison fell 70 feet and suffered serious injuries.
“She had fractures on her back, some of her vertebrae, her pelvis and her tailbone,” Celeen said.
But despite all odds, Kinnison can still walk. Her family from North Carolina paid her a visit in the hospital, alongside Celeen.
“I’m just glad she’s not paralyzed for life,” Celeen said. “There really was a guardian angel out there, looking out for her.”
But what still lies ahead in Kinnison’s journey is healing and the financial cost of it. That’s why Celeen is raising money on GoFundMe, and the community is already rallying behind her.
“It’s just amazing the community we have here. Everyone that’s been supporting her is just amazing,” Celeen said.

title: Woman accused of ‘extreme’ neglect that led to 12-year-old daughter’s death
text:
GADSDEN, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) — Police in Alabama have arrested a woman in connection with the death of a 12-year-old girl.
Leslie Denise Wilson, 35, is charged with felony murder in the death of her daughter, who had cerebral palsy, according to prosecutors.
Neglect allegations detailed in complaint
According to the complaint, between May 1 and June 17, Wilson subjected the child to “ongoing and extreme medical and/or physical neglect causing serious physical injury.”
The complaint said the child died as a result.
Gadsden police said officers initially responded to what was reported as a natural death. Because of the child’s age and the circumstances surrounding the death, the Gadsden Police Department’s Juvenile Unit and the Alabama Department of Human Resources began an investigation.
Aniah’s Law hearing held
An Aniah’s Law hearing was held Tuesday for Wilson.
Detective Alec Burgess with the Gadsden Police Department’s Major Crimes Division testified at the hearing and described what he saw when he was called to the home on reports of a natural death.
Burgess recalled finding a 12-year-old girl in a bedroom with marks on her body and live maggots inside her diaper. He described the girl as malnourished and dehydrated, and said she had pneumonia.
According to Burgess, the 12-year-old weighed 32 pounds and depended on a feeding tube. He said her younger siblings had been caring for her and that there was limited food inside the home.
Autopsy ruled homicide
An autopsy ruled the child’s death a homicide, and investigators developed evidence of abuse and neglect, according to police. At the hearing, Burgess said the autopsy showed the girl died from sepsis.
“Seeing a child, because I have children of my own, it’s heartbreaking. Prayers are with the family and the parents, and the family that is going through this hard time. Not only with that family, we want to pray for our police department. It’s tough to see our law enforcement going through the same thing because it hurts them also,” said Etowah County Assistant Coroner Dantez Robinson.
Police did not share the child’s name due to the nature of the case and her age.
Etowah County Judge Joe Nabors denied bond for Wilson.
Gadsden police said the case remains an active investigation.

title: Lawmakers make bipartisan push to save U.S. film industry
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Lawmakers say other countries have started offering stronger incentives to make movies than the United States, and if the U.S. does not keep up, it will lose a sizeable chunk of the industry.
Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said there is a shift happening in the film industry.
“What you’ll notice, if you’re in the theaters as I am all the time is that the actors are in different countries. They’re filming everywhere. And less and less are they filming at home,” Scott said.
Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) said the film industry creates a larger economic impact than many realize.
“It helps with tourism, and it creates jobs and opportunity all across the entertainment ecosystem, as well as industries that benefit from the net impact of this industry,” Warnock said.
The bill would offer base tax credits between 20 and 30 percent depending on various factors of how much the film is shot in the U.S. and where.
Lawmakers hope it can be a boon for all areas of the country.
“One thing we don’t want this to be is a bill for one state. Obviously I wouldn’t be here if that was the case,” Scott said.
Advocates of the bill say it would also benefit consumers by allowing more American stories to be told.
“Stories literally transform the world. And they give us a view of what’s possible,” Warnock said.
In addition to the support of President Donald Trump, the bill is backed by industry leaders like director Christopher Nolan and actor Jon Voight.
