title: Portland art exhibit contrasts 2 artists with a shared language in color
text:
Hot on the heels of the Impressionist and post-Impressionist movements in France, the painter Paul Sérusier founded Les Nabis, an almost devotional brotherhood of Symbolists who believed that usual modes of articulation and understanding had greater underlying powers that were elusive to most people (read: anyone who lacked the depth of what they perceived as their own spiritual profundity). Sérusier and fellow Nabis painters — Pierre Bonnard, Maurice Denis, Édouard Vuillard and others — determined that the artist’s mission was to unearth and release this abstract power from more common, intellectual and, so, superficial interpretations of their work.
Before each of their meetings, they would intone a kind of mantra, affirming that “Sounds, colors, and words have a miraculously expressive power beyond all representation, and even beyond the literal meaning of the words.” Especially in regards to color, “A Backwards Bloom” at Space gallery (through Nov. 14) asks us to attempt to tap into that subtler dimension of sensing and perception.
On the face of it, the connection between the two featured painters — Portland-based Stephen Benenson and Ellenville, New York-based Michael Berryhill — might seem tenuous. The former presents perfectly legible, if mysterious, paintings drawn from the story of “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.” The latter has only a cursory relationship with decipherable imagery, freely blending figuration with abstraction in a way that partially obfuscates both.
Benenson’s application of paint is thick and luscious and emanates a glossy reflectivity. Berryhill, on the other hand, deploys a nearly dry brush so that the paint’s texture feels thinner and chalky. Yet the paintings of both men nevertheless manage to convey an at times scalding luminosity.
As if to prove the Nabis’ thesis, we can intuit what unites the two painters in synchronous relationship as an intangible shared vibration arising from the language of color. Their palettes are similar, particularly a shade of bubblegum pink favored by Philip Guston that somehow seems to be able to convey, by turns, lush abundance (Berryhill’s “Palais Romantique”), fleshy vulnerability (Benenson’s “The Hatter’s Table #1”), or a slightly uncomfortable sense of ennui (Berryhill’s “Gloria” and Benenson’s “Transformation”).
For both artists, color, regardless of an image onto which we can affix rational interpretation, is the primary delivery system of meaning. Benenson and Berryhill both work on their paintings over time, often obsessively. Berryhill has been known to alter a painting 50 or 60 times before it feels complete. And if you follow a wall sign that reads “Rabbit Hole” and directs you to the backroom, there you will find a time-lapse video filmed over four months that elucidates the evolution of Benenson’s “The Hatters Table #2.” We see him deepening then lightening colors then darkening them again, scraping off hues and painting others over them. Clearly, both artists know intuitively that getting the color right ensures they have accurately portrayed something more essential about the image (whether representational or abstract) before us.
If you doubt the innate power of color to do this, there is no easier exercise than to very slowly circle the gallery and observe the emotions and sensations that arise in your body as you encounter each painting. For instance, we can be disoriented by a painting like Benenson’s “Golden Afternoon.” The title sounds idyllic, but the subject matter feels a little creepy. The more we contemplate it, the more we discern that what gives the work its disorienting quality is not the image itself. The tornado-sky greens that permeate “Golden Afternoon” and the inky blacks of the oversized flora are the primary vehicles of the eeriness we feel.
Conversely, our brains can be confounded by Berryhill’s “Unbound,” one of the most spectacular and beautiful paintings in the show. In its enveloping proportions (90 inches by 74 inches) we at first identify what looks like an enormous floral or fruit still life. But hang on. What is that figure on the right that seems to be walking around to the back of it? Why is the still life so outsized compared to the body? Where is that body in space exactly?
This is typical of the sort of confluence of abstraction and figuration that Berryhill trucks in, one that forces us to let go of our commitment to either and perceive the image from a more, shall we say, unbounded dimension. Once we surrender to his imperative, we can blissfully lose ourselves in the painting’s movement of color, which traverses various blues, oranges, greens, yellows and pinks. Despite its irrationality as an image — something that knocks us for a loop — the color is what pushes our confusion into the background and leaves us with a wistful, dreamy pleasure.
All the works in the show are also multilayered. Both painters build up their canvases through a sequential process of addition and subtraction, applying color, abrading it, then applying more, possibly different, color before abrading that too… and on and on. But the scraping away is not about obliteration, for Benenson and Berryhill actually want us to see through it. The aim is to add depth and understanding to their own processes and to imbed a visible record of history. This, in turn, adds still more layers of meaning. Benenson and Berryhill are both laying bare their own meticulous and exacting techniques — which give each painting a quality of something hard-won — and clear evidence of the work’s evolution and development within and through time.
An interesting side note: The show came about because Benenson, who maintains a studio above Space, had a show coming up at the gallery. To ramp up the curatorial quotient, he was asked to create a list of painters whose work he admired and with whom he’d like to be shown. Berryhill was one of those, primarily because Benenson considers him — as do others — one of the most important colorists of his time. Not only were their palettes symbiotic, but it also happened that both men had had a quasi-obsession with the same work, an obscure Piero della Francesca painting called “The Nativity.”
This, too, jibes splendidly with Les Nabis’ spiritual orientations. It mirrors a quantum physics concept that has given credence to the mystical belief that everything is connected. Entanglement theory proposes that one phenomenon affecting a particle can have the exact same effect on another particle regardless of the physical distance between them.
Which made me wonder about this profound ability of color to translate meaning. Does a specific shade of yellow resonate the same way, or elicit the same reaction, in all of us? Is there a common, identifiable sensorial experience associated with blue or lavender? “A Backwards Bloom” would be a great place to carry out this experiment. So, when you go, bring friends along too!
Jorge S. Arango has written about art, design and architecture for over 35 years. He lives in Portland and can be reached at [email protected]. This column is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.
“A Backwards Bloom,” through Nov. 14. Space, 534 Congress St., 207-828-5600, space538.org.

title: Tennessee prepares to execute a woman for a crime she committed at age 18
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee is preparing to put to death Christa Gail Pike for a 1995 murder she committed at age 18 in what would be the state’s first execution of a woman in at least 200 years.
Pike, now 50, is scheduled to be executed Wednesday morning by lethal injection at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of stabbing and beating 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville.
The case garnered widespread attention at the time in part because a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer’s body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s. As the execution date drew near, it renewed debate over the death penalty for young offenders.
Pike does not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argue the state should consider Pike’s age at the time, mental illness and a history of severe sexual abuse that included being raped from the time she was a toddler. Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike’s death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds sentenced to death in Tennessee have had their sentences vacated.
The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday denied a request from Pike’s attorneys to halt the execution. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee on Monday denied Pike clemency.
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”
Slemmer’s mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.
“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” May Martinez said in a telephone interview.
Martinez said a group helped raise money so she and her husband could travel from Florida to witness the execution.
The 1995 killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body.
Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.
Tennessee has not executed a woman for at least 200 years, according to Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Older records can be spotty, though, so it’s difficult to know precise details about the last woman who was put to death there.
It’s a rarity across the U.S. Since 1976, 18 women have been put to death in the country, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the center.
Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the U.S. In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the U.S. government put a female inmate to death.
___
Chandler reported from Montgomery, Alabama.

title: Pennsylvania records 5th measles death amid worst US year since 1991
text:
(AP) - Pennsylvania health officials reported a fifth measles-associated death Wednesday as the U.S. endures its worst year for the disease since 1991.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said the person was from Lancaster County and was unvaccinated. The state did not provide any further information about the person who died. Lancaster County’s coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said that his office did not handle the death and that state officials have not provided him with any details.
The state’s other deaths have included an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County, in the center of the state; a 40-year-old woman from Jefferson County, a rural area in western Pennsylvania; and two infants in Lancaster County, in the southeastern part of the state.
None of them were vaccinated, according to the state health department. The infants were too young for vaccinations, according to current recommendations.
The U.S. has now seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to grow, with 943 illnesses reported so far this year across 39 counties. The measles-associated deaths are the first reported in the state in 35 years, state officials say.
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
The problem has been years in the making, as fewer kids get routine vaccines because of parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation. More recently, Trump administration health officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have questioned and sown doubt about the established safety of vaccines at an unprecedented level while also defunding local efforts to improve vaccination rates.

title: The 10 largest credit unions in the US
text:
The 10 largest credit unions in the US
Key takeaways
- With over $200 billion in assets, Navy Federal is by far the largest credit union in the U.S.
- Most of the 10 largest credit unions restrict membership, but PenFed and Alliant are notable exceptions — anyone can join.
- Federal data shows that credit unions are growing steadily.
While the top ten largest credit unions still hold significantly less in assets than even the top five largest banks, they have been growing considerably in recent years.
In six years, total assets in federally insured credit unions have risen by over 48%, increasing from $1.64 trillion in March 2020 to just under $2.5 trillion in the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
Credit Unions may be drawing customers with their community focus, not-for-profit setup and tendency to offer competitive annual percentage yields (APYs).
The 10 largest credit unions collectively hold approximately $392.6 billion worth of deposits and $456.4 billion in total assets, according to the most recent NCUA data.
Here’s a breakdown of the biggest credit unions in the U.S. by total assets as of September 2026.
Some of these credit unions restrict membership based on factors such as residence or profession. Others — such as Pentagon Federal Credit Union (PenFed) and Alliant — make it easy for anyone to join.
Assets vs. deposits
You’ll see references to two different (large) numbers on this page — a credit union’s total assets and its total deposits.
- Deposits refers to the amount of money that members have put into deposit accounts, such as checking and savings accounts.
- Assets include deposits but also other financial instruments, like loans and investments.
1. Navy Federal Credit Union
Navy Federal is the largest credit union in the country. It has more than 15 and a half million members and holds over $170 billion in deposits. The credit union offers a full suite of financial products and services, including deposit products like checking and savings accounts along with credit products like credit cards and auto loans.
In order to be a member, you or a family/household member must have a tie to the armed forces, the U.S. Department of Defense or the National Guard.
- Assets: $204.46 billion
- Headquarters: Vienna, Virginia
- Footprint: More than 300 branches in 31 states and Washington, D.C.
- Members: 15.52 million
2. State Employees’ Credit Union
Chartered in 1937, State Employees’ is the second-largest credit union in the U.S. With just over $50 billion in deposits, State Employees’ has nearly 3 million members. Membership is open primarily to North Carolina state employees and their families.
- Assets: $59.97 billion
- Headquarters: Raleigh, North Carolina
- Footprint: Nearly 270 branches in North Carolina, plus CO-OP shared branches
- Members: 3 million
3. SchoolsFirst Federal Credit Union
SchoolsFirst is a California-based institution servicing nearly 1.6 million members. The credit union holds more than $30 billion in total deposits. The credit union serves educational communities in California.
As such, membership is open to current or retired school employees living in California or those with a family member who belongs to the credit union. Membership is also open to employees living in California whose company primarily offers direct services to a school or district in California, or college students enrolled in eligible education programs with a student teaching requirement.
- Assets: $37.23 billion
- Headquarters: Santa Ana, California
- Footprint: More than 70 branches in California
- Members: 1.58 million
4. Boeing Employees Credit Union
Boeing Employees’ Credit Union (BECU) is the fifth-largest credit union in the U.S. and the largest credit union in Washington state. BECU has nearly 1.6 million members, and holds more than $25 billion in deposits. Membership is currently open to those who live, work or go to school in Washington state, but residents of select counties in Oregon, Idaho and South Carolina, and those who are affiliated with partner companies and organizations are also eligible.
- Assets: $29.62 billion
- Headquarters: Tukwila, Washington
- Footprint: About 70 branches in Washington and South Carolina plus CO-OP shared branches
- Members: 1.6 million
5. Pentagon Federal Credit Union
Pentagon Federal Credit Union has more than 2.7 million members and deposits totaling over $25 billion. The credit union has branches scattered across the U.S., but provides a full spectrum of financial products, including certificates of deposit, money market, checking accounts and savings accounts. Unlike many other credit unions, PenFed membership is open to anyone.
- Assets: $29.2 billion
- Headquarters: McLean, Virginia
- Footprint: 38 branches in 10 states, Washington, D.C. and three territories
- Members: 2.75 million
6. First Technology Credit Union

title: How can we trust Susan Collins on the environment?
text:
I heat my home with a heat pump. It keeps the house warm through a Maine winter and costs less than the oil it replaced. It was one reason I was so disappointed that Sen. Susan Collins voted to advance the 2025 budget bill that rolled back the tax credits that help other Maine families make the same switch.
Sen. Collins often positions herself as an environmentalist, but her voting record doesn’t always reflect that. She earned a 0% rating from the League of Conservation Voters in 2024 and 31% in 2025, alongside her vote against the Inflation Reduction Act. Most recently, Collins voted to confirm Eighth Circuit judge Justin Smith, whose record as Missouri’s deputy attorney general included backing industry challenges to state clean water protections.
On May 18, Collins voted to confirm Stevan Pearce as director of the Bureau of Land Management, which oversees more than 245 million acres of public lands. Pearce has a track record of supporting the sell-off of public lands, conflicts of interest with the oil and gas industry and a history of trying to shrink and block the designation of national monuments.
Maine’s clean air, rivers and reduced dependence on heating oil didn’t happen by accident. Given her recent votes, how can Mainers trust Sen. Collins to protect our environment from big oil and gas?
Stephen Simpson
Portland

title: Bangor is a finalist for new refueling squadron
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Air Force has named Bangor as one of four finalists for a new air refueling squadron.
U.S. Sens. Susan Collins, a Republican, and Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, learned about that Tuesday from Michael Saunders, the Air Force’s principal deputy assistant secretary for energy, installations and environment, and Maj. Gen. Bryony Terrell, deputy director of the Air National Guard.
Bangor was among 14 Air National Guard bases under consideration. The other three finalists are: Forbes Field Air National Guard Base in Topeka, Kansas; Key Field Air National Guard Base in Meridian, Mississippi; and Rickenbacker Air National Guard Base near Columbus, Ohio; according to a spokesperson for King’s office.
“This announcement from the Air Force is an important step toward equipping the MAINEiacs with the advanced aircraft they need to carry out their critical mission,” Collins and King said in a statement. “Bangor’s strategic location and the proven excellence of the 101st Air Refueling Wing make a compelling case for bringing the KC-46 to Maine. We will continue to press for Bangor’s selection as the selection process continues.”
A decision will be made early next year, and if Bangor is selected, new military aircraft will begin moving here in 2030.
The 101st Air Refueling Wing, which calls Bangor home, is assigned the aging KC-135 Stratotankers, which could be replaced by the KC-46A, if the 101st makes the cut.
In making the announcement Tuesday afternoon, Collins touted tens of millions of dollars that she’s secured for air guard bases in Bangor and Saco, including $50 million for a universal fuel cell hanger in Bangor capable of accommodating the KC-46A.
BDN writer Marie Weidmayer contributed to this report.

title: Red Sox swept out of playoffs by Yankees
text:
NEW YORK — Max Fried dominated Boston in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the New York Yankees romped over the Red Sox 9-2 Wednesday night for a two-game AL Wild Card Series sweep.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston’s 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke the game open with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBI that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, was eliminated by the Yankees in the first round for the second straight year. The Red Sox hit .117 in the two-game series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and were outscored 18-2.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García’s fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead, and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just entered in relief. Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay Bellinger, who won a World Series with New York in 2000.
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, a throwing error, a stolen base, a bunt single and an intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger’s homer.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series opener, hadn’t pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation but entered to start the sixth. On a two-strike pitch to Jones, Crochet bounced a sweeper off catcher Adley Rutschman’s chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled out. The Yankees appealed, and the call was reversed by the video umpire.
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled, and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Austin Wells’ sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout, and Rice, who had four hits and six RBI in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats to make it 8-1.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
Nick Sogard hit a solo homer off Will Warren in the seventh.
UP NEXT
New York right-hander Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.

MaineHousing awards $2.7 million to fund winter warming shelters across state
MaineHousing is awarding $2.72 million to 12 organizations to operate short-term warming shelters for people who are homeless during dangerous winter weather.
MaineHousing awards $2.7 million to fund winter warming shelters across state
MaineHousing is awarding $2.72 million to 12 organizations to operate short-term warming shelters for people who are homeless during dangerous winter weather.
MaineHousing is awarding $2.72 million to 12 organizations to operate short-term warming shelters for people experiencing homelessness or housing instability during dangerous winter weather.
The grants will fund 474 beds across communities in eight of Maine’s nine homeless-service hubs. MaineHousing said the awards represent the largest amount of funding and the most beds supported since the warming shelter program began five years ago.
Most of the shelters are expected to operate overnight through April 30. Grant money can be used for staffing, supplies, transportation, extended hours and other operating expenses.
“Dangerous winter weather can put lives at risk, especially for people experiencing homelessness or housing instability,” MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan said. “These grants help communities open safe, heated spaces before severe cold arrives.”
When the temperature drops, people who live outside in tents and rely on portable heaters to stay warm face severe risks of deadly fires and carbon monoxide poisoning. Warming shelters offer a safer alternative.
A total of 12 organizations across Maine are receiving the funding, which will be used to create 474 new beds.
The warming shelter funding is part of the state’s broader winter preparedness efforts.
MaineHousing also administers the Home Energy Assistance Program, or HEAP, and the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which provide help with heating costs and emergency heating needs for eligible households.
With heating costs rising, MaineHousing is encouraging eligible residents to apply for assistance before an emergency occurs.
“We know many families are concerned about energy costs,” Brennan said. “Programs such as HEAP can help thousands of Maine households each year, and we urge people to seek help before they face a crisis.”
The organizations receiving the grants will work with municipalities, emergency management officials and community partners to connect people with shelter when winter conditions become hazardous.

MTA rolls out Red Sox, Sea Dogs and Hearts of Pine E-ZPass stickers
text:
Mainers can now show pride in some of their local sports teams while paying their highway tolls.
The Maine Turnpike Authority announced Wednesday that new $20 E-ZPass windshield sticker tags featuring the Boston Red Sox, Portland Sea Dogs and Portland Hearts of Pine are now available.
The MTA announced in March that it was rolling out windshield stickers as a cheaper and more environmentally friendly alternative to hardcase transponders. Unbranded stickers cost $5 compared to the $15 hardcase device, and the stickers use RFID technology, eliminating the need for a battery while using less plastic.
However, unlike the traditional device, the stickers cannot be shared between vehicles.
The new $20 sports stickers provide an optional “creative and personal” touch for Maine drivers to consider, said MTA Executive Director Andre Briere.
“We are constantly looking for smart technology that can improve cost efficiency, reduce our environmental impact, and make travel easier,” Briere said in a written statement. “When we can pair those benefits with something creative and personal, it is a win for Maine drivers.”
All of the proceeds from Portland Hearts of Pine stickers will benefit the Hearts of Pine Foundation.
“Every Hearts tag represents more than team pride — it helps us expand access to soccer, invest in places to play, and create opportunities for young people to build a sense of belonging,” Kevin Schohl, president of the Portland Hearts of Pine, said in the news release.
MTA says it plans to provide more of these “community driven” collaborations with New England sports teams in the future, and also teased that Maine Mariners stickers will be coming soon.
The stickers are available to purchase at the E-ZPass office at 2360 Congress St. in Portland, as well as through maineturnpikeauthority.com.
The MTA also released a new Maine E-ZPass App this week, through which Mainers can purchase the stickers. The app is live for Android users and coming soon for Apple users.

title: 3 GOP states go to US Supreme Court to challenge 3 Democratic-led states' abortion 'shield' laws
text:
Three Republican states went to the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to challenge abortion “shield laws” protecting providers in three Democratic states, escalating the legal conflict over pills that account for a majority of abortions.
The attorneys general of Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana contend that the laws in California, Massachusetts and New York undermine their abortion bans and their states’ sovereignty. Federal regulations allow prescriptions for abortion pills to be made by telehealth and filled by mail, and the three GOP states want to keep the pills out and punish out-of-state providers for sending them.
“This is the first time we’ve seen a state or group of states suing other states to challenge the validity of shield laws,” said Mary Ziegler, a University of California, Davis, law professor and author of seven books on abortion law and history.
The Supreme Court can hear disputes between states directly, though it rarely does. If the top court weighs in, it could short-circuit existing lawsuits.
Louisiana and anti-abortion activists have been frustrated with a lack of federal action by President Donald Trump’s administration against medication abortion. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill sued the U.S. Food and Drug Administration over its rules allowing mail-order prescriptions. The Supreme Court in May preserved access to abortion medications as that case plays out.
“We need and deserve the opportunity to be able to enforce our laws against those who have chosen, despite their knowledge of the illegality, to continue to foster abortion in our state,” Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall said during a news conference with Murrill and Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin.
Thirteen states ban abortion in all stages of pregnancy, which the Supreme Court allowed in its 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade. Most Democratic-controlled states adopted abortion protections, including eight with laws intended to protect providers who prescribe abortion pills for patients in states with bans.
Louisiana and Texas have pursued criminal charges and civil claims against doctors based in New York and California. Officials in California and New York have refused to cooperate, citing their shield laws.
“Louisiana, Alabama, and Arkansas are asking the Supreme Court to let them impose their abortion bans on New York and punish our doctors for providing legal health care,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said in a statement Wednesday.
Ziegler said Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana would have a stronger case if they had first tried to get the highest court in one of the three other states to force its officials to cooperate. She also said the lawsuit’s timing is odd — six weeks before November congressional midterm elections that could prove difficult for the GOP.
“This may be an example of the political incentives not being the same for state-level Republicans versus federal Republicans,” she said. “If you’re running in a contested race, calling attention to abortion is not a great idea, but if you’re Louisiana attorney general, you’re not really in that position.”
But Rachel Rebouche, a University of Texas law professor, said suing other states has been a potential legal strategy for GOP states since the first shield laws were enacted.
“That it’s taken this long is kind of remarkable,” she said.
Even before Roe was overturned, abortion pills were the most common means of ending pregnancies in the U.S., and telehealth makes abortion available even where it’s banned. The three GOP attorneys general said hundreds of patients in their states use pills to end pregnancies each month.
Also on Wednesday, Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana filed a lawsuit against 30 out-of-state abortion pill providers and their officers, accusing them of false advertising and other misconduct harming patients in states with abortion bans.
FDA scientists have repeatedly found the regimen safe and effective, though the agency is now reviewing its rules.

title: Portland-Thornton football grudge match, and other storylines for Week 5
text:
It’s clear by this point of the season which Maine high school football teams have potent offenses.
Now it’s time to find out if they also have the goods on defense.
CLASS A BATTLE
Saturday in Saco, two of the top three teams in the Varsity Maine poll meet when No. 3 Portland (4-0) takes on No. 1 Thornton Academy (4-0). These teams have met in three consecutive Class A title games. Thornton won in an upset in 2023 and rolled to a 28-0 win in 2025; Portland dominated in its 2024 victory.
Since 2018, Thornton has played in seven straight Class A championship games and is 72-8 against Maine teams (73-12 overall). Portland and Oxford Hills are the only in-state teams to beat Thornton more than once (both three times).
In its three-plus seasons back in Class A, Portland is 32-5 against Maine opponents (33-6 overall). Three of its five in-state losses were against Thornton (the other two vs. Bonny Eagle).
Both teams are more balanced offensively this season after the graduation of Thornton’s Fitzpatrick Trophy winner, Connor Ayoob, and Portland’s Cordell Jones, the Varsity Maine Male Athlete of the Year in 2025-26.
Thornton’s second-year starting quarterback, Noah Fullerton (26 of 32, 381 yards), has more touchdown passes (8) than incompletions (6) and hasn’t thrown an interception. He was 9 of 10 for 156 yards and 2 TDs last Friday in a 42-0 win against Westbrook.
Brennan Tabor (40 carries, 353 yards) and Josiah Blain (31 carries, 207 yards) are sharing the running reps with Caleb Parenteau (20 carries, 148 yards), who has been effective in a backup role. Thornton is averaging 328 yards and 45.4 points per game.
Portland sophomore David Gomes (38 carries, 414 yards) has emerged as a strong complement to top back Alex Martin (62 carries, 629 yards). With solid play from quarterback Reece Wildes (32 of 52, 499 yards), the Bulldogs are averaging 409 yards and 34.8 points.
This will be a competitive step up for both teams, though Thornton has beaten New Hampshire nemesis Bedford and South Portland (2-2). Portland’s four opponents are a combined 3-12.
Expect both Portland’s 10.1 yards per carry average and Fullerton’s 81.3% completion rate to dip Saturday. The winner will likely be the team that comes closest to its average production.
VARIETY IN TWO FORMS
Fun fact: This is the first time since 2018 that Cony vs. Lawrence will take place at Keyes Field in Fairfield. The B North rivals both enter Friday’s game 4-0. Cony’s spread offense, featuring a diverse passing game, contrasts sharply with the wing-T stylings that have defined Lawrence for decades.
“Lawrence can attack the A, B, C and D gap. They make you defend the full width of the field with their run game. That’s a challenge,” said Cony coach BL Lippert. “Against us, teams are always going to try to take away one thing and then we adapt.”
Lawrence and Cony have each beaten Fryeburg Academy, Skowhegan and Mt. Blue. In those three games, Lawrence had a cumulative 72-point margin. Cony (plus-25) had to rally to pull out wins against Fryeburg and Skowhegan.
Look for Lawrence’s top backs, Keegan Littlefield and Jaiden Hebert, to continue to chew up big yardage. The Bulldogs’ defense will try to dial up some pressure in an attempt to get Cony junior quarterback Drew Lindquist (55 of 87, 692 yards, 8 TDs, 1 INT) a bit flustered.
ANYTHING LEFT IN THE TANK?
How much energy will Marshwood and Noble have after Marshwood’s 52-51 win last week? That game had no punts, no turnovers and 10 lead changes — eight in the second half.
Marshwood (4-0) has momentum but now enters the heart of its B South schedule with a trip to Falmouth (2-2), which has won two straight.
After being pummeled by Marshwood’s wing-T (47 carries, 384 yards), the banged-up Knights (2-2) now have to figure out another option-style ground-and-pound offense in Massabesic’s Veer offense.
Massabesic (3-1) doesn’t have gaudy offensive numbers, but its 213-81 edge in rushing yards per game is telling. Plus, opposing QBs are completing less than 44% of their passes.
First-year Massabesic coach Cory Woodsome credits his offensive line — tackles Gavin Pomerleau and Isaac Best, guards Cam Goodson and Turner Knox, center Eli Tibbetts and tight end Nolan Pomerleau — for the team’s success. Best, Goodson and Knox are sophomores.
“It’s the guys up front. We really instill in these guys the importance of playing with a low pad level,” Woodsome said. “This style is how everybody used to teach blocking. The low man wins.”

title: Let’s have an honest discussion about Social Security
text:
Lenny Shine’s Aug. 22 op-ed (“Don’t fall for Republican distractions”) argues that the Social Security contribution cap unfairly favors higher earners because, once they earn more than $184,500, they “cease to pay a nickel into the program.” He calls eliminating that cap a matter of making them pay their “fair share.”
He leaves out an important fact: America’s working families who earn in excess of $184,500 will receive no additional Social Security retirement benefit based on those “excess” earnings. That is an important omission. Pay nothing in, get nothing out. How is that not “paying a fair share”?
Should American working families who earn more than $184,500 in a year be required to pay more into Social Security without receiving any additional benefit for those additional contributions?
If we are going to have an honest and helpful discussion about the challenges faced by Social Security, we should do so based on an honest and accurate statement of the facts.
Daniel Kagan
Lewiston

title: 2 killed, 1 injured after man allegedly shoots 3 coworkers at United Rentals, police say
text:
AUGUSTA COUNTY, Va. (WHSV/Gray News) - A man in Virginia is accused of killing two of his coworkers at United Rentals.
Marvin Grant, 37, was wanted for a shooting in Manassas City that was reported at 7:11 a.m. Wednesday.
Manassas City Police Department said Grant shot his coworkers at United Rentals around 7 a.m., then left the scene.
Police said Ricky Lamont, 48, and Christopher Serrano, 33, were both taken to the hospital but later died. The third victim remains in the hospital.
A Virginia State Police trooper saw Grant’s vehicle on southbound Interstate 81 in Augusta County before Grant pulled into the rest area at mile marker 232.
Troopers attempted a traffic stop. Grant then exited the vehicle, got back inside, and continued driving, prompting a pursuit.
Grant pulled over at mile marker 227 and exited the car with a firearm pointed at his head.
Police said Grant shot himself and was taken to a hospital, where he died.
Virginia State Police say troopers did not use force during the incident, which remains under investigation.

title: Insomnia is linked to higher risk of dementia and stroke, study finds
text:
(Gray News) - New research suggests insomnia may be linked to some serious long-term health risks.
A recent study published in “Sleep Medicine Reviews” found people with insomnia had a 26% higher risk of stroke.
The study also found that insomnia is linked to a higher risk of dementia, depression, suicide and hospitalizations.
Researchers analyzed 20 comprehensive review studies from multiple countries.
Another study, published on Sept. 9 in the journal “Neurology,” found that insomnia is a “modifiable risk factor” for cognitive decline.
In the study, 2,750 people underwent annual neurological assessments and brain imaging, along with evaluations of their sleep habits.
According to the study’s data, insomnia was linked to a 40% increased risk of cognitive impairment. It also found that people with insomnia who increased their sleep time or used medication to help them sleep did not experience as much harm to their cognitive health.
According to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 12% of Americans said they’ve been diagnosed with chronic insomnia.
Experts said staying on a regular sleep schedule is important.
According to Dr. Diego Carvalho, assistant professor of neurology and sleep specialist at the Mayo Clinic Center for Sleep Medicine, research shows that sleep helps clear unneeded synapses and waste from the brain that accumulates during the day. It is also necessary for memory consolidation, emotional regulation and overall brain health.
To get a good night’s sleep, experts suggest putting your phone and other distractions away about 30 to 60 minutes before bed. Practicing relaxing habits before bed and keeping your bedroom dark, quiet and cool can also help.
If insomnia persists after making these changes, experts say you should consult a doctor or sleep specialist.

title: Parents of college hockey player who collapsed during workout want coaches put on leave
text:
TEMPE, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - The parents of an Arizona State University hockey player who collapsed during a team workout last month and is unlikely to fully recover are calling for the coaches to be removed amid the investigation.
Matthew Mayich, a sophomore defenseman from Ontario, Canada, collapsed on Aug. 20 during an outdoor workout in Tempe, Arizona. The 21-year-old is still in the hospital and unlikely to fully recover, according to his family’s attorney.
In a statement provided on Tuesday through their attorney, Mayich’s parents, John and Christina, said they want the coaches involved in the workout removed during the investigation over concerns of possible retaliation.
“The coaches who ran that workout on August 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn’t have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day,” the statement read in part.
Mayich’s parents said they want the truth and accountability for what happened to their son.
The full statement is below:
“We’ve heard some things about what our family wants that aren’t right, so we want to be clear. We want this team to have a great season, and we’ll be cheering for you. But the coaches who ran that workout on August 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn’t have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day. And there are plenty of former college and pro players in the Valley who could step in and help.
“Nobody should keep quiet about what they think should happen because they believe that’s what we want. It isn’t. If anyone wants to know what we want, ask us. We want the truth, and we want it done in a way that lets the boys focus on hockey instead of wondering whether their coaches think they talked.
“Mostly, we want accountability for what happened to our son, and we want his teammates to be safe.”
Players challenge ASU’s report on workout
The statement comes a day after seven anonymous players sent a letter to ASU President Michael Crow challenging the university’s report on what happened the day Mayich collapsed.
The players’ letter claims former Green Beret Timothy Ziesel, who led the workout, was brought in with no background check or safety certifications. It was originally described as a team-building exercise, but in reality, it was a “military-style conditioning session,” players said.
The anonymous players reported that the only water break given lasted seconds, and only eight players got water. Mayich reportedly was not among them.
They said the workout continued even when some began falling to their knees and vomiting.
Like Mayich’s parents, the players are calling for the coaching staff to be placed on leave. They also asked that the investigation be turned over to an outside agency.
Trainer’s attorney pushes back on players’ account
Ziesel’s attorney, Buddy Rake, is pushing back on players’ accounts of the workout, saying no players vomited or were denied water.
He also said that Ziesel couldn’t have denied water to players since “he didn’t determine water breaks.” He added that water breaks were determined by coaching staff and based on the university’s hydration policy.
“The workout was not punishing unless you consider flutter kicks, pushups, planks, and sprints punishing,” said Rake in an emailed statement to Arizona’s Family. “Have you ever seen a D1 preseason workout?”
Rake explained that ASU’s hydration policy requires trainers to supervise pre-hydration requirements. Before exercise, he said ASU athletes under supervision are required to hydrate at least four hours prior and drink 8 to 12 fluid ounces about 10 to 15 minutes before starting the exercise.
The lawyer added that he has emails from a coach stating that Mayich didn’t show signs of struggle until after Ziesel left. During the workout, there were six coaches and trainers present, according to Rake.
“As Tim’s [Ziesel’s] attorney, I continue to be of the opinion that the family and parents of Matthew receive complete transparency. Instead of focusing on a non-existent hard workout, the focus should be on how could this happen during a workout that was not as hard as an average D1 conditioning program,” Rake said.
“There is not a definition of a military workout,” he added.
Rake claimed that Mayich’s case went off track by “trying to find blame before facts were known.” In his emailed statement, he listed questions about the case, including:
- What qualifies as a “military-style” workout?
- What conditioning was actually provided?
- Was water available and would it have made a difference?
- What was the temperature in Canada where Matthew was training beforehand?
- What kind of physical condition was Mayich in when he arrived in Arizona?
- What activities did Mayich participate in leading up to the incident?
ASU police are investigating the circumstances of the workout. They will submit their report to the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office for review.

title: Trump orders removal of ticks and mosquitoes from nation’s capital
text:
(CNN) — President Donald Trump signed a new executive order Wednesday that aims to slash the population of mosquitoes and ticks that spread disease in Washington, D.C.
The order directs federal agencies to cut the populations of Asian tiger and Egyptian mosquitoes in the nation’s capital by 90% by 2028.
It mandates a 50% cut in the tick population within the same time frame.
The Department of Health and Human Services, the EPA and the Department of the Interior would be involved in the effort.
HHS is tasked with hosting prize competitions to find the best ways to prevent and treat mosquito and tick illnesses.
Developing non-chemical ways to reduce mosquito and tick populations would also be prioritized.

title: Lewiston will offer funding to help business owners 'put ideas to work'
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The city of Lewiston is offering business owners the opportunity to receive development grants of up to $40,000 and loans up to $50,000.
The Business Opportunity Loan Program, now in its second year, is designed to support both startups and existing businesses to help create jobs and enhance the tax base.
Recipients can use the funds to expand their services in Lewiston or to relocate within the city, buy equipment, or address code issues.
A total of $415,000 is available between the grants and loans for this year’s program. Up to five grants and four loans can be awarded, and amounts will depend on the strength of the application and supporting materials.
Loans up to $50,000 will carry a 5% interest rate over 10 years. Grants are also available.
“Business owners looking to put their ideas to work will find Lewiston an ideal place to build and grow,” said Bryan Kaenrath, Lewiston city administrator. “Our location connects businesses to customers across the region, while our workforce gives them a foundation to grow.
“Being business-friendly also means helping owners overcome the financial hurdles of opening their doors or taking their business in a new direction,” Kaenrath added. “This program puts capital behind their plans, helping make that next step possible right here in Lewiston.”
The program was launched last year with $180,000 in funding, which supported 16 businesses.
More information
The city has scheduled complimentary training sessions for applicants. The first session will be held Tuesday, Oct. 13, from 8-9 a.m., at the Lewiston Auburn Metro Chamber of Commerce office, 415 Lisbon St., Suite 100.
Additional sessions are scheduled for Nov. 10 at 5 p.m., at the Lewiston Public Library, at 200 Lisbon St., and Dec. 8 at 5 p.m., at the Lewiston Colisée, at 190 Birch St.
More information can be found at www.lewistonmaine.gov/BOG2026, by calling 207-513-3126, or by emailing ECDGrantProgram@LewistonMaine.gov.

title: Central Maine Power removes job postings after Public Utilities Commission staff recommendation to deny temporary rate hike
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Central Maine Power (CMP) is removing all job postings from its website after Maine Public Utilities Commission (PUC) staff members called for the agency to deny the company’s request for a temporary rate increase, a CMP spokesperson confirmed to Maine’s Total Coverage.
As of Monday, CMP had 70 job postings listed.
CMP is requesting a $189 million increase to help upgrade equipment that failed or got close to failing this summer. But a number of groups have objected to the proposal, including the Maine Office of the Public Advocate, the Maine Department of Energy Resources, Efficiency Maine Trust, AARP Maine, CMP Ratepayers Unite and the Natural Resources Council of Maine.
In a recommended ruling, PUC staff members said the commission’s policy only allows it to approve rate changes if there are no objections to an amount, which is not the case in this instance.
CMP president and CEO Linda Ball released a statement reacting to the recommended ruling, which said that the recommendation “carries consequences that extend well beyond the rate case itself.”
“Prolonged revenue uncertainty puts pressure on the infrastructure investments, workforce, financing capacity, and grant-funded modernization efforts that customers and communities depend upon. Unfortunately, the consequences of prolonged uncertainty are no longer theoretical,” Ball said in her statement. “CMP has already been forced to defer planned capital work, including projects intended to strengthen reliability, improve resilience, and modernize the system, and will continue to do so. CMP will now also be forced to evaluate workforce levels and hiring plans that support current operations and future needs.”
Ball also sent a letter to CMP employees on Monday. In the letter, Ball said that the company will need to evaluate current workforce levels, hiring plans and apprenticeship programs as a result of the recommendation from PUC staff members.
“No decisions have been made beyond those already communicated, but it would be irresponsible not to assess all available options given the current circumstances,” Ball said in her letter, which was shared with Maine’s Total Coverage by a CMP employee.
PUC staff members noted in their recommended ruling, however, that the decision does not necessarily foreclose CMP from seeking a temporary rate increase later in the process should a clear agreement be reached between the parties.
“I think everybody recognizes we want costs as low as possible, but low also needs to be thoughtful,” said Patrick C. Woodcock, president of the Maine State Chamber of Commerce. “Just as in how you manage your house, you don’t want to put off investments that may increase costs later down the road.”
The PUC is expected to consider the recommendation at its meeting next Tuesday, Oct. 6. Parties must file comments or exceptions to the staff members’ recommended decision by 12 p.m. on Monday, Oct. 5, in order for the PUC to consider them in its deliberation on the matter.

title: Springworks Farm in Lisbon to be sold at auction
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Springworks Farm, the once-thriving aquaponics farm in Lisbon that supplied lettuce to grocers across New England, will be sold at auction next month.
Springworks was the exclusive supplier of organic and other lettuce to supermarket chain Hannaford from 2021 until earlier this year.
The farm was also a significant local taxpayer, having paid more than $77,000 in real estate taxes in fiscal year 2026.
According to Tranzon — a nationwide real estate auction company — the Lisbon farm is 168 acres, consisting of two abutting lots, 117,000 square feet of greenhouse growing space, 56,000 square feet of light industrial buildings and all related equipment.
The auction will be held Oct. 23 at 11 a.m.
Lisbon’s director of economic and community development, Ross Cunningham, did not respond to a request for comment on the auction.
Trevor Kenkel, the founder and CEO of Springworks Farm, purchased the farm in June 2014 for $457,500. Efforts to reach him have also been unsuccessful.
According to market intelligence platform traxcn.com, Springworks raised over $41.5 million of funding in seven rounds starting in 2014. In 2023, the company raised $22 million to fund the addition of its fourth and largest greenhouse.
Blue Highway Capital and Farm Credit East were listed as investors.
Springworks Farm announced in 2021 that it was the exclusive provider of whole head romaine lettuce to Hannaford in addition to being the exclusive supplier of certified organic green leaf lettuce.
The company also supplied all 184 Hannaford stores with baby romaine lettuce and Boston bibb, plus an assortment of pre-cut products in select stores, including single cut romaine, single cut Boston bibb, and salad mix.
In addition, the farm sold products to Whole Foods, Roche Bros. Supermarkets, Food City, Sysco of Northern New England, Lisbon K-12 schools, and other local institutions.

title: MAINE-LY GARDENING: Rain, rain, please come today
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
We’ve had some welcome rainfall recently, but unfortunately, we in Central Maine are still in a drought, as is the rest of the state. We wonder how long this can continue, especially as fall is usually an excellent time to plant trees, shrubs, and perennials. Weather reports offer only a few days of reliable forecasts. While the science has become more sophisticated decade by decade, the changes in worldwide temperatures continue to effect wind patterns, making the predictions increasingly more challenging. We may not feel that we can expect much more clarity from the weathermen and women than our grandparents did.
We might not repeat the old weather sayings – “Red sun at night…” – with as much confidence as in the past, but we don’t have much trust in the constancy of our climate. While we wait and see, we might remember a few facts about weather and water we may have learned in our elementary school science books.
Our planet has all the water it has ever had, and likely ever will – a closed system. It’s position in the solar system has given it the nickname the Goldilocks Planet – not too hot, not too cold, just right for life. We look at the globe and easily agree that 70 percent of Earth is covered by water.
Other water facts can be harder to understand. Science tells us that 97 percent of that water covering the world is saltwater and almost all of the remaining 3 percent that is fresh is actually locked up in glaciers or deep underground. That appears to be changing, but calculations done over years conclude that only 0.4 percent is available for human use. An almost unimaginably tiny amount! A gallon of water – an amount I can understand well enough – equals 128 fluid ounces and 0.4 percent of that is about three teaspoons. So much depends on so little.
The average annual rainfall in Central Maine is about 42 inches, or about .8 inch per week. Of course, that rainfall is never evenly distributed over the weeks or the acreage, but it is generally enough to keep most plants, and other living things like us, healthy.
That not-quite-inch of rainfall will move about six inches down into the soil – the typical root plant’s root zone. Even the largest trees’ roots those that actively provide water and nutrients, are in the top six or so inches of the surface, while larger roots provide anchorage.
Gardeners are advised to water at the surface of the ground so the water can soak right down into the roots zone, and to do it just once a week, unless we’ve had an inch rainfall, as small amounts given more frequently may not get deep enough. (Of course, the newest, littlest, seedlings need attention appropriate to their baby status.) If you’ve set up a sprinkler, soaker hose, or drip system, you can dig down six inches occasionally to see if that water is penetrating nicely.
While we watch and wait impatiently for the drought to end, we can try to use the water we do have wisely.
 © Judith Chute Hsiang
Jude Hsiang is a retired University Extension Master Gardener Program instructor and a member of the China Community Garden.

title: Drier, Brighter Weather Returns Today... Warmer Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - More clouds than sunshine expected for the remainder of the day. Temperatures will be warmer... more seasonable with highs in the 60s to near 70°. Skies will be partly cloudy tonight and we may see some patchy fog in spots too. Temperatures will drop to the upper 40s to mid-50s for nighttime lows.
High pressure will be centered to our south as we head into the end of the week... ushering some warmer air into the region for Thursday and Friday. Thursday looks a bit brighter than today with a mix of sun and clouds. High temperatures will be warmer... especially away from the coast with many spots seeing highs in the low to mid-70s while a breeze off the ocean keeps temps in the mid-60s to near 70° along the coast. A cold front is forecast to move through during the day Friday. This will bring more clouds and a good chance of showers from late morning through the afternoon and evening hours. It doesn’t look like a total washout but certainly looks like a much better chance of showers than previously forecast. Rainfall totals up to .5″ will be possible by later Friday evening as the front clears the state. Cooler... more seasonable air will move in behind the cold front for the upcoming weekend. High pressure will give us a beautiful day Saturday with sunshine and highs in the upper 50s to mid-60s. Sunday looks good too... maybe a bit more cloudiness leading to a mix of sun and clouds. Temperatures on Sunday will reach the mid-50s to low 60s for highs.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly cloudy. Highs in the mid-60s to around 70°. Light and variable wind.
Tonight: Partly cloudy. Patchy fog. Low between 48°-55°. Light south/southwest wind.
Thursday: Mix of sun and clouds. Highs in the upper 60s to mid-70s. South/southwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Friday: Partly to mostly cloudy with showers likely from late morning through the afternoon and evening. Highs in the upper 60s to mid-70s.
Saturday: Mostly sunny. Cooler with highs in the upper 50s to mid-60s.
Sunday: Mix of sun and clouds. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s.

title: Man dragged to death by subway train after his bag gets caught in doors
text:
NEW YORK (AP) - A man was dragged to death by a New York City subway train when a bag he was carrying got stuck in the door during the Monday evening rush hour commute, police said.
Yaw Boahene, 57, was exiting the train at a Brooklyn subway station around 6 p.m. when his bag, which police described as a shopping bag, snagged in the closing train doors. The Brooklyn resident was pulled onto the tracks and run over by the train as it left the station, police said in a statement.
Officers arrived to find Boahene “unconscious and unresponsive” on the train tracks, police said. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
The medical examiner’s office will determine the cause of death. The police investigation is ongoing.
The Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which runs the subway system, said both the train operator and conductor have been removed from service, as is routine while the investigation continues. The agency said the train was one of the fleet’s newest models. It was inspected after the man’s death and also previously in July, and no mechanical issues were found.
Dragging deaths happen from time to time on the nation’s largest subway system. In 2022, a 20-year-old commuter was killed after his backpack or a piece of his clothing got stuck in the door as he was trying to get onto a train at the Columbus Circle station in upper Manhattan.

title: Maine’s Blue Economy will form its future
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rhiannon Hampson serves on the Maine Blue Economy Week Planning Committee and is vice president for economic development at the Gulf of Maine Research Institute.
Long before we ever knew it as Maine, people lived and worked along the more than 3,500 miles of coastline we call home. For thousands of years, the Gulf of Maine has sustained our communities — we have harvested these waters, building our lives around its tides and seasons.
Our relationship with the sea has never been static. The movement of people and industry, changes in fish populations and the shifting demands of trade have continually pushed Maine’s coastal communities to reinvent themselves, to innovate and adapt.
That instinct to adapt is one of Maine’s oldest strengths. We see it in the fishing boats steaming out at dawn — evolving from small wooden dories to the fast boats that thrill kids and adults at summertime races, and now moving toward electrification. It shows up in the aquaculture farms growing food for their neighbors, and it drives the innovation of researchers and entrepreneurs who are creating solutions to the challenges those fishermen and farmers face.
The numbers set the stage but do not tell the whole story. The almost $6.8 billion in economic activity and 90,000 jobs supported by Maine’s ocean-related businesses are not legacy numbers. They are dynamic and reflect an economy that is still changing. The legislatively established Blue Economy Task Force 2.0 identified five sectors of opportunity for growth here in Maine: aquaculture and marine vegetation, marine biotechnology, ocean data and research, resilient coastal infrastructure and sustainable boatbuilding and marine propulsion.
This growth is not guaranteed, but the challenges we face can define our opportunity to support it. Climate change is not only rapidly warming the Gulf of Maine and reshaping the species available to our fishermen, but it is also pressuring our roads and working waterfronts — critical infrastructure for a thriving economy.
Few places in the country are as well positioned as Maine to turn those challenges into new solutions given the expertise we have developed here through investment in our colleges, scientific institutions and coastal industries. That expertise and experience in responding to these pressures and shifts are why our researchers, engineers, educators and community development organizations are in demand nationally as other states seek to solve these challenges.
This is why we are convening Maine’s first Blue Economy Week (Sept. 29-Oct. 2), because the time is now. It is a way to have scientists, investors, students, fishermen and educators come together to chart our course. It is an opportunity to collectively ask: How do we keep and build upon what Maine already does well while continuing to innovate to meet this moment?
We have never been a state that waits for the future to arrive, an identity demonstrated by our motto, Dirigo: “I lead.”
The blue economy is not a departure from our story; it is just the next chapter. We hope you will join us in writing it.

title: The US military says its withdrawal of troops from Iraq is complete
YWCA MDI welcomes new executive director
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR — Kari Burns is beginning a new chapter as the executive director of the YWCA MDI, with initiatives to implement further community programming and fundraising for the Hamilton Station Project.
Burns, originally from Indiana, was a military child and traveled across the U.S. with her family. She graduated from the University of Indianapolis with a bachelor’s degree in Visual Communications. After initially working in marketing and design, Burns yearned for the community-focused volunteer work she experienced growing up. She joined AmeriCorps with Colorado Youth for a Change, focusing on student engagement and helping high school seniors graduate.
“That year in AmeriCorps changed the trajectory of my life and gave me the confidence to see how my skillset could support me in succeeding in a leadership position,” said Burns. “The experience made me realize this is what I want to do with my life.”
Burns earned her master’s degree in Nonprofit Leadership from the University of Denver. She completed an ODI Fellowship in leadership in the university’s marketing and communications division. She created and embedded diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) policies and practices into the division’s infrastructure.
“The fellowship was a great learning opportunity working with DEI in a predominantly white, very affluent, elitist space at the university. Engaging in that work allowed me to learn the importance of meeting people where they are in their anti-racism work. Coming into this role at the YWCA MDI, I feel I can bring my learning to this community,” said Burns.
Outside of her educational experience, Burns has led several nonprofit organizations through mutual aid and advocacy programming. She was the executive director of Irvington Community Advocacy Network (ICAN), a social services nonprofit supporting the local community through an assistance center, food pantry, a community clothing closet, and hygiene kits.
Burns stepped into her new role as the executive director of the YWCA MDI in June, succeeding Jackie Davidson, who led the organization for 13 years. She expressed gratitude for Davidson’s support, along with appreciation for the staff and community’s warmth during her adjustment to the island and new position. “Jackie has been so wonderful throughout this transition. She served as the executive director of the YWCA MDI for 13 years and did such wonderful work. She has been so kind, gracious, and available to me as I’ve come into this role. I’m very appreciative of everyone here at the YWCA for welcoming me during this transition.”
Burns stated her commitment to supporting current community programs through the YWCA MDI, including initiatives like the YWCA Benni Mutual Aid Program and the Hamilton Station Project, which offers attainable, year-round housing to help address MDI’s housing shortage. She mentioned that the Hamilton Station Project has finished water testing and a traffic study and has received approval from the Town of Bar Harbor to move forward. The YWCA MDI is working with Flying Mountain Group to further develop the project.
In addition to new executive director leadership, the YWCA MDI has appointed Tracey Haskell as its new board president. Haskell, who served on the board for two years, assumed the presidency a few months ago. Additionally, the board has added several new members. This influx of new leadership is prompting the Hamilton Station Project to regroup, with plans to launch a community capital fundraising campaign as the next step.
“The YWCA MDI has provided attainable housing in-town Bar Harbor since 1904 and is currently the only YWCA in Maine that provides housing. With the Hamilton Station Project, we are taking that to the next level and meeting the critical need for year-round housing on the island. Jackie has done such incredible work to get the Hamilton Station project to where it is, and I feel so lucky to come in and bring it to the finish line,” said Burns.
Burns continued, speaking to the community’s impactful support of the project. “This project is doable when the community comes together to make it happen. I have a feeling this community is very active and compassionate with one another. I believe we are living in a time where we have a sense of urgency to step up and help each other, and I feel like residents of the island are really trying to do that here on MDI.”
Outside of the larger projects of the YWCA MDI, Burns shared her desire to create a space for community gatherings and conversations. In the future, the YWCA hopes to offer a speaker series and workshops to engage community members in conversations regarding community advocacy and current events.
“There’s a need for a community space where people can sit and talk about what current events mean to us individually and how we can act and show up as a community,” said Burns. “We’re thinking of ways to bring people together for those bigger conversations. Through the YWCA, and in collaboration with other local nonprofits, I think we can offer opportunities for people wherever they are in their journey to recognize how racism manifests in their world and internally as well, through socialization, and to investigate that for themselves. The YWCA has operated as a community space with recurring events, and I think it would be great for this space to have more of that flow, with the community coming in and out of the space.”
In September, the social services programming through the YWCA MDI, now known as the YWCA Resource Assistance Program, relaunched to serve the greater island community under the new leadership of Laura Merrill Bundy. Merrill continues the work that longtime local Linda Lunt started at the YWCA MDI back in 2022, when the program was known as “Linda’s Resource Locker.” To learn more, visit ywcamdi.org.

title: MTA rolls out Red Sox, Sea Dogs and Hearts of Pine E-ZPass stickers
text:
Mainers can now show pride in some of their local sports teams while paying their highway tolls.
The Maine Turnpike Authority announced Wednesday that new $20 E-ZPass windshield sticker tags featuring the Boston Red Sox, Portland Sea Dogs and Portland Hearts of Pine are now available.
The MTA announced in March that it was rolling out windshield stickers as a cheaper and more environmentally friendly alternative to hardcase transponders. Unbranded stickers cost $5 compared to the $15 hardcase device, and the stickers use RFID technology, eliminating the need for a battery while using less plastic.
However, unlike the traditional device, the stickers cannot be shared between vehicles.
The new $20 sports stickers provide an optional “creative and personal” touch for Maine drivers to consider, said MTA Executive Director Andre Briere.
“We are constantly looking for smart technology that can improve cost efficiency, reduce our environmental impact, and make travel easier,” Briere said in a written statement. “When we can pair those benefits with something creative and personal, it is a win for Maine drivers.”
All of the proceeds from Portland Hearts of Pine stickers will benefit the Hearts of Pine Foundation.
“Every Hearts tag represents more than team pride — it helps us expand access to soccer, invest in places to play, and create opportunities for young people to build a sense of belonging,” Kevin Schohl, president of the Portland Hearts of Pine, said in the news release.
MTA says it plans to provide more of these “community driven” collaborations with New England sports teams in the future, and also teased that Maine Mariners stickers will be coming soon.
The stickers are available to purchase at the E-ZPass office at 2360 Congress St. in Portland, as well as through maineturnpikeauthority.com.
The MTA also released a new Maine E-ZPass App this week, through which Mainers can purchase the stickers. The app is live for Android users and coming soon for Apple users.

title: UK says there are 'strong indications' Iran played a part in security incident at US-run air base
text:
UK says there are 'strong indications' Iran played a part in security incident at US-run air base
The U.K. has “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident that saw five men arrested near a U.S.-run military air base in England late at night, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday.
Burnham said U.K. and U.S. officials are carrying out a “complex and serious” investigation into how and why five men and three vans were near the perimeter of RAF Fairford, a base that has been used by American bombers striking Iran during this year's war.
Five British men in their 20s were arrested Sunday on suspicion of explosives offenses and planning an act of terror, before being released on bail a day later. Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in the vans, but no explosives.
Burnham did not provide details about what the suspects were planning or why the U.K. thinks Iran was involved. He said he would “update people more in due course.”
“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” Burnham told the BBC in one of a series of interviews with British broadcasters. “And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America.”
Iran has denied involvement in the incident. It has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
The base 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran.
Top U.S. officials have criticized the decision to grant the suspects bail, with President Donald Trump saying “I wouldn’t have done that" and Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying a lot of people were “disturbed” by the move.
Burnham said authorities have the investigation under “the strongest grip and the closest control,” and British officials had been “talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done.”
“I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this,” he told the BBC.
Laurence Taylor, the head of British counterterror policing, said Tuesday that the suspects remain under investigation and the decision to grant bail was grounded in “experience and strategy.”
He said a line of inquiry is whether the suspected offenses were committed by “proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.”
The arrests came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil. British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months to December 2025.
U.K. officials also say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.
