title: 2 Steves and a propeller
text:
Wiscasset's Steve Erskine said his grandfather Roy B. Rowe and Rowe's brothers Clarke and Frank started Eastern Steamship Company and owned the Winter Harbor and another steamboat. Winter Harbor did the Boothbay-Wiscasset mail run with over 100 passengers aboard, Erskine, of Wiscasset, said. He told Wiscasset Newspaper Sept. 24, Route 27’s paving “gradually put them out of business.” He has a logbook he said shows a Boothbay-Wiscasset trip with seven passengers.
Its income lost to the changing times, Erskine said the Winter Harbor was tied up “just abaft on the port side” of the Luther Little, which, along with its fellow four-masted schooner Hesper, became Wiscasset’s oft-captured image of two vessels in their final resting place.
The Rowe brothers could not afford Winter Harbor’s repairs and they “just left it abandoned,” Erskine said. “And then she went to the bottom in a hurricane, and that was history," Erskine said.
Not quite history for the Winter Harbor’s propeller, however.
Wiscasset author and Wiscasset Newspaper news contributor and columnist Phil Di Vece wrote in his book "Wiscasset And Its Times," divers cut off and brought up the propeller in 1978.
In last week's interview, Erskine recalled when, several years ago, friend Sidney Gammon was Wiscasset’s harbor master. “He said ‘Your granddad’s propeller is stored down at the storage locker and I’ve been told to clean out the locker, so would you like to have it?’ And then I said, ‘Yeah, I’d love to have it.’” Erskine considered it a “piece of Wiscasset history,” and wanted to preserve it.
Erskine worked at Bath Iron Works then and the company, he said, was going to soda-blast the propeller and put a preservative on it. “I had a group of 10 people and we were going to build an informational kiosk down at the waterfront, (telling) a little about the Winter Harbor and … Hesper and the Luther Little,” and return the propeller for display there.
He said publicity about the propeller’s being out of town hands led to the end of that prospect and the propeller went back to the town before it could be worked on.
Sept. 15, Steve Christiansen — known to Wiscasset Newspaper readers as a great resource in Phil Di Vece’s Salt ‘n Spar columns — told Wiscasset selectmen the old steel propeller, now sitting unpreserved at the waterfront, is "slowly eating itself to death." Christiansen said the Winter Harbor owner’s grandson (Erskine) told him he’d still like to improve the propeller’s condition for the town.
As this was the public comment portion, selectmen made no comment. Erskine told Wiscasset Newspaper he plans to talk with Town Manager Dennis Simmons about the idea.
Christiansen told Wiscasset Newspaper Sept. 22, when he was a kid, he could, in extreme low tides, see the Winter Harbor's ribwork. He said he has always known Erskine. Their fathers worked together at Mason Station.
"Hopefully, (this) will come to fruition," Christiansen said of the possible work on the propeller. "It's kind of sitting there rusting into oblivion ... I just think it's nice of Steve to want to do that."
Why does Christiansen like sharing Wiscasset's history, whether with Phil Di Vece for a column, or at a selectmen's meeting? Christiansen explained, his family goes back 290 years in Wiscasset. As a kid, he'd often look at Fanny Chase's book, "Wiscasset in Pownalborough." He has his great grandmother's copy she received as a Christmas gift in 1941.
"So I was always interested in stuff in Wiscasset, from my great grandmother's perspective. And my mother has a pretty good memory of stuff, and so I've just had an interest ... only because I've been here for so darn long. And I just think history is important, and I like talk in about it, and I've got a lot of stuff," he added.
Erskine is one of the captains on Maine's First Ship's the Virginia. He said he's a 40-year member of Wiscasset Yacht Club and that his roots run deep in the Boothbay area. "It's in my blood, and it means a lot to me."
Erskine said his mother Priscilla Rowe became, in 1949, the fifth female ever on the East Coast to get a hundred-ton captain’s license. At 12, she was captain of a 28-foot swampscott dorey taking people to Squirrel and Cabbage islands, Erskine said.
Erskine also recalled the late Ruth Applin, a Wiscasset Boston Post Cane honoree, telling him her senior class trip was on the Winter Harbor. He said she told him two seniors got a couple of empty pint bottles out of the trash and put ice tea in them; the two were up on the forecastle sipping when Erskine's grandfather, a "teetotaler ... grabbed them away from them and threw (the bottles) overboard and said 'I won't have any drinking on my boat.'"

title: Cornell gang rape allegation leads to renewed scrutiny of laws on intoxication and consent
text:
(AP) - A woman’s account of being sexually assaulted at a Cornell University fraternity house has advocates and lawmakers renewing their criticism of a New York law that makes it more difficult to prosecute people who have taken advantage of others too intoxicated to consent to sex.
Under state law, rape charges generally need to involve force or a clear refusal of sex, unless the victim is physically helpless due to being unconscious, or mentally incapacitated due to being drugged without their consent.
Those limitations have led to something nicknamed the “voluntary intoxication loophole.” Prosecutors can’t easily bring charges against someone who engaged in sex with someone who voluntarily became intoxicated to the point where their ability to say “yes” or “no” to sex was compromised.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited that law as he defended his office’s initial decision not to file criminal charges against any of the men sued by a woman who says she was the victim of a gang rape at Cornell in 2024.
Van Houten said that in her sworn statement to campus police in 2024, the woman didn’t allege that she became intoxicated against her will, or was physically forced into sex or was unconscious when it happened.
“That’s victim blaming, straight up,” in state law, said Stefan Turkheimer, vice president of public policy for RAINN, the largest anti-sexual violence organization in the U.S. “It prevents a lot of cases from coming forward, where prosecutors are reluctant to try to push forward on a case where the person is incapacitated due to voluntary intoxication.”
New York lawmakers renew push to change the law
New York state lawmakers have considered bills to change the law over the years, though the proposals have stalled, despite support from prominent district attorneys and advocates.
Jeffrey Dinowitz, a state Assembly member who has sponsored such measures starting back in 2019, said the Cornell case is “exactly the type of situation this legislation would address” and hoped that there would be additional urgency in the coming legislative session to change the law.
“It’s just outrageous and it makes me angry that we haven’t passed this yet,” he said, adding that “it would at least ensure that the survivor would get justice.”
The woman, identified only by a pseudonym in the civil lawsuit, filed the complaint Sept. 16, saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house on the Ivy League campus in October 2024 after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. She became completely incapacitated while frat members were sexually assaulting her, the lawsuit alleges.
Van Houten has since reopened the investigation, saying he would consider presenting the case to a grand jury for their consideration. But in a written statement issued Monday, he said his initial decision not to charge relied heavily on a statement the woman gave to police that was given to his office, in which he said she had described some of the male students exhibiting incapacitation but not herself.
Police have not released that document, and the prosecutor’s statement only included sparse redacted pieces of that document in his explanation.
Other states with intoxication laws are moving to change them
New York is one of 19 states with rape or sexual assault laws that consider intoxicated victims to be mentally incapacitated only if they became drunk or were drugged without their knowledge or consent, according to research by The Associated Press and a report published in The Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law.
Many of those laws have been in place for a long time. But states have been gradually moving to change them.
After the Minnesota Supreme Court overturned a sexual misconduct conviction in 2021 because the incapacitated victim had voluntarily become intoxicated, the state legislature revised its laws later that year to allow charges to be brought no matter whether an incapacitated victim had voluntarily or involuntarily become intoxicated. Michigan made a similar revision to its sexual assault laws in 2023, and Texas followed in 2025.
“That business of whether the victim was voluntarily intoxicated or involuntarily intoxicated should really not matter in the vast majority of cases, if not all of them,” said Chinmoy Gulrajani, a psychiatry professor at the University of Minnesota who has researched state sexual assault laws. That’s because “the assailant should have known that this is not a person who is in their right state of mind.”
Turkheimer said these laws can have a disproportionate effect on campuses, where people may be experiencing alcohol or drugs in social settings for the first time. He said mental incapacitation laws aren’t about someone having just a few drinks, but about situations in which a person has lost the capacity to consent.
“The movement is, to look at a person who is incapacitated, regardless of how they got there, and actually give that person protection,” he said. “This is a situation where a person has reached a state where they lack the capacity to consent. And in that situation, the law should be protecting those people because they simply can’t protect themselves.”

title: Presque Isle’s junior hockey team enters 2nd season with new lineup and playstyle
text:
If there was one thing the Northern Maine Pioneers lacked in their inaugural season, it was time.
The entire National Collegiate Development Conference franchise — from its roster to its coaching staff to branding — was cobbled together in three weeks after the season had already begun, after a different team slated for Presque Isle had collapsed.
The city’s first junior hockey franchise had little time to recruit, let alone structure a roster. The Pioneers went 11-37-3-1, finished fifth in their seven-team division and missed the playoffs by six points.
This year, the team had a full offseason to put together its team. Jack Lowry thinks the on-ice product will be better for it.
“At the end of every day, you can take a deep breath and think of what you want to do, what you need to do, which makes a huge difference,” Lowry, the Pioneers’ second-year head coach, said.
“Not taking away anything from last year, because I thought the guys on the team gave us a good season,” Lowry said. “That allowed us to have the time this year to be able to recruit, go after certain types of players.”
This year’s schedule, and team, look different. The NCDC doubled in the offseason, growing from 33 teams to 68. That boom triggered a league-wide realignment which moved the Pioneers into the newly-created Northeast Conference, now one of eight conferences in the league.
They are joined in the conference by four former divisional opponents: the St. Stephen County Moose, Lewiston MAINEiacs, Quebec Universel and the Woodstock Warriors, who rebranded from the Woodstock Slammers in the offseason.
Also in the Northeast Conference are the New Hampshire-based Thunder Hockey Club, the Montreal Black Vees and the Perth-Andover Bearcats. The Bearcats are under the same ownership as the Pioneers, and were brought to Perth-Andover, a mere 30-minute drive from Presque Isle, with the intention of creating a local rivalry.
Northern Maine is only returning 10 players from its inaugural season, and none of its top five scorers. But Lowry doesn’t believe scoring will be an issue for his team, which has tallied nine goals through its first three games.
Forward Grant Levins, who recorded 17 points in 48 games last season, started out hot this year with four goals and five points in three games. His linemate Luca DiSilvestro, a 19-year-old who played a handful of games in the NCDC in 2025-26, matched that point total.
“I think he’s going to be one of the top five forwards in the league,” Lowry said of DiSilvestro.
On the back end, the Pioneers are returning six of their defensemen from last season, among them Daniel Raskin, Jacob Heron and Owen Eckdahl.
Raskin, a top-pairing defenseman who logged 14 points in just 29 games with Northern Maine in his first junior season, is co-captaining the team with forward David Artenosi.
The Pioneers will have an entirely different playstyle this year that Lowry said attempts to mimic that of the defending Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes.
He wants his group to move the puck up the ice quickly, be relentless to force turnovers and transition aggressively with the aim of creating extended offensive zone possession. He also wants grit.
“We want to have size where we need size, have skill and speed throughout the lineup, but also have some grit,” Lowry said. “I thought last year in certain instances we got pushed around a little too much and didn’t respond.”
The Pioneers dropped their first two regular season games over the weekend, but pitched a shutout against Quebec Universel on Sunday where they only allowed 12 shots. They’ll host Montreal at 3:30 p.m. at the Presque Isle Forum on Saturday.
“I think that we have a really skilled team and when we’re playing the way we want to play, we’ll be able to play with anybody in the league,” Lowry said. “It’s going to come down to execution, but I’m excited about the team.”
Correction: An earlier version of the report misstated the Bearcats’ name.

title: Maine People’s Alliance protests LePage healthcare policies
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Mainers gathered at Cascade Park in Bangor on Wednesday in protest of former Governor Paul LePage amid his run for Congress, citing concerns about rural healthcare.
Organized by the Maine People’s Alliance, the group stated that LePage has a history of cutting healthcare during his terms as Governor, and that his election to Maine’s 2nd Congressional District will lead to further cuts to MaineCare, higher prescription prices, and longer wait-times for treatment.
The group claims LePage has supported the rich over his constituents already leaving thousands with limited or no access to the healthcare that they need- and that this pattern will only worsen if he is elected.
“Paul LePage does not care about those that have to travel sometimes for hours to get to a hospital. We’ve watched these hospitals close everywhere in our state and our friends lose their MaineCare. My son is on the chopping block for losing his MaineCare. All because the DC elite grabbing at our wallets to put our fuel in their planes and pay our money into their wallets from our health care needs.” said Rev. Tammy Taylor, a resident of Hancock County.
WABI reached out the the LePage campaign and the Maine GOP for comment. The Maine GOP’s Communications Director Kristina Parker responded with this statement:
“The Maine People’s Alliance is an unhinged radical-left mob, and their only reason for existence is to attack conservatives. The fact is, Paul LePage paid a massive hospital debt left behind by a previous Democrat Governor and saved rural healthcare for all Mainers. Paul LePage also implemented P.L. 90, which dropped healthcare costs before the Washington takeover. Matt Dunlap has done nothing to help healthcare. Matt Dunlap’s socialist policies will only cancel private health plans and harm access to care.”

title: Lawmakers make bipartisan push to save U.S. film industry
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Lawmakers say other countries have started offering stronger incentives to make movies than the United States, and if the U.S. does not keep up, it will lose a sizeable chunk of the industry.
Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said there is a shift happening in the film industry.
“What you’ll notice, if you’re in the theaters as I am all the time is that the actors are in different countries. They’re filming everywhere. And less and less are they filming at home,” Scott said.
Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) said the film industry creates a larger economic impact than many realize.
“It helps with tourism, and it creates jobs and opportunity all across the entertainment ecosystem, as well as industries that benefit from the net impact of this industry,” Warnock said.
The bill would offer base tax credits between 20 and 30 percent depending on various factors of how much the film is shot in the U.S. and where.
Lawmakers hope it can be a boon for all areas of the country.
“One thing we don’t want this to be is a bill for one state. Obviously I wouldn’t be here if that was the case,” Scott said.
Advocates of the bill say it would also benefit consumers by allowing more American stories to be told.
“Stories literally transform the world. And they give us a view of what’s possible,” Warnock said.
In addition to the support of President Donald Trump, the bill is backed by industry leaders like director Christopher Nolan and actor Jon Voight.

PSA or campaign ad? Lawmakers on both sides demanding answers about taxpayer-funded commercials
Democratic and Republican lawmakers are raising concerns about the Department of Homeland Security's reportedly spending $20 million on ads featuring President Trump, alleging misuse of taxpayer funds.
Democratic and Republican lawmakers are scrutinizing the Department of Homeland Security's reported $20 million spending on TV ads featuring President Donald Trump, with allegations of corruption and misuse of taxpayer money.
Sens. Patty Murray of Washington and Chris Murphy of Connecticut sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday, claiming the department's actions are corrupt and illegal.
The senators allege that the funds for the ads came from Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," which was partly for U.S. Customs and Border Protection. They are demanding that Mullin respond within 48 hours and clarify whether DHS-appropriated funds were used to create the ads.
The ads (which you can watch here, here, and here) reportedly feature Trump and even reboot an ad from his 2024 reelection campaign.
Republican lawmakers, including Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska and Brinker Harding, a Republican candidate for Nebraska's 2nd District, have also spoken out against the funding of these ads.
Kennedy said in a TV interview, "You can't spend public money to promote yourself."
Thune told reporters, "It shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars."
Harding wrote in a post, "We should be laser focused on spending the taxpayers' hard-earned dollars wisely, not funding political TV advertisements with their money."
Ricketts added in a TV interview, "I haven't seen the ad specifically you're talking about, but again, if you're using campaign ads and using federal dollars, that would not be appropriate."
Sen. Maggie Hassan, a Democrat from New Hampshire, said, "What the American people know is that Donald Trump is using their money, taxpayer money, to fund an ad promoting himself. It's propaganda. It's political. It's not lawful."
A White House spokesperson defended the ads, telling Hearst Television in a statement, "These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad. The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country."
The Department of Homeland Security referred inquiries to a previous White House statement.

title: Other states are banning deer urine lures for hunting. But should Maine?
text:
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Deer hunters like an edge, an advantage that increases the chances of success, if only slightly. The popularity and increased use of tree stands in recent years is a prime example. According to a 1993 magazine survey, 9.5 million of the 11 million U.S. deer hunters surveyed, or about 86%, used a tree stand. My wife and I fall within that percentage.
The popularity of urine-based deer lures is another example. I’m old enough and have hunted long enough to remember when these products were something of a novelty. Today, scent-control and lure products can be found on the shelves of practically every sporting goods store that sells hunting equipment.
Personally, I’ve never had much use for most of them. I don’t arrow a deer or fill my tags every year. Perhaps if I did, my success rate would be higher, but year in and year out, I do all right.
I do have friends and acquaintances who have used products designed to attract deer or negate a whitetail’s olfactory advantage for years and who swear by the edge they provide. Unless they’re telling hunting yarns, I don’t believe they tag out every year either, but that’s a whole different story for another time.
The use of natural deer urine products has taken on a different significance with the spread of chronic wasting disease, or CWD.
CWD was first recognized in captive mule deer at a Colorado research facility in the late 1960s. The first documented case in a wild cervid was identified in Colorado in 1981. The disease has since spread across much of North America. As of June 2026, CWD had been documented in 37 states and five Canadian provinces, but not in Maine or elsewhere in New England. New York detected CWD in two wild deer in 2005, but no additional cases have been detected in wild deer there since.
CWD is a fatal neurological disease caused by infectious proteins called prions. Prions can be shed in bodily fluids, including saliva, urine and feces, and can persist in the environment for years. CWD can spread through direct contact between animals and through contaminated soil, plants, food and water.
To help prevent the possible spread of CWD into Maine, the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife implemented an emergency rule in 2018 restricting the importation of cervid carcasses and high-risk body parts from all jurisdictions except New Hampshire. I remember it well because I was still hunting caribou in the province at the time and making occasional trips to Anticosti Island, Ohio and other states for deer.
The rules allow hunters to bring back boned-out meat, hardened antlers, cleaned skull caps, hides without the head, teeth and finished taxidermy mounts. Those restrictions remain in effect.
Because CWD can be detected in urine, wildlife officials have raised concerns about natural urine-based deer lures, which are often made from urine collected from captive deer or elk.
There is no direct evidence that a commercial urine lure has introduced CWD into a wild deer population, but wildlife agencies are concerned about the potential risk.
Several states have responded by banning or restricting natural deer urine products. Connecticut’s prohibition took effect in 2007. Vermont prohibited them beginning in 2016, Rhode Island adopted a ban in 2018 and Massachusetts prohibited deer-derived scent attractants beginning in 2026.
New Hampshire has taken a different approach. It does not prohibit natural urine-based lures, but its Fish and Game Department strongly discourages their use and recommends synthetic alternatives because of the potential CWD risk.
That leaves Maine.
At present, Maine does not ban natural urine-based lures. But MDIFW tells hunters not to use urine-based lures and instead recommends synthetic, non-urine-based products. The department says there are no standardized or widely accepted protocols for testing commercial deer lures for CWD prions and recommends using synthetic products until further research can show that deer urine does not contain infectious prions.
The scent industry has also taken steps to address the concern. The Archery Trade Association launched its Deer Protection Program in 2016, and the Responsible Hunting Scent Association took over management of the program in 2021. The program establishes guidelines and safeguards for manufacturers of urine-based scents.
Some manufacturers also have their urine products tested using RT-QuIC, a laboratory method designed to detect very small amounts of abnormal prion protein. Products that have undergone this testing may carry an RT-QuIC-tested label.
But those industry safeguards do not mean natural urine products are legal everywhere. States such as Vermont, Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts prohibit natural deer-derived lures regardless of industry certification.
For now, Maine has taken a precautionary approach without banning the products outright. The state restricts the importation of high-risk cervid parts and recommends that hunters use synthetic lures instead of natural urine-based products.
The question is, for how long?

title: A pilot on a flight carrying Israelis stabbed another and apparently tried to crash, Netanyahu says
text:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — A copilot stabbed a captain in an apparent attempt to crash a jetliner as it was flying 174 people to Israel on Wednesday. But passengers burst into the cockpit and wrestled with the attacker even as the plane descended sharply, witnesses and Israel’s government said.
The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The shaken passengers from the FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv landed Wednesday evening in Israel on another flight, as onlookers cheered. Israel’s emergency services said they treated three passengers with minor injuries.
It was not clear what motivated the attack, which led Israel to scramble warplanes amid concerns about a possible hijacking. In a CNN interview aired on Wednesday evening, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attacker was an Omani national and was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia, where he was arrested.
Aviation experts were surprised the plane did not crash after a descent so extreme that most of the rudder was ripped off the tail.
“We’re going to die,” passenger Naama Bershadski recalled thinking as she closed her eyes and prayed.
A video shared by Netanyahu’s office showed passenger Yaniv Hayoun, who grappled with the attacker, wearing a bloodied shirt and hugging the prime minister, who told Hayoun: “I look at you and I see a lion. I see a great hero.”
President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu discussed the incident “at length” by telephone and that it seemed as though the copilot “was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job. And, he stabbed the pilot.”
Responders said they knew they had seconds to act
Hayoun, who Netanyahu identified as a plumber, said he and others pushed their way into the cockpit, where he saw the alleged attacker seemingly trying to destroy the controls.
“The door apparently wasn’t locked, and we managed to open it,” Hayoun told journalists at the airport. “What made it difficult for us was the (other) pilot himself. He had been stabbed and was on the other side of the door.”
Hayoun told Netanyahu that as people wrestled with the attacker, he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television shows. Then other crew members took over. FlyDubai said the aircraft was secured by on-duty crew “who diverted and landed the aircraft safely.”
Another responder, dentist Shota Musayev, told journalists they realized they had just seconds to take control of the plane before a “critical event.” They also feared another attacker might be on the plane, so “we spread a few more people inside the plane so that if something happened, we would be able to simply take control.”
Musayev then attended to the wounded pilot: “He was just praying the whole time and was in contact with me, and I was afraid we would really lose him.”
Video footage on social media reviewed by The Associated Press showed two men on the plane’s floor, bloodied and wounded.
Netanyahu identified the captain as Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen, and noted his “extraordinary bravery.” The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was hospitalized in stable condition.
“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” Netanyahu said on X. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.”
Israel’s foreign ministry said the people on board were from Israel, India and the United Arab Emirates. The U.S. State Department said four passengers had American citizenship.
FlyDubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while an investigation takes place. Netanyahu said that he spoke with the UAE’s president, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.
The incident came at a busy travel time as the Jewish High Holy Days with school and work breaks wrap up. In addition, national elections will be held on Oct. 27 and many Israelis plan to fly back to vote, since Israel doesn’t permit absentee voting from abroad.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, heightened security threats. The country is a week away from the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which has triggered a series of wars.
Aviation experts marvel that the plane didn’t crash
In the chaos about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk about an hour later, according to Flightradar24, which identified the aircraft as a Boeing 737 Max 8.
According to a statement by Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, the plane landed there at 9:45 a.m., an hour after making a distress call.
“Suddenly the aircraft started to fall down, like, a massive turbulence, like a massive G force, for 20 or 30 seconds,” passenger Almog Italie said.
Former United Airlines pilot and aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said he was surprised that the plane was able to land safely after most of the rudder was ripped off the tail during the extreme descent.
“That was a serious descent and strong aerodynamic forces on that rudder for that to happen. I’m just amazed the aircraft didn’t come apart,” Arroyo said.
Another aviation safety expert, Jeff Guzzetti, said that given the rate of descent, it may not have been possible for the plane to level out if it had fallen below 10,000 feet.
“It is remarkable they were able to pull out of that dive. What saved them is there was enough altitude left for them to recover,” said Guzzetti, who used to investigate crashes for the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration in the U.S.
A panicked mayday call as the flight sought place to land
A person who heard the flight’s communications with air traffic control described the plane being turned away by Saudi Arabia and Jordan before eventually landing in Tabuk, while passengers screamed in the background.
The person said the pilot’s voice was trembling as he called “mayday” and said a hijacking was taking place and ambulances would be needed. But Saudi Arabia initially denied clearance to land and directed him to Jordan. The plane was told to wait for clearance from the Jordanian military and then turned away.
The pilot then returned to Saudi Arabia and said he had to land in Tabuk. The air control operators gave no reason for the refusals. The person who heard the communications spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said he spoke with his counterpart in the UAE and they agreed to work together “against extremist elements seeking to harm security and undermine stability in the region.” The general Civil Aviation Authority of the UAE said it was investigating a security incident.
An official confirmed that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a hijacking. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because the incident was under investigation.
Israelis have made emergency landings in Saudi Arabia before
Israelis were targeted in a string of hijackings and airplane attacks by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s. Israel has not experienced a hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world, including on Israel-bound flights.
The emergency landing in Saudi Arabia was not the first for a plane carrying Israelis home. The kingdom does not have formal diplomatic ties with Israel, but ended its longstanding ban on Israeli flights overflying its territory in 2022.
Since then, Saudi Arabia has coordinated emergency landings for Israeli passengers, including in 2023 when a plane experienced an electrical malfunction.
The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalized ties in 2020. FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates airlines.
___
Magdy reported from Cairo, Scharf from Jerusalem and Funk from Omaha, Nebraska. Associated Press writers Sam Metz, Aamer Madhani and Josef Federman in Jerusalem, Ami Ben Tov in Tel Aviv, Israel, Adam Schreck in Bangkok, Darlene Superville in Washington and Giovanna Dell’Orto in Minneapolis contributed to this report.

title: Route 69 And Route 9 Intersection In Newburgh Switching To Four-way Stop October 6th
text:
In just one week, motorists who travel along Routes 69 and Route 9/Route 202 in the Newburgh area will encounter a new traffic pattern along their commute.
Read More: Route 1A Paving Project Starts Monday In Brewer And Holden
As of October 6th, the intersection of those roads will become a full 4-way stop, and surrounding towns are trying to get the word out, so drivers aren't caught off guard.
Towns of Winterport and Hampden posted a notice on their social media pages.
"The Town of Winterport has been notified that the intersection of Route 69 and Route 9 will be converted to a full 4-way stop next week...Please use caution when traveling through the intersection and be aware of the new traffic pattern."
The town of Newburgh will also be affected by this, and took to their facebook page to address the changes, and ask folks to plan accordingly, as the there will be a time of transition as people get used to the new rules.
"The DOT will be placing all signage needed and flashing stop signs next week... They will be putting message boards out in these areas as well to notify drivers of the traffic pattern change. We know this will bring some frustrations for a bit while everyone gets used to the new pattern of everyone stopping. We ask that you give yourself a few extra minutes especially in those morning and evening commutes when the traffic flow there is heavier."
Earlier this summer, Maine DOT crews were in the same area working on tree and brush removal, along with taking other actions to make that specific area safer for folks traveling on the roads.
Read More: Old Town Bridge Closure Coming For Winter Prep Work
According to the Maine DOT website, crews also flatten slopes at the intersection, as well as removed guardrails so folks could see farther down the road. Maine DOT crews also paved about 500 feet at this intersection, and positioned a flashing beacon there "to alert drivers approaching the area."
Brittany Roberts from the Maine DOT says the decision was made after some other measures that were put into play did not result and safer travels for motorists.
"This intersection has historically been a high crash location. MaineDOT previously added signage intended to improve intersection visibility, but crash patterns did not improve significantly. Following a review by MaineDOT’s Safety Office, the office recommended converting the intersection to an all-way stop. MaineDOT met with town officials two months ago to review the project, and the town is aware of the changeover next week."
The change is supposed to take place next Tuesday, October 6th, if the weather allows. If there are issues with the weather, they will move the official change date to October 8th.

title: Work begins on 183-unit housing development in Topsham
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new apartment complex in the works in Topsham will feature 183 units and many communal spaces — a kitchen for cooking classes, movie theater, game room, gym and more.
“It’s the kind of building you would get in a big city, but it’s in a community setting like Topsham … and it’s a place that people really love living,” said The Lupine’s developer Dave Holman of Holman Homes.
Developers, contractors, and town officials gathered Sept. 30 in Topsham to celebrate the groundbreaking. Developers chose Topsham for the project in part because the town’s policies were friendlier than nearby towns, said Holman.
Most importantly, the town had a suitable site at 4 Union Park Road — close enough to amenities to be convenient, but tucked away from busy streets, Holman said.
The Lupine will largely be built on what is currently a parking lot. There is an existing office building at the site that will continue to be used.
Town Manager Mark Waltz said the project will include affordable housing. Ten units will be priced for people making 80% or less of the area median income, and 51 additional units for people making 120% or less.
“Hopefully it will ease the housing crunch a little bit,” Waltz said.
Rents have not been set yet, but Holman said he is confident that the most affordable units will be between $1,000 and $2,000 a month. The remaining apartments will likely be offered at a variety of price points.
“We like having a range of different demographics, and income-level folks, live in the same community and get to interact and make friends in the hallway,” Holman said. “It’s not all for one class or economic level.”
Holman said The Lupine intends to provide housing options for middle-class Mainers.
“You often don’t see housing for working folks, working families, retired folks that are on an average budget,” Holman said. “There’s not that many developers building those kind of units.”
The units are designed to facilitate connection to the outdoors for residents, featuring an abundance of natural light and open space. Holman said that this was a priority because people are happier and healthier when they have access to nature. He said it also leads to higher retention rates among renters.
The building was designed with sustainability in mind. Holman said it will be well insulated and many units will have heat pumps. Electric vehicle charging stations and bike storage will be available. The building will feature underground parking that will bolster its sustainability as less forested area will need to be paved, he said.
Solhem Companies, Lumen Design and Development, and Holman Homes are the developers for this project. The building was designed by Momentum Design Group, and construction will be carried out by Penobscot General Contractors. Construction for The Lupine is underway, and the complex is expected to be completed in the spring of 2028.

title: Pennsylvania records 5th measles death amid worst US year since 1991
text:
(AP) - Pennsylvania health officials reported a fifth measles-associated death Wednesday as the U.S. endures its worst year for the disease since 1991.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said the person was from Lancaster County and was unvaccinated. The state did not provide any further information about the person who died. Lancaster County’s coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said that his office did not handle the death and that state officials have not provided him with any details.
The state’s other deaths have included an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County, in the center of the state; a 40-year-old woman from Jefferson County, a rural area in western Pennsylvania; and two infants in Lancaster County, in the southeastern part of the state.
None of them were vaccinated, according to the state health department. The infants were too young for vaccinations, according to current recommendations.
The U.S. has now seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to grow, with 943 illnesses reported so far this year across 39 counties. The measles-associated deaths are the first reported in the state in 35 years, state officials say.
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
The problem has been years in the making, as fewer kids get routine vaccines because of parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation. More recently, Trump administration health officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have questioned and sown doubt about the established safety of vaccines at an unprecedented level while also defunding local efforts to improve vaccination rates.

title: Parents, teammates of hospitalized ASU hockey player call for coaches to be placed on leave
text:
Parents, teammates of hospitalized ASU hockey player call for coaches to be placed on leave
An Arizona State University hockey player remains in the hospital and is "unlikely to recover" after collapsing during an outdoor workout in August. Now, the player's parents and teammates are calling for the university's coaches involved to be placed on leave.
Related video: Which universities spent the most on college football coaches' salaries
ESPN said the parents of Matthew Mayich, 21, released a statement Tuesday through their family attorney, saying he suffered "from exertional heat stroke that reduced the flow of oxygen to his brain" after collapsing during a summer team workout on Aug. 20.
His family said he is unlikely to recover.
The statement comes after seven ASU hockey players sent an anonymous letter to the university's president on Monday, saying Mayich did not receive any water during the workout, which they said was more grueling than reported. They said the athletic staff was not prepared to deal with heat stroke.
The players also noted that Mayich was new to Arizona, having been in the area for only eight days and having been involved in the hockey program for five.
Drafted by the St. Louis Blues, Mayich is from Hamilton, Ontario, according to the NHL.
Players sent the letter anonymously due to fears of retribution from the coaching staff, ESPN said. The players asked for an interim coaching staff to be put in place if the coaches involved are placed on leave.
Arizona State police are investigating the incident. A report will be sent to the Maricopa County Attorney's Office for independent review when completed.
ESPN and the Associated Press contributed to this article.

title: The US military says its withdrawal of troops from Iraq is complete
text:
BAGHDAD (AP) — The U.S. military announced Wednesday that it completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group and prompting President Donald Trump to hail the conclusion of “a very expensive excursion into Hell.”
The last U.S. troops left an air base in northern Iraq under a deal between Baghdad and Washington.
Trump, in a social media post, described the withdrawal by a Sept. 30 deadline as “orderly.” Appearing soon after at a White House event celebrating Hispanics, he spoke at length about the withdrawal and said, “It’s been a long time with very bad decision making that got us involved in this quagmire in the first place. It was a quagmire. For many, many years it lasted. But soon that part of history will be over.”
He said the shift was a victory for the U.S., Iraq and a sign of victory over the Islamic State group.
The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups’ strongholds.
Trump’s comments came as his own decision earlier this year to launch the war with Iran has been compared to the Iraq war for its undefined mission as it nears its seventh month.
Appearing at the White House, Trump made that comparison, arguing both that his one-day military action in Venezuela earlier this year to capture now former President Nicolás Maduro and the Iran war compared favorably, taking far less time and with fewer deaths of U.S. troops.
In recent years, Washington has sought to shift its focus from the Middle East toward Asia, but that shift has been inconsistent, with the Pentagon alternating between reducing its Mideast presence and then finding itself engaging in new conflicts — including the ongoing war in Iran.
Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country’s increasing strength and sovereignty.
The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region, where many fear a resurgence of the Islamic State group as well as more attacks by Iran-linked groups, possibly emboldened by the departure of U.S. forces.
Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought to disarm, with little success so far.
A new phase in Iraq after decades of US involvement
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an “orderly departure” from the air base in Irbil, in northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” he said. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
He added that the U.S. military “will continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a “new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against IS and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons.
Trump in his remarks on Wednesday lavished praise on al-Zaidi, calling him “outstanding,” a “fantastic guy, friend of mine,” and someone who “will hopefully be able to handle things very well.” He also appeared to try to take credit for al-Zaidi’s leadership, saying that the Iraqi leader was “running for election” and “wasn’t given even a chance and I endorsed him and politicked for him a little bit, and he ended up winning in a virtual landslide.”
Al-Zaidi was not on the ballot but was selected as prime minister when Iraq’s dominant parliamentary bloc nominated him after weeks of internal debate among its member parties and Trump publicly announcing his opposition to the coalition’s previous choice.
U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight the Islamic State group, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory.
With the extremist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down.
U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen’s Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.
The future of militias remains unclear
The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.
While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet.
Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.
The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in Iraq’s Kurdish region have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems.
The Kurdish regional government’s Peshmerga Ministry said the Kurdish region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the statement said.
Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal.
“The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty,” Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.
He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that “any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means.”
Kataib Hezbollah leader Ahmad al-Hamidawi took a somewhat more conciliatory tone, calling on the group’s fighters to halt their military activities “with the exception of targeting hostile aircraft violating the country’s airspace.”
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, said in a statement that negotiations with the government over the regulation of weapons have not resulted in an agreement and that it was “not bound by any timeline or agreement” announced by the government or political entity. The group said it is open to “any dialogue that guarantees Iraq’s sovereignty and dignity.”
___
Price reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Abby Sewell in Istanbul contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: Kerri Rose Gilligan
text:
PORTLAND – Kerri Rose Gilligan passed away on Sept. 23, 2026, in Portland. She was born in Newburyport, Mass.
Today, as a family, we pause to honor the life of our Kerri Rose who, through the journey of her life, was deeply loved and will be dearly missed. We carry her memory with us and reflect on the moments and memories that made her life meaningful to those who knew her.
Today, we ask that you take a moment to hold your loved ones a little closer. Check on the people who matter to you, tell them you love them, and never take their presence for granted. Life is precious, and every moment with the people we love is a gift.

title: Bangor warming shelters prepare for winter as state awards record grants
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - MaineHousing has announced $2.7 million in grants for winter warming shelters across the state — the largest funding round in the program’s history.
The Bangor Area Homeless Shelter on Main Street and The Brick Church on Union Street are among the organizations receiving funding. Following a freeze in state funding last year, The Brick Church will receive direct support from the state as it enters its seventh operating season.
“I’ve never been paid, and we all just volunteer here,” said Pastor Leon Licata. “This year we’ll be able to give out some stipends and help some people along the way that way.”
Licata says while they are excited to be a recipient of this year’s funding, the church still faces issues related to capacity.
“I’m okay to hold 70 people, but last year there was 120 to 130 people out on the street,” Licata said. “That makes a big difference, especially if that’s your son, daughter, mother, father, grandparent.”
Licata said discussions are already underway to help support warming shelters that were not awarded state funds, including the neighboring Together Place and The Mansion Church on Center Street.
“They’ve always funded us in the past. I was a little set back by that. I really expected that we would get the funding again,” said Mansion Church Pastor Terry Dinkins.
Despite not receiving state funding, Dinkins plans to keep the warming center open and is turning to the community for support.
“We’re not going to let a lack of funds keep people from coming into the church to be warm and fed. We’ll just have to change some things around, maybe ask the community or our congregation to step up and donate finances,” Dinkins said, “Just because we didn’t get funding, we’re still going to open up the doors.”
Community members can support The Mansion Church by visiting its Facebook page.
The Brick Church is also seeking volunteers to help overnight and with crowd management this season.

title: New England’s winter forests need the Roadless Rule
text:
Anneka Williams is a writer and climate scientist who is originally from Vermont’s Mad River Valley. She currently serves as the policy director for Winter Wildlands Alliance.
Growing up in New England instilled in me a deep appreciation for trees. In the summers my family would hike sections of trail all over the state, relishing the shade provided by a dense, leafy canopy of sugar maple, beech and birch trees. In the winter, the trees would shed their leaves and my friends and I would go find hidden powder stashes, carving quick turns between tight glades.
While trees feel like an abundant resource in Vermont today, forests haven’t always been
plentiful in this part of the country. In the 17th century, early European settlers established the foundation for a booming logging industry across the Northeast. 
As the number of settlers grew through the 18th and 19th centuries, forests were cleared and converted to agricultural land and much of the region lost its major old growth forests, shifting lumber operations west because there simply weren’t enough trees left. Over the last century, New England forests have recovered through practices aimed at balancing timber harvesting with conservation and other uses, but much of New England is a patchwork of roads and very few large roadless areas are left.
The roadless areas that remain are vital resources for outdoor recreation and watershed
protection. But they are currently under threat. Last June, the Trump administration’s U.S. Department of Agriculture moved to rescind the Roadless Rule under the guise of more local forest control and wildfire management. 
The Roadless Rule is a piece of federal policy enacted in 2001. It protects more than 58 million acres of “inventoried roadless areas” — pieces of undeveloped land within the national forest system that remain in their natural, undeveloped state. These places offer abundant opportunities for outdoor recreation in all seasons, including undeveloped terrain that makes human-powered winter recreation some of the best in the country, while also protecting clean watersheds and natural ecosystem qualities.
While the rescission of the Roadless Rule doesn’t automatically greenlight logging and road development, it does remove an important layer of protection that has implications for the character of New England’s wild, unroaded lands and for backcountry winter recreationists.
New England is home to two national forests: the Green Mountain National Forest (GMNF) in Vermont and the White Mountain National Forest (WMNF) in New Hampshire and western Maine. GMNF, which is approximately 400,000 acres total, holds approximately 80,000 acres of inventoried roadless areas. WMNF is approximately 800,000 acres and encompasses an estimated 368,000 acres of inventoried roadless areas.
Collectively that’s roughly 448,000 acres of roadless areas across New England. These areas encompass lots of terrain for winter recreation, including world-class backcountry skiing in Jefferson Ravine, the Wildcat Valley Trail, maintained backcountry glades around Baldface Knob and sections of snowmobile trails.
When I think about roadless areas in New England, I picture quiet glades nestled in heavily forested areas, lovingly maintained and enjoyed by local communities. I picture second-growth forests that have worked hard to reach their current density. I picture the places I visit on my skis or snowshoes in search of untracked powder, wild experiences and the stillness of a forest stand in the middle of winter.
These are the places that create a community of people around shared outdoor experiences and that provide the backdrop for photographs that define entire regions. They are the places I think about when I think of home.
At a moment filled with attempts to sell off our public lands and dramatic cuts in funding and staff to the agency we rely on to manage our national forests, having a policy like the Roadless Rule to protect these places is more important than ever.
Intact forests are on the chopping block and it’s up to all of us to use our voices to speak for these places during the Roadless Rule Draft Environmental Impact Statement comment period. I hope that if you’re reading this you will reflect on what untrammeled forests mean for you, how outdoor recreation has played a role in your life and join me in standing up for those places and experiences now and for future generations.
The Forest Service is holding a public comment period on the Roadless Rule right now. Submit your comment before Oct. 6.

title: From scout fundraiser to fall staple: Inside Davis Family Farm’s 10-acre corn maze
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
KENDUSKEAG, Maine (WABI) - What started out as a simple fundraiser for local Cub Scouts has quickly grown into one of the region’s most anticipated autumn destinations.
Now in its third year of operation, Davis Family Farm in Kenduskeag has become a go-to seasonal hub for families across central Maine, blending traditional agriculture with community entertainment.
The Region’s Largest Corn Maze
The centerpiece of this year’s festivities is a sprawling 10-acre corn maze, which farm operators say is now the largest in Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts. The labyrinth expanded significantly from last year’s six-acre footprint.
Navigating the full adult maze can take anywhere from two to three hours.
“It’s the real deal,” said Davis, a fifth-generation farmer. “I’m not saying you have to pack a lunch, but you probably oughta bring a water.”
For younger visitors, the farm offers a smaller children’s maze complete with prizes at the finish.
Accessible Fun for All Generations
Beyond the maze, the farm was designed to be welcoming to every member of the family. Attractions include a pumpkin patch, pedal tractors, a corn play box, pumpkin and apple slingshots, and a giant slide accessed through a hay bale pyramid.
Accessibility was a top priority when designing the farm’s signature wagon ride.
“The ticket includes an accessible wagon ride. We’re really proud of that wagon,” Davis said. “I have set it up so there’s a ramp on the back so it’s accessible. I don’t know anybody that has something like that.”
Local food trucks, hot dogs, and popcorn are also on hand, alongside friendly farm animals ready for a visit once guests emerge from the stalks.
Giving Back to the Community
Community support remains at the heart of Davis Family Farm’s mission.
The farm has scheduled three “night mazes,” with 10% of ticket sales directly benefiting local high school Project Graduation programs. Additionally, on Oct. 10, the farm will partner with Tiller & Rye and Uno’s Pizzeria & Grill to host a special benefit for the Old Town Animal Orphanage.
For tickets, operating hours, and event schedules, visit the farm’s official page by following the link.

title: Gavin P. Martin Foundation donates $2,500 to Edgecomb Fire Dept.
text:
Gavin Martin lived a short, but remarkable life. Martin worked as a volunteer fireman in two communities. He began his public service in his hometown of Verona, New Jersey and later served in Edgecomb.
Shortly after his death in December 2025 at age 21, his family set up the Gavin P. Martin Foundation which benefits local fire departments. A board of directors was set up and, with a sponsorship from the Verona Local Policemen’s Benevolent Association No. 72, the foundation was established.
The fundraiser collected donations and sponsorships resulting into the contribution into the foundation.
According to its website, the Gavin P. Martin Foundation transforms compassion into action by supporting community-based initiatives that embody service, entrepreneurship and dedication. “We honor Gavin's legacy by investing in young and old alike, empowering service organizations, fostering entrepreneurial spirit, advancing vocational training, and strengthening civic engagement,” the website reads.

title: Pumpkin Pickin’ trains in Alna
text:
The WW&F Railway Museum will celebrate the Maine harvest season with its popular Pumpkin Pickin’ Train to SeaLyon Farm, operating Oct. 3, 12, 17 and 24. The family-friendly experience combines historic steam railroading, brilliant fall foliage, pumpkin picking and horse-drawn wagon rides for a distinctly Maine autumn adventure.
The journey begins at WW&F Railway Museum, 97 Cross Road in Alna, where passengers board a historic narrow gauge steam train for a trip through the forests and fields of the Sheepscot Valley. At Top of Mountain, passengers transfer to a wagon for the short ride to nearby SeaLyon Farm.
At the farm, visitors can head into the pumpkin patch to select a pumpkin to purchase and take home. Horse-drawn wagon rides are included with admission, and guests can enjoy games, seasonal food and the sights and atmosphere of a working Maine farm during the fall harvest season. Food, beverages, pumpkins and other farm offerings are available separately.
After their farm visit, passengers return by wagon to the railway and board the train for the steam-powered journey back to Sheepscot Station.
The Pumpkin Pickin’ Train has become one of WW&F’s signature autumn experiences, bringing together two Midcoast Maine attractions in a day that appeals to families, railroad enthusiasts and visitors looking for an unusual way to enjoy Maine’s fall colors.
Trains depart throughout the day, with guests able to choose between a 30 or 90-minute layover at the farm. Advance reservations are strongly recommended, as previous Pumpkin Pickin’ Trains have sold out. Information and reservations, wwfry.org;pnone: 207-882-4193

title: Transcript shows woman told Cornell police 2 years ago she was 100% confident she was raped
text:
A woman who filed a lawsuit saying she was sexually assaulted by seven men at a Cornell University fraternity house told police weeks after the incident that she could “say with 100% confidence I was raped,” according to a transcript obtained by CBS News New York.
The transcript, which has not been publicly released, raises new questions surrounding the local district attorney’s decision not to prosecute anyone at the time.
In recent days, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has maintained the woman’s first account to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex. Yet, he also said he had reopened the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which was filed this month.
The woman initially went to Cornell’s campus police about three weeks after the alleged attack that began on Oct. 19, 2024, then went back on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, to be interviewed.
“Yes. It was coercion, yes,” she told a campus police officer, according to the transcript. According to CBS News, she said she was “completely and totally incapacitated” before some of the sexual abuse.
The woman acknowledged she had been drinking alcohol and used drugs the night she visited the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, and that she had gaps in her memory.
She also told police she was comfortable with an initial sexual encounter with two of the men, but not with what happened later in the night, when other men began to enter the room.
“And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard,” she told police, according to the transcript. “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” she told investigators.
The woman, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in the lawsuit, filed a complaint Sept. 16 saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. She became completely incapacitated while fraternity members were sexually assaulting her, she said.
The district attorney, Van Houten, didn’t immediately respond to emails and phone messages from The Associated Press on Wednesday, but he told CBS News he never saw the transcript of the woman’s interview when his office declined to bring charges, and relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer but signed by the accuser.
Van Houten has released a summary of that statement, with some of her direct quotes included. He has defended his office’s decision not to do additional investigation after the woman first came forward in 2024.
“There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided,” Van Houten told CNN earlier this week.
Cornell University first publicly disclosed that it was investigating the woman’s allegations on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day she first went to police. The school sent students an email alert warning them that a person had reported they had been sexually assaulted at a fraternity house and coerced into consuming drugs. Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity the same day.
In another public statement to students in late November 2024, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said campus police were investigating “deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence” at the fraternity house.
Later, Cornell appointed a task force designed to address sexual assault on campus. But with the district attorney’s decision not to pursue charges and the university’s internal disciplinary investigation being shielded from the public, attention on the matter waned.
Cornell said in a statement this week that it supported the decision to reopen the criminal investigation, adding that its own investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled. The Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus, but the university has declined to release more information on discipline for individual students, citing privacy rules.

title: Blue Hill sues downtown restaurant over unpermitted buildings
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Blaze Blue Hill is being sued by the town for the restaurant’s alleged land-use violations and unpermitted structures, including a stage that’s drawn the ire of neighbors because of loud concerts.
The town of Blue Hill filed a lawsuit Tuesday in Ellsworth District Court against Pub Ciao LLC, doing business as Blaze Blue Hill, and John B. Warren and Kathryn N. Warren Trust, which owns the property at 66 Main St. Blaze Blue Hill is owned and operated by Matthew Haskell.
The lawsuit is the latest legal action involving businesses owned by Haskell, who as of June had more than half a million dollars in business and personal debts, which he attributed to a 2023 fire at a former Camden Blaze location. His restaurant empire has seen multiple closures in the last couple years, as well as the recent $1 million purchase of a Lincolnville winery.
The town wants a judge to order Blaze to remove the unpermitted structures and issue unspecified fines, according to the lawsuit. Blue Hill used satellite images, pictures, permitting records and statements by Blaze in compiling the lawsuit, it said.
“I prefer not to comment on pending litigation, other than to say I disagree with the allegations in the complaint,” Haskell said.
Blue Hill town officials were not immediately available for comment. Contact information for the Warren Trust could not be found.
Blue Hill’s Select Board voted to sue the restaurant at an Aug. 31 meeting. That decision came about three weeks after the town canceled a hearing about a settlement agreement because the two sides weren’t in agreement.
The unpermitted structures first started appearing in November 2021 when an outdoor kitchen and bar were built, the lawsuit said. In the following years a commercial meat smoker and an outdoor stage with a roof and three walls were added.
Neighbors complained about the noise from the summer concerts, saying they were too loud and went too late. Blue Hill found in July 2025 that the restaurant did not get the required special amusement permit.
During an October 2025 Select Board meeting, a town employee said he couldn’t find records of building permits for the stage and other recent construction. At the time Haskell said he knew the outdoor stage was built without permits.
Haskell was supposed to obtain the required permits and comply with town ordinances by March 31, which did not happen, according to the lawsuit. He submitted incomplete permit applications.
The structures were still on the property when a Blue Hill code enforcement officer checked on Sept. 16, according to the lawsuit.
In addition to being unpermitted, the outdoor kitchen is built within 25 feet of the high water line of Mill Stream, which violates shoreland zoning, the lawsuit said. The stage, kitchen, smoker, bar and a storage building on one of the restaurant’s lots takes up more than 90% of the space. Zoning laws say that no more than 20% of the lot can be non-vegetated, the lawsuit said.
The unpermitted structures are in a FEMA-designated flood hazard area but the company did not get the required permit before building, according to the lawsuit.
Fines for the alleged violations range from $100 to $5,000 per day, per violation, the lawsuit said. A fine of $15,000 plus $4,200 of the town’s legal fees had accrued by July 8, according to a letter from Blue Hill to Haskell and the property owner.

title: Should you buy a house now or wait?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Should you buy a house now or wait?
Key takeaways
- The housing market has become more friendly for homebuyers recently, but even so, many prospective buyers are sidelined by record-high prices.
- If your credit score is strong, your employment is stable and you have enough savings to cover a down payment and closing costs, buying now can still be a smart move.
- But if your personal finances are not ideal at the moment, or if home values in your area are on the decline, it might be better to wait.
Buy now, or wait? That’s the question prospective homeowners have been struggling to answer as home prices keep skyrocketing and rates keep rising.
So, is it a good time to buy a home? Or is it better to wait on the sidelines, in the hopes that either prices or rates see a significant drop soon? The combination of high home prices and mortgage rates has led many would-be buyers to pick the “wait” side of the equation, but these considerations can help you determine the way forward.
Is now a good time to buy a house?
No matter which way the real estate market is leaning, buying now means you can start building equity immediately. It also means avoiding the potential for mortgage rate fluctuations later: Rising rates can wreak havoc on your monthly budget, and they also result in paying more in interest over the life of the loan.
While they have backed off from the high of 8% hit in late 2023, they’re still elevated. Currently, mortgage rates are at their highest level in more than 18 months, with the 30-year fixed rate averaging 7.08% as of late September, according to Bankrate’s weekly survey of large lenders.
Home prices are also sky-high, with NAR’s data reflecting 38 consecutive months of year-over-year increases. The median sale price of an existing home in the U.S. was $429,100 in August 2026 — the highest August price ever recorded by the National Association of Realtors (NAR). Together, these factors might dissuade you from buying right now, and that’s understandable.
On the bright side, housing inventory is finally expanding a bit. There were 1.62 million homes for sale at the end of October 2025, marking the first time since November 2019 that inventory exceeded 1.6 million units, NAR says. That represented a 4.9-month supply of unsold inventory, up from 4.6 months in July 2026 and 4.6 months in August 2025.
If you’re ready to buy and you find a place you want to call home, pull the trigger. Timing the market is nearly impossible, and over the course of the 5 to 10 years you own the home, you’re likely to recoup your investment.
Whenever you buy, don't overpay for the loan
Bankrate research finds 87% of Americans overpay for their home loans. For the typical borrower, that adds up to $3,343 in extra costs each year. Don’t settle for the first offer — be sure to shop around.
How to know if you should buy a house or wait
Ultimately, the decision of when to buy a home is up to you, and it hinges on highly personal factors — the birth of a child, job changes, divorce, a death in the family. Life goes on, whether the timing is perfect or not. These questions can help guide your decision if you’re anxious to become a homeowner and start house-hunting.
- How is your credit? Before you start house-hunting, check your credit score. If you have demonstrated that you are a low-risk borrower with a history of on-time payments, you’ll be in line for the lowest mortgage rates a lender offers.
- Have you saved enough for a down payment? In addition to paying your bills on time, you should be sitting on a sizable chunk of change for a down payment. The more you can pay upfront, the less you’ll have to borrow (and so the less interest you’ll have to pay). You should also consider closing costs and other mortgage-related expenses
- Are you able to afford homeownership? More goes into the cost of owning a home than just the mortgage payment. You’ll need to be sure you can afford insurance costs, property taxes and any maintenance or emergencies that inevitably pop up along the way.
- How long are you planning to stay in the home? Beyond the purchase price, buying a home comes with closing costs that can run thousands more. So, to justify those one-time transaction costs, it’s wise to be reasonably certain that you won’t move again anytime soon — or that you’ll be financially stable enough to hold on to the property and rent it out. Selling a home very soon after buying can have serious tax implications.
- Are home values in your area dropping? The country’s overall median home price may be soaring to new heights, but some individual areas have still seen price declines. Such declines may not be done yet, so it could pay to be patient for a bit longer.
- Is the inventory in your area increasing substantially? When there are more properties on the market to choose from, buyers enjoy more bargaining power. Many areas have seen a jump in inventory recently, which certainly helps.
