Know your local market
Deciding whether to buy a house now or wait depends a lot on where you want to call home. Regardless of national headlines, real estate is a local game and can vary greatly from one market to another, even within the same state or metro area.
Consider this Redfin data from North Carolina’s Research Triangle cities of Raleigh and Chapel Hill, only about 30 miles from each other: In mid-2025, both cities had relatively similar median home prices of $450,000 and $495,000, respectively. But they’ve gone in opposite directions recently.
In Raleigh, the median price dipped to about $422,000, down 6% in a year. Meanwhile, the median price in Chapel Hill soared to nearly $660,000 in August 2026, up nearly 20% over the past year. They’re close in proximity, with similar pricing, but one market is in decline while the other is on the upswing. That can make a big difference for your buying strategy.
This is just one example of local markets going in different directions – and it’s another reason why it’s so hard to say whether it’s a “good” or “bad” time to buy. In today’s homebuying market, it’s more important than ever to find a real estate agent who really knows your local area — down to your specific neighborhood — and can help you successfully navigate its unique quirks
Next steps
Trying to buy a house right now might feel overwhelming, but waiting too long can present challenges as well. Review your finances in detail, and think about how much you’re able to pay upfront as a down payment. Your credit score is the single most important factor in determining your mortgage rate, so make sure you’ve cleaned up any outstanding issues.
Be sure to take the pulse of the town in which you’re hoping to live. Then, talk with an experienced local real estate agent to figure out whether you should buy now or wait until you’ve saved up enough to do a deal now.
Frequently asked questions
-  Should you wait for mortgage rates to drop? No. It’s almost impossible to know where mortgage rates are headed. The best advice: If you’re financially and emotionally ready to buy a house, then you should do so regardless of where mortgage rates are.
-  Is now a bad time to buy a house? Buying a house is a deeply personal decision, based on where you are in life. If you live in a one-bedroom apartment and are expecting twins, for instance, it’s a great time to buy a house, no matter what’s happening in the economy. Base your decision on your own individual circumstances rather than what’s happening in the housing market.
-  Is the housing market going to crash? Housing experts do not think so. While there is certainly some economic uncertainty swirling right now, most experts believe that the housing market will not crash. Home prices may decline in some areas, but it won’t be catastrophic — think of it as more of a soft landing.
-  What if there’s a recession? Talk of a possible recession has been increasing lately, and as you might imagine, recessions are a risky time to buy a home. If you lose your job, for example, a lender will be much less likely to approve your loan application. Even if a recession doesn’t affect you directly, if your geographic area is hard-hit, that could have a serious effect on the local real estate market. Fewer people with the means to buy means a lower chance of homes selling, which could keep homeowners from listing and decrease your options as a buyer. There are some potential upsides to buying a home during a recession, though, if you’re financially able to do so. Notably, there will be less competition, which could help you find a great property that you otherwise couldn’t.

title: Federal funding for tick-borne diseases extended until 2030
text:
A 2021 law that provided funding for studying and combating vector-borne diseases, including those carried by ticks, has been reauthorized through 2030.
The Kay Hagan Tick Reauthorization Act passed both houses of Congress and was signed into law by President Donald Trump on Wednesday, according to the office of U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, who sponsored the Senate version of the bill.
The law provides $10 million in funding for grants to regional centers of excellence in vector-borne diseases and for a national strategy around the diseases, which include such tick-borne illnesses as Lyme disease, Powassan virus, anaplasmosis and babesiosis, along with diseases carried by mosquitoes, such as dengue and West Nile virus.
Kay Hagan was a U.S. senator from North Carolina, who died in 2019 from complications of a Powassan virus infection believed to have been contracted from a tick bite.

title: Landowner banned from North Maine Woods says he can’t access his own property
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - A landowner in the North Maine Woods has been issued a lifetime ban and says he is no longer able to access his 400-acre property.
Mark Thomas was banned from the North Maine Woods on Oct.24, 2025. In a letter from North Maine Woods Incorporated to Thomas, officials claim since 2020 he committed several violations of Maine Inland Fish and Wildlife laws. The letter informed Thomas that he had been banned from the North Maine Woods and that if he’s found within an area he doesn’t have deeded access to he may face trespassing charges.
Organization responds
North Maine Woods Inc. Executive Director Bill Greaves wrote in a statement:
“North Maine Woods is a non-profit organization that manages public access on approximately 3.5 million acres of private timberlands. Public recreational access on these private lands is by permission. While the majority of public users are respectful of this permissive open access, on occasion there are users who are not and abuse this privilege. On such occasions, NMW takes steps to address this behavior, which can include prohibiting a person from using private lands for recreational use - i.e., those individuals no longer have permission.
“Each time a visitor enters the North Maine Woods, they agree to a Land Use and Camping Permit. Also, NMW prohibitions for recreational users are specific to permissive use and access. These steps help ensure permissive open access can remain for the majority of recreational users, especially during this time of year as we enter hunting season. Each individual situation is case-specific. NMW does not typically share details of such behaviors specific to any individuals out of privacy respect but may do so with cooperating law enforcement agencies. When a FOIA request is submitted to a government agency, this information then becomes available to the public. Whether someone has permission to use private lands is a wholly separate issue from whether an individual has, or does not have, certain property rights.”
Landowner disputes claims
Thomas calls the accusations unverified and incorrect and says he’d never harm the area.
“I love those woods up there. I literally stop in the spring and pick up trash because guys snowmobile down all the roads and I pick everything from gum wrappers to empty beer cans. It’s the most beautiful place in the world to me where I come from. It’s gorgeous. I cherish the place. I love it. I respect it and I want to bring my kid up there to have the memories that I had with my dad and the last thing I would do is do something harmful to the place,” he said.
Thomas denies every accusation against him. He says he never bypassed a gate and bought a season pass every year. He says the trespassing charge was dropped and denies vandalizing a bridge. He says a worker he hired stole the outhouse he’s been accused of taking and later confessed.
Family affected
Thomas said the situation has not only affected him, but his family as well.
“I’ve never stolen a thing in my life and never would and I have the money to buy something if I want it and it was just bizarre. I have 2 kids. I have my son and then me and my wife are in the process of becoming legal guardians of a 15-year-old boy that lost both his parents at a very young age. He moved in with us back in November and he loves the outdoors and this whole summer came and went. It makes me wanna cry and they’re like, ‘Let’s go up to camp,’ and I haven’t even told them because I keep thinking this is like a nightmare I’m gonna wake up from.”
Thomas says there is no appeal process. He just wants the ban lifted to reach and maintain his property, and enjoy it with family and friends.

title: 'America's Most Wanted' rerun leads to arrest in 1997 hit-and-run that killed man mowing lawn
text:
'America's Most Wanted' rerun leads to arrest in 1997 hit-and-run that killed man mowing lawn
Leslie Ruby, 64, died after he was struck outside his home on Easton Boulevard on Sept. 29, 1997.
'America's Most Wanted' rerun leads to arrest in 1997 hit-and-run that killed man mowing lawn
Leslie Ruby, 64, died after he was struck outside his home on Easton Boulevard on Sept. 29, 1997.
Nearly three decades after an Iowa man was killed in a hit-and-run, police say the suspected driver has been arrested.
Leslie Ruby, 64, died after he was struck outside his Des Moines home on Easton Boulevard on Sept. 29, 1997.
Police identified Gerardo Garcia-Michel, who was 28 at the time, as the suspected driver, but investigators said he left Iowa before he could be arrested.
Dan Anderson, who still lives next door to Ruby’s former home, recalled what happened that day. Anderson's wife had been inside their home when Ruby was hit.
“Les had been at his daughter’s house with his riding lawn mower and was on his way back,” said Anderson, who said Ruby was mowing his daughter's lawn. “He was hit in front of the driveway to the house next door and ended up in front of our driveway, so he was carried about 150 feet by the impact.”
Des Moines police Sgt. Paul Parizek said investigators in 1997 did not have access to the technology commonly used today.
“We didn’t have video evidence from Ring cameras. We didn’t have traffic cameras,” said Parizek. “So this was officers talking to witnesses.”
Those interviews led detectives to an officer on patrol days later, eventually finding a vehicle matching the description of the one involved, but it was abandoned. After working with what they knew, police later identified Garcia-Michel as the suspected driver.
“He apparently didn’t waste much time getting out of town, and the leads told us that he’d gone to Southern California,” said Parizek.
The warrant remained active for nearly 30 years. Sometime after the incident, there was an "America's Most Wanted" profile done on the case.
The case changed this August after someone watching a rerun of the episode submitted a Crime Stoppers tip.
“It was from a person who said, ‘I’m watching a rerun of 'America’s Most Wanted,' and I recognized the guy as being a person who lives in my building,’” said Parizek. "We were super excited about it. This is how it's supposed to work. This is why we tell these stories to raise awareness. As we read further down, this guy's in New Jersey."
Garcia-Michel, who police said has been living in New Jersey, was arrested by U.S. marshals on Aug. 26. He is awaiting extradition to Iowa.
“Kudos to the people for keeping track of this for 30 years and hopefully it works out as it should,” said Anderson.
Parizek said Ruby’s wife and daughter have died since that day in 1997, but police were able to notify his granddaughter.
“One of the things she said is that it was nice to know that justice was going to be served,” said Parizek. “And it was also nice to know that they weren’t forgotten about.”

title: Judge approves Paramount's settlement with states over Warner buyout, allowing merger to soon close
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — A federal judge has granted Paramount’s settlement agreement with 12 states that sued over the company’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, allowing the companies to soon close their $81 billion mega merger.
In a Wednesday order, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín ruled that the proposed consent decree was a “fair, reasonable, and good faith approach to address the competitive harms” alleged by the states’ lawsuit. Paramount — which was bought by Skydance just last year — previously called the antitrust challenge the last hurdle ahead of closing its Warner merger, and signaled that it aims to close its Warner acquisition in early October.
Shortly after Martínez-Olguín’s ruling Wednesday afternoon, the company announced Ynon Kreiz — current chief executive at toy giant Mattel — will join Paramount on Oct. 5 and serve as co-CEO alongside David Ellison after the merger’s closing.
In a statement, Ellison said Paramount’s merger with Warner marks a “transformational moment for our industry” and that he and his new co-CEO will lead a business that is “creator-first, tech-forward and built to scale globally.”
A Paramount-Warner marriage will bring together two of Hollywood’s last five legacy studios. HBO Max, a library full of titles including “Harry Potter” and cable networks such as CNN will also find themselves under the same roof with CBS, the likes of the “Top Gun” franchise and the Paramount+ streaming service.
That further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players. And many critics of the deal have decried the states’ settlement, arguing the terms are too weak.
The final antitrust fight
Paramount touted clearances for its Warner acquisition from regulators worldwide over recent months, including the Trump administration’s Justice Department in the U.S.
But in July, top prosecutors from 12 states — led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta — sued to block the merger altogether. They alleged a Paramount-Warner combination would “extinguish competition” in Hollywood and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly movie theatergoers and cable customers.
Last week, the states agreed to settle those claims through new commitments from Paramount, including pledges to increase film production in the U.S. over the next five years, grant millions of dollars to a fund aimed at supporting workers displaced by the merger and establish new editorial monitoring of CNN and CBS.
Martínez-Olguín didn’t greenlight the terms right away — maintaining at a Thursday hearing that the court isn’t merely a “rubber stamp” on a settlement of this kind and that she, like many others, had questions. The judge granted outside critics of the settlement (including members of the Block The Merger coalition and the League of United Latin American Citizens) a brief window to share their opposition. She also instructed Paramount and the states to respond to concerns raised by Democratic Sen. Cory Booker.
By Wednesday’s order, however, she concluded that the hopes for settlement terms to go further “do not rise to the level of legal violations upon which the Court can reject the parties’ negotiated resolution.”
The Writers Guild of America, which had filed its own suit shortly after the states in July, also reached a settlement agreement with Paramount last week — concluding that it couldn’t continue its legal fight alone.
Ongoing criticism of the deal
The Block the Merger coalition on Wednesday maintained the states’ settlement was a “toothless” deal.
“In years to come, we’ll be able to point to this failure to put consumers over the monied interests of corporate consolidation as the tipping-point moment for media in this country,” Block the Merger said in a statement. But, the group added, “if there is one discernible benefit to the approval of this corporate takeover, it’s that people are now wide awake and paying attention — and their anger is not going to fade away.”
Before agreeing to settle, Bonta previously said the states would only consider “robust” structural remedies. The bulk of the eventual settlement outlined behavioral requirements, at least in the immediate future, with some potential “court enforceable” penalties if Paramount breaks promises down the road.
Even so, most of the company’s new commitments only last five years. Paula Blizzard, an attorney for California, said in Thursday’s hearing that the states eventually settled on terms that didn’t “last forever” because the industry is changing — while immediate divestments, or even the complete blocking of the deal that they initially demanded, could open the door to further acquisitions.
Among those new commitments include a pledge from Paramount to increase spending on film production in the U.S. — by at least an additional $1.5 billion over the next five years — and promises to release at least 30 films each year, a figure Ellison already touted earlier in his quest for Warner.
The states’ settlement would require Paramount to distribute 30 films in theaters each year for the next two years — and 32 films in each of the three years after that. The fine print notes that only 50% of those movies would have to be “produced or jointly produced” by the combined company. If Paramount fails to meet these film outputs, the states say it will have to divest from Miramax Studios and pay $30 million for each missed film toward healthcare and retirement trust funds associated with the Writers Guild of America and other industry unions.
Paramount also agreed to commit $47.5 million to help fund training and career development for workers displaced by the merger, again over the next five years ($9.5 million each year).
Meanwhile, when it comes to cable, the states’ settlement orders the company to negotiate deals for current Paramount-owned and Warner-owned basic cable channels separately over the next five years. If Paramount violates those terms, a court may order future divestments.
The company must also form a “News Editorial Independence Board” to monitor news operations at CBS and CNN within 180 days of completing its Warner acquisition. But critics point to editorial turmoil already seen at CBS under Skydance ownership — and aren’t convinced this new body will move the needle much.
Per court documents outlining the settlement’s terms, Paramount’s new editorial body will be made up of five “active or retired” journalists with at least 10 years of experience — all appointed by, and reporting to, the combined company’s board of directors for three-year terms. Beyond his CEO title, Ellison is Paramount’s current chairman and is set to remain in the top spot after the Warner acquisition closes.
While joining the rest of the states in the wider settlement, Colorado and Washington declined to sign off on the editorial board terms. And prosecutors like Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, who wanted a full divestiture of CNN and CBS, said last week he wished the deal could have gone further.
Including billions of dollars in debt, Paramount’s buyout of Warner is currently valued at about $111 billion based on outstanding shares.

title: Gentle giant Backpack claims Fat Bear Week title in close finale at Alaska's Katmai National Park
text:
'Heavy is the bear that wears the crown. Like really heavy': Backpack declared winner of Fat Bear Week
After a week of fierce competition, Backpack emerged victorious as Fat Bear Week champion, the heftiest bear of Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.
The nonprofit running the longstanding contest announced that the bear, known for his pacifist nature, was the winner Tuesday with more than 100,000 votes, giving him a close win over Bear 910 with just over 50% of the poll.
In the player at the top: Contender video shows some of the bears that were in the 12th annual Fat Bear Week
The contest, which is in its 12th year, celebrates the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears that live in the preserve on the Alaska Peninsula, which extends from the state's southwest corner toward the Aleutian Islands. Fat Bear Week was started in 2014 as an interactive way to inform the public about brown bears, the coastal cousins of grizzlies.
Last year's winner, Chunk — known officially as Bear 32 — clinched his victory at an estimated 1,200 pounds. He was handily defeated in the first round of competition this year by Bucky, who went on to lose a faceoff against Backpack, known officially as Bear 89.
The event this year featured 16 bears vying for the heavyweight title in a single-elimination, bracket-style tournament. All voting is done online at www.fatbearweek.org, and the winner was declared Tuesday evening after the final poll closed. The public could watch the bears on explore.org's livestream cameras before deciding on their favorite.
"Fat bears are successful bears," the nonprofit says on its website. This group gorges itself on the abundant salmon that return to the Brooks River starting in late June. It's there that they can stuff themselves to accumulate the fat reserves they will need to survive the winter. To be featured in the contest, the bears must frequent the area around the river.
Backpack is the son of former Fat Bear Week champion Holly, who introduced him to the Brooks River when he was a first-year cub in 2006. His name was inspired by his habit of climbing onto his mother's back when they swam the river. This year's fans cheered on Backpack in the contest's Instagram comments, noting his lineage and reputation as a gentle giant.
"Unlike many large adult male bears, Backpack hasn't shown much aggression toward his competitors," his contestant profile reads.
Backpack uses his "quiet strength" rather than brawling and is often seen in wildlife cameras sitting on a rock downstream, appearing to take in the scenery around him.
He defeated Bear 910, who is also the daughter of a former champion: 409 Beadnose.
Adult male brown bears typically weigh 600 to 900 pounds (about 270 to 410 kilograms) in midsummer. By the time they are ready to hibernate after feasting on migrating and spawning salmon, large males can weigh well over 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms). Females are about one-third smaller. The bears may each eat as many as 30 fish a day this time of year, working hard to eat a year's worth of food in about six months.
During winter hibernation, the bears do not eat or drink and can lose one-third of their body weight.
Fat Bear Week's contestants also included five bear families, in recognition of the record high number of families and cubs at the river this summer. A mother must feed and protect her cubs while also eating enough calories to sustain herself through hibernation. Cubs often face the risk of attack by other bears due to territorialism or food scarcity.
Bear 132 and her three spring cubs advanced to the semifinals, but lost out to Bear 910.
Bear 132 has become one of the largest and most experienced mother bears at Brooks River, according to her contestant profile. In mid-July, one of her cubs became separated from the family for several days, wandering the river corridor alone. They were reunited a few days later.
The National Park Service posted the following after Backpack was named the champ:
We have a CHONKION!
The Fat Bear Week crown goes to: Bear 89 Backpack
Heavy is the bear that wears the crown. Like really heavy. Thank you to everyone who voted, shared, cheered, argued passionately about bears, defended your favorite chonk, and generally made Fat Bear Week the wonderfully amazing celebration of bears, salmon, the Alaskan ecosystem, and did we mention the bears?
Also, a BIG thank you to all 16 bears who involuntarily participated. They ate. They napped. They fished. They grew enormous. They understood the assignment. (Shoutout to runner-up Bear 910 as well) Here’s to a successful winter for Katmai’s fat bears!
___
Associated Press writer Jamie Stengle contributed from Dallas.

title: Letter to the Editor: Trevor Doiron has a plan
Secretary Hegseth confirms US military will cut 20% of its generals and admirals
text:
Secretary Hegseth confirms that the US military will cut 20% of its generals and admirals
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Wednesday that the U.S. military will cut 20% of its generals and admirals as he delivered what he is calling his “State of the Force” address.
Hegseth was speaking to junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, the second year in a row that he has given such an address. This time, the U.S. military is seven months into a war with Iran with no clear end in sight, has captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and killed more than 200 people in strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats in Latin America, among other actions worldwide.
The speech is not a usual fixture among Pentagon leaders. While Hegseth’s predecessors have regularly addressed troops and top officers, they have traditionally done so in small or private settings.
The Pentagon chief, however, again focused on how he has drastically retooled the U.S. military by targeting what he calls “woke” culture — through a rollback of diversity programs, a review of ground combat units with female troops and a new screening program for “testosterone deficiency” among male personnel.
Pentagon officials had previewed that Hegseth would announce more cuts to the number of generals and admirals. He directed all military services to double the 10% reduction he ordered last spring for roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, making it a total 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027.
“I call it accountability and long overdue,” he said.
Several senators viewed Hegseth’s move as nothing short of a “purge” of the military’s top ranks that will take years to rebuild.
“He’s got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., the former Navy combat pilot and NASA astronaut, who has been critical of Hegseth. “He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it.”
Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth’s reasoning behind the decision.
“If it’s simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first,” Rounds said.
Trump or Hegseth already have fired or pushed to retire more than two dozen military leaders since taking office, including the Army’s top uniformed officer, Gen. Randy George, a move that angered both Republicans and Democrats in Congress. They also have included a number of senior officers who are women or people of color.
Previous leaders who were ousted include Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. CQ Brown; Chief of Naval Operations Lisa Franchetti; and Vice Adm. Shoshana Chatfield, the U.S. military representative to the NATO Military Committee.
Although Hegseth never gave specific reasons for those firings, most were tied to the belief that they endorsed or spoke openly in support of diversity, equity and inclusion programs, which have been targets of Hegseth and Trump.
As part of last year’s cuts, Hegseth also ordered the active duty military to shed 20% of its four-star general officers — the highest-level leaders — and the National Guard to shed 20% of its top positions, but it is unclear if all those cuts have been made. The new cuts could include any one-star general or above, or an officer of equivalent Navy rank.
When Hegseth first announced the effort to trim the highest levels of the military ranks, he argued it was intended to remove “redundant force structure to optimize and streamline leadership.” In a memo released in May 2025, he said the aim was to free the military from “unnecessary bureaucratic layers.”
The number of general officer positions in the military is set by law, but it is possible to let positions remain unfilled by not submitting replacements to Congress.
Hegseth's efforts have extended well beyond personnel changes among the top ranks. He oversaw Trump’s ban on transgender troops, while announcing new directives for “gender-neutral” or “male-level” standards for physical fitness.
___
Associated Press writers Lisa Mascaro and Meg Kinnard contributed to this report.

title: Avesta Housing cuts the ribbon on new Westbrook apartment building
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Avesta Housing cuts the ribbon on new Westbrook apartment building
Avesta Housing held a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Wednesday morning for Seavey Crossing.
The new apartment building holds 61 one-bedroom units for adults who are at least 55 years old. Leasing is now open, and Avesta says rent will range from $1,300 to $1,600.
"Today, we're not just celebrating the new completion of a housing development," commented Southern Maine Area Agency on Aging with Ashley Perrone. "We're celebrating the creation of 61 new opportunities for older adults to have a safe, stable and comfortable place to call their own."
It comes as many are calling the current state of housing in Maine a crisis. Earlier this year, Gov. Janet Mills said in an address that to battle the crisis, the state will need to add 80,000 additional units by the year 2030.
She added that in 2025, the state's communities added 7,500, which is 9% over pace for that goal, but the annual demands are just going to grow.
"Across Cumberland County, the typical renter is facing affordability gaps throughout the past decade, and the gap is widening from 2022 to 2024 alone," said Director of Development for MaineHousing Laurie Warzinski. "The difference between the typical household income and the income needed to afford a typical rental grew from about $6,000 to $15,000."
According to Avesta, Seavey Crossing will emphasize independent living, healthy aging and a connection with the community.
The organization adds that the space has easy access to healthcare services, dining, shopping and other amenities.
"I hear all the time from seniors who are worried about when they give up their home, what if they have to move to another community that they're not familiar with," commented Westbrook Mayor David Morse. "They would like to stay here."
If you or a family member are interested, Seavey Crossing will be hosting an open house on Saturday. There, you can check out the space, speak with representatives from Seavey Crossing and learn about the leasing requirements.

title: New crisis center brings emergency mental health care to Bangor
text:
Starting next week, people facing a mental health crisis in the Bangor area will have a place to get immediate care and support.
Bangor’s Crisis Receiving Center at 68 First St., housed within Community Health and Counseling Services, will offer walk-in services for people experiencing mental health and substance use crises.
The center will add a low-barrier place for people to get help amid a shortage of mental health providers in the state, and as Bangor struggles to support homeless community members who often have trouble getting easy access to mental health services. It’s expected to ease the burden on law enforcement and local emergency rooms, who are often the first points of contact when someone is in crisis.
It’s the third such center that’s opened in the state, including a Portland-based pilot that began in 2022 and one that opened two weeks ago in Lewiston, as part of a push from the Mills administration.
“Crisis receiving centers work, which is why I asked the legislature to establish a network of them across Maine, so any person suffering a behavioral health crisis can get prompt and appropriate care instead of being left alone or languishing in an emergency room or jail, which is too often the case,” Gov. Janet Mills said at a ribbon-cutting Wednesday.
The center will be open 24/7 starting at 8 a.m. on Monday, Oct. 5, according to Dale Hamilton, executive director of Community Health and Counseling Services. It’s open to people ages 14 and older.
It adds a new component to the crisis response system at Community Health and Counseling Services, which already includes mobile outreach and a residential program, Hamilton said.
Four people will staff the center per shift, according to Hamilton, including nurses, a nurse practitioner, peer specialists and crisis workers. They’ll treat people for as long as they need, which could be just a couple hours or longer, and have space for up to eight people at a time, he said.
Patients can be referred or just show up to the center.
It’s made possible by a $3.35 million grant from Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services, which included nearly $1 million for a year-long building renovation as well as funds for ongoing operating costs.
While some insurance plans and MaineCare will reimburse for some of the services provided at the crisis receiving center, the state funding help means that no one should worry about their ability to pay when visiting, Hamilton said.
The Portland center has had more than 3,500 visitors in the four years it’s been open, according to Mills.

title: ‘Taking Care of Granny’: Hear this caregiver’s story of dementia, dignity and finding help
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of The Aging Untold Podcast, Dugan Meredith, who documents caring for his mother-in-law online through the “Taking Care of Granny” social media feeds, joins us to talk about what it’s really like to become a caregiver and how his family found their way through it.
Caring for an aging loved one can reshape a family, and it’s a responsibility more men are shouldering than ever before.
Watch the full podcast episode:
Today, an estimated 21 million men are in caregiving roles, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. They are navigating the daily challenges of aging and illness alongside their own jobs and children.
Meredith’s mother-in-law, known online as Granny, was originally living with her oldest daughter in the Charleston, South Carolina, area. Meredith described the signs that led the family to seek a diagnosis.
“She was experiencing symptoms, showing signs, forgetting how to go pick up the grandchildren from school, getting lost,” Meredith said. “Talking to random strangers and inviting them back to the house.”
The turning point came when Granny tried to cook soup by putting it in a baking pan in the oven instead of putting it in a pot and placing it on the stove. Granny was later diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia, also known as FTD.
Dividing caregiving duties wasn’t planned — it just happened
When Granny moved in with Meredith and his wife, there wasn’t a formal plan for who would do what.
“I think it was decided for us,” Meredith said. The family originally intended to split time with another sister-in-law, but when she had to return to full-time work, “the responsibility fell squarely on our shoulders,” Meredith said.
For a time, Meredith’s wife took Granny to work with her during the day and Dugan took over caregiving duties in the evenings. Eventually, his wife’s employer could no longer accommodate the arrangement, prompting the family to hire outside help.
Learning to ‘meet her where she’s at’
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, asked Meredith to reflect on his experience as a man stepping into a caregiving role that required hiring help rather than “fixing” the problem himself.
“Granny coming to live with us was a struggle for me mentally,” Meredith said. “I was exhausted because I could not figure out why I could not get a 72-, 73-year-old woman to understand, you can’t do this — it will hurt you.”
Meredith described one moment when Granny wanted to cut her hair and used a lighter to try to burn off a piece of it after he took away her scissors and said they would take her to get her hair cut.
“I could not understand in my mind, why does this woman do this? Why can I not get her to understand she’s going to hurt herself?” he said.
Meredith said he came to the realization that he needed to meet Granny where she is.
“Sam taught me that very early on,” Meredith said, referring to Aging Untold expert and gerontologist Sam Cradduck. “You have to meet them where they are.”
Meredith emphasized that lesson for other men in a similar situation.
“For men out there, you’re not going to fix it. The only thing you can do to help the situation is to swallow your pride, swallow your ego and learn to meet them where they’re at,” Meredith said.
Decoding Granny’s signature word: ‘heavy’
Viewers of Meredith’s videos on TikTok and Facebook are familiar with Granny’s repeated word, “heavy.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, asked how the family figures out what she means.
“What is she trying to tell me? Is her stomach hurt? Is her food cold? Is her food too hot?” Meredith said. “When she says ‘my heavy is heavy,’ I keep reiterating, and eventually she’ll move a certain way, she’ll do something with her hands, she’ll nod with her head, and we’ll figure it out.”
Meredith said much of the communication comes down to body language and behaviors learned from living with Granny every day.
Why Meredith started sharing the journey online
Meredith said the decision to document his caregiving journey online came from feeling isolated.
“I felt like I was alone. I felt like nobody in the world understood what was going on within my mind and in my heart,” Meredith said.
He recalled sitting at his kitchen table with a cup of coffee, recording himself talking about his frustrations before posting the video to TikTok. That post led him to a community of other caregivers he didn’t know existed.
Meredith said he’s still learning to manage the volume of response, including tens of thousands of messages and comments.
“You go through a whirlwind of emotions just reading the comments or the messages that come in,” he said.
Meredith said the online community has helped his family tremendously.
“For every one negative person, there’s 500 positives,” he said, and people in that community provide tips, which Meredith uses.
“Not only are they helping us, but they are helping the others that are reading the comments,” Meredith said.
The ‘sandwich generation’ and the cost of care
O’Rourke noted that Meredith and his wife are also raising children while caring for Granny — a dynamic often called the “sandwich generation.”
“We are 100% the sandwich generation,” Meredith said.
In the beginning, he said, the couple struggled to give their children enough attention because of the protocols required to care for Granny. Hiring additional caregivers allowed them “to still be parents for our children and give them the attention that they need and that they deserve as well.”
Meredith also spoke about the cost of care. The family looked into memory care facilities before deciding on the private route, which he described as the more affordable option.
“You go look at nice memory care facilities — we’re talking $10,000 to $15,000 a month,” Meredith said.
He said monetizing the family’s social media content has helped cover the cost of keeping Granny comfortable at home.
“Everyone always asks, are you going to keep her here until her last breath. We will,” Meredith said.
Meredith is also the founder of a nonprofit, also called Taking Care of Granny, which he said is focused solely on helping caregivers.
He said the idea for a nonprofit came from a conversation with another caregiver who documents caring for his wife, who has Parkinson’s disease.
“He was the one that started the idea with me. He was like, ‘What about a nonprofit? You do a nonprofit to provide care to the caregivers,’” Meredith said. “I was like, I like that idea. I don’t know how I’m going to do it, but let me start digging into it.”
Where things stand today
Asked how Granny is doing now, Meredith said the disease has progressed. The family now purees her food because of trouble swallowing, and he’s noticed her shuffling her feet while walking, so the family has removed rugs and other trip hazards from the house.
Hospice has also brought in a medical bed to help prevent falls.
“The disease has progressed, and we’re at that point now,” Meredith said. “But given what we’ve been through, I would say she’s doing well.”
See the full interview with Dugan Meredith
How to follow Taking Care of Granny
Key takeaways
- Male caregiving. An estimated 21 million men are currently in caregiving roles for aging or ill loved ones, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving.
- Meet them where they are. Dugan Meredith emphasized that trying to reason with a loved one with dementia rarely works. Caregivers need to adapt to the person’s reality instead.
- The “sandwich generation” faces unique pressure. Balancing young children and an aging parent or relative at the same time requires intentional systems so neither gets neglected.
- Online communities can ease caregiver isolation. Sharing the caregiving journey publicly connected Meredith with a wider community of caregivers facing similar experiences.

title: Trellis Health expands member-based primary care to Brunswick
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trellis Health, a MaineHealth subsidiary offering membership-based primary care through a collaborative care team model, has opened its second location at 4 Stephen Drive in Brunswick.
Trellis opened its first location in Portland in 2024, at 1945 Congress St. in the Gateway Business Park.
Trellis operates on a membership model rather than billing for individual visits or services. Clients can purchase memberships directly or join when membership is offered through their employer.
Growing trend
Trellis is part of a growing trend of direct primary care practices that provide direct provider access through a flat membership fee with no deductibles or coinsurance.
The model is designed to eliminate many of the barriers and fragmentation patients experience when care is spread across multiple offices and providers, according to a news release.
“Opening in Brunswick means more Mainers can have an ongoing relationship with a care team that knows them, understands their goals and is there to support their health over time,” said Matt Rector, chief business officer of Trellis.
Early results show Trellis members have approximately 30% fewer emergency department visits, inpatient admissions and specialist referrals, along with less imaging utilization, lowering the total cost of care, according to the release.
The Brunswick location offers a primary care provider, physical therapist, behavioral health clinician, clinical pharmacist, nurse and health coach, with same- and next-day appointments for urgent needs, 24/7 phone support and options to connect by secure text, video, or in person.

title: Group launches campaign opposing changes to Lewiston’s needle exchange program
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- A “No on Question 1” campaign launched Wednesday opposing Lewiston’s proposed syringe-service restrictions, which would require a 1-to-1 exchange, limit exchanges to 20 syringes per person per day, and require the city’s syringe service provider to operate from one fixed location.
- Speakers supporting “No on Question 1” said that beyond creating a reduction in access to sterile syringes, the restrictions could hurt other services without addressing waste, overdoses or infectious diseases.
- Proponents of Question 1 say the proposed ordinance changes would establish “a consistent, citywide standard that protects everyone.”
LEWISTON — A group calling itself Safe & Healthy Maine launched its campaign for “No on Question 1” in a news conference Wednesday.
Question 1 on the November city ballot asks voters if Lewiston’s Syringe Service Program should be amended to mandate a 1-for-1 needle exchange with a 20-syringe daily limit per person, require that each program provider operate from one fixed location, and prohibit mobile exchange units.
Speakers at the event included former state legislator Margaret Craven, Preble Street’s veterans director Laura Clark, the Rev. Sarah Bartlett of Norway’s Second Congregational Church, and doctors Paul Vinsel and Edward Walworth.
Speakers agreed that restricting syringe services programs would not only make syringe litter worse, but it could undermine public health services and exacerbate existing and future outbreaks of diseases such as HIV and hepatitis C.
Walworth, a retired general surgeon, said proponents of Question 1 are claiming that proposed restrictions would reduce syringe waste.
But restricting syringe programs is associated with more syringe waste, not less, Walworth said.
He added, “ When we restrict access to a proven public health tool without evidence that these restrictions will solve the problem we are trying to address, those problems don’t disappear,” Walworth said. “Instead, we risk creating new preventable costs and burdens for our healthcare system and our community.”
Vinsel said his experience as an emergency medicine and addiction medicine doctor in Lewiston brought him patients suffering from the consequences of shared needles and needle reuse, including skin infections, abscesses, sepsis, heart and lung infections, as well as HIV and hepatitis C.
If most of these patients had access to a syringe program, their ailments could have been preventable, Vinsel said.
“ People who use syringe service programs are five times more likely to enter treatment than people who do not use these services,” Vinsel said, adding that those who use syringe programs are three times more likely to stop using drugs. “The data is clear that these programs save lives. … Question 1 would set a dangerous precedent of ignoring evidence-based approaches to fighting the opioid epidemic.”
Despite Question 1 specifying it, the city’s existing rules governing the Lewiston Syringe Service Program already require syringe programs to obtain a city business license and to operate from a fixed location, and they prohibit mobile units. The state’s syringe-service requirements allow a person to receive up to 100 syringes per encounter.
During the long process of drafting those rules, then-Councilor Eryn Soule supported a 1-to-1 needle exchange that was rejected by the council.
Soule, who is running as an independent in Maine Senate District 21, and her husband, Marcel Leclair, who is running for Lewiston’s Ward 5 school board seat, spearheaded the Question 1 citizens petition earlier this year. The petition gathered 25 signatures more than the 941 required, putting it before the council.
The council voted not to pass the ordinance and to instead send it to voters for the Nov. 3 elections.
Soule said the referendum is about more than discarded needles — it is about “establishing a consistent, citywide standard that protects everyone” including those who utilize syringe programs and the broader Lewiston community.
“It is important to remember that a strict 1:1 exchange ratio was the Maine CDC’s original baseline prior to the pandemic … (when) our streets didn’t face the level of mass needle litter or open public drug use we see today,” she said. “What began as a well-intentioned harm reduction effort has evolved into a system that leaves hazardous conditions in the very neighborhoods where our families live, work and play.”
Soule said compassion and medical support must go hand in hand, and that without mandatory HIV and hepatitis C testing for those who use syringe services, “there is no way to ensure these programs are actually improving health outcomes or connecting people to the life-saving medical care they desperately need.”
“Meanwhile, every unreturned syringe represents a very real danger left behind in our community,” Soule said. “A strict 1:1 exchange ratio, paired with daily limits, restores accountability and helps keep our public spaces clean.”
In the first year following the implementation of Question 1, the public should see a noticeable and measurable drop in discarded needles across the city, Soule said.
Asked about the perception that a 100-syringe limit as required by the state means countless syringes are hitting Lewiston streets, No on Question 1 spokesperson Cara Courchesne said that perception is incorrect. She cited Lewiston’s only syringe program operator, Spurwink, actually having collected 38% more syringes than it gave out last year.
“It’s understandable that people have that perception, because we have had an SSP not do as well as we wished here,” Courchesne said, referring to a Syringe Service Program provider no longer in the city. “But if you want to see less needles and syringes in the street, you do not restrict the program that helps get you there.”
The Rev. Bartlett said syringe programs improve the overall health of communities.
“They are a critical part of preventing overdoses and disease, and help people find pathways to treatment,” she said. “That is important to saving people in our community.”

title: QUINN SIMPLE SCENES: Old Sayings
text:
Remember that old saying “A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush?”
I thought about this yesterday while chewing fried chicken. I don’t know what other birds are worth, but I had to pay for the chicken.
Seriously, the quote goes back to ancient times. Bird hunters reasoned that one bird already caught guaranteed dinner, while two birds uncaught (“in the bush”) meant more work plus the possibility of failure.
Why did the hunters want those other fowls, too? Maybe they expected guests for dinner, or maybe they just wanted to see if birds in the heather flock together.
See, you never can tell what our silly prehistoric pals thought! Back then, they drew stuff on their walls and called it art.
Today we call it graffiti. But if somebody famous sketched it, we call either a “mural” or “wallpaper.”
The birdie saying is much like another one claiming, “The grass is always greener on the other side of the fence.”
This means either (1) people always want what they can’t get, or (2) the neighbor buys better fertilizer.
What’s the lesson here? I’m guessing it is this:
“If you see two birds in a bush surrounded by green grass on the other side of a fence, don’t try to catch them, because they are probably in a zoo.”

title: Study ranks the most and least affordable states for retirees
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold)— Where retirees choose to live can make a significant difference in how far their savings go — and a study from Retirement Living identifies the states that offer the most financial breathing room.
Retirement Living ranked states based on housing costs, cost of living and tax-friendliness. Ella Gomes, a media relations specialist at Retirement Living, said the findings reflect a growing affordability challenge for retirees nationwide.
“Retirement affordability matters more than ever because many Americans are facing higher housing costs, health care expenses and everyday living costs than they did just a few years ago,” Gomes said. “And at Retirement Living, we wanted to understand which states provide retirees with the best opportunity to make their savings last longer.”
West Virginia ranked first as the most affordable state for retirees, with the lowest housing costs in the nation, according to the study. Median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the state is $643 a month. Mississippi, Alabama, Oklahoma and Arkansas round out the top five.
“What’s especially interesting is that these states aren’t just inexpensive in one area,” Gomes said. “They consistently perform well across housing, cost of living and taxes, making them well-rounded options for retirees who are looking to max their retirement savings.”
California tops the list of least affordable states for retirees, followed by Hawaii, Washington state, Oregon and Colorado.
“Here we see almost the opposite regional trend where the least affordable states are heavily concentrated in the West and the Northeast,” Gomes said. “Half of the bottom 10 are Western states, while New Jersey, Massachusetts, New York — those represent the Northeast. And these regions tend to have much higher housing costs, but they’re also more expensive when it comes to everyday expenses like groceries and transportation and taxes.”
For retirees considering relocation, Gomes said looking beyond a single expense category is essential. Day-to-day costs, health care access and proximity to specialists should all factor into the decision.
“It’s not only important to account for healthcare costs, but also picking a location where you can ensure you’ll have access to quality care and specialists for however your needs change over time,” Gomes said.
Retirement Living ranked all 50 states in the study. The full rankings and methodology are available on the organization’s website.

title: USDA, HUD sign agreement to streamline affordable housing process
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) Tuesday, officials say will make the homeownership process easier.
“Facing a lot of America today is the lack of affordable housing,” said USDA Sec. Brooke Rollins.
HUD and the USDA are teaming up to streamline standards related to housing, including environmental review, impact, regulations and physical inspections.
“We want to deregulate, make it easier for builders to build and for buyers to buy, and we want to make supply go up and costs go down, so more Americans, particularly in the rural areas of our country, can afford to buy a home,” explained HUD Sec. Scott Turner.
The partnership stems from the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which Congress passed at the end of June. Despite President Trump’s refusal to sign the bill, it eventually became law July 11.
“This MOU signifies and signals to the American people that USDA and HUD are indeed in partnership to make these processes easier, as we have been doing from day one,” Turner added.
Both agencies say the agreement also streamlines the housing approval process by cutting red tape and eliminating unnecessary paperwork to help communities build more homes, faster.
“The unprecedented level at which we’re all working together is a game changer for the American people,” Rollins said.
Average home prices are currently at an all-time high. The national median price for a single-family home is more than $434,000, according to the National Association of Realtors.

title: Maine employers say they need workers, so why is it hard to find a good job?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sheila Richardson has been hanging wallpaper since her youngest was in seventh grade. She learned the skill from her grandmother and her father, then grew it into a successful business with a broad customer base near her home in Turner — all by word of mouth.
“I take pride in my work,” she said. “I don’t have to advertise.”
Now 78 and a great-grandmother, she’s still working 35 years later, despite some health issues that cropped up last year.
“I’m up and down the ladder a hundred times a day,” she said. “I’m a doer. I don’t depend on anybody else.”
Richardson’s tenacity is serving her well these days, as rising costs for materials and fuel, and a shifting economic landscape make it more challenging to work or do business in Maine.
She is one of 824 Mainers who responded to a survey conducted in July by the Siena Research Institute for the Maine Trust for Local News. It found that the job market is daunting for many across the state — 51% of respondents rated their ability to get suitable employment as “only fair” or “poor,” while 41% rated their ability to make a living wage as “not very likely” or “not at all likely.”
Asked whether they could get a job with opportunities for advancement, 32% said it was “almost certain” or “very likely,” but 27% said it was “not very likely” or “not at all likely” and 39% said it was a toss-up.
The Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram interviewed a variety of people across the state who participated in the 62-question survey. While they see some bright spots, Richardson and others say workers and businesses face increasing economic headwinds.
Richardson has been working all her life, really, running a household with four kids, helping her husband with his excavation, wood harvesting and auto repair businesses, scrimping and saving to make ends meet when times got hard.
Social Security has eased her need to work, she said, but her healthcare savings are dwindling despite Medicare. She and her husband own the ranch-style home they built themselves, but it needs a new roof, and that’s going to be costly.
She sees others struggling, too, including her son, who has his own construction and excavation business, she said. Record-high diesel prices are eating up narrow profit margins.
“It’s terribly tough right now,” Richardson said. “The price of everything has gone up and you have to charge customers what it costs. You really have to pinch pennies when you don’t have money coming in.”
SHADOW OF UNCERTAINTY
In reviewing the survey results, Maine State Economist Amanda Rector said she was surprised that only 32% of respondents were positive about the potential for job advancement, especially since Maine has a worker shortage and its rapidly aging population is expected to increase retirements.
“Responses may have been overshadowed by near-term uncertainties,” Rector said, including rising costs that have led some businesses to throttle hiring and consider downsizing if artificial intelligence is used in the workplace.
She also noted significant regional differences in views of the job market — 51% of Southern/Coastal respondents (Cumberland and York counties) said they could get suitable employment, and 38% saw potential for workplace advancement. Responses in other regions were even lower.
Rector said that’s not surprising. “That’s where a lot of economic activity is in the state,” she said.
Respondents showed similar regional trends when asked whether Maine is a place where businesses can succeed — 46% rated the business climate positively, while 52% said it’s only “fair” or “poor.” Looking at that question regionally, 57% of Southern/Coastal participants had a positive response, with significantly lower rates in other areas where business owners say they’re facing tough economic conditions.
Rector also pointed out that the survey shows strong recognition — 75% statewide — of Maine’s access to affordable adult education and job training. Both have been bolstered in recent years by the state’s community colleges, building contractors, defense contractors and the U.S. Small Business Administration.
“It’s good to see that has such a strong positive response,” she said.
LACK OF RELIABLE WORKERS
Workforce training is helping Alex Thibodeau meet some of the challenges facing Maine’s manufacturing sector, including rising costs and logistical drawbacks of being at the end of the line geographically.
Thibodeau is director of operations at Kenway Composites, an Augusta company with 50 employees that makes fiber-reinforced plastic storage tanks and other equipment for heavy industry, public infrastructure and military uses.
In recent years, Thibodeau has hired seven students from the composites manufacturing program at the Foster Career and Technical Education Center in Farmington that serves several area high schools.
“They are some of our best employees,” said Thibodeau, 59. “Technical training is one of the only salvations for manufacturers who need workers. (The training programs) are so underrated and deserve more funding going forward.”
Still, a lack of reliable workers has forced Thibodeau to turn away about $2 million in contracts in recent years, he said. His hiring expectations are pretty basic — show up every day, be willing to learn and do quality work — but he’s often disappointed, despite offering benefits, bonuses and pay ranging from $23 to $35 an hour depending on the job, he said.
Recent tariffs, inflation, higher interest rates and rising fuel prices have increased the cost of procuring materials, having them delivered to Maine and transporting goods to customers, he said. Truck deliveries now come with fuel surcharges. Tariffs on one part needed for a government contract increased the price from $80,000 to $130,000.
“We as taxpayers end up paying for that,” Thibodeau said. “One of Maine’s greatest struggles is our location. Most of the truck traffic is outbound, so you have to pay for the trip in. We are disadvantaged in a lot of ways already. We don’t need additional costs.”
STARK DIFFERENCES STATEWIDE
Thibodeau’s experience and the survey’s findings align with aspects of a Maine State Chamber of Commerce goals report released this year in advance of the 2026 gubernatorial election, said Patrick Woodcock, chamber CEO.
Economic headwinds that have pummeled Maine for years have been exacerbated by recent federal policies that have increased costs and threaten to worsen the workforce shortage, he said, including immigration enforcement activities.
In reviewing the survey results, Woodcock noted that while 57% of respondents in the Southern/Coastal region said Maine is a place where businesses can be successful, 58%-60% of respondents in the rest of the state said the exact opposite.
“I found that gap to be pretty stark,” he said. “Some pessimism has taken root. There are distinct challenges between the regions, and we have to recognize and respect those differences.”
Woodcock also noted that 85% of respondents across the state said the lack of affordable housing is a problem.
“Housing has overwhelmed a lot of Maine families,” he said. “Our members have identified affordable housing as a workforce issue. We cannot attract workers, foster economic growth and have a robust business climate without addressing affordable housing.”
On the upside, Woodcock said, Maine businesses are resilient, with an uptick in recent retail sales corroborating anecdotal feedback that this summer was a fairly strong tourism season. He noted that lodging receipts increased 12.8% in July compared to 2025, and restaurants experienced 6.8% growth, according to the latest state sales tax reports.
THE GOOD AND NOT SO GOOD
Nathan Gurtman agrees — it was a successful summer for many businesses in Maine’s hospitality industry. A chef at the York Harbor Inn, he has worked in area kitchens for 30 years.
“It was a good season,” said Gurtman, 50. “We were booked up with plenty of events and functions and our daily business was good.”
But the inn has been affected by rising costs like every other business, he said. Whether ordering special ingredients from outside Maine or fresh produce from nearby farms, food prices and delivery fees are going up.
“We make everything from scratch,” Gurtman said. “We’ve definitely seen price fluctuations due to what’s going on because fuel is more expensive, insurance is more expensive, everything related to doing business is more expensive. At the same time, we’re trying to keep our quality up and our prices reasonable.”
Despite the challenges, Gurtman said he wouldn’t want to live anywhere else. A native Mainer, he has vacationed in western Maine all his life, visits Acadia National Park at least twice a year, and swims several times a week at beaches near his home in York.
He doesn’t mind the tourist traffic that takes over Memorial Day through Labor Day because it pays the bills — for him, the town and the state.
“I understand why people come here,” he said. “I live it. I don’t take it for granted.”
Zack Gauley, 28, is on the flip side of that experience. A California native, he lives in Rumford, in western Maine, with his girlfriend, who has a job in manufacturing. He has worked seasonal jobs in the skiing and commercial fishing industries for the last five years, he said.
This year, however, his $15.10-an-hour minimum wage job making snow and running chairlifts at Black Mountain Ski Resort kept him working into spring, then he was let go, he said. At that point, the fishing boats he had worked on in the past were all crewed up.
A high school graduate, Gauley has applied for jobs at local gas stations, grocery stores and fast-food restaurants without luck, he said. He plans to expand his search to manufacturing jobs that might pay more and include job training.
“I’m dismayed with a lot of things, but I just have to apply myself a little more,” he said. “I just hope I can get a job as soon as possible, and then I can get a better job and build a life for me and my girlfriend.”

title: Epstein lawsuit raises questions about child sexual abuse images, missing computers from mansion
text:
New Epstein lawsuit raises questions about child sexual abuse images, missing computers from Palm Beach mansion
Two women are suing Jeffrey Epstein’s estate, seeking an accounting of sexual abuse images and a process to identify and notify victims who may have been depicted as children.
New Epstein lawsuit raises questions about child sexual abuse images, missing computers from Palm Beach mansion
Two women are suing Jeffrey Epstein’s estate, seeking an accounting of sexual abuse images and a process to identify and notify victims who may have been depicted as children.
A new federal lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s estate is raising new questions about child sexual abuse images allegedly collected by the convicted sex offender and what happened to potentially critical electronic evidence missing when Palm Beach police searched his mansion two decades ago.
Two women are suing Epstein’s estate, alleging child sexual abuse material connected to Epstein has never been fully accounted for and that some victims depicted in the images may never have been identified or notified.
The lawsuit reaches back to the original Palm Beach investigation of Epstein.
Investigative Reporter Terri Parker was the first reporter in 2019 to broadcast video of Palm Beach police searching Epstein’s mansion on El Brillo Way during the investigation that began in 2005.
The search video shows detectives moving through the sprawling home, where they found erotic photographs, a massage table and a dentist’s chair.
But investigators did not find Epstein’s computers.
According to the new lawsuit, wires were left hanging where electronic equipment had been removed. Investigators believed Epstein’s computers could contain evidence of his sexual abuse of minors, including child pornography.
Law enforcement was advised at the time that Epstein’s attorneys or other agents had possession of the computers, according to the complaint.
The lawsuit says investigators never obtained access to those computers before Epstein entered into his controversial federal non-prosecution agreement in South Florida.
Years later, after Epstein was arrested on federal sex trafficking charges in 2019, federal agents searching his properties seized computers, hard drives and other electronic media.
The new lawsuit says that seized electronic evidence remains in federal government custody.
The women are now asking a federal judge to establish a court-supervised process to account for relevant material and identify and notify victims depicted in Epstein’s collection.
The complaint seeks cooperation with the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and its Child Victim Identification Program to help determine the identities of children depicted in the material.
The lawsuit also seeks information about relevant images, electronic devices and records that may be in the possession, custody or control of Epstein’s estate.
The estate has not yet filed a response to the allegations in court.
Epstein died in a New York jail in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.

title: It’s not about the quantity of Collins’ votes, it’s about the quality
text:
It is an undeniable fact that, in our nation’s history, the current administration has the least qualified and most incompetent cabinet members heading our important agencies.
While Sen. Susan Collins frequently cites her record of never missing a vote in the Senate, it is the merit of those votes that matters. If readers followed the Maine Sunday Telegram’s column on how our legislators voted in the prior week, they may recall that she votes for Trump’s right-wing judge nominees. If they check further, they will find that Collins’ vote was one of those that put the notorious Florida District Court Judge Aileen Cannon on the bench during Trump’s first term.
Mainers deserve more than a rubber stamp when the U.S. Senate acts on important nominations and policy issues.

Brunswick

title: ‘Super oversize’ load’s journey to South Portland taking longer than expected
text:
The transport of a “super oversize” load — approximately 220 feet long and roughly 20 feet wide — to South Portland has been delayed.
The heat recovery steam generator began its two-night journey from Jay on Tuesday night, and was originally due to arrive in South Portland by 6 a.m. Thursday.
But because its progress has been slower than anticipated, it’s now due to arrive in South Portland next Tuesday morning, with incremental progress each night, according to the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office.
Wednesday night, it was to travel from Turner to Oxford, including over Jumper Bridge. Over Thursday night, the generator will travel from Oxford to Gray, resulting in traffic delays on Route 26 in Mechanic Falls and Poland. It will be staged in Gray over the weekend and moved to Buxton on Sunday night.
Monday night will be the final push before it arrives in South Portland the next morning. Law enforcement officers, utility crews and other personnel are assisting the transport of the generator, which weighs more than 683,000 pounds.
These generators are typically used at industrial facilities or power plants, and while it’s on the road, it spans two travel lanes. Residents and businesses have been asked to avoid parking along the route while the load is being transported to avoid obstruction, and drivers have been encouraged to plan ahead and allow extra travel time.
It’s the first of nine oversize loads planned along this route. The schedule for the remaining eight loads will be released once the current one is complete, according to the Maine Department of Transportation.
A spokesman for the MDOT did not say whether the delay will impact the timelines for the other loads.
A spokesman for Barnhart Crane & Rigging, the company overseeing the transport, did not immediately respond to questions about the timeline.

title: ‘I need help’: Restaurant staff shields and protects woman from man following her on walk
text:
MONONA, Wis. (WMTV/Gray News) - A Wisconsin woman says a routine evening walk along Monona’s Lake Loop quickly escalated into a frightening situation.
Carly Major was out walking with her dog last Saturday evening when she said she noticed a man approaching her who then began to follow her.
Major was about to make her way home but immediately changed her path when this stranger suddenly appeared behind her so she wouldn’t lead him back to her front door.
“I turned around and noticed after about half a block that he started following me,” Major said. “So I diverted my course away from my home toward the courtyard around Buck & Honey’s [restaurant].”
As Major crossed the waterway, the situation escalated. She said the man took off his shirt and ran across four lanes of traffic, attempting to cut off her route.
Scared, Major ran directly into Buck & Honey’s restaurant to seek refuge.
“I need help. I am being followed,” Major said as she entered.
Inside the Monona restaurant, an all-woman crew working that shift immediately jumped into action outside of any typical job description.
Moments later, the man walked through the front doors, asking employees for Major and her dog.
Staff members immediately formed a protective barrier, blocking his view, directing him out of the building and contacting 911.
“I was immediately taken to a place of safety where I could not be seen outside, and I just received so much support from the staff,” Major said.
Buck & Honey’s manager, Katie Leiter, said her team reacted purely out of protective instinct.
“It was like everybody was going to their battle stations. Everybody was doing their part to make sure that this guy was not going to hurt anyone,” Leiter said. “I had one of my servers run down to the park to warn a woman who was down there by herself to make sure that she was safe too.”
Staff members stayed by Major’s side, even offering their shift meals, water for both her and her dog, and a ride home.
“I love my staff and seeing them behave instinctively this way was just heartwarming,” Leiter added. “They’re amazing people, and they did the right thing.”
The Monona Police Department confirmed officers were dispatched to the restaurant last Saturday night for a report of a suspicious person following Major.
Officers ended up making contact with the man in question. Police noted he showed signs of mental illness and was driven away from the area.
For Major, the relief of having complete strangers step up in a moment of vulnerability is something she says she will carry forever.
“I have strangers that don’t know me that care about me. And knowing that people really do have each other’s backs and care means everything,” Major said.
