title: Rivals for California governor to meet in only scheduled debate as mail ballots go to voters
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The candidates for California governor will meet face to face Tuesday in the only scheduled debate of the campaign, giving Republican Steve Hilton perhaps his best chance of gaining ground on Democrat Xavier Becerra.
The hourlong matchup on CNN comes just days before mail ballots are expected to begin arriving at homes in advance of the Nov. 3 general election. Looking to replace outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, Hilton is appealing to voters who he says are desperate for change in a state known for its punishing cost of living, high taxes and long-running homeless crisis.
Becerra is promising to bring down household costs, too, while continuing to push back against President Donald Trump’s agenda.
A September poll conducted by the University of California, Berkeley, Institute of Governmental Studies found that Becerra had a sizable lead over Hilton. A Republican has not won a statewide election in heavily Democratic California since 2006.
Hilton has Trump’s endorsement, but that could be a liability at a time when the president’s popularity has been sliding while voters grouse over climbing gas and grocery prices. Trump has had a long-strained relationship with left-leaning California, where he was trounced in his three runs for the White House.
The two rivals emerged from a chaotic primary that saw former Democratic U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell exit the race — then announce he would leave Congress — following allegations that he sexually assaulted a woman twice, including when she worked for him, while billionaire Tom Steyer ran the most expensive political advertising campaign in the country in a losing effort to win the Democratic nomination.
Hilton has vowed to bring down the price of gasoline to $3 a gallon, about half the current cost, cut residents’ utility bills in half, now among the nation’s highest, and eliminate state income taxes on the first $150,000 in earnings.
Becerra has been leaning into his long resume in government as he maneuvers to take charge of the state. He spent more than 35 years in state and federal office, including leadership roles in the U.S. House, as California’s attorney general, and as former President Joe Biden’s health secretary. “The governor’s office is not a place with training wheels,” he likes to say.

title: Springworks Farm in Lisbon to be sold at auction
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Springworks Farm, the once-thriving aquaponics farm in Lisbon that supplied lettuce to grocers across New England, will be sold at auction next month.
Springworks was the exclusive supplier of organic and other lettuce to supermarket chain Hannaford from 2021 until earlier this year.
The farm was also a significant local taxpayer, having paid more than $77,000 in real estate taxes in fiscal year 2026.
According to Tranzon — a nationwide real estate auction company — the Lisbon farm is 168 acres, consisting of two abutting lots, 117,000 square feet of greenhouse growing space, 56,000 square feet of light industrial buildings and all related equipment.
The auction will be held Oct. 23 at 11 a.m.
Lisbon’s director of economic and community development, Ross Cunningham, did not respond to a request for comment on the auction.
Trevor Kenkel, the founder and CEO of Springworks Farm, purchased the farm in June 2014 for $457,500. Efforts to reach him have also been unsuccessful.
According to market intelligence platform traxcn.com, Springworks raised over $41.5 million of funding in seven rounds starting in 2014. In 2023, the company raised $22 million to fund the addition of its fourth and largest greenhouse.
Blue Highway Capital and Farm Credit East were listed as investors.
Springworks Farm announced in 2021 that it was the exclusive provider of whole head romaine lettuce to Hannaford in addition to being the exclusive supplier of certified organic green leaf lettuce.
The company also supplied all 184 Hannaford stores with baby romaine lettuce and Boston bibb, plus an assortment of pre-cut products in select stores, including single cut romaine, single cut Boston bibb, and salad mix.
In addition, the farm sold products to Whole Foods, Roche Bros. Supermarkets, Food City, Sysco of Northern New England, Lisbon K-12 schools, and other local institutions.

title: Secretary Hegseth is set to announce more cuts to the military's general and admiral ranks
text:
Secretary Hegseth is set to announce more cuts to the military's general and admiral ranks
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is planning to announce further cuts to the number of generals and admirals serving in the military in an address set for Wednesday, the Pentagon confirmed.
According to Pentagon officials, Hegseth will direct all the military services to double the 10% reduction that he ordered last spring to the roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, making it a 20% total decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027.
President Donald Trump or Hegseth have already fired or pushed to retire more than two dozen military leaders since taking office, including the Army's top uniformed officer, Gen. Randy George, in April. They also have fired the only two women serving as four-star officers, as well as a disproportionate number of other senior female officers.
Hegseth plans to make the announcement in a speech to troops at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, the second year in a row he will deliver what the Pentagon is calling his “State of the Force” address. Fox News earlier reported the new reductions, which could include any one-star general or above or officer of equivalent Navy rank.
As part of last year's cuts, Hegseth also ordered the active duty military to shed 20% of its four-star general officers — the highest-level leader — and the National Guard to shed 20% of its top positions, but it is unclear if all those cuts have been made.
Hegseth gathered all the military's generals and admirals at the same time last year for an address in which he declared an end to “woke” culture and announced new directives for troops that include “gender-neutral” or “male-level” standards for physical fitness.
However, that speech was overshadowed by the attendance of President Donald Trump, who proposed using American cities as training grounds for the armed forces and spoke of needing U.S. military might to combat what he called the “invasion from within.”
When Hegseth first announced the effort to trim the highest levels of the military ranks, he argued it was intended to remove “redundant force structure to optimize and streamline leadership.” In a memo released in May 2025, he said the aim was to free the military from “unnecessary bureaucratic layers.”
The number of general officer positions in the military is set by law, but it is possible to let positions remain unfilled by not submitting replacements to Congress.
Hegseth's relationship with Congress is already strained, and he faces articles of impeachment from a Republican, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, over his leadership of the Pentagon and management of the Iran war.
Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said eliminating senior leadership positions must be done in consultation with Congress and warned that the planned cuts “should alarm every American.”
“Congress has been clear with the Secretary that he must consult this body and explain his reasoning for senior officer removals and promotion holds. To date, we have not received satisfactory answers," Reed said in a statement.
“Our military is conducting major operations around the world, and the force is already under strain," he added. "Eliminating senior positions and leaders now will add to that strain and disrupt command when continuity matters most."

title: Stephen King opens up about his new novel and a new ‘Carrie’ series
text:
It’s hard to imagine Stephen King needing another writer to make him look good.
But the Maine author says that’s what happened when he worked with Peter Straub. The two first collaborated on a dark fantasy called “The Talisman” in 1984 and then on the 2001 sequel, “Black House.”
Before Straub died in 2022 at 79, he wrote to King with ideas for a third book in the series. King thought the ideas were so powerful, so on point, that he used them as a basis for the new novel “Other Worlds Than These.” It goes on sale Oct. 6, with both authors’ names on the cover.
King wishes he had been able to work with Straub one more time, but is glad to have had the partnership at all.
“Oh man, he was so good. He was a better stylist than I ever was, and I thought this is going to make me look so good if I collaborate with him, and it really did,” said King in mid-September. “We kept saying we’re going to do it (a third book) next year, but I had things to finish and he had things to finish. Then time just ran out.”
The day after “Other Worlds Than These” comes out, Prime will debut a new limited series based on “Carrie,” King’s first book. The 1974 novel was made into a Hollywood film in 1976, starring Sissy Spacek. The new series stars Summer H. Howell and was created and written by Mike Flanagan, who has done several TV or film projects based on King’s work, including “The Life of Chuck” and “Dr. Sleep.”
King said he really likes the way the story has been updated to the present, with Carrie’s fellow students using cellphones and social media to bully and humiliate her.
“It’s really smart and it expands on the book, which was fairly slim. The miniseries is all about social media and it’s fantastic,” said King. “It’s a timeless story, which is too bad. You would hope at some point we as human beings would stop bullying each other for no good reason.”
NO SLOWING DOWN
At 79, King continues to be a pop culture powerhouse. He’s written more than 65 novels or novellas and his books have sold some 400 million copies. More than 80 films or TV series have been based on his work. Colleges around the country have held courses dedicated to his work.
Born in Portland and raised largely in Durham, King went to high school in Lisbon Falls and graduated with a degree in English from the University of Maine in 1970. He and his wife, Tabitha, have lived in Maine ever since. Their longtime Bangor home, a tourist attraction for its resemblance to a haunted house, now houses the couple’s charitable foundation and King’s archives. These days, King spends a little more than half the year in Maine and the rest in Florida.
King had only been a published author for a few years when he met Straub, in London, in the late 1970s. Straub had had success writing about the supernatural with his 1975 novel, “Julia.”
“The Talisman” focused on Jack Sawyer, who at the age of 12 starts an epic quest, walking from New Hampshire to the California coast to find a way to save his dying mother’s life. His trek takes him to the Territories, a parallel medieval universe, where people have lookalike counterparts known as twinners. Jack’s mother’s twinner is queen of the Territories, and is also dying.
“Black House” continues with Sawyer in his 30s, leaving his job as a police officer to live in small-town Wisconsin. A series of murders involving young children draws him out of retirement and into different worlds.
In “Other Worlds Than These,” Sawyer is called to journey to strange worlds again. He has to stop a rampaging group of infected teenagers in America-side and battle the forces of the mysterious Gullet at the edge of Mid-World. The book also wraps up the various worlds of King’s Dark Tower series.
Before Straub died, he sent King a letter with ideas for a third book. He also sent him the book “Redheaded Peckerwood” by artist and photographer Christian Patterson. The book uses photographs to retrace the route of teenagers Charles Starkweather and Caril Ann Fugate on a killing spree through Nebraska in the 1950s.
“Peter said to me, ‘Maybe somebody gets possesed by the spirit of Charles Starkweather and they go into the Territories, and all this stuff happens,” said King. “I thought, ‘Oh man, this is just tailor-made for a suspense novel.’ It really made me want to write this book.”
DO YOUR THING
As for the new “Carrie” series, King said he was sent scripts, had casting approval and was credited as an executive producer. But he really wasn’t very involved. He said he doesn’t like to use his approval power unless he feels he really has to, which is almost never.
“Making a film is different (than writing a book). My thought is, you do your thing and we’ll see what happens,” King said.
Besides Howell as Carrie, the cast includes Samantha Sloyan as her mother and Matthew Lillard as the high school principal. Though the book is set in a fictional Maine town, filming for the series took place in western Canada. Because Canada and states like Massachussetts and New York offer lucrative financial incentives and tax credits to production companies, Maine has rarely been the location of a big-budget King film or TV show in recent years. Film advocates have tried to increase Maine’s film incentives several times in recent years, without much success.
King liked the new series and was particularly impressed with the gym shower scene, where classmates taunt Carrie because she doesn’t realize she’s having her period. Her mother never explained it to her.
In the original movie, the scene is steamy and dreamlike, showing girls in the shower through what King called “a male gaze.” But in the new version, Carrie is crumpled on the floor of the shower while her classmates, fully clothed, crowd around her, recording her humiliation on their cellphones.
“Teenagers still bully each other, but with social media it’s supercharged,” said King. “He (Flanagan) really caught that idea with his shot of all these kids taking cellphone photos of this girl who’s in terror. It’s a wonderful moment.”
King is also happy that while Flanagan updated some things, he didn’t change the story basics, which include a girl who is mercilessly bullied but who has hidden powers.
“It doesn’t reinvent the wheel. The prom scene, the pig’s blood, it’s all there,” King said.

title: See photos from the Western Maine Conference golf qualifier
Maine employers say they need workers, so why is it hard to find a good job?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sheila Richardson has been hanging wallpaper since her youngest was in seventh grade. She learned the skill from her grandmother and her father, then grew it into a successful business with a broad customer base near her home in Turner — all by word of mouth.
“I take pride in my work,” she said. “I don’t have to advertise.”
Now 78 and a great-grandmother, she’s still working 35 years later, despite some health issues that cropped up last year.
“I’m up and down the ladder a hundred times a day,” she said. “I’m a doer. I don’t depend on anybody else.”
Richardson’s tenacity is serving her well these days, as rising costs for materials and fuel, and a shifting economic landscape make it more challenging to work or do business in Maine.
She is one of 824 Mainers who responded to a survey conducted in July by the Siena Research Institute for the Maine Trust for Local News. It found that the job market is daunting for many across the state — 51% of respondents rated their ability to get suitable employment as “only fair” or “poor,” while 41% rated their ability to make a living wage as “not very likely” or “not at all likely.”
Asked whether they could get a job with opportunities for advancement, 32% said it was “almost certain” or “very likely,” but 27% said it was “not very likely” or “not at all likely” and 39% said it was a toss-up.
The Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram interviewed a variety of people across the state who participated in the 62-question survey. While they see some bright spots, Richardson and others say workers and businesses face increasing economic headwinds.
Richardson has been working all her life, really, running a household with four kids, helping her husband with his excavation, wood harvesting and auto repair businesses, scrimping and saving to make ends meet when times got hard.
Social Security has eased her need to work, she said, but her healthcare savings are dwindling despite Medicare. She and her husband own the ranch-style home they built themselves, but it needs a new roof, and that’s going to be costly.
She sees others struggling, too, including her son, who has his own construction and excavation business, she said. Record-high diesel prices are eating up narrow profit margins.
“It’s terribly tough right now,” Richardson said. “The price of everything has gone up and you have to charge customers what it costs. You really have to pinch pennies when you don’t have money coming in.”
SHADOW OF UNCERTAINTY
In reviewing the survey results, Maine State Economist Amanda Rector said she was surprised that only 32% of respondents were positive about the potential for job advancement, especially since Maine has a worker shortage and its rapidly aging population is expected to increase retirements.
“Responses may have been overshadowed by near-term uncertainties,” Rector said, including rising costs that have led some businesses to throttle hiring and consider downsizing if artificial intelligence is used in the workplace.
She also noted significant regional differences in views of the job market — 51% of Southern/Coastal respondents (Cumberland and York counties) said they could get suitable employment, and 38% saw potential for workplace advancement. Responses in other regions were even lower.
Rector said that’s not surprising. “That’s where a lot of economic activity is in the state,” she said.
Respondents showed similar regional trends when asked whether Maine is a place where businesses can succeed — 46% rated the business climate positively, while 52% said it’s only “fair” or “poor.” Looking at that question regionally, 57% of Southern/Coastal participants had a positive response, with significantly lower rates in other areas where business owners say they’re facing tough economic conditions.
Rector also pointed out that the survey shows strong recognition — 75% statewide — of Maine’s access to affordable adult education and job training. Both have been bolstered in recent years by the state’s community colleges, building contractors, defense contractors and the U.S. Small Business Administration.
“It’s good to see that has such a strong positive response,” she said.
LACK OF RELIABLE WORKERS
Workforce training is helping Alex Thibodeau meet some of the challenges facing Maine’s manufacturing sector, including rising costs and logistical drawbacks of being at the end of the line geographically.
Thibodeau is director of operations at Kenway Composites, an Augusta company with 50 employees that makes fiber-reinforced plastic storage tanks and other equipment for heavy industry, public infrastructure and military uses.
In recent years, Thibodeau has hired seven students from the composites manufacturing program at the Foster Career and Technical Education Center in Farmington that serves several area high schools.
“They are some of our best employees,” said Thibodeau, 59. “Technical training is one of the only salvations for manufacturers who need workers. (The training programs) are so underrated and deserve more funding going forward.”
Still, a lack of reliable workers has forced Thibodeau to turn away about $2 million in contracts in recent years, he said. His hiring expectations are pretty basic — show up every day, be willing to learn and do quality work — but he’s often disappointed, despite offering benefits, bonuses and pay ranging from $23 to $35 an hour depending on the job, he said.
Recent tariffs, inflation, higher interest rates and rising fuel prices have increased the cost of procuring materials, having them delivered to Maine and transporting goods to customers, he said. Truck deliveries now come with fuel surcharges. Tariffs on one part needed for a government contract increased the price from $80,000 to $130,000.
“We as taxpayers end up paying for that,” Thibodeau said. “One of Maine’s greatest struggles is our location. Most of the truck traffic is outbound, so you have to pay for the trip in. We are disadvantaged in a lot of ways already. We don’t need additional costs.”
STARK DIFFERENCES STATEWIDE
Thibodeau’s experience and the survey’s findings align with aspects of a Maine State Chamber of Commerce goals report released this year in advance of the 2026 gubernatorial election, said Patrick Woodcock, chamber CEO.
Economic headwinds that have pummeled Maine for years have been exacerbated by recent federal policies that have increased costs and threaten to worsen the workforce shortage, he said, including immigration enforcement activities.
In reviewing the survey results, Woodcock noted that while 57% of respondents in the Southern/Coastal region said Maine is a place where businesses can be successful, 58%-60% of respondents in the rest of the state said the exact opposite.
“I found that gap to be pretty stark,” he said. “Some pessimism has taken root. There are distinct challenges between the regions, and we have to recognize and respect those differences.”
Woodcock also noted that 85% of respondents across the state said the lack of affordable housing is a problem.
“Housing has overwhelmed a lot of Maine families,” he said. “Our members have identified affordable housing as a workforce issue. We cannot attract workers, foster economic growth and have a robust business climate without addressing affordable housing.”
On the upside, Woodcock said, Maine businesses are resilient, with an uptick in recent retail sales corroborating anecdotal feedback that this summer was a fairly strong tourism season. He noted that lodging receipts increased 12.8% in July compared to 2025, and restaurants experienced 6.8% growth, according to the latest state sales tax reports.
THE GOOD AND NOT SO GOOD
Nathan Gurtman agrees — it was a successful summer for many businesses in Maine’s hospitality industry. A chef at the York Harbor Inn, he has worked in area kitchens for 30 years.
“It was a good season,” said Gurtman, 50. “We were booked up with plenty of events and functions and our daily business was good.”
But the inn has been affected by rising costs like every other business, he said. Whether ordering special ingredients from outside Maine or fresh produce from nearby farms, food prices and delivery fees are going up.
“We make everything from scratch,” Gurtman said. “We’ve definitely seen price fluctuations due to what’s going on because fuel is more expensive, insurance is more expensive, everything related to doing business is more expensive. At the same time, we’re trying to keep our quality up and our prices reasonable.”
Despite the challenges, Gurtman said he wouldn’t want to live anywhere else. A native Mainer, he has vacationed in western Maine all his life, visits Acadia National Park at least twice a year, and swims several times a week at beaches near his home in York.
He doesn’t mind the tourist traffic that takes over Memorial Day through Labor Day because it pays the bills — for him, the town and the state.
“I understand why people come here,” he said. “I live it. I don’t take it for granted.”
Zack Gauley, 28, is on the flip side of that experience. A California native, he lives in Rumford, in western Maine, with his girlfriend, who has a job in manufacturing. He has worked seasonal jobs in the skiing and commercial fishing industries for the last five years, he said.
This year, however, his $15.10-an-hour minimum wage job making snow and running chairlifts at Black Mountain Ski Resort kept him working into spring, then he was let go, he said. At that point, the fishing boats he had worked on in the past were all crewed up.
A high school graduate, Gauley has applied for jobs at local gas stations, grocery stores and fast-food restaurants without luck, he said. He plans to expand his search to manufacturing jobs that might pay more and include job training.
“I’m dismayed with a lot of things, but I just have to apply myself a little more,” he said. “I just hope I can get a job as soon as possible, and then I can get a better job and build a life for me and my girlfriend.”

title: Tick Reauthorization Act officially signed into law
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A new federal law aims to combat the growing threat of tick-borne illnesses in Maine and across the country.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-ME, and Sen. Tina Smith, D-MN, announced the Kay Hagan Tick Reauthorization Act has officially been signed into law.
The bipartisan measure extends funding through 2030 for regional research centers and provides CDC grants to state health departments to improve testing, tracking, and treatment.
It comes as Maine continues to see record-high levels of Lyme disease, with more than 4,200 cases reported statewide last year.
The funding also supports local efforts, including Lyme disease vaccine trials at MaineHealth Institute for Research.

title: ‘She’s gone’: Foster family mourns baby girl found dead in dumpster as mother arrested
text:
LOS ANGELES (KCAL/KCBS) - The foster family of a woman who was arrested after police say her 4-month-old daughter was found dead in a Los Angeles dumpster are speaking out amid their grief.
The Los Angeles Police Department says a woman found a 4-month-old girl in a dumpster around 10:30 p.m. Monday outside a South Los Angeles housing project. The baby was taken to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
Laura Lacy believes the baby was her 4-month-old foster granddaughter Luna; though she is still waiting on the coroner to confirm her identity.
“She’s gone, but it’s OK. The Lord has her,” Lacy said through tears.
Lacy says she and her husband, Herman Johnson, raised Luna while allowing her 19-year-old foster daughter, Takiyah Babers, who is also the baby’s mother, to visit her. The couple were worried Babers was suffering from postpartum depression, Johnson says.
Johnson and his wife dropped off Luna with Babers at the housing project Monday.
“She called me yesterday, told me to drop the baby off. I should have just kept her, like I started to do, but that’s just a back thought. It’s a sad situation. The baby can’t protect herself. She was just an innocent little baby,” Johnson said.
Lacy says the couple were at their home in Inglewood when they saw the news and rushed over, fearing the worst. Then, they couldn’t find Luna.
At the start of the police investigation, the foster family stood together – until officers put Babers in handcuffs and led her away. Police say she was booked for murder.
Lacy says she believes Babers is responsible for what happened.
“Why would you throw her away? She didn’t do anything,” Lacy said. “What did you call me to bring her home for? Why would you call me... and then do this to her? I don’t believe this. I’m still in disbelief.”
Police say Babers’ bail was set at $2 million. The case will be presented to the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office for filing consideration.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: Read the poem ‘How Memory Comes’ by Suzanne Langlois
text:
This week’s poem, Suzanne Langlois’ “How Memory Comes,” pulls us into rich, involuntary sense memories of a day in a rural childhood. I love how effortlessly an autumn cornfield conjures up itchy straw, june bugs, and boys in clanking trucks, and I love the poem’s bittersweet acknowledgement of memory’s nature: impossibly real, then gone again.
Langlois is a teacher from Portland. Her collection “Bright Glint Gone” won the Maine Writers and Publishers Alliance chapbook award. Her work has appeared in Leon Literary Review, Rust + Moth, Rogue Agent, and the Best New Poets Anthology. She holds an MFA from Warren Wilson College.
Poets, please note that submissions to Deep Water are open now and through the end of the year. Deep Water is especially eager to share poems by Black writers, writers of color, indigenous writers, LGBTQ+ writers, and other underrepresented voices. Submit your credits at mainewriters.org/deep-water
How Memory Comes
Sometimes memory is a splinter working
its way out. I drive by a field of corn stubble
and my skin itches, suddenly lost in an afternoon
spent in a friend’s barn, jumping from the loft
into a pile of half-baled hay until the straw
in our underwear sent us to the muddy pond
to rinse away the sweat and itch of summer.
The only other creatures in the barn that day
were pigeons roosting in the rafters
and mice darting across the packed dirt floor.
Wasps hung in the air, their bodies shiny
and lethal, the biggest threat for miles, except for
the local boys flying down the jagged road,
their trucks rattling like a nest of rusty chains.
And this was all just a slow blink ago—the days,
happy-sad, encased in amber light, the hum
of June bugs bumping against the screen, older
brothers appearing for dinner and then
disappearing, living on the other side of
a mysterious line we thought we’d never
be able to cross, no matter how fast we ran.
There was no event to mark this day, to set it
apart from all the others, and this is what seems
sad to me now—how unremarkable I thought it
at the time, like it was a place that would always
be there—somewhere I could go back to, even now.
This is how memory comes—unbidden.
This is how it leaves, without saying goodbye.
– Suzanne Langlois
Megan Grumbling is a poet and writer who lives in Portland. Deep Water: Maine Poems is produced in collaboration with the Maine Writers & Publishers Alliance. “How Memory Comes,” ©2026 by Suzanne Langlois, appears by permission of the author.

Current mortgage rates
The 30-year fixed mortgages in this week’s survey had an average total of 0.33 discount and origination points. Discount points are a way to lower your mortgage rate, while origination points are fees lenders charge to create, review and process your loan.
Shop smarter for mortgage rates

Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in August 2026 was $429,100, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.38% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,372 amounts to about 27% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 1.6% over the past year, and the median of $429,100 was an all-time high for the month of August. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late September showed national home prices grew 1.9% in the year ending in July, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation held at 3.4% in August, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have spiked amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, and 10-year Treasury yields hit 5.3% this week, well up from earlier in the year.
“Inflation as reported by PCE on Wednesday offered a potential respite for bonds but unfortunately, the trend is not our friend,” says James Sahnger of C2 Financial Corp. “Since mid-April, the 10-year has risen from 4.22% to as high as 5.30% mid-day Wednesday.”
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Body cam shows runaway 100-pound tortoise's 'slow-speed chase' end safely
text:
Body cam video shows officer helping carry wayward tortoise home after 'world's slowest escape'
A sheriff’s office in Colorado says the case of a nearly 100-pound tortoise on the run is “closed” and the “shellebrity” went viral for attempting the “world’s slowest escape.”
The Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office posted bodycam video to social media this week showing Animal Control Officer Sean McMullen responding to a report on Aug. 31 of a wandering tortoise in Littleton, which is around 11 miles south of Denver.
In the lighthearted post, the sheriff’s office said the tortoise, named Lard, had “big travel plans” but also had “absolutely no sense of urgency” after escaping a fenced-in yard and heading out for “a neighborhood adventure.”
“Lard’s owner was on scene, but efforts to negotiate a voluntary return were unsuccessful. Home was in one direction. Lard preferred the other,” the department said.
In the video, a kind bystander is seen helping Officer McMullen carefully lift the hefty explorer and return him home.
“Sometimes helping an animal means lending a hand. This time, it took a few,” JCSO said. “Thank you to Officer McMullen and the helpful neighbor for bringing this slow-speed adventure to a safe ending!”

title: How to take advantage of the campaign spending bonanza
text:
Dan Kolbert is a builder in Portland.
As summer turns to fall, the electoral campaigns in Maine are sure to heat up. Unprecedented sums of money are expected to flow into the state, in an effort to sway people one way or the other.
As a concerned citizen, I am anxious about the impact of all this spending. My first thought, like many of you no doubt, is “How do I get mine?”
Recently in Dallas, President Trump made his most important electoral reform yet, when he promised to buy our votes. Along with centralizing voter rolls under his control, sending the military to patrol voting sites and withholding funds from Democratic states, he is transforming our country in ways no one could have imagined. It is an exciting time to be a voter in America!
Unfortunately, he set a price for our votes, and apparently believes that all votes should cost the same. This seems shockingly short-sighted. If, as many analysts think, we hold the key to control of the Senate, shouldn’t we command top dollar for our votes? Does he really think our precious Maine votes are worth the same as those of people from Massachusetts? Fortunately, there is still time before the November elections, so let’s hope that he reconsiders this poorly thought out position.
We must, however, remain realists. For obscure historical reasons, vote-buying has negative connotations, and it seems likely that we won’t get our promised $5,000 before November. With that in mind, I have assembled a short list of alternatives that, while requiring more effort, promise greater gain for those with a little gumption.
Start a radio station.
There are a limited number of media outlets in Maine, and it seems likely that the ad budgets will quickly swamp the available slots. Campaigns will be desperate for alternatives. Put a speaker in your window and call it a low-power FM station. Play Chumbawumba’s “I Get Knocked Down” on the hour, every hour, and reserve the remaining 56 1/2 minutes for advertising.
Form a PAC.
There are plenty of identified groups — anti-abortion, pro-choice, gun rights and so on. But there are thousands of people just waiting for someone to stand up for their interests. Tax deductions for travel hockey teams. Banning lawn mowers on Sundays before 9 a.m. Making weed less smelly. Priority parking for big pickups. Campaigns will be so desperate to pick up a half dozen votes by Halloween that they’ll pull up to your house with truckloads of cash.
Become a pundit.
The short-lived Graham Platner campaign proved that there’s an insatiable appetite nationally for people who can explain our out-of-the-way state to a nationwide audience. Most people think of us as folks who talk funny and wear Grundens and plaid. Well, lean into it!
Listen to a few hours of Tim Sample and you’ll be able to pull off a 30- second interview on national news without breaking a sweat. Learn how to talk at length without getting to the point. Learn how to pronounce “Wytopitlock.” Pretend you like Moxie. You’ll have mobile TV trucks lined up around the block.
Those are just a few of the ideas out there. What are yours? Have fun.
As the old saying goes, the personal is political. And there’s nothing more personal than getting paid. Thank you for your attention to this matter!

title: Court halts execution of Christa Gail Pike in Tennessee for a murder she committed at age 18
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death Wednesday for a 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug. A death penalty expert said it was an unprecedented failure, and Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee halted the one remaining execution for the rest of the year.
Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn’t been told about her condition.
She had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay.
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday.
Gov. Bill Lee said in a statement that he has ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and that the remaining scheduled execution will not take place this year.
“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” he said.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that they “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”
The state’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is “singular and unparalleled.”
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Media witnesses detail the execution process
Media witnesses observing from a separate room said officials raised curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney.
“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love,” she said in her “last” words. She described herself as at peace.
But Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head and asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. It was not clear what she was referencing.
By 8:26 p.m., execution witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered.
Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday to the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit court and a district court.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution: In May state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. The case garnered widespread attention in part because of a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer’s body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s.
Stay of execution was swiftly appealed
Pike was initially scheduled to be put to death in the morning, and witnesses had gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay. That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.
The attorney general’s office appealed to the Supreme Court, saying that halting the execution at the last moment traumatized Slemmer’s family and rewarded “abusive delay tactics” by Pike’s attorneys.
Later in the day, the high court cleared the way for the execution to proceed. The conservative majority did not explain their order, while the three liberal members signed a dissent that said Pike’s claims deserved a closer look.
Pike did not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argued that the state should consider her age at the time, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse.
Case renewed debate on the death penalty for teens
As the execution date drew near, debate renewed over the death penalty for young offenders.
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike’s death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds in Tennessee have had such sentences vacated.
After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn’t “put the brakes on.”
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in a statement.
Victim’s mother says she is waiting for death sentence
Slemmer’s mother had traveled to Nashville in the hopes of witnessing the execution of her daughter’s killer. She told The Associated Press on Saturday that she had waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.
“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” May Martinez told The Associated Press in a telephone interview on Saturday.
Martinez could not be immediately reached by telephone for comment after the execution was halted.
The killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satan, into her body.
Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.
Executions of women are rare in the US
Since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976, 18 women have been put to death, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday.
Tennessee announced in 2024 that it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged that it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were tested properly.
___
This story has been updated to correct that Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. local time, not 11 a.m. and that the lawyers filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee Supreme Court, not U.S.
___
Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, Ed White in Detroit, Hallie Golden in Seattle and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

title: Trump touts $54 billion South Korea investment in Alaska gas pipeline
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump announced plans Wednesday for South Korea to invest $54 billion in a liquefied natural gas project in Alaska.
The project is expected to be completed in three years and would construct an 800-mile pipeline carrying natural gas from Alaska’s North Slope to the southern part of the state for export to Asian markets.
White House Correspondent Jon Decker asked Trump whether there was consideration of constructing another oil refinery in Alaska to lower gasoline prices, noting that energy costs in the state are high.
“I was in Alaska just a few weeks ago. Energy costs are exceedingly high. Is there any consideration of constructing another oil refinery - for gasoline to bring these prices down,” Decker asked.
“Gasoline prices in Alaska are going to tumble well as soon as the war ends which is going to be soon. Prices are going to come way down regardless. But gasoline prices, because of this project and a couple of others in Alaska are going to tumble,” Trump said.
Trump also commented on the Senate race between Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola (D). Peltola lost her bid for reelection to the House in 2024.
Decker asked Trump why he thought the race was as close as polls indicate.
“If the people of Alaska knew what I know, and I know the real facts, there wouldn’t even be a race,” Trump said.
Trump said he plans to travel to Alaska in the weeks before the midterms to energize Republicans and help Sullivan win a third term in the U.S. Senate.

title: Volleyball falls to GSA 3-0
text:
BAR HARBOR — The MDI volleyball team fell to a red-hot George Stevens Academy 3-0 at home on Tuesday, Sept. 29, continuing what has been a slight midseason dip for the defending state champs. The Trojans sit at 4-4 with 6 games remaining on the schedule.
After a strong start to the season with wins against Wells, Brewer, and Medomak Valley, the Trojans have now lost 4 of their last 5 in the month of September. That slide includes losses to Class B teams Yarmouth and Washington Academy, but also to rival Ellsworth and now a Class D team in GSA.

title: Trump administration considers scaling back border project in Texas' Big Bend National Park
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is considering reducing the scope of a planned border project through Big Bend National Park in Texas, a contentious undertaking that has drawn bipartisan opposition over concerns it will irrevocably mar the remote, majestic area.
The announcement on plans for the national park, made in two court filings late Tuesday, gave no details on what the government may do. In August, the Republican administration initiated a pause on construction-related activity in the park as it engaged in outreach efforts to opponents of the project. The pause ends Wednesday.
Customs and Border Protection is “actively considering adjustments” to the work “that would reduce its scope and avoid or minimize potential impacts, based on input received from the National Park Service and other stakeholders,” the government said in the court filing.
The agency said it will make a final decision the first week in October and will take “several weeks” after that announcement before any “ground-disturbing work” starts.
After intense opposition from environmentalists and local residents and business owners, CBP backed off plans this year to build a 30-foot-tall bollard wall through the park. But its intention to move forward with other measures such as a new road, lights, vehicle barriers and technology did not quell local resistance.
After bulldozers were spotted in August clearing land in Big Bend, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott announced a pause on all activity there and it was later expanded to the area upstream of the park. The agency has said it was only carrying out design and planning work, not full-scale construction activities.
Opponents of the border project called on the administration Wednesday to continue the pause while coming up with a new plan.
Bob Krumenaker, head of Keep Big Bend Wild and a former NPS superintendent at the park, said in a statement that the Border Patrol already works with the park service and local sheriffs to operate an “effective surveillance system” in Big Bend that includes ground sensors and patrols. The Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks said building in the park would be “mutilating an extraordinary landscape.”
The project is part of a $46 billion plan by the administration to line the U.S.-Mexico border with steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology to deter migrants and smugglers.
The government has also paused work on a 61-mile piece of land stretching north of the national park along the Rio Grande River, most of which is owned by private landowners. In that area, the government plans to build a 30-foot-tall steel bollard wall designed to prevent people on foot from crossing, roads and various types of surveillance technology where appropriate, according to the court filing.
CBP has started building the wall in a West Texas part of the broader Big Bend region, but has run into intense opposition there, including from landowners challenging the project in court.
Also in the court filing Tuesday, the government suggested it was facing resistance in getting permission from landowners to survey and build on their property and would be referring some cases to the Department of Justice to pursue condemnation.
The government also detailed efforts it had made to meet with people potentially affected by Big Bend projects and shared with them incidents of cartel-related violence that concerned the Border Patrol.
The administration has been pushing forward with the border wall projects that have long been a key part of President Donald Trump’s vision for border security. The agency said it is building 12 miles (19 kilometers) of wall per week.
But lining up against the work are private landowners, Native American tribes, environmental groups and others who question the necessity and cost of the project at a time when illegal immigration has fallen dramatically. Opponents also have accused the government of damaging Native American sites and sensitive ecology locations in its rush to finish construction.

title: NY man sentenced of mortgage fraud tied to illegal marijuana grow operation in Maine
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A New York man has been convicted of mortgage fraud in connection with an illegal marijuana grow operation in St. Albans.
Ken Yiu, 49, was sentenced Tuesday in federal court to time served.
According to court documents, Yiu bought a home in 2020 with an $80,000 residential mortgage loan. On the application, Yiu claimed the house would be used as his primary residence.
Investigators say Yiu admitted that he used the property for four years to grow and sell cannabis to out-of-state buyers.
Records show neither Yiu nor the property was licensed with the Maine Office of Cannabis Policy.

title: New 24/7 crisis receiving center to open in Bangor on Monday
Troy Jackson apologizes after linking Jewish Mainers' views on Gaza to their identity
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson apologized Wednesday for suggesting in a TV interview that some Mainers are uncomfortable calling Israel’s actions in Gaza a genocide because they are Jewish.
Jackson, who has called the war in Gaza a genocide on the campaign trail, including at a recent town hall, used the term again during an interview with News Center Maine that aired Wednesday. In it, he said some Mainers are uncomfortable with the word “only because, you know, they’re Jewish and … you know what that means to them with the Holocaust.”
The generalization drew quick attention from Republicans and Jewish publications during Jackson’s pivotal race against U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. The candidate offered an apology and issued a statement that sought to clarify his views in a Wednesday statement.
“I believe what’s happening in Gaza is genocide, and I also understand that word carries particular weight for many Jewish families given the Holocaust — the genocide of six million Jews,” he said. “In trying to acknowledge that, I misspoke and made a generalization about Jewish Mainers’ views that doesn’t reflect what I meant to say. I apologize for the pain that caused.”
Jackson noted that Mainers “hold a range of deeply considered views.” The Democrat said he would fight antisemitism and work for lasting peace and security in the Middle East.
Jackson’s comments on News Center Maine came during a discussion on foreign policy, which is new territory for the former Maine Senate president and former logger from Allagash. He took over the nomination in July from Graham Platner, a sharper Israel critic who ended his campaign following an ex-girlfriend’s rape allegation.
In the interview, Jackson criticized both Collins and President Donald Trump over the war in Iran impacting the Maine economy, acknowledging that the Israel-Gaza issue was something he “never had to deal with” as a state lawmaker. But he condemned the “horrendous” actions of Israel under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom Jackson has called a war criminal.
“I don’t want the United States sending money, a blank check, to him anymore,” he said.
Meanwhile, Jackson has faced pressure from some on the left on the issue. Jamila Levasseur who asked Jackson about his views at a recent town hall described his response as “tepid” in comments to the progressive Drop Site News. She is married to Ray Luc Levasseur, the former leader of a Marxist group who served prison time for bombings and robberies.
In a recent interview with the Wall Street Journal, Collins, a longtime Israel supporter, counted the Israel-Gaza conflict as one of Jackson’s central campaign issues, suggesting that Platner had required his replacement “to be very anti-Israel, to accuse Israel of committing genocide.”
“In fact it was Hamas, the terrorist group, that killed more Jewish citizens of Israel and Americans on [Oct. 7, 2023], the greatest loss of Jewish life in a single day since the Holocaust,” she said.
